Preface: Scope and Limits

What This Book Develops
This book is a work of epistemology. Its subject is the structure of explanatory cognition:
what any explanation must contain if it is to count as an explanation, how the elements of an
explanation are related, what makes a relation legible, and what the limits of finite cognition
are. The book’s aim is to reconstruct that structure explicitly, to state the conditions under
which an explanatory cognition is valid and adequate, and to state the limits that any finite
cognition must acknowledge.
    The book’s thesis is architectonic: the structure of explanatory cognition can be recon-
structed through four analytical roles—fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics,
and context—and the classical problems of identity, manifestation, and epistemic access can
be dissolved, rather than solved, once this four-column structure is made explicit. The thesis
is stated here as the book’s claim; its necessity and sufficiency are argued in Parts I and II,
and its consequences are developed in Parts III through VI. The preface does not assume the
thesis; it states it, and the body of the book is the argument for it.
    The book is written in a strictly epistemological register. Its arguments are offered to be
assessed on their own merits, and each claim is labeled with the kind of support it has and
the kind of criticism it invites. The reader who has no acquaintance with any philosophical
tradition can follow the argument from beginning to end, and can assess it on its own terms.
    The book is a self-contained epistemological apparatus. It states its own problem, defines
its own terms, gives its own arguments, and supplies its own standards of assessment. The
reader who has followed the book to its end has the analytical vocabulary, the criteria of
validity, and the measures of adequacy that the book itself uses; nothing further is required to
assess what the book has claimed.


The Scope of the Inquiry
The book is a work of epistemology. Its subject is the structure of explanatory cognition:
what an explanation must contain if it is to count as an explanation, how the elements of an
explanation are related, what makes a relation legible, and what the limits of finite cognition
are. Every technical term it introduces—including viability—is defined as a descriptive or
structural concept, and is to be understood as such throughout. Where the book speaks
of “adequacy,” “fidelity,” “sustainability,” or “recoverability,” these name structural relations
between an explanatory cognition and its object, not values, goods, or ends. They describe
what the relation is, not what it ought to be.
    The book makes no normative, ethical, or prescriptive claims. It does not follow, however,
that the book is indifferent to value, or that it treats the domain of value as unreal. The book
describes the epistemological structure within which inquiry into value is possible; it does not
supply the content of value, and it does not replace the inquiries that do. Its claim is that this
structure is reconstructible and assessable—not that it is self-sufficient, and not that nothing
lies beyond it.
xxvi                                                                  Preface: Scope and Limits


     The scope of the book is therefore exact: it is the reconstruction of the structure of
explanatory cognition, the statement of the conditions of epistemic validity and adequacy,
and the statement of the limits, errors, and unknownness that any finite cognition must
acknowledge. Everything the book claims falls within this scope; everything outside this scope
is marked as outside it, and is not claimed.
     A word on the phrase “complete explanation.” The book uses it in a defined, operative
sense: an explanation is complete, for the purposes of this book, when it specifies the four
analytical roles (fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context) for the
question at hand, and when its reconstruction satisfies the criteria of validity and adequacy
stated in Part IV. Completeness in this sense is relative to a cognitive context and to a question;
it is not an absolute metaphysical completeness. Where the book needs the stronger notion, it
says so, and it states the standard by which the stronger notion is assessed.


The Epistemic Architecture
The book develops a single epistemic architecture, and it is stated here in its positive form, so
that the reader knows from the outset what the book builds.

   1. The four columns. Explanatory cognition can be analyzed through four analytical
      roles: fixed elements (the entities held invariant within the explanation), fluid elements
      (the entities that convey effect between fixed elements), governing dynamics (the rule
      that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements), and context (the setting in which
      the cognition occurs). The four columns are analytical roles, not kinds of entity; they
      are the result of the book’s analysis of the four questions of Part I, and they are defined
      in Part II.

   2. Identity. The invariant structure that an explanatory cognition holds fixed across a
      class of allowable transformations of its manifestations. Identity is defined epistemically:
      it is what an explanation holds invariant, not a metaphysical posit.

   3. Manifestation. The contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving
      cognitive context, according to the capacity, aptitude, and constraints of that context.
      The book develops manifestation as an epistemic appearance in the cognitive context; it
      does not develop a doctrine of realization in an existential context.

   4. Context. The setting in which cognition occurs. The book develops the cognitive
      context—the frame fixed by the question—and states its structural role in Parts II
      and III.

   5. Epistemic light. The condition of possibility of legible relation; the medium by which
      an appearance is conveyed and by which a manifestation is rendered legible as an
      appearance of its source. The book does not claim to describe what light is in itself; it
      describes light as the active structure of legibility.

   6. Reconstruction. The epistemic process by which a finite subject recovers the structure
      of an identity from its manifestations. The book states the conditions under which a
      reconstruction is valid, the three ways in which it can fail, and the measures by which
      its adequacy is assessed.

   7. Validity and adequacy. The book states the criteria of context validity, manifestational
      adequacy, and the adequacy of a pseudo-identity. These criteria are the book’s own; they
      are stated in Part IV and used throughout.
Preface: Scope and Limits                                                                    xxvii


   8. Limits and unknownness. The book states the impossibility of super-identity, the
      fallacy of super-identity, configuration-dependence, the limits of self-knowledge, the
      impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light, and the distinction between
      intrinsic and temporary unknownness. These are structural results of the architecture,
      and they are stated in Part V.

   9. Viability. The structural character of the relation between an identity and its man-
      ifestations in a cognitive context, characterized through fidelity, sustainability, and
      recoverability. Viability is a descriptive concept: it states a condition on the relation
      between an identity and its manifestations, and attaches no value, end, or good to that
      condition. It is defined in Part VI.

    These nine items are the book’s positive architecture. Each is defined at its first occurrence,
collected in the Glossary, and used consistently throughout. The reader who has understood
these nine items has understood what the book builds; the body of the book is the argument
for each of them and the statement of their relations.


The Method of Reconstruction
The method of this book is a determinate epistemic process, and it is stated here in the order
in which it is practiced. The process has seven steps, and each step is observable in the body
of the book.

   1. Definition of the problem. The book begins by stating the problem exactly: what
      an explanation must contain if it is to count as an explanation, how the elements of
      an explanation are related, what makes a relation legible, and what the limits of finite
      cognition are. The problem is stated in Part I, and every later part is an answer to some
      part of it.

   2. Determination of the context. The book fixes the cognitive context of each question
      before answering it. The context is the frame fixed by the question; it determines what
      counts as an answer.

   3. Identification of elements and relations. The book identifies the elements that
      explanatory cognition must contain (the four columns) and the relations among them
      (the conveyor principle, non-sequential connectivity, context-dependence). This is the
      work of Part II.

   4. Reconstruction. The book reconstructs the structure of epistemic relations—identity,
      signature, pseudo-identity, manifestation, context, perspective, epistemic light, encom-
      passment in epistemic light—and states how a finite subject recovers an identity from
      its manifestations. This is the work of Part III.

   5. Test of validity. The book states the criteria of context validity, manifestational
      adequacy, and the adequacy of a pseudo-identity, and it tests each reconstruction against
      them. This is the work of Part IV.

   6. Assessment of adequacy. The book states the epistemic measures of intensity and
      breadth and uses them as two dimensions of the assessment of a reconstruction’s adequacy.
      Intensity and breadth are dimensions of assessment, not the whole of adequacy; the
      criteria of Part IV state the other conditions that a reconstruction must satisfy.

   7. Examination of limits. The book examines the limits, errors, and unknownness that
      any finite cognition must acknowledge, and it states them as structural results. This is
xxviii                                                               Preface: Scope and Limits


         the work of Part V; Part VI states the epistemic economy and the concept of viability
         that the whole process makes possible.

   The method has four characteristics, and each is worth stating at the outset.

   1. It proceeds by analysis, not by appeal to authority. Each principle is stated in
      philosophical prose, and its argument is given. Where a principle is adopted rather than
      argued, the adoption is declared and its cost is stated.

   2. It labels every claim with an epistemic status. The labels tell the reader what
      kind of argument is being offered, and therefore what kind of criticism is appropriate.
      The labels are not decorations; they are the book’s way of being honest about what it is
      doing.

   3. It distinguishes structure from telos. The book describes structure; it does not
      describe the end, purpose, or good for which anything exists. The question of telos is
      a real question, and the structure that the book describes points toward it; but the
      structure does not contain it, and the book cannot derive it from the structure alone.
      This boundary is stated as an axiom in Chapter 4, and it is observed throughout.

   4. It grounds its arguments in epistemological argument. The validity of the book’s
      foundational arguments rests on epistemological argument, not on confirmation from
      outside epistemology. Comparisons with other traditions and references to other domains,
      where they occur, have an explanatory or comparative role; they do not replace argument.
      The commitment is stated in Chapter 4, and it is observed throughout.


Structure and Dependency of the Book
The book is organized into six parts, a back matter, and three structural appendices. For each
part, the epistemic output is stated: what the reader has, epistemically, at the end of the part.

Part I (Foundations and Method of Explanatory Cognition). Explanatory cognition
     and the four questions; the method of the book; the finitude of the epistemic subject;
     the boundary between structure and telos; and cognitive architecture and the order of
     dependency in explanation (Chapter 5). Epistemic output: the exact statement of the
     problem, the method, and the boundary conditions of the inquiry.

Part II (Architecture of Explanatory Cognition). The four questions of Part I are here
     converted into and defined as the four analytical roles (the four columns): fixed elements,
     fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context. The part develops the four-column
     principle; the conveyor principle; non-sequential connectivity; context-dependence; and
     the infinity of cognitive contexts. Epistemic output: the analytical vocabulary of
     explanatory cognition—the four columns and their relations—in a defined and usable
     form.

Part III (Structure of Epistemic Relations). Identity, signature, and pseudo-identity;
     manifestation as epistemic appearance; context and perspective; epistemic light as the
     medium of relation; light as the active structure of legibility; encompassment in epistemic
     light; the desire to find; the unknownness of same-category identities; and the epistemic
     distinctions among self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness. Epistemic output: the
     reconstructed structure of epistemic relations, and the account of how a finite subject
     recovers an identity from its manifestations.
Preface: Scope and Limits                                                                  xxix


Part IV (Conditions of Epistemic Validity and Adequacy). The criteria of context
     validity; manifestational adequacy; the adequacy of a pseudo-identity; the three failures
     of reconstruction; category-relative predication; and the epistemic measures of intensity
     and breadth. Epistemic output: the criteria of validity and the dimensions of adequacy
     by which any reconstruction can be assessed.

Part V (Limits, Errors, and Unknownness). The impossibility of super-identity; the
     fallacy of super-identity; configuration-dependence; the limits of self-knowledge; the
     impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light; intrinsic and temporary un-
     knownness; the plurality of perspectives; the boundaries of epistemology; and the open
     questions. Epistemic output: the exact statement of the limits that any finite cognition
     must acknowledge, and the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness.

Part VI (Epistemic Economy and Viability). Viability as an epistemic structural char-
     acter; fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability; tendency and structural fidelity; the
     cost of cognition; cognitive sediment and its integration; the balance criterion; and the
     core epistemic commitments with their dependency map. Epistemic output: the concept
     of viability, the epistemic economy of cognition, and the dependency map of the book’s
     core commitments.

    Two orders must be distinguished here, and the distinction governs the reading of the
whole book. The order of presentation is the pedagogical and argumentative order of the six
parts: Part I through Part VI, each presupposing only what has come before in the order of
cognition. The order of dependency is the network of direct and indirect dependencies among
the book’s principles; it is stated in the dependency map at the end of Part VI, and it is
not identical with the order of presentation. The order of presentation is linear; the order
of dependency is a network. A reader who enters the book in the middle should consult the
dependency map to see what the entering point presupposes.
    The back matter contains a bibliography, a glossary of epistemic terms, an index of
epistemic principles, an index of arguments, and an index of formalizations. The back matter
is not an appendix: it contains no applications, and it adds no claims to the body. Its function
is to make the body assessable—to locate each principle in its context, to state the statuses of
the claims, and to make the framework’s formal apparatus visible in one place.
    The volume contains three structural appendices. They are not applications, and they
add no doctrinal claims to the body. Their function is assessability in three senses: the
Comparative Study (Appendix A) situates the framework’s structure in relation to earlier
philosophical architectures, so that the reader can see what is familiar and what is new; the
Formal Reconstruction (Appendix B) restates the framework’s core principles in a formal
apparatus, so that the reader can see the framework’s formal skeleton in one place; and the
Independence Stress Test (Appendix C) tests the framework’s core principles against the
question of what would refute them from within epistemology, so that the framework’s internal
coherence is assessable rather than merely asserted. In the present ordering of the volume,
the three appendices follow the body and precede the back matter; all three are referred to
identically in this preface, in the table of contents, and in the concluding note.


How to Read the Book
The book can be read in three ways, and each path is complete in its own terms.
    The reader of the whole architecture. Reads from beginning to end, in the order of
the chapters. Each part presupposes only what has come before. Each chapter is short enough
to be read in one sitting, and each ends with a transition to the next. This is the intended
path, and the reader who follows it has the framework in the order in which it was built.
xxx                                                                  Preface: Scope and Limits


    The reader of a part. Reads the part relevant to their inquiry, and follows the cross-
references backward to the foundations. The dependency map at the end of Part VI states
which principles depend on which, so that the reader who enters in the middle can see what
the entering point presupposes. The index of epistemic principles and the index of arguments
allow the reader to locate a specific claim in its context.
    The reader of the epistemic core. Reads Parts III and IV, which state the structure
of epistemic relations and the conditions of validity, and then follows the cross-references
backward to Parts I and II for the definitions, and forward to Parts V and VI for the limits
and the economy. This path is for the reader whose interest is in the epistemic structure itself.


The Meaning of Viability
The title names a concept that belongs entirely to the book’s epistemology. Identity does not
admit of degrees: a thing is the same one or it is not. But the relation between an identity
and its manifestations, as that relation is cognized in a cognitive context, can satisfy certain
structural conditions more or less completely. We call the structural character of that relation
viability. The viability of an identity in a cognitive context is characterized through three
structural components: the fidelity of its manifestations to its structure, the sustainability of
the cost of producing and maintaining them, and the recoverability of its capacity to manifest.
The three components are aspects of a single structural character; they are distinguished for
the purposes of analysis, and they are not asserted to be independent of one another.
    Viability admits of degrees; identity does not; and the two are related as what is expressed
to the structural character of its expression. The concept is defined in Chapter 36, and the
book returns to it in the chapters that follow. It is a descriptive concept: it states a condition
on the relation between an identity and its manifestations, and attaches no value, end, or good
to that condition. The concept is the epistemological counterpart of the concept of identity:
identity is the invariant an explanation holds fixed; viability is the structural character of how
that invariant is expressed in the explanation’s manifestations.


Epistemic Status of Claims
Every major claim in this book is tagged with one of six epistemic-status labels. These labels
tell the reader what kind of argument is being offered, and therefore what kind of criticism is
appropriate. The labels are aligned with the Status Labels file and with the Glossary; the
same six labels and the same definitions are used in all three places.

(A) Axiom or Foundational Commitment. A starting point that is adopted rather than
    proved. Its justification is coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness—not deduction.
    An (A) claim can be criticized by (i) showing incoherence with other commitments,
    (ii) showing a rival commitment that is more explanatory or more fruitful, or (iii) showing
    that the framework could do without it.

(T) Argued. An argument is given in the text—typically a reductio, a transcendental
     argument, or an inference to the best explanation. A (T) claim can be criticized
     by attacking its premises or its inferential step. Every (T) claim in this book depends on
     premises, and where those premises are themselves commitments ((A)) the text says so.

(E) Estimate. A claim that is offered as approximate and subject to revision—typically a
     structural estimate. An (E) claim can be criticized by showing that the architecture
     works as well or better with a different structure, or that the specific structure is doing
     no explanatory work.
Preface: Scope and Limits                                                                    xxxi


(Q) Open Epistemic Question. An epistemic question that has no final answer yet, but can
    be examined within the system. It is not handed to any other domain for measurement or
    testing. A (Q) question is not a gap in the argument; it is a question that the argument
    makes visible but does not settle, and it is stated at exactly that strength.

(S) Speculation. A speculative extension, flagged for caution. The framework does not claim
     that the speculation is true; it claims that it follows naturally from the framework’s
     structure and is worth investigating.

Proposed. A claim that the book states but does not place among its established results.
    It is offered for consideration, and its status remains deliberately proposed within the
    present framework. A proposed claim can be criticized by showing that it does no work,
    or that its work is done by a claim that is already in the framework.

    The reader is invited to assess each claim by the standard appropriate to its status. A (T)
claim is not refuted by saying “it is only an estimate”; an (E) claim is not refuted by saying “it
is not proved.” The labels are not decorations; they are the framework’s way of being honest
about what it is doing. The summary table of the labels, and the guidance on how to read a
labeled claim, are given in the Status Labels file and in the Glossary; the same definitions are
used there and here.


Terminology and Internal Assessability
The book uses a small number of technical terms, each of which is defined in the text and
collected in the Glossary. The most important are:

Identity. The invariant structure that an explanatory cognition holds fixed across a class of
     allowable transformations of its manifestations.

Manifestation. The contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving cognitive
    context, according to the capacity, aptitude, and constraints of that context.

Fixed element. An entity selected as an invariant term within a given explanatory cognition;
     its fixedness is methodological, not ontological.

Fluid element. An entity that conveys effect, connecting fixed elements to one another.

Governing dynamics. The rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements.

Context. The setting in which cognition occurs. The book develops the cognitive context—the
    frame fixed by the question.

Epistemic light. The condition of possibility of legible relation; the medium by which an
     appearance is conveyed and by which a manifestation is rendered legible as an appearance
     of its source.

Signature. The structural description of an identity’s invariance; what can be recorded,
     compared, and copied (as distinct from the identity itself).

Viability. The structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
    in a cognitive context, characterized through fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability; a
    descriptive concept, not a value, an end, or a good.
xxxii                                                                  Preface: Scope and Limits


    The technical terms are defined in the text and collected in the Glossary. Within the book
itself, the sense of each term is fixed by its definition and by nothing outside it. The Glossary
collects the definitions in one place; the index of epistemic principles locates each term’s first
occurrence and its uses.
    No term in this book carries normative or ethical weight. Every term is defined epistemically.
Where a term used in this book has a normative use elsewhere—“justice,” “care,” “sustainability,”
“flourishing”—its sense in this book is fixed entirely by the book’s own structural definitions,
and no normative use of the term outside the book determines its sense here.
    The book offers its arguments on their own merits, and asks to be assessed in that way. No
principle of it is justified by reference to an outside theory, tradition, or result. Its concepts
are defined within the book, and its arguments are stated so as to be assessed without any
other work. For each major claim, the book states (i) the claim itself, (ii) its premises, (iii) the
inferential step from the premises to the claim, and (iv) the epistemic status of the claim (A,
T, E, Q, S, or Proposed). The reader who wishes to assess a claim can locate its premises,
examine its inferential step, and apply the standard appropriate to its status. Nothing is
asserted without a stated premise; nothing is inferred without a stated step; nothing is labeled
without a stated reason for the label.
    The assessability of the book is therefore internal to the book. The reader does not need
to enter a tradition, consult an outside authority, or accept a result from another discipline in
order to assess what the book claims. The reader needs only the book’s own definitions, the
book’s own arguments, and the book’s own standards of assessment—all of which are stated
in the book itself.
    The book’s claim is not that its framework is the only possible one; it is that its framework
is stated in such a way that a reader can decide whether to accept it. A reader who disagrees
with the book’s conclusions can locate the premises on which the conclusions depend, and can
assess the premises on their own terms. This is what the book means by assessability: the
property of being stated so that a reader can decide.


The Appendices
The volume contains three structural appendices, and their place in the book is stated here
once, in the same terms that are used in the table of contents and in the concluding note.
Each appendix is introduced only by its epistemic function.

Appendix A: Comparative Study. A structural comparison of the framework developed
    in this volume with earlier philosophical architectures that are kin to it. Its epistemic
    function is comparative: it makes the framework’s novelty and its continuity visible at
    once, so that the reader can see what the framework shares with earlier architectures
    and what it adds. It adds no doctrinal claims to the body, and no argument in the body
    depends on it.

Appendix B: Formal Reconstruction. A formal restatement of the framework’s core
    principles—the four-column structure, the conveyor principle, the conditions of va-
    lidity, and the viability relation—in a single formal apparatus. Its epistemic function is
    formal: it makes the framework’s formal skeleton visible in one place, and it allows the
    reader to test the framework’s coherence formally. It adds no doctrinal claims to the
    body, and no argument in the body depends on it.

Appendix C: Independence Stress Test. A systematic test of the framework’s core prin-
    ciples, conducted by stress-testing each principle against the question of what would
    refute it from within epistemology. Its epistemic function is critical: it makes the
    framework’s internal coherence assessable rather than merely asserted, by displaying
Preface: Scope and Limits                                                                  xxxiii


      where each principle is vulnerable and what would count as its refutation. It adds no
      doctrinal claims to the body, and no argument in the body depends on it.

    None of the appendices is an application: the applications of the framework to anthropology,
religious phenomena, and ethics are not part of this volume. The distinction between a
structural appendix and an application is the distinction between an instrument of assessability
and a use of the framework; the present volume contains the former and not the latter.


A Note on the Two Orders and the Four Roles
The book distinguishes two orders from the outset: the order of cognition and the order of
dependency in explanation. The order of cognition is the order in which a finite subject comes
to understand the structure of explanatory cognition; the order of dependency in explanation
is the order in which the elements of an explanation depend on one another. The present
volume develops the order of cognition, and it states the order of dependency in explanation
insofar as that order is internal to explanatory cognition itself. The dependency map at the
end of Part VI states the order of dependency among the book’s principles.
    Within the order of cognition, the book’s architecture proceeds in two stages, and the two
stages must not be conflated. Part I (Foundations and Method) provides the four questions
and the method: it states what any explanation must address, and how the book will address
it. Part II (Architecture of Explanatory Cognition) converts those four questions into the
four analytical roles—fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context—and
defines them. The four roles are thus the result of Part II’s work on Part I’s questions, not
the starting point of Part I. This two-stage structure is stated in the table of contents, in the
“Map of the Book,” and in the body’s transition from Part I to Part II; the same two-stage
description is used in all three places.


Concluding Remark
This book is offered as a proposal, not as a finished system. It invites objection, revision, and
refinement. The reader who finds a claim unconvincing is invited to strengthen the objection
and continue the inquiry. The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.

Introduction: The Problem, the
Method, and the Map

The Central Problem
The central problem of this book is epistemological, and it can be stated in one sentence: how
is a subject of cognition reconstructed explanatorily, and how are the validity, the adequacy,
the limits, and the viability of that reconstruction assessed?
    The problem has four parts, and each part corresponds to a question that any explanatory
cognition must answer.

   1. The question of content. What must an explanation contain if it is to count as an
      explanation of its subject? This is the question of the elements of explanatory cognition.

   2. The question of relation. How are the elements of an explanation related to one
      another? This is the question of the structure that connects the elements.

   3. The question of legibility. What makes a relation between elements legible as a
      relation—that is, what makes it possible for a finite subject to recognize the relation as
      a relation between these terms? This is the question of the medium of relation.

   4. The question of limits. What are the limits of finite cognition, and how does a finite
      subject acknowledge them without abandoning the inquiry? This is the question of the
      boundaries of explanatory cognition.

    The book’s answer to these four questions is developed in six parts. The answer is not a
single proposition but an architecture: a structure of analytical roles, relations, conditions,
and measures that together make explanatory cognition reconstructible and assessable. The
book’s thesis is that this architecture can be stated explicitly, that its necessity and sufficiency
can be argued, and that its consequences for the classical problems of identity, manifestation,
and epistemic access can be drawn.


Explanatory Cognition
The subject of the book is explanatory cognition, and the term must be distinguished from a
closely related but different notion.

Definition 0.1 (Explanatory Cognition). Explanatory cognition is the cognitive activity by
which a finite subject reconstructs the structure of a subject of cognition from its manifestations,
states the reconstruction in a form that can be assessed, and assesses it by the criteria of
validity and adequacy that the reconstruction itself makes explicit.

    Explanatory cognition is not the passive reception of information. The passive reception of
information is the registration of a manifestation without the reconstruction of the structure
xxxvi                                  Introduction: The Problem, the Method, and the Map


that the manifestation manifests. A subject who registers a manifestation but does not
reconstruct the identity that the manifestation expresses has received information; the subject
has not yet cognized explanatorily. Explanatory cognition begins when the subject asks what
the manifestation is a manifestation of, and it is completed when the subject has reconstructed
the identity, stated the reconstruction, and assessed it.
    The distinction matters for the whole book. A theory of information can describe how a
signal is transmitted and received; it cannot, by itself, describe how a subject reconstructs
an identity from a manifestation, because the reconstruction is not a transmission. The
reconstruction is an activity of the finite subject, governed by the subject’s cognitive context,
its capacity, and its criteria of validity. The book’s subject is that activity, and the book’s
claim is that the activity has a structure that can be stated explicitly.
    Explanatory cognition has three structural features that the book develops.

   1. It is reconstructive. The subject does not receive the identity; the subject reconstructs
      it from its manifestations. The reconstruction is an achievement of the subject, not a
      given.

   2. It is context-bound. The reconstruction occurs in a cognitive context, and the context
      determines what counts as an answer. A reconstruction that is valid in one context may
      not be valid in another.

   3. It is assessable. The reconstruction can be assessed by criteria that the reconstruction
      itself makes explicit. The criteria are not imposed from outside; they are stated in the
      reconstruction, and the subject who states them can be assessed by them.

    These three features are the book’s starting point. The body of the book develops them,
states their consequences, and shows how they dissolve the classical problems of identity,
manifestation, and epistemic access.


The Four Questions and the Four Columns
The book’s architecture begins with four questions, and it converts them into four analytical
roles. The conversion is the work of Parts I and II, and it is stated here in outline so that the
reader knows what the book builds.


The Four Questions
Any explanatory cognition, if it is to be complete in the operative sense stated in the Preface,
must answer four questions.

What? What is the subject of the explanation? The question identifies the entity or structure
   that the explanation is an explanation of.

How? How does the subject of the explanation affect, or get affected by, what is around it?
   The question identifies the relations of effect that connect the subject to other entities.

On what basis? On what basis does the effect occur? The question identifies the rule or
    regularity that governs the effect.

Where? Where does the explanation occur? The question identifies the setting in which the
   cognition occurs and in which the manifestation is realized.
Introduction: The Problem, the Method, and the Map                                            xxxvii


   The four questions are stated in Part I, Chapter 1. They are the book’s starting point,
and they are not derived from any other principle. The book’s claim is that any explanatory
cognition that answers all four questions has the structure that the book reconstructs, and
that any explanatory cognition that omits one of the four is incomplete in a way that the book
can state.

The Four Columns
The four questions are converted, in Part II, into four analytical roles. The conversion is not a
renaming; it is a structural analysis that shows how each question corresponds to a role that
any explanatory cognition must fill.

Fixed elements. The entities held invariant within the explanation. The fixed elements
     answer the question What? : they are what the explanation is an explanation of, held
     fixed across the transformations that the explanation allows.

Fluid elements. The entities that convey effect between fixed elements. The fluid elements
     answer the question How? : they are the carriers of the effect that connects the fixed
     elements to one another.

Governing dynamics. The rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements. The
    governing dynamics answer the question On what basis? : they are the regularity that
    makes the effect intelligible.

Context. The setting in which the cognition occurs. The context answers the question
    Where? : it is the frame fixed by the question, and it determines what counts as an
    answer.

    The four columns are analytical roles, not kinds of entity. A single entity can occupy
different roles in different explanations, and the same explanation can be re-described by
assigning the roles differently. The book’s claim is that the four roles are necessary and sufficient
for explanatory cognition, and the argument for this claim is given in Part II, Chapters 6
and 7.
    The relation between the four questions and the four columns is stated in the following
diagram.

                            Question                     Column
                             What?           −→       Fixed elements
                              How?           −→       Fluid elements
                          On what basis?     −→     Governing dynamics
                             Where?          −→          Context

    The diagram is not a deduction; it is a statement of the book’s architectonic principle.
The principle is that the four questions and the four columns are the same structure stated
in two registers: the register of the questions that a finite subject asks, and the register
of the roles that the answers fill. The book’s argument, in Parts I and II, is that the two
registers are structurally identical, and that the identity is what makes explanatory cognition
reconstructible.


The Map of the Book
The book is organized into six parts, a back matter, and three structural appendices. The map
is stated here so that the reader knows the order of the argument and the output of each part.
xxxviii                                Introduction: The Problem, the Method, and the Map


Part I (Foundations and Method of Explanatory Cognition). The four questions and
     the method of the book; the finitude of the epistemic subject; the boundary between
     structure and telos; and cognitive architecture and the order of dependency in explanation.
    Output: the problem, the method, and the boundary conditions of the inquiry.

Part II (Architecture of Explanatory Cognition). The four questions are converted
     into the four analytical roles; the four-column principle; the conveyor principle; non-
     sequential connectivity; context-dependence; and the infinity of cognitive contexts.
    Output: the analytical vocabulary of explanatory cognition.

Part III (Structure of Epistemic Relations). Identity, signature, and pseudo-identity;
     manifestation as epistemic appearance; context and perspective; epistemic light as
     the medium of relation; light as the active structure of legibility; encompassment in
     epistemic light; the desire to find; the unknownness of same-category identities; and the
     epistemic distinctions among self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness. Output: the
     reconstructed structure of epistemic relations.

Part IV (Conditions of Epistemic Validity and Adequacy). The criteria of context
     validity; manifestational adequacy; the adequacy of a pseudo-identity; the three failures
     of reconstruction; category-relative predication; and the epistemic measures of intensity
     and breadth. Output: the criteria of validity and the dimensions of adequacy.

Part V (Limits, Errors, and Unknownness). The impossibility of super-identity; the
     fallacy of super-identity; configuration-dependence; the limits of self-knowledge; the
     impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light; intrinsic and temporary un-
     knownness; the plurality of perspectives; the boundaries of epistemology; and the open
     questions. Output: the exact statement of the limits of finite cognition.

Part VI (Epistemic Economy and Viability). Viability as an epistemic structural char-
     acter; fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability; tendency and structural fidelity; the
     cost of cognition; cognitive sediment and its integration; the balance criterion; and
     the core epistemic commitments with their dependency map. Output: the concept of
     viability, the epistemic economy of cognition, and the dependency map of the book’s
     core commitments.

    The dependency among the six parts is linear in the order of cognition: each part presup-
poses the parts above it, and no part presupposes a part below it. The dependency map at the
end of Part VI states the dependencies among the book’s principles; the pedagogical order and
the order of dependency are distinguished in the Preface, and the distinction is observed here.
    The back matter contains the bibliography, the glossary of epistemic terms, the index
of epistemic principles, the index of arguments, and the index of formalizations. The three
structural appendices (Comparative Study, Formal Reconstruction, Independence Stress Test)
follow the body and precede the back matter; their function is assessability, not doctrine, as
stated in the Preface.


How to Read the Book
The book can be read in three ways, and each path is complete in its own terms.

  1. The reader of the whole architecture. Reads from beginning to end, in the order of
     the chapters. Each part presupposes only what has come before. This is the intended
     path.
Introduction: The Problem, the Method, and the Map                                       xxxix


  2. The reader of a part. Reads the part relevant to their inquiry, and follows the
     cross-references backward to the foundations. The dependency map at the end of Part VI
     states which principles depend on which.

  3. The reader of the epistemic core. Reads Parts III and IV, and follows the cross-
     references backward to Parts I and II for the definitions, and forward to Parts V and VI
     for the limits and the economy.

   The reading paths are stated at greater length in the Preface, and the same paths are
described here in outline so that the reader who begins with the Introduction knows the
available routes.


The Basic Terminology
The book uses a small number of technical terms, and each is defined at its first occurrence
and collected in the Glossary. The most important are stated here so that the reader can
begin with a working vocabulary.

Explanatory cognition. The cognitive activity by which a finite subject reconstructs the
    structure of a subject of cognition from its manifestations, states the reconstruction, and
    assesses it.

Identity. The invariant structure that an explanatory cognition holds fixed across a class of
     allowable transformations of its manifestations.

Manifestation. The contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving cognitive
    context, according to the capacity, aptitude, and constraints of that context.

Fixed element. An entity selected as an invariant term within a given explanatory cognition.

Fluid element. An entity that conveys effect, connecting fixed elements to one another.

Governing dynamics. The rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements.

Context. The setting in which cognition occurs; the frame fixed by the question.

Epistemic light. The condition of possibility of legible relation; the medium by which an
     appearance is conveyed and by which a manifestation is rendered legible as an appearance
     of its source.

Reconstruction. The epistemic process by which a finite subject recovers the structure of
    an identity from its manifestations.

Viability. The structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
    in a cognitive context, characterized through fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.

    The terms are defined in the text and collected in the Glossary; the sense of each term is
fixed by its definition and by nothing outside the book. The Preface states the conventions of
terminology and the epistemic-status labels; the reader who wishes to see the labels and the
conventions in one place is directed to the Preface and to the Status Labels file.
xl                                       Introduction: The Problem, the Method, and the Map


What the Reader Will Have at the End
The book is an argument, and the argument has an output. The reader who has followed the
book to its end will have the following epistemic abilities.

     1. The ability to reconstruct an explanatory cognition. The reader will be able to
        identify the four analytical roles in any explanatory cognition, and to state how the roles
        are related.

     2. The ability to assess a reconstruction. The reader will be able to apply the criteria
        of validity and the dimensions of adequacy stated in Part IV, and to state what a
        reconstruction would have to satisfy in order to count as adequate.

     3. The ability to recognize the limits of a reconstruction. The reader will be able
        to state the limits of finite cognition stated in Part V, and to distinguish intrinsic from
        temporary unknownness.

     4. The ability to assess the viability of a reconstruction. The reader will be able
        to characterize the viability of a reconstruction through fidelity, sustainability, and
        recoverability, and to assess the epistemic economy of the reconstruction.

     5. The ability to locate a claim in the architecture. The reader will be able to use
        the dependency map, the indexes, and the Glossary to locate any claim in its context,
        and to assess it by the standard appropriate to its status.

   These abilities are the book’s output. The book does not claim that the abilities are the
whole of what epistemology can give; it claims that they are what this book gives, and that
they are assessable by the book’s own standards.


Concluding Remark
The Introduction states the problem, defines the subject, introduces the architecture, and maps
the book. The body of the book is the argument for the architecture and the development of
its consequences. The reader who has followed the Introduction has the map; the reader who
follows the body has the territory. The inquiry continues.

Epistemic Status Labels

Why the Book Uses Labels
Every major claim in this book is tagged with an epistemic-status label. The labels tell
the reader what kind of argument is being offered, and therefore what kind of criticism is
appropriate. They are not decorations; they are the book’s way of being honest about what
it is doing, and they are the reader’s way of knowing, at a glance, which claims are argued,
which are adopted, which are provisional, and which are left open.
     The labels are used consistently across the book. A claim that is argued in one chapter and
adopted in another carries the label appropriate to its role in each place; the book says which,
where the difference matters. The system applies to the body of the book (Chapters 1–42)
and to the three structural appendices (A, B, C); the appendices use the same six labels, and
they add no seventh label.
     The use of labels is itself a philosophical position, and it is worth stating at the outset.
The position is fallibilism: the book does not claim that its conclusions are certain, and it
does not pretend that they are. It claims that they are offered at the strength their arguments
support, and it marks, at each point, what that strength is. The labels are the vocabulary of
this fallibilism. A book that stated its conclusions without marking their strength would be
claiming more than it can support, and the reader would have no way of knowing which claims
are argued and which are adopted. The labels are the book’s refusal to make that claim.
     The labels are also a discipline on the book’s own claims. A claim labeled (T) must be
accompanied by an argument; a claim labeled (A) must state what it is adopted on the basis
of; a claim labeled (Q) must state what would settle it or show that it cannot be settled; a
claim labeled Proposed must state why it is left provisional. The labels are not a summary of
the book’s claims; they are a condition on how the claims are stated.


The Relation Among the Six Labels
The six labels are not a scale from weak to strong, and they are not nested. Each label names
a different kind of claim, and the kinds are distinguished by two questions: what is the claim’s
basis? and what is the claim’s present standing in the framework? The following statement
fixes the relation exactly.

   1. (A) is a basis-type. An (A) claim is adopted, not proved. It is a starting point. Two
      species fall under (A): a primitive commitment (a substantive claim the framework needs)
      and a stipulated definition (a decision about vocabulary). The species are distinguished
      in the note on (A) below.

   2. (T) is a basis-type. A (T) claim is argued. Its basis is an argument given in the text.

   3. (E) is a basis-type. An (E) claim is an estimate. Its basis is a substantive assess-
      ment offered at a declared strength, typically a structural judgment about sufficiency,
      minimality, order, or explanatory adequacy.
xlii                                                                  Epistemic Status Labels


   4. (Q) is a standing-type. A (Q) claim is an open epistemic question. Its basis is that
      the framework makes the question visible; its standing is that the framework does not
      settle it. A (Q) question is not a defective (T) claim; it is a question the framework
      states at exactly the strength of an open question.

   5. (S) is a standing-type. An (S) claim is a speculative extension. Its basis is that it
      follows naturally from the framework’s structure; its standing is conjectural, flagged for
      caution.

   6. Proposed is an independent, provisional status. A proposed claim is one the book
      states but does not place among its established results. It is not a subtype of (E) and
      not a subtype of (Q). It differs from (E) in that an (E) claim is offered as the book’s
      best current assessment, while a proposed claim is offered with its status deliberately
      undecided. It differs from (Q) in that a (Q) claim is a question, while a proposed claim
      is a statement whose status is left open. A proposed claim becomes an (A), (T), or
      (E) claim only if a later argument in the book assigns it that status; absent such an
      argument, it remains proposed within the present framework.

    The relation can be stated in one sentence: (A), (T), and (E) name the basis of a claim;
(Q) and (S) name the standing of a claim; and Proposed names a claim whose basis is stated
but whose standing is deliberately left undecided. The five labels (A), (T), (E), (Q), (S) are
exhaustive of the book’s settled statuses; Proposed is the book’s provisional status, used where
the book states a claim without settling its standing.


The Six Labels
For each label, four items are stated: the condition of use, the minimum evidence required,
the mode of assessment, and a real example from the book.

(A) Axiom or Foundational Commitment
Condition of use. The claim is a starting point that the framework adopts rather than
proves, and the chapter that states it declares the adoption and its cost.
     Minimum evidence required. A statement of (i) what the claim is adopted on the basis
of (coherence, explanatory power, fruitfulness), and (ii) what is lost if the claim is rejected.
     Mode of assessment. Attack by (i) showing incoherence with other commitments,
(ii) showing a rival commitment that is more explanatory or more fruitful, or (iii) showing that
the framework could do without it. For a stipulated definition, propose another vocabulary
and show what it does better.
     Real example from the book. C1 (Finitude of the Epistemic Subject, Chapter 3) is a
primitive commitment: it is adopted, its basis is stated, and its load-bearing role in Part V is
declared. The definition of identity (Chapter 12, Section 12.3) is a stipulated definition: it
fixes the sense of the term, and it is rejected only by proposing another vocabulary.

(T) Argued
Condition of use. An argument is given in the text—a reductio, a transcendental argument,
or an inference to the best explanation—and the argument’s premises and inferential step are
stated.
    Minimum evidence required. The premises, the inferential step, and the conclusion,
stated in the chapter that offers the argument. Where a premise is itself an (A) commitment,
the chapter says so.
Epistemic Status Labels                                                                     xliii


    Mode of assessment. Attack the premises, attack the inferential step, or show that the
argument does not reach the conclusion.
    Real example from the book. The removal-test argument for the necessity of the four
columns (Chapter 7, Section 7.3) is a (T) claim: it offers an argument, states its premises, and
invites attack on either the premises or the step.

(E) Estimate
Condition of use. The claim is a substantive assessment offered at a declared strength, not
presented as a necessary consequence. Structural estimates of sufficiency, minimality, order,
and explanatory adequacy are the typical cases.
    Minimum evidence required. A statement of what the estimate is an estimate of, the
strength at which it is offered, and what would count as a better estimate.
    Mode of assessment. Show that the architecture works as well or better with a different
structure, or that the specific structure is doing no explanatory work.
    Real example from the book. The reducibility-test conclusion that the four columns
are sufficient (Chapter 7, Section 7.4) is an (E) claim: it is offered as an estimate, subject to
revision if a candidate fifth column is found.

(Q) Open Epistemic Question
Condition of use. The claim is an epistemic question that the framework makes visible
but does not settle, and the chapter that states it states what would settle it or show that it
cannot be settled.
    Minimum evidence required. A statement of the question, of why the framework
makes it visible, and of what would count as settling it (or as showing that it is not a real
question).
    Mode of assessment. Settle the question (which extends the framework), or show that
the question is not real (which shows a limit of the framework’s formulation).
    Real example from the book. The fourteen open questions collected in Chapter 34
(The Boundaries of Epistemology) are (Q) claims: four conceptual, five argumentative, and
five epistemic. The fourteenth question (the temporal structure of self-awareness) is flagged in
Chapter 20 as a question the book makes visible but does not settle.

(S) Speculation
Condition of use. The claim is a speculative extension that follows naturally from the
framework’s structure and is flagged for caution. The chapter that states it marks it as not
established.
    Minimum evidence required. A statement of the structural reason the speculation
follows, and of what would make it worth investigating.
    Mode of assessment. Show that it does not follow from the framework’s structure, or
that it is not worth investigating.
    Real example from the book. The question whether the infinity of contexts (Chapter 11)
is countable or uncountable is the book’s one (S) claim in this volume; it is marked at exactly
that strength.

Proposed
Condition of use. The claim is stated but its status is deliberately left undecided within the
present framework. The chapter that states it says why the claim is left provisional, and what
would move it to a settled status.
xliv                                                                     Epistemic Status Labels


    Minimum evidence required. A statement of the claim, of why it is left provisional,
and of what would assign it a settled status (an (A), (T), or (E) status) if such an argument
were given.
    Mode of assessment. Show that the claim does no work, or that its work is done by a
claim already in the framework. Show, in the other direction, that the claim deserves a settled
status, and state the argument that would assign it.
    Real example from the book. The criteria of manifestational adequacy (Chapter 22)
and of contextual manifestational capacity (Chapter 13) are proposed claims: the book states
them, says what would put them in question, and does not count them as established.


A Note on the Use of (A)
The (A) label covers two things that are easily run together, and the book distinguishes them
where the difference matters.
     A primitive commitment is a substantive claim that the framework adopts rather than
proves. Its justification is coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness. A reader who rejects
a primitive commitment has a reason to reject the conclusions that depend on it, and the
dependency map at the end of Part VI states which conclusions those are. The ten core
commitments of Chapter 43 (C1–C10) are the book’s principal primitive commitments, and
the map states what depends on each.
     A stipulated definition is a decision about vocabulary. It fixes the sense of a term, and
it is true by stipulation. A reader who rejects a stipulated definition has proposed another
vocabulary, and the book can say where its own vocabulary was stipulated.
     Where the book needs to separate the two, it says so in the text. The reader who wishes
to know which (A) claims are primitive commitments and which are stipulated definitions is
directed to the dependency map at the end of Part VI, which states, for each load-bearing
commitment, what depends on it and what is lost if it is rejected. The reader who wishes
to see a stipulated definition in its own place is directed to the Glossary, where each term is
defined with the place of its definition.


The Labels and the Method
The labels are the vocabulary of the method stated in Chapter 2, and the connection is worth
stating explicitly. The method has three parts: the removal test for necessity, the reducibility
test for sufficiency, and the test of fruitfulness. Each part yields a conclusion at a declared
strength, and the labels are the declaration.
    The removal test, when it succeeds, yields a (T) conclusion: the column is necessary, given
the commitment that we can recognize an explanatory failure. The reducibility test, when it
succeeds, yields an (E) conclusion: the four columns are sufficient, as an estimate, subject to
revision if a candidate fifth column is found. The test of fruitfulness yields a reason in favor of
the framework, not a proof; the book states this at the strength of a consideration, not at the
strength of a (T) claim.
    The labels are the book’s way of keeping the method honest. A (T) claim that is offered
as an (E) claim would be false modesty; an (E) claim that is offered as a (T) claim would be
overstatement. The labels are the discipline that prevents both, and the reader who finds a
claim whose label does not match the method’s conclusion has found a defect in the book.


The Labels and the Conditional Architecture
The labels are also the vocabulary in which the book’s conditional architecture is stated
(Chapter 43). The book is a conditional architecture on a core of ten epistemic commitments
Epistemic Status Labels                                                                       xlv


(C1–C10); every other claim of the book is a definition, a consequence, an estimate, a proposal,
an open question, or a speculation. The labels are the vocabulary of this structure: they state
which claims are the core (A), which follow from the core (T), which are estimates (E), which
are open (Q), which are speculative (S), and which are proposed.
    The dependency map at the end of Part VI states, for each core commitment, which
conclusions depend on it, and what is lost if it is rejected. The labels and the map are
complementary: the labels state the kind of claim; the map states the dependence of the claim
on the core.

How to Read, Assess, and Criticize a Labeled Claim
The labels are not a ranking of importance. A (T) claim is not more important than an (A)
claim; it is a different kind of claim, and it invites a different kind of criticism. An (E) claim
is not a weaker version of a (T) claim; it is a claim offered at a different strength, and its
strength is exactly what the label says. A Proposed claim is not an (E) claim or a (Q) claim;
it is a claim whose status is deliberately undecided.

What the Labels Do Not Do
The labels are easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing, though the list is
short.
    They do not guarantee truth. A (T) claim is one for which an argument is given; it is not
a claim that the argument is sound.
    They do not rank importance. The book’s central claims are (A) claims—the ten core
commitments of Chapter 43—and the (T) claims are the arguments that show what follows
from them.
    They do not replace argument. The labels state what kind of argument is offered; they do
not state the argument. The reader who wishes to assess a claim is directed to the chapter
that states it.
    They do not close the book. The labels state the status of the book’s claims at the time
of writing; they invite the reader to revise the labels by showing that a (T) claim is not as
strong as the book thinks, or that an (E) claim is stronger, or that a proposed claim deserves
a settled status.
Epistemic Status Labels                                                                   xlvii


A Note on the Labels and the Book’s Audience
The labels are written for the reader who wishes to assess the book’s claims on their own
merits, and who wishes to know, at each point, what kind of claim is being made. They are
not written for the reader who wishes to be told what to think; the book does not tell the
reader what to think, and the labels are part of its refusal to do so.
     The reader who comes to the book from a tradition, or from another discipline, will find
the labels useful in a different way: they mark the places where the book’s claims are most
open to dialogue, and they mark the places where the book’s claims are most firmly held. A
dialogue that respects the labels is a dialogue that respects the book’s own statement of what
it is doing.


The labels are used consistently throughout the book. The reader who wishes to see them in use
is directed to any chapter; the reader who wishes to see the dependency of the book’s claims on
its commitments is directed to the dependency map at the end of Part VI.

          Part I

Foundations and Method of
  Explanatory Cognition
                                                                                                  3




Chapter 1

Explanatory Cognition and the Four
Questions

Scope
This chapter is a structural analysis of what it is for an explanatory cognition to be complete.
It states the four questions that any complete explanation must answer, introduces the scope in
which the questions are asked, and prepares the ground for the argument, given in Part II, that
the four are jointly necessary and jointly sufficient. Its claims are epistemic, not normative;
where it speaks of “understanding,” “explanation,” “cognition,” “element,” “rule,” or “context,”
these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter. The
chapter’s silence on questions of value is not a denial of their reality; it is the recognition that
the epistemic description is not the whole of what can be said.


1.1     A Scene: The Collapsed Bridge
Consider an engineer standing before a collapsed bridge. The bridge was new; the design was
standard; the materials were certified. Yet the bridge is in the river. The engineer is asked to
explain what happened.
    The engineer’s answer will not be a single sentence. It will identify the elements involved—
the deck, the piers, the cables, the load, the wind, the temperature, the quality of the concrete.
It will describe how these elements were connected—which element bore on which, through
what medium, by what path. It will state the rules that governed the connections—the laws of
stress and strain, the codes of design, the regularities of material behavior. And it will make
explicit the standpoint from which the explanation is given—the scale of the analysis, the
elements held fixed, the question the inquiry is asking.
    If any one of these four is missing, the explanation is incomplete. An engineer who names
the elements but says nothing about how they bore on one another has given a list, not an
explanation. An engineer who says that the cables failed but cannot say by what rule the
failure occurred has given a correlation, not an explanation. An engineer who gives the rule
but not the frame in which the rule is applied has given a formula, not an explanation of this
bridge.
    The scene is ordinary, but the structure it exhibits is general. Every explanatory cognition,
on inspection, assigns four roles: the elements that are related, the medium by which the
relation is carried, the rule that governs the medium, and the frame in which all three are
posed. The present chapter states these roles as four questions, and it fixes the scope in which
they are asked. The argument that the four are jointly necessary, and that no fifth is needed,
is the work of Part II.
4                                                           Chapter 1. Explanatory Cognition


Remark 1.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the four
roles at work in a familiar case. It does not prove that the four are necessary, or that no fifth
is needed. What it does is make the questions intelligible before they are stated: the reader
who has followed the scene knows what kind of thing the questions will ask. The argument for
necessity and sufficiency is given in Part II, and the scene carries no weight in it.


1.2     The Question of Understanding
When we say that we understand something, what have we done? The question is deceptively
simple. We may say that we understand a phenomenon, a text, a person, or a proof, and in
each case we seem to be claiming the same thing: that the matter is no longer opaque to us.
But what is it that has become transparent, and what has made it so?
    The question is not about the psychology of understanding. It is not a question about
what happens in the mind when we come to grasp something. It is a structural question: what
must an account of something contain, if the account is to count as an explanation of it? The
distinction between these two questions is the beginning of the inquiry of this book.
    To see the distinction, return to the collapsed bridge. A person may have a vivid mental
image of the collapse—the sound of the snapping cables, the dust, the silence afterward. The
image may be so vivid that the person says, “I understand what happened.” But the image is
not an explanation. It is an experience of the collapse, not an account of it. The engineer’s
explanation is an account: it identifies what was related, how the relation was carried, by
what rule it held, and from what standpoint it is stated. The image has none of these; the
explanation has all four.
    The distinction is not a denigration of experience. The person who saw the collapse knows
something the engineer does not—the sound, the dust, the silence. But the person’s knowledge
is not an explanation, and the engineer’s explanation is not an experience. The book is
concerned with the second, not the first. Its question is: what must an account of something
contain, if the account is to count as an explanation of it?
Remark 1.2 (The Two Questions Kept Apart). The question “what happens in the mind
when we understand?” and the question “what must an account contain if it is to explain?”
are different questions, and the book is concerned with the second. A psychological account
of understanding could be complete and leave the second question unanswered; a structural
account of explanation could be complete and leave the first unanswered. The book makes no
claim about the first, and it does not need to; its subject is the structure of explanation, not
the psychology of the explainer.
Remark 1.3 (What “Structural” Means Here). The word “structural” is used in this book in
a specific sense. A structural analysis asks what roles an account must assign, not what the
account is made of, and not what the account is about. It is the analysis of the form of an
explanation, not of its content. The distinction is the distinction between the architecture
of an explanation and the material the architecture is built with. The four questions are the
architecture; the elements, media, rules, and frames of any particular explanation are the
material.


1.3     The Four Questions
Every cognition that claims to “understand” something must answer four questions. The
questions are not posed here as a derivation from any premise; they are stated as an observation
about what any explanatory account, on inspection, must contain. Whether the four are truly
necessary, and whether no fifth is needed, is a matter for later argument; the present section
states the questions and prepares the ground for that argument.
1.3. The Four Questions                                                                           5


1.3.1    What?

The first question is: what are the elements that are known? Any explanatory account must
identify the entities or terms whose relations it is about. It must say what is being related to
what. Without such identification, the account has nothing to relate; it is a description of
process without terms.
    In the bridge case, the first question is answered by naming the deck, the piers, the cables,
the load, the wind, the temperature, the concrete. Each is an element the explanation holds
fixed while it explains the relations among them. The elements are not the explanation; they
are what the explanation is about.
    Epistemic output. The answer to What? must identify the fixed elements of the expla-
nation: the entities or terms that the explanation holds invariant across the transformations it
allows. The output is an identification, and it is assessed by whether the identified elements
are the ones the explanation actually needs, and whether the list is complete for the question
at hand. An answer that identifies the wrong elements, or omits an element the explanation
depends on, fails at this stage regardless of how well the other three questions are answered.


1.3.2    How?

The second question is: how are these elements connected? A list of entities is not an
explanation of how any one of them bears on another. The account must say by what the
relation is carried, or through what the effect of one element reaches another.
    In the bridge case, the second question is answered by describing the path by which the
load reaches the piers, the path by which the wind reaches the deck, the path by which the
temperature reaches the cables. The paths are the medium of the relation; without them, the
elements are a list, not a structure.
    Epistemic output. The answer to How? must describe the fluid elements and the paths
of effect that connect the fixed elements. The output is a description, and it is assessed by
whether the described paths are the ones through which the effect actually travels, and whether
the description specifies the direction and the medium of the effect. An answer that states
that two elements are connected but not through what, or in which direction, fails at this
stage: it gives a correlation, not a mechanism.


1.3.3    On What Basis?

The third question is: on what basis do the connections hold? The account must state the
rule or regularity that governs how the elements behave in one another’s presence. Without
such a rule, the account shows that things are connected, but not how the connection behaves,
and so cannot support prediction or counterfactual reasoning.
    In the bridge case, the third question is answered by stating the laws of stress and strain, the
codes of design, the regularities of material behavior. The rules are what make the explanation
predictive: given the elements and the medium, the rules say what will happen, and what
would have happened under different conditions.
    Epistemic output. The answer to On what basis? must state the governing dynamics:
the rule or regularity that governs the effect of the fluid elements on the fixed elements. The
output is a justification, and it is assessed by whether the stated rule is the one that actually
governs the connection, and whether the rule is stated at a level of generality that supports
prediction and counterfactual reasoning. An answer that names a rule but cannot say what
would happen under a different condition has not yet given the basis; it has given a label for it.
6                                                            Chapter 1. Explanatory Cognition


1.3.4    Where?
The fourth question is: where—from what standpoint—is the cognition carried out? Any
explanation is given from some position, in some frame, with some choice of what is held fixed
and what is allowed to vary. The account must make explicit the standpoint from which its
elements are individuated and its rule applied.
     In the bridge case, the fourth question is answered by stating the scale of the analysis (the
whole bridge, or a single joint), the elements held fixed (the load, or the wind, or the concrete),
and the question the inquiry is asking (why the bridge failed, or why the design was thought
adequate). The frame is what makes the explanation an explanation of this bridge, not of
bridges in general.
     Epistemic output. The answer to Where? must contextualize the explanation: it must
state the cognitive context (the frame fixed by the question), the scale of the analysis, and the
choice of what is held fixed and what is allowed to vary. The output is a contextualization, and
it is assessed by whether the stated context is the one the question actually fixes, and whether
the explanation would remain valid if the context were different. An answer that omits the
context gives a formula that could apply anywhere; it does not yet give an explanation of this
case.


1.3.5    The Four Together
The four questions are: what, how, on what basis, and where. They are not four questions about
the same thing. They are four questions about four different aspects of a single explanatory
account. The first asks about terms, the second about the medium between terms, the third
about the rule of the medium, and the fourth about the frame in which terms, medium, and
rule are posed.
    If any one of these questions remains unanswered, the cognition is incomplete as an
explanation. This claim, and the further claim that no fifth question is needed, are to be
argued in Part II. For the purposes of the present chapter, the four questions are to be
understood as the questions the book will call the four columns of explanatory cognition.
    The following table states, for each question, what defect an incomplete answer to that
question produces in the explanation. The table is operational: a reader who suspects that an
explanation is incomplete can locate the defect by asking which of the four questions has not
been answered.
