Remark 1.4 (The Four Are Stated as an Observation, Not Yet as a Principle). The four
questions are introduced here as an observation: on inspection, any explanatory account seems
to assign these four roles. The observation is not yet the principle. The principle—that the four
are jointly necessary and jointly sufficient—is stated and argued in Part II, and its argument
is what the present chapter prepares. A reader who is not yet persuaded that the four are
necessary is not asked to accept the principle on the strength of this chapter; the chapter
states the questions and leaves the argument to its place.

Remark 1.5 (The Four Questions Are Analytical, Not Ontological). The four questions are
questions about what an explanation must contain. They are not questions about what kinds
of entity reality contains. The distinction between the analytical structure of explanation
and the structure of what is explained is drawn in Chapter 5, and it is observed throughout
the book. Nothing in this chapter should be read as saying that the four questions are four
kinds of entity, or that reality has four levels. The four questions are the analytical roles of
an explanation, and the question of what reality contains is a different question, which the
present volume does not undertake.

Remark 1.6 (Why the Four Are Not Arbitrary). The four questions are not a list chosen at
will. They are the questions that any account must answer if it is to do what an explanation is
asked to do: to make something intelligible by identifying what is related, how the relation is
carried, by what rule it holds, and from what standpoint it is stated. A reader who proposes a
fifth question is invited to show that it is not a specification of one of the four—that it asks
about something the four do not cover. The argument for the four’s necessity and sufficiency
is the work of Part II; the present remark states the observation that motivates it.


1.4     The Scope: Explanatory Cognition
The four questions are questions about explanatory cognition, and the framework they lead to
is a framework for explanatory cognition. The term needs to be fixed at the outset, because
the framework does not claim to describe every mental state.

Definition 1.1 (Explanatory Cognition). Explanatory cognition is cognition whose aim is to
understand how some things stand to one another.

Remark 1.7 (What the Framework Does Not Claim). The framework does not claim to
describe every mental state. A momentary sensation, a mood, or a bare act of attention need
not answer all four questions. The framework concerns cognition whose aim is to understand
relations among things. Whenever this book says “cognition” without qualification, it means
explanatory cognition in the sense of Definition 1.1.

Example 1.1 (Two Cases). A negotiation is an explanatory cognition when the aim is to
understand how the parties affect one another. A city plan is an explanatory cognition when
the aim is to understand how districts and institutions bear on one another. A bare sensation
of warmth is not an explanatory cognition in this sense, because it does not aim to understand
how anything stands to anything.

    The scope is limited. It is also large enough to cover the inquiries of the book: the inquiries
into the structure of explanation, into the fixed and fluid elements of cognition, into the
epistemic structure of relation, into the conditions of validity, into the limits of finite cognition,
and into the epistemic economy of cognition. Every such inquiry is a cognition whose aim is
to understand how some things stand to one another. The framework of the four questions is
offered as the analytical structure of such cognition.
8                                                              Chapter 1. Explanatory Cognition


Remark 1.8 (The Scope Is the Scope of the Book). The reader who is interested in a mental
state that is not explanatory cognition—a bare sensation, a mood, an act of attention without
an aim to understand—will not find that state described in this book. The book’s silence
on such states is not a denial that they exist; it is the recognition that the book’s subject
is explanatory cognition, and that the four questions are questions about it. A reader who
wishes to extend the framework to other mental states is invited to do so; the framework is
offered at the scope it states, and the extension is a separate inquiry.

Remark 1.9 (The Scope and the Question of Telos). The scope of the book is explanatory
cognition, and the four questions are questions about its structure. They are not questions
about what explanatory cognition is for. The question of telos—the end, purpose, or good for
which cognition exists—is a real question, and the structure the book describes points toward
it; but the structure does not contain it, and the book cannot derive it from the structure
alone. This boundary is stated as an axiom in Chapter 4, and it is observed throughout. The
reader who seeks the telos of cognition will not find it in these pages; the reader who seeks the
structure within which the question of telos can be asked will find it.


1.5      A Minimal Procedure for Explanatory Inquiry
The four questions can be run as a procedure. The procedure is minimal: it states the steps
by which a subject of cognition is brought under the four questions, and it shows what the
output of each step is. The procedure is run here on the collapsed-bridge case, so that the
reader can see the four questions at work on a single problem.

    1. State the question and fix the context. Before the four questions can be asked, the
       question the inquiry is asking must be stated, and the context it fixes must be made
       explicit. For the bridge, the question is: why did this bridge collapse? The context fixes
       the scale (the whole bridge, the span between two piers, or a single joint), the time (the
       collapse, or the design, or the maintenance history), and the elements held fixed (the
       load, or the wind, or the concrete). The output of this step is the context; it is what the
       answer to Where? will state.

    2. Identify the fixed elements (What?). Name the entities the explanation holds
       invariant: the deck, the piers, the cables, the load, the wind, the temperature, the
       concrete. The output is the list of fixed elements, and it is assessed by whether the list is
       complete for the question at hand and whether each element is the one the explanation
       actually needs.

    3. Describe the paths of effect (How?). State how the fixed elements bear on one
       another: the path by which the load reaches the piers, the path by which the wind
       reaches the deck, the path by which the temperature reaches the cables. The output is
       the description of the fluid elements and the paths of effect, and it is assessed by whether
       the paths are the ones through which the effect actually travels.

    4. State the governing rule (On what basis?). State the rule or regularity that governs
       the effect: the laws of stress and strain, the codes of design, the regularities of material
       behavior. The output is the governing dynamics, and it is assessed by whether the rule
       supports prediction and counterfactual reasoning.

    5. Make the context explicit (Where?). State the context that the answer to Where?
       supplies: the scale of the analysis, the elements held fixed, and the question the inquiry
       is asking. The output is the contextualization, and it is assessed by whether the stated
       context is the one the question actually fixes.
1.6. What This Chapter Has Done                                                                 9


  6. Check for completeness. For each of the four questions, ask whether the answer sup-
     plies the epistemic output the question requires (identification, description, justification,
     contextualization). If any output is missing, the explanation is incomplete at that stage,
     and the defect is the one stated in the table of Section 1.3.5.




   The procedure is minimal because it does not yet state the criteria of validity and adequacy
that a complete explanation must satisfy; those criteria are developed in Part IV. What the
procedure states is the order in which the four questions are asked, and the output that each
question must supply. A reader who can run the procedure on a case has the four questions in
a usable form; a reader who cannot has the chapter’s first task before them.




Remark 1.10 (The Procedure Is Not Yet a Criterion). The procedure states the order of
the questions and the output of each step; it does not state the criteria by which a complete
answer is judged adequate. The criteria are developed in Part IV, and the present procedure
is the minimal form that the criteria will presuppose. A reader who takes the procedure as a
criterion has read it as more than it is; a reader who takes it as the order of the questions has
read it as it is.




1.6    What This Chapter Has Done


The chapter has done three things. It has distinguished the question of the psychology of
understanding from the question of the structure of explanation. It has stated the four
questions that any explanatory account, on inspection, must answer, and it has stated the
epistemic output that each question must supply. And it has fixed the scope of the inquiry, by
defining explanatory cognition and by stating what the framework does not claim. It has also
stated a minimal procedure by which the four questions can be run on a case.

     The chapter has not done three things, and they are worth naming. It has not argued that
the four questions are necessary; that argument is given in Part II. It has not argued that no
fifth question is needed; that argument is also given in Part II. And it has not developed the
criteria by which a complete answer is judged adequate; those criteria are the work of Part IV.
The present chapter is the foundation on which those parts build.

    The chapter’s contribution is therefore modest but exact. It has stated the observation that
the rest of the book will argue for, it has stated the epistemic output of each question, it has
stated the defect that an incomplete answer produces, and it has fixed the scope within which
the argument is to be assessed. A reader who accepts the observation has the framework’s
starting point; a reader who does not has the place where the argument must be pressed. The
book does not ask for more than the observation at this stage, and it does not claim more
than it has given.

A Question for Reflection
Can you name an explanatory account that fails to answer one of the four questions? What
is it about the account that makes the failure recognizable? Can you name the defect the
failure produces, using the table of Section 1.3.5? And can you name a question about the
same thing that the four questions do not answer—a question about what the thing is for ?
The first three questions test the observation of the present chapter; the fourth marks the
boundary between the structure of explanation and the question of telos, which is stated as an
axiom in Chapter 4. A reader who can answer all four has understood the chapter; a reader
who can answer none has the chapter’s tasks before them.

The next chapter states the method by which the four questions are to be assessed: the removal
test for necessity, the reducibility test for sufficiency, and the fruitfulness of the framework.
The chapter after that states the finitude of the epistemic subject, on which the limits of Part V
depend.

Chapter 2

Method: Removal, Reducibility, and
Fruitfulness

Scope
This chapter states the method by which the framework’s claims are to be assessed. It
introduces three tests—the removal test for necessity, the reducibility test for sufficiency, and
the test of fruitfulness—and it states what each test can and cannot deliver. It does not
yet apply the tests to the four columns; the application is the work of Part II. Its claims
are methodological; where it speaks of “completeness,” “removal,” “reducibility,” “role,” or
“fruitfulness,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this
chapter. Section 2.8 states the formal counterparts of the two tests and refers the reader to
Appendix .15 for the full definitions and proofs.


2.1     A Scene: The Reader Who Asks “How Do You Know?”
Consider a reader who has followed Chapter 1 and is persuaded that any explanatory account,
on inspection, seems to assign four roles: the elements that are related, the medium by which
the relation is carried, the rule that governs the medium, and the frame in which all three are
posed. The reader is persuaded—but not convinced. The reader asks: “How do you know that
these four are the right ones? How do you know that a fifth is not needed? And even if the
four are right, how do you know that the framework you build on them is worth having?”
    The reader’s questions are the questions of method. They are not hostile; they are the
questions any careful reader must ask, and the book would be asking the reader to accept its
claims on authority if it did not answer them. The present chapter is the answer. It states the
method by which the four questions of Chapter 1 are to be assessed, the method by which
the claim that no fifth is needed is to be assessed, and the method by which the framework’s
worth is to be assessed.
    The reader’s questions have a structure, and the structure is worth marking. The first
question—“are the four necessary?”—asks whether the four can be dropped without loss. The
second—“is a fifth needed?”—asks whether the four are enough. The third—“is the framework
worth having?”—asks whether the framework earns its keep. The three questions correspond
to the three tests of the present chapter: the removal test, the reducibility test, and the test
of fruitfulness. The tests are not arbitrary; they are the questions a careful reader must ask,
stated as method.

Remark 2.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the questions
of method at work in a careful reader. It does not prove that the three tests are the right ones;
12                                                                            Chapter 2. Method


it makes the tests intelligible before they are stated. The tests are stated and defended in the
sections that follow, and the scene carries no weight in them.


2.2      The Question of Method
The previous chapter stated four questions that any explanatory account, on inspection, must
answer: what, how, on what basis, and where. The questions were stated as an observation,
not as a principle. The present chapter asks: by what method are the questions to be assessed?
How is the reader to decide whether the four questions are the right ones, and whether no
fifth is needed?
     The question of method is not a preliminary to the inquiry; it is part of the inquiry. A
framework that stated its claims without stating how they are to be assessed would be asking
the reader to accept them on authority. The book does not ask for that. It states its method,
and it invites the reader to apply the method to the claims.
     The method has three parts, and each part answers a different question.


     1. The removal test answers the question: are the four questions necessary? If dropping
        a column leaves a recognizable explanatory failure, the column is necessary.

     2. The reducibility test answers the question: are the four questions sufficient? If every
        candidate fifth column can be reassigned to one of the four without loss, the four are
        sufficient.

     3. The test of fruitfulness answers the question: is the framework worth having? If the
        framework supports the arguments and distinctions of the chapters that follow, and if
        those chapters are clearer for the support, the framework’s fruitfulness is a reason in its
        favor.


    The three parts are stated in this chapter, and applied in Part II. The present chapter
states the method at the strength of a commitment: the method’s presuppositions are declared,
and the reader is invited to assess them alongside the claims they support.

Remark 2.2 (The Three Tests Answer Three Different Questions). The three tests are not
three ways of answering the same question. The removal test asks whether a column can be
dropped; the reducibility test asks whether a column can be added; the test of fruitfulness
asks whether the framework is worth having. The three questions are distinct, and an answer
to one is not an answer to the others. A reader who accepts the removal test has a reason to
accept that the four are necessary; that reader has no reason, from the removal test alone, to
accept that the four are sufficient. The distinction is stated here because the tests are easily
run together, and because the reader who runs them together will misjudge what each test
can deliver.

Remark 2.3 (The Asymmetry of the Three Tests). The three tests are asymmetric, and
the asymmetry is worth stating at the outset. The removal test is destructive: it proceeds
by looking for a failure. The reducibility test is constructive: it proceeds by looking for a
reduction. The test of fruitfulness is integrative: it proceeds by looking for support across the
book. The three are not three versions of one test; they are three different kinds of test, and
the reader who expects them to deliver the same kind of conclusion will be disappointed. The
asymmetry is not a defect; it is what the three questions require.
2.3. The Removal Test for Necessity                                                           13


2.3     The Removal Test for Necessity
2.3.1    The Test Stated
The removal test proceeds by removing each column in turn, and observing what remains. If
what remains is a recognizable explanatory failure, the column is necessary. If what remains is
a complete explanation, the column is not.
    The test is not a definition of “explanation,” and it is not a derivation of the four columns
from a prior principle. It is a test: it takes the four columns as proposed, and it asks whether
an explanation can be complete without one of them.
Definition 2.1 (The Removal Test). A proposed column of explanatory cognition is necessary
if the removal of that column from an otherwise complete explanation leaves an account that
is a recognizable explanatory failure in the sense of Criterion 2.2. The formal counterpart of
the definition is stated in Definition ?? of Appendix .15.
    The definition is stated at the strength of a test, not a proof. The test presupposes that
we can recognize an explanatory failure when we see one. The presupposition is a commitment
of the method, and it is declared as such; the criterion below makes the commitment explicit
and minimal.

2.3.2    The Presupposition of the Test
The removal test presupposes that we can recognize an explanatory failure when we see one.
The presupposition is not proved; it is a commitment of the method. The criterion stated in
the next subsection makes the commitment explicit.
Remark 2.4 (Why the Presupposition Is a Commitment, Not a Proof). The presupposition is
a commitment because the test cannot supply its own criterion of failure. To prove that we can
recognize an explanatory failure, we would need a prior account of what an explanatory failure
is; and that prior account would itself have to be assessed by a method. The removal test is
offered as the method, and its presupposition is declared as a commitment rather than derived.
A reader who denies the presupposition may still follow the argument that the four roles are
what an explanation, on inspection, assigns; what the reader denies is that the inspection has
the force of proof. The framework does not claim more than the inspection delivers.
Remark 2.5 (The Burden of Proof and the Removal Test). The removal test places the
burden of proof in a specific place. A reader who denies that a column is necessary must show
that an explanation can be complete without it. A reader who accepts that the column is
necessary need not show that it is necessary in every conceivable explanation; the reader need
only show that the removal leaves a recognizable failure in the explanations the framework
treats. The burden is on the denier, not on the asserter, and the framework states this so
that the reader knows where the argument must be pressed. A reader who shows that an
explanation can be complete without the column has refuted the test for that column; a reader
who shows that the removal leaves no recognizable failure has done the same. The framework
does not pretend otherwise.
Remark 2.6 (The Removal Test Is Not a Definition). The removal test is not a definition
of “explanation,” and it is not a derivation of the four columns from a prior principle. It is
a test: it takes the four columns as proposed, and it asks whether an explanation can be
complete without one of them. The test presupposes that the four columns have been correctly
identified; if they have not, the test may fail to reveal a column that should have been on
the list. This possibility is the concern of the reducibility test, which is stated in the next
section. The formal counterpart of the test, for the four columns, is stated in Theorem .1 of
Appendix .15.
14                                                                              Chapter 2. Method


2.3.3    A Minimal Criterion of Explanatory Failure
The removal test relies on our ability to recognize an explanatory failure, and the reliability of
the test depends on the clarity of the criterion by which the failure is recognized. The present
subsection states a minimal criterion, at the strength of a commitment. It is minimal because
it does not attempt to say what a complete explanation is; it attempts only to say what makes
an explanation fail in a way that the removal test can register.

Definition 2.2 (A Minimal Criterion of Explanatory Failure). (A) An account A is an
explanatory failure with respect to a question Q if at least one of the following three marks
holds:

(F1) Unanswered question. A leaves a question that Q requires to be answered without an
     answer, and no part of A supplies the missing answer.

(F2) Lost prediction or distinction. A removes a prediction or a distinction that the question
     Q requires, so that two situations that Q must distinguish are no longer distinguished,
     or a consequence that Q must support is no longer supported.

(F3) Incoherence. A asserts two claims that cannot both hold, or asserts a claim that
     contradicts a commitment the explanation is required to preserve.

The three marks are not a definition of “complete explanation.” They are the marks by which
the removal test registers failure. A reader who accepts the criterion can apply the removal
test; a reader who rejects the criterion has rejected the method’s criterion, and the argument
is offered at the strength of the criterion.

    The criterion is (A): it is stipulated. Its justification is that it is the weakest criterion that
suffices for the removal test. A criterion that required more would make the test harder to
apply and would import substantive claims about explanation that the chapter does not need.
A criterion that required less would not distinguish failure from mere incompleteness, and the
removal test would have no criterion to apply.

Remark 2.7 (The Criterion Is Minimal, Not Complete). The criterion is minimal: it states
the marks by which an account fails, not the marks by which an account is complete. The
distinction matters, because the removal test needs only the former. A reader who asks for a
full theory of explanation has asked for more than the removal test requires, and the framework
does not offer the full theory in this chapter. The criterion is the minimal instrument by which
the removal test registers failure; a fuller theory of explanation belongs to a different inquiry,
and the framework does not undertake it here.

Remark 2.8 (The Criterion and the Borderline Cases). The criterion is applied to borderline
cases, and the borderline cases are worth marking. Three cases are borderline, and the criterion
classifies each.
    Borderline case 1: a partial explanation. An account that answers some of Q’s sub-questions
but not all. The criterion classifies the account as a failure under (F1) if the unanswered
sub-question is one that Q requires, and as not a failure if the unanswered sub-question is
one that Q permits to remain open. The distinction is the distinction between a question the
explanation is required to answer and a question it is permitted to leave open; the criterion
applies to the former.
    Borderline case 2: a redescription. An account that restates Q’s content in different words,
without adding a relation, a rule, or a frame. The criterion classifies the account as a failure
under (F2) if the redescription removes a distinction or a prediction that Q requires, and as
not a failure if the redescription preserves both. The distinction is the distinction between a
restatement and a loss; the criterion applies to the latter.
2.3. The Removal Test for Necessity                                                           15


    Borderline case 3: an explanation with a missing role. An account that assigns only three
of the four roles. The criterion classifies the account as a failure under (F1), (F2), or (F3),
depending on which role is missing and why. The removal test’s application, in Chapters 7–11,
states for each role which mark of the criterion the removal produces; the criterion does not
itself fix the mark, and the chapter states the mark as part of the test’s application.

Remark 2.9 (The Criterion Is Applied, Not Proved). The criterion is applied, not proved.
Its application, in the removal test, is the test’s content; its proof is not available, because
the criterion is the method’s commitment. A reader who applies the criterion to a proposed
explanation has applied the method; a reader who shows that the criterion is too strict or too
lax has found a defect in the method, and the method can be revised accordingly.


2.3.4    A Step-by-Step Protocol for the Removal Test
The removal test is stated as a definition; the present subsection states it as a protocol that a
reader can run on a proposed explanation. The protocol has four steps, and each step has a
stated output.

   1. Define the role under test. State, in one sentence, what the role contributes to an
      explanation: the fixed elements identify the entities; the fluid elements carry the effect;
      the governing dynamics state the rule; the context fixes the frame. Output: a statement
      of the role’s contribution, against which the removal will be assessed.

   2. Remove the role experimentally. Take an explanation that assigns all four roles, and
      remove the role under test. The removal is experimental: the reader does not need to find
      a real explanation without the role; the reader needs to consider what the explanation
      would be if the role were absent. Output: a description of the explanation with the role
      removed.

   3. Record the defect. Apply Criterion 2.2 to the explanation with the role removed.
      State which mark, if any, the removal produces: (F1) an unanswered question, (F2) a
      lost prediction or distinction, or (F3) an incoherence. If no mark is produced, the role
      is not necessary by the test. Output: the mark of the defect, or the statement that no
      defect is produced.

   4. Diagnose necessity. If the removal produces a mark of failure, the role is necessary by
      the test, and the diagnosis states what the role contributes that the other three cannot
      supply. If the removal produces no mark, the role is not necessary by the test, and the
      diagnosis states what the other three roles do that makes the role dispensable. Output:
      the diagnosis, stated at the strength of the test.

   The protocol is applied in Chapter 7, where the four roles are removed in turn, and in
Chapters 8–11, where the conveyor principle, non-sequential connectivity, context-dependence,
and the infinity of contexts are examined. The protocol is stated here so that the reader can
run it on a proposed explanation before seeing the application.

Remark 2.10 (The Protocol Is Not a Criterion of Adequacy). The protocol states the order
of the removal test and the output of each step; it does not state the criteria by which a
complete answer is judged adequate. The criteria are developed in Part IV, and the protocol
is the minimal form that the criteria will presuppose. A reader who takes the protocol as a
criterion of adequacy has read it as more than it is; a reader who takes it as the order of the
removal test has read it as it is.
16                                                                           Chapter 2. Method


2.3.5    What the Test Can and Cannot Deliver
The removal test can deliver a conclusion about necessity, at the strength of an argument from
the meaning of “explanation.” It cannot deliver a conclusion about sufficiency; a demonstration
that each of the four is necessary does not show that no fifth is needed. It cannot deliver a
conclusion about the uniqueness of the four; a demonstration that these four are necessary
does not show that no other set of four would be. And it cannot deliver a conclusion about
the nature of what is explained; a demonstration that an explanation must contain the four
roles is not a demonstration that reality contains four kinds of entity.
    The limits are not deficiencies of the test. They are what the test is designed to deliver,
and the framework states them so that the reader knows what kind of conclusion the test
supports. A reader who asks the removal test to deliver a conclusion about sufficiency is asking
the test to do what the reducibility test does; the reader who asks the removal test to deliver
a conclusion about the nature of what is explained is asking the test to do what no epistemic
test can do. The limits are the framework’s honesty about what the test can support.


2.4     The Reducibility Test for Sufficiency
2.4.1    The Test Stated
Sufficiency cannot be proved from the definitions, because a new kind of explanation might
always turn up. It is therefore offered as an estimate and supported by a test.

Definition 2.3 (Reducibility). A candidate fifth column is reducible when its role in explanation
can be reassigned to one of the four columns without loss. The formal counterpart of the
definition is stated in Definition .9 of Appendix .15.

    The test proceeds by examining the standard candidates for a fifth column, and asking,
for each, whether its role can be reassigned. The criterion of loss is the same criterion by
which the removal test registers failure (Criterion 2.2): a role is reassigned without loss if the
resulting account does not exhibit any of the three marks.

Remark 2.11 (The Reducibility Test and the Burden of Proof). The reducibility test places
the burden of proof differently from the removal test. A reader who accepts that a candidate
fifth column is reducible need not show that every possible fifth column is reducible; the reader
need only show that the candidates the framework has examined are reducible. A reader who
denies that the four are sufficient must produce a candidate that resists reduction. The burden
is on the denier, and the framework states this so that the reader knows what would refute the
estimate. The framework does not offer a proof that no such candidate will ever be found; it
offers an estimate, supported by the examination of the candidates that have been proposed,
and it invites the reader to produce a counterexample.


2.4.2    The Standard Candidates
Four candidates have been proposed as a fifth column, and the test examines each in turn.
The first three are the classical candidates; the fourth is added because it is the most serious
challenge to the sufficiency half of the framework. The list of four is the reference list for the
volume: Chapter 7 (Section 7.4) examines the same four candidates, in the same order, and
offers the same reduction for each, so that the reader who has followed the argument of the
present chapter meets the same four candidates there. The two lists must not diverge; if a
later revision adds or removes a candidate, the change is made in both chapters at once.
2.4. The Reducibility Test for Sufficiency                                                        17


Candidate 1: Purpose or goal. A teleological explanation (“the knife is made in order
to cut”) states a rule of the form “the system tends toward state S.” That is a governing
dynamics. The role of purpose in the explanation is the role of a rule that governs the system’s
behavior, and the rule is one of the four columns.

Remark 2.12 (The Analytical Reduction of Purpose). The reduction here is analytical, not
metaphysical. The claim is that the role of purpose in an explanation can be reassigned
to the governing dynamics column without loss of explanatory content. The claim is not
that purposes are unreal, or that the things that have purposes do not really have them. A
teleological explanation is a particular kind of explanation; the framework’s claim is that its
form can be analyzed through the four columns, not that the reality it explains is exhausted
by the analysis. The distinction matters, because the analytical reduction of a role is not the
metaphysical reduction of a reality.


Candidate 2: Time. Temporal order enters an explanation either as a feature of the
dynamics (the rule concerns how states succeed one another) or as part of the frame (the scale
at which the elements are individuated). In either case, it is carried by the third or fourth
column.


Candidate 3: The observer. The standpoint of the cognizer is the content of the context
column: the question asked, the means used, the scale adopted. The observer is not a fifth
column; it is what the fourth column makes explicit.


Candidate 4: The normative dimension. A normative explanation (“the action was
right because it was just”) states what the agent ought to have done, and the “ought” seems to
be a feature of the explanation that is not carried by any of the four columns. The reduction
here is analytical: a normative explanation states a rule of the form “the system ought to tend
toward state S,” and the rule is a governing dynamics. The framework’s claim is that the form
of a normative explanation can be analyzed through the four columns, not that the content
of the norm is exhausted by the analysis. A reader who denies the reduction has a serious
challenge to the sufficiency half of the framework, and the framework invites the challenge.

Remark 2.13 (The Normative Candidate and the Boundary of the Book). The normative
candidate is the most serious challenge to the sufficiency half of the framework, and it is worth
marking why. The framework’s account of the four columns is an account of the form of an
explanation, not of its content; and the normative dimension concerns the content. A reader
who holds that the form of a normative explanation cannot be analyzed through the four
columns has found a candidate that resists reduction. The framework’s response is that the
form can be analyzed, and that the content belongs to a different inquiry (Chapter 4). The
response is stated at exactly that strength: the reader who rejects it has a reason to reject the
sufficiency half of the framework, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.

Remark 2.14 (The List of Four Is the Reference List). The four candidates are the reference
list for the volume, and the list is the same in Chapter 7. The reason for a single reference list
is not convenience but assessability: a reader who checks the reducibility test must be able to
see, in one place, which candidates the test examines. A framework that examined different
candidates in different chapters would leave the reader unable to tell whether the estimate of
sufficiency is supported by the whole examination or only by part of it. The present chapter
states the list; Chapter 7 repeats it; the repetition is deliberate, and the two lists are identical.
18                                                                            Chapter 2. Method


2.4.3    A Precise Criterion of Reducibility
The reducibility test is stated as a definition; the present subsection states the criterion by
which reducibility is recognized, and it distinguishes reducibility from two neighboring notions
that are easily confused with it.

Definition 2.4 (Criterion of Reducibility). (A) A candidate fifth column κ5 is reducible to
one of the four columns κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K} if and only if both of the following conditions hold:

(R1) Substitution. Every explanatory contribution that κ5 makes can be supplied by κ in an
     explanation that assigns the four roles, without adding a new role.

(R2) No loss. The explanation that results from the substitution exhibits none of the marks
     of explanatory failure (Criterion 2.2): no question required by the explanation is left
     unanswered (F1), no prediction or distinction required by the explanation is lost (F2),
     and no incoherence is introduced (F3).

A candidate that satisfies both (R1) and (R2) is reducible. A candidate that fails either
condition resists reduction, and the sufficiency half of the framework is in question for that
candidate.

   The criterion is (A): it is stipulated. Its justification is that it makes the reducibility test
applicable without importing substantive claims about explanation that the chapter does not
need. The two conditions are the minimal conditions under which a role can be reassigned
without loss.

Remark 2.15 (Removal Is Not Amalgamation). The criterion distinguishes two operations
that are easily confused: removal and amalgamation. Removal is the operation the removal
test performs: a role is dropped, and the explanation is assessed for failure. Amalgamation
is the operation the reducibility test performs: a candidate fifth role is absorbed into one of
the four, and the explanation is assessed for loss. The two operations are different, and the
difference matters.
    Removal asks: can the explanation survive without the role? If not, the role is necessary.
Amalgamation asks: can the candidate role be absorbed into an existing role without loss? If
so, the candidate is reducible. A role can be necessary (removal fails) and still be the target of
a reducible candidate (amalgamation succeeds), because the candidate is not the role itself but
a proposed fifth role that overlaps with an existing one. The removal test and the reducibility
test are therefore not two versions of one test; they are two tests that operate on different
objects.

Remark 2.16 (Amalgamation Is Not Elimination). Amalgamation is not elimination. To
say that a candidate role is reducible to an existing role is not to say that the candidate role
is unreal, or that the phenomena it describes do not exist. It is to say that the explanatory
role the candidate plays can be supplied by an existing role without loss. The distinction is
the distinction between the analytical reduction of a role and the metaphysical elimination of
a phenomenon. The framework’s claim is the former, not the latter; the latter belongs to a
different inquiry, and the framework does not undertake it.

Remark 2.17 (The Criterion and the Standard Candidates). The criterion is applied to the
four standard candidates in Section 2.4.2 and in Chapter 7 (Section 7.4). For each candidate,
the application states which of the four columns absorbs the candidate, and why the absorption
satisfies (R1) and (R2). A reader who wishes to challenge the sufficiency half of the framework
must produce a candidate that fails (R1) or (R2); a reader who accepts the criterion and the
applications has the estimate of sufficiency at the strength the method supports.
2.5. Fruitfulness                                                                              19


2.4.4    What the Test Can and Cannot Deliver
The reducibility test can deliver an estimate of sufficiency, at the strength of an examination of
the standard candidates. It cannot deliver a proof of sufficiency; the possibility of a new kind
of explanation cannot be ruled out in advance. It cannot deliver a proof that no candidate
will ever be found; it can deliver a conclusion about the candidates that have been examined,
and it can state what would refute the estimate.

Remark 2.18 (The Risky Claim). The framework makes a risky claim, and says in advance
what would refute it. A candidate fifth column that resists reduction to the four would refute
the sufficiency half of the four-column principle. The framework does not offer a proof that
no such candidate can be found; it offers an estimate, supported by the examination of the
candidates that have been proposed, and it invites the reader to produce a counterexample.
The formal counterpart of the test, for the standard candidates, is stated in Theorem .2 of
Appendix .15.


2.5     Fruitfulness
The third part of the method is not a test of necessity or of sufficiency; it is a test of whether
the framework is worth having. The test is stated here in the sense in which the book uses it,
and the sense is the one developed in Chapter 23.

Definition 2.5 (Fruitfulness). (A) A framework is fruitful to the extent that (i) it generates
distinctions that the book’s arguments require and that are not available without it, and (ii)
it makes possible the continuation of reconstruction—that is, it allows the book’s inquiries
to proceed to further questions without the framework collapsing or requiring replacement.
Fruitfulness in this sense does not include predictive success or practical success; those are
different measures, and the book does not use them as its criterion of fruitfulness.

    The definition is aligned with Chapter 23, where fruitfulness is distinguished from predictive
success and from practical success. The distinction matters, because a framework can be
fruitful in the book’s sense and still fail to predict, and a framework can predict successfully
and still be unfruitful in the book’s sense. The book’s claim is that its framework is fruitful in
the sense of Definition 2.5; it does not claim that the framework is predictively or practically
successful.

Remark 2.19 (Fruitfulness Is Not Predictive Success). Predictive success is the capacity of a
framework to generate predictions that are confirmed by observation. The book’s framework
does not make predictions in this sense, and it does not claim predictive success. Fruitfulness,
in the book’s sense, is the generation of distinctions and the continuation of reconstruction. A
reader who asks the framework to predict has asked for a different measure, and the framework
does not offer it.

Remark 2.20 (Fruitfulness Is Not Practical Success). Practical success is the capacity of
a framework to guide action toward a desired outcome. The book’s framework is not a
practical guide, and it does not claim practical success. Fruitfulness, in the book’s sense, is
the generation of distinctions and the continuation of reconstruction. A reader who asks the
framework to guide action has asked for a different measure, and the framework does not offer
it.

Remark 2.21 (Fruitfulness and the Audit of Chapter 43). The test of fruitfulness is retro-
spective: it is applied at the end of the book, when the reader can see whether the framework
has generated the distinctions the book needed and has allowed the reconstruction to continue.
The audit of Chapter 43 is the place where the test is applied. The audit states the framework’s
20                                                                          Chapter 2. Method


core commitments and their dependencies, and it states what would be lost if a commitment is
rejected. The reader who finds that the framework has generated the distinctions and allowed
the reconstruction to continue has found the framework fruitful; the reader who finds that it
has not has found a place where the framework needs revision. The audit is the framework’s
way of applying the test of fruitfulness to itself.


2.6      The Status of the Method
The method’s three parts have different statuses, and the difference is worth stating.

     1. The removal test is (T) relative to the commitment that we can recognize an explanatory
        failure. Its conclusion—that a column is necessary—is argued, given the commitment
        and the criterion of failure (Criterion 2.2).

     2. The reducibility test is (E). Its conclusion—that the four are sufficient—is offered as
        an estimate, supported by the examination of the standard candidates, and subject to
        revision if a candidate that resists reduction is found.

     3. The test of fruitfulness is a reason, not an argument. Its conclusion—that the
        framework is worth having—is offered as a consideration, not as a proof.

    The three statuses are stated so that the reader knows what kind of claim each part of the
method supports. A reader who accepts the removal test has a reason to accept the necessity
of the four; a reader who accepts the reducibility test has an estimate, not a proof, of their
sufficiency; a reader who accepts the test of fruitfulness has a reason to take the framework
seriously, not a proof that it is correct.

Remark 2.22 (Why the Method Is Not a Proof from Nothing). The removal test presupposes
that we can recognize an explanatory failure when we see one, and the criterion of failure
(Criterion 2.2) makes the presupposition explicit. The reducibility test presupposes that we
can recognize when a role has been reassigned without loss, and the criterion of reducibility
(Criterion 2.4) makes the presupposition explicit. Neither presupposition is itself proved. They
are commitments of the method, and they are declared as such. The method does not promise
certainty; it promises a discipline on the claims the book makes.

Remark 2.23 (The Method and the Epistemic Labels). The three statuses are the epistemic
labels introduced in the front matter, applied to the method. The removal test’s conclusion is
(T) relative to the commitment that we can recognize an explanatory failure, and relative to
the criterion of failure. The reducibility test’s conclusion is (E), because the possibility of a
new kind of explanation cannot be ruled out in advance. The test of fruitfulness’s conclusion
is (A) stipulated, because the test is the framework’s own statement of what it counts as
fruitfulness. The labels are the vocabulary in which the method’s conclusions are stated,
and the reader who wishes to see the labels in their full statement is directed to the note on
epistemic status labels that precedes Part I.


2.7      The Method and the Book
The method is applied in Part II, where the four columns are stated and argued. It is applied
again in Part IV, where the conditions of epistemic validity are stated and argued. It is applied
throughout the book, in the sense that every chapter states its claims at a declared strength
and invites the criticism appropriate to that strength.
   The method is not applied in a single chapter, once and for all. It is applied where the
framework states a principle, and it is stated here so that the reader knows, from the outset,
2.8. A Formal Sketch of the Two Tests                                                           21


what kind of argument the book offers. The method is the book’s way of being honest about
its claims, and it is the reader’s way of knowing what kind of criticism is appropriate at each
point. The formal counterpart of the method, for the two tests that admit a formal statement,
is given in Section 2.8 and in Appendix .15; the test of fruitfulness has no formal counterpart,
because it is an integrative assessment and not a formal test.
Remark 2.24 (The Method and the Conditional Architecture). The method is the vocabulary
of the framework’s conditional architecture (Chapter 43). The framework is a conditional
architecture on a core of ten epistemic commitments; every other claim of the framework is a
definition, a consequence, an estimate, a proposal, an open question, or a speculation. The
method states what kind of claim each part of the framework makes, and the labels state the
kind of criticism each claim invites. The two are complementary: the method states how the
claims are to be assessed; the labels state what kind of claim each is. The reader who has
followed the method has the vocabulary in which the framework’s conditional architecture is
stated.


2.8     A Formal Sketch of the Two Tests
The removal test and the reducibility test are stated in philosophical prose in Sections 2.3–2.4,
and they are applied to the four columns in Chapter 7. The present section states the formal
counterparts of the two tests, at the level of detail that the philosophical reader requires, and
it refers the reader to Appendix .15 for the full formal system and the proofs.
    The formal language was introduced in Chapter 6 (Section 6.9), and it is stated in full
in Appendix .15. It has four principal sorts (elements, rules, contexts, and explanations)
and four auxiliary sorts (states, subjects, acts, and times), four role predicates (for the fixed
elements, the fluid elements, the governing dynamics, and the context), a primitive predicate
of completeness, and a family of definitions and axioms. The present section uses the language
to state the formal counterparts of the two tests.

The formal counterpart of the removal test. The removal test is stated as a definition
of necessity. For a role κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K}:
        Necessary(κ) :≡ ∀x : StructuralComplete(x) ∧ Has(x, κ) → ¬Complete(x \ κ),
where StructuralComplete(x) is the condition that all four roles are assigned and the roles are
coherent with one another, Complete(x \ κ) is the primitive completeness predicate applied to
the explanation with the role κ removed, and x \ κ is the operation of removing the role κ
from the explanation x. The definition is the formal counterpart of Definition 2.1; the prose
version states the test in terms of “a recognizable explanatory failure,” and the formal version
states the test in terms of the primitive completeness predicate. The formal definition is stated
in full in Definition ?? of Appendix .15; the proof that the four roles satisfy the definition is
stated in Theorem .1 of the same appendix.

The formal counterpart of the reducibility test. The reducibility test is stated as a
definition of reducibility. For a candidate role κ5 ∈
                                                    / {F, Φ, D, K}:
               Reducible(κ5 ) :≡ ∃κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K} : RoleSet(κ5 ) ⊆ RoleSet(κ),
where RoleSet(κ) is the set of explanatory roles that the role κ plays. The definition is the
formal counterpart of Definition 2.3 and Criterion 2.4; the prose version states the test in terms
of “reassignment without loss,” and the formal version states the test in terms of the subset
relation among role sets. The formal definition is stated in full in Definition .9 of Appendix .15;
the proof that the standard candidates satisfy the definition is stated in Theorem .2 of the
same appendix.
22                                                                           Chapter 2. Method


Remark 2.25 (The Formal Statement and the Prose Statement). The formal statement and
the prose statement are not rivals. The prose statement is the substance, and the formal
statement is its precise form. The reader who is content with the prose statement has the
two tests, their presuppositions, and their limits; the reader who wishes to see the tests in a
precise form has the formal statement. The two are the same tests, stated at two levels of
detail; the formal statement does not replace the prose statement, and the prose statement
does not make the formal statement unnecessary.




Remark 2.26 (The Formal Statement and the Reader). The formal statement is offered for
the reader who wishes to see the two tests in a precise form, and for the reader who wishes to
assess the framework at the level of its formal structure. It is not offered as a requirement: the
philosophical reader who is content with the prose of Sections 2.3–2.4 has the tests and their
limits, and does not need the formal statement. The formal statement is a supplement, not a
substitute; it is the framework’s way of being assessable at the level of its formal structure,
and it is offered at the strength that a supplement can have.




Remark 2.27 (The Test of Fruitfulness Has No Formal Counterpart). The test of fruitfulness
has no formal counterpart, and the absence is worth marking. The test is an integrative
assessment of the framework as a whole; it asks whether the framework, taken together,
generates the distinctions the book requires and allows the reconstruction to continue. The
assessment is not a formal derivation from axioms, and it does not admit of a formal statement.
The test of fruitfulness is the framework’s way of being assessed as a whole, and it is offered
at the strength that an integrative assessment can have.

A Question for Reflection
Can you construct an explanation that you would accept as complete and that does not assign
one of the four roles? If so, the reducibility test has failed for that case, and the sufficiency
half of the four-column principle is in question. If not, what is it about the explanation that
makes the missing role unrecognizable as missing—and which mark of Criterion 2.2 registers
the failure? And consider the fourth candidate—the normative dimension: does a normative
explanation state a rule of the form “the system ought to tend toward state S,” and if so, is
24                                                                          Chapter 2. Method


the rule a governing dynamics? The first question tests the reducibility test; the second tests
the criterion of failure; the third tests the sufficiency half of the framework. A reader who can
answer all three has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s
three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the finitude of the epistemic subject, on which the limits of Part V
depend. The chapter after that states the boundary between structure and telos, and the
autonomy of epistemic justification. The formal reconstruction of the two tests, with their
definitions and the proofs that apply them to the four columns, is given in Appendix .15.
                                                                                               25




Chapter 3

Finitude of the Epistemic Subject

Scope
This chapter states the finitude of the epistemic subject as an axiom of the framework. It
gives the principle, states why it is adopted rather than proved, names the parts of the book
in which it does load-bearing work, and states what a denial of the principle would require. Its
claim is epistemic, not ontological: it is a claim about what any cognizing subject we know of
can do, not about what kinds of being there are. The chapter’s silence on questions of value or
of ontology is not a denial of their reality; it is the recognition that the epistemic description
is not the whole of what can be said. A section (Section 3.8) states the formal counterpart of
the principle and refers the reader to Appendix .15 for the full statement.


3.1     A Scene: The Reader in the Library
Consider a scholar in a library at the end of a working day. She has read for ten hours. She has
followed a question through a dozen books, and each book has opened a further question. She
has taken notes; the notes fill a folder. She has formed a hypothesis; the hypothesis explains
some of what she has read, and leaves some of it unexplained. She knows that there are books
in the library she has not opened, and that the books she has opened refer to books the library
does not hold. She knows that tomorrow she will read more, and that the day after she will
read more still. She knows that she will not, in her lifetime, read everything, and she knows
that even if she did, the reading would raise questions the reading could not answer.
    The scholar’s situation is not a failure. It is not a sign that she has been careless, or that
she has chosen the wrong question, or that the library is inadequate. It is the condition under
which her inquiry is possible. She knows what she knows because she has been able to hold
some things fixed while she examined others; she has formed a hypothesis because she has
been able to gather some manifestations and compare them; she has a folder of notes because
she has been able to write some things down and leave others for later. Her knowledge is real,
and it is partial, and the partiality is not a defect of the knowledge. It is what knowledge is,
for a subject like her.
    The scene poses a question. What kind of subject is the scholar? The answer the framework
gives is: a finite subject. The scholar occupies finitely many cognitive contexts at a time; she
completes finitely many acts of reconstruction in a finite span. Her finitude is the condition
under which her inquiry is possible, not a limit on what inquiry can reach. The present chapter
states the principle, states why it is adopted, and names the parts of the book in which it does
its work.

Remark 3.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows finitude at
work in a familiar case. It does not prove that every cognizing subject is finite; it makes the
26                                                Chapter 3. Finitude of the Epistemic Subject


principle intelligible before it is stated. The principle is stated and defended in the sections
that follow, and the scene carries no weight in them.


3.2     The Question
The previous two chapters have stated the four questions of explanatory cognition and the
method by which the framework’s claims are to be assessed. The present chapter introduces a
premise that the framework needs before it can proceed: a premise about the subject who
asks the questions and applies the method.
    The premise is not a principle of the four-column framework. The four questions are
questions about what an explanation must contain; the premise is a claim about the explainer.
The two are different, and the distinction is worth marking. A framework could state the four
questions correctly and be wrong about the subject who asks them; a framework could be
right about the subject and wrong about the questions. The present chapter is about the
subject, and its claim is offered as an axiom.
    The question the chapter answers is: what kind of subject is the cognizing subject? The
framework’s answer is that the cognizing subject is finite. The answer is not derived from the
four questions, and it is not derived from the method. It is adopted, and its cost is stated.
Remark 3.2 (Why the Premise Is Needed Before the Framework Can Proceed). The frame-
work’s claims about the limits of cognition (Part V) and about the conditions of epistemic
validity (Part IV) are claims about what a subject can and cannot do. The claims presuppose
a subject; the present chapter states what kind of subject the framework’s claims are about.
Without the premise, the framework’s claims about limits would have no subject to be about;
with the premise, the claims are stated at exactly the strength they can support. The premise
is therefore not a preliminary; it is a condition of the framework’s claims being assessable at
all.


3.3     The Principle of Finitude
Principle 3.1 (Finitude of the Epistemic Subject). Every cognizing subject is finite: at any
time it occupies finitely many cognitive contexts, in any finite span of inquiry it completes
only finitely many acts of reconstruction, it has finitely many resources available to it, and
it surveys only a finite span of time. The formal counterpart of the principle is stated in
Definition .11 of Appendix .15.
    The principle has four bounds, and all four are needed. The first two are the bounds stated
in the earlier form of the principle; the second two make the bounds exact.

Bound 1: finitely many contexts at a time. A cognitive context is a frame in which
an explanation is posed—the question asked, the scale adopted, the elements held fixed, the
rule applied. The principle says that at any time a subject occupies finitely many such frames.
The subject may move among frames, may adopt one after another, may combine them; but
at any one time the subject stands in finitely many. The claim is not that the subject cannot
occupy a new frame; it is that the number of frames occupied at a time is finite.

Bound 2: finitely many acts of reconstruction in a finite span. A reconstruction is
the act by which a subject forms a pseudo-identity of an identity from its manifestations—the
act described in Chapter 12 and developed in Chapter 23. The principle says that in any finite
span of inquiry, the subject completes only finitely many such acts. The subject may continue
indefinitely, may refine an act indefinitely, may return to an act and revise it; but in any finite
span, the number of completed acts is finite.
3.3. The Principle of Finitude                                                                   27


Bound 3: finitely many resources. The subject has finitely many resources available to
it: finite time, finite attention, finite memory, finite computational capacity, finite access to
evidence. The principle says that the resources available to the subject at any time are finite.
The bound is not a claim that the subject cannot acquire more resources; it is a claim that
at any time the resources available are finite, and that the inquiry is conducted under that
condition.

Bound 4: a finite span of time. The subject surveys only a finite span of time. Its inquiry
begins at some time and ends at some time; its reconstructions occur within that span; its
resources are spent within that span. The principle says that the span is finite. The bound is
not a claim that the subject cannot continue after the span; it is a claim that the span within
which the inquiry is conducted is finite, and that the inquiry’s conclusions are offered within
that span.
    The four bounds are not four versions of one bound, and none entails the others. A subject
could occupy finitely many contexts and still have infinite resources (if the resources were not
consumed by the contexts); a subject could complete finitely many reconstructions and still
survey an infinite span (if the reconstructions were not distributed across the span); a subject
could have finite resources and still occupy infinitely many contexts (if the contexts were not
frames of inquiry). The principle states all four, and all four are used in the arguments that
follow.
Remark 3.3 (The Four Bounds Are Not Redundant). The four bounds are not four ways of
saying the same thing. The first bound concerns the subject’s synchronous situation—how
many contexts it occupies at a moment. The second concerns the subject’s diachronic situation—
how many reconstructions it completes in a span. The third concerns the subject’s material
situation—what resources it has. The fourth concerns the subject’s temporal situation—what
span it surveys. A subject could be finite in one bound and infinite in another; the framework
needs all four because its arguments use all four: the impossibility of super-identity uses the
first and second bounds (the subject occupies finitely many contexts and completes finitely
many reconstructions, so it cannot survey the non-finitely many contexts); the account of
reconstruction uses the second and third (the subject completes finitely many reconstructions
with finitely many resources, so its pseudo-identity is always partial); the account of the
limits of self-knowledge uses the fourth (the subject surveys only a finite span of time, so its
self-knowledge is bounded by the span). A reader who accepts only one bound has accepted
only part of the premise; the framework states all four so that the reader knows what the
arguments depend on. The formal counterparts of the four bounds are stated in Definition .11
of Appendix .15.
Remark 3.4 (Finitude Is a Claim About the Subject, Not About the Object). The principle
says that the subject is finite. It does not say that the object of inquiry is finite, that the
identity is finite, or that the manifestations are finitely many. The distinction is the distinction
between the order of inquiry and the order of being, and it is observed throughout the book. A
reader who takes the principle as a claim about the object has misread it; a reader who takes it
as a claim about the subject has read it correctly. The distinction is the same distinction that
Chapter 5 states between the cognitive and the ontological architecture; the present chapter
states it in its specific application to the subject.
Remark 3.5 (Finitude Is a Claim About the Subject We Know Of). The principle is stated
at the strength of what the framework knows. It says that every cognizing subject we know
of is finite. It does not say that no infinite subject is possible; it says that the framework
offers no account of such a subject, and that its arguments are about finite subjects. The
distinction matters, because the framework’s claims about the limits of cognition are claims
about finite subjects, not claims about the limits of what is. The framework’s silence on the
28                                                Chapter 3. Finitude of the Epistemic Subject


infinite subject is not a denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the framework’s
method is the method of finite inquiry, and that the limits of finite inquiry are not the limits of
what is. The formal statement of the principle is restricted to finite subjects, in Definition .11;
the formal system contains no axiom that asserts the existence of an infinite subject, and it
does not deny that one might exist.


3.4     Why Finitude Is an Axiom
The principle is (A): it is adopted as an axiom, not proved. The justification is stated, and
the cost of adopting it is stated with it.
     The justification is that every cognizing subject we know of—a person, an institution,
a tradition—is bounded in what it can survey. A person occupies finitely many contexts
at a time, completes finitely many acts of reconstruction in a finite span, has finitely many
resources, and surveys a finite span of time. An institution occupies finitely many contexts,
its inquiries are bounded by its resources, and its conclusions are offered within a finite span.
A tradition occupies finitely many contexts, its reconstructions are bounded by what it has
received, and its span is finite. The framework does not know of a subject that is not bounded
in these ways.
     The principle is not proved from these observations; the observations are the support
of an axiom, not a derivation of it. To prove the principle, the framework would need a
demonstration that no infinite subject is possible, and it does not have one. It adopts the
principle because its denial would require an argument the framework does not have, and
because the principle is supported by every case the framework knows of.

Remark 3.6 (Why the Principle Is Not Derived from the Four Questions). The principle is
not derived from the four questions of Chapter 1, and the reader should not expect it to be.
The four questions are about what an explanation must contain; the principle is about the
subject who gives the explanation. A framework could state the four questions correctly and
be wrong about the subject; a framework could be right about the subject and wrong about
the questions. The two are independent claims, and the framework states them independently.
The principle is adopted because it is needed for the arguments of Parts IV and V, and because
its denial would require an argument the framework does not have. It is not adopted because
it follows from the four questions; it is adopted because the framework needs it, and because
the framework can support it at the strength it is adopted.

Remark 3.7 (What a Denial of Finitude Would Require). A critic who denies finitude must
say what an unbounded subject would be. The framework offers no account of such a subject,
and it does not claim that one is impossible. The critic who offers such an account has a reason
to reject the principle; the framework does not pretend otherwise. The framework’s claim is
that its arguments are about finite subjects, and that the arguments are stated at that strength.
A reader who has an account of an infinite subject—a divine intellect, a computational oracle,
a tradition that has received all things—has a reason to reject the principle, and the framework
invites the reader to produce the account.

Remark 3.8 (The Cost of the Axiom). The cost of the axiom is that the framework’s claims
about the limits of cognition are claims about finite subjects, not claims about what is. The
cost is not a defect of the principle; it is what the principle makes possible, and it is stated so
that the reader knows what kind of claim the framework’s limits are. The framework does not
claim that nothing can know what the finite subject cannot know; it claims that the finite
subject cannot know it, and that the framework’s arguments are about the finite subject. The
cost is the price of the precision; the precision is the framework’s gain.
3.5. The Uses of the Principle                                                                 29


3.5     The Uses of the Principle
The principle does load-bearing work in two parts of the book, and its uses are named here so
that the reader knows where the principle is going.

Part IV: Conditions of epistemic validity and adequacy. The principle is used in the
account of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity. A pseudo-identity is the subject’s approximation
of an identity, formed from the available manifestations. The principle explains why the
approximation is always partial: the subject completes finitely many acts of reconstruction,
has finitely many resources, and the manifestations available are finitely many. The adequacy
of a pseudo-identity is assessed against the criteria stated in Part IV, and the principle is one
of the premises of that assessment.

Part V: Limits, errors, and unknownness. The principle is used in the argument for
the impossibility of super-identity, in the account of the limits of self-knowledge, and in the
account of intrinsic and temporary unknownness. The impossibility argument combines the
principle with the infinity of cognitive contexts (stated in Chapter 11) and with the premise
that manifestation is a product of identity and receiving context (stated in Chapter 13). The
argument is given in Chapter 27. The account of the limits of self-knowledge is given in
Chapter 30; the account of intrinsic and temporary unknownness is given in Chapter 32.
