consequences has accepted the principle in its practical form; the subject who ignores them
has not.
Remark 3.9 (The Table and the Limits of Part V). The table’s third row is the practical
counterpart of the limits stated in Part V. The intrinsic unknownness of Chapter 32 is the
structural unknownness that the subject cannot eliminate, no matter how many resources
it has; the temporary unknownness is the unknownness that the subject could in principle
eliminate, given more resources. The distinction is the practical form of the principle: the
subject’s finitude means that some unknownness is temporary (given more resources, it could
be removed) and some is intrinsic (no amount of resources would remove it). The table states
the consequence at the strength the principle supports; the reader who wishes to see the
argument is directed to Chapter 32.
Remark 3.10 (The Uses Are Named, Not Yet Made). The principle is stated here, and its
uses are named. The arguments that use it are given in their own places, and the reader who
wishes to see the principle at work is directed to those places. The present chapter states
the principle, its cost, and its practical consequences; it does not yet give the arguments that
depend on it. The reader who wishes to see the principle in action is invited to return to it
after reading Parts IV and V; the reader who wishes to assess the principle on its own terms
has it here.
Remark 3.11 (The Principle Is Not Used in Part II). The principle is not used in Part II,
where the four columns are stated and argued. The four-column principle is a claim about
what an explanation must contain; it is not a claim about the subject, and it does not depend
on the finitude of the subject. A reader who rejects the principle of finitude can still accept
the four-column framework; the two are separable, and the dependency map at the end of
Part VI states which conclusions depend on which.
Remark 3.12 (The Principle Is Not Used in Part III). The principle is not used in Part III
either, where the structure of epistemic relations is developed. Part III’s claims about identity,
manifestation, and epistemic light are claims about the structure of the relation, not about
the subject who stands in the relation. The principle becomes load-bearing in Part IV, where
the conditions of validity are stated for a finite subject, and in Part V, where the limits of
finite cognition are stated. The reader who is interested in the structure of the relation can
read Part III without the principle; the reader who is interested in the limits of the subject
will find the principle at work in Parts IV and V.


3.6     The Four Bounds of the Principle and the Method
The four bounds of the principle correspond to parts of the method stated in the previous
chapter.
     The first bound—finitely many contexts at a time—corresponds to the removal test and the
reducibility test. The tests proceed by examining the standard candidates for a fifth column;
the examination is a survey of the candidates, and the survey is finite because the subject
is finite. The principle explains why the survey is an estimate rather than a proof: a finite
subject cannot rule out a candidate it has not surveyed.
     The second bound—finitely many acts of reconstruction—corresponds to the test of
fruitfulness. The framework’s fruitfulness is assessed by the chapters that follow; the assessment
is a series of reconstructions, and the series is finite because the subject is finite. The principle
explains why the fruitfulness is a reason rather than a proof: a finite subject cannot complete
the survey of the framework’s consequences.
     The third bound—finitely many resources—corresponds to the selection of evidence. The
tests are conducted with the resources available; the selection of candidates is bounded by the
resources; the estimate is offered at the strength the resources support.
3.7. Limits of the Argument                                                                   31


    The fourth bound—a finite span of time—corresponds to the retrospective application
of the tests. The audit of Chapter 43 is conducted within a finite span; the retrospective
assessment of fruitfulness is bounded by the span; the reasons offered are the reasons available
within the span.
    The correspondence is not a coincidence. The method is the method of a finite subject,
and the principle states what finitude means. The method and the principle are the same
claim, stated in two vocabularies.
Remark 3.13 (The Method and the Principle Are Not Independent). The method and the
principle are not independent claims; they are the same claim, stated in two vocabularies.
The method states the tests by which the framework’s claims are to be assessed; the principle
states the subject’s condition under which the tests yield the conclusions they yield. If the
subject were not finite, the tests could yield conclusions of a different kind—proofs rather
than estimates, reasons rather than arguments. The method’s statuses (T, E, reason) are
the method’s statuses for a finite subject; the principle states what the finitude means. The
reader who accepts the method has accepted the principle in its methodological vocabulary;
the reader who accepts the principle has accepted the method in its subject-side vocabulary.
The two are not rivals; they are the same claim, stated from two angles. The formal statement
of the principle, in Section 3.8, makes the correspondence precise.


3.7    Limits of the Argument
Two limits of the argument must be stated.
    First, the principle is (A), not (T). It is adopted, not proved. A reader who denies it has
a reason to reject the conclusions that depend on it, and the dependency map at the end of
Part VI states which conclusions those are. The framework does not claim that the principle
is certain; it claims that the principle is the one the framework adopts, and that its adoption
is supported by every case the framework knows of.
    Second, the principle is about the subject, not about the object. It does not say that the
identity is finite, that the manifestations are finitely many, or that the contexts are finitely
many. The infinity of cognitive contexts is argued in Chapter 11, on independent grounds, and
the two claims are compatible: the subject is finite, and the contexts are not finitely many.
The combination is what makes super-identity impossible, and the combination is stated in
Chapter 27.
Remark 3.14 (The Two Limits Are Not Defects). The two limits are not defects of the
argument; they are the conditions under which the argument is offered. The first limit states
the status of the principle (A); the second states the scope of the principle (the subject, not
the object). The framework states both so that the reader knows what kind of claim the
principle is, and what kind of claim it is not. A reader who accepts the limits has accepted the
principle at the strength the framework states it; a reader who rejects the limits has rejected
the principle, and the framework invites the rejection.


3.8    A Formal Statement of the Principle of Finitude
The principle of finitude is stated in philosophical prose in Section 3.3, and its uses are named
in Section 3.5. The present section states the formal counterpart of the principle, at the level
of detail that the philosophical reader requires, and it refers the reader to Appendix .15 for
the full statement.
    The formal language was introduced in Chapter 6 (Section 6.9), and it is stated in full
in Appendix .15. It has four sorts (elements, rules, contexts, and explanations), four role
predicates (for the fixed elements, the fluid elements, the governing dynamics, and the context),
32                                                   Chapter 3. Finitude of the Epistemic Subject


a primitive predicate of completeness, and a family of definitions and axioms. The present
section uses the language to state the formal counterpart of the principle of finitude.
    The formal counterpart is a single definition, stated in Definition .11 of Appendix .15. The
definition has four clauses, one for each of the four bounds stated in Section 3.3.

The formal counterpart of Bound 1 (finitely many contexts). The first clause uses a
predicate Occupies(s, c, t), read: the subject s occupies the context c at the time t. The clause
states that, for every subject s and every time t, the set of contexts occupied by s at t is finite:

                                ∀s, t : |{c : Occupies(s, c, t)}| < ∞.

This is the formal counterpart of Bound 1. It is stated in the first clause of Definition .11.

The formal counterpart of Bound 2 (finitely many acts of reconstruction). The
second clause uses a predicate Completes(s, a, t), read: the subject s completes the act of
reconstruction a at the time t. The clause states that, for every subject s and every finite
interval of time [t1 , t2 ], the set of acts completed by s in the interval is finite:

                  ∀s, t1 , t2 : |{a : Completes(s, a, t) for some t ∈ [t1 , t2 ]}| < ∞.

This is the formal counterpart of Bound 2. It is stated in the second clause of Definition .11.

The formal counterpart of Bound 3 (finitely many resources). The third clause uses
a predicate Available(s, r, t), read: the resource r is available to the subject s at the time t.
The clause states that, for every subject s and every time t, the set of resources available to s
at t is finite:
                                ∀s, t : |{r : Available(s, r, t)}| < ∞.
This is the formal counterpart of Bound 3. It is stated in the third clause of Definition .11.

The formal counterpart of Bound 4 (a finite span of time). The fourth clause uses
the predicate Surveys(s, t1 , t2 ), read: the subject s surveys the span of time from t1 to t2 . The
clause states that, for every subject s, if s surveys [t1 , t2 ], then the span is finite:

                           ∀s, t1 , t2 : Surveys(s, t1 , t2 ) → |t2 − t1 | < ∞.

This is the formal counterpart of Bound 4. It is stated in the fourth clause of Definition .11.

The formal statement of the whole principle. The four clauses together are the formal
counterpart of the principle of finitude. The principle is stated as a single definition with
four clauses in Definition .11 of Appendix .15. The definition is restricted to finite subjects:
the formal system contains no axiom that asserts the existence of an infinite subject, and it
contains no axiom that denies the possibility of one.

The formal statement and the four bounds. The formal statement makes the relationship
between the four bounds precise. The first clause is a condition on the synchronous situation of
the subject; the second is a condition on its diachronic situation; the third is a condition on its
material situation; the fourth is a condition on its temporal situation. The four conditions are
independent: none entails the others, as the prose of Section 3.3 says. The formal statement
does not merge them into a single condition; it states them separately, exactly as the prose
does.
3.8. A Formal Statement of the Principle of Finitude                                              33


Remark 3.15 (The Formal Statement and the Prose Statement). The formal statement and
the prose statement are not rivals. The prose statement is the substance, and the formal
statement is its precise form. The reader who is content with the prose statement has the
principle, its justification, its cost, and its uses; the reader who wishes to see the principle in a
precise form has the formal statement. The two are the same principle, stated at two levels of
detail; the formal statement does not replace the prose statement, and the prose statement
does not make the formal statement unnecessary.




Remark 3.16 (The Formal Statement and the Reader). The formal statement is offered for
the reader who wishes to see the principle of finitude in a precise form, and for the reader
who wishes to assess the framework at the level of its formal structure. It is not offered as a
requirement: the philosophical reader who is content with the prose of Sections 3.3–3.5 has the
principle, its justification, and its uses, and does not need the formal statement. The formal
statement is a supplement, not a substitute; it is the framework’s way of being assessable at
the level of its formal structure, and it is offered at the strength that a supplement can have.




Remark 3.17 (The Formal Statement and the Infinity of Contexts). The formal statement of
the principle of finitude is compatible with the formal statement of the infinity of cognitive
contexts (Chapter 11). The first says that the subject occupies finitely many contexts at a
time; the second says that the contexts in which an identity can be cognized are not finite
in number. The two are compatible: the subject is finite, and the contexts are not. The
combination is what makes super-identity impossible (Chapter 27), and the formal statement
of the combination is given in Appendix .15, together with the formal statement of the principle
of finitude.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a subject you know well—a person, an institution, a tradition. What does it mean
to say that the subject is finite? Is the finitude a limit on what the subject can know, or is it
the condition under which the subject knows at all? Which of the four bounds—the bound on
contexts, the bound on acts, the bound on resources, the bound on the span of time—is most
visible in the subject’s situation? What does your answer tell you about the relation between
finitude and the possibility of knowledge?
    And consider the scholar in the library: her knowledge is real and partial; she knows some
things and not others. Is her partiality a defect of her knowledge, or is it what makes her
knowledge the kind of knowledge it is? If the former, what would non-partial knowledge
look like? If the latter, what does that tell you about the relation between finitude and the
possibility of knowledge? A reader who can answer both questions has understood the chapter;
a reader who can answer neither has the chapter’s two tasks before them.

architecture, on which the epistemology-only scope of this volume depends. The formal statement
of the principle of finitude, with its four bounds and its compatibility with the infinity of contexts,
is given in Appendix .15.

Chapter 4

Structure, Not Telos

Scope
This chapter states two axioms on which the book’s method depends: that epistemology
describes structure, not telos; and that epistemic justification is autonomous with respect to
other domains. It gives the two principles, states why they are adopted rather than proved,
draws the consequences for the book’s method, and marks the boundary that they set. Its
claims are epistemic and meta-epistemic; where it speaks of “structure,” “telos,” “justification,”
“autonomy,” or “boundary,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions
in this chapter. The chapter’s silence on questions of value, of ontology, and of theology is not
a denial of their reality; it is the recognition that the epistemic description is not the whole of
what can be said.


4.1     A Scene: The Reader Who Asks “What Is It For?”
Consider a reader who has followed the first three chapters. The reader has understood the
four questions of explanatory cognition, has seen the method by which the framework’s claims
are to be assessed, and has accepted the finitude of the epistemic subject. The reader is
persuaded that the framework is doing something real. And then the reader asks a question
that the framework has not yet answered: “But what is cognition for ? What is the purpose of
understanding? Why does any of this matter?”
    The reader’s question is not hostile. It is the question any thoughtful reader must ask, and
the book would be evading it if it did not respond. The present chapter is the response. It
says: the question is real, and the framework does not answer it. The framework describes
the structure of explanatory cognition—what any complete explanation must contain, how its
elements are related, what makes a relation legible, what the limits of finite cognition are. It
does not, and by its method cannot, establish the end, purpose, or good for which cognition
exists.
    The reader’s question has two parts, and the chapter treats them separately. The first
part—“what is cognition for?”—is the question of telos, and the chapter’s first principle states
that the framework does not answer it. The second part—“why should I accept what the
framework says?”—is the question of justification, and the chapter’s second principle states
that the framework’s justification is internal to epistemology, not drawn from another domain.
The two parts are related, and the chapter states their relation.
    The reader who accepts the chapter’s answer has accepted the boundary within which
the book’s claims are made; the reader who rejects it has asked the book to do what it was
not written to do. The chapter does not ask the reader to stop asking “what is it for?”—the
question is real, and the book points toward it. The chapter asks the reader to recognize
38                                                            Chapter 4. Structure, Not Telos


that the question is not answered here, and that the book’s silence on it is not a denial of its
importance.

Remark 4.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the boundary
at work in a thoughtful reader. It does not prove that the boundary is the right one; it makes
the boundary intelligible before it is stated. The two principles are stated and defended in the
sections that follow, and the scene carries no weight in them.


4.2    The Question
The previous chapters have stated the four questions of explanatory cognition, the method by
which the framework’s claims are to be assessed, and the finitude of the epistemic subject.
The present chapter asks a question that must be settled before the argument can proceed:
what kind of question can the framework answer?
     The question is not what the framework describes; the previous chapters have said that
it describes explanatory cognition. The question is what kind of claim the framework can
make, and what kind of claim it cannot. A framework that did not know the boundary of its
own competence would claim more than it can support, and its claims would be vulnerable to
criticism it should have anticipated. The present chapter states the boundary, and states it as
an axiom so that the reader knows, from the outset, what the framework claims and what it
does not.
     The chapter states two principles. The first is the boundary between structure and telos:
epistemology describes the structure of explanatory cognition, and it does not, by its method,
establish the end, purpose, or good for which anything exists. The second is the autonomy
of epistemic justification: the validity of no epistemic principle in this book depends on
confirmation from outside epistemology.
     The two principles are related, and their relation is worth marking from the outset. The
first sets the boundary of what the framework describes; the second sets the boundary of how
the framework’s description is justified. The first says what the framework can say; the second
says how it can say it.

Remark 4.2 (The Two Questions Are the Two Principles). The reader who asks “what is
cognition for?” is asking the question that the first principle answers, by saying that the
framework does not answer it. The reader who asks “why should I accept what the framework
says?” is asking the question that the second principle answers, by saying that the framework’s
justification is internal to epistemology. The two questions are not the same, and the two
principles are not the same; but each question corresponds to one principle, and the chapter
states both so that the reader can see which question each principle answers.


4.3    Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos
Principle 4.1 (Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos). Epistemology, as practiced in
this book, describes the structure of explanatory cognition: the relations among the elements
of an explanation, the rules that govern those relations, and the frames in which both are
posed. It does not, and by its method cannot, establish the telos of cognition: the end, the
purpose, or the good for which anything exists. The question of telos is a real question, and
the structure that epistemology describes points toward it; but the structure does not contain
it, and epistemology cannot derive it from the structure alone.

   The principle is (A): it is adopted as an axiom. It is not derived from the four-column
framework, and it does not follow from any of the definitions stated so far. It is adopted
because the method of the book is structural: the book asks what roles an explanation must
4.3. Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos                                                 39


assign, and it answers by analysis, not by appeal to purpose. A method that answers by
analysis cannot, by the same analysis, deliver a purpose. To claim otherwise would be to
confuse the description of a structure with the justification of an end.

Remark 4.3 (Why the Principle Is an Axiom, Not a Conclusion). The principle is not a
conclusion of the framework; it is a condition of the framework’s method. A framework that
derived the boundary from its own principles would be claiming that its method can establish
its own limits, which would be a claim the method cannot deliver. The boundary is stated as
an axiom so that the framework’s claims are assessable: the reader knows what kind of claim
is being made, and therefore what kind of criticism is appropriate.

   The principle has two sides, and both must be stated.

The first side: structural epistemology. A structural epistemology asks how the elements
of an explanation stand to one another. It identifies the elements, the medium of their relation,
the rule of the medium, and the frame in which all three are posed (the four questions of
Chapter 1). It answers by description: it says what the structure is, and it states the conditions
under which the structure holds. Its claims are assessed by coherence, explanatory power, and
fruitfulness—the criteria stated in Chapter 2. This is the kind of epistemology the present
book practices.

The second side: teleological inquiry. A teleological inquiry asks for the sake of what a
thing exists. It identifies the end toward which a structure is ordered, and it states the good
that the structure serves. Its claims are assessed by a different standard: by the adequacy of
the end it proposes, by the coherence of that end with the structure it is said to serve, and by
the authority of the source from which the end is received. This is not the kind of inquiry the
present book undertakes.
    The two inquiries are not rivals. They answer different questions about the same reality.
A structural description can be true while a teleological account is also true, and the two can
be compatible without either reducing to the other. The structural description says what the
structure is; the teleological account says what the structure is for. The first does not entail
the second, and the second does not replace the first. But the first is not complete without
the second, and the second is not intelligible without the first. The structure is the condition
of possibility of the teleological account, and the teleological account is the completion of the
structure’s meaning.

4.3.1    Why Knowing the Structure Is Not the Same as Knowing the Telos
The distinction between describing a structure and determining its telos is easily stated and
easily lost. The present subsection makes the distinction exact, with a worked example, so
that the reader can see what the chapter’s first principle claims and what it does not.

Definition 4.1 (Structural Description and Teleological Determination). (A) A structural
description of a thing states the roles its parts play, the relations among the parts, and the
conditions under which the roles and relations hold. A teleological determination of a thing
states the end for which the thing exists, or the good it serves. The two are different kinds of
claim: a structural description can be complete while the teleological determination remains
open, and a teleological determination can be true while the structural description remains
incomplete.

    The definition is (A): it is a stipulation of the chapter’s vocabulary. Its purpose is to make
the distinction exact, not to argue for a particular view about the relation between structure
and telos.
40                                                              Chapter 4. Structure, Not Telos


Example 4.1 (The Structure of a Court and the Purpose of a Court). Consider a court of
law. A structural description of the court states the roles it assigns: the judge, the advocates,
the witnesses, the jury, the defendant, the record. It states the relations among the roles: the
judge presides over the advocates, the advocates examine the witnesses, the jury deliberates
on the evidence, the record preserves the proceedings. It states the conditions under which the
roles and relations hold: the rules of procedure, the rules of evidence, the rules of jurisdiction.
    The structural description can be complete, and the question of the court’s purpose can
remain open. One inquirer may say that the court exists in order to render justice; another
may say that it exists in order to resolve disputes peacefully; another may say that it exists in
order to preserve the authority of the sovereign. Each of these is a teleological determination,
and each is a different claim from the structural description. The structural description does
not entail any of them, and none of them replaces it.
    The point is not that the court has no purpose, or that the purpose is unknowable. The
point is that the structural description and the teleological determination are different kinds of
claim, and that a method that describes the structure is not, by the same method, in a position
to determine the purpose. A reader who has the structural description has the structure; the
reader who wants the purpose must undertake a different inquiry—whether that inquiry is
jurisprudence, political philosophy, or something else—and the structural description is the
condition of possibility of that inquiry, not its substitute.

    The example makes the distinction exact. The structural description answers the question
“what is the court?” The teleological determination answers the question “what is the court
for?” The two questions are different, and the method that answers the first is not, by itself,
the method that answers the second.

Remark 4.4 (The Example and the Framework). The example of the court is the chapter’s
central illustration of the distinction. The framework of the four columns is a structural
description of explanatory cognition, in the sense of Definition 4.1. It states the roles that
any explanation assigns, the relations among the roles, and the conditions under which the
roles and relations hold. It does not state the end for which explanatory cognition exists, and
the example of the court shows why the two claims are different. A reader who takes the
framework’s structural description as a teleological determination has confused the two kinds
of claim; a reader who takes it as a structural description has read it correctly.

Remark 4.5 (The Analogy of the Grammar and the Poem). A grammar describes the
structure of a language: its syntax, its morphology, its phonology. A poem written in that
language has a structure that the grammar describes, and a meaning that the grammar does
not describe. The grammar can be complete and the poem can still have a meaning the
grammar cannot reach. The grammar is the condition of the poem’s being intelligible; the
meaning is what the poem is for. The relation between structure and telos is like the relation
between grammar and poem: the one is the condition of the other, and neither is the other.
A grammar that claimed to describe the poem’s meaning would be claiming more than a
grammar can deliver; a grammar that said nothing about the poem would be silent about
what makes the poem worth reading. The framework is the grammar; the telos is the poem’s
meaning. The framework describes the grammar of explanatory cognition; it does not describe
the meaning.

Remark 4.6 (Why the Boundary Is Not a Weakness). The boundary is not a deficiency of
the framework. It is a condition of its precision. A framework that claimed to establish both
structure and telos by a single method would be claiming more than its method can deliver.
The framework’s honesty about its boundary is part of what makes its structural claims
assessable: the reader knows exactly what kind of claim is being made, and therefore what
kind of criticism is appropriate. A structural claim is criticized by showing that the structure
4.4. The Autonomy of Epistemic Justification                                                      41


is misdescribed; a teleological claim is criticized by showing that the end is inadequate or
unauthorized. The two criticisms are different, and the framework keeps them apart.

Remark 4.7 (What the Framework Does Not Say About Telos). The framework does not
say that telos is unreal, unknowable, or unimportant. It says only that telos is not established
by the method of this book. Whether telos is real, and if so how it is known, is a question the
framework leaves open. The question belongs to a different inquiry—whether that inquiry is
revelation, intuition, practical reason, or religious experience—and the framework takes no
position on which inquiry is the right one. It takes a position only on what its own method
can deliver, and telos is not among the things its method delivers.

Remark 4.8 (Structure Is Not Self-Sufficient). The framework describes structure. But the
framework does not claim that structure is the whole of what is. The order through which
what is becomes intelligible is real, and the framework’s claim is that this order is invariant
and describable. But the order is not self-sufficient: it is the order of something, and the
something is not exhausted by its order. The framework’s silence on telos is therefore not a
denial of telos; it is the recognition that a description of order is not a description of the whole.
The structure is a condition of intelligibility, not a substitute for being.

Remark 4.9 (The Boundary Is a Threshold, Not a Wall). The boundary between structure
and telos is a threshold, not a wall. It marks the point at which description gives way
to indication, and indication is not a lesser form of knowledge but a different form. The
framework’s silence on telos is not a denial of telos; it is the recognition that the description of
structure is not the description of the whole. The structure is real, and the framework’s claim
is that the structure is invariant and describable. But the structure is the order of what is, and
what is is not exhausted by its order. The threshold is the framework’s way of marking where
its competence ends without claiming that the end of its competence is the end of what is.

Remark 4.10 (The Formal Reconstruction and the Boundary). The formal reconstruction
of the four columns (Chapter 6, Section 6.9; Chapter 7, Section 7.8; Appendix .15) respects
the boundary stated in this chapter. The formal language states the analytical roles of an
explanation and the conditions under which the roles are assigned; it does not state the telos
of explanation, and it does not claim to establish the end for which cognition exists. The
formal theorems (necessity, sufficiency, distinctness, and consistency) are theorems about the
structure of explanation, not about its purpose. The formal reconstruction is therefore an
instance of the boundary: it is a structural description, offered at the strength of a structural
description, and it leaves the question of telos to the inquiry that undertakes it. A reader who
takes the formal reconstruction as a claim about the purpose of explanation has misread it; a
reader who takes it as a claim about the structure of explanation has read it correctly.


4.4     The Autonomy of Epistemic Justification
Principle 4.2 (Autonomy of Epistemic Justification). The validity of no epistemic principle
in this book depends on confirmation from outside epistemology—including from science, from
theology, from authority, or from any other discipline. Every principle is derived from within
the four-column framework and from epistemic arguments.

    The principle is (A): it is adopted as an axiom. It states what counts as justification in
the book, and it is observed throughout.
    The principle does not forbid the book from speaking of other domains. It forbids the
book from using other domains as a ground of justification for its principles. References to
other domains appear in the book in one role only: as a coherence test. A coherence test
shows that an inquiry in another domain can develop itself within the epistemic framework
42                                                             Chapter 4. Structure, Not Telos


without contradiction. It is marked in the text by a dedicated box, headed “Coherence Test
(not evidence, not justification),” and it is never used as a premise in any argument of the
book.

Remark 4.11 (Why the Principle Is an Axiom, Not a Conclusion). The principle is not a
conclusion of the framework; it is a condition of the framework’s method. A framework that
justified its principles by appeal to another domain would be claiming that its method is not
autonomous, which would be a claim about its method, not a claim within it. The principle is
stated as an axiom so that the reader knows, from the outset, what kind of justification the
book offers.

Remark 4.12 (Autonomy Is Not Isolation). The principle of autonomy is easily misread
as isolation. A framework that claimed to have nothing to do with other domains would
be isolated, and isolation is not what the principle requires. The principle requires that the
framework’s justification be internal to epistemology—that the framework’s principles not
depend on confirmation from outside. It does not require that the framework be unaware of
other domains, or that it refuse to speak of them. The framework may speak of science, of
theology, of ethics; it may use the coherence test to show that its claims are not at odds with
what those domains say. What it may not do is rest its principles on the authority of those
domains. The distinction is the distinction between speaking of another domain and being
justified by it. The framework does the first; it does not do the second.

     The principle has three consequences, and each is worth stating.

First consequence: the book is not a philosophy grounded in science. The reader
who seeks a philosophy grounded in science will not find one here. The book does not draw
its premises from empirical data, and it does not claim that its principles are confirmed by
empirical inquiry. Its principles are epistemic principles, and they are assessed by epistemic
standards.

Second consequence: the book is not a philosophy that ignores science. The reader
who seeks a philosophy that ignores science will also not find one. The book is coherent with
the inquiries it does not depend on, and it uses coherence tests to show that an inquiry in
another domain can develop itself within the framework without contradiction. The coherence
tests are not justifications; they are checks on the framework’s own claims.

Third consequence: the coherence test is a discipline on the book’s own claims.
If an epistemic principle is incompatible with the way an established inquiry actually works,
the principle is defective as a principle of the structure of cognition, and the coherence test
reveals the defect. The test does not confirm the principle; it exposes the principle to a kind of
check. A principle that passes the coherence test is not thereby justified, and a principle that
fails it is not thereby refuted—but the failure is a reason to examine the principle further.

Remark 4.13 (What the Coherence Test Shows and Does Not Show). A coherence test shows
that an inquiry in another domain can develop itself within the epistemic framework without
contradiction. It does not show that the framework’s principles are correct. It does not show
that the inquiry confirms the framework, or that the framework confirms the inquiry. It shows
only that the framework’s principles are not at odds with the way the inquiry describes its
own structure. The test is offered at exactly that strength.

Remark 4.14 (The Coherence Test Is Not a Concession to Science). The coherence test is
not a concession to science, and it is not a concession to any other domain. It is a discipline
on the book’s own claims. The book uses the coherence test because the book takes its
4.5. The Relation Between the Two Principles                                                    43


own claims seriously enough to check them against the way other inquiries actually work.
A framework that refused to check its claims against anything would be a framework that
could not be assessed. The coherence test is the framework’s way of being assessable; it is
not the framework’s way of borrowing authority from another domain. The distinction is the
distinction between checking and grounding. The framework checks its claims against other
domains; it does not ground them in other domains.


4.5     The Relation Between the Two Principles
The two principles are related, and the relation is worth marking.
     The first principle sets the boundary of what the framework describes: it describes structure,
not telos. The second principle sets the boundary of how the framework’s description is justified:
its justification is internal to epistemology, not drawn from another domain.
     The two boundaries are different. The first is a boundary between the structure of cognition
and the end of cognition. The second is a boundary between epistemic justification and the
justification of other domains. The first says what the framework cannot say; the second says
how it can say what it says.
     The two boundaries are also related. The first principle is stated as an axiom because the
second principle requires it: if the framework’s justification is internal to epistemology, the
framework cannot derive the boundary of its own competence from another domain, and it
cannot derive it from its own principles without claiming more than its method delivers. The
first principle is therefore stated as an axiom, and its adoption is part of what the second
principle requires.
Remark 4.15 (The Two Principles Are Not the Same). The two principles are not the same,
and neither entails the other. A framework could be autonomous in its justification and still
claim to establish telos; a framework could describe structure and still draw its justification
from another domain. The first principle is about what the framework describes; the second is
about how it is justified. The book adopts both, and the two are stated separately so that the
reader can assess them separately.
Remark 4.16 (The Two Principles Together Define the Framework’s Competence). The
two principles together define the framework’s competence. The first principle says that the
framework’s competence is the description of structure, not the establishment of telos. The
second principle says that the framework’s competence is exercised by epistemic justification,
not by appeal to another domain. The two principles are the framework’s two boundaries,
and together they state what the framework can and cannot do. A framework that accepted
only the first would describe structure but might justify its description by appeal to another
domain; a framework that accepted only the second would have autonomous justification but
might claim to establish telos. The framework accepts both, and the two together state its
competence.


4.6     The Boundary and the Reader
The boundary has a consequence for the reader. The reader who seeks a structural description
of explanatory cognition will find one in this book. The reader who seeks an account of the
end for which cognition exists will not find one here; the book points beyond itself, to the
inquiry that undertakes that question.
    The pointing is not a refusal. It is the recognition that an epistemological framework,
honestly practiced, knows where its competence ends—and that the end of its competence is
not the end of what is. The pointing is itself a kind of claim: the claim that structure is not
the whole, and that the whole is not exhausted by what epistemology can describe.
44                                                             Chapter 4. Structure, Not Telos


Remark 4.17 (The Reader’s Two Paths). The boundary gives the reader two paths. The
first path is the path of the reader who seeks a structural description: that reader will find the
framework’s claims in Parts I–VI, and the framework’s arguments for them in the chapters
that state them. The second path is the path of the reader who seeks an account of telos:
that reader will not find the account in this book, but will find the framework’s indication of
where the account belongs. The two paths are not rivals; they are two ways of reading the
same book. The reader who takes the first path has the framework’s structural claims; the
reader who takes the second has the framework’s indication of what it does not claim. The
two paths are complementary, and the framework invites both.


4.7     The Role of Structural Analysis in Epistemic Justification
The chapter’s first principle sets a boundary; the chapter’s positive contribution is the role
that structural analysis plays in epistemic justification. The present section states that role,
so that the reader knows what the chapter gives, not only what it declines.
    The chapter gives the framework three things, and each is a contribution to the method of
the book.

First contribution: a criterion for when an explanation is assessable. A structural
analysis makes an explanation assessable by making its roles explicit. When the roles are
stated—the fixed elements, the fluid elements, the governing dynamics, the context—the
explanation can be assessed role by role, and the assessment can locate the point at which
the explanation succeeds or fails. The court example (Example 4.1) makes the point concrete:
the structural description of the court makes the court’s operation assessable in a way that a
teleological claim alone cannot. A reader who has the structural description can ask whether
the judge’s role is well-defined, whether the advocates’ relations are well-ordered, whether the
rules of evidence are coherent. A reader who has only the teleological claim (“the court exists
to render justice”) cannot ask these questions, because the claim does not state the roles. The
structural analysis is therefore not a preliminary to assessment; it is what makes assessment
possible.

Second contribution: a criterion for the scope of a claim. A structural analysis makes
a claim’s scope explicit. When the roles are stated, the claim can be assessed at the scope the
roles define, and the claim can be marked as valid within that scope and not beyond it. The
court example again: the structural description of the court makes explicit that the description
is of this court, in this jurisdiction, under these rules. A claim about the court that went
beyond the scope—a claim that the court, wherever it is found, must have these roles—would
be a different claim, and the structural analysis makes the difference visible. The framework’s
claim about explanatory cognition is offered at the scope the framework states: the cognitive
context fixed by the question. The structural analysis is what makes the scope explicit, and
what makes the claim assessable at that scope.

Third contribution: a criterion for the relation between structure and justification.
A structural analysis makes explicit the relation between what a claim says and how it is
justified. When the roles are stated, the claim’s premises can be located in the roles, and the
claim’s justification can be assessed role by role. The court example: the claim that the judge
presides is justified by the rules of procedure, and the claim that the advocates examine the
witnesses is justified by the rules of evidence. The structural analysis makes the justification
explicit, and it makes the claim assessable by the justification the claim actually offers. The
framework’s principle of autonomy (Principle 4.2) is the application of this contribution to
epistemology: the framework’s claims are justified within epistemology, and the structural
4.7. The Role of Structural Analysis in Epistemic Justification                                45


analysis makes the justification explicit by locating each claim in the roles the framework
states.




Remark 4.18 (Structural Analysis Is Not Justification). The chapter’s positive contribution
is not that structural analysis justifies an epistemic claim. Structural analysis makes a claim
assessable; it does not make the claim true. The justification of a claim is the argument the
claim offers, and the argument is assessed by the criteria of Chapter 2. The structural analysis
is the condition under which the argument can be located and assessed; it is not the argument
itself. A reader who takes the structural analysis as a substitute for argument has misread the
chapter; a reader who takes it as what makes argument assessable has read it correctly.




Remark 4.19 (Structural Analysis Is Not Neutral). Structural analysis is not neutral about
what counts as an explanation. It states the roles that an explanation must assign, and the
statement is a claim about the structure of explanatory cognition. The claim is assessed by
the method of Chapter 2, and it is not offered as a neutral description of all possible accounts.
A reader who takes the structural analysis as neutral has misread it; a reader who takes it as
a claim, offered at the strength the method supports, has read it correctly.




Remark 4.20 (The Positive Output of the Chapter). The chapter’s positive output is threefold.
It gives the framework a criterion for when an explanation is assessable (the explicit roles), a
criterion for the scope of a claim (the roles define the scope), and a criterion for the relation
between structure and justification (the roles locate the justification). The three criteria are
the chapter’s contribution to the method of the book; they are what the boundary makes
possible, not what the boundary denies. The boundary states what the framework cannot do;
the three criteria state what it can do. The chapter’s contribution is the three criteria, offered
at the strength the method supports.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a claim you accept about the structure of something—a legal system, a language, a
scientific theory. Does the claim tell you what the thing is for ? If it does not, is the claim
incomplete, or is it complete in its own terms? What does your answer tell you about the
relation between structure and telos?
     And consider the court example (Example 4.1): a structural description of the court can
be complete, and the question of the court’s purpose can remain open. Is the structural
description thereby incomplete, or is it complete in its own terms? What does your answer
tell you about the difference between knowing a structure and knowing its purpose? A reader
who can answer both questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer neither
has the chapter’s two tasks before them.
