Chapter 5

Cognitive Architecture and the Order
of Explanatory Dependence

Scope
This chapter closes Part I by stating the distinction on which the epistemology-only scope of
this volume depends: the distinction between the order of cognitive reconstruction and the
order of explanatory dependence represented within an explanation. It states the principle
that the two are distinct, states the consequence for the book’s method, and distinguishes the
order of cognition from the order of explanatory dependence that an explanation represents.
It makes no ontological claim, and it defers none: the distinction is internal to epistemology,
and everything the chapter says is said within epistemology.
    The distinction between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence
is not a preliminary remark, stated once and then left idle; it is a working tool that the
later chapters use to make their own distinctions precise (identity/signature in Chapter 12,
viability/identity in Chapter 36, singularity/manifestation in Chapter 37, balance/measure in
Chapter 42, and the conditional architecture on a core in Chapter 43). The chapter therefore
adds, at the end, a section that lists where the distinction is operationalized, so that the reader
knows that the distinction is load-bearing and not merely terminological.
    Its claims are epistemic and meta-epistemic; where it speaks of “architecture,” “role,” “order,”
“dependence,” or “distinctness,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter.


5.1     A Scene: The Map and the Territory
Consider a map of a mountain range. The map is accurate: every peak is in its place, every
valley is where the map says it is, every river follows the course the map records. A hiker
who follows the map will reach the summit the map marks. The map is a description of the
mountain range, and it is a good description.
    Now ask: is the map the mountain range? The question sounds absurd, and it is meant
to. The map is a description; the mountain range is what is described. The map has features
the mountain range does not have (a legend, a scale, a north arrow, a border); the mountain
range has features the map does not have (the smell of pine, the sound of wind, the weight
of a stone). The map and the mountain range are related—the map describes the mountain
range, and the description is accurate—but they are not the same, and they are not even on
the same level.
    Now consider a subtler case. Suppose a cartographer claims that the map’s features—its
legend, its scale, its border—are features of the mountain range itself. The cartographer says:
“The mountain range has a legend; the legend is written on the rock.” The claim is not merely
50             Chapter 5. Cognitive Architecture and the Order of Explanatory Dependence


false; it is a category mistake. The legend is a feature of the map, not of the mountain range.
The cartographer has confused the description with the described.
    The framework’s distinction is the distinction between the order of reconstruction and the
order of dependence that the reconstruction represents. The four columns—fixed elements,
fluid elements, governing dynamics, context—are the features of the map: they are the
analytical roles that any complete explanation must assign, and they describe the structure of
the explanation, not the structure of what is explained. The order of explanatory dependence
is the order that the explanation represents: it is the order in which the elements of the
explanation depend on one another as the explanation represents them. To say that the four
columns are the analytical structure of explanation is not to say that reality consists of four
kinds of entity; to say that the explanatory dependence has a certain order is not to say that
the real order of beings has that order. The two claims are different, and the framework keeps
them apart.
    The scene poses a question. What is the distinction between the order of reconstruction
and the order of explanatory dependence, and why does the distinction matter for the book’s
claims? The present chapter answers. Its answer is the chapter’s principle, stated and defended
in the sections that follow, and the distinction is the tool the rest of the book uses to keep its
claims precise.

Remark 5.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the distinction
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove that the distinction is the right one; it makes the
distinction intelligible before it is stated. The principle is stated and defended in the sections
that follow, and the scene carries no weight in it.


5.2     The Question
Part I has stated the four questions of explanatory cognition, the method by which the
framework’s claims are assessed, the finitude of the epistemic subject, and the boundary
between structure and telos. The present chapter asks a question that the previous chapters
have prepared but not yet answered: when the book says that an explanation requires four
roles, what kind of claim is it making? Is it making a claim about the order in which a
finite subject reconstructs an explanation, or a claim about the order of dependence that the
explanation represents?
    The distinction is easily run together, and the consequences of running it together are
large. If the four roles were read as four kinds of entity, the framework would become a
metaphysics of four substances—a view the book does not hold and does not need. If the
four roles were read as four levels of reality, the framework would become an ontology, and
the epistemology-only scope of this volume would be lost. The present chapter states the
distinction that prevents both readings, and it states it as a principle.
    The question has a second face, which the present chapter also treats. The book presents
its architecture in an order—the order of cognition, the order in which a finite subject comes
to understand the structure of explanatory cognition. Is that order the same as the order
of dependence that the explanation represents? The framework’s answer is that the two
orders are distinct, and that the present volume develops both insofar as they are internal
to epistemology: the order of cognition, and the order of explanatory dependence as the
explanation represents it. The distinction is stated here, at the end of Part I, so that the
reader enters Part II with both distinctions in hand.

Remark 5.2 (Why the Question Comes Here, at the End of Part I). The question comes at the
end of Part I, not at the beginning, because the reader now has the vocabulary to understand
the answer. If the question had come before the four questions, the method, and the finitude,
the reader would have had no way to see what the distinction was a distinction between. The
5.3. The Two Orders                                                                            51


distinction between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence is
a distinction between the structure of an explanation and the order of dependence that the
explanation represents; without the vocabulary of the four questions (Chapter 1) and of the
method (Chapter 2), the reader would not know what “the structure of an explanation” meant.
The delay is intentional.


5.3     The Two Orders
The book distinguishes two orders, and the distinction is stated as a principle.

Principle 5.1 (The Order of Reconstruction and the Order of Explanatory Dependence Are
Distinct). The four columns are four analytical roles that any complete explanation must
assign. From the definition of the columns alone it does not follow that the order of explanatory
dependence that the explanation represents is the real order of beings. The distinction between
the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence is internal to epistemology;
no claim about the real order of beings follows from it, and no such claim is needed for it.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of the four columns. The removal test,
when it is applied, shows what an explanation must contain. A statement about what an
explanation must contain is a statement about the explanation; it becomes a statement about
the real order of beings only with a further premise, namely that the roles are carved out by
the real order of beings. That premise is not part of the four-column principle. Hence the
principle is silent on the real order of beings. Whatever is said on that matter must be argued
on its own ground.

Proof of Principle 5.1. The removal test shows what an explanation must contain. It does not
show what the real order of beings contains. The step from the first to the second requires
the premise that the roles are carved out by the real order of beings. That premise is not
supplied by the definition of the columns, and it is not supplied by the removal test. Hence
the principle is silent on the real order of beings. If a particular claim about the real order of
beings is to be made, it must be argued on its own ground, not inferred from the four-column
framework.

   The two orders can be stated side by side.

The order of cognitive reconstruction. The order of cognitive reconstruction is the order
in which a finite subject comes to understand the structure of explanatory cognition. It begins
with the four analytical roles that any complete explanation must assign (Part I); it continues
with the architecture of explanatory cognition (Part II); it develops the structure of epistemic
relations (Part III); it states the conditions of epistemic validity and adequacy (Part IV); it
states the limits, errors, and unknownness that any finite cognition must acknowledge (Part V);
and it develops the epistemic economy of cognition and the concept of viability (Part VI). The
order of reconstruction is the order of the present book.

The order of explanatory dependence. The order of explanatory dependence is the
order in which the elements of an explanation depend on one another as the explanation
represents them. It is not the order in which a finite subject comes to know, and it is not
the real order of beings; it is the order that an explanation represents when it states which
elements depend on which, through which medium, by which rule, and within which frame.
The present volume develops the order of explanatory dependence insofar as it is internal
to the explanation: it states what a complete explanation must contain, and it states the
relations among the elements as the explanation represents them.
52             Chapter 5. Cognitive Architecture and the Order of Explanatory Dependence


Remark 5.3 (The Two Orders Answer Different Questions). The two orders answer different
questions, and neither is a rival of the other. The order of reconstruction answers the question:
how does a finite subject come to understand the structure of explanatory cognition? The
order of explanatory dependence answers the question: how does the explanation represent
the dependence of its elements on one another? The first is the order of inquiry; the second is
the order of the representation. The present volume develops both, at the strength internal to
epistemology. It makes no claim about the real order of beings, and it does not need to.
Remark 5.4 (An Analogy: The Recipe and the Meal). An analogy may help to fix the
distinction. A recipe is a description of how to prepare a meal: the ingredients, the steps, the
order in which the steps are taken. The recipe represents an order of dependence among its
ingredients and steps: the flour depends on the water for becoming dough, the dough depends
on the oven for becoming bread. That represented order is internal to the recipe; it is not a
claim about the real order of the ingredients in the kitchen, and it is not the order in which
a cook comes to prepare the meal. The recipe’s order is the order in which a cook comes to
prepare the meal; the meal’s order is the order the recipe represents. A cook who followed
the recipe perfectly might still produce a meal whose actual order differs from the recipe’s
represented order, because the actual order depends on factors the recipe does not describe
(the heat of the pan, the freshness of the ingredients, the altitude of the kitchen). The order of
reconstruction is the order of the cook’s activity; the order of explanatory dependence is the
order the recipe represents. The framework develops both orders; the real order of the meal is
a different question, and it is not the framework’s claim.
Remark 5.5 (The Same Structure From Two Questions). The structural order—the four
columns, the epistemic relations, the conditions of validity—appears in both orders, but from
two different questions. In the order of reconstruction, it is the analytical architecture that
an explanation must articulate. In the order of explanatory dependence, it is the form that
the explanation’s representation of dependence takes. The appearance in both is not an
inconsistency; it is the same structure viewed from two questions. The book’s claim is that
both orders are real, invariant, and describable as epistemological structures, and that the two
orders are compatible. The present book states both, and it makes no claim about the real
order of beings.


5.4     The Cognitive Architecture
The cognitive architecture of the book is the four-column structure that any complete ex-
planation must assign. The present section states what the architecture is, and what it is
not.

What the cognitive architecture is. The four columns answer the question: what roles
must be told apart if something is to be understood? The four columns are fixed elements,
fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context. They are analytical roles, not kinds of entity.
They are the architecture of explanatory cognition, and they are the subject of Part II.

What the cognitive architecture is not. The cognitive architecture is not a doctrine of
what reality contains. It does not say that reality consists of four kinds of entity, or four levels
of being, or any particular number of either. The question of what the real order of beings
is—whether there are levels, and if so how many, and how they are related—is a different
question, and the present volume does not undertake it. The cognitive architecture is silent on
that question, and it is silent by method, not by denial.
Remark 5.6 (No Conflict Between the Four Columns and Any Doctrine of Levels). There is
no conflict between a cognition that has four columns and any doctrine of levels of being. The
5.4. The Cognitive Architecture                                                                  53


four columns apply to the study of any level, and to the study of the relations among levels.
Within the study of a single level, its manifestations are the fixed elements, epistemic light is
the fluid element, the rules of that level are the governing dynamics, and the level together
with the cognitive standpoint is the context. Nothing in this chapter should be read as saying
that each column is a level, or that each level is a column. The cognitive architecture and any
doctrine of levels are distinct, and the distinction is what allows the book to argue for each
on its own terms—the book argues for the cognitive architecture; it does not argue for any
particular doctrine of levels.

Remark 5.7 (Why the Distinction Matters for This Volume). The distinction is not a small
point. If the four columns were read as four kinds of entity, the framework would become a
metaphysics of four substances, and the epistemology-only scope of this volume would be lost.
The book’s claim is that the four columns are the analytical structure of explanation, and that
any claim about the real order of beings is a different claim. The present volume develops the
analytical structure, and it makes no claim about the real order of beings. The reader who
takes the four columns as a doctrine of what reality contains has misread the book’s scope;
the reader who takes them as analytical roles has read it correctly.

Remark 5.8 (The Analogy of the Grammar, Revisited). The analogy of the grammar and
the poem (Chapter 4) applies here as well, and the application is worth stating. The grammar
describes the structure of a language; the poem uses the language to say something the
grammar does not describe. To say that the grammar has four parts is not to say that the
poem has four parts; to say that the poem has a meaning the grammar does not capture is
not to say that the grammar is wrong. The four columns are the grammar of explanation; the
meaning of the poem is a different order of question. The two are distinct, and the distinction
is what allows the grammar to be assessed on its own terms and the poem to be read on its
own terms.

Remark 5.9 (The Two Realities: The Activity and the Structure). The distinction between
the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence is related to a second
distinction that the chapter keeps throughout, and the second is easily conflated with the first.
The second is the distinction between two realities: the reality of the explanatory activity, and
the reality of the structure that the activity represents.
    The first reality: the reality of the explanatory activity. The activity of explaining is a real
activity, performed by real subjects in real contexts. Its reality is not in question; it is the
reality of an event in the world, and the framework assumes it. The existence of the activity is
not the framework’s claim; it is a precondition of the inquiry.
    The second reality: the reality of the structure the activity represents. The structure of
explanatory cognition—the four columns, the relations among them, the conditions of their
adequacy—is the structure that the activity represents. Its reality is the framework’s claim,
and the claim is stated at the strength the framework’s arguments support. The framework
does not claim that the structure is a substance, or that it exists independently of the activity;
it claims that the structure is real, invariant, and describable, and it states the claim at the
strength the arguments support.
    The transition from the first reality to the second is the transition from “there are explana-
tory activities” to “the structure that those activities represent is real.” The transition is not a
logical consequence of the first; it is a claim about the second, and the framework states it
at the strength of a (T) claim relative to the arguments of Parts I–IV. A reader who accepts
the first reality and rejects the second has rejected the framework’s claim about the structure;
the framework does not pretend that the second follows from the first by itself. The two are
distinct, and the framework keeps them distinct.
54             Chapter 5. Cognitive Architecture and the Order of Explanatory Dependence


5.5     The Order of Explanatory Dependence
The order of explanatory dependence is the order in which the elements of an explanation
depend on one another as the explanation represents them. The present section states what
that order is, distinguishes it from the order of reconstruction, and states the epistemological
consequence of the distinction.

What the order of explanatory dependence is. The order of explanatory dependence
is the order that an explanation represents when it states which elements depend on which,
through which medium, by which rule, and within which frame. It is an order within the
explanation: it is the order that the explanation’s representation assigns to its elements, and it
is assessed by the criteria of Part IV.

What the order of explanatory dependence is not. The order of explanatory depen-
dence is not the real order of beings. It is not a claim that, in reality, this element depends on
that element in the way the explanation represents. It is a claim about what the explanation
represents, and it is assessed by the criteria that apply to representations—coherence, explana-
tory power, adequacy—not by a comparison with the real order of beings, which the present
volume does not undertake to survey.

Remark 5.10 (The Order of Dependence Is Internal to the Explanation). The order of
explanatory dependence is internal to the explanation in the sense that it is what the explanation
says, not what the world is. An explanation can represent an order of dependence, and
the representation can be assessed for coherence, for explanatory power, and for adequacy,
without the assessment requiring a survey of the real order of beings. The assessment is an
epistemological assessment, and it is offered at the strength that an epistemological assessment
can have. A reader who asks the framework to compare its represented order with the real
order of beings has asked for a comparison the framework does not undertake; a reader who
asks the framework to state and assess the represented order has asked for what the framework
offers.

Remark 5.11 (The Epistemological Consequence of the Distinction). The distinction between
the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence has an epistemological
consequence, and the consequence is worth stating. The consequence is that the framework’s
claims are assessable on their own terms: the claims about the order of reconstruction
are assessed by the criteria of the method (Chapter 2), and the claims about the order of
explanatory dependence are assessed by the criteria of validity and adequacy (Part IV). The
two sets of criteria are distinct, and the distinction is what allows the framework to be assessed
without a survey of the real order of beings. A framework that conflated the two orders
would have to defend its epistemological claims by appeal to a survey of the real order of
beings, and it would be unable to do so without undertaking an inquiry it does not undertake.
The distinction is therefore not a terminological nicety; it is the condition under which the
framework’s claims are assessable at all.

Remark 5.12 (An Analogy: The Recipe and the Meal, Revisited). The analogy of the recipe
and the meal (Section 5.3) applies here as well. The recipe’s represented order of dependence
is internal to the recipe: it is what the recipe says about how the ingredients depend on one
another. The cook who follows the recipe assesses it by the criteria of cookery—coherence,
workability, the quality of the meal—not by a survey of the real chemical order of the ingredients.
The recipe is assessable on its own terms, and the assessment is what the recipe is for. The
framework’s represented order of explanatory dependence is analogous: it is internal to the
explanation, and it is assessed by the criteria of Part IV, not by a survey of the real order of
beings.
5.6. Where the Distinction Operates                                                          55


5.6    Where the Distinction Operates
The distinction between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence
is not a preliminary remark, stated once and then left idle. It is a working tool that the later
chapters use, each time they need to distinguish the analytical structure of an explanation
from the order of dependence the explanation represents. The present section states where the
distinction is operationalized, so that the reader knows that it is load-bearing and not merely
terminological.

Identity and signature (Chapter 12). The identity is the invariant that an explanatory
     cognition holds fixed (an analytical role); the signature is the structural description of
     that invariance (an analytical description); the distinction is the analytical form of the
     distinction between the invariant and the description of it. The doctrine that identity
     is more than its signature (Chapter 12, primitive thisness) is the statement that the
     analytical description does not exhaust the invariant.

Manifestation and manifestational effect (Chapter 13). The manifestation is the con-
    textually realized appearance of an identity (an analytical role); the manifestational
    effect is what the appearance brings about in the receiving context. The distinction is
    the analytical form of the distinction between the appearance and its effect.

Viability and identity (Chapter 36). Identity is rigid and admits no degrees; viability is
    graded and admits of degrees. The distinction between the two (Chapter 36, Principle ??)
    is the analytical form of the distinction between the invariant and the character of its
    expression; the identity is the invariant, and viability is the analytical character of the
    relation between the invariant and its manifestations.

Singularity and manifestation (Chapter 37). The singularity is the analytical threshold
     at which the cost of restoring a manifestation exceeds the cost of producing a new one;
     the manifestation is the event that the threshold concerns. The distinction between
     the threshold of manifestation and the manifestation itself (Chapter 37, Definition 37.5
     and the Remarks that follow it) is the analytical form of the distinction between the
     analytical threshold and the event that it marks.

Balance and the relation (Chapter 42). The balance is a measure of the relation between
    an identity and the epistemic light it receives; the relation is what the measure is a
    measure of. The distinction between the measure and the relation (Chapter 42, the
    Remark that the balance is a measure and not a character) is the analytical form of the
    distinction between the analytical measure and the relation it measures.

Conditional architecture on a core (Chapter 43). The framework is a conditional ar-
    chitecture on a core of ten epistemic commitments; the architecture is the analytical
    structure that the framework states, and the core is the set of commitments on which the
    architecture depends. The distinction between the architecture and its core (Chapter 43,
    Principle 43.1) is the analytical form of the distinction between the analytical structure
    and the commitments that ground it. The core is the framework’s own statement of its
    analytical commitments; it is not a claim about what reality contains.

    The six operationalizations are not six different distinctions; they are one distinction,
applied six times. The distinction is between the order of reconstruction and the order of
explanatory dependence; each of the six operationalizations is a particular case of that general
distinction, applied to the particular concepts that the chapter in question introduces. The
reader who has understood the general distinction (Principle 5.1) will recognize it in each of
the six cases; the reader who has not will find the six cases disconnected.
56             Chapter 5. Cognitive Architecture and the Order of Explanatory Dependence


Remark 5.13 (The Six Operationalizations Are Not Arbitrary). The six operationalizations
are not an arbitrary list; they are the places where the distinction does its most important
work in the book. The first two (identity/signature, manifestation/effect) are the places where
the distinction is most easily lost, because identity and signature, and manifestation and effect,
are easily confused. The third and fourth (viability/identity, singularity/manifestation) are the
places where the distinction is most important for the book’s central concept, because viability
and singularity are the concepts the book’s title names. The fifth and sixth (balance/relation,
conditional architecture/core) are the places where the distinction is most important for the
book’s self-description, because the balance criterion and the conditional architecture are the
book’s own statements of what it is. The six are the places where the reader most needs the
distinction, and the framework states their location so that the reader can see the distinction
at work in each of them.

Remark 5.14 (The Distinction Is Analytical, Not Ontological). The distinction between the
order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence is itself an epistemological
distinction. It does not claim that reality is divided into an order of reconstruction and an
order of explanatory dependence; it claims that the structure of an explanation is distinct
from the order of dependence that the explanation represents, and that the two must be kept
apart so that the explanation is not mistaken for what it represents. The distinction is a tool
of the inquiry, not a claim about the furniture of the world. A reader who takes the distinction
as an ontological thesis has misread it; a reader who takes it as an epistemological tool has
read it correctly.


5.7     The Consequence for the Method
The distinction between the two orders has a consequence for the book’s method, and the
consequence is worth stating.
    The method of the book is the method of a finite subject, stated in Chapter 2. Its tests—
the removal test, the reducibility test, and the test of fruitfulness—are tests of the cognitive
architecture, not of the order of explanatory dependence. A reader who applies the tests to
the four columns is testing the analytical structure of explanation; a reader who applies them
to the order of explanatory dependence is testing the order that the explanation represents,
and the test is an assessment of the representation, not of the real order of beings.
    The distinction is what makes the book’s claims assessable. A reader who knows that the
four columns are analytical roles knows what kind of criticism is appropriate: to attack the
four-column principle, the reader must show that an explanation can be complete without one
of the roles, or that a candidate fifth role cannot be reduced to the four. To attack the order
of explanatory dependence, the reader would have to engage a different argument, which is
given in Part IV. To attack any claim about the real order of beings, the reader would have to
engage an argument the present volume does not give—and the framework invites the reader
to engage it on its own terms, not as an inference from the epistemological claims.

Remark 5.15 (The Distinction Is Not a Separation). The distinction between the two orders
is not a separation of two worlds. The order of reconstruction is the order through which what
is becomes intelligible; the order of explanatory dependence is the order that the explanation
represents. The two are distinct, and neither is reducible to the other; but the first is the
condition of possibility of the second. A manifestation is realized in a context before it is known
in a frame; and the frame is the order through which the manifestation becomes intelligible.
The framework keeps the two apart so that the study of cognition is not confused with the
study of the represented order of dependence—but the keeping-apart is not a denial that the
two are related.
5.8. The Epistemological Result of the Distinction                                            57


Remark 5.16 (The Distinction Is Observed Throughout the Book). The distinction is observed
throughout the book. Part II states the four columns and the principles of their relation;
Part III states the structure of epistemic relations; Part IV states the conditions of validity
and adequacy; Part V states the limits, errors, and unknownness; Part VI states the epistemic
economy and the concept of viability. None of these parts develops a doctrine of the real order
of beings. The distinction is what allows each part to state its claims at the strength the
method supports, and it is what allows the reader to assess the claims on their own terms.


5.8    The Epistemological Result of the Distinction
The chapter’s positive contribution is the epistemological result of the distinction between
the two orders, and the present section states that result, so that the reader knows what the
chapter gives, not only what it declines.
    The result has three parts, and each is a contribution to the method of the book.

First part: the framework’s claims are assessable on their own terms. The distinc-
tion makes the framework’s claims assessable without a survey of the real order of beings. The
claims about the order of reconstruction are assessed by the criteria of the method (Chapter 2);
the claims about the order of explanatory dependence are assessed by the criteria of validity
and adequacy (Part IV). The two sets of criteria are distinct, and the distinction is what
allows the framework’s claims to be assessed at the strength they can support.

Second part: the framework’s scope is stated exactly. The distinction makes the
framework’s scope exact. The framework’s claims are claims about the cognitive architecture
and about the order of explanatory dependence as the explanation represents it. They are not
claims about the real order of beings. The scope is stated so that the reader knows what the
framework claims and what it does not; the reader who seeks a claim about the real order of
beings will not find one in this volume, and the framework does not present its epistemological
claims as a substitute.

Third part: the framework’s relation to other inquiries is stated exactly. The
distinction makes the framework’s relation to other inquiries exact. The framework’s claims
can be used by any inquiry that asks about the real order of beings, but the framework does
not itself make such claims, and it does not need to. The other inquiry is free to use the
framework’s analytical vocabulary, to assess its own claims by the framework’s criteria of
validity, and to state its own claims about the real order of beings on its own ground. The
framework’s silence on that order is not a denial of the inquiry; it is the recognition that the
inquiry is a different inquiry, and that the framework’s contribution to it is the analytical
vocabulary, not a conclusion.
Remark 5.17 (The Three Parts Are Not Three Claims). The three parts of the epistemological
result are not three separate claims. They are three aspects of a single result: the framework’s
claims are assessable on their own terms, and the terms are the analytical terms of the cognitive
architecture and of the represented order of explanatory dependence. The first part states
the assessability; the second states the scope; the third states the relation to other inquiries.
The three together are the chapter’s positive contribution, and they are what the distinction
makes possible.
Remark 5.18 (The Result Is Epistemological, Not Metaphysical). The result is epistemological,
not metaphysical. It states what the framework’s claims are, how they are assessed, and how
they relate to other inquiries; it does not state what reality contains, and it does not claim
to. The result is offered at the strength that an epistemological result can have, and it is
58             Chapter 5. Cognitive Architecture and the Order of Explanatory Dependence


what the chapter contributes to the method of the book. A reader who takes the result as a
metaphysical claim has misread it; a reader who takes it as an epistemological result has read
it correctly.

A Question for Reflection
Consider an explanation you accept—of a legal decision, a biological process, a historical event.
Is the explanation a description of the order of reconstruction, or a description of the order of
explanatory dependence that the explanation represents? What does the difference tell you
about the relation between the four columns and the real order of beings?
    And consider the map and the mountain range—the scene that opened the chapter. If a
cartographer claimed that the map’s legend was written on the rock, what would be wrong
with the claim? Is the wrongness a matter of fact, or a matter of category? What does your
answer tell you about the difference between the order of reconstruction and the order of
explanatory dependence, and about why the framework keeps the two apart? Finally, consider
the epistemological result of Section 5.8: can you state the three parts of the result, and can
you assess the framework’s claims at the strength the result supports? A reader who can
5.9. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                              59


answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the
chapter’s three tasks before them.

Part I is complete. Part II defines the four columns, states the four-column principle, and
gives the argument that the four are jointly necessary and jointly sufficient. The chapter that
opens Part II defines the four columns as analytical roles, and gives each a control question by
which a proposed instance can be tested.

               Part II

Architecture of Explanatory Cognition
                                                                                                  63




Chapter 6

The Four Columns Defined

Scope
This chapter defines the four analytical roles that Chapter 1 introduced as the four questions
of explanatory cognition. It defines fixed element, fluid element, governing dynamics, and
context; it gives each a control question, a diagnostic criterion, and a role-diagnosis table by
which a proposed instance can be tested; and it states the distinction between the two kinds
of context that the framework employs. It does not argue that the four roles are necessary,
nor that no fifth is needed; those arguments belong to the chapters that follow.
    The four columns are analytical roles in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes: they are the
structure of an explanation, not the structure of what is explained. The present chapter
defines them, and it adds, at the end, a remark on where each column is developed in the
volume, so that the reader knows that the four roles are analytical and that their development
is distributed across the parts. It also adds a section (Section 6.9) that introduces a formal
language for the four columns and refers the reader to the formal appendix (Appendix .15) for
the full proofs.
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not
a denial but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be said.
Where the chapter speaks of “element,” “effect,” “rule,” “standpoint,” “limit,” or “aptitude,”
these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


6.1     A Scene: Two Explanations of the Same Event
Consider a single event—a bridge that collapsed on a Tuesday morning— and two explanations
of it, given by two inquirers with different questions.
    The first inquirer is an engineer. She asks: why did the bridge fall? Her explanation
identifies the elements: the deck, the piers, the cables, the load, the wind, the temperature,
the concrete. It identifies the medium: the path by which the load reaches the piers, the path
by which the wind reaches the deck, the path by which the temperature reaches the cables. It
identifies the rule: the laws of stress and strain, the codes of design, the regularities of material
behavior. And it identifies the frame: the scale of the analysis, the elements held fixed, the
question the inquiry is asking.
    The second inquirer is a historian. She asks: why was this bridge built here, at this time,
in this style? Her explanation identifies different elements: the city, the river, the engineers,
the budget, the political moment, the architectural fashion. It identifies a different medium:
the path by which the political moment reached the engineers, the path by which the budget
reached the design, the path by which the architectural fashion reached the style. It identifies
a different rule: the regularities of municipal decision-making, the conventions of engineering
64                                                       Chapter 6. The Four Columns Defined


practice, the dynamics of architectural influence. And it identifies a different frame: the scale
of the historical analysis, the elements held fixed, the question the inquiry is asking.
    The two explanations are of the same event, and they are not rivals. The engineer explains
why the bridge fell; the historian explains why the bridge was built as it was. Each explanation
assigns four roles— elements, medium, rule, frame—and each assigns them to different entities,
by different rules, in a different frame. The roles are the same; the content is different. The
roles are the analytical structure of the explanation; the content is the material the structure
is realized in.
    The scene poses a question. What are the four roles, exactly, such that two explanations of
the same event can assign them to different entities and still be complete? The present chapter
answers. Its answer is the four definitions, each with a control question, a diagnostic criterion,
and a role-diagnosis table by which a proposed instance can be tested, and the distinction
between the two kinds of context in which the roles are assigned.

Remark 6.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the four
roles at work in two familiar cases. It does not prove that the four roles are necessary, or that
no fifth is needed; it makes the definitions intelligible before they are stated. The reader who
has followed the scene knows what kind of thing the definitions will name, and knows that the
roles are analytical (they are the same across the two explanations) and that their content is
not (the entities, rules, and frames differ). The arguments for necessity and sufficiency are
given in Chapters 7–11, and the scene carries no weight in them.


6.2     The Four Roles, the Control Question, and the Diagnostic
        Criterion
Before the four definitions are stated, two methodological remarks are worth making, because
they govern how each definition is to be read.
    The first remark concerns the control question. Each definition names a role, and each role
is accompanied by a control question—a question that a proposed instance must be able to
answer if it is to count as an instance of the role. The control question is not a definition; it is
a test. It does not say what the role is; it says what an instance of the role must be able to do.
    The second remark concerns the diagnostic criterion. The control question is answered
by the proposed instance; the diagnostic criterion is what the answer must exhibit. The
distinction is the distinction between asking the question and judging the answer. The control
question without the diagnostic criterion is a question without a standard of judgment; the
diagnostic criterion without the control question is a standard of judgment without a question
to apply it to. The two are stated together so that the reader can both ask the question and
judge the answer.

Remark 6.2 (The Control Question Is a Discipline on the Definitions). The control question
is a discipline on the definitions. A definition that could not be accompanied by a control
question would be a definition that could not be applied; a role that could not be tested would
be a role that could not be distinguished from its rivals. The four definitions of this chapter
are each accompanied by a control question, and the control question is the test by which
the definition is applied. The reader who finds a proposed instance that answers the control
question has found an instance of the role; the reader who finds a proposed instance that does
not answer the control question has found something else. The distinction is the framework’s
way of keeping its definitions usable.

Remark 6.3 (The Diagnostic Criterion Is a Discipline on the Control Question). The diagnostic
criterion is a discipline on the control question. The control question asks the proposed instance
to state a fact; the diagnostic criterion states which fact counts. Without the criterion, two
6.3. Fixed Elements                                                                             65


readers could answer the same control question in incompatible ways and both claim that the
role is assigned. The criterion narrows the answer to what the role requires, and it makes the
assignment assessable. The four criteria stated in the sections that follow are stated at the
strength of stipulations, and they are the tests by which the control questions are answered.


6.3     Fixed Elements
The first role is the fixed element.

Definition 6.1 (Fixed Element). A fixed element is an entity selected as an invariant term
within a given explanatory cognition. Its fixedness is methodological: it is held stable for the
purpose of explaining its relations, and does not by itself imply that the entity is ontologically
immutable. A fixed element is present in the cognition as a node. The formal counterpart of
this definition is given in Appendix .15; see the entry for the fixed-element predicate in that
appendix.

    Two things in this definition deserve emphasis.
    First, the fixedness is methodological, not ontological. To hold an entity fixed in an
explanation is to decide, for the purposes of the explanation, not to vary it. It is not to claim
that the entity cannot vary. A river may be held fixed as a boundary in political geography,
and the same river may be treated as a fluid route of transport in the geography of trade. In
the first frame it is a fixed element; in the second it is not. The fixedness is a role the entity
plays in a frame, not a property the entity has in itself.

Remark 6.4 (Relativity of Fixedness). Fixedness is relative, not absolute. An element may
be fixed in one context and fluid in another. A river is a fixed boundary in the context of
political geography, and a fluid route of transport in the context of trade. This relativity is
the context-dependence principle, which is stated and argued in Chapter 10; here it is only
named. The reader who wishes to see the principle in its own place is directed to Chapter 10;
the reader who wishes to see its application to the fixed element has it here.

    Second, the fixedness of an element within a cognition must not be confused with the
ontological invariance of an identity. The former concerns the conditions of an explanation;
the latter would concern what persists through transformation. The framework of the present
volume treats identity as the invariant an explanatory cognition holds fixed (Chapter 12); it
does not develop a doctrine of what persists in itself. The two notions are distinguished at
length in Chapter 12. For the present, it is enough to see that the fixed element is a role in an
explanation, not a metaphysical posit.

Remark 6.5 (Fixed Element and Ontological Invariance). The distinction between the fixed
element and the ontological invariant is an instance of the distinction that Chapter 5 states
between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence. The fixed
element is the analytical role; the ontological invariant would be the structure of what is. The
framework treats identity as the fixed element (Chapter 12), and it does not claim that what
identity is in itself is exhausted by its being a fixed element. The distinction is the framework’s
way of keeping its analytical claims from becoming claims about what is; the reader who takes
the fixed element as a metaphysical posit has misread the distinction, and the reader who
takes it as an analytical role has read it correctly.

Remark 6.6 (Control Question for a Fixed Element). For any proposed fixed element, ask:
in which context is it held fixed, and what is being explained while it is held fixed? A fixed
element with no answer to the first part is not yet a fixed element of any cognition.
66                                                       Chapter 6. The Four Columns Defined


Remark 6.7 (Diagnostic Criterion for a Fixed Element). A proposed fixed element passes
the criterion when its role in the explanation meets two conditions: (i) the explanation treats
the entity as constant while the relations are explained, and (ii) if the entity were allowed to
vary, the explanation’s answer to the question it addresses would change. The two conditions
are the test; an entity that meets them is a fixed element, an entity that fails them is not.

6.3.1    Role-Diagnosis Table for the Fixed Element
The following table collects the items by which a proposed fixed element is diagnosed. The
table is the operational form of Definition 6.1, the control question, and the diagnostic criterion.

Item                        Content
Definition                  An entity selected as an invariant term within a given explanatory
                            cognition.
Diagnostic question         In which context is it held fixed, and what is being explained
                            while it is held fixed?
Mark of presence            The explanation treats the entity as constant while the relations
                            are explained, and varying it would change the answer to the
                            question.
Mark of absence             The explanation varies the entity with the relations, or varying
                            the entity would not change the answer to the question.
Example                     The deck, the piers, and the cables in the engineer’s explanation.
Common error of diagno- Treating an entity as fixed because it is mentioned, without
sis                     checking whether the explanation holds it constant or whether
                        varying it would change the answer.


Remark 6.8 (A Borderline Case for a Fixed Element). A borderline case is the price of a
commodity in an economic explanation of a market’s behavior. The price is sometimes held
fixed (the explanation treats it as a parameter, and the quantities are explained relative to
it), and sometimes treated as fluid (the explanation treats it as varying, and the market’s
adjustment is explained relative to it). The criterion resolves the case: the price is a fixed
element when the explanation’s question is about quantities given a price, and it is a fluid
element when the explanation’s question is about the price’s adjustment. The borderline case
is not a contradiction; it is a case in which the entity’s role depends on the question, and the
criterion’s first condition (the question being addressed) is what resolves it.
Example 6.1 (The Engineer and the Historian). In the engineer’s explanation, the deck, the
piers, and the cables are fixed elements. In the historian’s explanation, the city, the river, and
the engineers are fixed elements. The same event, two explanations, different fixed elements:
the role is the same, the content is different.
     The definition and its remarks are summarized in the control question and the diagnostic
criterion: a fixed element is whatever an explanation holds invariant, and the criterion by
which it is recognized is the change in the explanation’s answer if the entity were allowed to
vary. The role is defined by what the explanation does with the entity, not by what the entity
is in itself.


6.4     Fluid Elements
The second role is the fluid element.
6.4. Fluid Elements                                                                              67


Definition 6.2 (Fluid Element). A fluid element is an entity that conveys effect. A fluid
element is an edge in the network of cognition, connecting fixed elements to one another and
explaining their behavior in one another’s presence. The formal counterpart of this definition
is given in Appendix .15; see the entry for the fluid-element predicate in that appendix.
    The word “fluid” in this definition does not mean “liquid.” It means “conveying”: an
element is fluid in the framework’s sense if it carries the effect of one fixed element to another.
Language, information, force, signals, processes—all of these can be fluid elements in the
appropriate context. The framework’s use of the word is fixed by the definition and by nothing
else.
Remark 6.9 (The Fluid Element Is Not the Effect). The fluid element is not the effect itself;
it is what carries the effect. The distinction will matter when Part III turns to epistemic light,
which is the framework’s name for the fluid element in its most general role. For the present,
the distinction is the difference between a message and the meaning it carries, between a wire
and the current it conducts, between a language and the thought it conveys. The fluid element
is the message, the wire, the language; the effect is the meaning, the current, the thought. The
framework’s claim is that an explanation of how one thing reaches another must invoke the
carrier, not merely the effect.
Remark 6.10 (The Fluid Element as Condition of Possibility). A fluid element is the condition
of possibility of cognizing relations. Without a fluid element, fixed elements are disconnected
nodes, not a network of cognition. The argument for this claim—that no explanation of how
one fixed element bears on another is complete without a fluid element—is given in Chapter 8,
the conveyor principle. Here the claim is stated as part of the definition’s import.
Remark 6.11 (Control Question for a Fluid Element). For any proposed fluid element, ask:
what does it convey, and between which fixed elements? If it conveys nothing between anything,
it is not functioning as a fluid element in that cognition.
Remark 6.12 (Diagnostic Criterion for a Fluid Element). A proposed fluid element passes the
criterion when its role in the explanation meets two conditions: (i) the explanation identifies
the entity as the means by which an effect of one fixed element reaches another, and (ii) if the
entity were absent, the explanation’s account of the effect’s transmission would be missing a
step. The two conditions are the test; an entity that meets them is a fluid element, an entity
that fails them is not.

6.4.1    Role-Diagnosis Table for the Fluid Element

Item                        Content
Definition                  An entity that conveys effect, connecting fixed elements to one
                            another.
Diagnostic question         What does it convey, and between which fixed elements?
Mark of presence            The explanation identifies the entity as the means by which an
                            effect reaches from one fixed element to another, and without it
                            the transmission would be missing a step.
Mark of absence             The explanation identifies no effect transmitted by the entity, or
                            the transmission is accounted for without it.
Example                     The load path, the wind path, and the thermal path in the
                            engineer’s explanation.
Common error of diagno- Treating the effect itself (the meaning, the current, the thought)
sis                     as the fluid element, rather than the carrier of the effect.
68                                                      Chapter 6. The Four Columns Defined


Remark 6.13 (A Borderline Case for a Fluid Element). A borderline case is a promise in an
explanation of why a transaction occurred. The promise is sometimes a fluid element (it carries
the effect of one party’s commitment to the other party’s expectation, and the transaction is
explained relative to it), and sometimes a governing dynamics (the rule by which the parties
are bound in the transaction). The criterion resolves the case: the promise is a fluid element
when the explanation’s question is about the transmission of the commitment between the
parties, and it is a governing dynamics when the explanation’s question is about the rule that
governs the parties’ behavior. The borderline case is not a contradiction; it is a case in which
the entity’s role depends on the question, and the criterion’s first condition (the explanation
identifying the transmission) is what resolves it.
Example 6.2 (The Engineer and the Historian). In the engineer’s explanation, the load path,
the wind path, and the thermal path are fluid elements. In the historian’s explanation, the
political moment, the budget, and the architectural fashion are fluid elements. The same event,
two explanations, different fluid elements: the role is the same, the content is different.
   The fluid element is the second column. It is what an explanation invokes when it says
how one thing reaches another. The definition is generic: it names the role, not the entity
that plays the role.
Remark 6.14 (The Fluid Element Is Defined Generically Here). The definition of the fluid
element is generic: it names the role, not the entity that plays the role. The framework’s claim
is that epistemic light plays this role in its most general form (Chapter 15), and that other
fluid elements—language, force, signals, processes—are specific conveyors that appear in the
mode of a particular cognitive context (Chapter 17). The present chapter defines the role; the
chapters that follow develop its specific forms. The distinction between the generic role and
its specific forms is an instance of the distinction that Chapter 5 states between the analytical
role and the material in which it is realized; the role is analytical, and its specific forms are
the material in which the role is instantiated.


6.5    Governing Dynamics
The third role is governing dynamics.
Definition 6.3 (Governing Dynamics). Governing dynamics is a rule that explains how fluid
elements affect fixed elements. Dynamics determines the behavioral pattern of the network of
cognition. The formal counterpart of this definition is given in Appendix .15; see the entry for
the dynamics predicate in that appendix.
    Governing dynamics is not itself an element. It is a rule of effect. The distinction is not
always obvious, because in some cognitions a fluid element and a rule may coincide: a custom,
for example, is both “a thing that conveys” and “a rule of effect.” The framework’s way of
handling the coincidence is the one it uses everywhere: the role an entity plays in a given
cognition decides how it is classified there, and the same entity may play both roles in different
cognitions.
Remark 6.15 (The Rule and the Element: A Custom). A custom is a useful example of
the coincidence of a fluid element and a governing dynamics. In one frame, the custom is a
thing that conveys: it carries the effect of one generation on the next, or of one community on
another. In another frame, the custom is a rule of effect: it determines how the members of
the community behave in one another’s presence. The same custom, two roles, neither role
more real than the other. The framework’s claim is that the roles are distinct as roles, and
that the same entity may play both roles in different frames; the distinction is the distinction
between what the entity does and what the entity is, and the framework keeps it throughout.
6.6. Context                                                                                          69


Remark 6.16 (Control Question for a Governing Dynamics). For any proposed governing
dynamics, ask: what kind of change does it explain, and what would count as a violation of
it? A rule that no event could violate explains nothing.

Remark 6.17 (Diagnostic Criterion for a Governing Dynamics). A proposed governing
dynamics passes the criterion when its role in the explanation meets two conditions: (i) the
explanation identifies the entity as the rule that the fluid elements’ effects obey, and (ii) the
explanation specifies what would count as a departure from the rule. The two conditions are
the test; an entity that meets them is a governing dynamics, an entity that fails them is not.


6.5.1    Role-Diagnosis Table for the Governing Dynamics


Item                          Content
Definition                    A rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements.
Diagnostic question           What kind of change does it explain, and what would count as
                              a violation of it?
Mark of presence              The explanation identifies the entity as the rule the fluid elements’
                              effects obey, and specifies what would depart from it.
Mark of absence               The explanation invokes no rule, or the rule is stated so vaguely
                              that nothing could count as a departure from it.
Example                       The laws of stress and strain in the engineer’s explanation.
Common error of diagno- Treating a mere regularity (a pattern noted) as a governing
sis                     dynamics, without specifying what would count as a violation.


Remark 6.18 (A Borderline Case for a Governing Dynamics). A borderline case is a habit in
an explanation of how an agent acts. The habit is sometimes a governing dynamics (the rule
that the agent’s actions follow), and sometimes a fluid element (the means by which a prior
decision reaches the present action). The criterion resolves the case: the habit is a governing
dynamics when the explanation’s question is about the pattern the actions follow, and it is
a fluid element when the explanation’s question is about the transmission of the decision to
the action. The borderline case is not a contradiction; it is a case in which the entity’s role
depends on the question, and the criterion’s second condition (the specification of what would
count as a departure) is what resolves it.

Example 6.3 (The Engineer and the Historian). In the engineer’s explanation, the laws of
stress and strain are the governing dynamics. In the historian’s explanation, the regularities of
municipal decision-making are the governing dynamics. The same event, two explanations,
different governing dynamics: the role is the same, the content is different.

   The third column is the rule. It is what an explanation invokes when it says not merely that
one thing reaches another, but how the reaching is governed: what regularities the connection
obeys, and what would count as a departure from them. Without such a rule, the network of
cognition shows that things are connected, but not how the connection behaves.


6.6     Context
The fourth role is context.
70                                                      Chapter 6. The Four Columns Defined


Definition 6.4 (Context). A context is the background in which cognition occurs. Context
determines what counts as a fixed element, what counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics
governs. The formal counterpart of this definition is given in Appendix .15; see the entry for
the context predicate in that appendix.

   Context is not itself an element. It is the condition of possibility of defining elements. The
framework’s fourth column is not one more item on the list; it is what makes the list possible.
Context is the frame within which the other three columns take the specific content they have.

Remark 6.19 (Context Is Not an Element Among Elements). The context is easily misread as
a fourth element, alongside the fixed elements, the fluid element, and the governing dynamics.
The misreading is worth distinguishing. The context is not an element that is related to the
other elements; it is the frame in which the other elements are individuated and the rule is
applied. A reader who treats the context as an element will find the framework’s claim that
the context is the condition of possibility of the elements puzzling; a reader who treats it as
the frame will find the claim clear. The distinction is the distinction between what is in the
frame and what the frame is; the framework keeps it throughout.

Remark 6.20 (Control Question for a Context). For any proposed context, ask: what limit
or aptitude does it set for what can appear in it? A context that sets no limit and favors no
appearance is an empty label.

Remark 6.21 (Diagnostic Criterion for a Context). A proposed context passes the criterion
when its role in the explanation meets two conditions: (i) the explanation’s partition of entities
into fixed and fluid, and the rule it applies, depend on the context’s limits or aptitudes, and
(ii) if the context were replaced by a different one, the partition or the rule would change. The
two conditions are the test; a context that meets them is a context, a context that fails them
is not.

Item                        Content
Definition                  The background in which cognition occurs, determining what
                            counts as fixed, what counts as fluid, and which dynamics gov-
                            erns.
Diagnostic question         What limit or aptitude does it set for what can appear in it?
Mark of presence            The explanation’s partition and rule depend on the context’s
                            limits or aptitudes, and a different context would change them.
Mark of absence             The context is named but sets no limit, favors no appearance,
                            and changing it would leave the partition and rule unchanged.
Example                     The physics of the bridge in the engineer’s explanation; the
                            history of the bridge in the historian’s explanation.
Common error of diagno- Treating the context as one more element to be related, rather
sis                     than as the frame in which the other elements are individuated.


Remark 6.22 (A Borderline Case for a Context). A borderline case is a legal jurisdiction in
an explanation of a contract’s validity. The jurisdiction is sometimes a context (the frame
within which the parties, the contract, and the rule of validity are assigned), and sometimes
a fixed element (one of the entities whose relations the explanation traces). The criterion
6.7. The Four Roles Together                                                                     71


resolves the case: the jurisdiction is a context when the explanation’s question is about what
counts as a contract within it, and it is a fixed element when the explanation’s question is
about the jurisdiction’s relations to the parties. The borderline case is not a contradiction; it is
a case in which the entity’s role depends on the question, and the criterion’s second condition
(the change under a different context) is what resolves it.
    The word “context” is used in this book in two senses, and the distinction is kept throughout.

The cognitive context. A cognitive context, or frame, is any background that fixes a
partition of entities into fixed and fluid, together with a governing dynamics. A negotiation, a
city plan, and a legal case are cognitive contexts. A cognitive context is fixed by the question
being asked, and there are indefinitely many of them; the infinity of cognitive contexts is
argued in Chapter 11.

The existential context. An existential context is the setting in which a manifestation
is realized, with the capacity and the constraints of that setting. The present volume uses
the notion only to distinguish it from the cognitive context; the existential context is not
developed as an ontology here. The distinction between the order of reconstruction and the
order of explanatory dependence is stated in Chapter 5; the existential context is named here
to be marked off, not to be developed.
Remark 6.23 (Two Kinds of Context). A cognitive context is fixed by the question being
asked. An existential context is fixed by the identity and the receiving setting, not by the
question. An existential context does not require a cognizing subject in order to be real: a
manifestation may be realized in a setting without being known, observed, or reconstructed by
any subject. A cognitive context conditions the knowledge of a manifestation; an existential
context conditions its realization. The present volume is concerned with the first; the second
is named here to be marked off.
Example 6.4 (The Engineer and the Historian). The engineer’s context is the physics of the
bridge: the elements held fixed, the laws applied, the scale adopted. The historian’s context is
the history of the bridge: the elements held fixed, the regularities applied, the scale adopted.
The same event, two contexts: the role is the same, the content is different.
    The fourth column is the frame. It is what an explanation invokes when it says not merely
how something is connected and by what rule, but from what standpoint the connection and
the rule are posed. Without a frame, the same entities can be partitioned into fixed and fluid
in different ways, and the rule alone does not say which partition is intended.
    The distinction between the cognitive context and the existential context is a distinction
between two orders, not a separation of two worlds. The existential context is the order of
realization; the cognitive context is the order of inquiry. The two are distinct, and neither is
reducible to the other; but the first is the condition of possibility of the second. A manifestation
is realized in a setting before it is known in a frame; and the frame is the order through which
the setting becomes intelligible. The framework keeps the two apart so that the study of
cognition is not confused with the study of realization—but the keeping-apart is not a denial
that the two are related. The existential context is the ground of the cognitive context, and
the cognitive context is the intelligibility of the existential context. The distinction is the
distinction of Chapter 5, applied to the word “context.”


6.7     The Four Roles Together
The four columns are not four items on a list. They are four roles in a single structure. The
fixed elements are what is related; the fluid element is the medium of relation; the governing
72                                                     Chapter 6. The Four Columns Defined


dynamics is the rule of the medium; the context is the frame in which all three take their
specific content.
