6.7.1     A Single Example with All Four Roles
The following example identifies all four roles simultaneously, so that the reader can see the
structure in a single explanation. The example is the engineer’s explanation of the collapsed
bridge.
    The question. Why did the bridge fall?
    The fixed elements. The deck, the piers, the cables, the load. These are the entities the
explanation holds invariant while it explains their relations.
    The fluid elements. The load path (the path by which the load reaches the piers), the
wind path (the path by which the wind reaches the deck), and the thermal path (the path by
which the temperature reaches the cables). These are the carriers of effect between the fixed
elements.
    The governing dynamics. The laws of stress and strain, the codes of design, the regularities
of material behavior. These are the rules the fluid elements’ effects obey, and the explanation
specifies what would count as a departure from them (a load that exceeds the design capacity;
a wind that exceeds the design tolerance).
    The context. The physics of the bridge, with the scale of the analysis (the whole bridge, or
the span between two piers), the choice of elements held fixed (the load, or the wind, or the
temperature), and the question the inquiry is asking (why the bridge fell). The context is the
frame within which the four roles take their specific content.
    The four roles are identified in a single explanation, and each role meets its diagnostic
criterion: the deck is a fixed element (varying it would change the answer); the load path is a
6.7. The Four Roles Together                                                                    73


fluid element (without it, the transmission would be missing a step); the laws of stress and
strain are a governing dynamics (they state the rule, and what would depart from it); the
physics of the bridge is a context (a different context would change the partition and the rule).

Remark 6.24 (The Example and the Role-Diagnosis Tables). The example shows the four
roles in a single explanation, and the role-diagnosis tables (Sections 6.3.1 through 6.6.1) show
how each role is diagnosed. A reader who wishes to test a proposed instance of a role can use
the table; a reader who wishes to see the four roles in a single example can use the present
section. The two are complementary: the tables state the diagnosis role by role; the example
shows the diagnosis at work on a single explanation.

6.7.2    One Element, Two Roles: The Custom in Two Contexts
The example of the custom is worth analyzing in full, in two contexts, so that the role-change
is visible and so that the reader can see why the change is not a contradiction.
    Context 1: The historian of a community. The question is: how did the community’s
practice of hospitality pass from one generation to the next? The custom is a fluid element: it
is the means by which the practice of one generation reaches the next. The fixed elements
are the successive generations; the governing dynamics is the regularity of transmission (the
custom is transmitted by imitation and by explicit instruction); the context is the historian’s
question, which fixes the generations as fixed elements and the transmission as the object of
explanation. The custom’s role in this context is fluid.
    Context 2: The anthropologist of the community’s internal life. The question is: why do
the members of the community behave toward strangers in the way they do? The custom
is a governing dynamics: it is the rule by which the members’ behavior toward strangers
is governed. The fixed elements are the members; the fluid element is the expectation that
passes between them (the expectation of hospitality, carried by the custom’s prescriptions);
the context is the anthropologist’s question, which fixes the members as fixed elements and the
rule of behavior as the object of explanation. The custom’s role in this context is governing
dynamics.
    The custom is the same entity in both contexts. It is a fluid element in Context 1 and a
governing dynamics in Context 2. The change is not a contradiction, because the role is not a
property of the entity; it is a position in an explanatory structure, and the structure is fixed by
the question. The criterion for the fluid element (Remark 6.12) is met in Context 1: without
the custom, the transmission’s step is missing. The criterion for the governing dynamics
(Remark 6.17) is met in Context 2: the custom is the rule, and a departure from it (a member
who refuses hospitality) would count as a violation. The same entity meets both criteria, in
different contexts, without either criterion being violated.

Remark 6.25 (Role-Change Is Not Contradiction). The example of the custom shows that
role-change is not contradiction. The same entity can be a fluid element in one context and
a governing dynamics in another, because the role is a position in an explanatory structure,
not a property of the entity. The role-diagnosis tables (Sections 6.3.1 through 6.6.1) make the
diagnosis explicit role by role; the present example shows the diagnosis at work on a single
entity in two contexts. A reader who takes the role as a property of the entity will find the
role-change puzzling; a reader who takes it as a position in a structure will find it clear.

6.7.3    Distinctness and Separability
Distinctness does not imply absolute separability. Two analytical roles may be instantiated
by the same entity, or one role may constrain the content of another (the rules of a cognition
may be constrained by the structure of its elements), without the roles thereby becoming
conceptually identical. The four roles are distinct as roles; they may be carried by fewer than
74                                                       Chapter 6. The Four Columns Defined


four entities in a given cognition. A custom may be both a fluid element and a governing
dynamics, depending on the question the cognition asks; a context may be both the frame of
one cognition and an element of another. The framework’s claim is that the roles are distinct
as roles, not that they are separate as entities. The formal counterpart of this distinction is
Theorem .3 in Appendix .15.

6.7.4     The Four Roles and the Four Questions
The four roles are not the four questions of Chapter 1, though they correspond to them. The
four questions are what an explanation must answer; the four roles are what an explanation
must assign. The questions are asked of the explanation; the roles are assigned by the
explanation. A reader who takes the roles as the questions, or the questions as the roles, will
find the relationship between Chapters 1 and 6 puzzling; a reader who keeps them apart will
find the relationship clear. The distinction is the distinction between what is asked and what
is assigned; the framework keeps it throughout.
    The four roles are analytical tools. They describe the structure of an explanation, not the
furniture of the world. The distinction matters, because the analytical description is not the
whole of what can be said about what is explained. The structure is the order through which
what is explained becomes intelligible; but the order is not the explained, and the explanation
is not the whole of what is explained. The four columns are the framework’s way of describing
the order; they do not claim that the order is self-sufficient, and they do not claim that nothing
lies beyond it.

Remark 6.26 (Where Each Column Is Developed). The four columns are analytical roles;
their development is distributed across the parts of the volume, not gathered in one chapter.

     • The fixed elements are developed in Chapters 12–13 (identity and manifestation).

     • The fluid element is developed in Chapters 15–17 (epistemic light: the medium of relation,
       the active structure of legibility, the foundational fluid element and its specific forms).

     • The governing dynamics are developed where the rules of the specific cognitive contexts
       are stated: in Chapter 13, on the capacity and constraints of the receiving context; in
       Chapter 21, on the criteria of context validity; and in the later parts of the volume,
       where the rules of the specific contexts are stated in the form the context requires. The
       framework does not gather the rules of the cognitive contexts in a single chapter, because
       the rules differ across contexts.

     • The context is developed in Chapters 10–11 (the cognitive context and the infinity of
       contexts) and in Chapter 14 (the distinction between context and perspective).

The distribution is not a deficiency; it is what the four roles are. Because the four columns are
analytical roles, their development is the articulation of the roles in the specific contexts in
which they are put to work, and the articulation is distributed across the parts.

Remark 6.27 (The Four Roles and the Distinction of Chapter 5). The four roles are
analytical, not ontological (Chapter 5, Principle 5.1). The distinction between the order
of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence is the distinction between the
structure of an explanation and the order of dependence the explanation represents; the four
roles are the analytical structure, and the later chapters’ specific instantiations of each role
(identity/manifestation, epistemic light, rules of cognitive contexts, cognitive context) are the
material in which the analytical structure is realized. The reader who has understood the
distinction of Chapter 5 will recognize it in each of the roles; the reader who has not will find
the four roles, and their distribution across the volume, disconnected.
6.8. The Definitions and the Method                                                            75


6.8     The Definitions and the Method
The definitions of this chapter are offered at the strength the method of Chapter 2 allows.
They are (A): they are stipulations of the framework’s vocabulary, not argued conclusions.
Their justification is their fruitfulness in the chapters that follow, and their cost is stated
where the cost is relevant.
    The argument that the four are jointly necessary, and the estimate that they are jointly
sufficient, are given in Chapter 7. The chapter that follows this one states the four-column
principle (Chapter 7); the chapters after that state the conveyor principle (Chapter 8), non-
sequential connectivity (Chapter 9), and context-dependence (Chapter 10). The definitions of
the present chapter are the vocabulary those arguments use; they are stated here so that the
arguments can be stated there. The formal reconstruction of the four columns, and the formal
proofs of the four-column principle, are given in Appendix .15; the present chapter states the
informal vocabulary, and the appendix states the formal system.

Remark 6.28 (The Definitions Are Stipulations). The four definitions are stipulations of the
framework’s vocabulary. A reader who rejects one of them has proposed another vocabulary,
and the framework can say where its own vocabulary was stipulated. The framework does not
claim that its vocabulary is the only possible one; it claims that its vocabulary is the one its
arguments need, and that the arguments are stated so as to be assessed without any other
vocabulary. A reader who proposes a different vocabulary has proposed a different framework,
and the comparison of the two frameworks is a different inquiry; the present chapter states
the framework’s vocabulary at the strength a stipulation can have.

Remark 6.29 (What the Chapter Has Done). The chapter has done six things. It has defined
the four analytical roles that the four questions of Chapter 1 correspond to. It has given each
role a control question, a diagnostic criterion, and a role-diagnosis table by which a proposed
instance can be tested. It has distinguished the two kinds of context that the framework
employs. It has analyzed a single example in which all four roles are identified simultaneously,
and a single example (the custom) in which one element takes two roles in two contexts. It
has stated, in a dedicated remark, where each column is developed in the volume. And it has
introduced, in Section 6.9, a formal language for the four columns, and referred the reader
to Appendix .15 for the full formal system and the proofs of the four-column principle. The
chapter has not argued that the four are necessary, and it has not argued that no fifth is needed;
those arguments are the work of Chapters 7–11. The chapter’s contribution is the framework’s
vocabulary, stated at the strength a stipulation can have, and the control questions, diagnostic
criteria, and role-diagnosis tables that make the vocabulary usable.


6.9     A Formal Language for the Four Columns
The definitions of the four columns are stated in philosophical prose, and they are sufficient
for the arguments of Chapters 7–11. But the four-column principle—the claim that the four
roles are jointly necessary and jointly sufficient—invites a more precise formulation, and a
more precise formulation is what a formal language can supply. The present section introduces
the formal language at the level of detail that the philosophical reader requires, and it refers
the reader to Appendix .15 for the full system, the definitions, the axioms, and the proofs.

The sorts of the language. The formal language has four principal sorts, corresponding
to the four categories of the material in which the four roles are assigned:

   • E: elements;

   • R: rules;
76                                                       Chapter 6. The Four Columns Defined


     • C: contexts;

     • X: explanations.

The fixed elements and the fluid elements are both elements (E), distinguished by the role
they play in an explanation; the governing dynamics is a rule (R); the context is a context (C);
and the explanation is the structured object (X) in which the roles are assigned. The four
principal sorts thus respect the distinction, stated in Chapter 5, between the analytical roles
and the material in which they are realized: the four columns are roles, and the four principal
sorts are the categories of the material in which the roles are assigned.
    The formal language also has four auxiliary sorts, which are used in the finitude axioms
(Group F of Appendix .15) and in the application predicate:

     • S: states;

     • P: subjects or cognizers;

     • A: acts or reconstructions;

     • T: times.

The auxiliary sorts are not a fifth column and not a fifth kind of entity; they are the sorts
needed to state the finitude claims of Chapter 3 (subjects, acts, times) and the state parameter
of the application predicate (states). The distinction between principal and auxiliary sorts is
stated here so that the reader who has followed the philosophical prose of this chapter meets,
in the formal system, the same four principal sorts, and so that the addition of the auxiliary
sorts is visible as an addition, not as a silent change of the language.

The predicates. The formal language introduces, for each of the four columns, a predicate
that assigns the role to an element in an explanation:

     • InF (e, x): the element e is a fixed element of the explanation x;

     • InΦ (e, x): the element e is a fluid element of the explanation x;

     • Dyn(x, r): the rule r is the governing dynamics of the explanation x;

     • Ctx(x, c): the context c is the context of the explanation x.

The predicates are the formal counterparts of the control questions of Section 6.2: each
predicate is the formal statement of the role, and the control question is the test by which a
proposed instance is assigned to the role. The diagnostic criteria of Remarks 6.7–6.21 are the
informal counterparts of the conditions under which the predicates are applied; the formal
system states the conditions as part of its definitions and axioms.

The completeness predicate. The formal language also introduces a predicate of com-
pleteness, Complete(x), which is the formal counterpart of the methodological commitment,
stated in Chapter 2, that we can recognize an explanatory failure when we see one. The
predicate is primitive: it is not defined in terms of the four roles, and it is the commitment on
which the argument for necessity rests. The formal language states the relationship between
the primitive completeness predicate and the structural completeness of an explanation (the
condition under which all four roles are assigned, and the roles are coherent with one another)
in the axioms of Appendix .15.
    The formal language is stated at the strength of a stipulation, not at the strength of a
proof. It is offered as the framework’s way of making the four-column principle precise; it does
not claim to be the only possible formalization, and it does not claim that the formalization is
6.9. A Formal Language for the Four Columns                                                      77


a substitute for the philosophical argument. The formalization is a tool, and the philosophical
argument is the substance. The reader who wishes to see the formal system in full—the sorts
(principal and auxiliary), the predicates, the axioms, the definitions of necessity and sufficiency,
and the four theorems (necessity, sufficiency, distinctness, and consistency)—is directed to
Appendix .15. The reader who wishes to see the philosophical argument, in its own terms, is
directed to Chapter 7.




Remark 6.30 (The Formal Language and the Distinction of Chapter 5). The formal language
is an instance of the distinction that Chapter 5 states between the order of reconstruction and
the order of explanatory dependence. The four columns are analytical roles; the four principal
sorts of the formal language are the categories of the material in which the roles are assigned.
The formal language does not say that the four principal sorts are four kinds of entity; it says
that the four roles are assigned to entities of those sorts. The distinction is the distinction
between the role and the material; the formal language keeps it, and the reader who takes the
four sorts as a metaphysical division has misread the formalization.




Remark 6.31 (The Formal Language and the Control Question). The formal predicates are
the formal counterparts of the control questions. The control question for a fixed element is:
in which context is it held fixed, and what is being explained? The formal counterpart is the
predicate InF (e, x), which assigns the element e to the fixed-element role in the explanation x,
together with the predicate Ctx(x, c), which assigns the context c to the explanation x. The
two predicates together state what the control question asks: the element is held fixed in the
explanation, and the explanation is posed in the context. The formal language thus makes the
control question precise, without replacing it: the control question is the test, and the formal
predicate is the statement of the role that the test assigns.




Remark 6.32 (The Formal Language and the Reader). The formal language is offered for
the reader who wishes to see the four-column principle in a precise form, and for the reader
who wishes to assess the framework at the level of its formal structure. It is not offered as a
requirement: the philosophical reader who is content with the prose of Sections 6.3–6.6 has
the definitions, the control questions, the role-diagnosis tables, and the distinctions, and does
not need the formal language. The formal language is a supplement, not a substitute; it is the
framework’s way of being assessable at the level of its formal structure, and it is offered at the
strength that a supplement can have.

A Question for Reflection
Take an explanation you accept—of a historical event, a biological process, a legal decision.
Can you identify, in that explanation, the four roles as this chapter has defined them, and can
you apply the diagnostic criterion of each role to a proposed instance? Which role is most
easily identified, and which is most easily overlooked? What does the overlooking tell you
about the structure of the explanation you have taken?
    And consider the single example with all four roles (Section 6.7.1): can you identify the
four roles in a different explanation of your own choosing, and can you apply the role-diagnosis
tables to each? Finally, consider the custom in two contexts (Section 6.7.2): can you give a
further example of an entity that plays two roles in two contexts, and can you show, using the
diagnostic criteria, that the role-change is not a contradiction? A reader who can answer all
three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s
three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the four-column principle: the argument that the four roles are jointly
necessary, and the estimate that they are jointly sufficient. The chapter after that states and
proves the conveyor principle, which supplies the proof of necessity for the fluid element. The
formal reconstruction of the four columns, and the formal proofs of the four-column principle,
are given in Appendix .15.
                                                                                                   81




Chapter 7

The Four-Column Principle

Scope
This chapter argues that the four roles defined in the previous chapter are jointly necessary
for any explanatory cognition, and offers an estimate that they are jointly sufficient. It states
the four-column principle, gives the removal test for necessity, gives the reducibility test for
sufficiency, and argues that the four roles are distinct.
    The chapter is written after the rewrites of Chapters 5 and 6, and it reflects them. The
principle is stated as analytical, not ontological, in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes (Principle 5.1);
the distinction between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence
is the distinction between the structure of an explanation and the order that the explanation
represents, and the four-column principle is a claim about the first. The four roles whose
necessity and sufficiency the chapter argues are the roles that Chapter 6 defined and, in its
Remark on where each column is developed, distributed across the volume (Remark 6.26).
Section 7.8 states the formal counterparts of the three arguments and refers the reader to
Appendix .15 for the full formal proofs.
    Its claims are analytical; where the chapter is silent on questions of value or purpose, the
silence is not a denial but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole of what
can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “completeness,” “removal,” “reducibility,” “role,” or
“distinctness,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter
and in the previous chapter.


7.1     The Question
An explanation, we said in the previous chapter, assigns four roles: fixed elements, fluid
element, governing dynamics, context. The definitions were given, and a control question was
supplied for each. But two questions remain unanswered.
    First: are the four roles necessary? Could an explanation omit one of them and still
be complete? If a role can be omitted without loss, then it is not a column of explanatory
cognition, but a convenience of some explanations.
    Second: are the four roles sufficient? Could an explanation require a fifth role that the four
do not cover? If a fifth role is needed, the framework is incomplete, and the book’s architecture
must be revised.
    This chapter addresses both questions. The first it answers by argument: the four roles
are necessary, and their necessity can be shown by removing each in turn and observing what
remains. The second it answers by estimate: the four roles are sufficient, in the sense that
every candidate fifth role examined so far has been reducible to one of the four. The estimate
is offered as an estimate, not as a proof, because the possibility of a new kind of explanation
cannot be ruled out in advance. The chapter states in advance what would refute the estimate.
82                                                      Chapter 7. The Four-Column Principle


7.2     The Four-Column Principle
The two questions are answered together by a single principle.

Principle 7.1 (The Four-Column Principle). Necessity (T). Every explanatory cognition
requires the simultaneous presence of four columns: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing
dynamics, and context. If any one of the four is absent, the cognition is incomplete as
an explanation. The formal counterpart of the necessity half is stated in Theorem .1 of
Appendix .15.
    Sufficiency (E). No fifth column is needed among the candidates that have been examined :
every candidate fifth column in the standard list (purpose, time, observer, normative dimension)
reduces to one of the four. The formal counterpart of the sufficiency half is stated in Theorem .2
of Appendix .15, whose content is restricted to the standard candidates and is stated precisely
in Section 7.8, below.

     The principle has two halves with different statuses. The necessity half is (T): it is argued,
and the argument is given below. The sufficiency half is (E): it is an estimate, supported by a
test, and it is subject to revision if a candidate fifth column is found that cannot be reduced
to any of the four. The two halves are stated together because they concern a single claim
about the analytical structure of explanatory cognition, but the reader is invited to assess
them separately.
     The principle is not a stipulation. It is not a definition of “explanation” by fiat. The
necessity half follows from what an explanation is asked to do, as the removal test shows.
The sufficiency half is an estimate about the space of possible explanations, and it is offered
at exactly that strength. The phrase “among the candidates that have been examined” is
deliberate: it states the scope of the estimate, and it directs the reader to Section 7.4 for the
list of candidates and to Section 7.8 for the formal statement of the estimate’s scope.

Remark 7.1 (The Principle Is Analytical, Not Ontological). The principle is a claim about
what an explanation must contain. It is not a claim about what kinds of entity reality contains.
The distinction between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence
was stated in Chapter 5 (Principle 5.1), and it is observed here. The distinction is the one that
Chapter 5 uses, in its Section on where the distinction operates, to distinguish the analytical
structure of an explanation from the order of dependence that the explanation represents; the
four-column principle is the abstract statement of what those operationalizations instantiate.
A reader who takes the four-column principle as a claim about the furniture of the world has
misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim about the structure of explanation has read it
correctly.

Remark 7.2 (The Roles Whose Sufficiency Is Estimated). The sufficiency half of the principle
is an estimate about the four roles that Chapter 6 defined. The roles are not a bare list;
they are the analytical structure whose development Chapter 6 distributes across the volume
(Chapter 6, Remark 6.26): the fixed elements are developed in Chapters 12–13, the fluid
element in Chapters 15–17, the governing dynamics in the chapters that state the rules of the
specific cognitive contexts, and the context in Chapters 10–11 and 14. The estimate’s force is
the force of the structure those chapters articulate; a reader who rejects one of the developments
has a reason to question the sufficiency half, in the respect in which the development matters.


7.3     Proof of Necessity: The Removal Test
The argument for necessity proceeds by removing each column in turn, and observing what
remains. If what remains is a recognizable explanatory failure, the column is necessary. If
what remains is a complete explanation, the column is not.
7.3. Proof of Necessity: The Removal Test                                                      83


    The argument depends, as Chapter 2 stated, on a criterion of explanatory failure that is
independent of the four columns. If the criterion were stated in terms of the four columns, the
argument would be circular: it would assume the four columns to prove that the four columns
are necessary. The present chapter therefore restates the criterion in a form that does not
mention the four columns, and it uses that criterion in the proof.
Definition 7.1 (Criterion of Explanatory Failure, Independent Form). (A) An account A is
an explanatory failure with respect to a question Q when at least one of the following three
conditions holds, and none of the conditions mentions any of the four columns:
(F1) A leaves a question that Q requires to be answered without an answer, and no part of A
     supplies the missing answer.
(F2) A removes a distinction or a prediction that Q requires, so that two situations that Q
     must distinguish are no longer distinguished, or a consequence that Q must support is
     no longer supported.
(F3) A asserts two claims that cannot both hold, or asserts a claim that contradicts a
     commitment the explanation is required to preserve.
The three conditions are stated without reference to the four columns, to the framework’s
vocabulary, or to the framework’s principles. They are the criterion by which the removal test
registers failure, and they are stated here so that the proof of necessity does not presuppose
the conclusion it argues for.
   The definition is (A): it is stipulated. Its purpose is to state the criterion of failure
independently of the four columns, so that the proof of necessity can use it without circularity.
The criterion is minimal: it does not attempt to say what a complete explanation is; it attempts
only to say what makes an explanation fail in a way that the removal test can register. A
reader who accepts the criterion can apply the removal test; a reader who rejects the criterion
has rejected the method’s criterion, and the argument is offered at the strength of the criterion.

Proof of Necessity (Removal Test). By the definitions of the previous chapter, an explanation
says what is related, by what the relation is carried, according to what rule, and from what
standpoint. We remove each column in turn and observe what remains. Each removal is
assessed by the criterion of Definition 7.1, which is independent of the four columns.

 (a) Without fixed elements. The account has no terms to relate. It leaves unanswered the
     question Q requires to be answered—the question of what is related—and no part of the
     account supplies the missing answer. The account is a failure under (F1).
 (b) Without fluid elements. The account has the terms but no medium through which one
     term reaches another. It removes a distinction that Q requires: the distinction between
     two terms being connected and two terms merely both being present is no longer drawn.
     The account is a failure under (F2); the argument that this is so is the conveyor principle,
     which is stated and proved in the next chapter (Chapter 8), and here it is only named.
 (c) Without governing dynamics. The account shows that the terms are connected, but
     not by what rule the connection behaves. It removes a prediction that Q requires: the
     account cannot say what would happen if the conditions were different, because it has
     no rule by which the connection’s behavior is fixed. The account is a failure under (F2).
 (d) Without context. The account states a rule without a standpoint. The same terms can
     be partitioned into fixed and fluid in different ways, and the rule alone does not say
     which partition is intended. The account is a failure under (F1): it leaves unanswered
     the question of which partition the explanation is about, and no part of the account
     supplies the missing answer.
84                                                      Chapter 7. The Four-Column Principle


   Each removal produces a failure under the independent criterion. Hence each column is
necessary, given the criterion and the commitment that we can recognize an explanatory failure
when we see one.

    The proof depends on the commitment that we can recognize an explanatory failure when
we see one, and on the criterion of Definition 7.1. The commitment is declared in Chapter 2,
and the criterion is stated above in a form that does not presuppose the four columns. A
reader who denies the commitment may still follow the argument that the four roles are what
an explanation, on inspection, assigns; what the reader denies is that the inspection has the
force of proof. The framework does not claim more than the inspection delivers. The formal
counterpart of the proof, with the four cases stated as formal derivations from the definitions
and the axioms of Appendix .15, is Theorem .1.

Remark 7.3 (The Criterion Is Independent of the Four Columns). The criterion of Defini-
tion 7.1 is stated in terms of the question Q, the account A, and the requirements Q places on
A. None of the three conditions mentions the four columns, the framework’s vocabulary, or
the framework’s principles. The criterion is therefore independent of the conclusion the proof
argues for, and the proof is not circular. A reader who has followed Chapter 2 will recognize
the criterion as the criterion stated there (Criterion 2.1); the present definition restates it in
the form the proof requires, and the two criteria are the same.

Remark 7.4 (The Removal Test Is Not a Definition). The removal test is not a definition
of “explanation,” and it is not a derivation of the four columns from a prior principle. It is
a test: it takes the four columns as proposed by the previous chapter, and it asks whether
an explanation can be complete without one of them. The test presupposes that the four
columns have been correctly identified; if they have not, the test may fail to reveal a column
that should have been on the list. This possibility is the concern of the reducibility test, which
is stated in the next section.

Remark 7.5 (What the Proof Establishes). The proof establishes that each of the four
columns is necessary for an explanation, given the commitment that we can recognize an
explanatory failure and given the independent criterion of failure. It does not establish that
no fifth column is needed; a demonstration that each of the four is necessary does not show
that the list is complete. Nor does it establish that the four columns are jointly sufficient; that
is the concern of the reducibility test. The proof is offered at exactly that strength.


7.4     Support for Sufficiency: The Reducibility Test
Sufficiency cannot be proved from the definitions, because a new kind of explanation might
always turn up. It is therefore offered as an estimate and supported by a test.

Definition 7.2 (Reducibility). A candidate fifth column is reducible when its role in explanation
can be reassigned to one of the four columns without loss. The formal counterpart of the
definition is stated in Definition .9 of Appendix .15.

     The test proceeds by examining the standard candidates for a fifth column, and asking,
for each, whether its role can be reassigned. The candidates examined here are the four that
Chapter 2 examined (Section 2.4.2): the first three are the classical candidates; the fourth is
added because it is the most serious challenge to the sufficiency half of the framework. The
list is the same in both chapters, and the reduction offered for each is the same, so that the
reader who has followed the argument of Chapter 2 meets the same four candidates here.
7.4. Support for Sufficiency: The Reducibility Test                                            85


7.4.1    The Scope of the Candidates Examined



The sufficiency half is an estimate about the candidates that have been examined, and the
scope of the examination is stated here so that the reader knows what the estimate covers.
The candidates fall into three groups, and the estimate is offered for the first two; the third is
the group in which a counterexample would most plausibly be found.




   1. The classical candidates. Purpose, time, and the observer. These are the candidates
      that the philosophical tradition has most often proposed as an addition to the elements,
      the medium, and the rule. They are examined in the standard list, and the reduction for
      each is stated below.




   2. The normative candidate. The normative dimension. This is the most serious
      challenge to the sufficiency half, because it concerns the content of an explanation, not
      merely its form. It is examined in the standard list, and the reduction is stated below,
      at the strength the reduction supports.




   3. The further candidates. The interpretive, probabilistic, institutional, and agential
      candidates. These are examined in the classification of types (Section 7.4.2), at the
      strength of a systematic search. A counterexample to the estimate is most plausibly
      found in this group, and the framework invites the reader to look for one.




    The following table lists the candidates in all three groups, states the proposed fifth-column
role of each, and states the reason for its reducibility or non-reducibility. The table is the
reference statement of the estimate’s scope; the prose below states the reduction for each
candidate in the standard list, and the classification states the reduction for each candidate in
the further group.

    The table is offered at the strength of a systematic search, not a proof. A reader who finds
a candidate whose role resists the reduction stated in the table has found a counterexample to
the sufficiency estimate, and the framework invites the counterexample. A reader who finds a
candidate not listed in the table has extended the search; the estimate’s scope is extended
accordingly, and the framework’s answer is the same: the candidate’s role must be shown to
resist reduction to the four columns.

Remark 7.6 (The Table and the Standard List). The standard list of four candidates is the
list that Chapter 2 examined (Section 2.4.2) and the list that the formal theorem of sufficiency
covers. The table above includes the standard list and adds the further candidates of the
classification. The standard list remains the reference list of the volume; the table’s further
rows are offered at the strength of a systematic search, and the formal theorem does not cover
them. A reader who wishes to assess the estimate’s scope should consult the table; a reader
who wishes to assess the formal result should consult the theorem, whose scope is the standard
list only (Section 7.8).

Candidate 1: Purpose or goal. A teleological explanation (“the knife is made in order
to cut”) states a rule of the form “the system tends toward state S.” That is a governing
dynamics. The role of purpose in the explanation is the role of a rule that governs the system’s
behavior, and the rule is one of the four columns.

Remark 7.7 (The Analytical Reduction of Purpose). The reduction here is analytical, not
metaphysical. The claim is that the role of purpose in an explanation can be reassigned
to the governing dynamics column without loss of explanatory content. The claim is not
that purposes are unreal, or that the things that have purposes do not really have them. A
teleological explanation is a particular kind of explanation; the framework’s claim is that its
form can be analyzed through the four columns, not that the reality it explains is exhausted
by the analysis. The distinction matters, because the analytical reduction of a role is not the
metaphysical reduction of a reality.

Candidate 2: Time. Temporal order enters an explanation either as a feature of the
dynamics (the rule concerns how states succeed one another) or as part of the frame (the scale
at which the elements are individuated). In either case, it is carried by the third or fourth
column.

Candidate 3: The observer. The standpoint of the cognizer is the content of the context
column: the question asked, the means used, the scale adopted. The observer is not a fifth
column; it is what the fourth column makes explicit.

Candidate 4: The normative dimension. A normative explanation (“the action was
right because it was just”) states what the agent ought to have done, and the “ought” seems to
be a feature of the explanation that is not carried by any of the four columns. The reduction
here is analytical: a normative explanation states a rule of the form “the system ought to tend
toward state S,” and the rule is a governing dynamics. The framework’s claim is that the form
of a normative explanation can be analyzed through the four columns, not that the content
of the norm is exhausted by the analysis. A reader who denies the reduction has a serious
challenge to the sufficiency half of the framework, and the framework invites the challenge.

Remark 7.8 (The Normative Candidate and the Boundary of the Book). The normative
candidate is the most serious challenge to the sufficiency half of the framework, and it is worth
88                                                      Chapter 7. The Four-Column Principle


marking why. The framework’s account of the four columns is an account of the form of an
explanation, not of its content; and the normative dimension concerns the content. A reader
who holds that the form of a normative explanation cannot be analyzed through the four
columns has found a candidate that resists reduction. The framework’s response is that the
form can be analyzed, and that the content belongs to a different inquiry (Chapter 4). The
response is stated at exactly that strength: the reader who rejects it has a reason to reject the
sufficiency half of the framework, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.
    These four are the standard candidates. The test would fail, and the principle would have
to be revised, if an explanation accepted as complete could be exhibited whose content cannot
be redistributed over the four columns in this way. The formal counterpart of the test, for the
standard candidates, is stated in Theorem .2 of Appendix .15.
Remark 7.9 (The Candidates and the Distinction of Chapter 5). The four candidates are
candidates for a fifth analytical column, not for a fifth kind of entity. The distinction is the
one Chapter 5 states: the four columns are analytical roles, and the question of a fifth column
is the question of whether an explanation needs a fifth role, not the question of whether reality
contains a fifth kind of thing. The observer, for instance, is a real subject; the question is
whether the observer’s standpoint requires a fifth analytical role, and the answer is that it does
not, because the standpoint is the content of the context column. The same applies to the
normative dimension: a norm is a real feature of the world (if norms are real at all), and the
question is whether the form of a normative explanation requires a fifth analytical role. The
framework’s answer is that it does not; the reader who disagrees has found the place where
the sufficiency half is most vulnerable.
Remark 7.10 (The Risky Claim). The framework makes a risky claim, and says in advance
what would refute it. A candidate fifth column that resists reduction to the four would refute
the sufficiency half of the four-column principle. The framework does not offer a proof that
no such candidate can be found; it offers an estimate, supported by the examination of the
candidates that have been proposed, and it invites the reader to produce a counterexample.
Remark 7.11 (The Test Is an Estimate, Not a Proof). The reducibility test yields an estimate
of sufficiency, at the strength of an examination of the standard candidates. It does not yield
a proof; the possibility of a new kind of explanation cannot be ruled out in advance. The
estimate’s status is (E), and it is stated at that strength so that the reader knows what kind
of claim it is.

7.4.2    The Candidates Classified by Type of Explanation
The standard list of four candidates is the reference list of the volume, and the reducibility test
of the previous subsection examines each of the four. The list, however, is not a classification
of the types of explanation that could produce a candidate; it is a list of the candidates that
have been proposed. The present subsection states a classification of the types of explanation,
and it states, for each type, whether it has a candidate that resists reduction to the four
columns. The classification is offered as an organizing frame; it does not replace the standard
list, and the standard list remains the reference list.
Remark 7.12 (The Classification and the Standard List). The classification is stated at the
strength of a classification, not a test. Its purpose is to make the search for a counterexample
to the sufficiency half systematic, and to state, for each type of explanation, whether the type
has been examined. The standard list of four is a subset of the classification’s candidates; the
classification adds four types whose candidates the standard list does not name (interpretive,
probabilistic, institutional, and agential) and whose examination is stated below. A reader
who finds a type of explanation whose candidate is not classified here has found a gap in the
classification, and the framework can be revised accordingly.
7.4. Support for Sufficiency: The Reducibility Test                                            89


Causal explanation. A causal explanation states how one event brings about another. Its
    candidate for a fifth column is causal connection. The candidate is reducible to the four:
    the causal connection is carried by the fluid element, and the rule that governs it is the
    governing dynamics. The reduction is analytical, not metaphysical: it does not claim
    that causation is unreal, only that the form of a causal explanation can be analyzed
    through the four columns.

Teleological explanation. A teleological explanation states the end toward which a system
     tends. Its candidate is purpose. The candidate is reducible to the four: purpose is a
     governing dynamics (the rule “the system tends toward state S”). The reduction is stated
     in the first candidate of the standard list.

Normative explanation. A normative explanation states what an agent ought to have done.
    Its candidate is the normative dimension. The candidate is reducible to the four: the
    norm is a rule of the form “the system ought to tend toward state S,” and the rule is a
    governing dynamics. The reduction is stated in the fourth candidate of the standard list,
    and it is the most serious challenge to the sufficiency half (Remark on the normative
    candidate).

Interpretive explanation. An interpretive explanation states the meaning of a text, an
     action, or a practice. Its candidate is interpretation. The candidate is reducible to the
     four: the interpretation is carried by the fluid element (the meaning that passes from
     the text to the interpreter), and the rule that governs it is the governing dynamics (the
     conventions of interpretation). The reduction is offered at the strength of a conceptual
     analysis, not a proof; a reader who finds an interpretive explanation whose form resists
     the four columns has found a counterexample to the estimate.

Probabilistic explanation. A probabilistic explanation states the probability of an event
    given some conditions. Its candidate is probability. The candidate is reducible to the
    four: the probability is a feature of the governing dynamics (the rule that assigns the
    probability), and the conditions are the fixed elements. The reduction is offered at the
    same strength as the interpretive one.

Institutional explanation. An institutional explanation states how an institution’s rules
      produce an outcome. Its candidate is the institution. The candidate is reducible to the
      four: the institution is the context (the frame within which the rules are applied), and
      the rules are the governing dynamics. The reduction is offered at the same strength.

Agential explanation. An agential explanation states what an agent does and why. Its
    candidate is agency. The candidate is reducible to the four: the agent is a fixed element,
    the intention is carried by the fluid element, and the rule of action is the governing
    dynamics. The reduction is offered at the same strength; a reader who finds an agential
    explanation whose form resists the four columns has found a counterexample to the
    estimate.

    The classification does not close the list of types of explanation. It states seven types, and
it states the reduction for each. A reader who finds an eighth type whose candidate resists
reduction has extended the estimate’s scope; a reader who shows that one of the seven types
is not reducible has found a counterexample to the estimate. The classification is offered at
the strength the estimate requires: it is a systematic search, not a proof.

Remark 7.13 (The Classification and the Open Question of Chapter 34). The classification
is related to the open question of Chapter 34 about the exhaustiveness of the four columns
(Question 2 in the list of the fourteen open questions). The open question states that the
90                                                     Chapter 7. The Four-Column Principle


exhaustiveness is not settled; the classification is the framework’s current statement of which
types of explanation have been examined. A reader who settles the open question has extended
the classification; a reader who shows that a type of explanation resists the classification has
shown the estimate’s limit. The two are complementary: the open question states the limit of
the estimate; the classification states the search by which the estimate is supported.


7.5      The Distinctness of the Four Analytical Roles
The four columns are necessary only if they are also distinct. If one column could be supplied
by another, the removal test would not show what it claims to show: the removal of a column
that is not distinct from another would not produce an explanatory failure, because the other
column would supply the role.
    The distinctness of the four roles is therefore argued separately.

Principle 7.2 (The Distinctness of the Four Analytical Roles). (T) The four questions are
distinct: an answer to any one of them does not, by itself, supply the answer to any other.
The formal counterpart of the principle is stated in Theorem .3 of Appendix .15.

Proof of Principle 7.2.  1. Knowing what the elements are does not say what, if anything,
      passes between them. Two things may be fully described, and yet nothing be said of
      how one bears on the other.

     2. Knowing that something passes between them does not say by what rule it behaves. A
        conduit may be named without any law of its working.

     3. Knowing the rule does not say from what standpoint the elements are partitioned as
        they are, since the same rule can be applied to different partitions.

   4. Knowing the standpoint does not supply the elements, the conduit, or the rule that are
      to be found from it.
    Hence no one of the four answers is supplied by another taken alone, and the four roles are
distinct.

    The proof shows that the four roles are distinct as roles. It does not show that they are
distinct as entities. The distinction is important, and it is stated in the next remark.

7.5.1     Counterexamples and Borderline Cases
The proof of distinctness is a proof that the four roles are not interchangeable. It is worth
supporting the proof with examples of the cases in which the roles are most easily confused,
so that the reader can see what the distinctness principle is asserting and what it is not.

Counterexample 1: The rule that seems to supply the elements. A proposed
counterexample to distinctness is a mathematical proof in which the rule of inference seems to
determine the elements to which it is applied. The proof’s rule (the rule of inference) and the
proof’s elements (the propositions) seem to be supplied together: the rule of inference is stated
in terms of the kind of proposition it applies to, and the propositions are individuated by the
kind of inference they support. The distinctness principle’s response is that the rule does not
supply the elements; the rule constrains the elements, but the elements are the propositions,
and the rule is the pattern of inference. The constraint is real, and the distinctness principle
does not deny it; what the principle asserts is that an answer to “what are the elements?” is
not, by itself, an answer to “what is the rule?” The counterexample shows that the roles are
related, not that they are interchangeable.
7.5. The Distinctness of the Four Analytical Roles                                            91


Counterexample 2: The context that seems to supply the fixed elements. A
proposed counterexample is a legal case in which the jurisdiction (the context) seems to
determine the parties (the fixed elements). The jurisdiction’s rules determine who can be
a party, what counts as a claim, and what counts as a remedy. The distinctness principle’s
response is that the jurisdiction constrains the parties, but the parties are the entities whose
relations the explanation traces, and the jurisdiction is the frame within which the relations
are assessed. The constraint is real; the distinctness principle does not deny it. What the
principle asserts is that the answer to “what are the parties?” is not supplied by the answer to
“what is the jurisdiction?” The same jurisdiction can be the frame for different parties, and
the same parties can be assessed under different jurisdictions.

Counterexample 3: The fluid element that seems to supply the governing dynamics.
A proposed counterexample is a language in which the medium of communication (the fluid
element) seems to determine the rules of grammar (the governing dynamics). The language
carries the effect of one speaker’s intention to another, and the rules of grammar are the
regularities that govern the language’s use. The distinctness principle’s response is that the
language and its grammar are related, but the language is the medium and the grammar is
the rule; the answer to “what is the medium?” is not supplied by the answer to “what is the
rule?” The same medium can be governed by different rules (a dialect and a standard), and
the same rules can be carried by different media (speech and writing).

Borderline case 1: A custom. A custom is the case in which the distinction is most
easily lost. In one context, the custom is the medium by which a practice passes from one
generation to the next (a fluid element); in another context, the custom is the rule by which
the members of the community behave toward one another (a governing dynamics). The
distinctness principle’s response is that the custom is the same entity, but it plays two roles
in two contexts, and the roles are distinct. The custom is a fluid element in the first context
and a governing dynamics in the second; the role is not a property of the entity, and the
distinctness principle is not violated by the same entity playing two roles. The example is
analyzed in full in Chapter 6 (Remark on the custom in two contexts).

Borderline case 2: A promise. A promise is the case in which a fluid element and a
governing dynamics seem to coincide. In one context, the promise carries the effect of one
party’s commitment to the other party’s expectation (a fluid element); in another context, the
promise is the rule by which the parties are bound (a governing dynamics). The distinctness
principle’s response is the same as in the case of the custom: the promise is the same entity,
but it plays two roles in two contexts, and the roles are distinct.

Borderline case 3: A jurisdiction. A jurisdiction is the case in which a context and a
fixed element seem to coincide. In one context, the jurisdiction is the frame within which the
parties, the contract, and the rule of validity are assigned (a context); in another context, the
jurisdiction is one of the entities whose relations the explanation traces (a fixed element). The
distinctness principle’s response is the same: the jurisdiction is the same entity, but it plays
two roles in two contexts, and the roles are distinct.

Remark 7.14 (The Counterexamples and Borderline Cases Support the Principle). The
counterexamples and borderline cases are offered in support of the distinctness principle, not
against it. Each shows that the roles are related, and each shows that the relation does
not collapse the roles into one. The distinctness principle asserts that the roles are not
interchangeable; the cases show that the assertion survives the most plausible attempts to
confuse the roles. A reader who finds a case in which the roles genuinely collapse (not merely
92                                                       Chapter 7. The Four-Column Principle


constrain one another) has found a counterexample to the distinctness principle, and the
framework invites the counterexample.

Remark 7.15 (Distinctness Is Not Separability). Distinctness does not imply absolute
separability. Two analytical roles may be instantiated by the same entity, or one role may
constrain the content of another (the rules of a cognition may be constrained by the structure
of its elements), without the roles thereby becoming conceptually identical. A custom may be
both a fluid element and a governing dynamics, depending on the question the cognition asks.
What the distinctness principle asserts is that the roles are not interchangeable: an answer to
one question does not, by itself, answer another.

Remark 7.16 (The Limit of the Distinctness Argument). The conclusion is limited. It shows
that the roles are distinct and all required. It does not show that they are carried by four
distinct kinds of thing in reality; one entity can play several roles in different cognitions, and
this is the point of the context-dependence principle, which is stated in Chapter 10. The
framework’s claim is analytical, not ontological.

Remark 7.17 (The Analytical and the Real). The analytical necessity of the four columns is
a claim about the structure of explanation, not a claim about the composition of reality. The
two are related, but they are not the same. If explanation is possible, then the structure of
explanation is real; but the reality of the structure is not the reality of the things explained.
The four columns describe the order through which what is becomes intelligible; they do not
claim that the order is the whole of what is. The framework keeps the analytical and the
real distinct, because the confusion of the two would turn a description of explanation into a
metaphysics of substances—a view the book does not hold and does not need.

Remark 7.18 (The Two Realities: The Activity and the Structure). The remark on the
analytical and the real is easily read as a single claim, and the single claim hides a distinction
that the framework keeps. The distinction is between two realities, and the two are not the
same.
    The first reality: the reality of the explanatory activity. The activity of explaining is a real
activity, performed by real subjects in real contexts. Its reality is not in question; it is the
reality of an event in the world, and the framework assumes it.
    The second reality: the reality of the structure the activity represents. The structure of
explanatory cognition—the four columns, the relations among them, the conditions of their
adequacy—is the structure that the activity represents. Its reality is the framework’s claim,
and the claim is stated at the strength the framework’s arguments support. The framework
does not claim that the structure is a substance, or that it exists independently of the activity;
it claims that the structure is real, invariant, and describable, and it states the claim at the
strength the arguments support.
    The transition from the first reality to the second is the transition from “there are explana-
tory activities” to “the structure that those activities represent is real.” The transition is not a
logical consequence of the first; it is a claim about the second, and the framework states it
at the strength of a (T) claim relative to the arguments of Parts I–IV. A reader who accepts
the first reality and rejects the second has rejected the framework’s claim about the structure;
the framework does not pretend that the second follows from the first by itself. The two are
distinct, and the framework keeps them distinct.


7.6     The Limit of the Argument
Three limits of the argument must be stated, and each is worth stating with the argument it
limits.
7.7. The Principle and the Method                                                               93


    First, the removal test presupposes that we can recognize an explanatory failure, and the
criterion by which the failure is recognized is stated in Definition 7.1 in a form that does not
mention the four columns. A reader who denies the criterion denies the force of the argument,
not its content; the argument itself remains intelligible, and its conclusion remains a claim
that the reader can assess on other grounds.
    Second, the reducibility test is an estimate, not a proof. Its support consists in the
examination of the standard candidates for a fifth column; it does not exclude the possibility
that a new kind of explanation will be found that resists reduction to the four. The framework
states this limit openly and offers the estimate at exactly that strength.
    Third, the distinctness principle shows that the roles are distinct, not that they are
separable. The framework’s four columns are analytical roles, not four substances. Where a
single entity plays more than one role, the framework does not multiply entities; it distinguishes
roles.
    These limits are not deficiencies of the argument. They are the conditions under which
the argument is offered, and the framework states them so that the reader knows what kind
of claim is being made. A reader who accepts the limits may still accept the framework; a
reader who rejects the framework is invited to attack it at the limits, since those are where
the framework is most vulnerable.
Remark 7.19 (The Limits Have a Positive Side). The framework’s claim is analytical, and
the analytical claim points toward the reality it analyzes. The four columns describe the order
of explanatory cognition; the order is real, and the framework’s claim is that it is invariant.
But the order is not self-sufficient. The analytical description is not the whole of what can
be said about what is explained. The framework’s silence on what lies beyond the analytical
structure is not a denial; it is the recognition that the analytical structure is the order of what
is, not the whole of what is.


7.7     The Principle and the Method
The principle is stated at the strength the method of Chapter 2 allows.
    The necessity half is (T): it is argued by the removal test, relative to the commitment
that we can recognize an explanatory failure and relative to the independent criterion of
failure (Definition 7.1). The argument is given in this chapter, and the reader who accepts the
commitment and the criterion has a reason to accept the conclusion. The formal counterpart
of the argument is stated in Theorem .1 of Appendix .15.
    The sufficiency half is (E): it is supported by the reducibility test, and it is offered as an
estimate, subject to revision if a candidate that resists reduction is found. The estimate is at
the strength of an examination of the standard candidates, not at the strength of a proof. The
formal counterpart of the estimate, for the standard candidates, is stated in Theorem .2 of
Appendix .15; the theorem’s content is restricted to the standard candidates, and the reader
who wishes to see the restriction stated precisely is directed to Section 7.8, below.
    The distinctness principle is (T): it is argued from the definitions of the previous chapter,
and it establishes that the four roles are not interchangeable. The argument is given in this
chapter, and the reader who accepts the definitions has a reason to accept the conclusion. The
formal counterpart of the argument is stated in Theorem .3 of Appendix .15.
    The three statuses—(T), (E), and (T)—are stated so that the reader knows what kind
of claim each part of the principle supports. The dependency map at the end of Part VI
(Chapter 43) states which conclusions depend on which, and the reader who wishes to see the
structure of the whole is directed there. The formal system itself, with its sorts, predicates,
axioms, and the four theorems (necessity, sufficiency, distinctness, and consistency), is stated
in Appendix .15; the present section states the informal argument, and the appendix states
the formal counterpart.

7.8     Formal Formulation of the Four-Column Principle
The four-column principle is stated in philosophical prose in Section 7.2, and its three arguments
are given in Sections 7.3–7.5. The present section states the formal counterparts of the principle
and its arguments, at the level of detail that the philosophical reader requires, and it refers
the reader to Appendix .15 for the full formal system and the proofs.
    The formal language was introduced in Chapter 6 (Section 6.9), and it is stated in full
in Appendix .15. It has four principal sorts (elements, rules, contexts, and explanations)
and four auxiliary sorts (states, subjects, acts, and times), four role predicates (for the fixed
elements, the fluid elements, the governing dynamics, and the context), a primitive predicate
of completeness, and a family of definitions and axioms. The present section uses the language
to state the formal counterparts of the four-column principle and its three arguments.

The formal counterpart of necessity. The necessity half of the four-column principle is
stated as:
                         ∀κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K} : Necessary(κ),
where Necessary(κ) is defined in Definition .7 of Appendix .15 as the claim that the removal of
the role κ from a structurally complete explanation yields an explanation that is not complete.
The formal proof is stated in Theorem .1. The proof is a reductio for each of the four roles,
and its force is the force of the axioms and the primitive completeness predicate, exactly as
the prose proof’s force is the force of the commitment that we can recognize an explanatory
failure and the independent criterion of failure (Definition 7.1).

The formal counterpart of sufficiency. The sufficiency half of the four-column principle
is stated, in the prose of this chapter, as an estimate about the standard candidates. The
formal counterpart of the estimate is:
                                   ∀κ5 ∈ Cstd : Reducible(κ5 ),
where Cstd = {purpose, time, observer, normative dimension} is the standard list of candidates,
and Reducible(κ5 ) is defined in Definition .9 of Appendix .15 as the claim that the role of κ5 is
a subset of the role of one of the four columns. The formal proof, for the standard candidates,
is stated in Theorem .2.
    The formal result is explicitly separated from the broader prose claim. The
theorem’s title and statement are restricted to the standard candidates: it is a theorem about
the reducibility of the four candidates that have been proposed and examined, not a theorem
that no fifth column is possible. The prose of Section 7.4 states the same restriction, the
classification of Section 7.4.2 states the broader search that supports the estimate, and the
estimate of sufficiency in Section 7.2 is stated at the strength the restriction supports. A
reader who reads the theorem as a proof of general sufficiency has read more into the title than
the theorem contains; the title is the theorem’s scope, and the scope is stated in the prose and
in the formal statement. The broader prose claim—that the four columns are sufficient among
the candidates examined—is (E), and it is supported by the examination, not by the theorem
alone.

The formal counterpart of distinctness. The distinctness principle is stated as:
              ∀κ1 , κ2 ∈ {F, Φ, D, K} : κ1 ̸= κ2 → ¬(RoleSet(κ1 ) ⊆ RoleSet(κ2 )),
where RoleSet(κ) is the set of explanatory roles that the column κ plays. The formal proof is
stated in Theorem .3. The proof is a construction of countermodels for each pair of columns,
and its force is the force of the definitions of the four roles and the axioms of the formal system,
exactly as the prose proof’s force is the force of the definitions and the counterexamples and
borderline cases of Section 7.5.1.
7.8. Formal Formulation of the Four-Column Principle                                          95


The formal counterpart of consistency. The formal system also states a consistency
theorem (Theorem .4): the axioms of the formal system have a model, and therefore the
system is consistent. The consistency theorem is the formal counterpart of the claim, stated in
Chapter 34, that the framework is coherent. The consistency theorem is stated at the strength
of a formal result; it does not claim that the framework is true, and it does not claim that the
framework is complete. It claims that the formal system is consistent, and it is offered as the
formal counterpart of the framework’s coherence.




Remark 7.20 (The Formal Statement and the Prose Statement). The formal statement and
the prose statement are not rivals. The prose statement is the substance, and the formal
statement is its precise form. The reader who is content with the prose statement has the
principle, the arguments, and the limits; the reader who wishes to see the principle in a precise
form has the formal statement. The two are the same principle, stated at two levels of detail;
the formal statement does not replace the prose statement, and the prose statement does not
make the formal statement unnecessary.




Remark 7.21 (The Formal Statement and the Reader). The formal statement is offered for
the reader who wishes to see the four-column principle in a precise form, and for the reader
who wishes to assess the framework at the level of its formal structure. It is not offered as a
requirement: the philosophical reader who is content with the prose of Sections 7.2–7.5 has the
principle and the arguments, and does not need the formal statement. The formal statement
is a supplement, not a substitute; it is the framework’s way of being assessable at the level of
its formal structure, and it is offered at the strength that a supplement can have.




Remark 7.22 (The Formal Statement and the Dependency Map). The formal statement
is related to the dependency map of Chapter 43. The dependency map states, for each core
commitment, which conclusions depend on it. The formal statement makes the dependencies
among the four-column principle, the definitions, and the axioms explicit; it is the formal
counterpart of the dependency map, restricted to the four-column principle. The reader who
wishes to see the full dependency map is directed to Chapter 43; the reader who wishes to see
the dependencies of the four-column principle in a precise form is directed to Appendix .15.




Remark 7.23 (The Theorem’s Title and the Scope It Records). The formal counterpart of
sufficiency is stated in Appendix .15 under the title “Reducibility of the Standard Candidates.”
The title is deliberate. The theorem establishes that the four standard candidates (purpose,
time, observer, normative dimension) are reducible to the four columns; it does not establish
that no fifth column is possible. The prose of Section 7.4 states the same restriction, the
classification of Section 7.4.2 states the broader search that supports the estimate, and the
estimate of sufficiency in Section 7.2 is stated at the strength the restriction supports. A
reader who reads the theorem as a proof of general sufficiency has read more into the title
than the theorem contains; the title is the theorem’s scope, and the scope is stated in the
prose and in the formal statement.

A Question for Reflection
Can you construct an explanation that you would accept as complete and that does not assign
one of the four roles? If so, the reducibility test has failed for that case, and the sufficiency half
of the principle is in question. If not, what is it about the explanation that makes the missing
role unrecognizable as missing? Consider also one of the four standard candidates—purpose,
time, the observer, and the normative dimension—and ask whether the reduction of its role
to one of the four columns is lossless, or whether something is lost in the reduction. What
does your answer tell you about the difference between the analytical reduction of a role and
the metaphysical reduction of a reality? And consider the classification of Section 7.4.2: can
you find a type of explanation whose candidate is not classified, or a type whose reduction
to the four columns is not lossless? What does your answer tell you about the scope of the
sufficiency estimate? And consider the counterexamples and borderline cases of Section 7.5.1:
can you give a further case in which the roles are easily confused, and can you show, using the
distinction between constraint and interchangeability, that the case does not collapse the roles
into one? The first question tests the reducibility test; the second tests the four reductions;
the third tests the classification; the fourth tests the distinctness principle in its most difficult
form.

The next chapter states and proves the conveyor principle: the claim that no explanation of
how one fixed element bears on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element. The
principle is the first of the four columns to receive a proof of its own, and it supplies the proof of
necessity for the fluid element that the removal test of the present chapter named. The formal
reconstruction of the four-column principle, with its four theorems, is given in Appendix .15.
