Chapter 8

The Conveyor Principle

Scope
This chapter states and proves the conveyor principle: the claim that no explanation of how
one fixed element bears on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element. It states what
would falsify the principle, and it distinguishes the principle from a stronger claim that it
does not entail—the claim that the effect must pass through every intermediate element. The
distinction is developed in the next chapter, under the heading of non-sequential connectivity.
    The principle is analytical, not causal, in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes (Principle 5.1): it is
a claim about the structure of an explanation, not about the structure of what is explained. The
fluid element whose necessity it proves is the role that Chapter 6 defines (Definition 6.2) and
distributes across the volume (Remark 6.26): the specific form of the fluid element—epistemic
light—is developed in Chapters 15–17. The principle supplies the proof of necessity that
Chapter 7’s removal test named but did not prove (Chapter 7, Section 7.3, step (b)).
    Its claims are analytical; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is
not a denial but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be
said. Where the chapter speaks of “effect,” “carrier,” “medium,” “signal,” “process,” “passage,”
or “route,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and
in the previous chapters.


8.1     A Scene: The Switch and the Wall
Consider a room with a lamp, a switch, and a wall. The switch is flipped; the wall becomes
bright. Something has happened between the switch and the wall, or so we say. The wall was
dark; now it is bright. The switch was off; now it is on.
    Now consider two explanations of what happened, both of which a person might offer, and
both of which are, in different ways, incomplete.
    The first explanation says: “When the switch is flipped, the wall becomes bright.” The
explanation records a correlation. It says that the two events happen together, and it says that
one follows the other. But it does not say how the switch reaches the wall. It does not say by
what the effect of the switch is carried to the wall. A person who accepted this explanation
and no more would know that the wall becomes bright when the switch is flipped, and would
not know why. The explanation is not complete as an explanation of how; it is a description
of what happens, offered in the place of an account of why.
    The second explanation says: “The switch closes a circuit; the circuit carries a current to
the lamp; the lamp converts the current to light; the light travels from the lamp to the wall.”
This explanation is better, and it is still incomplete, in a way that the next paragraph will
state. But it is better because it invokes a medium at each step: the circuit, the current, the
100                                                          Chapter 8. The Conveyor Principle


light. It says by what the effect of the switch reaches the wall. It does not merely record the
correlation; it explains how the correlation is produced.
    The difference between the two explanations is not a difference in accuracy. Both explana-
tions are accurate; both describe what happens. The difference is in what the explanation
contains. The first explanation contains the two fixed elements (the switch, the wall) and the
correlation between them; it does not contain the medium. The second explanation contains
the two fixed elements, the correlation, and the medium. The medium is what makes the
second explanation an explanation of how, and its absence is what makes the first explanation
incomplete.
    The scene poses a question. What is the difference between an explanation that records a
correlation and an explanation that explains how the correlation is produced? The present
chapter’s answer is the conveyor principle: no explanation of how one fixed element bears
on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element. The principle is stated in the next
section, proved in the section after, and distinguished from a stronger claim in the section
after that.
Remark 8.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the principle
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the conveyor principle; it makes the principle
intelligible before it is stated. The proof of the principle is given in Section 8.5, and the scene
carries no weight in it. The reader who has followed the scene knows what kind of thing the
principle will claim—that the difference between the two explanations is the medium—and
knows why the principle is stated as a claim about completeness. The reader who has not will
find the principle stated and proved on its own terms.
Remark 8.2 (The Second Explanation Is Also Incomplete). The second explanation is better
than the first, and it is still incomplete. It invokes a medium at each step, but it does not say
by what rule the medium operates: it does not say how the current is produced by the circuit,
or how the lamp converts the current to light, or how the light travels from the lamp to the
wall. The missing rule is the governing dynamics, and its absence is what the removal test of
Chapter 7 named (step (c)). The present chapter is about the medium, not about the rule;
the rule is the concern of the chapters that state the rules of the specific cognitive contexts.
The distinction is stated here so that the reader does not mistake the present chapter’s claim
(the medium is necessary) for a claim the chapter does not make (the medium is sufficient).


8.2     The Question
In Chapter 7, the four-column principle was stated and argued. The four columns are necessary
(the necessity half of Principle 7.1), and the four roles are distinct (Principle 7.2). One of the
four columns—the fluid element—was defined in Chapter 6 as the entity that conveys effect
(Definition 6.2). The definition was given, and a control question was supplied for it.
    The present chapter asks a further question about the fluid element. The definition says
what a fluid element is; it does not yet say why an explanation must invoke one. The question
is:

      Why is no explanation of how one fixed element bears on another complete, unless
      it invokes a fluid element?

   The question is not idle. An explanation that names the two fixed elements and states
that one changes when the other does records a correlation. It does not say how the one bears
on the other. If the correlation is offered as a complete explanation, something has been left
out, and the present chapter identifies what.
   The chapter’s answer is the conveyor principle. The principle is stated in the next section,
proved in the section after, and distinguished from a stronger claim in the section after that.
8.3. The Scope of the Principle                                                                   101


The distinction from the stronger claim is developed further in Chapter 9, where it is stated
as the principle of non-sequential connectivity.
Remark 8.3 (The Question Is About the Meaning of “How”). The question the chapter asks
is, at bottom, a question about the meaning of the word “how.” An explanation of how one
thing bears on another must say how; and to say how is to say by what the bearing is carried.
A reader who accepts the meaning of “how” that the framework employs has accepted the
premise of the proof, and the proof’s conclusion follows. A reader who denies the meaning has
denied the premise, and the framework does not claim that the denial is impossible; it claims
that the denial is a different use of the word “how,” and that the framework’s use is the one
its argument needs. The distinction is the distinction between the framework’s vocabulary
and a rival vocabulary; the framework states its own, and it invites the reader to assess the
argument in the vocabulary it states.


8.3     The Scope of the Principle
The conveyor principle is stated for one kind of relation and not for others, and the present
section makes the scope exact. The principle is a claim about relations of effect: relations in
which one term brings about, produces, or alters another. The principle is not a claim about
every relation that an explanation may record. The distinction matters, because the principle
would be false if it were stated for every relation, and it is true only for the relation it is stated
for.
     Three kinds of relation must be distinguished.

   1. Co-occurrence. Two terms occur together, or one occurs after the other, with no claim
      that one produces the other. An explanation that records a co-occurrence is complete as
      a description of the co-occurrence, and the conveyor principle does not apply to it. The
      principle applies only when the explanation claims that one term bears on the other.
   2. Correlation. Two terms vary together, in a statistical or regular way, without a claim
      that one produces the other. An explanation that records a correlation is complete as
      a description of the correlation, and the conveyor principle does not apply to it. The
      principle applies only when the explanation claims that the correlation is produced by
      an effect.
   3. Effect. One term brings about, produces, or alters another. An explanation that
      claims an effect is an explanation of how, and the conveyor principle applies to it: the
      explanation must invoke a medium by which the effect is carried.

    The distinction is the distinction between three kinds of relation that an explanation
may record, and the principle’s scope is the third. A reader who applies the principle to
co-occurrence or correlation has applied it beyond its scope; a reader who applies it to effect
has applied it within its scope.
Remark 8.4 (The Principle and the Three Kinds of Relation). The three kinds of relation
are not three versions of one relation; they are three different claims that an explanation may
make. The co-occurrence claim is the weakest: it says only that the terms occur together. The
correlation claim is stronger: it says that the terms vary together in a regular way. The effect
claim is strongest: it says that one term produces the other. The conveyor principle is a claim
about the third, not about the first two. A reader who says “but the explanation records the
co-occurrence, and it is complete as a description of the co-occurrence” has not refuted the
principle; the reader has stated a different claim, and the principle is not a claim about that
claim. The principle is a claim about the explanation that says one thing bears on another,
not about the explanation that says two things happen together.
102                                                        Chapter 8. The Conveyor Principle


Remark 8.5 (Why the Distinction Matters for the Framework). The distinction matters for
the framework because it prevents the conveyor principle from being read as a demand that
every explanation invoke a medium. The framework’s claim is not that every explanation
must invoke a medium; it is that every explanation of how one thing bears on another must
invoke a medium. An explanation that records a co-occurrence, or a correlation, or a logical
dependence, is not an explanation of how one thing bears on another, and the principle does
not apply to it. The principle is a claim about a specific kind of explanation, and its scope is
the kind of explanation it is about.

Remark 8.6 (The Principle and Logical Dependence). A logical dependence (“if P , then Q”)
is not a relation of effect in the sense the principle requires. The principle does not require a
medium for logical dependence; it requires a medium for effect. The two are different, and
the framework keeps them apart. A reader who asks whether the principle applies to logical
dependence has asked a question about a relation outside the principle’s scope; the answer is
that the principle does not apply to logical dependence, and that the principle is silent on it.


8.4    The Conveyor Principle
Principle 8.1 (Conveyor Principle). (T) No explanation of how one fixed element bears on
another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element: a carrier, medium, signal, or process by
which the effect passes.

    The principle is stated as a claim about completeness. It does not say that every explanation
must name a particular kind of fluid element; it says that every explanation of how one element
bears on another must invoke some fluid element or other. The principle is deliberately broad
in the range of what counts. A thing, a signal, a process, a medium, a field—any of these can
be a fluid element, provided it conveys effect. What the principle excludes is the explanation
that says how one thing bears on another without invoking anything by which the bearing is
carried.
    The breadth is not a weakness. It is what makes the principle hard to evade. An explanation
that tries to avoid naming a fluid element will fail, not because the framework insists on a
particular kind of medium, but because the explanation will leave unanswered the question of
how. The proof of the principle, given below, makes this precise.

Remark 8.7 (The Principle Is Not a Definition). The conveyor principle is not a definition
of “explanation,” and it is not a stipulation that every explanation must contain the word
“medium.” It is a claim about the structure of any explanation of how one thing bears on
another. The claim can be denied; a reader who denies it is invited to produce an explanation
of how, that names no carrier, and that is nonetheless complete. The proof below shows
that the denial is difficult to sustain; it does not show that the denial is impossible in every
conceivable case.

Remark 8.8 (The Principle Is Not a Demand for Mechanism). The principle is not a demand
that every explanation of how be a mechanistic explanation. A mechanistic explanation is
one that invokes a physical mechanism; the conveyor principle does not require a physical
mechanism, and it does not privilege the physical over the non-physical. A medium may be
physical (a wire, a wave), or it may be non-physical (a logical implication, a semantic relation,
a convention). What the principle requires is that some medium be named, not that the
medium be of a particular kind. The breadth of the term “fluid element” is deliberate: it is
what allows the principle to cover explanations of all kinds, not only the physical ones.

Example 8.1 (Conversation). If language is removed from the negotiation, the two parties
are disconnected nodes. Language is therefore the condition of possibility of the explanation
8.5. The Proof                                                                               103


of how one bears on the other. The example is not a proof of the principle; it is an illustration
of what the principle says.
Example 8.2 (The Switch and the Wall). The second explanation of the scene (Section 8.1)
invokes the circuit, the current, and the light as media. Each is a fluid element; each is
what the principle requires. The first explanation, which names no medium, is the kind of
explanation the principle excludes. The example is not a proof; it is an illustration of the
difference the principle marks.


8.5    The Proof
The principle is proved by reductio.

Proof of the Conveyor Principle.      1. Suppose an explanation of how A bears on B is com-
      plete, and invokes no fluid element.

  2. Then it says only that A and B are fixed elements, and that B changes when A does.

  3. That statement records a correlation between two nodes. It does not say how A bears
     on B, since by hypothesis no route, medium, or process is specified.

  4. An explanation that does not say how is incomplete as an explanation of how.

  5. This contradicts the supposition. Hence every complete explanation of how one thing
     bears on another invokes a fluid element.


    The proof is short, and its brevity is the point. The principle is not a substantive
metaphysical claim about the furniture of the world; it is a claim about what a certain kind of
explanation must contain. The argument turns on a single distinction—between recording a
correlation and explaining how the correlation is produced—and the distinction is one that
any explanation of how must respect.
    The proof’s scope is the scope stated in Section 8.3: the principle applies to explanations
of effect, not to explanations of co-occurrence or correlation. The proof’s premise is that an
explanation of how, which does not say how, is incomplete as an explanation of how; the
premise is not a claim about all explanations, and it is not applied to all explanations. It is
applied to explanations of effect, and the principle’s scope is stated so that the reader knows
what kind of explanation the principle is about.
Remark 8.9 (The Proof Is Relative to a Premise). The proof depends on the premise that
an explanation that does not say how is incomplete as an explanation of how. The premise is
not proved; it is what the word “how” means in the context of an explanation. A reader who
accepts the premise accepts the proof; a reader who denies the premise denies the meaning
of “how” that the framework employs. The framework does not offer an argument for the
meaning; it states the meaning, and offers the proof as what follows from it.
Remark 8.10 (The Proof Is a Reductio, Not a Construction). The proof is a reductio, and
the reductio’s form is worth marking. The proof does not construct a positive account of what
a medium is; it shows that the denial of the principle is incoherent. The reader who accepts
the reductio has accepted that the principle cannot be denied without contradiction, but has
not thereby learned what a medium is. The positive account of the medium is the work of
the chapters that follow: Chapter 6 defines the role, and Chapters 15–17 develop the specific
medium (epistemic light). The distinction is the distinction between the proof of the principle
and the development of its content; the present chapter gives the first, and the later chapters
give the second.
104                                                         Chapter 8. The Conveyor Principle


Remark 8.11 (The Proof Is Not Circular). The proof is not circular, and the non-circularity
is worth stating. The proof does not assume that a medium exists; it assumes only that an
explanation of how that does not say how is incomplete. From this assumption it derives that
some medium must be invoked. The assumption is a claim about the meaning of “how,” not a
claim about the existence of media. A reader who accepts the assumption has accepted the
meaning of “how,” and the derivation follows. A reader who denies the assumption has denied
the meaning, and the framework does not claim that the denial is impossible; it claims that
the denial is a different meaning, and that the framework’s meaning is the one its argument
needs.

Remark 8.12 (The Principle Is Analytical, Not Causal). The conveyor principle is a principle
about explanation, not a principle about causation. It says that any explanation of how
one thing bears on another requires a medium; it does not say that every instance of one
thing bearing on another requires a medium. The two claims are different, and the difference
is the difference that Chapter 5 states between the order of reconstruction and the order
of explanatory dependence (Principle 5.1): the first is a claim about the structure of an
explanation, the second would be a claim about the structure of what is explained. The
framework’s claim is the first. It does not claim that reality is exhausted by what an explanation
can contain, and it does not claim that nothing happens without a medium. It claims that
nothing can be explained as happening without a medium. The distinction is crucial, because
it prevents the principle from being read as a denial of direct action—whether that action is
human, natural, or divine.

Remark 8.13 (The Proof Establishes the Necessity of the Fluid Element). The proof
establishes the necessity of the fluid element, given the meaning of “how” that the framework
employs. It does not establish the necessity of any particular fluid element; it establishes that
some fluid element or other is required. The specific fluid element that the framework invokes
in its most general role is epistemic light, which is developed in Part III (Chapter 15). The
present chapter establishes the necessity of the role; Part III develops the specific medium.
The distinction between the role and its specific form is the distinction that Chapter 6 states
in its Remark on the fluid element being defined generically (Remark following Definition 6.2).


8.6     What Would Falsify the Principle
The principle is only as strong as the breadth of the term “fluid element,” and the term is
deliberately broad. Because of that breadth, the principle could not be refuted by merely
renaming a mediator. A genuine counterexample must satisfy two conditions.

   1. It must name no mediating medium, signal, or process.

   2. It must nonetheless be accepted as complete.

   The standard candidate is unmediated action at a distance. One thing bears on another
across a gap with nothing passing between them, and the account is held to leave no further
question about how.
   The framework’s position on the candidate is stated in the next remark.

Remark 8.14 (The Framework’s Position on Unmediated Action). The framework holds that
an account of unmediated action at a distance always leaves the question of how unanswered.
The account may be accepted as a description of what happens; it is not accepted as an
explanation of how what happens is produced. Whoever exhibits an accepted complete account
of that kind refutes the conveyor principle. The framework does not claim that no such account
will ever be exhibited; it claims that no such account has been exhibited, and it states what
8.7. Counterexamples and a Borderline Case                                                      105


such an account would have to be. The framework does not deny that unmediated action is
real. It denies that unmediated action can be explained without a medium. The two claims
are different. The first is a claim about what can happen; the second is a claim about what
can be said about what happens. The framework’s principle is the second, not the first.

    The remark is not a dogmatic refusal to consider the candidate. It is a statement of what
the framework would need in order to revise the principle. The framework is not committed
to the principle come what may; it is committed to the principle as the best account currently
available, and it says in advance what would show the account to be wrong.

Remark 8.15 (The Principle Is a Commitment to a Standard). The framework’s commitment
to the conveyor principle is a commitment to a standard of explanation: that an explanation of
how must say how, and that saying how requires a medium. A reader who rejects the standard
rejects the principle; the framework does not pretend otherwise. The reader who accepts
the standard accepts the principle, and with it the consequence that unmediated action at a
distance, if it is real, cannot be explained.

Remark 8.16 (What the Framework Does Not Claim About Direct Action). The framework
does not claim that direct action is unreal, and it does not claim that direct action is impossible.
It claims that direct action, if it is real, cannot be explained without a medium. The distinction
is the distinction between what can happen and what can be said about what happens. A
reader who takes the principle as a denial of direct action has misread it; a reader who takes
it as a claim about explanation has read it correctly. The framework’s silence on whether
direct action is real is not a denial; it is the recognition that the question belongs to a different
inquiry, and that the present chapter’s claim is about explanation, not about what is.


8.7     Counterexamples and a Borderline Case
The falsification section stated what a genuine counterexample would have to be. The present
section states two counterexamples that the framework recognizes as serious, and one borderline
case in which the application of the principle is limited. The section is offered so that the
reader can see the principle’s scope in its most difficult cases, not only in its easy ones.

8.7.1    Counterexample 1: Quantum Entanglement as Described
A description of quantum entanglement, as it is often stated in popular and even in some
technical presentations, says that two particles are correlated in such a way that a measurement
on one fixes the outcome of a measurement on the other, with no signal passing between them.
The description is offered as an account of how the correlation is produced, and it explicitly
denies that any signal or medium passes between the particles.
    The framework’s response is the distinction of Section 8.3. The description, as it is stated,
is an account of a correlation, not an account of an effect. It says that the outcomes are
correlated, and it denies that one outcome brings about the other through a medium. An
account of a correlation is complete as an account of the correlation, and the conveyor principle
does not apply to it. The principle would apply only if the description claimed that one
measurement brings about the other; and the description, as it is stated, does not claim that.
A reader who offers the description as a counterexample to the conveyor principle has applied
the principle outside its scope; a reader who offers it as a description of a correlation has
stated a case the principle does not cover.

Remark 8.17 (The Framework’s Response to the Entanglement Case). The framework’s
response is not a dismissal of the case. It is the statement that the case, as it is stated, is a
case of correlation, not of effect. If a future physics states that the correlation is produced by
106                                                        Chapter 8. The Conveyor Principle


an effect, and states that the effect passes through no medium, the conveyor principle would
be refuted by that physics. The framework does not claim that no future physics could do so;
it claims that the present physics does not, and that the present description is a description
of correlation. The distinction is the distinction between the correlation and the effect; the
principle is a claim about the effect, and the case, as stated, is a case of the correlation.


8.7.2    Counterexample 2: Logical Implication
A logical implication (“if P , then Q”) is sometimes offered as a case in which one proposition
bears on another without any medium passing between them. The implication is held to be
complete as an account of the bearing, and no medium is invoked.
     The framework’s response is the same distinction. A logical implication is a relation of
logical dependence, not a relation of effect. The conveyor principle is a claim about effect;
it is not a claim about logical dependence. An account of logical dependence is complete
as an account of logical dependence, and the principle does not apply to it. The principle
would apply only if the account claimed that one proposition brings about the other; and the
account of logical implication does not claim that. A reader who offers logical implication as a
counterexample has applied the principle outside its scope.

Remark 8.18 (The Framework’s Response to the Logical Case). The framework’s response is
not a denial of logical dependence. It is the statement that logical dependence is a different
kind of relation from effect, and that the conveyor principle is a claim about effect. The two
are distinguished in Section 8.3, and the distinction is what makes the principle’s scope exact.
A reader who holds that logical dependence is a kind of effect has found a case in which the
principle might apply; the framework’s answer is that logical dependence is not an effect, and
that the principle is silent on it. The reader who disagrees has stated a disagreement about
the classification of logical dependence, not about the principle itself.


8.7.3    Borderline Case: Institutional Causation
An institutional explanation (“the law caused the behavior”) is a borderline case. The law
is sometimes treated as a medium (it carries the effect of the legislature’s decision to the
citizen’s behavior), and sometimes treated as a rule (it governs the behavior without carrying
an effect through a medium). The framework’s response is that the case is resolved by the
question the explanation is asking. If the question is “how did the legislature’s decision reach
the citizen?” the law is a medium, and the principle applies. If the question is “what rule
governs the citizen’s behavior?” the law is a governing dynamics, and the principle does not
apply, because the explanation is not an explanation of effect. The borderline case is not a
counterexample to the principle; it is a case in which the principle’s application depends on
the question, and the question is what the framework’s scope-statement (Section 8.3) requires
the reader to state.

Remark 8.19 (The Borderline Case and the Scope of the Principle). The borderline case
shows that the principle’s application depends on the question the explanation is asking. The
principle applies to explanations of effect, and it does not apply to explanations of rule or of
correlation. The institutional case can be either, depending on the question; the framework’s
response is to ask which question the explanation is answering, and to apply the principle only
to the explanation that answers the question of effect. The distinction is the distinction of
Section 8.3, applied to a case in which the distinction is not obvious. A reader who takes the
borderline case as a counterexample has not asked which question the explanation is answering;
a reader who asks the question has the principle’s scope in hand.
8.8. The Conveyor Principle and the Four Columns                                               107


8.8     The Conveyor Principle and the Four Columns
The conveyor principle is the first of the four columns to receive a proof of its own. In Chapter 7,
the necessity of the four columns was argued by the removal test; the test presupposed that the
fluid element is necessary (Chapter 7, Section 7.3, step (b)), and the present chapter supplies
the proof of that presupposition.
    The principle’s place in the framework can be summarized as follows.

Column              Role in the argument of this chapter
Fixed elements      The two terms whose relation is to be explained.
Fluid element       The medium by which the effect of one term reaches the other. The
                    conveyor principle asserts its necessity.
Governing           The rule of the medium’s operation. The conveyor principle does not
dynamics            assert anything about it; the rules are distributed across the chapters
                    that state the rules of the specific cognitive contexts (Chapter 6,
                    Remark 6.26).
Context             The frame in which the relation is posed. The conveyor principle is
                    silent on it; the frame is what makes the relation a relation between
                    these terms rather than others.
    The table is a summary, not a new argument. Its purpose is to locate the conveyor principle
in the framework’s architecture: the principle is about the second column, and it presupposes
the first and fourth. The third column—the governing dynamics—is not addressed by the
principle; the rules are distributed across the chapters that state the rules of the specific
cognitive contexts, as Chapter 6’s Remark on where each column is developed states.

Remark 8.20 (The Principle and the Order of the Columns). The conveyor principle is about
the second column, and it presupposes the first and fourth. The order in which the chapters
treat the columns is the order of the book, not the order of the principle’s dependence. The
fixed element is defined first (Chapter 6), the fluid element second (Chapter 6), the governing
dynamics third (Chapter 6), and the context fourth (Chapter 6). The conveyor principle is
about the fluid element, but it presupposes the fixed element (there must be terms for the
effect to hold between) and the context (the frame must pose the relation). The principle is
stated here, and its dependence on the first and fourth columns is stated with it.

Remark 8.21 (The Principle and the Non-Sequential Claim). The conveyor principle requires
that some fluid element carry the effect. It does not say that the effect must traverse, one
after another, every element that lies between two fixed elements in some ordering of them.
The distinction is important, and it is stated as a principle of its own in the next chapter,
under the heading of non-sequential connectivity. The present chapter establishes that some
fluid element is required; the next chapter establishes what the principle does not require.


8.9     The Principle and the Method
The principle is (T): it is argued, relative to the meaning of “how” that the framework employs.
Its argument is the reductio given in Section 8.5, and the reader who accepts the meaning has
a reason to accept the conclusion.
    The principle’s status is stated at the strength its argument supports. It is not a proof
from nothing; it depends on the meaning of “how,” and the framework states the meaning
so that the reader can assess the argument. A reader who denies the meaning denies the
argument, and the framework does not claim more than the argument delivers.
108                                                         Chapter 8. The Conveyor Principle


Remark 8.22 (The Principle and the Analysis of Epistemic Explanations). The conveyor
principle is not only a constraint on explanation; it is a tool for the analysis of epistemic
explanations. When an explanation of how a subject comes to know something is offered, the
principle directs the analysis to the medium by which the subject’s cognition reaches its object.
The medium is the epistemic light of Part III: the condition of possibility of legible relation,
by which an appearance is conveyed and by which a manifestation is rendered legible as an
appearance of its source. The principle’s function in the analysis of epistemic explanations is
to make the medium explicit, and to prevent an explanation of knowing from being offered as
complete when it names only the subject and the object and leaves the medium unnamed.
The function is stated positively here, so that the reader knows what the principle is for, not
only what it excludes.




Remark 8.23 (The Principle and the Other Columns). The conveyor principle is the first
of the four columns to receive a proof of its own. The other three columns are argued in the
chapters that follow: the context column is argued in Chapters 10–11 and 14; the fixed element
column is argued in Chapters 12–13; and the governing dynamics column is not argued by
a proof of its necessity in this volume—the rules are stated where the rules of the specific
cognitive contexts are stated (Chapter 6, Remark 6.26), and their necessity is left to the
chapter that states them. The reader who wishes to see the whole of the four-column argument
is directed to the dependency map in Chapter 43.




Remark 8.24 (What the Chapter Has Done). The chapter has done five things. It has stated
the conveyor principle, and it has proved it by reductio. It has stated the scope of the principle,
distinguishing effect from co-occurrence, correlation, and logical dependence. It has stated
what would falsify the principle, and it has examined two counterexamples (entanglement,
logical implication) and one borderline case (institutional causation). It has located the
principle in the four-column framework, and it has stated the principle’s dependence on the
first and fourth columns. And it has stated the principle’s function in the analysis of epistemic
explanations, so that the reader knows what the principle is for, not only what it excludes.
The chapter has not established the necessity of any particular fluid element; that is the work
of Chapters 15–17. The chapter’s contribution is the conveyor principle itself, proved at the
strength its argument supports, its scope, its falsification conditions, and its function in the
analysis of epistemic explanations.
