Chapter 10

Context-Dependence

Scope
This chapter states and argues the first of the two principles about the context column: the
claim that the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on the
element’s essence. It distinguishes the cognitive context, which the principle concerns, from
the context represented in the inquiry, which is the context that the explanation’s content
states. It states the limits of the argument, and it prepares the ground for the second principle
about the context column, the infinity of cognitive contexts, which is stated and argued in
Chapter 11.
     The principle is analytical, not ontological, in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes (Principle 5.1):
it is a claim about the roles that an explanation assigns, not a claim about what the elements are
in themselves. The two kinds of context (cognitive context, context represented in the inquiry)
are the same distinction that Chapter 6 introduced (Definition 6.4 and the remarks that follow
it) and that Chapter 14 develops systematically: the present chapter restates the distinction,
and it refers the reader to Chapter 14 for the full treatment. The principle’s generalization to
category-relative predication is the claim that Chapter 25 states (Principle 25.1); the present
chapter names the generalization, and it states the principle in its own place.
     Its claims are analytical; where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not
a denial but a recognition that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be said.
Where the chapter speaks of “fixedness,” “fluidity,” “essence,” “frame,” “role,” or “represented
context,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and
in the previous chapters.


10.1      A Scene: The River, the Word, the Coin
Consider three things that a single entity can be, in three different inquiries, and the apparent
contradictions that arise when the three are run together.
    A river. The political geographer asks: where does the border lie? For her, the river is
a boundary—a fixed element, held stable while the relations of the two banks are explained.
The trader asks: how do goods travel from this bank to that? For him, the same river is a
route—a fluid element, carrying effect from one side to the other. The geographer’s river and
the trader’s river are the same water, and they play different roles. Neither role is a mistake;
each is correct in its own frame. But if the geographer’s river is taken to be the river, and the
trader’s river is taken to be not the river but a mere appearance, then something has gone
wrong: a role that belongs to a frame has been mistaken for a property of the thing.
    A word. In a dictionary, the word is a fixed element: an entry whose meaning is held
constant while its relations to other entries are explained. In a conversation, the same word
is a fluid element: a conveyor of meaning between speakers. The dictionary’s word and the
126                                                            Chapter 10. Context-Dependence


conversation’s word are the same word, and they play different roles. If the dictionary’s word
is taken to be the word, and the conversation’s word is taken to be not the word but a misuse,
then the same mistake has been made: a role has been mistaken for an essence.
    A coin. In an economic analysis, the coin is a fixed unit of value. In a metallurgical analysis,
the same coin is a fluid sample of copper, carrying the effect of the alloy’s composition from
the mine to the market. The economist’s coin and the metallurgist’s coin are the same metal,
and they play different roles. The same mistake, if the roles are run together, is available here
too.
    The scene poses two questions. First: if fixedness is not a property of the thing, what is it
a property of? Second: how many such frames are there—is there a finite list of them, or does
the list run on without end? The present chapter answers the first question. The second is the
subject of Chapter 11.

Remark 10.1 (The Scene Shows a Pattern, Not Three Accidents). The three cases—river,
word, coin—are not three accidental coincidences; they exhibit the same structure. In each
case, an entity is held fixed in one frame and treated as fluid in another, and neither frame is
mistaken about what the entity is. The structure is what the principle names, and the pattern
is what the proof uses. A reader who takes the three cases as isolated curiosities has missed
the pattern; a reader who takes them as three instances of one structure has the principle.

Remark 10.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the
distinction at work in three familiar cases. It does not prove the context-dependence principle;
it makes the principle intelligible before it is stated. The proof of the principle is given in
Section 10.4, and the scene carries no weight in it.


10.2     The Question
The previous chapters of this part have developed the four columns (Chapter 6), the four-column
principle (Chapter 7), the conveyor principle (Chapter 8), and the principle of non-sequential
connectivity (Chapter 9). The present chapter turns to the fourth column, the context, and
asks a question about the roles the other three columns assign.
     The question is this. When an explanation holds an element fixed, or treats it as fluid, is
it identifying a property the element has in itself, or is it assigning a role that depends on the
explanation? The essentialist answer is that the element is fixed, or is fluid, in virtue of what
it is, and so in every frame alike. The framework’s answer is that fixedness and fluidity are
roles, assigned by the frame.
     The question is not merely terminological. If fixedness were a property of the thing, then
two frames that assign different roles to the same thing could not both be correct; one of them
would have to be mistaken about what the thing really is. If fixedness is a role, then both
frames can be correct in their own terms, and the apparent conflict between them is a conflict
between the frames, not between the thing and itself.
     The chapter’s answer is the context-dependence principle. The principle is stated and
proved in the next two sections. The chapter then distinguishes the cognitive context from the
context represented in the inquiry, states the limits of the argument, and prepares the ground
for the infinity of contexts in Chapter 11.

Remark 10.3 (The Question Is About the Source of the Role). The question is not whether
an element plays a role in an explanation; that is not in dispute. The question is what the
role depends on. The essentialist says: on the element’s essence. The framework says: on the
context. The two answers have different consequences. If the role depends on the essence,
then two frames that assign different roles to the same element cannot both be correct. If the
role depends on the context, then two frames that assign different roles to the same element
10.3. The Principle                                                                            127


can both be correct, because each role is indexed to its own context. The framework’s claim is
the second answer, and the chapter’s proof is what makes the second answer the better one.


10.3     The Principle
Principle 10.1 (Context-Dependence). (T) The fixedness or fluidity of an element depends
on the cognitive context, not on the element’s essence. A single element can be fixed in one
context and fluid in another.
    The principle is (T): it is argued, and the argument is given in the next section. Its
argument is a counterexample argument, and its force is the force of the counterexamples.
The principle is not a stipulation, and it is not an empirical generalization; it is a claim about
the structure of the roles that explanatory cognition assigns, and it is offered at the strength
of the argument that supports it.
    The principle has two halves, and both are worth marking.

The first half: the role depends on the context. Fixedness and fluidity are not
properties the element has in itself. They are roles the element plays in a frame, and the
frame is fixed by the question the cognition asks. The same element can play different roles in
different frames, and neither role is a mistake.

The second half: the role is not the essence. The element’s essence—whatever it is
that makes the element the element it is—does not determine its role. The role is assigned by
the frame, not read off the essence. The distinction between the role and the essence is what
allows two frames to assign different roles to the same element without either frame being
mistaken about what the element is.
Remark 10.4 (The Principle Concerns the Cognitive Context). The principle concerns the
cognitive context. It must not be read as saying that the context an explanation represents
depends on how it is studied. The context that an explanation represents is the context
its content states; it is fixed by the identity and the setting the explanation is about, not
by the question asked. The distinction between the two kinds of context was introduced in
Chapter 6 (Definition 6.4 and the remarks that follow it), and it is developed systematically in
Chapter 14; the present chapter restates the distinction, and it refers the reader to Chapter 14
for the full treatment. The cognitive context fixes the roles of elements in an explanation. The
context represented in the inquiry fixes what the explanation states about the setting of the
manifestation. The two are not the same, and the context-dependence principle concerns the
first alone.
Remark 10.5 (The Principle Is About Roles, Not About Value). The principle is a claim
about what fixedness is, not a claim about which assignments are good. It says that fixedness
is a role, and it leaves the question of which role assignments are adequate to the criteria of
context validity (Chapter 21). The distinction is the distinction between the kind of thing
fixedness is and the adequacy of a particular assignment; the framework keeps it apart, and
the reader who takes the principle as licensing arbitrary frames has misread it.


10.4     The Proof
The proof of the principle is a counterexample argument. Essentialism makes a universal claim;
the counterexamples show that the universal claim is false.

Proof of the Context-Dependence Principle.          1. Essentialism says: each element is fixed, or
      is fluid, in virtue of what it is, and so in every context.
128                                                          Chapter 10. Context-Dependence


   2. But a river is a fixed element (a boundary) in political geography and a fluid element
      (a route of transport) in the geography of trade. A word is a fixed element (an entry
      whose meaning is held constant) in a dictionary and a fluid element (a conveyor of
      meaning between speakers) in a conversation. A coin is a fixed element (a unit of value)
      in economic analysis and a fluid element (a sample of copper) in metallurgical analysis.

   3. So there are elements whose status differs between contexts. This contradicts the
      universal claim of essentialism.

   4. Hence fixedness and fluidity are not essential properties of elements. They are roles,
      assigned by the question a context asks: which relations it holds constant, and which it
      treats as carrying effect.


    The proof is a counterexample argument. Essentialism makes a universal claim; the
counterexample shows that the universal claim is false. The argument does not prove that
every element’s role varies with the frame; it proves that some do, and that is enough to refute
essentialism.

Remark 10.6 (The Counterexamples Are Not Controversial). The counterexamples are not
controversial, and this is what gives the proof its force. The river is a boundary in political
geography and a route in the geography of trade; the word is an entry in a dictionary and a
conveyor in a conversation; the coin is a unit of value in economics and a sample of copper in
metallurgy. These are not exotic cases; they are the ordinary furniture of inquiry. A reader
who denies that the river plays these roles has denied something that the geographers and
the traders who use the river take for granted; and the denial, if pressed, would have to show
that one of the two inquiries is mistaken about what the river is. The framework does not
claim that no such showing could be made; it claims that none has been made, and that the
ordinary cases the framework knows of support the principle.

Remark 10.7 (What the Proof Establishes and What It Does Not). The proof establishes
that essentialism is false: there are elements whose role differs between contexts, and the
difference cannot be explained by the element’s essence. The proof does not establish what
fixedness and fluidity are in positive terms. The framework’s positive account is that they
are roles assigned by the question a context asks; this account is stated, not proved, and a
reader who prefers a different positive account is invited to develop it. The proof establishes
the negative conclusion; the positive conclusion is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary,
and it is stated as such.

Remark 10.8 (The Proof Is Relative to the Counterexamples). The proof depends on the
counterexamples. A reader who denies that the river is a fixed element in political geography,
or that the word is a fluid element in a conversation, denies the force of the argument. The
framework does not claim that the counterexamples are beyond dispute; it claims that they
are the cases the framework knows of, and that the essentialist claim is false for them. A
reader who wishes to challenge the principle knows where to press.


10.5     Cognitive Context and Represented Context
The principle concerns the cognitive context, and the distinction between the cognitive context
and the context represented in the inquiry must be stated, because the two are easily run
together. The distinction was introduced in Chapter 6 (Definition 6.4 and the remarks that
follow it) and is developed systematically in Chapter 14; the present section restates it in the
form the present chapter requires.
10.5. Cognitive Context and Represented Context                                                 129


Definition 10.1 (Cognitive Context (restated)). A cognitive context is the frame in which
something is cognized: the question asked, the elements held fixed, the rule applied, and the
standpoint from which the partition into fixed and fluid is made. A cognitive context is fixed
by the question, and there are indefinitely many of them.

Definition 10.2 (Context Represented in the Inquiry (restated)). A context represented in
the inquiry is the setting that the explanation’s content states: the identity the explanation is
about, the setting the explanation says the manifestation occurs in, and the constraints the
explanation says the setting imposes. A context represented in the inquiry is fixed by the
explanation’s content, not by the question the explanation answers.

    The two definitions are different, and the difference is the difference between the frame in
which cognition occurs and the content that the cognition states. The cognitive context is the
frame through which what is becomes intelligible; the context represented in the inquiry is
the content that the explanation says about the setting. The two are distinct, and neither is
reducible to the other; but the first is the condition of possibility of the second. A manifestation
is realized in a setting before it is known in a frame; and the frame is the order through
which the setting becomes intelligible. The context that the explanation represents is the
explanation’s content about the setting; the cognitive context is the frame in which the
explanation’s content is stated.

Remark 10.9 (The Distinction Is the Analytical/Ontological Distinction of Chapter 5). The
distinction between the cognitive context and the context represented in the inquiry is a
particular case of the distinction that Chapter 5 states between the order of reconstruction
and the order of explanatory dependence (Principle 5.1). The cognitive context is the frame
through which what is becomes intelligible; the context represented in the inquiry is the
content that the explanation states about the setting. The distinction is the same distinction,
applied to the word “context”; and the two kinds of context are not two worlds, but two orders,
in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes.

Remark 10.10 (The Present Volume Is Concerned With the Cognitive Context). The present
volume is concerned with the cognitive context. The context represented in the inquiry is
named here to be marked off from the cognitive context; it is not developed as an ontology.
The question of what the setting of a manifestation is in itself, and of how the manifestation is
realized in the setting, is left to the chapter that states the framework’s account of manifestation
(Chapter 13). The context-dependence principle concerns the cognitive context alone; it does
not say that the setting the explanation represents depends on how it is studied.

Remark 10.11 (The Two Contexts Are Not Two Worlds). The distinction between the two
kinds of context is a distinction between two orders, not a separation of two worlds. The
context represented in the inquiry is the explanation’s content about the setting; the cognitive
context is the frame through which the content is stated. The framework keeps the two apart
so that the study of cognition is not confused with the study of the explanation’s content—but
the keeping-apart is not a denial that the two are related.

Remark 10.12 (The Two Contexts Answer Different Questions). The two kinds of context
answer different questions, and the difference is worth marking. The cognitive context answers
the question: in which frame is the element individuated and the rule applied? The context
represented in the inquiry answers the question: what does the explanation say about the
setting in which the manifestation occurs, and about the constraints the setting imposes?
The first is a question about the frame of the explanation; the second is a question about
the content of the explanation. The framework keeps the two apart so that the first is not
mistaken for the second; a reader who takes the cognitive context as the represented context
has confused the frame of the explanation with its content.
130                                                           Chapter 10. Context-Dependence


10.6     What the Principle Generalizes
The context-dependence principle is a special case of a broader structural claim, and the
broader claim is worth naming, because the book will use it in Part IV.
    The broader claim is that epistemic predicates are not absolute: they are defined relative
to a level or a respect. The present principle applies the broader claim to the level of the
cognitive context: just as a predicate is true or false relative to a respect, an element is fixed
or fluid relative to a context. The broader claim is stated and argued in Part IV, under the
heading of category-relative predication (Chapter 25, Principle 25.1). The present principle is
one of its applications, and it does not depend on the broader argument for its establishment.

Remark 10.13 (The Principle Is One Application of a General Claim). The principle is one
application of the general claim that predicates are relative. The general claim is stated in
Chapter 25, and the present principle is stated here, in its own place, because it is needed for
the infinity of contexts (Chapter 11) and for the impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27).
The reader who wishes to see the general claim in its own place is directed to Chapter 25; the
reader who wishes to see the present principle in its own place has it here.


10.7     Where This Principle Is Used
The principle is one of the structural tools of the volume, and the present section states
where it is used, so that the reader knows that the principle is load-bearing and not merely a
preliminary remark.

Infinity of contexts (Chapter 11). The principle says that fixedness and fluidity are roles;
      the infinity principle says that the frames in which roles are assigned are not finite
      in number. The two together imply that no finite survey of an element’s roles can
      be completed, and the implication is used in the argument for the impossibility of
      super-identity (Chapter 27).

Context and perspective (Chapter 14). The systematic treatment of the two kinds of
    context, and of the distinction between context and perspective, is given in Chapter 14.
    The present chapter states the principle that the systematic treatment presupposes; the
    reader who wishes to see the distinction in its own place is directed to Chapter 14.

Criteria of context validity (Chapter 21). The principle says that fixedness is a role; the
     criteria of context validity say which role assignments are valid. The criteria presuppose
     the principle, and the principle is stated at the strength the criteria require.

Category-relative predication (Chapter 25). The principle is one application of the gen-
    eral claim that epistemic predicates are relative (Principle 25.1). The general claim is
    stated and argued in Chapter 25; the present principle is its application to the cognitive
    context.

Impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27). The impossibility argument uses the in-
    finity of contexts (Chapter 11) and the context-bound character of manifestations
    (Chapter 13). The context-dependence principle is what makes the infinity of contexts
    applicable to the roles an element plays; without it, the infinity would be an infinity of
    frames with no bearing on the elements the frames cognize.

Fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28). The fallacy is the error of treating a record
     formed by aggregating manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the identity.
     The principle states that the roles of elements depend on the contexts; the fallacy is
     what happens when the roles are treated as if they did not.
10.8. The Criteria for Valid Role Assignments                                                  131


   The six uses are not six different principles; they are one principle, applied six times. The
reader who has understood the principle (Principle 10.1) will recognize it in each of the six
uses; the reader who has not will find the six uses disconnected.
Remark 10.14 (The Six Uses Are Not Arbitrary). The six uses are not an arbitrary list; they
are the places where the principle does its most important work. The first and second (infinity
of contexts, context and perspective) are the places where the principle is most immediately
needed for the argument of Part II and Part III; the third and fourth (criteria of context
validity, category-relative predication) are the places where the principle is most important for
the conditions of validity and for the general structural claim; the fifth and sixth (impossibility
of super-identity, fallacy of super-identity) are the places where the principle is most important
for the limits of Part V. The six are the places where the reader most needs the principle, and
the framework states their location so that the reader can see the principle at work in each of
them.


10.8     The Criteria for Valid Role Assignments
The principle says that fixedness and fluidity are roles. It does not say that every assignment
of roles is equally adequate. Some assignments will explain the phenomenon better than others;
some will fail to explain it at all. The criteria by which a role assignment is assessed are the
criteria of context validity, and the present section states them in the form the present chapter
requires, aligned with the full statement in Chapter 21.
Definition 10.3 (Criteria of Context Validity (summary form)). (A) A role assignment in a
cognitive context is valid when it satisfies the following conditions, stated in summary form
here and in full in Chapter 21:
(V1) Identifiability. The role assignment identifies the elements and the relations the explana-
     tion is about, so that a reader can locate them in the explanation.

(V2) Minimality. The role assignment does not introduce elements or relations that the
     explanation’s question does not require; the context is the smallest that explains the
     phenomenon.

(V3) Consistency. The role assignment is consistent with other valid contexts in which the
     same element appears, in the sense that the roles it assigns do not contradict the roles
     assigned elsewhere without a stated reason for the difference.

(V4) Completeness. The role assignment, together with the other three columns, leaves no
     question that the explanation’s question requires to be answered; the criterion is the one
     stated in Chapter 7 (Definition 7.1).
The four conditions are stated in summary form here; the full statement is in Chapter 21.
The summary is offered so that the reader can see, in the present chapter, what makes an
assignment valid, and can assess an assignment by the criteria without leaving the chapter.
    The definition is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s criteria. Its justification is
the account in Chapter 21, and the present definition is a summary of that account. The
four conditions are the criteria by which a role assignment is assessed; the principle says that
fixedness is a role, and the criteria say which roles are assignable.
Remark 10.15 (The Criteria and the Principle Are Complementary). The criteria and the
principle are complementary. The principle says that fixedness is a role; the criteria say which
assignments of roles are valid. A reader who accepts the principle and the criteria has a
complete account of what fixedness is and which assignments are adequate. A reader who
132                                                               Chapter 10. Context-Dependence


accepts the principle and not the criteria has an account of what fixedness is, but not of
which assignments are adequate; the framework states both so that the reader can assess an
assignment, not only recognize one.

Remark 10.16 (The Principle Does Not License Arbitrary Frames). The principle is easily
misread as licensing arbitrary frames: if fixedness is a role, then any role is as good as any
other. The misreading is not the principle. The principle is about the kind of thing fixedness is;
the criteria are about which assignments are correct. A frame that fails the criteria of validity
is not a legitimate frame, even though it is a frame; the principle does not claim otherwise.

Remark 10.17 (The Criteria Are Stated in Full in Chapter 21). The criteria are stated in
summary form in Definition 10.3, and in full in Chapter 21. The present chapter states the
principle and the summary of the criteria; the full statement is in its own place. The reader
who wishes to see the criteria in full is directed to Chapter 21; the reader who wishes to see
the principle that the criteria presuppose has it here.


10.9      The Principle’s Use in Classifying and Assessing Explana-
          tions
The principle is not only a constraint on explanation; it is a tool for classifying and assessing
explanations. The present section states the principle’s use in classification, and its use in
assessment, so that the reader knows what the principle is for, not only what it excludes.

The principle’s use in classification. The principle permits an explanation to be classified
by the roles it assigns, not by the entities it names. Two explanations that name different
entities may be instances of the same role structure; two explanations that name the same
entities may be instances of different role structures. The river that is a boundary in political
geography and the river that is a route in the geography of trade are two explanations with
different role structures, and the classification by role structure is what makes the difference
visible. The principle’s use in classification is to make the role structure the unit of classification,
and to treat the entities as the material in which the roles are realized.

The principle’s use in assessment. The principle permits an explanation to be assessed
by the validity of its role assignments, not by the entities it names. An explanation that assigns
roles validly is assessed as valid, whatever entities it names; an explanation that assigns roles
invalidly is assessed as invalid, whatever entities it names. The criteria of Definition 10.3 are
the criteria by which the assessment is made, and the principle’s use in assessment is to make
the validity of the role assignments the criterion of the explanation’s validity. The assessment
is an assessment of the explanation, not of the entities; the entities may be any entities, and
the assessment is the same.

Remark 10.18 (The Two Uses Are Complementary). The two uses are complementary.
The classification use groups explanations by role structure; the assessment use evaluates
explanations by role validity. The two together give the reader a way to place an explanation
in the space of explanations and a way to assess it within that space. The reader who uses
the principle for classification but not for assessment has a taxonomy without a standard; the
reader who uses it for assessment but not for classification has a standard without a taxonomy.
The framework provides both, and the two are stated together so that the reader can use them
together.

Remark 10.19 (The Uses Are Not Reductions of the Principle). The two uses are not
reductions of the principle; they are the principle’s application to two tasks of the inquiry.
10.10. The Limit of the Argument                                                              133


The principle itself is the claim that fixedness is a role; the uses are what the claim enables.
A reader who takes the uses as the principle has confused the claim with its application; a
reader who takes the principle as what the uses apply has the claim in hand.


10.10      The Limit of the Argument
Two limits of the argument must be stated, and each is worth stating with the argument it
limits.
     First, the context-dependence principle is proved by counterexample, and counterexample
proves only that essentialism is false. It does not establish what fixedness and fluidity are
in positive terms. The framework’s positive account is that they are roles assigned by the
question a context asks; this account is stated, not proved, and a reader who prefers a different
positive account is invited to develop it.
     Second, the principle concerns the cognitive context, not the context represented in the
inquiry. It does not say that the setting the explanation represents depends on how it is
studied. A reader who takes the principle as a claim about the represented context has misread
it; a reader who takes it as a claim about the cognitive context has read it correctly.
Remark 10.20 (The Limits Are Not Deficiencies). The limits are not deficiencies of the
argument. They are the conditions under which the argument is offered, and the framework
states them so that the reader knows what kind of claim is being made. A reader who accepts
the limits may still accept the principle; a reader who rejects the principle is invited to attack
it at the limits, since those are where the principle is most vulnerable.


10.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
     First, the chapter does not establish what fixedness and fluidity are in positive terms.
The proof establishes that essentialism is false; the positive account is a stipulation of the
framework’s vocabulary. A reader who prefers a different positive account is invited to develop
it, and the framework can say where its own account was stipulated.
     Second, the chapter does not develop the infinity of cognitive contexts. That is the subject
of Chapter 11. The present chapter states the principle that the infinity argument presupposes;
the argument itself is given in its own place.
     Third, the chapter does not develop the setting the explanation represents as an ontology.
It distinguishes the represented context from the cognitive context, and it leaves the account
of manifestation to Chapter 13. A reader who seeks a doctrine of levels of being will not find
it here; a reader who seeks the distinction between the cognitive context and the represented
context will find it.
     Fourth, the chapter does not settle the question of which role assignments are valid. The
criteria of context validity are stated in full in Chapter 21, and the present chapter leaves the
question to them. A reader who seeks the criteria in full will not find them here; a reader who
seeks the principle that the criteria presuppose, and a summary of the criteria, will find both.
Remark 10.21 (What the Chapter Has Done). The chapter has done five things. It has
stated the context-dependence principle, and it has proved it by counterexample. It has
distinguished the cognitive context from the context represented in the inquiry, and it has
stated the distinction in the terms the present volume requires. It has stated the criteria for
valid role assignments in summary form, aligned with Chapter 21. It has stated the principle’s
use in classifying and assessing explanations, so that the reader knows what the principle is
for, not only what it excludes. And it has stated the limits of the argument, so that the reader
knows what kind of claim the principle is. The chapter has not established what fixedness and
134                                                           Chapter 10. Context-Dependence


fluidity are in positive terms, has not developed the infinity of contexts, has not developed the
represented context as an ontology, and has not settled the question of which role assignments
are valid. The chapter’s contribution is the principle itself, proved by counterexample, the
distinction between the two kinds of context, the summary of the criteria, and the statement
of the principle’s uses.




10.12      The Principle and the Method




The principle is (T): it is argued, by counterexample. Its argument is given in Section 10.4,
and the reader who accepts the counterexamples has a reason to accept the conclusion.



   The principle’s status is stated at the strength its argument supports. It is not a proof from
nothing; it depends on the counterexamples, and the framework states the counterexamples so
that the reader can assess the argument. A reader who denies the counterexamples denies the
argument, and the framework does not claim more than the argument delivers.




Remark 10.22 (The Principle and the Next Chapter). The principle is the first of the two
principles about the context column. The second is the infinity of cognitive contexts, stated
and argued in Chapter 11. The two are related: the present principle says that fixedness is a
role; the next principle says that the frames in which roles are assigned are not finite in number.
The two together imply that no finite survey of an element’s roles can be completed, and the
implication is used in Chapter 27, in the argument for the impossibility of super-identity.
