A Question for Reflection
Can you name an element that plays a fixed role in one frame and a fluid role in another, and
whose roles in the two frames are both correct? What would it mean to say that one of the
two frames has got the element’s role wrong? And can you assess the two role assignments by
the criteria of Definition 10.3: are both assignments identifiable, minimal, consistent with each
other, and complete?
    And consider the three cases that opened the chapter—the river, the word, the coin. In
each case, the same entity plays different roles in different frames, and neither role is a mistake.
136                                                          Chapter 10. Context-Dependence


What does the pattern tell you about the difference between a role and an essence? If the
roles were essences, what would follow about the two frames? And if the roles are not essences,
what follows about the relation between the frames? Finally, consider the principle’s use in
classifying and assessing explanations (Section 10.9): can you classify an explanation by its
role structure, and can you assess it by the validity of its role assignments? A reader who can
answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the
chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter states and argues the infinity of cognitive contexts: the claim that the frames
in which roles are assigned are not finite in number. The two principles together imply that
no finite survey of an element’s roles can be completed, and the implication is used in the
argument for the impossibility of super-identity in Part V.
                                                                                              137




Chapter 11

Infinity of Cognitive Contexts

Scope
This chapter states and argues the second of the two principles about the context column: the
claim that the cognitive contexts in which an identity can be cognized are not finite in number.
It states the openness of relations as an axiom, derives the unbounded openness of contexts
from it, states the two principles about the context column in tandem, and states the limits of
the argument. It closes Part II.
     A word on what the chapter claims and what it does not. The claim is unbounded openness,
not mathematical infinity. The chapter argues that no finite list of cognitive contexts can be
complete, and that the generation of new contexts does not terminate. It does not claim that
the contexts form a set of a particular cardinality; the cardinality question is marked (S) and
left open. The distinction between unbounded openness and mathematical infinity is stated in
Section 11.4, and it is observed throughout.
     The subject-side character of the openness is a particular case of the distinction that
Chapter 5 states (Principle 5.1): the openness is an openness of the standpoints of cognition,
not of the levels of being. The context column whose openness the chapter argues is the
role that Chapter 6 defines (Definition 6.4) and distributes across the volume (Remark 6.26).
The context-dependence principle (Chapter 10) is the first of the two principles in tandem
(Principle 10.1); the present chapter states the second. The open questions of Chapter 34
include the present chapter’s claim among their fourteen: the (S) claim about the countability
of the generated contexts is one of the questions the framework leaves open.
     The openness argued here is an openness of cognitive contexts, not an openness of being;
the distinction is stated in the chapter itself and observed throughout. Its claims are analytical;
where the chapter is silent on questions of value, the silence is not a denial but a recognition
that the analytical description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks
of “openness,” “generation,” “frame,” “inquiry,” or “survey,” these are structural terms; their
sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the previous chapter.


11.1      A Scene: The Footnote and the Thesis
Consider a single sentence in a doctoral thesis. The sentence is: “The city was not only a place
but also a project.”
    The sentence is a manifestation of the author’s identity in the context of the thesis. It is a
fixed element of the thesis; the thesis is about the sentence among other things.
    Now consider the same sentence in a footnote of a later article. The article’s author quotes
the sentence and criticizes it: she says the sentence confuses two senses of “project,” and that
the confusion is characteristic of the author’s school. The sentence is no longer a fixed element
138                                                  Chapter 11. Infinity of Cognitive Contexts


of the thesis; it is a fixed element of the criticism. The criticism is a different context, and the
sentence plays a different role in it.
    Now consider the criticism in a review of the article. The reviewer says that the critic’s
reading of the sentence is uncharitable, and that the critic has missed the sentence’s irony.
The criticism is now a fixed element of the review, and the sentence is a fixed element of the
criticism, and the review is a fixed element of a further context.
    At each step, the previous product becomes a fixed element of a new context. The sentence
is never exhausted. The thesis is not the last word on the sentence; the criticism is not the
last word on the thesis; the review is not the last word on the criticism. The sequence does
not terminate. There is no final context in which the sentence is exhausted, because every
context produces a new element that can be the starting point of a further context.
    The scene poses a question. Is the sequence finite? Is there a last context, after which
no further context can be generated? The present chapter’s answer is that there is not. The
sequence is non-terminating, and the non-termination is structural, not contingent on the
subject’s effort or the subject’s resources. The present chapter states the argument.

Remark 11.1 (The Scene Shows Generation, Not Just Repetition). The scene shows more
than repetition: it shows generation. The criticism does not merely repeat the thesis; it
produces something the thesis did not contain—a claim about the thesis’s confusion, which
becomes itself a fixed element of the review. The sentence is not merely passed from hand
to hand; it is transformed at each step, and each transformation opens a new context. The
generation is what the argument uses, and the scene shows the generation at work in a familiar
case.

Remark 11.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the
generation of contexts at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the openness of contexts;
it makes the claim intelligible before it is argued. The argument is given in Section 11.5.1,
and the scene carries no weight in it.


11.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated and argued the context-dependence principle (Principle 10.1):
the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on the element’s
essence. The principle left a question open. If fixedness depends on the context, and if the
context is fixed by the question, then how many questions are there? If the number of questions
is finite, then the number of contexts is finite, and a complete survey of the roles an element
can play might be possible in principle. If the number of questions is open-ended, no such
survey can be completed, and the epistemic humility the book will state in Chapter 35 has a
structural ground.
     The question is not whether we, in fact, have surveyed all the contexts. The question is
whether the survey could, in principle, be completed. The next sections argue that it cannot.
The argument has two parts. The first part states an assumption about the openness of
relations. The second part uses the assumption to generate a non-terminating sequence of
contexts.

Remark 11.3 (The Question Is About the Structure of the Survey, Not Its Fact). The
question is not about how many contexts we have surveyed, or how many we could survey with
more effort. It is about whether the survey has a terminus in principle. The claim will be that
it does not, and that the non-termination is structural. A subject that had more resources
would not complete the survey; it would only proceed further along a sequence that has no
end.
11.3. The Openness of Relations                                                              139


Remark 11.4 (The Question Is Not Rhetorical). The question is not rhetorical, and the
answer is not assumed. A reader who thinks the answer is obviously yes is invited to say what
the last context would be; a reader who thinks the answer is obviously no is invited to say
what would prevent the generation. The framework offers an argument, and the argument
can be assessed; a reader who accepts the argument accepts the conclusion, and a reader who
denies the argument denies the conclusion. The question is not settled by rhetoric, and the
chapter does not settle it by rhetoric.


11.3     The Openness of Relations
The first part of the argument is an assumption about what happens when a manifestation is
produced in a context. The assumption is stated as a definition and adopted as an axiom.
Definition 11.1 (Openness of Relations). (A) Openness of relations: for every cognitive
context C and every manifestation m that an identity has in C, there is a cognitive context
C ′ in which m is itself a fixed element, related by fluid elements and dynamics that are not
available in C.
     The definition says that any manifestation, once produced, can become an element in a
further context. The manifestation is not merely a label for the identity that produced it;
it is a thing in its own right, and it can be related to other things in ways the producing
context did not consider. The definition uses “fluid elements and dynamics” in the generic
sense that Chapter 6 fixes (Definition 6.2 and Definition 6.3); the specific form of the fluid
element (epistemic light) is developed in Chapters 15–17, and the specific rules (governing
dynamics) are distributed across the chapters that state the rules of the specific cognitive
contexts (Chapter 6, Remark 6.26).
Remark 11.5 (Why Openness Is Plausible). The assumption is plausible because a mani-
festation is not a mere label for the identity; it is the product of the identity’s interaction
with a receiving cognitive context. Once produced, it is a thing in its own right, and it
can be related to other things in ways the producing context did not consider. A speech is
manifested in a conversation and then becomes a fixed element in an analysis of rhetoric; a
building is manifested in a street and then becomes a fixed element in the history of a city.
The assumption is that this step never runs out. It is the framework’s version of the familiar
observation that every answer in inquiry opens further questions.
Remark 11.6 (Openness Is Not a Claim About Reality). The assumption is a claim about the
structure of inquiry, not a claim about reality. It says that any manifestation, once produced,
can become an element of a further context; it does not say that every manifestation will, in
fact, become an element of a further context. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure of inquiry and the contingent history of inquiry; the framework claims the first, not
the second. A reader who takes openness as a claim about reality has misread it; a reader who
takes it as a claim about the structure of inquiry has read it correctly.
Example 11.1 (A Speech). A speaker says something in a conversation. The utterance is a
manifestation of the speaker’s identity in the relational context of conversation. In a subsequent
inquiry, the same utterance is a fixed element—a text to be analyzed for its rhetorical structure.
In a further inquiry, the analysis is itself a fixed element—a document to be studied for its
assumptions. At each step, the previous product becomes an element of a new context. The
example illustrates the assumption; it does not prove it.
    The assumption is adopted, not proved. Its justification is that it is plausible in light
of what manifestations are, and that its denial would require an argument the framework
does not have. A reader who denies the assumption can still accept the context-dependence
principle; what the reader denies is the basis for the openness of contexts.
140                                                  Chapter 11. Infinity of Cognitive Contexts


Remark 11.7 (What a Denial of Openness Would Require). A critic who denies openness
must say what a closed space of contexts would be: a list of contexts that exhausts, in advance,
every context in which a manifestation can appear. The framework offers no such list, and it
does not know of one. The critic who offers such a list has a reason to reject the assumption;
the framework does not pretend otherwise.
Remark 11.8 (Openness Is Not a Guarantee of a Particular Cardinality). Openness is not
a guarantee of a particular cardinality. A sequence generated from openness might be finite
in a particular case (if, say, the sequence terminates for some reason the framework does not
foresee). Openness is a structural claim that the generation can proceed; the openness-of-
contexts argument (Principle 11.1) uses the claim to show that no finite list can be complete.
The distinction is the distinction between the possibility of generation and the impossibility
of completion; the framework claims the possibility of generation and the impossibility of
completion, and it does not claim a particular cardinality.


11.4     Unbounded Openness, Not Mathematical Infinity
The chapter’s conclusion is easy to misread, and the present section states the distinction that
prevents the misreading. The conclusion is unbounded openness: the generation of contexts
from any given context does not terminate, and no finite list of contexts is complete. The
conclusion is not mathematical infinity: the chapter does not claim that the contexts form a
set of a particular cardinality, and it does not claim that the number of contexts is countably
or uncountably infinite. The two claims are different, and the chapter’s argument supports
the first, not the second.
Definition 11.2 (Unbounded Openness of Potential Contexts). (T) The cognitive contexts in
which an identity can be cognized are unboundedly open when, for every finite list of contexts,
there is a context not on the list. Unbounded openness does not assert a cardinality for the
collection of contexts; it asserts that no finite list is complete.
    The definition is (T): it follows from the openness assumption (Definition 11.1) by the
generative argument of Section 11.5.1. The definition’s scope is the finite list: it says that no
finite list is complete, and it says nothing about the cardinality of the collection beyond that.
Remark 11.9 (The Two Claims Are Different). Unbounded openness and mathematical
infinity are different claims, and the difference is worth marking. Unbounded openness says:
no finite list is complete. Mathematical infinity says: the collection has a cardinality greater
than every finite cardinality. The first is a claim about the failure of finite lists; the second is
a claim about the size of a set. The first is established by the generative argument; the second
is not, and the chapter does not claim it. A reader who takes the chapter’s conclusion as a
claim of mathematical infinity has read more than the chapter contains; a reader who takes it
as a claim of unbounded openness has read it correctly.
Remark 11.10 (Why the Distinction Matters). The distinction matters for two reasons. First,
the generative argument establishes unbounded openness by showing that from any context, a
further context can be generated; it does not establish that the generated contexts form a set,
and the question of cardinality is not settled by the argument. Second, the distinction matters
for the framework’s claim about the limits of finite inquiry: the claim is that the finite subject
cannot complete the survey, not that the survey’s object has a particular cardinality. The
distinction is the difference between a claim about the subject’s inquiry and a claim about the
object of the inquiry; the framework’s claim is about the first, not the second.
Remark 11.11 (The Cardinality Question Is Marked (S)). Whether the contexts, if they
form a set, are countable or uncountable is marked (S) in Principle 11.1, and the framework
11.5. The Openness of Contexts                                                                   141


does not settle it. The question is one of the fourteen open questions of Chapter 34. A reader
who settles it is invited to do so; the framework’s claim is stated at the strength of unbounded
openness, and the cardinality is left open.


11.5      The Openness of Contexts
The second part of the argument uses the openness assumption to generate a non-terminating
sequence of contexts.
Principle 11.1 (Unbounded Openness of Contexts). (T) Given the openness assumption of
Definition 11.1, the cognitive contexts in which an identity can be cognized are unboundedly
open in the sense of Definition 11.2: no finite list of them is complete.
   (S) Whether the collection of contexts, if it forms a set, is countable or uncountable is left
open.
    The principle has two halves, with different statuses. The first half is (T): given openness,
the non-terminating generation argument below establishes that no finite list is complete.
The second half is (S): whether the collection is countable or uncountable is a question the
framework does not settle. The two halves are stated together because they concern a single
claim, but the reader is invited to assess them separately.

11.5.1    The Proof
Proof of Unbounded Openness of Contexts.       1. Let C0 be any cognitive context for an iden-
      tity I, and let m0 be a manifestation of I in C0 .
   2. By openness, there is a context C1 in which m0 is a fixed element, related by new fluid
      elements and dynamics. I has a manifestation m1 in C1 , and m1 differs from m0 , since
      it is the product of I with a different context.
   3. Apply the same step to m1 , and so on. The sequence C0 , C1 , C2 , . . . never repeats: each
      Cn+1 contains an element mn that is not a fixed element of Cn or of any earlier context,
      since manifestations are context-bound products.
   4. So no finite list of cognitive contexts is complete.


    The proof depends on a premise that is not established here: that manifestations are
context-bound products. The premise is developed in Part III, in the chapter on manifestation
as epistemic appearance (Chapter 13). Here it is stated as a premise of the argument, and the
argument is offered as what follows from it.
Remark 11.12 (The Proof Establishes Unbounded Openness, Not Cardinality). The proof
establishes that no finite list of contexts is complete. It does not establish whether the collection
of contexts, if it forms a set, is countable or uncountable; that question is marked (S) in
Principle 11.1, and the framework does not settle it. The proof’s conclusion is unbounded
openness in the sense of Definition 11.2, not mathematical infinity. A reader who wishes
to settle the cardinality question is invited to do so; the framework’s claim is stated at the
strength of unbounded openness, and the cardinality is left open.
Remark 11.13 (The Proof Is a Generative Argument). The proof is a generative argument,
and its form is worth marking. It does not enumerate the contexts; it shows that from any
context, a further context can be generated. The generation is what does the work, and the
generation is the content of the openness assumption. A reader who accepts the generation
accepts the conclusion; a reader who denies the generation denies the assumption, and the
framework states the assumption so that the denial can be directed.
142                                                Chapter 11. Infinity of Cognitive Contexts


Remark 11.14 (The Proof Depends on Openness and on Context-Bound Products). The
proof depends on two premises: the openness of relations (Definition 11.1) and the premise
that manifestations are context-bound products (Chapter 13). A reader who denies either
premise denies the argument. The framework states both premises so that the reader can
assess the argument, and it does not claim more than the premises deliver.

Remark 11.15 (The Proof Is Not a Proof by Induction). The proof is not a proof by induction,
and the difference is worth marking. A proof by induction would establish a property of every
member of a sequence; the present proof establishes that the sequence cannot be completed.
The first is a claim about each member; the second is a claim about the whole. The distinction
is the distinction between a claim that every context in the sequence has a successor and a
claim that no finite list exhausts the sequence; the framework claims the second, and the proof
establishes it by showing that from any context, a further one can be generated.


11.6     The Openness Is on the Side of the Subject
The openness established here is an openness of contexts, not an openness of being. The
distinction is crucial, and it is worth stating with care.
    The framework does not claim that reality is open-ended in itself. It claims that the frames
in which reality can be cognized are unboundedly open. The distinction is the distinction
between the order of inquiry and the order of being, and it is observed throughout the book.
The openness is on the side of the subject: it is the subject’s inquiry that is non-terminating,
not the object of the inquiry that is inexhaustible. The framework’s claim is that the finite
subject cannot complete the survey; it does not claim that the survey has no object, or that
the object is beyond all survey.

11.6.1    The Subject’s Role in Producing or Identifying New Contexts
The openness is on the side of the subject, and the subject’s role in producing or identifying
new contexts is worth stating with an example. The subject does not merely find contexts that
were already there; the subject produces them, by asking a question that the earlier context
did not ask, and by treating the earlier context’s product as an element of the new inquiry.
The following example shows the subject’s role at each step.

Example 11.2 (The Subject’s Role at Each Step). Consider the sentence of the scene
(Section 11.1), and the subject’s activity at each step.
    Step 1. The thesis author writes the sentence “The city was not only a place but also a
project.” The subject (the author) produces the sentence as a manifestation of her identity in
the thesis’s context. The sentence is a fixed element of the thesis.
    Step 2. A later critic reads the thesis and asks: does the sentence confuse two senses of
“project”? The critic’s question is a new question; the thesis did not ask it, and the thesis’s
context did not contain it. The critic produces a new context (the criticism) by asking the
new question, and she treats the sentence as a fixed element of the criticism. The step is the
subject’s production of the new context.
    Step 3. A reviewer reads the criticism and asks: is the critic’s reading uncharitable, and
has the critic missed the sentence’s irony? The reviewer’s question is a new question; the
criticism did not ask it, and the criticism’s context did not contain it. The reviewer produces
a new context (the review) by asking the new question, and she treats the criticism as a fixed
element of the review. The step is the subject’s production of the new context.
    The pattern. At each step, the subject produces a new context by asking a question the
earlier context did not ask, and treats the earlier context’s product as a fixed element of the
new context. The openness is the structure of this production: the subject can always ask a
11.7. The Two Principles in Tandem                                                          143


new question, and the new question always produces a new context. The subject’s role is not
to find contexts that were already there; it is to produce them by asking new questions.
    The example shows the subject’s role at each step. The openness is on the side of the
subject because the production of new contexts is the subject’s activity: the subject asks the
new question, and the new question produces the new context. A subject that did not ask
new questions would not produce new contexts; the openness is the structure of the subject’s
activity, not a feature of the object that the subject studies.
Remark 11.16 (The Subject’s Role Is Production, Not Discovery). The subject’s role is
production, not discovery. The subject does not find contexts that were already there, waiting
to be discovered; the subject produces them by asking questions that the earlier context did
not ask. The distinction is the distinction between the discovery of a pre-existing structure
and the production of a new context; the framework claims the second, not the first. A reader
who takes the openness as a claim about a pre-existing infinity has misread it; a reader who
takes it as a claim about the subject’s activity of producing new contexts has read it correctly.
Remark 11.17 (The Subject’s Role Is Structural, Not Contingent). The subject’s role
is structural, not contingent. The subject can always ask a new question, because the
manifestation the earlier context produced is a thing in its own right, and a thing in its own
right can always be made the subject of a new question. The structural character of the role is
what makes the openness unbounded; a role that depended on the subject’s effort or resources
would be contingent, and the openness would be a contingent fact, not a structural one. The
framework’s claim is the structural one.
Remark 11.18 (The Openness Is a Particular Case of the Distinction of Chapter 5). The
distinction between the openness of contexts and the openness of being is a particular case
of the distinction that Chapter 5 states between the order of reconstruction and the order of
explanatory dependence (Principle 5.1). The openness of contexts is an openness on the side
of reconstruction: it is an openness of the standpoints of cognition, not of the levels of being.
The openness of being would be a claim about what is, and the present volume does not make
it. The distinction is the same distinction, applied to the word “openness”; and the two kinds
of openness are not two worlds, but two orders, in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes.
Remark 11.19 (The Object May Be Fully Known to a Subject That Is Not Finite). The
framework’s claim is about the finite subject, not about the object. The object may be fully
known to a subject that is not finite; the framework’s silence on the infinite subject is not a
denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the framework’s method is the method of
finite inquiry, and that the limits of finite inquiry are not the limits of what is. The reader
who takes the openness of contexts as a claim about reality has misread it; the reader who
takes it as a claim about finite inquiry has read it correctly.
Remark 11.20 (An Image, Not an Argument). A cone cut by planes at different angles yields
different figures. The image illustrates how one structure shows different faces under different
cuts. It is not an argument for the openness of contexts: the number of ways of cutting a cone
says nothing about the number of cognitive contexts. The argument is the generative one
above, and its force is exactly that of the openness assumption.


11.7     The Two Principles in Tandem
The two principles of the context column are distinct, but they are related, and their relation
is worth stating.
    The context-dependence principle (Chapter 10, Principle 10.1) says that fixedness is a
role, not an essence. The openness principle says that the frames in which roles are assigned
144                                                  Chapter 11. Infinity of Cognitive Contexts


are unboundedly open. Together, they imply that an element can be fixed in some contexts
and fluid in others, and that the production of new contexts does not terminate. No finite
survey of an element’s roles can be completed, because the roles depend on the frames, and
the frames are unboundedly open.
    This consequence will matter for the framework’s claim about super-identity. The claim is
that no finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts. The openness of
contexts is one of the premises of that claim; the other is the finitude of the subject (Chapter 3).
The two premises together yield the conclusion. The argument for super-identity is given
in Chapter 27; for the present, it is enough to see that the openness principle is one of its
structural grounds.

Principle                   What it establishes
Context-dependence          Fixedness and fluidity are roles, assigned by the frame, not
                            properties of the element.
Unbounded openness of       The frames in which roles are assigned are unboundedly open;
contexts                    no finite list of them is complete.
Both together               An element can play roles in unboundedly many contexts; no
                            finite survey of its roles can be completed.


Remark 11.21 (Epistemic Humility Is Not Skepticism). The framework’s epistemic humility
is the recognition of the limits of finite inquiry, not a denial that knowledge is possible. The
finite subject can know; what the finite subject cannot do is complete the survey. The two
claims are different, and the difference matters. A skeptic claims that knowledge is impossible;
the framework claims that knowledge is partial. The first is a denial of knowledge; the second
is a description of its condition. The framework’s claim is that the partiality is structural: it
belongs to the relation between a finite subject and an identity, not to the identity itself, and
not to the object of knowledge. The identity may be fully known to a subject that is not finite;
the framework’s claim is about the finite subject, not about the identity. The distinction is
developed in Chapter 35, in the account of epistemic humility; the present remark states the
version of the distinction that the present chapter requires.

Remark 11.22 (The Two Principles Are Separable). The two principles are separable. A
reader who denies openness can accept the context-dependence principle and deny the openness
principle; the two are related but distinct. The context-dependence principle is proved by
counterexample (Chapter 10); the openness principle is derived from openness (the present
chapter). A reader who accepts one and rejects the other has a coherent position, and the
framework does not claim otherwise. The separability is what allows the two principles to be
assessed independently; a reader who is persuaded by one and not by the other has a position
that the framework recognizes as coherent.

Remark 11.23 (The Tandem Is What Makes the Fallacy Possible). The two principles in
tandem are what make the fallacy of super-identity possible. The fallacy is the error of treating
a record formed by aggregating manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the
identity; the possibility of the error depends on the roles being context-dependent (Chapter 10)
and on the contexts being unboundedly open (the present chapter). A reader who accepts the
two principles can see why the fallacy is tempting: the record seems to capture everything,
and the temptation is to treat the finite record as if it were the whole. The framework states
the two principles in tandem so that the fallacy can be stated precisely, and the fallacy is
stated in Chapter 28.
11.8. A Method for Managing New Contexts                                                    145


11.8     A Method for Managing New Contexts
The chapter’s positive contribution is a method for managing the new contexts that the
openness principle makes inevitable. The method is stated here as the chapter’s epistemic
result, so that the reader knows what the principle is for, not only what it excludes.

11.8.1    The Method
The method has four steps, and each step is a practice that the principle recommends to a
finite subject.

  1. Track the contexts already surveyed. The subject records the contexts in which it
     has cognized the identity, and the roles the identity played in each. The record is finite,
     and it is the subject’s current survey. The record is not the identity; it is the subject’s
     finite sample of the identity’s roles.

  2. Identify the open questions that the current contexts leave unanswered. For
     each context in the record, the subject asks: what question does this context not ask?
     The unanswered questions are the points at which new contexts can be produced. The
     questions are the subject’s entry points into the unbounded openness.

  3. Produce new contexts by asking the open questions. For each open question,
     the subject asks the question, treats the earlier context’s product as a fixed element of
     the new inquiry, and produces a new context. The production is the subject’s activity,
     and it is what the openness principle makes possible.

  4. Assess the new contexts by the criteria of validity. For each new context, the
     subject assesses its role assignments by the criteria of context validity (Chapter 21). A
     new context is not thereby valid; it is a new candidate, and the criteria decide whether
     it is a legitimate context for the identity’s roles.

   The method is a practice, not a proof. It does not complete the survey; it states how
the finite subject manages the survey it cannot complete. The method’s four steps are the
operational form of the openness principle, and the two are stated together so that the reader
can move from the principle to the practice without a gap.

11.8.2    The Method’s Relation to the Other Parts of the Framework
The method is related to the other parts of the framework, and the relations are worth stating.

The two principles of the context column (Chapters 10–11). The method applies both
    principles: the context-dependence principle (Chapter 10) is what makes the roles depend
    on the contexts, and the openness principle (the present chapter) is what makes the
    contexts unboundedly open. The method’s four steps are the practice that the two
    principles recommend.

The criteria of context validity (Chapter 21). The method’s fourth step is the applica-
    tion of the criteria of validity to the new contexts. The criteria are what decide whether a
    new context is a legitimate context; the method’s fourth step is the criteria’s application.

The impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27). The method’s first step (track the
     contexts already surveyed) is the finite subject’s alternative to the impossible super-
     identity. The subject cannot know the identity’s roles in all contexts; it can track the
     roles in the contexts it has surveyed, and it can manage the unbounded openness by the
     method’s four steps.
146                                                 Chapter 11. Infinity of Cognitive Contexts


The fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28). The method’s second step (identify the open
    questions) is what prevents the fallacy. The fallacy is the error of treating the finite
    record as the identity; the method’s second step is the practice of identifying what the
    record leaves out, and it is the practice that the fallacy fails to perform.

Epistemic humility (Chapter 35). The method is the practice that epistemic humility
     recommends. Humility is the disposition that recognizes the limits of finite inquiry;
     the method is the practice that the disposition takes. The two are complementary:
     the disposition without the practice would be a sentiment; the practice without the
     disposition would be a procedure.

    The five relations are the method’s place in the framework. The method is not a new
principle; it is the practice that the framework’s principles and criteria recommend. The reader
who has followed the framework to this point has the principles and the criteria; the method
is what they recommend in the management of new contexts.

Remark 11.24 (The Method Is a Practice, Not a Guarantee). The method is a practice, not
a guarantee. It does not guarantee that the subject will produce the right new contexts, or
that the new contexts it produces will be valid. It states what the finite subject can do to
manage the unbounded openness; it does not promise that the management will be complete,
because no finite management can be. The method’s value is that it is the finite subject’s
best available practice, not that it is a complete solution. A reader who takes the method as
a guarantee has misread it; a reader who takes it as the finite subject’s practice has read it
correctly.

Remark 11.25 (The Method’s Steps Are the Operational Form of the Principles). The
method’s four steps are the operational form of the two principles of the context column and
the criteria of validity. The first step (track the contexts already surveyed) is the recognition
that the roles are context-dependent (Chapter 10). The second step (identify the open
questions) is the recognition that the contexts are unboundedly open (the present chapter).
The third step (produce new contexts) is the practice that the openness principle makes
possible. The fourth step (assess the new contexts) is the criteria’s application. The four steps
are the practice that the principles and the criteria recommend, and the method’s statement
is the framework’s way of making the principles usable.


11.9     Where This Principle Is Used
The principle is one of the structural tools of the volume, and the present section states
where it is used, so that the reader knows that the principle is load-bearing and not merely a
preliminary remark.

Impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27). The principle is one of the two premises
    of the impossibility argument: no finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity
    in all contexts, because the contexts are unboundedly open (the present chapter) and
    the subject is finite (Chapter 3). The impossibility argument would not go through
    without the openness principle; and the openness principle, in turn, is what makes
    the context-dependence principle (Chapter 10) bear on the impossibility of a complete
    survey.

Fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28). The fallacy is the error of treating a record
     formed by aggregating manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the identity.
     The openness principle states that the contexts are unboundedly open; the fallacy is
     what happens when a subject treats a finite record as if it exhausted an open space. The
11.10. The Limit of the Argument                                                            147


      principle is the structural background of the fallacy; without it, the fallacy would be an
      error about a finite space, not about an open one.

Epistemic humility (Chapter 35). The principle is the structural ground of epistemic
     humility: the finite subject cannot complete the survey, and humility is the disposition
     that recognizes the limits of finite inquiry. The principle states what the limit is;
     Chapter 35 states the disposition that the limit requires. The method of Section 11.8 is
     the practice that the disposition takes.

Limits of self-knowledge (Chapter 30). The limits of self-knowledge are a particular case
     of the openness principle, applied to the subject’s own identity: the contexts in which
     the subject’s own identity can be cognized are unboundedly open, and the subject’s
     self-knowledge is therefore a reconstruction from a finite sample, not a complete survey.

    The four uses are not four different principles; they are one principle, applied four times.
The reader who has understood the principle (Principle 11.1) will recognize it in each of the
four uses; the reader who has not will find the four uses disconnected.

Remark 11.26 (The Four Uses Are Not Arbitrary). The four uses are not an arbitrary
list; they are the places where the principle does its most important work. The first two
(impossibility of super-identity, fallacy of super-identity) are the places where the principle
is most immediately needed for the argument of Part V; the third (epistemic humility) is
the place where the principle is most important for the disposition that Part V requires; the
fourth (limits of self-knowledge) is the place where the principle is most important for the
subject’s own identity. The four are the places where the reader most needs the principle, and
the framework states their location so that the reader can see the principle at work in each of
them.


11.10      The Limit of the Argument
Three limits of the argument must be stated, and each is worth stating with the argument it
limits.
    First, the openness principle depends on the openness assumption. A reader who denies
openness can accept the context-dependence principle and deny the openness principle; the two
are related but separable. The framework adopts openness because its denial would require an
argument the framework does not have, and because the assumption is plausible in light of
what manifestations are. The framework does not claim that openness is necessary in every
conceivable framework.
    Second, the principle of openness is a structural claim about cognitive contexts, not a
claim about the world. It does not say that the world is open-ended; it says that the frames in
which the world can be studied are unboundedly open. A reader who is concerned that the
framework is making a metaphysical claim about openness is invited to read the principle at
its stated strength: it is a claim about the analytical structure of cognition, not about the
extent of being.
    Third, the principle leaves the cardinality of the collection of contexts open. Whether the
collection, if it forms a set, is countable or uncountable is marked (S), and the framework does
not settle it. The claim is the non-termination of the generation, not the cardinality of what
is generated.
    These limits are not deficiencies of the argument. They are the conditions under which the
argument is offered, and they are stated so that the reader knows what kind of claim is being
made.
148                                                 Chapter 11. Infinity of Cognitive Contexts


Remark 11.27 (The Limits Have a Positive Side). The limits are limits of finite inquiry, not
limits of reality. The framework does not claim that reality is inexhaustible; it claims that the
finite subject’s survey of reality is non-terminating. The distinction is the distinction between
the order of inquiry and the order of being, and it is kept throughout the book. A reader who
takes the framework’s claim as a claim about reality has misread it; a reader who takes it as a
claim about finite inquiry has read it correctly.


11.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not establish the openness of relations. The openness is adopted as
an axiom, and its justification is that its denial would require an argument the framework does
not have. The chapter states the axiom and its cost, and it leaves the axiom to the reader’s
assessment.
    Second, the chapter does not establish the cardinality of the collection of contexts. Whether
the collection is countable or uncountable is marked (S), and the framework does not settle it.
The chapter’s claim is the non-termination of the generation, not the cardinality of what is
generated.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the argument for the impossibility of super-identity.
That argument is given in Chapter 27, and it uses the present chapter’s principle as one of its
premises. The present chapter states the principle; the later chapter uses it.
    Fourth, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the openness of contexts is an
openness of being. It states that the openness is on the side of the subject, not of being, and it
leaves the question of being to the chapter that states the framework’s account of manifestation
(Chapter 13). A reader who seeks a doctrine of the openness of being will not find it here; a
reader who seeks the distinction between the openness of inquiry and the openness of being
will find it.

Remark 11.28 (What the Chapter Has Done). The chapter has done five things. It has
stated the openness of relations as an axiom, and it has stated what a denial of the axiom
would require. It has argued the unbounded openness of cognitive contexts as a consequence
of openness, and it has stated the proof’s dependence on the context-bound character of
manifestations. It has stated the distinction between unbounded openness and mathematical
infinity, and it has stated the subject’s role in producing new contexts with a step-by-step
example. It has stated the two principles of the context column in tandem, showing that the
tandem is what makes the fallacy of super-identity possible. And it has stated a method for
managing the new contexts, together with the method’s relation to the other parts of the
framework. The chapter has not established the openness of relations, has not established the
cardinality of the collection of contexts, has not developed the argument for the impossibility
of super-identity, and has not settled the question of the openness of being. The chapter’s
contribution is the principle of unbounded openness, argued from openness, the distinction
between unbounded openness and mathematical infinity, the subject’s role in producing new
contexts, the tandem with the context-dependence principle, and the method for managing
new contexts.


11.12      Closing Part II
Part II has stated the four columns, the four-column principle, the conveyor principle, the
principle of non-sequential connectivity, the context-dependence principle, and the principle of
the unbounded openness of cognitive contexts. The summary is worth giving, because the
parts that follow build on it.
11.12. Closing Part II                                                                       149


   1. The four columns. Fixed elements, fluid element, governing dynamics, context
      (Chapter 6). Each is defined, and each has a control question.



   2. The four-column principle. The four roles are jointly necessary (removal test), and
      they are jointly sufficient as an estimate (reducibility test). The four roles are distinct
      (Chapter 7).



   3. The conveyor principle. No explanation of how one fixed element bears on another is
      complete without a fluid element (Chapter 8).



   4. Non-sequential connectivity. The conveyor principle does not require sequential
      passage through every intermediate element (Chapter 9).



   5. Context-dependence. Fixedness and fluidity are roles, assigned by the cognitive
      context, not properties of the element’s essence (Chapter 10).



   6. Unbounded openness of contexts. Given openness, the cognitive contexts in which
      an identity can be cognized are unboundedly open in the sense of Definition 11.2 (the
      present chapter).




    Part III turns from the architecture of explanatory cognition to the structure of epistemic
relations. It defines identity, signature, and pseudo-identity; it defines manifestation as
epistemic appearance; it develops epistemic light as the fluid element in its most general
role; and it states the desire to find, the unknownness of same-category identities, and the
distinction among self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness. The reader who has followed
Part II has the vocabulary; Part III puts it to work.



Remark 11.29 (The Six Claims Are Not Independent). The six claims of Part II are not
independent; they support one another, and the reader who has followed the argument can
see the support. The four columns (Chapter 6) are the analytical structure; the four-column
principle (Chapter 7) argues that they are necessary and sufficient; the conveyor principle
(Chapter 8) and non-sequential connectivity (Chapter 9) state what the fluid element requires
and does not require; context-dependence (Chapter 10) states that the roles are assigned by
the context; and unbounded openness of contexts (the present chapter) states that the contexts
are unboundedly open. The six together are the architecture of explanatory cognition, and
the reader who has understood all six has the architecture on which Parts III–VI build. A
reader who has understood only some of them has part of the architecture; the framework
invites the reader to return to the parts that are not yet clear, and to read them again in the
light of the parts that are.

A Question for Reflection
Consider an inquiry you have followed to its end. Did the inquiry have a natural terminus, or
did it open further questions that you did not pursue? If it opened further questions, was the
opening a consequence of the object, or of the structure of inquiry itself? What does your
answer tell you about the relation between the unbounded openness of contexts and the limits
of the finite subject?
    And consider the scene that opened the chapter—the sentence, the thesis, the criticism,
the review. At each step, the previous product becomes a fixed element of a new context, and
11.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                           151


the sentence is never exhausted. Is the sequence finite? If it were finite, what would the last
context be? And if it is not finite, what does the non-termination tell you about the difference
between the unbounded openness of contexts and the openness of being? Finally, consider
the method of Section 11.8: can you apply its four steps to an inquiry of your own, and can
you show, using the criteria of Chapter 21, which of the new contexts you produce are valid?
A reader who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can
answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

Part II is complete. Part III begins with the fixed elements of epistemic relations: identity,
signature, and pseudo-identity. It defines the terms that the four columns presuppose, and it
prepares the ground for epistemic light, which is the framework’s name for the fluid element in
its most general role.

Chapter 12

Identity, Signature, and
Pseudo-Identity

Scope
This chapter opens Part III by defining the first of the fixed elements of epistemic relations:
identity. It defines identity as the invariant that a cognitive reconstruction identifies and
holds fixed across a class of allowable transformations of its manifestations; it states the
criterion and the procedure of allowable transformations (Section 12.4); it distinguishes
identity from signature (the structural description of the invariance) and from pseudo-identity
(the reconstruction’s approximation of the signature); it separates the epistemic principles
from the framework’s assumptions and from the consequences of reconstruction; it states the
thread-and-beads model of identity and the conservation-under-reduction theorem that follows
from it; it gives the formal distinction among qualitative similarity, structural repetition, causal
continuity, and numerical identity, together with a comparison table (Section 12.10); and it
gives a template for the output of a reconstruction (Section 12.13).
    The chapter makes no ontological claim about what persists in itself. It treats the classical
puzzles of identity as epistemic puzzles about what a finite subject can reconstruct, not as
metaphysical puzzles about what there is. Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks
of “invariance,” “transformation,” “signature,” “reconstruction,” “conservation,” “duplication,”
“thisness,” or “adequacy,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions
in this chapter. The principles of rigidity, conservation, and non-duplicability are the backing
for the framework’s core commitments C4 and C10 (Chapter 43); the criteria of adequacy of a
pseudo-identity are stated here and developed in Chapter 23; the fallacy of super-identity is
stated in Chapter 28.


12.1      A Scene: The Ship, the Song, and the Self
Consider three cases, and the same question in each.
    A ship. It leaves harbor with planks of wood, a mast, a sail. Over the years, its planks are
replaced one by one. A plank rots; a new plank is fitted in its place. The mast is replaced; the
sail is replaced; the rudder is replaced. After a century of repairs, every plank of the original
ship has been replaced. The ship in the harbor is made of entirely new wood. Is it the same
ship?
    A song. It is composed by a musician who plays it once, on a single instrument, for a
single audience. The musician dies; the instrument is lost; the audience disperses. The song is
transmitted by ear, from singer to singer, across generations. The melody changes; the words
change; the rhythm changes. After a century of transmission, the song is sung in a form the
composer would not recognize. Is it the same song?
156                                      Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


    A self. A person is born, grows, learns, forgets, changes her beliefs, changes her habits,
changes her name. She remembers some things from her childhood and forgets others; she
feels continuous with the child she was and also estranged from her. Nothing about her—not
a single atom, not a single belief—has remained unchanged. Is she the same person?
    The three questions have the same form, and the same apparent paradox. In each case,
a thing persists through change, and the persistence seems both obvious and impossible. It
seems obvious because we speak of the ship as the same ship, the song as the same song, the
person as the same person. It seems impossible because everything about the ship, the song,
and the person has changed. The paradox is not a puzzle about language; it is a question
about what makes a thing the same thing across change, when everything about it has become
different.
    The three cases are the Ship of Theseus, the folk song, and the problem of personal identity.
The framework’s question about them is not the traditional one. The traditional question
is: what is the identity of the ship—the matter, the form, the continuity, the memory, or
something else? The framework’s question is: what does a cognitive reconstruction identify
and hold fixed when it treats the ship as the same ship, and how does the reconstruction relate
to the identity that the ship, if it has one, has? The first question is metaphysical; the second
is epistemic. The present volume takes up the second.

Remark 12.1 (The Three Cases Show the Same Structure). The three cases are not three
different puzzles; they exhibit the same structure. In each case, an entity persists through
change, and the persistence is not the persistence of any of its parts. The ship’s planks are all
new; the song’s notes are all new; the person’s cells are all new. What persists is not the parts
but something the parts express—and the framework’s question is what that something is,
and how a cognitive reconstruction holds it fixed. The three cases are the framework’s way of
showing that the question is general, not confined to any one domain.

Remark 12.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the epistemic
question at work in three familiar cases. It does not prove any of the definitions or principles
that follow; it makes them intelligible before they are stated. The definitions are offered as the
framework’s analytical vocabulary, and their use in the reconstruction of identity is argued in
the chapters that follow.


12.2     The Question
The previous part of the book developed the four columns of explanatory cognition: fixed
elements, fluid element, governing dynamics, context. It defined the four roles, argued their
joint necessity, and stated the principles of their relation. The present part turns to the
structure of epistemic relations, and it begins with the first of the fixed elements.
    The question is: what is identity, as the first fixed element of a cognitive reconstruction?
The question is not merely terminological. It is the question of what a reconstruction identifies
and holds fixed when it treats a thing as the same thing across change, and the question of
what distinguishes the thing, as the reconstruction holds it, from the appearances through
which the reconstruction has access to it.
    The chapter’s answer has seven parts. Identity is the invariant that a cognitive reconstruc-
tion identifies and holds fixed across a class of allowable transformations of its manifestations
(Section 12.3). The class of allowable transformations is specified by a criterion and by
a procedure that distinguishes the goal of the question, the level of analysis, the features
preserved, the features allowed to vary, and the criterion of selection (Section 12.4). The
signature is the structural description of that invariance, and it is what reconstruction recovers
(Section 12.5). The pseudo-identity is the reconstruction’s approximation of the signature,
and it has a stated output, a degree of confidence, its supporting evidence, its gaps, and its
12.3. The Definition of Identity                                                                157


probability of error (Section 12.13). Identity is rigid: it admits of no degrees (Section 12.7).
Identity is conserved across temporal transformations of its manifestations (Section 12.8).
Identity cannot be duplicated: a copy of a signature is a new thing, not a second instance of the
same identity (Section 12.9). The formal distinction among qualitative similarity, structural
repetition, causal continuity, and numerical identity is stated in Section 12.10.
   The chapter does not argue that identity exists in itself; that is a question the present
volume does not undertake. It argues for what identity must be if it is to do the work the
framework requires of it: the work of being the invariant that a reconstruction identifies and
holds fixed, and the work of being the target that the reconstruction approximates.

Remark 12.3 (The Question Is Epistemic, Not Metaphysical). The question the chapter
asks is not the traditional metaphysical question about identity. The traditional question is:
what is the identity of a thing in itself? The chapter’s question is: what does a cognitive
reconstruction identify and hold fixed when it treats a thing as the same thing across change?
The two questions are related, but they are not the same. The first is not answered here; the
second is the subject of the present chapter. A reader who takes the chapter’s answer as an
answer to the traditional question has misread the chapter; a reader who takes it as an answer
to the epistemic question has read it correctly.

Remark 12.4 (The Chapter Opens Part III). The chapter opens Part III, and it does so
by defining the first of the fixed elements. The fixed elements are the terms whose relations
the four columns describe; the present chapter defines the first of them, and the chapter that
follows defines the second. The reader who has followed Parts I and II has the architecture;
the present chapter begins to fill the architecture with its terms.


12.3      The Definition of Identity
The first thing to be said about identity, for the purposes of this book, is that it is not
a substance, not a property, not a thing. It is a pattern of invariance that a cognitive
reconstruction identifies and holds fixed across a space of possible transformations. To say
that a reconstruction has identified a thing’s identity is to say that the reconstruction has
identified a class of transformations under which the thing’s manifestations remain the same.

Definition 12.1 (Identity (Epistemic Form)). An identity, for the purposes of a cognitive
reconstruction, is the invariant that the reconstruction identifies and holds fixed across a
specified class of allowable transformations of the thing’s manifestations.

    The definition’s subject is explicitly epistemic: identity is the invariant that a reconstruction
identifies and holds fixed, not an invariant that is posited to exist independently of any
reconstruction. The definition does not say that there is no reconstruction-independent
invariant; it says that the framework’s claim is about the invariant as identified and held fixed
in a reconstruction. The distinction is the distinction between what the reconstruction does
and what the thing is in itself, and the present volume’s claim is about the first, not the
second.
    The definition raises an immediate question. The phrase “specified class of allowable
transformations” invites the further question: who specifies the class, and how? If the
reconstruction specifies it arbitrarily, identity becomes a construction, and the framework’s
claim that the reconstruction tracks something is in question. If the structure specifies it
independently of any reconstruction, the definition risks circularity: the class of allowable
transformations is defined by the identity, and the identity is defined by the class.
    The framework’s answer is that the class of allowable transformations is determined by the
identity’s defining invariants, and that the defining invariants are taken as primitive in the
framework. The reconstruction’s task is to discover the defining invariants, not to choose them.
158                                       Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


The discovery is fallible, and the criteria by which it is checked are given later in this chapter
and in Chapter 23. The procedure by which the class is determined is stated in Section 12.4.
   Two further definitions are needed to make the first precise.

Definition 12.2 (Defining Invariants). (A) The defining invariants of an identity are the
features that constitute its determination: those that distinguish it from its alternatives and
are fixed by what it is. They are taken as primitive in the framework.

Definition 12.3 (Identity-Preserving Transformation). An identity-preserving transformation
is a transformation whose resulting state remains within the range of structural possibilities
compatible with the identity’s defining invariants.

    The defining invariants are primitive in the framework. They are not obtained by asking
which transformations preserve identity; they are what the allowable transformations are
defined in terms of. This is a commitment of the framework, and its cost is stated: the
framework offers no observer-independent procedure for listing an identity’s defining invariants.
A reconstruction reaches them only fallibly, by identification, and the criteria of adequacy given
later in this chapter are the check on that identification, not a derivation of the invariants.

Remark 12.5 (Why the Class of Allowable Transformations Is Not Defined Circularly). The
allowable range cannot be defined merely by saying that identity is preserved; that would
define the class by the very identity it is meant to fix. It is specified through the defining
invariants: a transformation is allowable when it respects them. The defining invariants are
not themselves obtained by asking which transformations preserve identity; they are taken as
primitive. What would put the commitment in question is a case in which two accounts of the
defining invariants of one identity are both fully adequate by the criteria of adequacy and yet
incompatible.

Remark 12.6 (Identity Is Defined at the Level of the Reconstruction). The definition states
what an identity is for the purpose of a cognitive reconstruction: it is the invariant that the
reconstruction identifies and holds fixed across a class of allowable transformations. It does
not state what persists in itself. The distinction between the reconstruction’s invariant and
the reconstruction-independent invariant is the distinction that Chapter 5 states between the
order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence (Principle 5.1), and it is
observed here. A reader who takes the definition as a claim about what persists in itself has
misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim about the invariant a reconstruction identifies and
holds fixed has read it correctly.

Remark 12.7 (The Definition Is a Stipulation, Not a Discovery). The definition is a stipulation
of the framework’s vocabulary, not a discovery about the nature of identity. It fixes the sense of
“identity” for the purpose of the framework, and it is offered at exactly that strength. A reader
who proposes a different definition has proposed a different vocabulary, and the comparison of
the two vocabularies is a different inquiry. The framework’s claim is that its definition is the
one its arguments need, not that it is the only possible definition.


12.4     The Criterion and the Procedure of Allowable Transfor-
         mations
The definition of identity (Definition 12.1) makes the class of allowable transformations load-
bearing: the identity is what the reconstruction identifies as invariant across the class, and if
the class is not specified, the identity is not specified. The present section states the criterion
by which the class is specified, and it gives the procedure by which the class is determined.
12.4. The Criterion and the Procedure of Allowable Transformations                               159


12.4.1    The Criterion
The criterion has three parts, corresponding to three questions the reconstruction must answer.

Who specifies the class. The reconstruction does not arbitrarily choose the class; it discov-
   ers the class that the identity’s defining invariants fix. The reconstruction’s identification
   is a hypothesis about the class, and the criteria of adequacy (Section 12.13) are the check
   on the hypothesis.

At what level. The class is specified at the level of the kind of identity the reconstruction
    is treating: the level of the individual identity, the level of the kind, or the level of the
    context. The level is fixed by the question the reconstruction addresses, not chosen
    arbitrarily. The same entity may be treated as an individual identity in one reconstruction
    and as an instance of a kind in another, and the change of level is a consequence of the
    context-dependence principle (Chapter 10).

By what criteria. The class is checked by the criteria of adequacy: consistency, stability, and
    fruitfulness. The criteria do not choose the class; they check whether the reconstruction’s
    identification of the class has correctly identified the defining invariants.

12.4.2    The Procedure
The criterion is stated abstractly; the procedure states the steps by which the reconstruction
applies it to a case. The procedure has five steps, and each step has a stated output.

   1. State the goal of the question. The reconstruction states the question it is answering,
      and the answer’s intended use. The goal fixes the level of the class (individual, kind, or
      context). Output: a statement of the question and the level.

   2. Identify the level of analysis. The reconstruction states the level at which it is
      treating the identity, and the features it is treating as part of the identity and the features
      it is treating as manifestations. Output: a statement of the level and of the partition
      between identity-features and manifestation-features.

   3. State the features that must be preserved. The reconstruction states the features
      that it takes to be the identity’s defining invariants, and that any allowable transformation
      must preserve. Output: a list of defining invariants, stated as the reconstruction’s
      hypothesis.

   4. State the features that are allowed to vary. The reconstruction states the features it
      takes to be manifestations, and that the allowable transformations may change. Output:
      a list of variable features.

   5. State the criterion of selection. The reconstruction states the criterion by which a
      proposed transformation is admitted as allowable: the transformation is allowable if and
      only if it preserves the defining invariants of step 3 and alters only the variable features
      of step 4. Output: the criterion, stated explicitly, together with the fallibility of the
      hypothesis (the hypothesis is a candidate, not a certified identification).

    The procedure is the operational form of the criterion. It does not certify the reconstruction’s
hypothesis; it states what the hypothesis must contain, and it makes the hypothesis assessable
by the criteria of adequacy. A reader who applies the procedure to a case has the class of
allowable transformations in a form that can be checked; a reader who does not has only a
label.
160                                       Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


Remark 12.8 (The Procedure Is Not a Decision Procedure). The procedure is not a decision
procedure for the defining invariants. It states the form that the reconstruction’s hypothesis
must take; it does not derive the invariants from anything more basic. The invariants are
primitive (Definition 12.2), and the procedure is the form in which a reconstruction offers its
hypothesis about them. A reader who takes the procedure as a derivation of the invariants
has read more into it than it contains; a reader who takes it as the form of the hypothesis has
read it correctly.

12.4.3    The Objections and the Answers
The criterion and the procedure are open to two objections, and the framework’s answers are
worth stating.

The subjectivity objection. If the reconstruction specifies the class, identity becomes
    subjective. Answer. The reconstruction does not arbitrarily choose the class; it offers a
    hypothesis about the class that the defining invariants fix, and the criteria of adequacy
    check the hypothesis. The subjectivity objection confuses the hypothesis with a choice.
The circularity objection. If the class is specified by the identity, and the identity by the
    class, the definition is circular. Answer. The class is specified by the identity’s defining
    invariants, and the defining invariants are primitive. The circularity objection assumes
    that the defining invariants are derived from the class; they are not. They are the
    framework’s starting point, and the class is defined in terms of them.

   Neither objection is met by definition; both are met by the structure of the framework’s
account. A reader who rejects the framework’s primitive defining invariants has rejected the
framework’s starting point; the framework states the starting point openly, and invites the
reader to assess it.
Remark 12.9 (The Problem of the Class of Allowable Transformations Is an Open Epistemic
Question of This Book). The procedure of Section 12.4.2 states the form that the reconstruc-
tion’s hypothesis must take; it does not settle, for any particular identity, which features are
defining invariants and which are manifestations. That question is the open epistemic question
of the class of allowable transformations, and the framework records it as an open question of
the present book (it is one of the questions collected in Chapter 34). The framework does not
defer the question to another work; it records it as open, and it states what would settle it for
a particular case: a reconstruction that satisfies the criteria of adequacy for the case, together
with a demonstration that no incompatible reconstruction satisfies the criteria equally well. A
reader who settles the question for a case has extended the framework; a reader who shows
that the question is not settleable in a case has shown a limit of the framework’s formulation
for that case.
Remark 12.10 (The Criterion Is Stated, Not Applied). The criterion of allowable transfor-
mations is stated here at the strength of a stipulation, and it is applied in the chapters that
follow. The present section states the criterion and the procedure; the chapters that treat
particular identities (Chapters 13, 27, 28, 29, 36, and 37) apply them, and the reader who
wishes to see the criterion at work is directed to those chapters.
Remark 12.11 (The Criterion and the Definition Are Not the Same). The criterion of
allowable transformations is not the definition of identity. The definition states what identity
is, for the purposes of a cognitive reconstruction (the invariant that the reconstruction identifies
and holds fixed across a class); the criterion and the procedure state how the class is specified.
The two are distinct, and the framework keeps them distinct. A reader who takes the criterion
as the definition has confused the specification of the class with the definition of the invariant;
a reader who keeps them distinct has the framework’s account.
12.5. Identity Is Not Signature                                                              161


12.5     Identity Is Not Signature
The definition of identity is easily conflated with the definition of its structural description.
The two must be kept apart.

Definition 12.4 (Signature). The signature of an identity is the structural description of
its invariance: what can be read off, compared, recorded, and reproduced about the pattern.
Signatures are what reconstruction recovers, and what copying copies.

Remark 12.12 (Identity and Signature). Two things must be kept apart. The signature
is a pattern; it can be shared by many things and it can be duplicated. The identity is the
invariance as identified and held fixed by a reconstruction, and it is what the signature is
the signature of. Everything that a reconstruction can establish is a fact about signatures.
The claim that identity is more than its signature is a commitment of the framework, and
its epistemic consequence is stated in what follows: a reconstruction that has recovered the
signature has not thereby recovered the identity.

    The distinction between identity and signature is not the distinction between the real and
the unreal. Both are real; the signature is what reconstruction recovers, and the identity is
what the signature is the signature of. The distinction is between the pattern and what the
pattern is a pattern of, and it is what allows the framework to state, without paradox, that a
reconstruction can know the signature without knowing the identity, and that an identity can
be conserved across changes of its signature (Section 12.8).

Remark 12.13 (The Epistemic Consequence of the Distinction). The distinction has an
epistemic consequence that the framework uses throughout Part III. A reconstruction has
access to manifestations, not to the identity itself. From the manifestations, the reconstruction
recovers a signature. From the signature, the reconstruction forms a pseudo-identity of the
identity. The reconstruction is fallible at every step, and the criteria of adequacy are the
check on the fallibility. The distinction between identity and signature is what makes the
reconstruction intelligible as a reconstruction of something, and not as a construction of
nothing.

Remark 12.14 (The Signature Is Not the Manifestation). The signature is not the man-
ifestation. The manifestation is the contextually realized appearance of an identity in a
receiving cognitive context (Chapter 13); the signature is the structural description of the
identity’s invariance. The manifestation is what a reconstruction has; the signature is what
the reconstruction recovers from the manifestations. The two are related, but they are not
the same, and the framework keeps them apart. A reader who takes the signature as the
manifestation has confused the structural description with the appearance it describes.


12.6     Three Features of Identity
Three features of identity follow from the definition, or are added to it as commitments. They
are stated here, with an indication for each of whether it follows from the definition, whether
it is an independent commitment, and whether an argument is offered.


Relational. Identity is not a property that a thing has in isolation; it is a relation between
a reconstruction and a class of transformations—the relation of invariance as identified. The
feature follows from the definition, and no separate argument is needed.
162                                       Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


Hierarchical. Identity is not a single, flat property; it is a hierarchy of invariances. A thing
may be invariant under a narrow class of transformations (its specific identity) and also under
a broader class (its generic identity). The feature follows partly from the definition: nested
classes of transformations give nested invariances. It is partly an independent commitment:
that such nesting is the general case. The commitment is supported by example, not proved.

Dynamic (enactment). Identity is not a static property that a thing has once and for
all; it is a dynamic achievement, maintained through the ongoing process of expression. The
identity of a thing is not given; it is enacted. The feature does not follow from the definition;
it is an independent commitment, and its epistemic reading is supported in Chapter 38, in the
discussion of the tendency to express.
