   A feature is not established merely because the definition is. Only the first is. The second
and third are commitments of the framework, stated as such, and the reader who wishes to
challenge them knows where to press.

Remark 12.15 (Dynamic and Rigid). The third feature may look at odds with the rigidity of
identity, which is argued in Section 12.7. The two statements concern different things. What
is dynamic is the enactment, that is, the ongoing expression through which the identity shows
itself. What is rigid is the invariant that is enacted. The difference is an instance of a broader
structural claim about predication, which the framework develops in Chapter 25; here the
distinction is named, and the reader is asked to suspend the fuller treatment until it is given.

Remark 12.16 (The Three Features Are Not Independent of Each Other). The three features
are not independent of each other. The relational feature is what makes the hierarchical
feature possible: because identity is a relation to a class of transformations, nested classes
give nested invariances. The hierarchical feature is what makes the dynamic feature possible:
because identity is a hierarchy of invariances, the enactment can be an achievement at different
levels. The three features are three aspects of one structure, and the framework states them
separately so that the reader can see each, not because they are three separate claims.


12.7      Identity Rigidity
The definition of identity (Definition 12.1) states that the reconstruction identifies an invariant
across a class of allowable transformations. The present section states the consequence: the
identity, as identified, does not come in degrees. The claim is presented in three parts: the
epistemic principle, the framework’s assumption, and the reconstruction-consequence. The
distinction is stated at each step so that the reader can see what is argued and what is assumed.

Principle 12.1 (Identity Rigidity (Epistemic Form)). (T) As identified by a reconstruc-
tion, identity does not admit of degrees. A structure either is invariant under the specified
transformations, or it is not.
12.7. Identity Rigidity                                                                            163


   The epistemic principle. The principle is (T): it follows from the definition and from
the argument from the logic of identity, given below. Its content is epistemic: it is a claim
about the identity as identified, not about the identity as it might be in itself.

Argument from the Logic of Identity.

   1. Strict sameness is an equivalence relation: it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. If a
      is the same as b, and b is the same as c, then a is the same as c.

   2. A relation that comes in degrees (“more or less the same”) is not transitive. A chain of
      small differences can connect two things that are very unlike; this is the structure of the
      sorites.

   3. So a degree-based “sameness” is not strict sameness. It is resemblance, which is a matter
      of degree and has no tendency to settle whether something is the same one.

   4. Hence identity, as strict sameness under the allowed class of transformations, admits
      no degrees. The apparent degrees of ordinary language (“not himself today,” “no longer
      the same”) are degrees of manifestation, or of resemblance between signatures, not of
      identity.

    The argument turns on step (3). If a degree-based sameness could be strict sameness,
the sorites would be a paradox of identity; but the sorites is a paradox of resemblance, and
resemblance is not identity. The framework’s claim is that identity is strict, and that the
language of degrees belongs to the manifestations, not to the identity.
    The framework’s assumption. The principle’s claim that the identity as identified is
strict has a companion assumption: that the features the reconstruction identifies as defining
invariants are genuinely invariant under the allowable transformations. The assumption is (A),
and its cost is that a reconstruction may misidentify the invariants. The assumption is stated
here, not proved; the criteria of adequacy are the check on the misidentification.
    The reconstruction-consequence. Given the principle and the assumption, the recon-
struction’s output has the form: either the reconstruction has identified an invariant under the
allowable transformations, or it has not. The output does not admit of degrees; the degrees
belong to the confidence in the reconstruction, not to the identity itself. The distinction
between the identity’s strictness and the reconstruction’s confidence is stated in the template
of Section 12.13.

Remark 12.17 (The Contrast with Properties). Rigidity must be distinguished from the
degrees of properties. Properties admit of degrees: a room can be more or less warm, a person
more or less tall. Identity is not a property; it is the condition of persistence itself, as identified
by a reconstruction, and as such it is not a matter of degree. The framework’s way of speaking
of “degrees” belongs to viability, which is a structural feature of the relation between identity
and manifestation (Chapter 36), not of identity.

Remark 12.18 (Rigidity of Identity Is Not Rigidity of Manifestation). Two propositions must
be kept apart: (i) identity is invariant in itself, which belongs to the definition of identity;
(ii) identity appears in the same way under all conditions and relations, which does not follow
from (i). Hence the rigidity of identity does not mean the rigidity of its manifestations.
Manifestations may differ widely while the identity does not change. The distinction is
developed in Chapter 25, in the resolution of the tension between rigidity and dynamism; here
it is named, and the reader is asked to suspend the fuller treatment until it is given.

Remark 12.19 (The Cost of Rigidity). The cost of the principle is that it rules out graded
readings of identity, and it reinterprets the apparent degrees of ordinary language as degrees
164                                        Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


of manifestation or of resemblance. A reader who thinks that identity itself can be more or
less (“she is no longer the same person”) is invited to consider whether the apparent degrees
are degrees of identity or degrees of manifestation. The framework’s claim is that they are
degrees of manifestation; the identity is strict. A reader who finds the cost unacceptable has
located the place where the framework should be challenged.


12.8      Identity Conservation
Identity is rigid (Section 12.7). The present section states the temporal consequence: identity
is conserved across the changes of its manifestations. As in the previous section, the claim
is presented in three parts: the epistemic principle, the framework’s assumption, and the
reconstruction-consequence.

Principle 12.2 (Identity Conservation (Epistemic Form)). (T) As identified by a reconstruc-
tion, identity is invariant under the temporal transformations of its manifestations that the
reconstruction treats as allowable. Manifestations may vary with time; identity, as identified,
is conserved.

    The epistemic principle. The principle is (T): it follows from the rigidity principle
together with the reconstruction’s identification of the allowable temporal transformations. It
is not a claim that identity persists in itself; it is a claim that the identity as identified persists
across the temporal transformations the reconstruction treats as allowable.

First Argument: Transcendental, to the Presumption of Sameness. We have
experiences of temporal continuity: we remember the past, anticipate the future, and recognize
objects and persons across time. Such experiences are possible only if we presume that what
is remembered, anticipated, or recognized is the same one across the interval. Hence the
presumption of sameness is a transcendental condition of temporal experience, and cannot be
coherently denied by one who is describing such experience.
    The conclusion is a statement about a presumption, and a presumption might be a useful
construct rather than a fact. The first argument therefore establishes less than the principle
asserts. It does not, by itself, tell us that identity is really conserved. The gap is closed, to the
extent that it can be closed, by the second argument.

Second Argument: Abductive, to the Reality of the Invariant. Reconstructions
of the same thing, carried out independently by observers in different contexts, converge
on a single pseudo-identity up to isomorphism; the result is stable under perturbation; and
it yields successful predictions (the three criteria of adequacy stated in Section 12.13, and
developed in Chapter 23). The best explanation of this convergence is that the observers are
tracking something that is the same across the contexts and across time: an invariant. The
rival explanation, namely that the convergence reflects shared convention or psychological
projection, predicts convergence only among observers who share the convention, and does not
explain why predictions made from the pseudo-identity succeed in domains the convention
never touched. Hence it is reasonable to hold that there is an invariant that the reconstruction
tracks.
    The framework’s assumption. The principle’s claim that the identity as identified
persists across the temporal transformations has a companion assumption: that the temporal
transformations the reconstruction treats as allowable are the ones the defining invariants
permit. The assumption is (A), and its cost is that a reconstruction may misclassify a temporal
transformation as allowable or as non-allowable. The assumption is stated here, not proved;
the criteria of adequacy are the check on the misclassification.
12.9. Non-Duplicability of Identity                                                           165


    The reconstruction-consequence. Given the principle and the assumption, the recon-
struction’s output has the form: either the identity as identified persists across the temporal
transformations, or the reconstruction has misclassified the transformations. The output does
not settle whether identity persists in itself; that question is outside the present volume’s
scope. The output settles whether the reconstruction’s identification is internally consistent
with its allowable temporal transformations.
Remark 12.20 (The Three Moments of Temporal Experience). The transcendental argument
can be put in terms of three moments of temporal experience. In memory, I remember a past
event as mine. In anticipation, I anticipate a future event as one that will happen to me. In
recognition, I recognize an object or a person as the same one across time. The three are
aspects of one structure, and all three presuppose the presumption of sameness. The abductive
argument is what supports the further claim that the presumption is a tracking of something
real.
Remark 12.21 (The Limit of the Transcendental Argument). The transcendental argument
establishes that the concept of a persisting identity is structurally necessary for temporal
experience. It does not establish that an identity actually persists in every realm and after
every kind of transformation. The gap between the two is the gap between a presumption
and a fact. A presumption might be a useful construct rather than a fact; a concept might be
structurally necessary for experience even if nothing in reality answers to it. The abductive
argument is what closes the gap, to the extent that the gap can be closed.
Remark 12.22 (Conservation Is Not the Persistence of Manifestation). That an identity is
conserved does not mean that its manifestations are conserved: a manifestation in a context
may cease while the identity is conserved. The distinction is the structural point on which
the framework’s account of the relation between identity and manifestation depends. A song
whose every performance has ceased is still the song, in the sense the principle of conservation
gives to “still”; a person whose every manifestation in a given context has ceased is still the
person, in the same sense.
Remark 12.23 (The Two Arguments Support Different Things). The two arguments support
different things, and the difference is worth marking. The transcendental argument supports
the structural necessity of the presumption of sameness; it shows that we cannot experience
time without presuming that something persists. The abductive argument supports the reality
of the invariant; it shows that the best explanation of our convergent reconstructions is that
they are tracking something that is really there. The first argument supports the presumption;
the second supports the tracking. Together, they support the principle of conservation at the
strength the framework claims.


12.9     Non-Duplicability of Identity
Identity is conserved across time (Section 12.8). The present section states a further principle:
identity is not duplicated across space. The claim is presented in three parts, as in the previous
two sections.
Principle 12.3 (Non-Duplicability (Epistemic Form)). (T) As identified by a reconstruction,
identity cannot be copied. Signatures, pseudo-identities, and information can be duplicated;
identity, as identified, cannot. A copy of a system reproduces its signature. If the copy
expresses at all, it expresses an identity of its own.
    The epistemic principle. The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of identity
as the invariant identified by a reconstruction together with the argument from the logic of
numerical identity, given below.
166                                       Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


First Argument: The Logic of Numerical Identity.
   1. Suppose I1 and I2 are numerically distinct, and each is identical to the identity I.

   2. Identity is symmetric and transitive: from I1 = I and I2 = I it follows that I1 = I2 .

   3. This contradicts the supposition that they are distinct. Hence numerical duplication of
      an identity is impossible.
    The argument is short, and its brevity is the point. Numerical identity is an equivalence
relation: it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. If two things are each identical with a third,
they are identical with each other, and so they are not two things. The philosophical content
of the principle, however, is not in the logic of numerical identity; it is in the further claim
that identity is more than signature—that a thing’s identity is not exhausted by the pattern it
exhibits.

Second Argument: The Dilemma from Indiscernibles. The identity of indiscernibles
(PII) is the principle that two things sharing all their qualitative features are one thing. It is
contested; Black argued against it with a world of two exactly similar spheres. The principle
of non-duplicability does not depend on how this dispute comes out.
   1. First horn: PII holds. Then two things cannot share all qualitative features. A copy of a
      signature therefore differs from the original in some respect (at least in its relations or
      its position), so it is a second thing with its own features, and not a second instance of
      the same thing.

   2. Second horn: PII fails. Then there can be two things that share every qualitative feature,
      as in Black’s spheres. They are two, and so have two identities (the argument from
      the logic of numerical identity). An exact qualitative duplicate is still not a numerical
      duplicate.

   3. In both horns, copying does not yield a second thing that is the original identity.

   4. Conclusion: identity cannot be duplicated, whether or not PII is true.
    The argument removes the dependence of the principle on PII. Its force is that the two
horns exhaust the possibilities: either PII holds or it does not, and in either case the principle
follows.
    The framework’s assumption. The principle’s claim that the identity as identified
cannot be duplicated has a companion assumption: that identity is more than its signature, in
the sense that a thing’s identity is not exhausted by the pattern the reconstruction recovers. The
assumption is the doctrine of primitive thisness: an individuating feature that is not qualitative,
and that distinguishes one thing from an exact qualitative duplicate. The assumption is (A),
and its cost is stated below.
    The reconstruction-consequence. Given the principle and the assumption, the recon-
struction’s output has the form: a copy of the signature does not deliver a second instance
of the identity as identified. The output does not settle what the identity in itself is; that
question is outside the present volume’s scope. The output settles what the reconstruction
can and cannot claim about a copy.

The Cost of the Assumption. The cost of the doctrine of primitive thisness is that, in a
case where the signature is perfectly copied, nothing observable settles which of the resulting
systems, if any, carries the original identity. The framework accepts this cost, and states
it as the price of the commitment. A reader who finds the cost unacceptable has located
the place where the framework should be challenged. The assumption is supported by three
12.10. Four Notions That Must Be Distinguished                                                 167


considerations. First, it explains why the rigidity of identity holds: strict sameness is not a
matter of resemblance, and the invariance of identity is not the invariance of a pattern shared
by many. Second, it is consistent with Black’s two exactly similar spheres, in which two things
share every qualitative feature and yet are two. Third, it explains why reconstruction can
converge on a signature without ever delivering the identity: the signature is what can be read
off, and the identity is what is enacted by a source.

Consequences: Cloning, Teleportation, and Fission. The principle of non-duplicability
has consequences for the classical puzzles. They are stated here with their epistemic statuses.

   • Cloning ((T)). A clone reproduces a genetic signature. It is not the original and does
     not carry the original’s identity; if it expresses at all, it expresses an identity of its own,
     with its own manifestations and its own structural trajectory.

   • Teleportation ((E)). If a machine scans a body, destroys it, and builds an exact copy
     elsewhere, the copy has the original’s signature. The framework’s commitment is that
     copying does not transfer the identity, so the copy is a new system. This verdict is a
     consequence of the doctrine of primitive thisness and cannot be decided by observation;
     it is offered as the framework’s answer, not as an empirical result.

   • Fission ((S)). If a system divides into two systems that both continue its signature, then
     by the logic of identity the original identity can continue in at most one of them, or in
     neither. The framework does not say that the question has no answer, but that nothing
     observable fixes it. It is a case where the further fact is real and inaccessible.

Remark 12.24 (Independence from Qualitative Similarity). The principle of non-duplicability
is independent of the degree of qualitative similarity between things: it is neither strengthened
nor weakened by finding two things more or less alike. The argument is that similarity of
entities, or of forms, is a relation among products or appearances; the numerical unity of
identity is a fact about a source; and from a fact about products one cannot, without a further
premise, infer a fact about the number of sources. Hence similarity, however complete, is not
numerical unity of identity.

Remark 12.25 (What Has Value in Survival Is Not Addressed). The framework’s account
of non-duplicability is a structural account of identity, not a normative account of what has
value in survival. Whether viability has value, and what value it has, is not a question this
book answers. The distinction between the structural question and the normative question is
stated in the boundaries of epistemology (Chapter 34).


12.10      Four Notions That Must Be Distinguished
The distinction between identity and signature, and the principle of non-duplicability, are
easily run together with three other notions that are related but distinct. The present section
gives the formal distinction among the four, a comparison table, and two counterexamples
that show that the distinctions are not merely verbal.

Definition 12.5 (Qualitative Similarity). Two things are qualitatively similar when they
share some of their qualitative features. Qualitative similarity is a matter of degree: two things
can be more or less similar, and the degree is the extent of the shared features.

Definition 12.6 (Structural Repetition). Two things are structural repetitions of one another
when they share the same signature: the structural description of their invariance is the same,
and the pattern is what can be read off, compared, recorded, and copied.
168                                     Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


Definition 12.7 (Causal Continuity). Two things are causally continuous when the second is
the effect of the first, or when both are effects of a common cause, in a chain that preserves
some structural feature across the causal link.
Definition 12.8 (Numerical Identity). Two things are numerically identical when they are
one thing: the same source, the same thisness, the same enactment of the pattern, as identified
by the reconstruction. The relation is strict, and it admits of no degrees (Section 12.7).

12.10.1       The Comparison Table
The four notions are related, and the relations are worth stating in a table. Each is implied
by the next, but none is implied by the previous; the table states the implications and the
counterexamples that separate the notions.

Remark 12.26 (Two Counterexamples: The Copy and the Continuity). The distinctions
among the four notions are made vivid by two counterexamples.
    The copy. Consider a machine that scans a system and builds an exact structural copy of
it. The copy shares the original’s signature (structural repetition holds); it is qualitatively
similar to the original (qualitative similarity holds); it may even be causally continuous with
the original (if the scanning process preserves the causal chain, causal continuity holds). But
12.11. The Thread and the Beads                                                               169


the copy is not numerically identical with the original: it is a second thing, with its own source
and its own thisness (numerical identity fails). The copy is a counterexample to the inference
from structural repetition to numerical identity, and it shows that the first three notions do
not entail the fourth.
    The continuity. Consider a system whose structure has changed so much that its signature
is no longer recognizable, but whose causal chain has been preserved throughout. A person
whose beliefs, habits, and memories have all changed, but whose body and brain have continued
without interruption, is an example: the signature has changed, the causal continuity has been
preserved, and the numerical identity is conserved (in the framework’s commitment). The
continuity is a counterexample to the inference from numerical identity to structural repetition,
and it shows that the fourth notion does not entail the second.

    The two counterexamples are the framework’s way of stating the distinctions at the strength
the arguments support. The first shows that structural repetition is not sufficient for numerical
identity; the second shows that numerical identity is not sufficient for structural repetition.
The two together show that the four notions are pairwise distinct, and that the framework’s
claim that identity is more than signature is not a verbal claim but a structural one.

Remark 12.27 (The Four Notions and the Classical Puzzles). The four notions are the
framework’s answer to the classical puzzles of identity. The Ship of Theseus is a case in which
structural repetition holds (the planks are replaced, but the pattern is preserved), causal
continuity holds (the ship is repaired, not replaced), and numerical identity is the question
at issue. The folk song is a case in which structural repetition is questionable (the melody
changes, the words change), causal continuity holds (the song is transmitted), and numerical
identity is the question at issue. The problem of personal identity is a case in which all three
of the first notions are questionable (the person’s structure changes, her causal continuity
is interrupted by sleep and by forgetting), and numerical identity is the question at issue.
The framework’s answer to all three is that the question of numerical identity is not settled
by the first three notions; it is settled by the framework’s commitment to primitive thisness
(Section 12.9), and the commitment is stated at the strength the framework can support.

Remark 12.28 (The Four Notions and the Audit of Chapter 43). The four notions are
the framework’s contribution to the audit of Chapter 43, and they are the backing for the
audit’s statements about C4 (identity rigidity and conservation) and C10 (non-duplicability).
The audit’s statement of C4 uses the distinction between identity and signature; the audit’s
statement of C10 uses the distinction between structural repetition and numerical identity.
The four notions are the framework’s way of making those distinctions precise, and the audit’s
statements are stated at the strength the four notions support.


12.11      The Thread and the Beads
Conservation (Section 12.8) states that identity is invariant under temporal transformations;
non-duplicability (Section 12.9) states that identity is enacted by a single source. The present
section states a model that unifies the two, and the theorem that follows from it.

Definition 12.9 (Identity as Thread). An identity, as identified by a reconstruction, is a
thread : a structural invariant that holds a sequence of manifestations together. It is not the
sequence, and it is not any of its members.

Principle 12.4 (The Invisibility of the Thread). (T) The thread is not visible in the field of
manifestations. What is visible are the beads (the manifestations); the thread is not visible
because the field does not have the capacity to display it.
170                                        Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


Proof. By Definition 12.9, the thread is the invariant, not the varying. What is displayed in a
context is the varying (the manifestations). The invariant is the structural condition of the
display, not an item in it. Hence the thread is not visible in the field of manifestations.  □
Remark 12.29 (Parallel with the Invisibility of Epistemic Light). The invisibility of the
thread is structurally parallel to the invisibility of epistemic light (Chapter 15). In both cases,
a condition of possibility is not one of the things made possible.
Theorem 12.1 (Conservation Under Reduction). (T) If the number of manifestations of
an identity is reduced, the identity, as identified, is not thereby destroyed. The thread is
conserved; only the beads are lost.
Proof. By Definition 12.9, the identity is the thread, not the beads. The thread is the condition
of possibility of the sequence, not the sequence itself. Hence the loss of some beads does not
entail the loss of the thread. The identity is conserved.                                       □
Example 12.1 (Amputation and Hydrocephalus). A person who loses a limb, or whose brain
is significantly compressed by fluid (hydrocephalus), loses some manifestations but not her
identity. The thread is conserved; the beads are reduced. This is consistent with the empirical
findings cited in the literature, and it illustrates the structural principle: identity, as identified,
is not reducible to its material substrate.
Remark 12.30 (The Empirical Examples Are Coherence Tests). The empirical examples are
coherence tests, not justifications. They show that the structural principle is compatible with
the empirical facts; they do not establish it. The structural argument (Theorem 12.1) is what
establishes the principle.
Remark 12.31 (The Model Is a Model, Not a Metaphysics). The thread-and-beads model
is a model, not a metaphysics. It gives a precise form to the invariance of identity and to
the conservation of identity under the loss of lower manifestations. It does not claim that
the identity is literally a thread, or that the manifestations are literally beads. The model is
offered as the framework’s way of stating the relation between identity and manifestation, and
its use is analogical. A reader who takes the model as a metaphysical claim has misread it; a
reader who takes it as a structural model has read it correctly.


12.12       Unity and Multiplicity
Identity is one (Section 12.3). Its manifestations are many (Chapter 13). The present section
states the relation between the two, so that the identity’s unity is not confused with the
multiplicity of its manifestations.

Two distinctions. The first distinction is between the plurality of manifestations and the
plurality of identities. The manifestations of one identity are many; the identities are one.
These are two different pluralities. If they are run together, the many manifestations are
mistaken for many identities, and the one identity is lost in the multiplicity of its appearances.
    The second distinction is between the unity of a source and the unity of an aggregate. The
unity of an identity, as identified, is the unity of a source; it is not the unity of an aggregate.
An aggregate is one thing only in the sense that its parts are collected under a name; a source
is one thing in the sense that it is a single invariance, a single thisness. If the two unities are
run together, the unity of the source is mistaken for the unity of the aggregate, and the source
is treated as if it were the sum of its manifestations.
Principle 12.5 (Distinction of Plurality of Manifestations from Plurality of Identities). (T)
The plurality of the manifestations of one identity is not a plurality of identities, and recursive
manifestation is not numerical multiplication of the identity.
12.12. Unity and Multiplicity                                                                171


Definition 12.10 (Recursive Manifestation). Recursive manifestation is the structure by
which a manifestation that is realized in one context can itself be the occasion for further
manifestations of the same identity, in the same context or another, without the identity being
multiplied.
    The definition states a structure, not a process. The structure is that of a manifestation
serving as the occasion for further manifestations. The occasions are not temporal stages;
they are structural positions. A manifestation, once realized, is an element of the context
in which it is realized, and as an element it can enter into relations that occasion further
manifestations of the same identity. The identity is not multiplied by this; it remains one, and
its manifestations are many.

Argument for the Resolution.
  1. A manifestation is a product of a source identity and a receiving context, and is not an
     identity (Chapter 13).

  2. So many manifestations of one source are many products of one source; the number of
     products does not fix the number of sources.

  3. A manifestation may itself be the occasion of further manifestations (Definition 12.10);
     each further one is again a product of the same source and a receiving context.

  4. Hence the manifestations may be many, and recursively so, while the identity remains
     one.

  5. The unity of the identity is therefore not the unity of an aggregate and not the unity of
     a thing underlying its manifestations; it is the numerical unity of a source.
    The argument’s force is in step (2). If the manifestations were not products of the identity—
if they were the identity itself, or separate things alongside the identity—the plurality of the
manifestations would be a plurality of identities, and the contradiction would be real. The
framework’s account of manifestation is what blocks this: the manifestations are products, not
the identity, and the number of products does not fix the number of sources.
Remark 12.32 (The Source Is Not a Thing Behind the Appearances). The unity of a source
is not the unity of a thing behind the appearances. The framework does not posit a hidden
entity whose appearances are the manifestations; it posits a structural source whose invariance
is what the manifestations manifest. The source is not hidden; it is what the manifestations
exhibit. The manifestations do not conceal the source; they express it.

Three Consequences.
  1. The reality of multiplicity ((T)). The many are real in their own contexts. The mani-
     festations are not illusions, not appearances of an underlying reality that alone is real;
     they are real products of real sources, with their own modes of existence and their own
     structural relations.

  2. The unity of identity ((T)). The unity of identity is the unity of a source. It is not the
     unity of an aggregate, nor the unity of a pattern, nor the unity of a thing behind the
     appearances. It is the numerical unity of a source, as identified by the reconstruction.

  3. The structural possibility of reconstruction ((T)). Since an identity is expressed in its
     manifestations, a finite subject can reconstruct a pseudo-identity of it through those
     manifestations; the reconstruction is always partial, as the impossibility of super-identity
     establishes (Chapter 27).
172                                      Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


    The three consequences are not separate. They are three aspects of one structural fact:
the identity is one, the manifestations are many, and the relation between them is the relation
of expression. The first names the reality of the many; the second names the unity of the one;
the third names the epistemic access to the one through the many.


12.13      Pseudo-Identity
The definition of identity, together with the distinction between identity and signature, leaves
open what a reconstruction can know. The reconstruction does not have access to the identity
itself; it has access to manifestations, and from them constructs an approximation. The
approximation has a name, and its output has a stated form.

Definition 12.11 (Pseudo-Identity). A pseudo-identity is the reconstruction’s approximation
of an identity, constructed from the available manifestations. It is an estimate of a signature,
not a rival identity.

     A pseudo-identity is not a falsehood; it is a working model: the best approximation the
reconstruction can achieve, given the available manifestations and the costs of reconstruction.
It is a hypothesis about the identity, subject to revision in light of new manifestations. In the
vocabulary of the previous section, a pseudo-identity is an estimate of a signature.
     A pseudo-identity can be more or less adequate. Its adequacy is measured by three criteria.

   1. Consistency. Reconstructions working in different contexts, who carry out the process
      of reconstruction, must arrive at the same pseudo-identity, up to isomorphism.

   2. Stability. The pseudo-identity must be stable under small perturbations of the recon-
      struction’s context or cognitive apparatus.

   3. Fruitfulness. A system that operates according to the pseudo-identity must be able to
      operate within its environment, predict future manifestations, and preserve the structural
      viability of its expressions.

    These criteria do not prove that a pseudo-identity is adequate in an absolute sense. They
provide a fallibilist account of adequacy, of the same kind that scientific theories have. The
criteria are developed in Chapter 23; the present chapter states them so that the reader knows
what kind of thing a pseudo-identity is, and what kind of assessment it is open to.

12.13.1     The Template for the Output of a Reconstruction
The definition of pseudo-identity is abstract; the template states the form that the reconstruc-
tion’s output must take, so that the output can be assessed by the criteria. The template has
five parts, and each part is stated with what it must contain.

   1. Reconstruction output. A statement of the pseudo-identity that the reconstruction
      has formed: the signature it has recovered, stated in a form that can be compared,
      recorded, and assessed. Example: “the ship is the pattern P of planks, mast, and sail,
      held across the replacement sequence.”

   2. Degree of confidence. A statement of the confidence the reconstruction has in the
      output, on a stated scale (for example: low, moderate, high), together with the reason
      for the confidence. The confidence belongs to the reconstruction, not to the identity; the
      identity as identified is strict (Section 12.7). Example: “moderate, because the available
      manifestations cover the replacement sequence but not the ship’s earlier history.”
12.14. Four Things That Must Not Be Run Together                                               173


   3. Supporting evidence. A statement of the manifestations on which the reconstruction’s
      output rests, and of the relations among them that the reconstruction has used. Example:
      “the manifests of the planks, the records of the replacements, and the continuity of the
      ship’s use.”

   4. Gaps. A statement of the manifestations the reconstruction has not surveyed, and of
      the questions it has left unanswered. The gaps are the reconstruction’s explicit record
      of its partiality (Section 12.12, consequence 3). Example: “the ship’s history before the
      survey began, and the ship’s relations to other ships.”

   5. Probability of error. A statement of the reconstruction’s estimate of the probability
      that its output is mistaken, at a stated strength, together with what would change
      the estimate (new manifestations, a different level of analysis, a different goal of the
      question). Example: “low, given the quality of the manifests; higher if the ship’s history
      before the survey is unknown.”

     The template is the operational form of the criteria. It does not certify the pseudo-identity;
it states the form that the reconstruction’s output must take so that the criteria can be applied.
A reader who fills the template for a case has the pseudo-identity in a form that can be
assessed; a reader who does not has only an intuition.

Remark 12.33 (The Template Is Not a Guarantee of Adequacy). The template is not a
guarantee of adequacy. A reconstruction can fill all five parts and still fail the criteria (for
example, its output can be inconsistent with other reconstructions’ outputs, or its confidence
can be misplaced). The template is the form of the output; the criteria are the test of the
output. A reader who takes the template as a guarantee has confused the form with the test;
a reader who takes it as the form of the output has read it correctly.

Remark 12.34 (The Template and the Problem of the Class of Allowable Transformations).
The template records the reconstruction’s identification of the class of allowable transformations
(Section 12.4) in its first and third parts, and it records the reconstruction’s estimate of its own
fallibility in its second and fifth parts. The problem of the class of allowable transformations
(Remark 12.9) is therefore visible in the template: the reconstruction states its identification
of the class, and it states its confidence and its estimated error. A reader who wishes to assess
a reconstruction’s identification of the class can do so from the template; a reader who wishes
to settle the question for a case is invited to do so, and the framework records it as an open
question of the present book.

Remark 12.35 (Signatures and Pseudo-Identities). The relation between the notions intro-
duced so far is this: the identity is the invariance identified by a reconstruction; its signature
is the structural description of that invariance; a pseudo-identity is a reconstruction’s estimate
of the signature. Reconstructions deal only with the last two. This is why identity is never
exhausted by any record of it, and why the distinction between identity and signature is the
epistemic ground of the distinction between identity and pseudo-identity.


12.14      Four Things That Must Not Be Run Together
A representation that falls short of the identity is not a rival identity. Four cases differ, and
the difference is worth marking.

   1. Cognitive error : a mistake in reconstruction, correctable by further manifestations.

   2. Incomplete representation: a pseudo-identity that is accurate as far as it goes but does
      not exhaust the signature. Every pseudo-identity is incomplete in this way.
174                                       Chapter 12. Identity, Signature, and Pseudo-Identity


   3. Misattribution: assigning a manifestation to an identity of which it is not a manifestation.

   4. An independent identity: a different source with an identity of its own.

    A pseudo-identity may be a cognitive error or an incomplete representation; it is not, by
being so, an independent identity that rivals the original. Calling a reconstruction “pseudo”
states its epistemic standing, and gives it no ontological standing of its own.

Remark 12.36 (The Epistemic Diagnosis of the Four Cases). The four cases are distinguished
by what kind of epistemic failure they involve, and by what kind of remedy they admit.
Cognitive error admits of correction by further manifestations. Incomplete representation does
not admit of a remedy that makes it complete, because every pseudo-identity is partial; it
admits only of increase in adequacy. Misattribution admits of sorting. An independent identity
is not a failure at all, but a distinct object of inquiry. The framework uses the distinction in
Part V, in the account of the three failures of reconstruction (Chapter 24).


12.15      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not argue that identity exists in itself. It defines identity as the
invariant a cognitive reconstruction identifies and holds fixed, and it does not develop a
doctrine of what persists in itself. The question of what persists in itself is outside the present
volume’s scope, and the present volume is silent on it by method, not by denial.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the notion of category-relative predication. The
distinction between what is rigid and what is dynamic, and the distinction between what is
invariant in an identity and what varies in its expression, are instances of the broader structural
claim, which the framework develops in Chapter 25. The reader who wishes to see how the
claim is argued will find it there.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the fallacy of super-identity. The fallacy is the
error of treating an aggregate of manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the
identity; it is stated and argued in Chapter 28, on the basis of the impossibility of super-
identity (Chapter 27). The present chapter states the principles on which the fallacy argument
depends—the distinction between identity and signature, the distinction between identity and
manifestation, and the conservation and non-duplicability of identity—and it leaves the fallacy
itself to its place.
    Fourth, the chapter does not settle the classical puzzles of personal identity. The puzzles
are treated here as epistemic puzzles about what a finite subject can reconstruct, not as
metaphysical puzzles about what there is. The reader who seeks a metaphysical solution to the
puzzles will not find one here; the reader who seeks an epistemic account of the reconstruction
of identity will find one in Part IV, in the account of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity
(Chapter 23).

Remark 12.37 (The Problem of the Class of Allowable Transformations Is Recorded as Open).
The problem of the class of allowable transformations is recorded as an open epistemic question
of the present book (Remark 12.9). The chapter states the criterion and the procedure, and it
records the question of which features are defining invariants for a particular identity as open.
The framework does not defer the question to another work; it records it, and it states what
would settle it for a case. The reader who settles the question for a case has extended the
framework; the reader who shows that the question is not settleable in a case has shown a
limit of the framework’s formulation for that case.

Remark 12.38 (What the Chapter Has Done). The chapter has done eight things. It
has defined identity as the invariant a cognitive reconstruction identifies and holds fixed.
12.15. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                 175


It has stated the criterion and the procedure of allowable transformations, with the five
steps of the procedure (goal, level, features preserved, features allowed to vary, criterion of
selection) (Section 12.4). It has distinguished identity from signature and from pseudo-identity.
It has separated the epistemic principles from the framework’s assumptions and from the
reconstruction-consequences in the accounts of rigidity, conservation, and non-duplicability.
It has given the formal distinction among the four notions, with the comparison table and
the two counterexamples (Section 12.10). It has stated the thread-and-beads model and the
conservation-under-reduction theorem. It has distinguished the unity of a source from the
plurality of its products, and it has stated the four things that must not be run together. And
it has stated the template for the output of a reconstruction (Section 12.13.1). The chapter
has not argued that identity exists in itself, has not developed the notion of category-relative
predication, has not developed the fallacy of super-identity, and has not settled the classical
puzzles of personal identity. The chapter’s contribution is the framework’s account of identity,
stated at the strength its arguments support, the procedure of allowable transformations, the
template for the output of a reconstruction, and the distinctions that the later parts of the
book require.

A Question for Reflection
Take a thing you have known for a long time—a friend, a place, a practice. What has remained
the same across the time you have known it, and what has changed? If you were asked to
say what the thing is, would you point to what has remained, or to what has changed? If the
thing had been perfectly copied, would you say that there are two of it, or that there is one
thing in two places? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the identity,
the signature, the pseudo-identity that your reconstruction of the thing gives you, and the
non-duplicable thisness that the framework holds the identity to be?
    And consider the three cases that opened the chapter—the ship, the song, the self. In each
case, the persistence seems both obvious and impossible. Is the persistence the persistence
of the parts, or of something the parts express? If the parts, what would the ship, the song,
the self be after all the parts were replaced? If something the parts express, what is that
something, and how does a cognitive reconstruction hold it fixed? And consider the four
notions of Section 12.10: can you give a further case in which two things are qualitatively
similar and structurally repetitive but not numerically identical, or a further case in which
a thing is numerically identical with itself across a change of signature? What does your
answer tell you about the relation between the four notions and the classical puzzles? Finally,
consider the template of Section 12.13.1: can you fill its five parts for an identity of your own
choosing, and can you assess the resulting pseudo-identity by the three criteria? A reader who
can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has
the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter defines the second of the fixed elements of epistemic relations: manifestation.
It states what it is for an identity to appear in a receiving cognitive context, distinguishes
essential from non-essential features, and prepares the ground for the chapters on epistemic
light.

Chapter 13

Manifestation as Epistemic
Appearance

Scope
This chapter defines the second of the fixed elements of epistemic relations: manifestation.
It defines manifestation as the contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving
cognitive context, according to that context’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints; it states
an explicit model of the relation among the subject of cognition, its accessible features, the
receiving context, and the epistemic output (Section 13.3); it distinguishes essential from
non-essential features and aligns the criterion with Chapter 12; it argues that a manifestation
is a product of the interaction between an identity and an active receiving context, with a
complete example of change of appearance under change of context (Section 13.7); it states
the two-sided model of manifestation and its input-process-output diagram (Section 13.4);
it states the four propositions that locate the identity–manifestation relation; it states the
principle of essential homogeneity; and it distinguishes context from perspective. It completes
the framework’s treatment of the fixed elements: with identity defined in Chapter 12 and
manifestation defined here, the two fixed elements are in place.
     The reader who has followed Chapter 12 has: the definition of identity (Definition 12.1), the
distinction between identity and signature (Definition 12.4), the definition of pseudo-identity
(Definition 12.11), identity rigidity (Principle 12.1), identity conservation (Principle 12.2), non-
duplicability (Principle 12.3), the thread-and-beads model (Definition 12.9; Theorem 12.1), and
the distinction between the unity of a source and the plurality of its products (Principle 12.5;
Definition of recursive manifestation, Definition 12.10). The present chapter states what a
manifestation is, given those definitions, and how it stands to the identity that it manifests.
     Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “capacity,” “aptitude,” “constraint,”
“effect,” “nature,” “homogeneity,” or “perspective,” these are structural terms, and their sense
is fixed by the definitions in this chapter. The word “aptitude” does not name a value or an
end; it names the structural suitability of a cognitive context for a kind of appearance.


13.1      A Scene: The Same Person, Three Appearances
Consider a daughter, forty years old, a surgeon. Three people look at her, and each sees
something different.
    Her mother sees the child she raised: the small hands, the face that once cried at nightmares,
the girl who learned to ride a bicycle. The daughter is now a surgeon, married, with a practice
of her own. But what the mother sees is not the surgeon; it is the daughter, whom the mother
has known since before the daughter knew herself.
180                                       Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


    Her colleague in the operating room sees a hand, steady and precise; a judgment, quick
and reliable; a voice, calm under pressure. The colleague does not see the child; the colleague
sees the professional, the one whose competence has been tested and proven.
    Her patient, waking from anesthesia, sees a face, blurred; a voice, reassuring; a name, half-
remembered. The patient does not see the mother’s daughter or the colleague’s professional;
the patient sees the one who saved her life, or the one who failed to.
    Three appearances, one person. The appearances are not merely different perspectives
on the same facts. Each is real; each makes visible something the others cannot. And none
is reducible to another. The mother’s love is not the colleague’s respect, and neither is the
patient’s gratitude. Each appearance is shaped by the relation between the daughter and the
one who sees her—by the mother’s memories, by the colleague’s shared work, by the patient’s
dependence.
    The scene poses a question that the previous chapter left open. The previous chapter
defined identity as the invariant an explanatory cognition holds fixed across a class of allowable
transformations, and it distinguished identity from signature and from pseudo-identity. But it
did not yet say what an appearance of an identity is. If the daughter’s identity is one, and
her appearances are many and different, what is the structure of the relation between the
one and the many? Is she nothing more than her appearances, or is there something she is,
which they manifest? And if there is something she is, how can appearances so different all be
appearances of it?

Remark 13.1 (The Scene Shows a Structural Point, Not a Psychological One). The scene
is easily read as a psychological observation about three people who happen to know the
daughter differently. The psychological reading is not wrong, but it is not the chapter’s point.
The chapter’s point is structural: the same identity appears differently in different receiving
cognitive contexts, and each appearance is real in its own context. The three viewers are three
contexts—three questions asked of the same identity—and the scene would work with one
viewer in three contexts. The distinction between context and perspective, which the present
chapter states in Section 13.10, is what makes the point precise: the scene varies the context,
not the perspective within a context.

Remark 13.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the relation
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove any of the definitions that follow; it makes them
intelligible before they are stated. The definitions are the framework’s analytical vocabulary,
and their use in the reconstruction of identity is argued in the chapters that follow.


13.2     The Question
The scene raises three questions, and the chapter treats them in turn.
     The first is: what is a manifestation? The previous chapter used the term in a minimal
working sense—the determinate appearance of an identity in a receiving context—and promised
that the full definition would be given here. The definition must state what a manifestation is,
what its components are, and how it is related to the identity it manifests.
     The second is: what distinguishes the features of a manifestation that belong to the
identity from the features that belong to the receiving context? The daughter’s steadiness
under pressure is a feature of her identity; the specific appearance of that steadiness to a
colleague is a feature of the receiving context. The chapter must provide the criterion by which
the two kinds of feature are distinguished, and it must state the two-sided model that locates
each feature on one side or the other.
     The third is: is the receiving context passive or active in the production of a manifestation?
Is it a neutral vessel that receives whatever the identity pours into it, or does its own capacity
shape what appears? The scene suggests the latter: the mother’s love makes visible what
13.3. The Definition of Manifestation                                                         181


another cannot see. The chapter must state the framework’s answer to this question, and
state its status.
    The chapter’s method is structural. It defines manifestation, states the model of the
relation among subject, accessible features, receiving context, and epistemic output, defines
essential feature, states the two-sided model with its diagram, states the principle of the active
capacity of the receiving context (as a proposal), states the principle of essential homogeneity,
and distinguishes context from perspective. The chapter’s task is to complete the treatment of
the fixed elements, and to prepare the ground for the treatment of the fluid element, epistemic
light, in Chapter 15.

Remark 13.3 (The Question Is Not About the Reality of Appearance). The question the
chapter asks is not whether appearances are real. The scene shows three appearances, and the
framework takes all three to be real. The question is about the structure of appearance: what
it is, how it relates to the identity it manifests, and what distinguishes the features it gets
from its source from the features it gets from its context. A reader who takes the chapter’s
question as a question about the reality of appearance has misread it; a reader who takes it as
a question about the structure of appearance has read it correctly.


13.3     The Definition of Manifestation
Definition 13.1 (Manifestation). A manifestation is the contextually realized appearance
of an identity according to the capacity, aptitude, and constraints of the receiving cognitive
context.

   What is new in this definition is that the receiving cognitive context is not only the place
where an appearance happens to occur. Its capacity, aptitude, and constraints take part in
determining the form of the appearance. The vocabulary used from now on is fixed.

Source identity. The identity that appears.

Receiving cognitive context. The context in which it appears. The cognitive context was
defined in Chapter 6 and again in Chapter 10; the receiving context is a cognitive context
considered as the setting in which an appearance is realized. Any cognitive context can be a
receiving context for an identity whose manifestations are at issue.

Capacity and aptitude of the receiving context. What kinds of appearance the context
can bear, and what it is structurally suited to. The terms are structural: they name what a
context can receive and what it is suited to receive, not a value, a purpose, or an end.

Form of manifestation. The determinate appearance that results.

Manifestational effect. The effect of the manifestation in the receiving cognitive context—
what the appearance brings about in the context in which it is cognized. The effect is stated
here in summary; its fuller account—in terms of hard and soft manifestation, and of the action
chain by which an effect is received and sedimented—is given in Chapter 40.

13.3.1    The Model of the Relation Among Subject, Features, Context, and
          Output
The definition names the terms of the relation; the model states how the terms are connected.
The model has four elements, and each element is distinguished from the others.
182                                       Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


Definition 13.2 (The Manifestation Model). (A) A manifestation is the epistemic output of
a four-place relation:

(M1) The subject of cognition: the identity that appears, with its defining invariants (Chapter 12,
     Definition 12.2).

(M2) The accessible features: the features of the subject that can be conveyed to a receiving
     context, as distinguished from the features that cannot (the distinction is stated in
     Section 13.5, and the criterion is aligned with Chapter 12).

(M3) The receiving context: the cognitive context, with its capacity, aptitude, and constraints
     (Definition 13.1, above).

(M4) The epistemic output: the determinate appearance that results, and that the receiving
     context can recognize as an appearance of the subject.

The model is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s way of decomposing the relation.
Its justification is its use in the analysis of examples; its cost is that the decomposition is
analytical, and a given manifestation may resist a sharp separation of the four elements.

    The model is the framework’s way of making the definition precise. The definition states
what a manifestation is; the model states the four places in the relation that the manifestation
occupies. The model does not add a new claim; it states the structure of the claim the
definition already makes.

Remark 13.4 (The Four Elements Are Not Four Substances). The four elements of the
model are not four substances. The subject is the identity; the accessible features are what
the subject can convey; the receiving context is the cognitive context; the epistemic output is
the appearance. None of the four is a fifth kind of entity, and none is a metaphysical posit.
The model is analytical, in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes: it distinguishes the places in the
relation, not the kinds of thing the relation contains.

Remark 13.5 (The Model and the Two-Sided Model). The model of this subsection is the
general statement of the relation; the two-sided model of Section 13.4 is the decomposition of
the manifestation into source features, contextual features, transmission features, and result
features. The two models are related: the general model names the terms of the relation; the
two-sided model locates the contributions of each term in the resulting appearance. A reader
who has followed the general model will recognize the two-sided model as its application to a
single manifestation; a reader who has followed the two-sided model will recognize the general
model as its abstract statement.

Remark 13.6 (Manifestation Is Not Illusion). The structural account is not a claim that
manifestation is an illusion. A manifestation is real at its own level: it is a determinate
appearance in a receiving cognitive context, with its own mode of givenness and its own relations
to other manifestations in that context. The framework’s claim is that the manifestation
is real as a product, not that it is unreal because it is not the source. The distinction is
the distinction between the reality of the source and the reality of the product; it is not the
distinction between the real and the unreal. A reader who takes the definition of manifestation
as a claim that manifestations are appearances in the sense of illusions has misread it; a reader
who takes it as a claim that manifestations are real products of a real source has read it
correctly.

Remark 13.7 (Manifestation Is Not the Effect). The manifestation is not the manifestational
effect, and the two must be kept apart. The manifestation is the appearance itself; the effect is
what the appearance brings about in the receiving context. A patient who sees the daughter’s
13.4. The Two-Sided Model of Manifestation                                                   183


face has a manifestation of the daughter; the patient’s gratitude, or her fear, is the effect of
that manifestation. The distinction is the distinction between what appears and what the
appearance does; the framework keeps it apart, and the fuller treatment of the effect is given
in Chapter 40.

Remark 13.8 (Source and Higher Context). “Source” in this book means the source identity
of a manifestation. It does not mean a higher cognitive context. By the non-necessity of
sequential passage (Chapter 9), an identity may be manifested in a context that is not adjacent
to the context in which the identity is first cognized, so the source of a manifestation need
not be the context immediately above the one in which it appears. The context in which an
identity’s invariant is first exhibited is a different matter, and is said so when meant.

Remark 13.9 (Three Features of Manifestation). Three features follow from the definition.
    Contextual. A manifestation is always a manifestation in a receiving cognitive context.
The context influences what aspects are expressed and how.
    Partial. No single manifestation exhausts the identity. This is why super-identity is
impossible, as argued in Chapter 27.
    Plural. An identity is expressed in many manifestations. Plurality is a structural condition
of expression, not a structural deficiency. The plurality may be recursive: a manifestation,
once realized, can become the occasion for further manifestations of the same identity, without
the identity being multiplied (Chapter 12, Definition 12.10; Principle 12.5). The plurality of
manifestations is therefore not a plurality of identities; it is the plurality of the products of
one source.
    The plurality of manifestations is not a falling-away from the identity; it is the condition
under which the identity is expressed. What the traditions call the manifestation of the one in
the many is, in the framework’s vocabulary, the structural plurality of epistemic expression.
The framework’s claim is structural: it says that the plurality is a condition of expression, not
that the plurality is a defect.


13.4     The Two-Sided Model of Manifestation
The definition of manifestation says that a manifestation is the contextually realized appearance
of an identity in a receiving context. The definition does not, by itself, say which features of
the appearance belong to which side of the relation. The present section states the model by
which the question is answered, and it states the model’s input-process-output diagram.

Definition 13.3 (The Two-Sided Model of Manifestation). (A) A manifestation has four
kinds of component, and the model locates each kind on one side or the other of the relation:

  (i) Source features: the features that the manifestation receives from the identity, and that
      are essential to the identity’s determination (the essential features of Definition 13.4).

 (ii) Contextual features: the features that the manifestation receives from the receiving
      cognitive context’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints.

 (iii) Transmission features: the features that the manifestation receives from the rules by
       which the source’s effect is carried into the receiving context (the conveyor principle of
       Chapter 8, and the epistemic light of Chapter 15).

 (iv) Result features: the features that the manifestation has as a determinate product, which
      are not attributable to any one of the three contributions alone, but are the joint result
      of all three.
184                                       Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


    The model is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s way of decomposing a manifestation.
Its justification is its use in the analysis of examples, and its cost is stated in the examples
themselves. A reader who proposes a different decomposition has proposed a different model,
and the comparison of the two models is a different inquiry.

13.4.1    The Input-Process-Output Diagram
The two-sided model can be displayed as an input-process-output diagram. The diagram
separates the four kinds of feature, and it shows where the contributions of the subject, the
receiving context, the constraints, and the rules of transmission enter the result.
