    The diagram is a summary of the two-sided model. It does not add a new claim; it
displays the four kinds of feature, and it shows the order in which the contributions enter the
appearance. The input is the subject’s features; the process is the transmission; the constraints
are the receiving conditions; the output is the appearance’s features.
Remark 13.10 (The Diagram Is a Guide, Not a Formula). The diagram is a guide to
the analysis of a manifestation, not a formula that mechanically assigns each feature to a
component. In a given case, the analysis is the work of the inquiry; the diagram states the four
components among which the analysis distributes the features. A reader who uses the diagram
as a formula will find that the features of a manifestation resist mechanical assignment; a
reader who uses it as a guide will find that the analysis becomes clearer.
Remark 13.11 (The Diagram and the Four Elements of the General Model). The diagram’s
four columns correspond to the four elements of the general model (Definition 13.2): the input
column is (M1) and (M2), the subject and its accessible features; the process column is the
rules of transmission (the fluid element of the framework); the constraints column is (M3),
the receiving context; the output column is (M4), the epistemic output. The diagram is the
general model’s display at the level of a single manifestation, and the two-sided model is the
display’s decomposition of the output into the four kinds of feature.

Example 1: The Daughter Seen by Her Mother. The daughter’s appearance to her
mother has (i) source features: the daughter’s identity, its essential determination, the features
that belong to her as a person; (ii) contextual features: the mother’s memories, the mother’s
relation to the daughter, the mother’s question (“who is this?” answered by “my daughter”);
(iii) transmission features: the rules by which the daughter’s identity is conveyed to the mother
(the visual, auditory, and affective channels, and the epistemic light that makes the conveyance
legible); (iv) result features: the determinate appearance of the daughter as the mother sees
her, which is the joint result of the three.

Example 2: The Daughter Seen by Her Colleague. The daughter’s appearance to her
colleague has (i) source features: the same identity; (ii) contextual features: the colleague’s
13.5. Essential and Non-Essential Features                                                   185


professional relation, the operating room’s demands, the colleague’s question (“can I trust this
surgeon?”); (iii) transmission features: the same channels and the same epistemic light, under
the rules of professional perception; (iv) result features: the determinate appearance of the
daughter as a competent surgeon, which is the joint result of the three.

Example 3: The Daughter Seen by Her Patient. The daughter’s appearance to her
patient has (i) source features: the same identity; (ii) contextual features: the patient’s
dependence, the patient’s anesthesia, the patient’s question (“who is this?” answered by
“the one who saved me”); (iii) transmission features: the same channels under the rules of
post-anesthetic perception; (iv) result features: the determinate appearance of the daughter as
the one who saved the patient’s life, which is the joint result of the three.
    The three examples are not three different identities; they are three different two-sided
analyses of the same identity. The source features are the same; the contextual features are
different; the transmission features are the same in kind, different in mode; the result features
are different. The model thus preserves the source identity across the analyses, and it accounts
for the difference in appearances by the difference in the other three components.
Remark 13.12 (The Two-Sided Model and the Essential Homogeneity Principle). The
two-sided model is what the principle of essential homogeneity (Principle 13.2) presupposes.
The principle says that a manifestation is essentially homogeneous with its source insofar
as it preserves the source’s essential determination. The model says where the essential
determination is located: it is the source features, and the other three components are not
essential to the source. The principle is (T) relative to the model; without the model, the
principle would be a verbal formula whose application could not be checked.
Remark 13.13 (The Two-Sided Model and the Contextual Manifestational Capacity). The
two-sided model is what the principle of contextual manifestational capacity (Principle 13.1)
would need to be supported by. The principle says that the form of the manifestation is
fixed jointly by the source and by the context’s capacity. The model states where the two
contributions are: the source features are the first contribution, the contextual features are
the second, and the transmission and result features are the joint outcome. The principle is
still proposed, not established, because the independent account of capacity is still lacking
(Section 13.7.2); but the model locates the place where the missing account would do its work.
Remark 13.14 (The Two-Sided Model and the Four Columns). The two-sided model is a
particular case of the four-column architecture, and it is worth marking how. The source
features are the fixed element (the identity); the transmission features are the fluid element
(epistemic light); the contextual features are the context (the receiving cognitive context); the
rules by which the transmission is governed are the governing dynamics. The result features
are the manifestation itself, which is not a fifth column but the product of the four analytical
roles. The model thus applies the four columns to the study of a manifestation, and it does
so in the way Chapter 6 stated: the four are analytical roles, and the manifestation is the
product of their joint operation.


13.5     Essential and Non-Essential Features
The second question of the chapter was: what distinguishes the features of a manifestation that
belong to the identity from those that belong to the receiving context? The answer requires a
distinction between two kinds of feature, and the criterion must be aligned with Chapter 12.
Definition 13.4 (Essential Feature). An essential feature of an identity is a feature that
belongs to its defining invariants (Chapter 12, Definition 12.2). A non-essential feature is
one that may vary among the manifestations of the identity without altering its essential
determination.
186                                       Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


     The definition uses the notion of defining invariants, which was introduced in Chapter 12.
The defining invariants are the features that constitute an identity’s determination and
distinguish it from its alternatives; they are taken as primitive in the framework. An essential
feature is one that belongs to them; a non-essential feature is one that does not.
     It follows that an identity without one of its essential features would not be the identity
it is. But that counterfactual is a consequence of the definition, and is not used to define
the term; to define essential features by it would make the definition circular with that of an
identity-preserving transformation.

Remark 13.15 (The Criterion of Essence Is the Criterion of Chapter 12). The criterion for
identifying an essential feature is the criterion stated in Chapter 12 (Remark 12.9, on the class
of allowable transformations). The criterion is: an essential feature is one whose removal would
place the identity in question, in the sense that the reconstruction of the identity would no
longer be consistent with the reconstruction’s identification of the allowable transformations.
The removal may be conceptual (we cannot conceive the identity without this feature) or
structural (the feature is a condition of the identity’s recognizable persistence). The two are
not the same; the conceptual removal is a mark, not a test, and the structural removal is what
the framework takes as the criterion.
    The framework does not offer an observer-independent procedure for listing the essential
features of an identity; the observer reaches them fallibly, by reconstruction, and the criteria of
adequacy stated in Chapter 23 are the check on that reconstruction. The problem of the class
of allowable transformations (Chapter 12, Remark 12.9) is the same problem in the present
chapter’s vocabulary: it is the problem of identifying which features are defining invariants
and which are manifestations. The chapter records the problem as open, and it states what
would settle it for a case.

Remark 13.16 (The Distinction Is a Consequence, Not an Addition). The distinction between
essential and non-essential features is not an addition to the definition of manifestation. It is
what the definition already implies: if a manifestation is the appearance of an identity in a
receiving context, then some features of the appearance are contributed by the identity, and
some by the context. The distinction names the two contributions. It is stated separately
because the naming is useful, not because the distinction is new.

Remark 13.17 (The Distinction Is Not a Claim About Essence in the Metaphysical Sense).
The distinction between essential and non-essential features is a distinction within the frame-
work’s analytical vocabulary; it is not a claim about a metaphysical essence that a thing has
in itself. The essential features are the identity’s defining invariants (Chapter 12), and the
defining invariants are features that constitute the identity’s determination for the purpose
of an explanation. The distinction is epistemic, not metaphysical; a reader who takes it as a
claim about essence in the traditional sense has misread it, and a reader who takes it as a
distinction between what belongs to the identity and what belongs to the context has read it
correctly.


13.6     Manifestation as a Node in a Cognitive Context
In its own cognitive context, a manifestation is a fixed element in the network of that context.
From the standpoint of a frame concerned with a different identity, it may be studied as a
fluid element, since it appears differently as the frame varies. The two roles are the ones the
framework’s four columns distinguish; the same manifestation can play either role, depending
on the question the frame asks.
    The point is an instance of the context-dependence principle, which was stated and argued
in Chapter 10: the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on
13.7. Manifestation as a Product of Interaction                                               187


the element’s essence. What the principle says of elements generally, it says of manifestations
in particular. A manifestation is a fixed element in one frame and a fluid element in another;
neither role is more real than the other.

Remark 13.18 (Two Independences That Must Not Be Mixed). A manifestation can be a
real and independent entity in the order of the cognitive context in which it appears. It is
not independent of its source as an identity. The first is independence of context; the second
would be independence of identity. The first is affirmed; the second is denied.
    A manifestation is a structural element in its context, with its own mode of givenness and
its own relations to other manifestations in that context. It is not, for that, a second identity.
It has the reality of a product, not the reality of a source. The distinction between the two
kinds of reality is what the framework’s account of manifestation is meant to preserve. Both
are real; neither is an illusion. The product is real at its own level; the source is real at its
own level. The framework’s claim is that the two levels are distinct, not that one is real and
the other is not.


13.7     Manifestation as a Product of Interaction
A manifestation is not an independent column. It is the product of an interaction in which
three things take part: the source identity, the aptitude of the receiving cognitive context, and
the action and interaction between the two.
    That a manifestation is a product of the source and the receiving context is not a definitional
triviality. It is a substantive claim, and it was used as a premise in the argument for the
impossibility of super-identity in Part V. The claim is a commitment of the framework, and it
is supported by the fact that one identity appears differently in contexts of different capacity.
It would be refuted by a case in which the appearance in a context is fixed by the source alone.

13.7.1    A Complete Example of Change Under Change of Context
The claim that the receiving context is active is abstract; the following example shows the
claim at work in a single case, with the receiving context changed and the identity held fixed.

The case. The daughter of the scene (Section 13.1) is the subject of cognition. The identity
is her identity, with its defining invariants: the features that make her the person she is. The
accessible features are the features that can be conveyed to a receiving context: her voice, her
face, her manner, her professional competence, her history.

The first receiving context: the colleague in the operating room. The colleague’s
question is: “can I trust this surgeon?” The receiving context’s capacity includes the professional
norms of the operating room, the colleague’s training, and the practical demands of surgery.
The receiving context’s constraints exclude features that are not relevant to the question:
the daughter’s childhood, her family relations, her private life. The epistemic output is the
appearance of the daughter as a competent surgeon, with the features that bear on the question:
steadiness, precision, judgment, calm.

The second receiving context: the mother in the family home. The mother’s question
is: “who is this?” answered by “my daughter.” The receiving context’s capacity includes the
mother’s memories, her relation to the daughter, and her affective disposition. The receiving
context’s constraints exclude features that are not relevant to the question: the daughter’s
professional competence, her surgical technique, her operating-room manner. The epistemic
output is the appearance of the daughter as the child the mother raised, with the features
188                                       Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


that bear on the question: the small hands, the face that once cried at nightmares, the girl
who learned to ride a bicycle.

The comparison. The identity is held fixed across the two contexts. The accessible features
are the same. The receiving context is changed, and the change produces a change in the
epistemic output: the same identity appears as a competent surgeon in the first context and
as a raised child in the second. The appearance is not contradictory; it is the same identity,
manifested differently in different receiving contexts. The example shows the active role of the
receiving context: the context’s question, capacity, and constraints shape what appears.

Remark 13.19 (The Example Shows the Active Role, Not a Contradiction). The example is
easily read as a contradiction: the same person appears as two different things. The reading
is not the framework’s. The appearance is the epistemic output of the relation between the
identity and the receiving context, and the identity is one while the outputs are many. The
plurality of outputs is not a contradiction; it is the condition of expression (Section 13.3,
Remark on the three features). A reader who takes the example as a contradiction has confused
the identity with its appearances; a reader who takes it as an illustration of the active role of
the receiving context has read it correctly.

13.7.2    The Active Role of the Receiving Context
The receiving cognitive context is not a neutral vessel. Its capacity bears on what can appear;
its constraints exclude some forms and favor others. This is not an addition to the identity’s
appearance by an outside force: it is part of what it is for the appearance to be in that context.
    The point can be put in a slogan: a manifestation is not the identity plus the context,
but the identity as manifested in the context. The two contributions are not separable, and
the manifestation is not the sum of two independent parts. It is one thing, produced by the
interaction of two conditions, and its form reflects both. The two-sided model of Section 13.4
is the framework’s way of stating how the contributions are located.

Remark 13.20 (The Active Role of the Context Is Not Creation). The active role of the
receiving cognitive context is not a creation of the manifestation. The context does not produce
the identity, and it does not produce the manifestation from nothing. It is the condition under
which the identity appears in a determinate form. The distinction is the distinction between
a condition of appearance and a creator of appearance. The framework’s claim is that the
context is the first, not the second. A reader who takes the active role as a creation has
misread it; a reader who takes it as a condition has read it correctly.

    The distinction matters because it preserves the structural asymmetry between the source
and the receiving context. The source is the identity; the context is the condition. The identity
is not produced by the context, and the context is not produced by the identity. The two are
distinct conditions of one manifestation. The framework’s claim is that the manifestation is
the product of both, and that neither is the whole cause of the manifestation. The framework
does not claim that the manifestation is created by the context, and it does not claim that the
manifestation is created by the source alone. It claims that the manifestation is the structural
result of the interaction between the two.
    The framework states the point as a principle, but the principle is proposed, not adopted,
because its independent definition and support are not yet given.

Principle 13.1 (Contextual Manifestational Capacity (proposed)). Status: proposed; not yet
assigned (A) or (T). The form that a manifestation takes in a receiving cognitive context is
fixed jointly by the source identity and by the capacity of the context, and contexts differ in
capacity.
13.8. The Relation Between Identity and Manifestation                                          189


   The principle states what the definition of manifestation presupposes, but a definition
cannot also be the argument for itself. Two things are still lacking, and they are worth stating
precisely, because the chapter’s status depends on them.

First thing lacking: an independent account of “capacity.” The principle uses the
notion of capacity; the notion is defined in this chapter as what a context can bear and what
it is suited to. But the definition is circular with the use of the notion in the principle: the
principle says that the context must have the capacity for the appearance, and the definition
says that capacity is what the context can bear. What is lacking is an independent account of
what capacity is, not defined as the structural capacity to produce what is observed.

Second thing lacking: an argument that capacity is not merely the name of the
difference in appearances. The principle would be trivial if capacity were merely the
name of the difference in appearances: the context would be said to have the capacity for the
appearance because the appearance is what the context produces, and the principle would
reduce to the tautology that the context produces what it produces. What is lacking is
an argument that capacity is not merely the name of the difference in appearances, but a
structural feature of the context that is independent of the particular appearance the context
happens to produce.
     Until these two things are supplied, the principle is examined in the text and not counted as
a principle of the book. It is retained here because the definition of manifestation presupposes
it, and because the audit of Chapter 43 lists it as a proposal, not as an established principle.
The reader who seeks the principle as established will not find it in Book I; the reader who
seeks it as a proposal whose settlement is left open will find it here.

Remark 13.21 (What Would Settle the Principle). The principle would be settled by supplying
the two things that are lacking: an independent account of capacity, and an argument that
capacity is not merely the name of the difference in appearances. The present volume does not
supply them; the account of cost (Chapter 39) is a partial development, not a settlement. A
reader who supplies them has extended the framework; a reader who shows that they cannot
be supplied has shown that the principle is not a principle at all. The framework’s claim is
that the principle is a proposal whose settlement is open, not that the principle is established.


13.8      The Relation Between Identity and Manifestation
The relation between identity and manifestation is not identity, and it is not opposition. It is
one of expression. Four propositions state it.

First proposition: a manifestation is not the identity. It is a new entity in its own
cognitive context. The daughter’s appearance to her mother is not the daughter; it is the
appearance.

Second proposition: a manifestation is not unrelated to the identity. It makes the
identity visible, legible, recognizable; this is what makes it a manifestation of that identity
rather than an unrelated event. The daughter’s appearance to her mother is recognizable as
the daughter; it is not a random event.

Third proposition: manifestations of one identity may differ in structure. Two
manifestations of the same identity, in different contexts or in one, may have different structures.
The daughter’s appearance to her mother and her appearance to her patient differ in structure.
190                                        Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


Fourth proposition: a manifestation is homogeneous in essence with its source.
Whatever its structure, it must not have a feature that conflicts with the essential determination
of its source. The daughter’s appearance to her patient, however different, must not be an
appearance in which the daughter is not recognizable at all; if it were, it would not be a
manifestation of the daughter.
    The four propositions together locate manifestation in a conceptual space: not the identity,
not unrelated to the identity, not necessarily similar in structure to other manifestations, and
yet bound by the essential determination of the source.

Remark 13.22 (The Four Propositions Are Not Independent). The four propositions are not
independent of each other. The first establishes the distinctness of the manifestation from
the identity; the second establishes the relation that the distinctness might seem to deny; the
third establishes the plurality of the appearances; the fourth establishes the constraint under
which the plurality is permitted. If the first were denied, the second would be unnecessary; if
the second were denied, the manifestation would not be a manifestation of anything; if the
third were denied, the plurality of appearances would be impossible; if the fourth were denied,
any appearance could count as a manifestation of any identity. The four together state what
the relation of expression requires.

     The relation is one of expression, and expression points beyond itself. The manifestation
expresses the identity; the identity is what is expressed; and the identity is what it is because
of a ground that the manifestation does not contain. The manifestation shows the identity,
but it does not exhaust the identity; and the identity is real, but its reality is not the reality of
the manifestation. The distinction is the distinction between the expressing and the expressed;
it is kept throughout the book, and it is the structural ground of the framework’s account of
manifestation.

Remark 13.23 (Expression Is the Middle Term). “Expression” is the middle term between
identity and manifestation, and the term is worth marking. It is not identity, because the
manifestation is not the identity; it is not opposition, because the manifestation is not unrelated
to the identity. It is the relation that holds when the identity shows itself in the manifestation—
the relation that the four propositions describe. A reader who takes “expression” as a third
entity, alongside identity and manifestation, has misread it; a reader who takes it as the name
of the relation between the two has read it correctly.

    The relation is also the relation that the thread-and-beads model states in its epistemic
form (Chapter 12, Definition 12.9): the identity is the thread that holds the sequence of
manifestations (the beads) together; the manifestations are many, and the thread is one. The
present chapter’s four propositions are the statement, at the level of a single manifestation, of
what the thread-and-beads model states at the level of a sequence.

Level                 Question
Identity              What is the source of the appearance?
Manifestation         What of it is realized in the receiving context?
Manifestational ef- What change does it bring about in the receiving context?
fect
    The table is a conceptual separation, not a principle. Its use is that the effect of a
manifestation does not show the whole of the manifestation, and the manifestation does not
reveal the whole of the identity. The three are distinct levels; confusion among them is the
source of several errors, including the fallacy of super-identity, which Chapter 28 will state in
its epistemic form.
13.9. Essential Homogeneity                                                                    191


13.9     Essential Homogeneity
The fourth proposition of the previous section requires a principle of its own, because it is the
criterion by which a manifestation is recognized as a manifestation of its source rather than of
another.

Principle 13.2 (Essential Homogeneity of Manifestation). (T) A manifestation is essentially
homogeneous with its source insofar as it preserves the source’s essential determination.
Structural variation among manifestations of one identity is permissible where it does not
introduce a feature incompatible with that determination; a manifestation cannot have a
feature that conflicts with an essential feature of its source.

    The principle is empty unless it says what counts as the essential determination of an
identity and as a conflict with it. The criterion adopted is this.
    The essential determination of an identity is the totality of its defining invariants, as those
were defined in Chapter 12. A feature conflicts with that determination when it is incompatible
with an essential feature. Hence differences of form, scale, or mode in non-essential features
are allowed; incompatibility with an essential feature is not.
    The criterion is internal: it uses only the defining invariants of the identity. The principle
is (T) relative to the definition of identity (Chapter 12) and to the definition of manifestation;
it adds that manifestations are bound by the essential determination of the source. What
would refute it is a manifestation that is acknowledged to be of an identity and yet has a
feature incompatible with an essential feature; the framework would then hold either that the
thing is not a manifestation of that identity (a case of misattribution, of the kind Chapter 12
distinguished) or that the principle fails.

Remark 13.24 (The Principle Is Epistemic, Not Ontological). The principle states a condition
on recognition: a manifestation that is to count as a manifestation of a given identity must
not carry a feature that would exclude the identity’s essential determination. It does not claim
that the manifestation shares a metaphysical essence with the source. The word “homogeneous”
is epistemic: it names the structural compatibility that makes recognition possible. A reader
who takes the principle as a metaphysical claim about shared essence has misread it; a reader
who takes it as an epistemic condition on recognizability has read it correctly.

Remark 13.25 (Structural Difference Is Not Change of Nature). That manifestations differ
in structure does not mean that the essential determination of the identity changes. The
daughter’s structure as a professional and her structure as a daughter are different, and the
daughter’s essential determination is not thereby two. The point is one of the instances of a
broader structural claim, which the framework develops in Chapter 25; here it is named, and
the reader is asked to suspend the fuller treatment until it is given. The structural difference
is not a change of nature; it is the richness of expression.

Remark 13.26 (Essential Homogeneity Is Not Similarity). Essential homogeneity is not
similarity, and the two must be kept apart. Similarity is a relation between the structures
of two manifestations; essential homogeneity is a relation between a manifestation and the
essential determination of its source. A manifestation may be very unlike other manifestations
of the same source (the daughter’s appearance to a patient versus her appearance to her
mother) and still be essentially homogeneous with the source; a manifestation may be similar
to another manifestation of a different source (a portrait of one person resembling another)
and still fail essential homogeneity with the source it is supposed to manifest. The distinction
is the distinction between structural resemblance and essential compatibility; the framework
keeps it apart, and the present chapter’s principle is about the second, not the first.
192                                       Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


13.10      Context and Perspective

A terminological clarification is needed here and later. Cognitive context and perspective are
different things, and the framework uses the two terms with fixed senses.

Definition 13.5 (Cognitive Context (restated)). A cognitive context is the frame in which
something is cognized: the question asked, the elements held fixed, the rule applied, and the
standpoint from which the partition into fixed and fluid is made. A cognitive context is fixed
by the question.

Definition 13.6 (Perspective). A perspective is the structural position of an observer within
a cognitive context: the point from which, the means by which, and the conceptual structure
through which a manifestation is apprehended. A perspective is located at a position, is partial
in what it can apprehend, and is revisable in light of further manifestations.

    The two definitions are different, and the difference is worth marking. A cognitive context is
the frame; a perspective is the position within the frame. Two observers in the same cognitive
context may occupy different perspectives; one observer may move among perspectives within
the same context. The distinction is what allows the framework to say that a difference in
understanding is not, as such, a difference in the manifestation.

Remark 13.27 (The Distinction Is Epistemic, Not Ontological). The distinction between
context and perspective is a distinction within the epistemic order. A manifestation may
be realized in one cognitive context and still be understood in different ways from different
perspectives. A difference in understanding is not, as such, a difference in the manifestation.
To treat the one as the other is to confuse the epistemic with the ontic. The framework’s
claim is that the two are distinct, and that the distinction is what allows it to state, without
paradox, that a manifestation is one thing and its apprehensions are many.

Remark 13.28 (The Fallacy of Super-Identity Concerns Contexts, Not Perspectives). The
fallacy of super-identity, argued in Chapter 28, and the broader structural claim about
predication, which the framework develops in Chapter 25, concern contexts, not perspectives.
The fallacy is not that an observer has a partial perspective (that is inevitable); it is that
manifestations from contexts that cannot be translated into one another are gathered into a
single flat record. The distinction between context and perspective is what allows the fallacy
to be stated precisely, and what allows the framework to say that partial perspectives are not
a defect of cognition but a structural condition of it.

Remark 13.29 (Partiality of Perspective Is Structural). The partiality of the perspective
is not a deficiency; it is the condition under which a finite subject can cognize at all. The
framework’s claim is that the partiality is structural: it belongs to the relation between a finite
subject and an identity, not to the identity itself. The identity may be fully known to a subject
that is not finite; the framework’s claim is about the finite subject, not about the identity.

With the definition of manifestation in place, the framework’s use of the four columns can be
stated for the specific case of a manifestation.

a map of the analytical roles has read it correctly.


13.12      The Epistemic Consequences of Manifestation for Recon-
           struction and Assessment
The chapter’s positive contribution is not only the definition of manifestation and the two-
sided model; it is also the statement of the epistemic consequences of manifestation for the
reconstruction and assessment of identity. The present section states those consequences, so
that the reader knows what the chapter gives, not only what it defines.

First consequence: reconstruction is always from manifestations, never from the
identity itself. A reconstruction has access to manifestations, and from them it recovers
a signature and forms a pseudo-identity (Chapter 12). The reconstruction does not have
access to the identity itself; it has access to what the identity manifests. The consequence is
structural: the reconstruction’s output is always a reconstruction from a finite sample, never a
direct acquaintance with the identity.

Second consequence: the reconstruction’s adequacy is relative to the receiving
context. The manifestation is the epistemic output of the relation between the identity and
the receiving context; the reconstruction of the identity from the manifestation is therefore
relative to the context in which the manifestation was realized. A reconstruction that is
adequate in one context may not be adequate in another; the criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23)
are the check on the reconstruction, and the check is relative to the context.

Third consequence: the plurality of manifestations is the reconstruction’s resource,
not its obstacle. The identity is manifested in many appearances; the reconstruction’s
resource is the plurality of appearances, and its task is to recover the invariant from the many.
The plurality is not a defect; it is the condition under which the reconstruction can proceed.
A reconstruction that treated the plurality as an obstacle would be treating the condition of
its own possibility as an obstacle.
194                                      Chapter 13. Manifestation as Epistemic Appearance


Fourth consequence: the assessment of a reconstruction is the assessment of a
pseudo-identity, not of an identity. The reconstruction’s output is a pseudo-identity, and
the assessment of the reconstruction is the assessment of the pseudo-identity by the criteria
of adequacy. The assessment does not deliver a verdict on the identity in itself; it delivers a
verdict on the reconstruction’s approximation. The distinction is the distinction between the
assessment of the reconstruction and the assessment of the identity; the framework keeps it
apart, and the criteria of Chapter 23 are the instrument of the first, not of the second.

Remark 13.31 (The Four Consequences Are Not Four Separate Claims). The four conse-
quences are not four separate claims; they are four aspects of the single consequence that
manifestation is the epistemic condition of reconstruction. The first names the condition
(the reconstruction is from manifestations); the second names the relativity (the adequacy is
relative to the receiving context); the third names the resource (the plurality is the condition
of reconstruction); the fourth names the limit (the assessment is of a pseudo-identity). The
four together state what the chapter’s account of manifestation contributes to the framework’s
account of reconstruction and assessment.

Remark 13.32 (The Consequences and the Later Parts of the Book). The four consequences
are stated here as the chapter’s positive contribution; their development is in the chapters that
follow. The first consequence is developed in Chapter 23 (the adequacy of a pseudo-identity).
The second is developed in Chapter 21 (the criteria of context validity) and in Chapter 23.
The third is developed in Chapter 27 (the impossibility of super-identity) and in Chapter 28
(the fallacy of super-identity). The fourth is developed in Part IV (the conditions of validity
and adequacy) and in Part V (the limits of finite cognition). The chapter states the four
consequences; the chapters that follow develop them.


13.13      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Five things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not give an independent account of the notion of capacity, and it
does not settle the principle of contextual manifestational capacity. The principle remains
proposed (Principle 13.1 and the remark that follows it). The account of cost in Chapter 39
develops what a context can bear, but it does not supply the independent account the principle
needs; the settlement of the principle is left open, and the audit of Chapter 43 lists it as a
proposal.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the hard/soft distinction of manifestation, nor the
action chain by which an effect is received and sedimented. Both are developed in Chapter 40,
where the definitions of hard and soft manifestation, and the notion of crystallization, are
stated.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the broader structural claim about predication, of
which the distinction between structural difference and change of nature is an instance. The
claim is developed in Chapter 25. The present chapter has named the distinction; the later
chapter argues for it.
    Fourth, the chapter does not develop the full account of the relation between manifestation
and effect. The manifestational effect is named in the definition of manifestation, but its full
treatment is deferred to Chapter 40, where the hard/soft distinction and the action chain give
the effect a fuller structural description.
    Fifth, the chapter does not claim to have fully described the relation of manifestation. It
claims to have described the structure of the relation, and the structure points beyond itself
to the source that manifests. The framework’s claim is that the structure is real, invariant,
and describable; it does not claim that the structure is the whole of what is, and it does not
claim that nothing lies beyond it. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of
13.13. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                 195


manifestation and the ground of manifestation; it is kept throughout the chapter, and it is
stated here as the chapter’s explicit limit.




Remark 13.33 (What the Chapter Has Done). The chapter has done seven things. It has
defined manifestation as the contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving
cognitive context, and it has stated the model of the relation among the subject, its accessible
features, the receiving context, and the epistemic output. It has stated the two-sided model
of manifestation and its input-process-output diagram, and it has analyzed three examples
under the model. It has distinguished essential from non-essential features, with the criterion
aligned with Chapter 12. It has argued that a manifestation is a product of interaction with
an active receiving context, and it has stated a complete example of change under change of
context. It has stated the four propositions that locate the identity–manifestation relation,
and it has stated the principle of essential homogeneity. It has distinguished context from
perspective, and it has stated the epistemic consequences of manifestation for reconstruction
and assessment. The chapter has not given an independent account of capacity, has not
developed the hard/soft distinction, has not developed the broader structural claim about
predication, has not developed the full account of the manifestational effect, and has not
claimed to have fully described the relation of manifestation. The chapter’s contribution is the
framework’s account of manifestation, stated at the strength its arguments support, the model
and the two-sided diagram, the complete example of change under change of context, and the
epistemic consequences for reconstruction and assessment.




Remark 13.34 (The Chapter Prepares the Ground for Epistemic Light). The chapter’s
task was to complete the treatment of the fixed elements, and to prepare the ground for the
treatment of the fluid element. With identity defined in Chapter 12 and manifestation defined
here, the two fixed elements are in place. What remains is the medium of their relation:
the fluid element by which the appearance of an identity is conveyed, and by which the
manifestation is rendered legible as an appearance of the identity. The next chapter opens the
treatment of that medium, epistemic light.

A Question for Reflection
Take a person you know well. Consider three of their appearances: to you, to someone who
does not know them, to themselves. What is preserved across the three? What is different?
And what does the answer tell you about the relation between the person’s identity and the
appearances in which it is manifested? Apply the two-sided model of Section 13.4 to the three
appearances: which features are source features, which are contextual features, which are
transmission features, which are result features?
    And consider the complete example of Section 13.7.1: the daughter in the operating room
and the daughter in the family home. The identity is held fixed; the receiving context is
changed; the appearance changes. Is the change a contradiction, or is it the condition of
expression? What does your answer tell you about the epistemic consequences of manifestation
for reconstruction and assessment (Section 13.12)? Finally, consider the model of Section 13.3.1:
can you apply its four elements (subject, accessible features, receiving context, epistemic
output) to a case of your own choosing, and can you show what the reconstruction of the
identity from the resulting manifestation must contain? A reader who can answer all three
questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s three
tasks before them.

With this chapter, the framework’s treatment of the fixed elements is complete. The next chapter
opens the treatment of the fluid element: epistemic light, the condition of possibility of legible
relation, by which the appearance of an identity is conveyed, and by which the manifestation is
rendered legible as an appearance of the identity.

Chapter 14

Context and Perspective

Scope
This chapter develops the distinction between context and perspective that the previous chapter
named. It distinguishes the cognitive context from the existential context, defines perspective
as the structural position of a subject within a cognitive context, argues that the two are
distinct, and draws two consequences: first, that the fallacy of super-identity concerns contexts
and not perspectives; and second, that the partiality of perspective is a structural condition of
finite cognition and not a defect.
    The chapter’s relation to Chapter 13 is worth stating at the outset. Chapter 13 used
“cognitive context” and “perspective” as minimal working terms, and it gave them as definitions
(13.3 and 13.4) with the label “restated” (from Chapters 6 and 10). Those definitions were
sufficient for Chapter 13’s purpose, which was to state what a manifestation is and how it
stands to the identity it manifests. The present chapter is the systematic treatment of the
two terms: it states the two kinds of context in their own place, it defines perspective with
the three parts that Chapter 13’s brief definition anticipated, and it argues that the two are
distinct. The brief definitions of Chapter 13 and the systematic treatment of the present
chapter are not two different definitions; they are the same distinction, stated at two levels of
detail.
    It does not yet state the impossibility of super-identity; that is the work of Part V. Its claims
are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “context,” “perspective,” “position,” “partiality,”
“standpoint,” or “apprehension,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter and in the previous chapters.


14.1      A Scene: The Courtroom and the Six Descriptions
Consider a courtroom. The same event—a contract signed on a Tuesday afternoon—is described
by six people, each of whom is present in the room, and each of whom describes the event
differently.
    The judge describes it as the formation of a binding obligation, with conditions of offer,
acceptance, and consideration. The clerk describes it as a document entered into the record
on a particular page, at a particular time. The plaintiff describes it as the moment her claim
arose. The defendant describes it as the moment he was misled. The reporter describes it as a
fact to be reported, with a lead and a quotation. The bailiff describes it as a quiet interval in
a long day.
    Six descriptions, one event. The descriptions differ, and the difference is not a mistake.
Each is correct in its own frame, and each makes visible something the others do not. The
judge’s description is not the clerk’s, and the plaintiff’s is not the defendant’s, and the reporter’s
is not the bailiff’s. Yet the event is one.
200                                                      Chapter 14. Context and Perspective


      The scene exhibits two distinctions at once, and the chapter’s task is to keep them apart.

The first distinction. The six descriptions belong to different cognitive contexts. The
judge’s context is defined by the question of legal obligation; the clerk’s by the question of
record; the plaintiff’s by the question of claim; the defendant’s by the question of reliance;
the reporter’s by the question of public interest; the bailiff’s by the question of order in the
room. Each context fixes what counts as a fixed element, what counts as a fluid element, and
which dynamics governs. The contexts are not the same, and the difference between them is
the difference between the questions they ask.

The second distinction. Within each context, the observer occupies a perspective. The
judge’s perspective is the bench; the clerk’s is the record; the plaintiff’s is the bar; the
defendant’s is the dock; the reporter’s is the press row; the bailiff’s is the door. Each
perspective is a position within the context: the point from which, the means by which, and
the conceptual structure through which the event is apprehended. The perspectives are not
the same, and the difference between them is the difference between the positions the observers
occupy.
    The two distinctions are not the same. Two observers in the same context may occupy
different perspectives; one observer may move among perspectives within the same context;
and two observers in different contexts may, by coincidence, occupy the same perspective.
The chapter’s claim is that the two distinctions must be kept apart, and that running them
together is the source of a class of epistemic errors that the framework is designed to diagnose.
    The scene poses a question. What is the difference between the two distinctions, and why
does it matter? The present chapter’s answer is that the first distinction is between questions,
and the second is between positions within a question. The first determines what counts as an
element and as a rule; the second determines what an observer can see and how. The two are
distinct, and the framework’s account of finite cognition depends on keeping them apart.

Remark 14.1 (The Scene Shows Two Distinctions, Not One). The scene is easily read as a
single observation about six people who happen to see the same event differently. The single
observation is not wrong, but it conflates two distinctions. The first distinction is between the
six questions the six people ask; the second is between the six positions the six people occupy.
The judge and the plaintiff’s attorney both ask the question of the plaintiff’s claim (so they
share a context), and yet they occupy different positions (the bench and the bar). The judge
and the clerk both occupy positions of authority in the room (so they share a perspective, by
a loose analogy), and yet they ask different questions (so they differ in context). The two
distinctions are orthogonal, and the scene shows both at work.

Remark 14.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the two
distinctions at work in a familiar case. It does not prove that the two are distinct; it makes
the distinction intelligible before it is argued. The argument is given in Section 14.5, and the
scene carries no weight in it.


14.2       The Question
The previous chapter defined manifestation as the contextually realized appearance of an
identity in a receiving cognitive context. It named three things that must not be run together:
the identity, the manifestation, and the manifestational effect. It named, in passing, the
distinction between context and perspective, and it promised that the distinction would be
developed in its own place. The present chapter is that place.
    The question is: what is the distinction between a cognitive context and a perspective,
and why does the distinction matter for the framework’s account of finite cognition? The
14.3. The Two Kinds of Context                                                               201


question is not merely terminological. It is the question of what it is for a manifestation to be
cognized in a frame, and of what it is for an observer to occupy a position within that frame.
If the two are run together, the framework cannot state what a manifestation is (a product
of identity and receiving context), and it cannot state what the observer’s apprehension of
a manifestation is (a pseudo-identity formed from a perspective within a context). The two
statements would collapse into one, and the framework would lose the distinction between the
manifestation and its apprehension.
    The chapter’s answer has three parts. It distinguishes the two kinds of context—the
cognitive context, which is fixed by the question, and the existential context, which the present
volume uses only to mark off the ontological question. It defines perspective as the structural
position of an observer within a cognitive context, with its determining parameters. It argues
that the two are distinct, and it draws the consequences for the fallacy of super-identity and
for the partiality of perspective.

Remark 14.3 (The Question Is About the Structure of Apprehension). The question the
chapter asks is not about what an observer believes, or about how an observer feels. It is
about the structure of apprehension: what it is for an observer to occupy a position within a
context, and how that position conditions what the observer can see and how. The structure
is what the chapter describes, and the description is at the level of the epistemic order, not at
the level of psychology. A reader who takes the chapter’s question as a psychological question
has misread it; a reader who takes it as a structural question has read it correctly.


14.3     The Two Kinds of Context
The word “context” is used in this book in two senses, and the distinction is kept throughout.
The two senses were introduced in Chapter 6, restated in Chapter 10, and used in their minimal
form in Chapter 13; they are restated here in their own place, with exact names, definitions,
and relations, because the present chapter’s argument depends on them.


14.3.1    The Two Kinds of Context Stated Exactly
Definition 14.1 (Cognitive Context). A cognitive context is the frame in which something is
cognized: the question asked, the elements held fixed, the rule applied, and the standpoint
from which the partition into fixed and fluid is made. A cognitive context is fixed by the
question, and there are indefinitely many of them (Chapter 11).

Definition 14.2 (Existential Context). An existential context is the setting in which a
manifestation is realized, with the capacity and the constraints of that setting. An existential
context is fixed by the identity and the receiving setting, not by the question.

    The two definitions are different, and the difference is the difference between the order
of inquiry and the order of being. The cognitive context is the order through which what is
becomes intelligible; the existential context is the order of what is. The two are distinct, and
neither is reducible to the other; but the first is the condition of possibility of the second. A
manifestation is realized in a setting before it is known in a frame; and the frame is the order
through which the setting becomes intelligible.


14.3.2    The Relation Between the Two Kinds of Context
The two kinds of context are related, and the relation is worth stating exactly.
202                                                         Chapter 14. Context and Perspective


The first relation: distinctness. The cognitive context is not the existential context.
A cognitive context can change while the existential context remains the same (the same
manifestation can be cognized under a different question, with a different frame); and the
existential context can change while the cognitive context remains the same (the same question
can be asked of a manifestation in a different setting). The distinctness is what the two
definitions establish.

The second relation: condition and conditioned. The cognitive context is the condition
under which the existential context becomes intelligible. The existential context is the setting
in which the manifestation is realized; the cognitive context is the frame through which the
setting is cognized. The cognitive context does not produce the existential context, and
the existential context does not produce the cognitive context. The first is the condition of
intelligibility; the second is the condition of realization.

The third relation: non-reducibility. Neither kind of context is reducible to the other.
The cognitive context is not a construction of the existential context (the frame is not a
setting); the existential context is not a construction of the cognitive context (the setting is not
a frame). The framework keeps the two apart so that the study of cognition is not confused
with the study of being.

14.3.3     Examples of the Two Kinds of Context
Two examples make the distinction concrete.

Example 14.1 (The River: Cognitive Context and Existential Context). Consider a river.
Its existential context is the setting in which the river is realized: the physical channel, the
water, the banks, the surrounding terrain, with their capacities and constraints. The river is
realized in that setting whether or not any observer cognizes it.
    The river’s cognitive contexts are the frames in which the river is cognized. The political
geographer’s context is the question of the border; the river is a fixed element (a boundary),
held stable while the relations of the two banks are explained. The trader’s context is the
question of transport; the river is a fluid element (a route), carrying effect from one side to
the other. The hydrologist’s context is the question of flow; the river is a network of fluid
elements (channels) governed by the rules of hydrology.
    The three cognitive contexts are different, and the existential context is one. The river
is the same river in all four; the cognitive contexts in which it is cognized are different; the
existential context in which it is realized is one. The example shows the distinction: the
existential context is the setting; the cognitive contexts are the frames.

Example 14.2 (The Contract: Cognitive Context and Existential Context). Consider the
contract of the courtroom scene. Its existential context is the setting in which the contract
was signed: the room, the parties, the paper, the ink, the time, with their capacities and
constraints. The contract is realized in that setting whether or not any observer cognizes it.
    The contract’s cognitive contexts are the frames in which it is cognized. The judge’s
context is the question of legal obligation; the clerk’s is the question of record; the plaintiff’s is
the question of claim; the defendant’s is the question of reliance; the reporter’s is the question
of public interest; the bailiff’s is the question of order in the room. The six cognitive contexts
are different, and the existential context is one. The contract is the same contract in all seven;
the cognitive contexts in which it is cognized are different; the existential context in which it
is realized is one.

Remark 14.4 (The Examples Show the Distinction at Work). The two examples show the
distinction at work in familiar cases. In each, the existential context is the setting in which
14.4. The Perspective                                                                       203


the manifestation is realized, and the cognitive contexts are the frames in which it is cognized.
The plurality of cognitive contexts is a plurality of questions, not a plurality of settings; the
existential context is one even when the cognitive contexts are many.
Remark 14.5 (The Present Volume Is Concerned With the Cognitive Context). The present
volume is concerned with the cognitive context. The existential context is named here to be
marked off, and it is not developed as an ontology. The question of what levels of being there
are, and of how a manifestation is realized in a setting, is outside the present volume’s scope.
The distinction between the two kinds of context is stated so that the reader knows which
kind the framework’s arguments concern; it is not stated so that the reader will take it as an
ontological thesis.
Remark 14.6 (The Two Contexts Are Not Two Worlds). The distinction between the two
kinds of context is a distinction between two orders, not a separation of two worlds. The
existential context is the ground of the cognitive context, and the cognitive context is the
intelligibility of the existential context. The framework keeps the two apart so that the study
of cognition is not confused with the study of being—but the keeping-apart is not a denial
that the two are related. A reader who takes the distinction as a denial that there is a setting
in which manifestations are realized has misread it; a reader who takes it as a distinction
between two orders has read it correctly.
Remark 14.7 (The Two Kinds of Context Answer Different Questions). The two kinds
of context answer different questions, and the difference is worth marking. The cognitive
context answers the question: in which frame is the element individuated and the rule applied?
The existential context answers the question: in which setting is the manifestation realized,
with what capacity and what constraints? The first is a question about the structure of the
explanation; the second is a question about the structure of what is explained. The framework
keeps the two apart so that the first is not mistaken for the second; a reader who takes the
cognitive context as the existential context has confused the order of inquiry with the order of
being.


14.4     The Perspective
Within a cognitive context, a subject occupies a position. The position is the perspective, and
it is defined as follows.

14.4.1    The Definition of Perspective
Definition 14.3 (Perspective). A perspective is the structural position of a subject within a
cognitive context: the point from which, the means by which, and the conceptual structure
through which a manifestation is apprehended. A perspective is located at a position, is partial
in what it can apprehend, and is revisable in light of further manifestations.
   The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.

The point from which. A perspective is located. The judge’s perspective is the bench; the
reporter’s is the press row. The location is not a physical location only; it is the structural
position from which the subject has access to the manifestation, and it conditions what the
subject can apprehend.

The means by which. A perspective has means of apprehension. The judge has the record
and the argument; the reporter has the notebook and the interview; the plaintiff has the
memory and the contract. The means are part of the perspective, and they condition what
the subject can make of the manifestation.
204                                                       Chapter 14. Context and Perspective


The conceptual structure through which. A perspective has a conceptual structure.
The judge’s concepts are legal concepts; the reporter’s are narrative concepts; the clerk’s are
administrative concepts. The concepts are part of the perspective, and they condition what
the subject can articulate.
    The three parts are not separable. A perspective is the structural position taken as a
whole: the point from which, the means by which, and the conceptual structure through which
a manifestation is apprehended.

14.4.2    The Determining Parameters of a Perspective
The definition states what a perspective is; the parameters state what determines a perspective
in a given case. The parameters are the features by which a perspective can be identified,
compared, and assessed.
Definition 14.4 (The Determining Parameters of a Perspective). (A) A perspective is
determined by five parameters:
(P1) Location: the position within the context from which the subject has access to the
     manifestation (the bench, the bar, the dock, the press row, the door).
(P2) Access channel : the means by which the subject receives the manifestation (the record,
     the argument, the interview, the memory, the direct observation).
(P3) Conceptual repertoire: the concepts through which the subject articulates the manifesta-
     tion (legal concepts, narrative concepts, administrative concepts, technical concepts).
(P4) Interest and question-focus: the aspect of the manifestation that the subject’s interest
     makes salient (the legal obligation, the claim, the reliance, the public interest, the order).
(P5) Epistemic stance: the attitude the subject takes toward the manifestation (accepting,
     doubting, testing, recording, observing).
The five parameters are (A): they are a stipulation of the framework’s way of decomposing a
perspective. Their justification is their use in the analysis of cases; their cost is that a given
perspective may not exhibit all five parameters distinctly.
    The parameters are the framework’s way of making the definition of perspective exact.
The definition states what a perspective is; the parameters state what determines a perspective
in a given case. The parameters do not add a new claim; they state the structure of the claim
the definition already makes.
Remark 14.8 (The Parameters Are Analytical, Not Metaphysical). The five parameters are
analytical roles, in the sense that Chapter 5 fixes. They are the features by which a perspective
can be identified, compared, and assessed; they are not five substances, and they are not five
kinds of entity. The model of a perspective as a five-parameter structure is the framework’s
way of making the definition usable; it does not claim that a perspective is composed of five
parts.
Remark 14.9 (The Parameters and the Two-Sided Model of Chapter 13). The parameters of
a perspective are related to the two-sided model of manifestation (Chapter 13, Definition 13.3).
The receiving context of a manifestation is the context (the question); the perspective of the
subject who cognizes the manifestation is the position within the context. The parameters
of the perspective (location, access channel, conceptual repertoire, interest, stance) are the
features that distinguish one subject’s apprehension of the manifestation from another’s. The
two-sided model locates the source and the context; the parameters locate the subject’s
position. The distinction is the distinction between the context and the perspective, and the
parameters are the framework’s way of making the perspective exact.
14.5. The Distinction                                                                        205


14.4.3    The Properties of Perspective
Three properties follow from the definition and the parameters, and each is worth marking.
    Located. A perspective is at a position. It is not a view from nowhere; it is a view from
somewhere. The location is what makes the perspective a perspective, and not a view of the
whole.
    Partial. A perspective is partial in what it can apprehend. No perspective can apprehend
everything about a manifestation, because every perspective is at a position, and every position
excludes what it is not.
    Revisable. A perspective is revisable in light of further manifestations. The subject
may move to a new position, adopt new means, or revise the conceptual structure, and the
perspective thereby changes. The revision is not a defect of the perspective; it is a structural
feature of finite cognition.
Remark 14.10 (Perspective Is Not the Same as Context). A perspective is within a context;
a context is not within a perspective. Two subjects in the same context may occupy different
perspectives; one subject may move among perspectives within the same context; and two sub-
jects in different contexts may, by coincidence, occupy the same perspective. The distinctions
are the distinctions of the chapter, and the present remark states them so that the reader does
not run them together.
Remark 14.11 (The Perspective Is the Position of the Pseudo-Identity). The pseudo-identity
defined in Chapter 12 is formed from a perspective within a context. The subject does not
reconstruct the identity from nothing; the subject reconstructs it from the manifestations
that are accessible from the perspective, and with the means and the conceptual structure
that the perspective provides. The partiality of the pseudo-identity is the partiality of the
perspective, and the adequacy of the pseudo-identity (Chapter 23) is assessed relative to the
perspective and to the context. The distinction between context and perspective is what makes
the assessment possible.
Remark 14.12 (The Perspective Is Not the Subject). The perspective is not the subject. The
subject is the one who occupies the perspective; the perspective is the position that the subject
occupies. The distinction is the distinction between the one who sees and the position from
which the seeing is done. The distinction matters because the subject may occupy different
perspectives at different times, or may move among perspectives within the same context;
the perspective is what changes, not the subject. A reader who takes the perspective as the
subject has confused the position with the one who occupies it; a reader who takes it as the
position has read it correctly.


14.5     The Distinction
The two definitions are different, and the difference is what the chapter argues. The distinction
is not merely verbal; it marks two different things, and running them together is the source of
a class of epistemic errors.

Argument for the Distinctness of Context and Perspective.   1. A cognitive context is fixed
     by the question. It determines what counts as a fixed element, what counts as a fluid
     element, and which dynamics governs. The context is shared by all subjects who ask the
     same question.

   2. A perspective is the structural position of a subject within a cognitive context. It
      determines the point from which, the means by which, and the conceptual structure
      through which a manifestation is apprehended. The perspective is occupied by one
      subject, or by a group of subjects who share a position.
206                                                       Chapter 14. Context and Perspective


   3. Two subjects in the same context may occupy different perspectives. The two plaintiffs’
      attorneys in the same trial, both asking the question of the plaintiff’s claim, may
      occupy different perspectives—one at the bar, the other at counsel’s table—and the two
      perspectives condition different apprehensions of the same manifestation.
   4. One subject may move among perspectives within the same context. The judge may move
      from the bench to the record to the colloquy, and the move is a change of perspective
      within the same context.
   5. Two subjects in different contexts may, by coincidence, occupy the same perspective.
      The bailiff and the plaintiff’s attorney may both occupy the bar, but the bailiff asks the
      question of order in the room and the attorney asks the question of the plaintiff’s claim.
      The perspective is the same; the context is different.
   6. Hence context and perspective are distinct: an answer to one is not an answer to the
      other, and a difference in one is not, as such, a difference in the other.


    The argument’s force is in steps (3)–(5). If context and perspective were the same, the
cases described in those steps would not be possible. The cases are not contrived; they are the
ordinary cases of cognition, and the framework’s claim is that they are intelligible only if the
two are distinguished.
Remark 14.13 (The Argument Is a Counterexample Argument). The argument is a coun-
terexample argument, and its form is worth marking. It does not prove that context and
perspective are distinct by definition; it shows that the two cannot be the same, because the
same context can contain different perspectives (step 3), and the same perspective can occur
in different contexts (step 5). The counterexamples are the ordinary cases of cognition, and
the framework’s claim is that they are intelligible only if the two are distinguished. A reader
who denies the counterexamples denies the argument; a reader who accepts them has a reason
to accept the distinction.
Remark 14.14 (The Distinction Is Analytical, Not a Doctrine of What Is). The distinction
between context and perspective is a distinction within the epistemic order. It is not a
claim about what reality must contain, and it is not a claim about the route that any real
manifestation must take. The framework’s claim is analytical: it describes the structure of
apprehension, not the structure of what is apprehended. A reader who takes the distinction as
a claim about reality has misread it; a reader who takes it as a distinction within the epistemic
order has read it correctly.
Remark 14.15 (The Distinction Resolves an Apparent Paradox). Without the distinction,
an apparent paradox arises. The same manifestation is apprehended differently by different
subjects, and it seems to follow either that the manifestation is many (one per subject) or that
the apprehensions are illusory (none per subject). Neither consequence is acceptable. With
the distinction, the paradox disappears: the manifestation is one, the contexts are many, the
perspectives are many, and the apprehensions are many. The manifestation is not multiplied
by the apprehensions, and the apprehensions are not illusory because they are partial. The
distinction is what allows the framework to state, without paradox, that a manifestation is
one thing and its apprehensions are many.


14.6     Comparative Examples and the Decision Table
The distinction is stated abstractly; the present section states it in a form that can be applied.
The section gives two comparative examples, and a decision table for deciding, in a given case,
whether a difference is a difference of context or a difference of perspective.
14.6. Comparative Examples and the Decision Table                                              207


14.6.1     Two Comparative Examples


Example 1: Two Lawyers, One Question. Two lawyers both ask the question of the
plaintiff’s claim. They occupy different positions in the courtroom: one at the bar, the other
at counsel’s table. They have access to the same record, but different access channels (one
examines the witnesses directly, the other reads the transcript); they have different conceptual
repertoires (one is trained in contract law, the other in tort law); they have different interest
and question-focus (one emphasizes the plaintiff’s claim, the other the defendant’s reliance);
and they have different epistemic stances (one accepts the plaintiff’s account, the other tests it).
The two lawyers share a context (the question of the plaintiff’s claim) and differ in perspective
(the five parameters of Definition 14.4).




Example 2: One Lawyer, Two Questions. The same lawyer asks the question of the
plaintiff’s claim in one hearing, and the question of the defendant’s reliance in another. The
lawyer occupies the same position in the courtroom (the bar), has the same access channel
(the record and the witnesses), the same conceptual repertoire (contract and tort law), and
the same epistemic stance (testing). But the question is different, and the context is different:
the same perspective, two contexts. The two examples show the two distinctions in opposite
directions: Example 1 holds the context fixed and varies the perspective; Example 2 holds the
perspective fixed and varies the context.




Remark 14.16 (The Two Examples Are Not the Only Combinations). The two examples are
the two simplest combinations of the two distinctions: same context, different perspectives
(Example 1); different contexts, same perspective (Example 2). Other combinations are
possible: different contexts, different perspectives; same context, same perspective (which is
what two subjects in the same context and the same position share). The examples are not
the only combinations; they are the combinations that make the distinction visible.

apprehensions differ, the table states the questions by which the difference is diagnosed as a
difference of context, a difference of perspective, or both.
