Remark 14.17 (The Decision Table and the Criteria of Diagnosis). The decision table is
the criteria of diagnosis for the distinction between context and perspective. The criteria are
the four diagnostic questions; the diagnosis is the assignment of the difference to context, to
perspective, or to both. The table does not replace the argument of Section 14.5; it states the
criteria by which the argument’s distinction is applied to a case.

Remark 14.18 (The Decision Table Is Not a Decision Procedure for the Truth). The decision
table is not a decision procedure for the truth of an apprehension. It states how to diagnose
whether a difference is a difference of context or of perspective; it does not state whether either
apprehension is correct. The truth of an apprehension is a separate question, and the criteria
of adequacy (Chapter 23) are the framework’s account of how it is assessed. A reader who
takes the table as a decision procedure for truth has confused the diagnosis of the difference
with the assessment of the apprehension; a reader who takes it as a decision procedure for the
diagnosis has read it correctly.


14.7     The Fallacy of Super-Identity Concerns Contexts, Not
         Perspectives
The distinction between context and perspective is what allows the framework to state the
fallacy of super-identity precisely.
    The fallacy of super-identity is the error of treating a record formed by aggregating manifes-
tations drawn from contexts whose elements are not mutually translatable as a reconstruction
of the identity. It is stated in Chapter 28 in its epistemic form. The present section states the
distinction that the fallacy presupposes: the fallacy concerns contexts, not perspectives.
14.8. Partiality of Perspective Is Structural                                                      209


The point. The fallacy is not that a subject has a partial perspective. The partiality of
perspective is inevitable, and the framework does not treat it as a defect. The fallacy is
that manifestations from contexts that cannot be translated into one another are gathered
into a single flat record. The contexts are different, and the difference is not a difference of
perspective; it is a difference of the question asked, and the question determines what counts
as a fixed element, what counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics governs.

The illustration. The courtroom scene illustrates the point. The judge’s description, the
clerk’s, the plaintiff’s, the defendant’s, the reporter’s, and the bailiff’s are six descriptions in six
contexts. A record that gathered all six into a single flat record would not be a reconstruction
of the event; it would be a context-confounded record, an object that corresponds to no event.
The record would confuse the six contexts, and it would treat the six perspectives as if they
were differences within a single context. The fallacy is the confusion of the two, and the
distinction between context and perspective is what makes the confusion visible.
Remark 14.19 (Partial Perspective Is Not the Fallacy). The partiality of perspective is
not the fallacy. The fallacy is the aggregation of manifestations across contexts, not the
partiality of a perspective within a context. A reader who takes the fallacy as a criticism of
partial perspectives has misread it; a reader who takes it as a criticism of the aggregation of
manifestations across contexts has read it correctly.
Remark 14.20 (The Fallacy and the Criteria of Validity). The criteria of context validity,
stated in Chapter 21, are what discipline the use of contexts. A context that fails the criteria is
not a valid context, and the manifestations drawn from it are not candidates for a reconstruction
of the identity. The fallacy of super-identity is the error of aggregating manifestations across
contexts without subjecting the contexts to the criteria. The present chapter states the
distinction that makes the fallacy visible; Chapter 21 states the criteria that make the fallacy
avoidable.
Remark 14.21 (The Fallacy Is a Failure of Translation, Not of Vision). The fallacy is a
failure of translation, not of vision, and the distinction is worth marking. A perspective is
partial, but its partiality is not a failure: the partiality is what it is to see from somewhere.
The fallacy is not that the subject sees partially; it is that the subject treats the partial record
as if it were the whole, because the subject has failed to recognize that the records come
from contexts that cannot be translated into one another. The failure is a failure to recognize
the difference between contexts, not a failure of the subject’s vision. A reader who takes the
fallacy as a criticism of partial vision has confused the two; a reader who takes it as a failure
of translation has read it correctly.


14.8      Partiality of Perspective Is Structural
The distinction between context and perspective has a further consequence, which the present
section states: the partiality of perspective is structural, not a defect.
Principle 14.1 (The Partiality of Perspective). (T) The partiality of a perspective is a
structural condition of finite cognition, not a defect. A perspective is partial because it is
located; the location is what makes it a perspective, and not a view of the whole.
    The principle follows from the definition of perspective. A perspective is at a position; a
position excludes what it is not; the exclusion is what makes the perspective a perspective. To
demand a perspective that is not partial is to demand a perspective that is not at a position,
which is to demand a view from nowhere. The framework does not claim that such a view
is impossible in itself; it claims that it is not the view of a finite subject, and that the finite
subject’s view is partial by structural necessity.
210                                                        Chapter 14. Context and Perspective


Remark 14.22 (The Principle Is About the Finite Subject). The principle is about the finite
subject. It does not claim that no subject whatsoever can have a non-partial view; it claims
that no finite subject can. The object may be fully known to a subject that is not finite; the
framework’s claim is about the finite subject, not about the object. The framework’s silence on
the infinite subject is not a denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the framework’s
method is the method of finite inquiry, and that the limits of finite inquiry are not the limits
of what is.

Remark 14.23 (The Partiality Is Not Skepticism). The partiality of perspective is not
skepticism. A skeptic claims that knowledge is impossible; the framework claims that knowledge
is partial. The first is a denial of knowledge; the second is a description of its condition. The
framework’s claim is that the partiality is structural: it belongs to the relation between a finite
subject and an identity, not to the identity itself, and not to the object of knowledge. A partial
apprehension can be a real apprehension, and a located perspective can yield real knowledge.

Remark 14.24 (The Partiality Is Not a Deficiency to Be Overcome). The partiality of
perspective is not a deficiency that a better perspective would overcome. It is a structural
condition of finite cognition, and a subject that had no partiality would not be a finite subject.
The framework’s claim is that the partiality is the condition under which finite cognition
is possible, and that the recognition of the condition is the beginning of epistemic humility
(Chapter 35), not the end of epistemic hope.

Remark 14.25 (The Partiality and the Plurality of Perspectives). The partiality of perspective
is what makes the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33) intelligible. If a perspective were
not partial, there would be no reason for there to be more than one; the plurality would be
an oddity. Because a perspective is partial, the plurality is a structural condition of finite
cognition: each perspective sees something the others do not, and the plurality is what makes
the apprehension of an identity more complete than any single perspective could be. The
partiality and the plurality are two aspects of one structural fact; the framework states them
separately so that each can be assessed, not because they are separate.

in the framework’s architecture: the cognitive context is the frame; the existential context is
14.10. The Distinction and the Method                                                          211


the setting; the perspective is the position. The three are distinct, and the distinctions are what
allow the framework to state, without paradox, that the same manifestation is apprehended
differently from different perspectives, and that the apprehensions are not a defect of cognition
but a structural condition of it.

Remark 14.26 (The Distinctions Are Epistemic, Not a Doctrine of What Is). The three
distinctions are distinctions within the epistemic order. They do not claim that reality is
divided into contexts, or that a manifestation is realized in a setting that is separate from the
setting in which it is cognized. They claim that cognition is structured by context, perspective,
and the setting in which a manifestation is realized, and that the three must be distinguished
so that the structure of cognition can be stated. The reader who takes the distinctions as
claims about reality has misread them; the reader who takes them as distinctions within the
epistemic order has read them correctly.

Remark 14.27 (The Three Distinctions Are Not the Same Kind). The three distinctions
are not the same kind of distinction, and the difference is worth marking. The distinction
between cognitive context and existential context is a distinction between two orders (the
order of inquiry and the order of being). The distinction between context and perspective is a
distinction within the epistemic order (the frame and the position within the frame). The two
distinctions are not parallel; the first is between orders, the second is within an order. A reader
who treats the three as parallel distinctions has misread the chapter; a reader who treats the
first as between orders and the second as within the epistemic order has read it correctly.


14.10      The Distinction and the Method
The distinction is stated at the strength the method of Chapter 2 allows. It is (T): it is argued,
and the argument is given in Section 14.5. The argument’s force is in the counterexamples
(steps 3–5 of the proof), and a reader who accepts the counterexamples has a reason to accept
the conclusion.
    The two consequences—the fallacy of super-identity concerns contexts and not perspectives,
and the partiality of perspective is structural—are (T) relative to the definitions of the chapter.
They are argued in Sections 14.7 and 14.8, and the reader who accepts the definitions has a
reason to accept the consequences.
    The principles are stated at the strength their arguments support. They are not proofs
from nothing; they depend on the definitions and on the counterexamples, and the framework
states the definitions and the counterexamples so that the reader can assess the arguments.

Remark 14.28 (The Chapter Prepares the Ground for Later Parts). The chapter’s distinction
is used throughout the parts that follow. Part IV uses it to state the criteria of context
validity (Chapter 21) and the three failures of reconstruction (Chapter 24). Part V uses it
to state the impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27) and the fallacy of super-identity
(Chapter 28). Part VI uses it to state the cost of cognition (Chapter 39) and the cognitive
sediment (Chapter 40). The distinction is stated here, in its own place, so that the later parts
can presuppose it.


14.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
   First, the chapter does not state the impossibility of super-identity. That is the subject
of Chapter 27. The present chapter states the distinction that the impossibility argument
presupposes; the argument itself is given in its own place.
212                                                        Chapter 14. Context and Perspective


    Second, the chapter does not state the criteria of context validity. That is the subject of
Chapter 21. The present chapter states the distinction between context and perspective; the
criteria that discipline the use of contexts are stated in their own place.




    Third, the chapter does not develop the existential context as an ontology. It names the
existential context only to mark it off, and it leaves the ontological question to the chapter
that states the framework’s account of manifestation (Chapter 13) and to the chapters that
state the conditions of validity (Part IV). A reader who seeks a doctrine of levels of being
will not find it here; a reader who seeks the distinction between the cognitive context and the
existential context will find it.




   Fourth, the chapter does not settle the question of which perspectives are more adequate
than others. The assessment of perspectives is a matter for the inquiry, and the criteria of
adequacy (Chapter 23) are the framework’s account of what makes an assessment possible.
The present chapter states the distinction; the assessment is a separate inquiry.




Remark 14.29 (What the Chapter Has Done). The chapter has done six things. It has
distinguished the cognitive context from the existential context, and it has stated the two kinds
of context in their own place, with exact names, definitions, relations, and examples. It has
defined perspective as the structural position of a subject within a cognitive context, and it has
stated the five determining parameters of a perspective (location, access channel, conceptual
repertoire, interest, epistemic stance). It has argued that context and perspective are distinct,
by a counterexample argument whose force is in the ordinary cases of cognition. It has stated
two comparative examples and a decision table for the diagnosis of a difference as a difference
of context, of perspective, or of both. It has drawn the two consequences: that the fallacy of
super-identity concerns contexts and not perspectives, and that the partiality of perspective is
structural and not a defect. And it has prepared the ground for the later parts, which use
the distinction in their own arguments. The chapter has not stated the impossibility of super-
identity, has not stated the criteria of context validity, has not developed the existential context
as an ontology, and has not settled the question of which perspectives are more adequate.
The chapter’s contribution is the distinction between context and perspective, stated at the
strength its argument supports, the five parameters of a perspective, the comparative examples
and decision table, and the two consequences that the later parts of the book require.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a disagreement you have witnessed or participated in. Was the disagreement a
difference of context (the parties were asking different questions) or a difference of perspective
(the parties were in the same context, but at different positions)? Use the decision table of
214                                                       Chapter 14. Context and Perspective


Section 14.6.2 to diagnose the difference: do the two parties ask different questions (a difference
of context), or do they differ in one or more of the five perspective parameters (a difference of
perspective), or both? What does your answer tell you about the relation between context,
perspective, and the possibility of disagreement?
    And consider the courtroom scene that opened the chapter. The six descriptions are six
descriptions in six contexts. Are they rivals? If not, what makes them compatible? And if
they are compatible, what would a record that gathered them into a single flat record be—a
reconstruction of the event, or a context-confounded record? What does your answer tell you
about the difference between a manifestation and its apprehension, and about the relation
between the partiality of perspective and the plurality of perspectives? Finally, consider
the two comparative examples of Section 14.6.1: can you give a third example in which two
subjects share a context but differ in perspective, or share a perspective but differ in context,
and can you diagnose the difference with the decision table? A reader who can answer all
three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s
three tasks before them.

With this chapter, the framework’s treatment of the epistemic structure of relation is deepened:
identity and manifestation are the fixed elements; context and perspective are the structure
of their apprehension. The next chapter opens the treatment of the fluid element: epistemic
light, the condition of possibility of legible relation, by which the appearance of an identity is
conveyed.

Chapter 15

Epistemic Light: The Medium of
Relation

Scope
This chapter opens the framework’s treatment of the fluid element. Epistemic light is the
framework’s name for the condition of possibility of legible relation: the medium by which an
appearance is conveyed and by which a manifestation is rendered legible as an appearance
of its source. The chapter maps the human answers to the question “what is light?” into
four structural patterns, identifies the common presupposition that underlies them, defines
epistemic light as the medium of legible relation, proves the regress argument that makes the
definition necessary, and states the distinctness test that exhibits the specific work epistemic
light does (Section 15.9). It does not yet sharpen the definition; the sharpening (light as an
active structure of legibility, and the encompassment in light) is the work of Chapters 16
and 17.
    The chapter is the first of the three chapters that develop the fluid element that Chapter 6
defined (Definition 6.2) and that Chapter 6’s Remark on where each column is developed
(Remark 6.26) distributes across the volume: the fluid element is developed in Chapters 15–17,
of which the present chapter is the first. The chapter presupposes the conveyor principle
of Chapter 8 (Principle 8.1), which established that some fluid element is necessary for any
explanation of how one fixed element bears on another, and the non-sequential connectivity
of Chapter 9 (Principle 9.1), which established that the carrier need not be a sequence of
carriers. The chapter’s central claim, that epistemic light is the condition of possibility of
legible relation, is one of the six operationalizations of the distinction that Chapter 5 states
between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory dependence; the reader who
has understood that distinction will recognize it here.
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “light,” “legibility,” “medium,” “sub-
stance,” “relation,” or “condition,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter.


15.1     A Scene: The Table in the Dark and the Table in the Light
Close your eyes. In the dark, objects are—you reach out, you touch a table. The table is there:
its edge, its grain, its coolness. But it is not seen. Then you open your eyes. The same table,
the same distance, the same hand. But something has been added: the table is seen. What is
that added thing?
    The question seems simple. The table did not change; the hand did not move; the distance
is the same. What changed is that the table is now visible. But “visible” is not a thing added to
the table, as a fourth leg would be. It is a relation—between the table, the eye, and something
216                                     Chapter 15. Epistemic Light: The Medium of Relation


else, something that was absent when the eyes were closed and present when they opened.
What is that something else?
    The ordinary answer is: light. The room was dark; now it is lit. But the ordinary answer
names a candidate for the something else; it does not yet say what the candidate is. When
we press the question—what is light, such that its presence makes the table visible and its
absence leaves the table in the dark?—the ordinary answer begins to dissolve. Is light a stream
of particles? A wave in a medium? A field? A condition of visibility that is not itself visible?
Each answer has its difficulties, and each has been defended.
    The scene is small, but the question it raises is not. It is the question of what makes
relation possible—not only the relation between the eye and the table, but any relation of
appearing at all. If the framework’s four columns are correct (Chapter 7), the second column
is the fluid element: the entity that conveys effect between the fixed elements. What is that
entity? The present part of the book answers: it is epistemic light, in a sense that must be
defined with philosophical precision. The present chapter prepares the definition by showing
why the question is an epistemic question, by mapping the answers that have been given, and
by exhibiting what difference epistemic light makes (Section 15.9).

Remark 15.1 (The Scene Shows the Same Object, Two Conditions). The scene shows the
same table, two conditions: the dark and the light. The table does not change; what changes
is whether the table is visible. The distinction is the distinction between the object and its
legibility—between the thing and its appearing. The scene is the framework’s way of showing
that legibility is a condition, not a property of the thing. The table is the same table in the
dark and in the light; what differs is the condition under which the table is legible. Epistemic
light is the framework’s name for that condition.

Remark 15.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the definition that follows; it makes the definition
intelligible before it is stated. The argument for the definition is given in Section 15.8, and the
scene carries no weight in it.


15.2     The Question
Part III has treated the fixed elements of epistemic relations. Identity was defined as the
invariant an explanatory cognition holds fixed across a class of allowable transformations of its
manifestations (Chapter 12); manifestation was defined as the contextually realized appearance
of an identity in a receiving cognitive context, according to that context’s capacity, aptitude,
and constraints (Chapter 13); context and perspective were distinguished (Chapter 14). The
relation between identity and manifestation was stated: a manifestation is not the identity,
and is not unrelated to it; it makes the identity visible, legible, recognizable.
    But the relation has a gap. If the manifestation is the appearance of the identity in a
context, what carries the effect of the identity into the manifestation, and what carries the
manifestation back to the identity? The relation is not automatic; it is not a mere logical
implication. It is a relation in which something passes—from the identity to its manifestation,
and from the manifestation to its source, and from one manifestation to another in the same
context. What is that something?
    The four-column framework has a name for it: the fluid element. The conveyor principle,
stated and proved in Chapter 8 (Principle 8.1), says that no explanation of how one fixed
element bears on another is complete unless it invokes a fluid element. The present part of the
book asks what the fluid element is, in its most general role. The answer is epistemic light.
    The question is not: what is light in the physicist’s sense? That is a question for empirical
inquiry, and the book does not address it. The question is: what is light in the framework’s
sense—the medium of legible relation between identity and manifestation? The answer must
15.3. Why Epistemic Light Is an Epistemic Problem                                               217


be a philosophical definition, not an empirical description. It must state what epistemic light
is, in a way that is precise enough to be argued about, and general enough to cover the role
the framework assigns to it.
     The chapter’s method is fourfold. First, it maps the human answers to the question “what
is light?” into structural patterns, and shows that the patterns are not accidental. Second, it
identifies the common presupposition that underlies all four patterns. Third, it shows that
the presupposition is the source of the tension among them—and that the tension is what
motivates the definition of epistemic light that the chapter proposes. Fourth, it states a
distinctness test that exhibits what difference the presence or absence of epistemic light makes.
Remark 15.3 (The Question Is About the Structural Place of Light). The question the
chapter asks is not: what is light in itself? The question is: what is the structural place of light
in the architecture of relation? The two questions are different, and the chapter is concerned
with the second. The first question is not answered in the present chapter; the second is. A
reader who takes the chapter’s question as a question about light in itself has misread it; a
reader who takes it as a question about the structural place of light has read it correctly.


15.3      Why Epistemic Light Is an Epistemic Problem
Before the map, a preliminary question: why is light an epistemic problem at all? Why not
leave the question to physics, which has studied light for centuries and has produced a body
of theory of extraordinary precision?
     The answer is not that physics is wrong. The answer is that physics answers a different
question. Physics asks how light behaves: how it propagates, how it interacts with matter,
how it is emitted and absorbed. It answers this question with mathematical precision, and
the answers are among the most successful in the history of science. But physics does not ask
what light is, in the sense the framework requires. It describes the behavior; it does not state
the medium of legibility.
     The distinction is not a criticism of physics. It is a distinction between two kinds of
question. The question “how does light behave?” is an empirical question; the question “what
is light, as the medium by which relation is rendered legible?” is an epistemic one. The two
are related, but neither is reducible to the other. A complete physics of light would not answer
the epistemic question, and a complete epistemology of light would not replace the physics.
The framework’s claim is that the epistemic question is real, and that it must be answered if
the conveyor principle is to have a determinate content.
Principle 15.1 (Epistemic Light Is an Epistemic Problem). (T) The question “what is
epistemic light?” cannot be answered by empirical methods alone, because epistemic light is
the condition of possibility of legible relation—and a condition of legibility is not itself an
object of empirical inquiry in the ordinary sense.
Argument for the Principle.       1. Empirical methods answer questions about objects of expe-
     rience.

   2. Epistemic light is the condition of possibility of legibility: without it, no relation is
      legible, and the legible is the paradigm of the empirically accessible.

   3. A condition of possibility is not itself an object of experience in the same sense. The eye
      sees by light, but does not see light (except by reflection or scattering, which is light as
      an object, not light as the condition).

   4. Hence the question “what is epistemic light?” cannot be answered by empirical methods
      alone.
218                                     Chapter 15. Epistemic Light: The Medium of Relation


    The argument is not a proof that epistemic light is unknowable. It is a proof that the
question of what epistemic light is cannot be settled by the methods that presuppose it. The
epistemic question remains, and the framework addresses it.

Remark 15.4 (The Question Is Not Merely Terminological). The epistemic question “what
is epistemic light?” is not a question about the essence of light in isolation. It is a question
about the structural place of light within the architecture of relation. The framework’s answer
will be a structural answer: epistemic light is the condition of possibility of legible relation,
not a thing that enters into relations. The structural answer is not a denial that light points
beyond itself. The condition of possibility of relation is a real condition, and its reality is the
reality of an order. The framework’s claim is that the structural place of light is real, invariant,
and describable; it does not claim that the structural place is the whole of what light is.

Remark 15.5 (The Diversity of Answers Is Not Accidental). The diversity of answers to
the question “what is light?”—across traditions, across centuries, across disciplines—is not
accidental. It is a sign that light is, before being a “thing” in the world, a structural condition
for understanding the world. When a condition is mistaken for a thing, the answers multiply,
because each answer captures an aspect of the condition while missing the others. The
multiplication is the symptom; the condition is the cause. The framework’s claim is that the
condition is real, and that its reality is the reality of an order that the categories of thinghood
presuppose but cannot exhaust.


15.4      Four Structural Patterns
The human answers to the question “what is light?” can be classified into four structural
patterns. The patterns are not historical; they are structural. In every period, all four are
present. The classification is offered as a map, not as a history.

Light as experience. The first pattern answers the question “how is seeing possible?” It
treats light as the condition of visual experience, and studies it through the phenomenology
of perception, the psychology of vision, or the analysis of what it is like to see. The pattern
is present in every period; in the modern period it appears in phenomenology and in the
psychology of perception.

Light as metaphor. The second pattern answers the question “what does it illuminate?”
It treats light as a figure for something else—for knowledge, for truth, for the good, for the
divine. The pattern is present in every period; it is the dominant pattern in mystical, poetic,
and theological traditions, and it recurs in philosophical traditions whenever light is used to
figure the intelligible. The word “metaphor” in the name of the pattern is a structural label; it
does not mean that the pattern is arbitrary or merely ornamental. The pattern treats light as
a figure for something that the categories of substance and relation cannot capture—a figure
that points, rather than a figure that substitutes.

Light as substance. The third pattern answers the question “what is it made of?” It treats
light as a thing with a nature of its own—a subtle substance, a stream of particles, a stuff of
which reality is made. The pattern is present in every period; it is the dominant pattern in
cosmological and physical traditions, and it recurs in metaphysical traditions whenever light is
treated as a constituent of being.

Light as relation. The fourth pattern answers the question “what does it mediate?” It
treats light as a medium, a carrier, a connection—something that holds between two things
15.5. The Common Presupposition                                                                  219


and makes their relation possible. The pattern is present in every period; it is the dominant
pattern in optical and physical traditions, and it recurs in philosophical traditions whenever
light is treated as a condition of relation rather than a thing in relation.

Pattern         Question                        Typical Examples
Experience      How is seeing possible?         Phenomenology of perception; psychology
                                                of vision
Metaphor        What does it illuminate?        Mystical, poetic, and theological traditions;
                                                figures of the intelligible
Substance       What is it made of?             Cosmological and physical traditions; meta-
                                                physical traditions that treat light as a con-
                                                stituent of being
Relation        What does it mediate?           Optical and physical traditions; philosophi-
                                                cal traditions that treat light as a condition
                                                of relation
    The table is structural, not historical. Its rows are not periods; they are patterns. A single
thinker may exemplify more than one pattern; a single period may exemplify all four. The
classification is not a claim about who held what, but about what kinds of answer have been
given.
Remark 15.6 (The Four Patterns Are Not a Historical Classification). The four patterns are
not a historical classification, and the distinction is worth marking. A historical classification
would place the experience pattern in the modern period, the substance pattern in the ancient,
the metaphor pattern in the medieval, and the relation pattern in the contemporary. The
framework’s classification does not do this. It holds that all four patterns are present in every
period, and that a single thinker may exemplify several of them. The claim is that the patterns
are structural positions, not temporal stages; the positions are what the question “what is
light?” can be answered from, and the answers have recurred across the centuries because the
question has a structure that the answers are trying to capture.
Remark 15.7 (The Metaphor Pattern Is Not Mere Metaphor). The second pattern is called
“metaphor” because the word is the least misleading structural label for it. But the label must
not be read as a claim that the pattern is ornamental or arbitrary. The traditions that speak
of light as a figure for the divine, for truth, or for the good are not engaged in a decorative
exercise; they are pointing to something that the categories of substance and relation cannot
capture. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not
exhausted by the figure. The word “figure” names the relation between the light of experience
and the light that the traditions call divine; it does not identify the created light with God.
The distinction is the distinction between the figure and the figured; it is kept throughout the
chapter.


15.5       The Common Presupposition
The four patterns differ in what they say about light. They do not differ in what they
presuppose about it. All four take light to be something that is in space and time—a wave
that propagates, a particle that moves, a field that oscillates, a condition that is realized in a
particular place and moment. This common presupposition is so deeply embedded that it is
rarely noticed. Yet it is the source of the tension among the patterns.
    The presupposition can be stated in a sentence. Light is a thing in space-time. The
sentence is not a definition; it is a diagnosis. It states what the four patterns share, and it
identifies what the next section puts in question.
220                                     Chapter 15. Epistemic Light: The Medium of Relation


     If light is a thing in space-time, it must be either a substance or an accident, either a
process or a relation. And each of these categories fails to capture the whole. If light is a
substance, its being a relation—its role as the conveyor of effect—is unexplained. If it is an
accident, its independent existence is unexplained. If it is a process, its stability is unexplained.
If it is a relation, its physical reality is unexplained. The deadlock is not an accident of the
four patterns; it is the consequence of their common presupposition.

Remark 15.8 (The Presupposition Is Not a Mistake). The presupposition is not a mistake.
It is the natural presupposition of any inquiry that treats light as an object of study. The
physicist who studies light as a wave or a particle is not wrong; the physicist is studying light
as an object, and an object is what the physicist’s methods presuppose. The framework’s
claim is not that the physicist is mistaken, but that the presupposition is not the only possible
one, and that an epistemic treatment of light may require a different starting point. The
present chapter proposes such a starting point.

Remark 15.9 (The Common Presupposition Is Not the Only One). The common presupposi-
tion is not the only presupposition possible. The traditions that speak of light as transcending
space and time are not committing an error; they are working with a different presupposition,
one on which light is not a thing among things but a condition that precedes the distinction
among things. The framework’s claim is not that the traditional presupposition is the correct
one, and it is not that the common presupposition is the correct one. It is that the tension
among the patterns is generated by the common presupposition, and that an epistemic treat-
ment of light may require examining whether the common presupposition is the only one
available.


15.6      What the Map Shows
Four observations follow from the map.

First observation: multiplicity is patterned. The four patterns recur across history,
not randomly, but structurally. The recurrence is not a sign of confusion; it is a sign that the
question has a structure that the answers are trying to capture.

Second observation: no pattern eliminates another. Each pattern captures an aspect
of light, and leaves another aside. The experience pattern captures light as the condition
of seeing; it leaves aside light as a thing studied. The metaphor pattern captures light as a
figure of the intelligible; it leaves aside light as a physical phenomenon. The substance pattern
captures light as a constituent of being; it leaves aside light as a relation. The relation pattern
captures light as a conveyor; it leaves aside light as a thing.

Third observation: no pattern is complete. All four are incomplete, and this very
incompleteness motivates the proposal of the next section. The proposal is not the elimination
of one pattern in favor of another; it is the change of level at which the question is asked.

Fourth observation: all patterns share a common presupposition. All four take light
to be something in space-time. The presupposition is the source of the tension among them,
and it is the presupposition that the proposal puts in question.
     The fourth observation is the most important. It shows that the four patterns, for all their
differences, share a common ground—and that the common ground is what must be examined
if the tension among the patterns is to be resolved. The next section examines it, and proposes
a definition of epistemic light that does not rest on it.
15.7. The Definition of Epistemic Light                                                         221


15.7     The Definition of Epistemic Light
The proposal is a definition. The definition does not rest on the common presupposition of
the four patterns; it changes the level at which the question is asked. The definition is stated
in terms of the function that epistemic light performs in the framework’s account of relation,
and it is distinguished from the neighboring notions with which it is easily confused.

Definition 15.1 (Epistemic Light). Epistemic light is the condition of possibility of legible
relation: the condition under which a relation between two terms is recognizable as a relation
between those terms, and the manifestation of an identity is recognizable as an appearance of
that identity. The definition states light’s function in legibility; it does not state what light is
in itself.

   The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.

The first part: epistemic light is a condition. It is not a term in the relation it makes
legible. It is what the relation is legible under. The word “condition” is structural: it names
the role, not a physical substance.

The second part: epistemic light is the condition of recognizability. Without it, a
relation could not be recognizable as a relation between these terms. The condition is not a
logical condition only, and it is not a physical condition only; it is the structural condition
under which a relation is recognizable.

The third part: epistemic light is defined by its function. The definition states what
epistemic light does: it makes relation legible. It does not state what epistemic light is made
of, whether it travels, or what its source is. Those questions are not the definition’s subject;
the definition’s subject is the function.
    The definition is stated at the strength of a proposal. It is offered as the framework’s
answer to the question of the fluid element in its most general role, and it is supported by the
argument of the next section and by the distinctness test of Section 15.9. The reader who
rejects the proposal is invited to propose a different answer to the question; the framework
does not claim that its answer is the only one.

15.7.1    What Epistemic Light Is Not
The definition is easily conflated with four neighboring notions, and the present subsection
distinguishes epistemic light from each.

Not the context. The context is the frame fixed by the question: what counts as fixed and
    fluid, and which dynamics governs. Epistemic light is not the frame; it is what makes
    a relation legible within the frame. A context can be fully specified, and the relation
    within it can still fail to be legible, if epistemic light is absent (the distinctness test of
    Section 15.9 exhibits exactly this case).

Not the relation. The relation is between two terms; epistemic light is the condition under
    which the relation is legible. The relation is what is legible; epistemic light is what makes
    it legible. The regress argument (Section 15.8) establishes that epistemic light is not a
    relation among relations.

Not the carrier. The carrier is the entity that conveys effect between fixed elements (the
    fluid element of Chapter 6). Epistemic light is the condition under which the carrier’s
    effect is legible as a conveying of effect. A carrier can be present, and the effect can still
222                                     Chapter 15. Epistemic Light: The Medium of Relation


      fail to be legible, if epistemic light is absent. The carrier is the means; epistemic light is
      the condition of legibility of the means.

Not the cognitive process. The cognitive process is the activity by which a subject recon-
    structs a signature from manifestations (Chapter 12). Epistemic light is not the activity;
    it is the condition under which the activity’s object is legible. A cognitive process can
    be carried out, and its object can still fail to be legible, if epistemic light is absent.

    The four distinctions are the framework’s way of keeping the definition precise. Epistemic
light is not the context, not the relation, not the carrier, and not the cognitive process; it is
the condition under which a relation, a carrier, and a process are legible.
Remark 15.10 (The Four Distinctions Are Not Verbal). The four distinctions are not verbal,
and the distinctness test of Section 15.9 shows why. In the test’s two cases, the context,
the relation, the carrier, and the cognitive process are held constant, and only the state of
epistemic light differs. The difference in legibility that results is the work of epistemic light,
and the sameness of the other four notions excludes their being the source of the difference. A
reader who treats the distinctions as verbal is invited to run the test on a case; a reader who
has run the test has seen the distinctions at work.
Remark 15.11 (The Definition Is Epistemic, Not a Doctrine of What Is). The definition
states what epistemic light is for the purpose of explanation: it is the condition of possibility
of legible relation. It does not state what light is in itself. The distinction between the
analytical role and the claim about what is was stated in Chapter 5 (Principle 5.1), and it
is observed here. The definition is one of the six operationalizations of that distinction: the
distinction between the condition of legibility and the things related is the analytical form of
the distinction between the structure of an explanation and the order of dependence that the
explanation represents. A reader who takes the definition as a claim about what light is in
itself has misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim about the condition of legible relation
has read it correctly.
Remark 15.12 (The Definition Is Not a Denial of Physics). The definition does not deny that
physics studies light, or that the physical description of light is a real description at its own
level. It claims that the physical description and the epistemic description answer different
questions, and that both can be true. The distinction is the distinction between two levels of
description, not the distinction between the real and the unreal.
Remark 15.13 (The Definition and the Conveyor and Non-Sequential Principles). The
definition specifies what the fluid element is, in its most general role. It presupposes the
conveyor principle of Chapter 8 (Principle 8.1): the conveyor principle established that some
fluid element is necessary for any explanation of how one fixed element bears on another; the
present definition specifies what that element is. The definition also presupposes the non-
sequential connectivity of Chapter 9 (Principle 9.1): the non-sequential principle established
that the carrier need not be a sequence of carriers; the present definition specifies the carrier
as the condition of legibility, which may connect directly. The three chapters are the analytical
structure of the fluid element, stated from three angles: necessity (Chapter 8), indifference to
the route (Chapter 9), and the specific function (the present chapter).


15.8     The Regress Argument
The definition is not arbitrary. It is forced by a regress argument, and the regress argument is
the chapter’s principal contribution to the treatment of the fluid element. The argument’s
premise—that every legible relation requires a condition of legibility—is stated and defended
independently in the present section, and the cases that seem to contradict it are examined.
15.8. The Regress Argument                                                                       223


15.8.1     The Premise
Definition 15.2 (The Legibility Premise). (T) Every legible relation requires a condition
of legibility: a condition that is not itself one of the terms of the relation, and not itself a
relation among relations, and under which the relation is recognizable as a relation between
these terms.
    The premise is (T): it is argued, and the argument is given below. The premise is not a
definition of legibility; it is a structural claim about what legibility requires. Its defense has
two parts: a positive argument, and a review of the cases that seem to contradict it.

The positive argument. A relation is legible when it can be read off the terms it relates.
But reading off is not automatic: the terms must be presented in a way that makes the relation
recognizable. The presentation is not itself one of the terms (the terms are what is related);
it is not itself the relation (the relation is what is presented); and it is not a further relation
among relations (a further relation would need its own presentation, and the regress would
begin). The presentation is therefore a condition of the relation’s recognizability, distinct from
the terms and from the relation. The condition is what the present chapter calls epistemic
light.

The cases that seem to contradict the premise. Three cases are worth examining.
     First case: logical implication. The relation between the premises and the conclusion of a
valid argument is legible without any sensory medium. The relation is formal, and its legibility
is the legibility of a formal structure.
     The framework’s response. The logical relation is legible under a condition: the condition is
the framework of logical form, which is not itself one of the premises, not itself the conclusion,
and not itself a further relation among relations. The condition is epistemic light in its formal
mode: it is the condition under which the relation between the premises and the conclusion
is recognizable as a relation of implication. The case does not contradict the premise; it
illustrates the premise at a different level of the medium.
     Second case: direct perception. In ordinary perception, the relation between an object and
one’s perception of it seems legible without any medium beyond the perception itself. The
relation is immediate.
     The framework’s response. The immediate perception is legible under a condition: the
condition is the epistemic light of the perceptual context, which is not itself the object, not
itself the perception, and not itself a further relation among relations. The condition is what
the framework calls epistemic light in its perceptual mode. The case does not contradict the
premise; it illustrates the premise in a mode where the condition is easily overlooked because
it is universal in the context.
     Third case: self-relation. A subject’s relation to itself (its self-awareness) seems legible
without any medium beyond the self-relation itself. The relation is immediate.
     The framework’s response. The self-relation is legible under a condition: the condition is
the epistemic light of the self’s context, which is not itself the self, not itself the self-relation,
and not itself a further relation among relations. The condition is what the framework calls
epistemic light in its reflexive mode. The case does not contradict the premise; it illustrates
the premise in a mode where the condition is most easily missed, because the self-relation
appears to be its own condition.
Remark 15.14 (The Three Cases Illustrate the Premise, Not Refute It). The three cases
are the most plausible candidates for a relation that is legible without a condition. In each
case, the framework’s response is that the relation is legible under a condition that is distinct
from the terms and from the relation, and that the condition is epistemic light in a mode
appropriate to the case. The cases do not refute the premise; they illustrate it in the modes
224                                     Chapter 15. Epistemic Light: The Medium of Relation


where the condition is most easily overlooked. A reader who accepts the premise in these cases
has accepted the premise in the cases that are most difficult for it; a reader who rejects the
premise in these cases has located the place where the argument must be pressed.
Remark 15.15 (The Premise Is Relative to the Meaning of “Legible”). The premise depends
on the meaning of “legible” that the framework employs. “Legible” names the recognizability
of a relation as a relation between these terms. A reader who accepts the meaning accepts the
premise; a reader who denies it denies the premise, and the framework does not claim more
than the meaning delivers. The framework states the meaning so that the reader can assess
the premise; it does not claim that the meaning is the only possible one.

15.8.2    The Argument
Principle 15.2 (Epistemic Light as the Condition of Possibility of Legible Relation). (T)
Epistemic light is not a relation—it is the condition of possibility of legible relation. Without
epistemic light, no relation is legible. But epistemic light itself is not legible in the same
sense—it is legibility-making.
Argument for the Principle.      1. Every relation is between two terms.

   2. By the legibility premise (Definition 15.2), for a relation to be legible—for it to be
      recognizable as a relation between these terms—there must be a condition of legibility
      distinct from the terms and from the relation.

   3. This condition cannot itself be a relation. If it were, it would need another condition of
      legibility to connect it to the terms it relates, and that condition would need another,
      and so on without end. This is a regress.

   4. So there must be a condition that comes before relation—its condition of possibility.

   5. This condition is what we call epistemic light.


   The argument is a reductio of the view that epistemic light is a relation. If epistemic light
were a relation, the regress would be unavoidable. The only way to avoid the regress is to hold
that epistemic light is the condition of possibility of relation, not a relation among relations.
Remark 15.16 (What “Legible” Means Here). “Legible” in this chapter is a structural term.
It names the recognizability of a relation as a relation between these terms. A relation is legible
when it can be read off the terms it relates—when the terms, in their relation, are recognizable
as related. The term is not a metaphor for psychological comprehension; it is a structural
condition. Epistemic light is what makes a relation legible, in this sense, and epistemic light
itself is not legible in the same sense, because it is what makes legibility possible.
Remark 15.17 (The Regress Argument Is Not a Skeptical Argument). The regress argument
is not a skeptical argument, and the distinction is worth marking. A skeptical argument
would conclude that no relation is legible, because the regress cannot be stopped. The present
argument concludes the opposite: that relations are legible, and that their legibility requires a
condition of possibility that is not itself a relation. The regress is stopped, not by finding a
first relation, but by recognizing that the condition of possibility of relation is not a relation.
The argument’s conclusion is positive, not negative; it is that epistemic light is real, not that
nothing is.
Remark 15.18 (The Argument Establishes the Function, Not the Nature). The argument
establishes that epistemic light cannot be a relation among relations, and that it must be
the condition of possibility of legible relation. It does not establish what epistemic light is
15.9. The Distinctness Test for Epistemic Light                                                 225


in itself; it establishes its function in the framework’s account of relation. The distinction is
the distinction between the function and the nature of the medium. The framework’s claim is
about the function; the question of the nature of the medium is not addressed in the present
chapter.


15.9      The Distinctness Test for Epistemic Light
The regress argument establishes the structural place of epistemic light—that it is the condition
of possibility of legible relation, not a relation among relations. It does not, by itself, show
that epistemic light does any work that the other columns do not already do. The present
section states the distinctness test that is meant to show this, and it states what the test
would have to exhibit.

15.9.1    The Test Stated
The test proceeds by comparing two cases. The two cases are alike in their fixed elements,
in their context, in their governing dynamics, in their carrier, and in their cognitive process.
They differ only in the state of epistemic light. If the two cases differ in legibility—in what
can be read off the relation—the difference must be attributed to epistemic light, because
the other notions are held constant. If the two cases do not differ in legibility, epistemic light
does no work that the other notions do not already do, and the definition’s claim is restricted
accordingly.

Definition 15.3 (The Distinctness Test for Epistemic Light). (A) Let C1 and C2 be two cases
such that:

  (i) the fixed elements of C1 and C2 are the same;

 (ii) the receiving cognitive contexts of C1 and C2 are the same;

 (iii) the governing dynamics of C1 and C2 are the same;

 (iv) the carrier of C1 and C2 is the same;

 (v) the cognitive process of C1 and C2 is the same;

 (vi) the state of epistemic light in C1 differs from the state of epistemic light in C2 .

The cases are a distinctness test when the legibility of the relation in C1 differs from the
legibility of the relation in C2 . The difference, if it occurs, is the work of epistemic light; the
sameness of the other notions excludes their being the source of the difference.

15.9.2    Three Cases
The test is applied to three cases, and the cases are stated below. The first is the case of the
printed page; the second and third are cases from other domains, chosen to show that the test
is not confined to vision.

Case 1: The same text, in the dark and in the light. A reader holds a printed page
whose text she has never seen. The fixed elements are the printed characters (their shapes,
their order, the relations among them). The context is the reader’s question (“what does the
page say?”), the means (her eyes, her memory, her language), and the scale (the page, the
room). The governing dynamics are the rules of reading: the grammar, the conventions of the
script, the norms of interpretation. The carrier is the light reflected from the page to the eye.
The cognitive process is the reader’s act of reading.
226                                     Chapter 15. Epistemic Light: The Medium of Relation


    Case 1a: the room is dark. The state of epistemic light is absent. The fixed elements, the
context, the dynamics, the carrier, and the cognitive process are all present, but the relation
between the characters and the reader’s cognition is not legible. The reader cannot read the
page. Measurable result: the reader produces zero words from the page.
    Case 1b: the room is lit. The state of epistemic light is present. The fixed elements, the
context, the dynamics, the carrier, and the cognitive process are the same. The relation is
legible. The reader reads the page. Measurable result: the reader produces the words of the
page.
    The difference in measurable result (zero words vs. the words of the page) is the work of
epistemic light, and it is not attributable to the other notions, which are held constant.


Case 2: The same argument, with and without the inferential medium. A logician
considers a valid argument, whose premises and conclusion are fully specified. The fixed
elements are the premises and the conclusion (their content, their form, their relations). The
context is the logician’s question (“does the conclusion follow?”), the means (the logician’s
logical competence), and the scale (the argument as a whole). The governing dynamics are the
rules of inference. The carrier is the formal structure of the argument. The cognitive process
is the logician’s act of inference.
     Case 2a: the inferential medium is absent. The logician has the premises and the con-
clusion, but the inferential medium (the framework of logical form under which the relation
of implication is legible) is absent. The relation is not legible as a relation of implication.
Measurable result: the logician cannot say whether the conclusion follows.
     Case 2b: the inferential medium is present. The inferential medium is present. The relation
is legible. Measurable result: the logician says that the conclusion follows (and can give the
inference).
     The difference in measurable result (cannot say vs. can say) is the work of epistemic light
in its formal mode.


Case 3: The same action, with and without the practical medium. A subject
considers an action she is about to take. The fixed elements are the action, the circumstances,
and the subject (their content and relations). The context is the subject’s question (“what
should I do?”), the means (her practical competence), and the scale (the situation). The
governing dynamics are the norms of practical reason. The carrier is the practical deliberation.
The cognitive process is the subject’s act of deliberation.
    Case 3a: the practical medium is absent. The subject has the action, the circumstances,
and the deliberation, but the practical medium (the condition under which the action is legible
as the action the situation calls for) is absent. The relation is not legible as a relation of
practical requirement. Measurable result: the subject cannot say what she should do.
    Case 3b: the practical medium is present. The practical medium is present. The relation is
legible. Measurable result: the subject says what she should do (and can give the reason).
    The difference in measurable result (cannot say vs. can say) is the work of epistemic light
in its practical mode.

Remark 15.19 (The Three Cases and the Modes of Epistemic Light). The three cases exhibit
the same structure in three modes. In each case, the fixed elements, the context, the dynamics,
the carrier, and the cognitive process are held constant; only the state of epistemic light differs;
and the difference in legibility is measurable. The modes are different (perceptual, formal,
practical), and the framework does not claim that the modes are reducible to one another. The
claim is that in each mode, epistemic light does work that the other notions do not already do.
15.10. The Medium Is Not a Thing Among Things                                                    227


15.9.3     What the Test Establishes
The test establishes that epistemic light does work that the other notions do not already
do: it makes a relation legible that would not be legible without it, and the legibility cannot
be attributed to the fixed elements, the context, the dynamics, the carrier, or the cognitive
process. The work is not a mysterious addition; it is the specific work of the condition of
legibility, as the regress argument (Section 15.8) established.
    The test does not establish the full content of the definition of epistemic light. It establishes
that the definition is not idle: the term “epistemic light” names a condition that does work in
the framework’s account of relation, and the work cannot be done by the other notions. The
full content of the definition is the subject of Chapters 16 and 17, where light is sharpened as
an active structure and as an encompassing medium.

Remark 15.20 (The Test Is Measurable, Not Merely Illustrative). The test is measurable,
not merely illustrative, and the distinction is worth marking. In each case, the difference in
legibility is stated as a difference in a measurable result: the words produced, the inference
given, the reason given. The measurability is the test’s way of excluding the possibility that
the difference is merely apparent. A reader who wishes to run the test can do so, and the
result is a difference that can be observed, not a difference that is merely asserted.

Remark 15.21 (What the Test Would Not Show). The test would not show that epistemic
light is a substance, a relation, or any other category of thing. The test is a distinctness test:
it shows that the term is not idle, not what kind of thing the term names. The framework’s
claim is that the term names a condition of possibility, and the distinctness test is consistent
with that claim; it would also be consistent with the claim that the term names a substance,
if a substance could do the work the test exhibits. The framework’s commitment to the first
claim is the definition of Section 15.7, not the distinctness test.

Remark 15.22 (The Test and the Restriction of the Claim). If the test failed—if no two cases
could be exhibited that differ only in the state of epistemic light and differ in legibility—the
definition’s claim would be restricted. The restriction would be to the claim that epistemic
light is a name for the condition of legibility, not a distinct condition over and above the
other notions. The framework does not claim that the test cannot fail; it claims that the test
succeeds in the cases examined, and it invites the reader to produce a case in which it does
not.


15.10      The Medium Is Not a Thing Among Things
The regress argument establishes that epistemic light is the condition of possibility of legible
relation. The present section draws the consequence: the medium is not a thing among things.


First consequence: epistemic light is not a term of the relation. It is the medium of
relation, not one of the terms related. When we say that epistemic light connects an identity
and its manifestation, we do not mean that epistemic light is a third term alongside the
identity and the manifestation; we mean that epistemic light is the condition under which the
connection is legible. The distinction is the distinction between being in a relation and being
the relation’s condition of legibility.


Second consequence: epistemic light is not a relation among relations. The regress
argument establishes this. If epistemic light were a relation, the regress would be unavoidable,
and no relation would be legible.
228                                     Chapter 15. Epistemic Light: The Medium of Relation


Third consequence: epistemic light is not a thing. It is not a substance, not an
accident, not a process. The four patterns of Section 15.4 treat light as one of these, and the
deadlock of the patterns is the consequence of so treating it. The framework’s proposal is
that epistemic light is of a different order: it is the condition of legibility, not a thing whose
legibility is at issue.

Remark 15.23 (The Medium Is the Framework’s Answer to the Deadlock). The four patterns
of Section 15.4 are in deadlock because each treats light as a thing among things, and each
captures an aspect while missing another. The framework’s proposal is that the deadlock is
dissolved by changing the level at which the question is asked: not “what kind of thing is
light?” but “what kind of being is light, such that the categories of thinghood are not adequate
to it?”. The proposal’s answer is that epistemic light is the condition of legible relation. The
answer is not a fifth kind of thing; it is the condition of possibility of the distinction among
kinds of things.

Remark 15.24 (The Medium and the Categories). The framework’s claim is that the categories
of substance, accident, process, and relation are adequate for things among things, but not for
the condition through which things among things are related. The condition is not a thing
among things, and the categories do not apply to it without remainder. The claim is not that
the categories are inadequate in general; it is that they are inadequate for the condition of
legibility. The next chapter sharpens the point by distinguishing the medium’s function (active
making-legible) from the categories’ structure, and by stating what the medium is for.

Remark 15.25 (The Medium Is Not the Relation). The medium is not the relation, and
the distinction is worth marking. The relation between an identity and its manifestation is a
relation between two terms; the medium is what makes the relation legible. The relation is
between the terms; the medium is the condition under which the relation can be read off the
terms. The distinction is the distinction between the relation and its condition of legibility;
the framework keeps it throughout, and the present chapter’s definition is about the condition,
not the relation.


15.11      The Epistemic Function of Epistemic Light
The chapter’s positive contribution is the epistemic function of epistemic light in the framework’s
model of relation. The present section consolidates that function, so that the reader knows
what epistemic light does, not only what it is defined to be.


First function: making relation legible. Epistemic light makes a relation legible as a
relation between these terms. Without it, the terms can be present, the relation can hold, and
the relation is not legible. The function is exhibited by the distinctness test (Section 15.9):
the same terms, the same context, the same dynamics, the same carrier, the same cognitive
process, and the relation is legible in one case and not in the other, and the difference is the
work of epistemic light.


Second function: making manifestation recognizable as appearance. Epistemic
light makes a manifestation recognizable as an appearance of its source. Without it, the
manifestation can be present, and it is not recognizable as an appearance of the identity that
manifests itself in it. The function is the counterpart, at the level of manifestation, of the first
function at the level of relation.
15.11. The Epistemic Function of Epistemic Light                                             229


Third function: providing the condition of assessment. The criteria of adequacy of a
pseudo-identity (Chapter 23) presuppose that the manifestation is legible as an appearance of
its source. Without epistemic light, the manifestation is present, and the criteria cannot be
applied, because there is nothing recognizable to assess. Epistemic light is the condition under
which the assessment of a pseudo-identity is possible.




Fourth function: structuring the epistemic economy. The cost of cognition (Chap-
ter 39) and the cognitive sediment (Chapter 40) presuppose that the cognitive process operates
on a legible object. The legibility is the work of epistemic light; the economy of cognition is
the economy of a process that operates under the condition of legibility. Epistemic light is the
condition under which the epistemic economy is intelligible.


    The four functions are not four separate claims; they are four aspects of the single function
of epistemic light: making legible. The first names the function at the level of relation; the
second at the level of manifestation; the third at the level of assessment; the fourth at the
level of the economy of cognition. The four together state the place of epistemic light in the
framework’s model.




Remark 15.26 (The Function Is the Definition’s Content). The four functions are the defini-
tion’s content, stated at the level of what epistemic light does. The definition (Definition 15.1)
states what epistemic light is: the condition of possibility of legible relation. The four func-
tions state what the condition does: it makes relations legible, manifestations recognizable,
assessment possible, and the economy of cognition intelligible. The definition and the functions
are the same claim, stated at two levels of description; the functions do not add a new claim,
they state the definition’s content.




Remark 15.27 (The Function Is Not a Denial of What Light Is in Itself). The function is
not a denial of what light is in itself. The definition states what epistemic light does in the
framework’s model; it does not state what light is in itself. The distinction is the distinction
between the function and the nature of the medium. A reader who takes the definition as a
claim about what light is in itself has misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim about the
function has read it correctly.

A Question for Reflection
If epistemic light is the condition of possibility of legible relation, can we speak of a “relation
to epistemic light”—or is that a category mistake? What would it mean to be related to what
makes relation possible? And if the word “light” is used in both a structural sense and a
traditional sense, does the question of their relation belong to epistemology, or to another
inquiry?
     And consider the scene that opened the chapter—the table in the dark and the table in
the light. The table does not change; what changes is whether the table is legible. Is the light
that makes the table legible a thing among things, or is it the condition under which the table
is legible? If it is the condition, what does that tell you about the difference between the light
of physics and epistemic light? If it is a thing, what does that tell you about the difference
between the four patterns and the framework’s proposal? And consider the distinctness test
of Section 15.9: can you give a further case in which the fixed elements, the context, the
dynamics, the carrier, and the cognitive process are held constant, and the presence or absence
of epistemic light makes a measurable difference in legibility? If you can, the test is confirmed;
if you cannot, the framework’s claim is restricted to the cases it examines. Finally, consider the
four epistemic functions of Section 15.11: can you show, for an identity of your own choosing,
how the four functions operate together in the reconstruction of that identity? A reader who
can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has
the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter sharpens the definition. If epistemic light is the condition of legible relation, it
cannot “move” in the ordinary sense, because motion requires time, and time is a category of the
related. The next chapter argues that epistemic light does not travel, but is an active structure
of legibility. The chapter after that states the encompassment in light, and the consequence
that complete knowledge of epistemic light is impossible.
