Chapter 16

Epistemic Light as Active Structure

Scope
This chapter sharpens the definition of the previous chapter. If epistemic light is the medium
of legible relation, and if a medium is the condition of possibility of a relation rather than a
term in it, then epistemic light cannot “move” in the ordinary sense, because motion requires
time, and time is a category of the related. The chapter defines the active structure of legibility
and states its process model (Section ??), argues that epistemic light is such a structure,
proves that epistemic light does not travel, distinguishes two senses of “fluidity,” re-reads the
three directions of the structure of legibility in a comparison table (Section 16.9), and states a
second distinctness test (Section 16.10) for the active-structure claim.
    The chapter is the fourth of the four chapters that articulate the fluid element from different
angles: Chapter 8 established the necessity of some fluid element; Chapter 9 established that
the conveyor principle is indifferent to the route; Chapter 15 specified the medium as epistemic
light; the present chapter states the structure of the medium, as active structure rather than
traveler. The “activation” language that the chapter uses is the same language that Chapter 40
develops into the hard/soft distinction, the action chain, and the crystallization of effect; the
present chapter states the structure, and Chapter 40 states what the structure produces.
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “structure,” “edge,” “activation,”
“direction,” “descent,” or “travel,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter. The chapter makes no claim about what epistemic light is in itself;
the claims of the chapter are claims about the structure of the medium.


16.1      A Scene: The Flashlight and the Shadow
Consider a flashlight and a shadow. In a dark room, you switch on the flashlight, and a circle
of light appears on the wall. Move the flashlight slowly, and the circle moves across the wall.
Move it quickly, and the circle moves quickly. What moves?
     The shadow moves; the circle of illumination moves. But does the light move? We say
“the light moves across the wall,” and the sentence seems obvious. But consider: the light on
the wall at one moment and the light on the wall at the next moment are not the same light.
They are successive patterns of illumination, each produced by the flashlight’s relation to the
wall at a given moment. Nothing has traveled from one part of the wall to another; what has
changed is the relation between the flashlight and the wall, and the pattern of illumination
reflects that change.
     The scene can be described in two ways. In the first, the light travels: it leaves the flashlight,
crosses the room, and lands on the wall. In the second, the light does not travel: the flashlight’s
relation to the wall activates a pattern of illumination, and moving the flashlight deactivates
one pattern and activates another. The two descriptions agree on what happens—the circle of
234                                            Chapter 16. Epistemic Light as Active Structure


light moves—and disagree on what “the light” is doing. In the first, the light is a traveler. In
the second, the light is a structure of illumination, whose edges are activated and deactivated
according to the flashlight’s position.
    The scene poses a question. Which description is appropriate to what epistemic light is—the
medium of legible relation? The ordinary language of light’s travel is so deeply embedded that
the second description sounds strange. But the strange description may be the more accurate
one, and the ordinary one may be a projection of a category that does not apply. The present
chapter argues that the second description is the correct one for epistemic light—not because
the first is false of light as physics studies it, but because the first imports a category (motion)
that does not apply to the medium of legibility.
Remark 16.1 (The Scene Shows Two Descriptions of One Event). The scene is not a puzzle
about the flashlight; it is a display of two descriptions of the same event. The circle of light
moves; the two descriptions agree on this. What they disagree on is what the light is doing.
In the first description, the light is a thing that travels from the flashlight to the wall; in the
second, the light is a structure whose edges are activated and deactivated. The framework’s
claim is that the second description is the correct one for epistemic light, because the first
imports the category of motion, which does not apply to the medium of legibility.
Remark 16.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the chapter’s claim; it makes the claim intelligible
before it is stated. The argument is given in Section 16.5, and the scene carries no weight in it.
The reader who finds the second description strange is invited to follow the argument; the
reader who finds it natural is invited to see whether the argument supports it.


16.2     The Question
The previous chapter defined epistemic light as the medium of legible relation: the condition
of possibility of a relation’s being legible as a relation between these terms. The definition was
given, and the regress argument that supports it was given. The definition is now in place.
    The present chapter asks a question that the definition raises. If epistemic light is the
medium of legibility, and if a medium is the condition of possibility of a relation rather than a
term in it, then how does the medium relate to the change that is observed when a relation
changes? The ordinary language of light’s travel is the language of motion—of a thing that
moves from one place to another. If epistemic light moves, it is subject to time, and time is a
category of the related. If epistemic light is subject to time, it is not the medium of legibility
but a thing among things, and the previous chapter’s definition is in question.
    The question is therefore not a small one. It is the question of whether the definition
of the previous chapter can survive the most obvious feature of light: that the pattern of
illumination changes, and that the change is naturally described as the light’s moving. The
chapter’s answer is that it can, and that the change is not what it seems. Epistemic light does
not travel; what changes is the pattern of legibility, and the pattern is not the medium. The
medium is the structure that makes the pattern possible; the structure does not move; its
edges activate.
    The chapter’s method is fourfold. First, it exhibits the problem: the apparent conflict
between the fluidity of the medium and its stability. Second, it defines the active structure of
legibility and states its process model. Third, it proves that epistemic light does not travel,
distinguishes two senses of “fluidity,” and re-reads the three directions of the structure of
legibility. Fourth, it states a distinctness test for the active-structure claim, exhibiting what
difference the activations make.
Remark 16.3 (The Question Is About the Compatibility of Two Requirements). The question
is not about whether epistemic light is fluid; the framework has already claimed that it is.
16.3. The Problem: Fluidity and Motion                                                              235


The question is about whether the fluidity of epistemic light is compatible with its being the
medium of legibility. The two requirements seem to conflict: fluidity suggests motion, and
motion suggests time; but the medium of legibility cannot be subject to time, because time
is a category of the related. The chapter’s task is to show that the two requirements are
compatible, by distinguishing the sense of “fluidity” that applies to epistemic light from the
sense that does not.


16.3      The Problem: Fluidity and Motion
The four-column framework defines the fluid element as the entity that conveys effect. The
conveyor principle, proved in Chapter 8, says that no explanation of how one fixed element
bears on another is complete without a fluid element. Epistemic light, in the framework’s
sense, is the fluid element: it is what conveys effect between identity and manifestation.
    But the word “fluid” is usually understood as “flowing” and “in motion.” A fluid is what
flows; it is what moves from one place to another. If epistemic light is fluid in this sense, it
flows; if it flows, it moves; if it moves, it travels; and if it travels, it contains time within itself.
    The argument can be stated compactly:

   1. If epistemic light moves, it travels.

   2. If epistemic light travels, time is part of what epistemic light is.

   3. But epistemic light is the medium of legibility, and time is a category of the related.

   4. Therefore epistemic light cannot move in the sense that requires time.

    The conclusion is not that epistemic light is motionless in the way a stone is motionless. A
stone is motionless because it is at rest; its rest is defined against motion. Epistemic light is
not at rest; it is not in the category of things that can be at rest or in motion. The category
of motion does not apply to it. To say that epistemic light does not travel is not to say that it
is stationary; it is to say that the vocabulary of station and motion is not the vocabulary in
which epistemic light is to be described.
    The problem, then, is this. The framework needs epistemic light to be the fluid element—
the conveyor of effect. But if fluidity means motion, epistemic light cannot be the fluid element
without being subject to time, and epistemic light cannot be subject to time without ceasing
to be the medium of legibility. The framework is caught between two requirements: epistemic
light must be fluid, and epistemic light must be the medium of legibility. The next section
proposes a solution that satisfies both.
Remark 16.4 (The Problem Is Not Merely Terminological). The problem is not merely a
matter of words. One might think that the framework could simply redefine “fluid” to mean
“conveying” rather than “flowing,” and the problem would disappear. But the redefinition
would be empty unless it could be applied. What does it mean for epistemic light to convey
without flowing? What kind of structure is a structure of conveyance that does not move?
The next section answers these questions by defining the structure and its process model. The
definition is what makes the redefinition substantive.
Remark 16.5 (The Problem and the Generic Character of the Fluid Element). The problem
arises because the fluid element, as Chapter 6 defines it, is a generic role: it is the role of
conveying effect, not a particular entity that plays the role. Because the role is generic, the
question of what kind of structure can play it is open; the present chapter answers that the
structure is the active structure of legibility. The generic character of the role is what makes
the present chapter’s answer possible: if the role were tied to a particular kind of entity, the
question of the structure of the entity would be a question of physics, not of epistemology.
236                                            Chapter 16. Epistemic Light as Active Structure


16.4     The Solution: Active Structure of Legibility
The framework’s solution is to distinguish two things that are easily run together: a structure
that moves, and a structure whose edges are activated. Epistemic light is the second kind of
structure, not the first.
Definition 16.1 (Active Structure of Legibility). (A) An active structure of legibility is a
structure that:
 (a) always is—not that it is built and then moves;

 (b) is a structure of connection—not a path of connection;

 (c) has edges that are activated or deactivated according to rules;

 (d) itself does not move—its connections change.
     The definition is stated as a commitment ((A)). It is not derived from anything more basic;
it is the framework’s proposal for the kind of structure that epistemic light is. The definition
is supported by its fruitfulness in what follows: if epistemic light is an active structure of
legibility, then the three directions of the structure (descending, ascending, reflective) can be
re-read as three directions of one structure, the problem of fluidity versus motion is solved,
the definition of the previous chapter is preserved, and the distinctness test of Section 16.10
exhibits the specific work the activations do.
     The metaphor of the scaffold is used for illustration, but the formal term is “active structure
of legibility.” The scaffold suggests a pre-existing framework of connection, not a physical
object located in space. To avoid spatial baggage, the formal term is preferred, and the
metaphor is retained only for illustration.
Remark 16.6 (The Scaffold Metaphor). The word “scaffold” suggests a structure that is built
and then used. But the definition says the structure “always is,” not that it is built. The
scaffold metaphor is meant to evoke the idea of a pre-existing framework of connection; it is
not meant to suggest a construction process. The reader who finds the metaphor misleading
should prefer the formal term.
Remark 16.7 (The Definition Is Not a Description of a Thing). The definition does not
describe a thing; it describes a structure. The distinction is the distinction between a thing
and the structure of a thing. The active structure of legibility is not a thing; it is the structure
of connection that makes legibility possible.

16.4.1    The Process Model of the Active Structure
The definition states what the active structure is; the process model states how it works. The
model has four elements: an input, a direction, an effect, and an output. Each element is
stated with its role in the activation.
Definition 16.2 (The Process Model of the Active Structure). (A) An activation of the active
structure of legibility has four elements:
  (i) Input: the cognitive context’s question and the fixed elements the question makes salient.
      The input is what the activation is an activation of.

 (ii) Direction: the edge of the structure that is activated—descending, ascending, or reflective.
      The direction is what the activation connects.

 (iii) Effect: the change in legibility that the activation produces—what becomes readable
       that was not readable before, or what becomes readable through a different path.
16.4. The Solution: Active Structure of Legibility                                             237


 (iv) Output: the legible relation that results, as the receiving cognitive context can recognize
      it. The output is what the activation leaves as its result.
    The model is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s way of decomposing an activation.
Its justification is its use in the analysis of cases; its cost is that a given activation may not
exhibit all four elements distinctly.

    The table is the operational form of the process model. It states the four elements and
how each is recognized in a given case. A reader who has followed the table has the model in
a form that can be applied to a case.
Remark 16.8 (The Process Model Is Not a Temporal Process). The process model is not
a temporal process, and the distinction is worth marking. The model’s four elements are
structural positions in an activation, not stages in a sequence that unfolds in time. The
activation is not “first the input, then the direction, then the effect, then the output”; the
activation is a single structure whose four elements are analytically distinguished. The reader
who reads the model as a temporal sequence has misread it; the reader who reads it as a
structural decomposition of the activation has read it correctly.
Remark 16.9 (The Process Model and the Two-Sided Model of Chapter 13). The process
model is related to the two-sided model of manifestation (Chapter 13, Definition 13.3). The two-
sided model decomposes a manifestation into source features, contextual features, transmission
features, and result features; the process model decomposes an activation of epistemic light into
input, direction, effect, and output. The two models are not the same: the two-sided model
concerns the manifestation, and the process model concerns the activation of the medium by
which the manifestation is legible. The two models are complementary: a manifestation is
legible under an activation, and the activation has the structure the process model states.
Principle 16.1 (Epistemic Light Is an Active Structure). (E) Epistemic light is an active
structure of legibility—not a traveler. It does not move; the edges of the structure, according
to the rules of the receiving cognitive context, connect different nodes to one another.
    The principle is the framework’s identification of epistemic light with the structure of the
definition. It is not derived from the definition; it is the framework’s claim that epistemic light
is what the definition describes. The principle is supported by the same considerations as the
definition: if epistemic light is an active structure of legibility, the problem of fluidity versus
motion is solved, the definition of the previous chapter is preserved, and the distinctness test
succeeds.
238                                            Chapter 16. Epistemic Light as Active Structure


Remark 16.10 (The Structure and the Operationalization of Chapter 5). The identification
of epistemic light with an active structure is one of the six operationalizations of the distinction
that Chapter 5 states between the order of reconstruction and the order of explanatory
dependence: the distinction between the medium and the things related is the analytical form
of the distinction between the structure of an explanation and the order of dependence that
the explanation represents. The present chapter adds a further analytical distinction within
the medium: the distinction between the structure and its activations. The structure is what
it is; the activations are what change. The distinction is analytical, not a claim about two
kinds of entity.

Remark 16.11 (What “Stability” Means Here). The principle says that epistemic light does
not move. It does not say that epistemic light is static in the way a stone is static. The
stability of epistemic light is the stability of a structure: the structure is what it is, and its
edges activate according to rules that are themselves stable. The rules do not change; the
activations change. The stability is in the structure and the rules, not in the activations.

Remark 16.12 (The Structure Is Not the Pattern). The structure is not the pattern, and
the distinction is worth marking. The pattern is the arrangement of activated edges at any
given moment; the structure is the framework of possible connections that the pattern realizes.
The pattern changes as the activations change; the structure does not. The distinction is the
distinction between the actual and the possible; the structure is the space of possibilities, and
the pattern is the actualization of some of those possibilities at a moment.


16.5     Why Epistemic Light Does Not Travel
The previous section defined the active structure of legibility and identified epistemic light
with it. The present section states the principle that follows, and proves it.

Principle 16.2 (Non-Travel of Epistemic Light). (T) Epistemic light does not travel.

Argument for the Principle.       1. Travel requires time.

   2. Time is the order of succession of the stages by which changes are realized in a receiving
      cognitive context. The definition is stated here in the framework’s vocabulary; it does not
      depend on any external account of time, and it is the only sense of “time” the argument
      uses.

   3. Epistemic light is the medium of legibility, and time is a category of the related (of the
      things whose relations epistemic light makes legible).

   4. Therefore epistemic light does not travel.


    The proof depends on the premise that time is a category of the related. The premise
is stated in step 2 with an explicit definition of the sense of “time” the argument uses. The
reader who accepts the premise accepts the conclusion; the reader who denies it denies the
argument, and the framework does not claim more than the premise delivers.
    The proof also depends on the premise that epistemic light is the medium of legibility.
This premise is the principle of the previous chapter, argued there. The two premises together
yield the conclusion that epistemic light does not travel.

Remark 16.13 (The Proof Is a Modus Tollens). The proof is a modus tollens, and the form
is worth marking. The argument establishes that if epistemic light travels, then time is part
of what epistemic light is (the first two steps). But time is a category of the related, and
16.6. Two Senses of “Fluidity”                                                                  239


epistemic light is the medium of legibility (the third step). Therefore epistemic light does not
travel. The argument’s force is in the third step: the medium of legibility cannot be subject
to the categories of the related, because it is the condition of their legibility.

Remark 16.14 (Why This Is Not a Denial of Physics). Physics describes light as propagating
at a finite speed. The framework does not deny this. What the framework denies is that
the propagation is a motion of epistemic light in the ordinary sense. Physics describes the
behavior of light in time; the framework describes what epistemic light is, as the medium of
legibility. The two are compatible, because they answer different questions. The framework’s
claim is epistemic; the physicist’s claim is empirical. Neither replaces the other, and neither
contradicts the other.

Remark 16.15 (Why This Is Not a Denial of Carriers of Light). The framework’s claim is
that epistemic light—in the structural sense defined in the previous chapter—does not travel.
The claim is not that nothing associated with light travels. The framework does not deny that
there may be physical carriers of light, and that they move as they carry it. Whether such
carriers exist, and what their relation to epistemic light is, is a question the framework does
not address, and does not foreclose.

Remark 16.16 (Motion Is Our Language). We say “light goes from the sun to the earth,”
because time and motion are categories of the related, and we can speak only within the
related. But epistemic light, in the structural sense, is the medium of legibility, and the
categories of the related do not apply to it. The sentence “light goes from the sun to the earth”
is not false; it is a description of the appearance of light in the related, in the categories of the
related. The epistemic claim is that the appearance is not the medium. Epistemic light does
not go; the structure of epistemic light activates an edge between the sun and the earth, and
the activation appears to us as a going.


16.6      Two Senses of “Fluidity”
The problem of the earlier section was that “fluidity” seems to imply motion, and motion is
incompatible with the character of epistemic light as the medium of legibility. The solution is
to distinguish two senses of “fluidity.”

Kinetic Fluidity                               Structural Fluidity
Having flow                                    Having the capacity to convey
Moving                                         Being a medium
Traveling                                      Establishing connection
Requires time                                  Independent of time
    The first sense is the ordinary one: a fluid is what flows, and flowing requires motion and
time. The second sense is the framework’s: a fluid is what conveys, and conveying does not
require motion or time. The two senses are not the same, and the framework uses the second.
When the framework says that epistemic light is the fluid element, it means that epistemic
light is what conveys effect, not that epistemic light flows from one place to another.
    The distinction is not a verbal trick. It names two different structures. Kinetic fluidity is a
structure of matter: a liquid flows because its molecules move past one another. Structural
fluidity is a structure of relation: a medium conveys because it connects the terms it relates.

Remark 16.17 (The Distinction Is Structural, Not Verbal). The distinction between kinetic
and structural fluidity is a distinction between two structures, not a distinction between two
uses of a word. The word “fluid” applies to both because both involve a kind of passing; but
240                                           Chapter 16. Epistemic Light as Active Structure


the passing of a liquid is a motion, and the passing of a medium is a conveying. The two are
structurally different, and the framework’s claim is that epistemic light is fluid in the second
sense, not the first.

Remark 16.18 (Why Not Use a Different Word). The framework retains the word “fluid”
because it is the word the four-column framework uses for the second column. To call the
column something else would require a revision of the framework’s vocabulary, and the revision
would obscure the connection between the present chapter and the chapters that introduced
the column. The word is retained with a stipulation: “fluid” in this book means “conveying,”
not “flowing.”

Remark 16.19 (The Distinction Is the Framework’s Answer to the Problem). The distinction
between the two senses of fluidity is the framework’s answer to the problem of the earlier
section. The problem was that fluidity seemed to imply motion, and motion seemed to imply
time, and time seemed to contradict the character of epistemic light as the medium of legibility.
The answer is that fluidity, in the sense the framework needs, does not imply motion; it implies
conveyance, and conveyance does not imply time.


16.7     Fluidity as Role, Not Essence
The distinction between kinetic and structural fluidity raises a further question. Is structural
fluidity a property of epistemic light—something epistemic light has in itself—or is it a role
that epistemic light plays in the framework’s analysis?

Principle 16.3 (Structural Fluidity Is a Role). (T) “Fluid element” is an analytical role—not
an ontological essence. Epistemic light, in the four-column framework, plays the role of
conveyor—so it is the fluid element. This role is independent of whether epistemic light moves
or not.

    The principle follows from the context-dependence principle, stated in Chapter 10: the
fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive context, not on the element’s
essence. Epistemic light is the fluid element in the framework’s analysis because it plays the
role of conveyor. It would play this role whether or not it moved; the role is analytical, not
ontological.

Remark 16.20 (The Analytical and the Ontological). The distinction between analytical role
and ontological essence is one of the framework’s recurring distinctions. It is the distinction
between the four columns, which are analytical roles, and the structure of what is explained,
which is a different question. The present principle applies the distinction to the fluid element:
epistemic light plays the role of conveyor, and the role does not make epistemic light essentially
fluid.

Remark 16.21 (The Principle Is a Particular Case of the Context-Dependence Principle).
The principle is a particular case of the context-dependence principle. The context-dependence
principle says that fixedness and fluidity are roles, not essences; the present principle applies
the general claim to epistemic light.


16.8     Epistemic Descent, Not Travel
A further distinction is needed, between two ways in which epistemic light can be said to “go”
from one cognitive context to another. The two are easily confused, and the confusion is the
source of the apparent conflict between the framework’s claim that epistemic light does not
travel and the ordinary language of light’s descent.
16.9. The Three Directions Re-Read                                                            241


Epistemic Descent                          Travel
Structural                                 Kinetic
In the levels of cognitive context         In space
Simultaneous                               Gradual
Does not require time                      Requires time
Epistemic light descends                   (No corresponding epistemic claim)

   Epistemic descent is structural: it is the appearance of epistemic light in the mode of a
lower cognitive context, without epistemic light going from one context to another. Travel is
kinetic: it is the motion of a thing from one place to another, requiring time and space. The
framework’s claim is that epistemic light descends, not that it travels. The descent is not a
motion; it is an appearance.


Principle 16.4 (Epistemic Descent Is Structural). (T) The epistemic descent of light is not its
motion from a higher cognitive context to a lower one, but its appearance in the mode of the
lower context. Epistemic light in each context appears in the mode of that context—without
going from one context to another.


    The principle is the framework’s account of how epistemic light is present in the lower
cognitive contexts. It is supported by the non-necessity of sequential passage, argued in
Chapter 9. If epistemic light does not have to pass through every context between, its presence
in a lower context must be explained by something other than passage. The principle explains
it by appearance: epistemic light appears in the mode of the lower context, without going
from one context to another.


Remark 16.22 (Epistemic Descent and Non-Sequential Passage). The principle is a special
case of non-sequential connectivity. The general principle says that an explanation of how
one fixed element bears on another does not require the connection to pass through every
intermediate fixed element. The present principle says the same for epistemic light: epistemic
light’s presence in a lower context does not require passage through every context between.


Remark 16.23 (Epistemic Descent and the Appearance in the Mode of the Apparatus). The
principle is developed in Chapter 17, where epistemic light is stated to be the foundational fluid
element that appears in the mode of each cognitive apparatus. The descent that the present
chapter states is the same structural relation that Chapter 17 develops into the hierarchy of
apparatuses: light in each context appears in the mode of that context, and the appearance is
not a new light but the same light in a different mode.

structure. The three directions are three directions of a single structure: the edge from
identity to manifestation, the edge from manifestation to identity, and the edge between two
manifestations. The structure is one; the edges are three; the directions are three.
Remark 16.24 (The Three Directions Are Not Three Things). The three directions are not
three separate entities. They are three directions of one structure, distinguished by what they
connect. The structure is one; the edges are three; the directions are three. The unity of the
structure is what makes the three directions directions of one thing, not three things.
Remark 16.25 (The Re-Reading Is a Translation, Not a Replacement). The re-reading of
the three directions is a translation, not a replacement. The old reading (“light goes,” “light

returns,” “light flows”) is not abandoned as false; it is translated into the new reading (“the
edge is activated”). The two readings describe the same phenomena, but the new reading uses
the category of activation, which does not import the category of motion.

Remark 16.26 (The Cycle of Epistemic Light). The three directions together form a cycle:
an identity manifests, and its manifestation refers back to it, and manifestations are related to
one another. The cycle is not described as having a beginning in time; the framework states
the cycle as a structural feature of the active structure of legibility, not as a temporal process.


16.10      The Distinctness Test for the Active Structure
The first distinctness test (Chapter 15) exhibited the difference that the presence or absence
of epistemic light makes. The present section states a second distinctness test, for the claim
that epistemic light is an active structure: that the activation of edges does work that the
other columns do not already do.


16.10.1     The Test Stated
The test proceeds by comparing two cases. The two cases are alike in their fixed elements, in
their context, and in their governing dynamics; the structure of epistemic light is present in
both. They differ only in which edges of the structure are activated. If the two cases differ
in legibility—in what can be read off the relation—the difference must be attributed to the
activation of the edges, because the other columns are held constant and the structure itself is
the same.

Definition 16.3 (The Distinctness Test for the Active Structure). (A) Let C1 and C2 be two
cases such that:

  (i) the fixed elements of C1 and C2 are the same;

 (ii) the receiving cognitive contexts of C1 and C2 are the same;

 (iii) the governing dynamics of C1 and C2 are the same;

 (iv) the structure of epistemic light is present in both C1 and C2 ;

 (v) the edges of the structure that are activated in C1 differ from the edges that are activated
     in C2 .

The cases are a distinctness test when the legibility of the relation in C1 differs from the
legibility of the relation in C2 .


16.10.2     Two Cases
Case 1: The library with the catalogue. A reader is in a library, and the books are
arranged on the shelves. The fixed elements are the books (their contents, their titles, their
authors). The context is the reader’s question (“what is in these books?”). The governing
dynamics are the rules of reading. The structure of epistemic light is present: the library is lit.
The activation of the edges: the edges from the reader’s question to the catalogue’s entries, and
from the catalogue’s entries to the books, are activated; the edges from the reader’s question
to the books’ contents are not activated directly. The legibility of the relation between the
reader’s question and the books’ contents is mediated by the catalogue.
244                                             Chapter 16. Epistemic Light as Active Structure


Case 2: The library without the catalogue. The same reader, the same library, the
same books, the same question, the same dynamics, the same lit library. The only difference
is that the catalogue is not available. The activation of the edges: the edges from the reader’s
question to the books’ contents are activated directly. The legibility of the relation is direct.
    The two cases satisfy the conditions of Definition 16.3. The difference in legibility is not
attributable to the fixed elements (they are the same), to the context (it is the same), to the
governing dynamics (they are the same), or to the presence of the structure (it is the same).
The difference is attributable to the activation of the edges, and to the activation alone.

16.10.3     What the Test Establishes
The test establishes that the activation of edges does work that the other columns and the
structure do not already do: it makes a relation legible through one path rather than another,
and the path cannot be attributed to the fixed elements, the context, the governing dynamics,
or the structure. The work is the work of the active structure: the structure does not merely
enable legibility; its activations determine which legibility occurs.
Remark 16.27 (What the Test Would Not Show). The test would not show that the active
structure is the only possible account of the activation of edges. It shows that the activation
does work, not that the framework’s vocabulary for describing the work is the only one
available.


16.11       A Coherence Test
The chapter’s claim is that epistemic light does not travel, but is an active structure of legibility.
The claim is epistemic, not empirical. But it may be asked whether the claim is coherent with
the way physics describes light. The question is a coherence test, not a justification.

  Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification) The Non-Travel of Epistemic Light and the Propagation of

   What this test shows. That the framework’s claim that epistemic light does not travel is
   not at odds with the way physics describes light’s propagation.
   The test. Physics describes light as propagating at a finite speed. This description is a
   description of light’s behavior in time. It does not say what light is; it says how light behaves.
   The framework’s claim is about what epistemic light is: epistemic light is an active structure of
   legibility, not a traveler. The two claims are about different things.
   What this test does not show. It does not show that the framework’s claim is correct.
   It shows only that the framework’s claim and the physicist’s claim can both be true, because
   they answer different questions.


Remark 16.28 (The Coherence Test Is Not a Concession to Science). The coherence test
is not a concession to science. It is a discipline on the book’s own claims. The test does not
confirm the principle; it exposes the principle to a kind of check.


16.12       What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the epistemological consequences of the claim that
epistemic light does not travel. The consequences—that we are encompassed in light, and that
complete knowledge of epistemic light is therefore impossible—are developed in Chapter 17.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between epistemic light and energy. The
present chapter has stated that epistemic light is an active structure; the question of what the
structure carries, if anything, is not the chapter’s subject.
16.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                  245


    Third, the chapter does not develop the full account of the three directions. The directions
are named, compared, and their re-reading is stated, but the detailed treatment of each is
deferred to Chapter 17 and to the later parts.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described what epistemic light is in itself. It
claims to have described the structure of the medium, and the structure points beyond itself.

Remark 16.29 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has distinguished the structure of legibility from the travel of a thing, and defined the active
structure of legibility. It has stated the process model of the active structure, with its four
elements (input, direction, effect, output). It has argued that epistemic light is such a structure.
It has proved that epistemic light does not travel, and distinguished two senses of “fluidity.” It
has compared the three directions in a table with definition, role, activation condition, and
effect on legibility. And it has stated the distinctness test that exhibits the specific work the
activations do (Section 16.10). The chapter’s contribution is the framework’s account of the
structure of the medium, stated at the strength its arguments support, the process model, the
comparison table, and the distinctness test.

A Question for Reflection
If epistemic light does not travel, how can we speak of “the light of the sun reaching us”—is this
a category mistake? If it is, what does the sentence “the light of the sun reaches us” actually
say? Does it say something false, or something true in a language that is not the language of
the framework?
    And consider the flashlight and the shadow—the scene that opened the chapter. The circle
of light moves; the two descriptions agree on this. But one description says the light travels,
and the other says the light is a structure whose edges activate. Which description is correct?
If the second, what does that tell you about the difference between the behavior of light and
the being of epistemic light?
    And consider the process model of Section 16.4.1: can you apply its four elements (input,
direction, effect, output) to an activation of epistemic light in a case of your own choosing?
Can you state the input, the direction, the effect, and the output, and can you show that the
effect on legibility is not attributable to the other columns? A reader who can answer all three
questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s three
tasks before them.

The next chapter draws the epistemological consequence of the definition. If epistemic light is
the medium of legibility, and if we are in relation to epistemic light in every act of cognition,
then we are encompassed in epistemic light—not floating in it. The consequence is that complete
knowledge of epistemic light is impossible, and the chapter states why.

Chapter 17

Encompassment in Epistemic Light

Scope
This chapter locates epistemic light in the framework’s architecture. It argues that epistemic
light is the medium of relation, not a term of relation—it belongs to the second of the two pairs
into which the four columns divide. It argues that epistemic light is the foundational fluid
element, appearing in the mode of each cognitive apparatus. It argues that we are encompassed
in epistemic light, not floating in it, with the consequence that complete knowledge of epistemic
light is impossible for the finite subject. It distinguishes three levels of knowledge (Section 17.8),
so that the claim of impossibility is stated at the strength the argument supports, and it states
the relation of the chapter to Chapter 31. Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks
of “medium,” “term,” “apparatus,” “encompassment,” or “window,” these are structural terms,
and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


17.1      A Scene: The Fish and the Water
Consider a fish in water. The fish swims; the water surrounds it; the fish breathes the water;
the water is the medium in which the fish moves and lives. But the fish does not know the
water as we know it. The fish has no standpoint outside the water from which to see the water
as an object. The water is not one of the things the fish encounters; it is the condition under
which the fish encounters things at all. If the fish could speak, it would not say “here is water”;
it would say “here is what there is”—and the water would be invisible in its speech.
    Now consider us, in relation to epistemic light. We see by light; we do not see light.
Epistemic light is the medium in which things appear to us, but it is not one of the things that
appear. When we study light, we study it as an object—as a wave, a particle, a field—and in
doing so we treat it as one of the things that appear. But the light by which we study it is
the light we are trying to study, and that light is not one of the things that appear. It is the
condition under which things appear.
    The fish and the water, we and the epistemic light: the two scenes have the same structure.
In both, a medium makes appearance possible without itself appearing. The medium is not one
of the things; it is what makes the things possible. And the relation between the knower and
the medium is not the relation between the knower and an object; it is the relation between
the knower and the condition of the knower’s objects.
    The scene poses three questions. First: where does epistemic light stand in the framework’s
architecture? Second: how does it relate to the various apparatuses of cognition that study
the world? Third: what is our relation to epistemic light, if we are in it as the fish is in water?
The present chapter answers these questions.
Remark 17.1 (The Scene Shows Two Kinds of Relation to a Medium). The scene shows two
kinds of relation to a medium, and the distinction is worth marking. The first is the relation
248                                           Chapter 17. Encompassment in Epistemic Light


of a thing to an external medium: the fish is in the water, and the water is around it, but
the water is not in the fish. The second is the relation of a thing to a pervading medium:
the fish breathes the water, and the water is in the fish’s gills, in its blood, in its cells. The
framework’s claim is that our relation to epistemic light is the second kind, not the first. We
are not floating in epistemic light, as a fish floats in water; we are encompassed in it, as the
air is in the lungs.

Remark 17.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the chapter’s claims; it makes them intelligible
before they are stated. The arguments are given in the sections that follow, and the scene
carries no weight in them.


17.2     The Question
The previous chapter argued that epistemic light is an active structure of legibility, not a
traveler. The present chapter asks a further question: where does epistemic light stand, in the
framework’s architecture?
    Three aspects of the question must be distinguished.

The structural aspect. The four columns are divided into two pairs: fixed elements with
context, and dynamics with fluid element. Which pair does epistemic light belong to?

The apparatus aspect. Epistemic light is the fluid element. But there are many fluid
elements—language, information, force, chemical bonds, metabolic processes. Is epistemic
light one of these, or is it the foundational fluid element of which the others are specific
manifestations?

The epistemic aspect. What is our relation to epistemic light? Do we stand outside it and
study it as an object, or are we encompassed in it? The answer has consequences for what we
can know about it.
    The chapter treats the three aspects in turn. It then distinguishes three levels of knowledge
(Section 17.8), and it states the relation of the chapter to Chapter 31.

Remark 17.3 (The Three Aspects Are Not Independent). The three aspects are not in-
dependent. The structural aspect (which pair) is what makes the apparatus aspect (which
level) possible: because epistemic light is the medium of relation, it is the foundational fluid
element of the hierarchy. The apparatus aspect is what makes the epistemic aspect (what our
relation to it is) possible: because epistemic light is foundational, we are in it in every act of
cognition, and the question of our relation to it arises. The three aspects are three stages of
one argument.


17.3     The Two Pairs of Columns
The four columns are not four isolated roles. They form two structural pairs, and the pairing
is not arbitrary. It follows from the structure of relation itself.

17.3.1    The Diagram of the Two Pairs
The relation of the two pairs, and the place of epistemic light in the cognitive structure, can be
displayed as a diagram. The diagram has two pairs, and it shows where epistemic light enters.
17.3. The Two Pairs of Columns                                                               249


Pair 1: The Terms of the Relation                  Pair 2: The Medium of the Relation
Fixed elements (what is related)                   Governing dynamics (the rule of the rela-
                                                   tion)
Context (the frame in which the terms are          Fluid element (the conveyor of the relation)
posed)

                                                   Epistemic light
                                                   (the fluid element in its foundational form)

   The diagram is a summary of the pairing. Pair 1 gives the terms; Pair 2 gives the medium.
Epistemic light is the fluid element, and so it belongs to Pair 2. The diagram does not add a
new claim; it displays the pairing that the principle of the chapter will state.

17.3.2    A Single Worked Example
The pairing can be applied to a single case, so that the reader can see where epistemic light
enters. The example is the courtroom scene of Chapter 14, but the point is general.

The case. A contract is signed in a courtroom; a judge, a clerk, and a plaintiff each cognize
the event.

Pair 1 in the case. The fixed elements are the contract, the parties, the signatures, the
date. The context is the judge’s question (“is the contract binding?”). The fixed elements are
what the judge’s cognition is about; the context is the frame in which the question is posed.

Pair 2 in the case. The governing dynamics are the rules of contract law. The fluid
element is what conveys the effect of the contract to the judge’s cognition—the documents,
the testimony, the record. In the framework’s sense, this fluid element is epistemic light in the
mode of the legal apparatus: it is the condition under which the contract’s effect is legible to
the judge as the effect of a binding obligation.

The place of epistemic light. Epistemic light is not the contract (a fixed element), not the
judge’s question (the context), not the rules of contract law (the dynamics). It is the medium
by which the contract’s effect reaches the judge’s cognition, in the mode of the legal apparatus.
The example shows the place of epistemic light: it is in Pair 2, alongside the dynamics, and it
is the conveyor of the relation.

Remark 17.4 (The Diagram and the Example Are Illustrations, Not Arguments). The
diagram and the example are illustrations of the pairing; they do not prove the pairing. The
pairing is argued in the principle that follows. The reader who has followed the diagram and
the example has the pairing in a form that can be applied; the reader who wishes to see the
argument for the pairing is directed to Section 17.4.

17.3.3    The Principle of the Two Pairs
Principle 17.1 (Pair 2 as the Medium of Relation). (T) Dynamics and fluid element form the
medium of the relation. Without fluid element, dynamics is meaningless. Without dynamics,
fluid element is unordered. The two are mutually dependent.

   The principle is (T): it is argued from the structure of relation itself. Any relation between
two terms must have a medium through which the relation is established, and the medium is
250                                            Chapter 17. Encompassment in Epistemic Light


distinct from the terms. It would be refuted by showing that a relation can hold without a
medium, which the conveyor principle (Chapter 8) denies.
Remark 17.5 (The Pairing Is Not a Division of the Columns into Two Kinds). The pairing is
not a division of the four columns into two kinds of thing. It is a structural grouping: the four
columns answer two questions, and the two questions group the columns into two pairs. A
reader who takes the pairing as a claim that there are two kinds of columns—fixed and fluid,
say—has misread it; a reader who takes it as a grouping of the four columns by the questions
they answer has read it correctly.


17.4       Epistemic Light Belongs to Pair 2
Epistemic light is the fluid element. It follows that epistemic light belongs to Pair 2, not Pair 1.
The consequence is not trivial; it has three implications.

First implication: epistemic light is not a term of relation. Epistemic light is the
medium of relation, not one of the terms related. It is not what is related; it is what conveys
the relation.

Second implication: epistemic light is inseparable from dynamics. Without the
rules of the receiving cognitive context—the governing dynamics—epistemic light is unordered.
The rules determine what connections epistemic light carries, in what modes, under what
conditions.

Third implication: epistemic light is the condition of possibility of the relation
between fixed elements and context. Without epistemic light, the fixed elements are
disconnected islands, and the context is an empty frame. Epistemic light is what makes the
relation possible—not the relation itself, but its condition.
Remark 17.6 (Epistemic Light Is Not the Relation). Epistemic light is the condition of
possibility of relation, not the relation itself. The relation between an identity and its
manifestation is one thing; the epistemic light that makes the relation legible is another.


17.5       The Hierarchy of Cognitive Apparatuses
The framework distinguishes two kinds of cognitive apparatus: primary and secondary.
Definition 17.1 (Primary Cognitive Apparatus). (A) A primary cognitive apparatus is one
whose fixed elements are general and whose fluid element is foundational. Its dynamics has a
general formalization, and its context is foundational.
Definition 17.2 (Secondary Cognitive Apparatus). (A) A secondary cognitive apparatus is
one whose fixed elements are specific and whose fluid element is derived. Its dynamics has
specific rules, and its context is composite.
      The hierarchy of apparatuses is as follows.

Level              Apparatus                 Fluid Element               Dynamics
Foundational       General cognition         Epistemic light             General rules
Primary            Specific cognition (gen- Epistemic light              General rules
                   eral fixed elements)
Secondary          Specific cognition (spe- Derived conveyors            Specific rules
                   cific fixed elements)
17.6. Epistemic Light as the Foundational Fluid Element                                        251


Remark 17.7 (“Primary” Does Not Mean “More Fundamental”). The word “primary” is a
structural label, not an evaluative one. Primary apparatuses are those whose fixed elements
are general; secondary apparatuses are those whose fixed elements are specific. A primary
apparatus is not more fundamental than a secondary one; it is simply more general.

Remark 17.8 (The Hierarchy Is Not a Ladder of Increasing Reality). The hierarchy is a
classification of cognitive apparatuses by their structural generality; it does not rank them by
reality. The foundational level is not more real than the secondary; it is more general, and its
fluid element is foundational.


17.6     Epistemic Light as the Foundational Fluid Element
Principle 17.2 (Epistemic Light as Foundational Fluid Element). (E) Epistemic light, in the
framework’s sense, is not one of the fluid elements—it is the foundational fluid element that
appears in the mode of each apparatus.

    The principle is (E): it is an estimate, supported by the structural parallel between epistemic
light and the specific conveyors.

Principle 17.3 (Appearance in the Mode of the Apparatus). (T) Epistemic light in each
cognitive apparatus appears in the mode of that apparatus—without becoming many epistemic
lights.

Argument for the Principle.   1. Epistemic light is the foundational fluid element, appearing
     in the mode of each apparatus.

   2. An appearance in the mode of an apparatus is an appearance shaped by the apparatus’s
      specific character.

   3. The shaping does not multiply epistemic light. The specific character that a medium
      takes in a domain is not a new medium.

   4. Hence epistemic light in each apparatus appears in the mode of that apparatus, without
      becoming many epistemic lights.


Remark 17.9 (The Analogue, Not the Identity). What appears as a chemical bond, a
metabolic process, or a flow of water in secondary apparatuses are not epistemic light in
the framework’s sense. They are structural analogues of epistemic light, manifested in their
respective apparatuses.

Remark 17.10 (The Modal Language Is Structural). The principle speaks of epistemic
light appearing “in the mode of” each apparatus. “Mode” here is a structural term, not a
modal-metaphysical one. It names the specific character that epistemic light takes when it
operates within a given apparatus.


17.7     Encompassment in Epistemic Light
The hierarchy of apparatuses locates epistemic light structurally. The present section turns
from structure to epistemology. What is our relation to epistemic light, given that epistemic
light is the foundational fluid element?
    The framework distinguishes two possible relations: floating in a medium and being
encompassed by it.
252                                            Chapter 17. Encompassment in Epistemic Light


Floating                                  Encompassed

Preserving full independence              Without full independence
A fish in water                           Air in the lungs
The environment is external               The environment is pervading
      Floating is a relation of exteriority. Encompassment is a relation of pervasion.

Principle 17.4 (Encompassment in Epistemic Light). (E) We are not floating in epistemic
light—we are encompassed in epistemic light. Epistemic light has taken us up—not that we
have taken up epistemic light.

    The principle is (E): it is adopted, not proved. It is supported by the argument that
follows.

Argument for Encompassment.          1. Epistemic light is the condition of possibility of legible
     relation (Chapter 15).

  2. We, in every act of cognition, are in a relation.

  3. Therefore we, in every act of cognition, are in epistemic light.

  4. But this “being in epistemic light” is not “being in an external environment”—it is “being
     taken up by the condition of possibility.”

  5. Therefore we are encompassed in epistemic light—not floating in it.



17.7.1      The Model of Encompassment
The argument’s step (4) is abstract; the model makes it concrete. The model states why the
epistemic subject is not fully independent of the conditions of its own legibility.

Definition 17.3 (The Encompassment Model). (A) The epistemic subject is related to
epistemic light in three ways:

(E1) Dependence: the subject’s every act of cognition presupposes epistemic light as its
     condition of legibility. Without epistemic light, the subject’s cognition would not be
     legible to the subject itself.

(E2) Non-exteriority: the subject cannot occupy a standpoint outside epistemic light from
     which to survey it. The subject’s standpoint is always within the light, not outside it.

(E3) Pervasion: epistemic light is not merely around the subject, but in the subject’s every
     act of cognition. The light is in the subject’s cognition as its condition, not around it as
     an environment.

The three ways together are the encompassment: the subject is not fully independent of the
conditions of its own legibility, because (E1) it depends on them, (E2) it cannot stand outside
them, and (E3) they pervade its cognition.

   The model is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s way of decomposing the encom-
passment. Its justification is its use in the analysis of cases; its cost is that a given case may
not exhibit all three ways distinctly.

    The model states why the subject is not fully independent of the conditions of its own
legibility. If the subject were independent, it would be related to epistemic light by exteriority
(as a fish is related to water); the model states that the relation is encompassment (dependence,
non-exteriority, pervasion).

Remark 17.11 (The Model Is an Analysis of the Encompassment). The model is not a separate
argument for encompassment; it is an analysis of what encompassment is. The argument for
encompassment is the argument of the proof; the model states why the argument’s conclusion
(we are encompassed) explains the subject’s epistemic situation.

Remark 17.12 (Encompassment Is Not Identity). To say that we are encompassed in epistemic
light is not to say that we are epistemic light. The air in the lungs is not the lungs. We are
encompassed in epistemic light as the light is in us, not as the light is us.

Remark 17.13 (Encompassment Is Not a Prison). The encompassment is not a restriction on
knowledge; it is the condition under which knowledge is possible. The fish is not imprisoned
in the water; the water is what makes the fish’s motion possible. We are not imprisoned in
epistemic light; the light is what makes our cognition possible.


17.8      Three Levels of Knowledge
The claim that complete knowledge of epistemic light is impossible for the finite subject
is ambiguous, and the ambiguity must be resolved. Three levels of knowledge must be
distinguished, and the chapter states which level it claims to be impossible and which level
it claims to be possible. The distinction is also the distinction between this chapter and
Chapter 31, which treats the same subject at the level of the limits of self-knowledge.

17.8.1    The Three Levels Defined
Definition 17.4 (Complete Knowledge of Structure). Complete knowledge of structure is
knowledge of the full structural description of epistemic light: its place in the framework’s
architecture, its character as the medium of legibility, its relation to the four columns, its
appearance in the modes of the apparatuses. The criterion of completeness at this level is the
criterion of the framework’s own completeness: the structural description is complete when it
states all the roles and relations that the framework’s architecture assigns.

Definition 17.5 (Partial Knowledge). Partial knowledge is knowledge of some of the instances
of epistemic light: some of the activations, in some of the apparatuses, under some of the
conditions. The criterion of partiality at this level is the criterion of the finite subject’s actual
survey: the knowledge is partial when it covers some but not all of the instances the subject
could encounter.
254                                           Chapter 17. Encompassment in Epistemic Light


Definition 17.6 (Estimative Knowledge). Estimative knowledge is knowledge of what the
subject reaches toward beyond the instances it can survey: knowledge of the source, of the
ground, of what lies beyond the structural window. The criterion of estimative knowledge is
the criterion of the reach: the knowledge is estimative when it is real at its own level but does
not claim completeness of the instances or of the ground.

    The three definitions distinguish three levels of knowledge, and each level has its own
criterion of assessment. The three levels are not three degrees of one knowledge; they are three
kinds of knowledge, each with its own structure.

    The table states the three levels, their criteria, and whether each is possible for the finite

knowledge is possible as estimate, not as complete knowledge of the source.


17.8.3    The Impossibility Claim, Stated Precisely
Principle 17.5 (Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light). (T) We cannot
know epistemic light completely at the level of instances, nor at the level of final encompass-
ment—because we are encompassed in it. Complete knowledge of instances would require
standing outside the object of knowledge from a standpoint from which all instances could be
surveyed; final encompassment would require standing outside epistemic light. We can stand
outside neither. We can have complete knowledge of structure, and we can have partial and
estimative knowledge; these are real knowledge, and they are the knowledge available to the
finite subject.

Argument for the Principle.    1. Complete knowledge of instances requires standing outside
     the object of knowledge, from a standpoint from which all its instances can be surveyed
     as a whole. Final encompassment requires standing outside epistemic light entirely.

   2. We are encompassed in epistemic light (Principle 17.4; the model of Definition 17.3).
      To stand outside epistemic light would be to stand outside the condition of our own
      cognition.

   3. We cannot stand outside the condition of our own cognition, and we cannot survey an
      infinity of instances from a finite standpoint.
17.9. The First Consequence: Epistemic Light as the Structural Window                          255


   4. Therefore we cannot know epistemic light completely at the level of instances or of
      final encompassment. We can have complete knowledge of structure, and partial and
      estimative knowledge; these are real knowledge.


    The argument is a reductio of the claim to complete knowledge of epistemic light at the
levels of instances and final encompassment. The claim is impossible, not because we lack the
resources, but because the relation between the knower and the known is not the relation of
exteriority that complete knowledge of instances or final encompassment would require. We
can know epistemic light in its modes and in its structure; we cannot know all its instances,
and we cannot occupy the standpoint of final encompassment.
Remark 17.14 (The Relation of This Chapter to Chapter 31). The present chapter states
the impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light at the levels of instances and final
encompassment. The same subject is treated in Chapter 31, at the level of the limits of
self-knowledge: the subject’s self-knowledge is bounded by the same encompassment, and the
two chapters are two aspects of one structural fact. The present chapter states the impossibility
from the side of the structure of epistemic light; Chapter 31 states the impossibility from the
side of the subject’s self-knowledge. The two chapters are not two arguments for the same
conclusion; they are two statements of the same fact, from two sides, and the reader who has
followed both has the fact at the strength the framework can support.
Remark 17.15 (The Impossibility Is Not a Defect). The impossibility of complete knowledge
of instances and of final encompassment is not a defect of the finite subject; it is the structural
condition of finite cognition. A subject that was not encompassed in epistemic light would not
be a finite subject.
Remark 17.16 (What We Can Know). The principle does not say that we cannot know
epistemic light at all. It says that we cannot know epistemic light completely at the levels of
instances and final encompassment. What we can know is the structure of epistemic light, and
the modes of epistemic light in the instances we can survey. The partial knowledge is real, and
the estimative knowledge is real; only the complete knowledge at the two levels is impossible.


17.9     The First Consequence: Epistemic Light as the Structural
         Window
Principle 17.6 (Epistemic Light as the Structural Window). (E) Within the structure of
finite cognition, epistemic light is the only window through which an identity reaches the
receiving context in which it is cognized—and that too in the mode of that context. What
we have of an identity is its manifestation, conveyed by epistemic light; we do not have the
identity itself.
    The principle follows from the non-necessity of sequential passage (Chapter 9) and from
the definition of manifestation (Chapter 13). If an identity’s presence in a context does not
require passage through every context between, then the identity’s relation to the context is
carried by something other than passage. That something is epistemic light.
Remark 17.17 (The Window Is a Structural Description). The word “window” is a structural
metaphor. It does not mean that epistemic light is transparent; it means that epistemic light
is what allows an identity to be legible from within a receiving context.
Remark 17.18 (The Window Is Not a Barrier). The window is not a barrier. A window lets
in light; it does not block it. The claim that epistemic light is the only window is not the
claim that it blocks us from what lies beyond; it is the claim that it is the medium through
which what lies beyond reaches us.
256                                               Chapter 17. Encompassment in Epistemic Light


17.10      The Second Consequence: Estimate, Not Complete Knowl-
           edge
Principle 17.7 (Estimate, Not Complete Knowledge). (T) We can estimate, from the
properties of epistemic light in the receiving context, something about the identities whose
manifestations epistemic light conveys—but our estimate is not complete knowledge. The
estimate is real knowledge at its own level; it is not complete knowledge of the source.

    The principle is a consequence of the two previous ones. If we are encompassed in
epistemic light, we cannot know epistemic light completely at the levels of instances and final
encompassment; if epistemic light is the structural window to identities, then what we have of
identities is what we have of epistemic light, in its mode in the receiving context. And what
we have of epistemic light is estimate at the level of the source, and partial knowledge at the
level of the instances.

Remark 17.19 (Estimate and Inference). Estimate is not the same as inference. An inference
proceeds from premises to a conclusion by a rule; an estimate proceeds from what is given to
something beyond what is given, by analogy and indication.

Remark 17.20 (The Estimate Points Beyond Itself). The estimate points beyond itself.
What the estimate estimates is not contained in the estimate; it is the source that the estimate
reaches toward.

Remark 17.21 (The Three Consequences Are One Structure). The consequences are not
separate results; they are aspects of one structural fact. The fact is that we are encompassed
in epistemic light. The first consequence states what the fact implies for our knowledge of
epistemic light (impossibility at the levels of instances and final encompassment). The second
states what it implies for our access to identities (epistemic light is the window). The third
states what it implies for the character of that access (estimate, not complete knowledge).


17.11      A Coherence Test
  Coherence Test (not evidence, not justification) The Hierarchy of Apparatuses and the Self-Description of th

   What this test shows. That the hierarchy of cognitive apparatuses—primary and sec-
   ondary, with epistemic light as the foundational fluid element—is not at odds with the way at
   least some established inquiries describe their own structure.
   The test. Physics studies general fixed elements under general rules; its fluid element is
   general. Chemistry studies specific fixed elements under specific rules; its fluid element (the
   chemical bond) is a specific conveyor. Ecology studies specific fixed elements under specific rules;
   its fluid elements (flows of water, air, energy) are specific conveyors. In each case, the apparatus
   has a fixed element, a fluid element, a dynamics, and a context. The specific fluid elements
   are structural analogues of the general one: a chemical bond conveys effect between atoms as
   epistemic light conveys effect between identities. The analogy is structural, not substantial: the
   specific conveyors are not epistemic light, but they are what epistemic light looks like when it
   appears in the mode of the specific apparatus.
   What this test does not show. It does not show that the framework’s claim is correct.
   It shows only that the framework’s hierarchy of apparatuses is coherent with the way these
   inquiries describe their own structure.


17.12      The Positive Epistemic Result
The chapter’s positive contribution is the epistemic result of the encompassment, stated so
that the reader knows what the chapter gives, not only what it excludes.
17.13. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                    257


First result: the framework’s architecture has two pairs. The four columns divide
into two pairs: the terms of the relation (fixed elements and context) and the medium of the
relation (dynamics and fluid element). Epistemic light belongs to the second pair. The result
is the framework’s structural location of epistemic light.

Second result: epistemic light is the foundational fluid element. The hierarchy of
cognitive apparatuses distinguishes foundational, primary, and secondary levels. Epistemic
light is the foundational fluid element that appears in the mode of each apparatus. The result
is the framework’s structural location of epistemic light in the hierarchy.

Third result: we are encompassed in epistemic light. The encompassment model states
why the subject is not fully independent of the conditions of its own legibility: dependence,
non-exteriority, and pervasion. The result is the framework’s epistemic location of the finite
subject.

Fourth result: three levels of knowledge. The three levels of knowledge—complete
knowledge of structure, partial knowledge, estimative knowledge—are defined with independent
criteria. The impossibility claim of the chapter covers the levels of instances and final
encompassment; the levels of structure and partial knowledge are real knowledge. The result
is the framework’s precise statement of what the finite subject can and cannot know.

Remark 17.22 (The Four Results Are Not Four Separate Claims). The four results are
aspects of one epistemic result: the framework’s location of epistemic light, of the finite subject,
and of the knowledge the finite subject can have. The first two results locate epistemic light;
the third locates the subject; the fourth states the knowledge available. The four together are
the chapter’s positive contribution.


17.13      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the full implications of encompassment. The results
are stated, but their further implications are left for later parts of the book.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the hierarchy of apparatuses
has other levels. It states the hierarchy as three levels (foundational, primary, secondary);
whether a fourth level exists is a question the chapter leaves open.
    Third, the chapter does not claim to have described what epistemic light is in itself. It
claims to have described the structural place of epistemic light, and the structural place is
what the framework’s architecture assigns. The question of what grounds epistemic light is
not addressed in the present chapter.

Remark 17.23 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed five things. It
has located epistemic light in the analytical framework, as the medium of relation belonging
to Pair 2, with a diagram and a worked example. It has classified cognitive apparatuses into
primary and secondary, and argued that epistemic light is the foundational fluid element
appearing in the mode of each apparatus. It has argued that we are encompassed in epistemic
light, with a model that states why the subject is not fully independent of the conditions of
its own legibility. It has distinguished three levels of knowledge with independent criteria,
and stated the impossibility claim precisely. And it has stated the positive epistemic result
of the chapter. The chapter’s contribution is the framework’s location of epistemic light in
the architecture, the model of encompassment, the three levels of knowledge, and the positive
result that the later parts of the book require.

A Question for Reflection
If we are encompassed in epistemic light, can we speak of an “experience of epistemic light”—or
is experience always experience of something other than epistemic light? What would it mean
to experience what makes experience possible?
    And consider the fish and the water—the scene that opened the chapter. The fish is in
the water, but does not know the water as an object; we are in epistemic light, but do not
know epistemic light as an object. Are the two cases the same? If they are, what does that
tell you about the difference between being in a medium and being related to an object? If
they are different, what does that tell you about the difference between a physical medium
and epistemic light?
17.14. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                               259


    And consider the three levels of knowledge (Section 17.8): which level does the chapter’s
impossibility claim cover, and which level is possible for the finite subject? Can you give
a further case in which the structural knowledge is possible but the complete knowledge of
instances is not? Finally, consider the diagram and the worked example (Sections 17.3.1
and 17.3.2): can you apply the two pairs to a case of your own choosing, and can you locate
epistemic light in it? A reader who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter;
a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter draws the final consequence of the definition. It distinguishes epistemic light
from what it conveys, and it argues that every explanation requires a conveyor, that without
epistemic light no explanation is possible, and that epistemic light is the condition of possibility
of every fluid element. The chapter after that states the desire to find, which the theorem of
Chapter 24 will prove.
