Chapter 18

The Desire to Find

Scope
This chapter states and proves a theorem about the structural relation by which an identity is
rendered legible in the reflection of its expression in another identity’s expression. The theorem
is stated in its epistemic form. Its proof uses the definition of manifestation (Chapter 13), the
definition of epistemic light as the medium of legible relation (Chapter 15), and the reflective
character of epistemic light (Chapter 16). It does not use the principle of expression; that
principle is argued in Chapter 38, and the theorem’s fuller form—which states that every
identity, manifest or not, stands in the relation of finding—is stated there. The theorem is
(T) in the form given here, and it is stated at the strength its premises support. Its claims
are epistemic; the terms “desire” and “finding,” which appear in the title and in the theorem,
are used in a purely structural sense, defined in this chapter; neither names a mental state, a
motivation, a want, a value, or an end. Section 18.5.1 states the definition of “desire” as a
technical term, together with the criterion that distinguishes it from psychological desire and
behavioral motivation, and lists the structural positions that the term occupies. The chapter
is silent on psychological and evaluative questions; the silence is not a denial, and it is stated
as a limit at the end of the chapter.


18.1     A Scene: The Speaker, the Listener, and the Reflection
Consider two people in conversation. One speaks; the other listens. The speaker says something
about herself—not a fact about the world, but something that reveals what she is like, what
she cares about, what she fears, what she hopes for. The listener hears the words and, in
hearing them, understands something about the speaker. The understanding is not the words;
the words are the expression. The understanding is the recognition of what the expression
expresses.
     What happens in the listener? The listener does not enter the speaker’s mind; the listener
does not have direct access to the speaker’s identity. The listener has the words, and from the
words the listener forms an impression—a partial, fallible, revisable impression of what the
speaker is like. The impression is not the speaker; it is a reconstruction, from the expression,
of the identity that the expression manifests.
     Now consider the reverse. The speaker, in speaking, is also listening to herself. She hears
her own words; she sees, in the listener’s response, something of what she has said. The
listener’s response is another expression, and the speaker, in hearing it, comes to understand
her own expression better. What she said, and how it was received, and what the reception
reveals about what she meant—the three are not separate. The listener’s response is a reflection
of the speaker’s expression, and in the reflection the speaker finds her expression rendered
legible in a new way.
262                                                             Chapter 18. The Desire to Find


    The scene is not about psychology. It is about a structural relation that holds between
expressions, whether or not the expressions belong to persons in conversation. Whenever
one expression reflects another, the reflection renders the reflected expression legible as the
expression of its source. And whenever an expression is rendered legible in this way, something
has been found—not the identity itself, which is never directly accessible, but the identity as
it appears in the reflection of its expression.
    The scene poses a question. What is the structure of this relation? Is it a contingent
feature of some expressions, or a structural feature of expression as such? And does the relation
carry any implication for what an identity is, or for how identities stand to one another? The
present chapter answers these questions. Its answer is a theorem: that every manifest identity
stands in a structural relation of finding, given the reflective character of epistemic light.

Remark 18.1 (The Scene Shows Two Directions of One Relation). The scene shows two
directions of one relation, and the distinction is worth marking. The first direction is ascending:
from the speaker’s expression to the listener’s understanding of the speaker. The second
is reflective: from the listener’s response back to the speaker’s understanding of her own
expression. The two directions are not two different relations; they are two ways in which one
relation of finding can run.

Remark 18.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the relation
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the theorem; it makes the theorem intelligible
before it is stated. The proof is given in Section 18.4, and the scene carries no weight in it.


18.2     The Question
The preceding chapters of this part have developed the structure of epistemic relations. Identity
was defined as the invariant an explanatory cognition holds fixed (Chapter 12); manifestation
was defined as the contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving cognitive
context (Chapter 13); context and perspective were distinguished (Chapter 14); epistemic light
was defined as the medium of legible relation (Chapter 15); epistemic light was sharpened
into an active structure of legibility (Chapter 16); and we were argued to be encompassed in
epistemic light, with the consequence that complete knowledge of epistemic light is impossible
at the levels of instances and final encompassment (Chapter 17).
    The present chapter asks a different kind of question. The previous chapters have argued
for what identity is, and for what the medium of its appearance is, and for what our relation
to that medium is. The present chapter asks how identities stand to one another—specifically,
how an identity is rendered legible in the expression of another identity.
    The question is: is there a structural relation by which every manifest identity is rendered
legible in the reflection of its expression in another identity’s expression? The chapter’s answer
is that there is, and that the relation is a consequence of the principles already established in
this part: the definition of manifestation, the definition of epistemic light, and the reflective
character of epistemic light.
    The chapter’s method is fourfold. First, it states the theorem, and defines the terms
“finding” and “desire” in the structural sense they will have in the argument. Second, it
proves the theorem from the three principles, distinguishing the logical part of the proof from
its interpretive part. Third, it defines “desire” as a technical term, with the criterion that
distinguishes it from psychological desire and behavioral motivation, and states its structural
content (Section 18.5.1). Fourth, it draws the consequences: the dependence of the theorem
on its premises, the distinction between finding through manifestation and finding through a
successive downward route, the two directions of finding, and a step-by-step example of the
process of finding.
18.3. The Theorem                                                                               263


Remark 18.3 (The Question Is About Relations Among Identities). The question the chapter
asks is not about what an identity is (that is Chapter 12), nor about what the medium of its
appearance is (that is Chapters 15–17), but about how identities stand to one another through
their expressions. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of a single identity’s
relation to its manifestation, and the structure of the relation between two identities through
their manifestations. The present chapter is concerned with the second.

Remark 18.4 (The Theorem Is in Its Epistemic Form). The theorem is stated in its epistemic
form: it concerns manifest identities, and the reflection of their expressions in another expression.
The fuller form—which concerns every identity, manifest or not, and which depends on the
principle of expression—is stated in Chapter 38. The present chapter states the theorem at
the strength its premises support, and it does not claim more than that.


18.3      The Theorem
18.3.1     The Premises of the Theorem
The theorem has exactly three premises, and they are stated here so that the reader can
identify each in the proof.

(P1) The Manifestation Premise (Chapter 13, Definition 13.1): every manifest identity appears
     in a receiving cognitive context, and its appearance is a manifestation in the sense defined
     there.

(P2) The Epistemic Light Premise (Chapter 15, Definition 15.1): the appearance of an identity
     in a receiving cognitive context is conveyed by epistemic light, which is the condition of
     possibility of legible relation.

(P3) The Reflectivity Premise (Chapter 16, Principle 16.1 and the three-directions re-reading):
     epistemic light has a reflective direction; the structure-edge between two manifestations
     in the same receiving context is activated according to the rules of the context.

    The three premises are established in the chapters named. The theorem uses no fourth
premise. The premise that connects the three to the conclusion is the interpretive premise
stated in Section 18.4.1: it identifies the rendering of an expression in the reflection of another
expression with the relation of finding. The interpretive premise is the chapter’s contribution,
and it is distinguished from the three premises so that the logical part of the proof is visible.

18.3.2     The Theorem Stated
Theorem 18.1 (The Desire to Find). (T) Given (P1) the Manifestation Premise, (P2) the
Epistemic Light Premise, and (P3) the Reflectivity Premise, every manifest identity stands in
a structural relation of finding: it is, in its manifestation, such that it is rendered legible in
the reflection of its expression in the expression of another identity.

    The theorem has three premises and one conclusion. The conclusion is stated in terms of
“finding,” which is defined in Section 18.5, and in terms of “rendered legible,” which is defined
in Chapter 15. The conclusion’s scope is manifest identities: identities that have appeared in
some receiving cognitive context. The theorem does not state that every identity (manifest or
not) stands in the relation; that stronger form depends on the principle of expression, which is
established in Chapter 38.

Remark 18.5 (The Scope of the Conclusion). The conclusion’s scope is exact. It states that
every manifest identity stands in the relation of finding; it does not state that every identity
264                                                              Chapter 18. The Desire to Find


(including the unmanifest) stands in the relation. The scope is the scope of the three premises:
the premises concern manifest identities, and the conclusion is stated at that scope. A reader
who reads the conclusion as a claim about every identity has extended its scope beyond what
the premises support; a reader who reads it as a claim about manifest identities has read it
correctly.
Remark 18.6 (The Logical and the Interpretive Parts of the Theorem). The theorem has
two parts, and the distinction is worth marking. The logical part is the derivation of the
conclusion from (P1)–(P3): this is the part that the proof establishes, and it is the part that is
(T) relative to the premises. The interpretive part is the identification of the rendered-legibility
of an expression in the reflection of another expression with the relation of finding: this is
the chapter’s contribution, and it is stated at the strength of a stipulation (the definition of
“finding”). A reader who accepts the three premises and the interpretive stipulation has the
theorem; a reader who accepts the premises and rejects the interpretive stipulation has the
derivation of a relation, but not the name “finding” for it. The distinction is the distinction
between the logical structure and the vocabulary the chapter uses to state it.
Remark 18.7 (The Theorem Is Structural, Not Empirical). The theorem is not an empirical
claim about how often identities are actually found. It is a structural claim about the relation
between expression and legibility. It says that a manifest identity’s expression is, by its nature,
legible in the reflection of another expression; it does not say that every manifest identity is,
in fact, reflected in another’s expression, or that every reflection is adequate.
Remark 18.8 (The Theorem Is Conditional on the Principle of Expression). The stronger
form of the theorem—which states that every identity, manifest or not, stands in the relation
of finding—depends on the principle of expression, which is argued in Chapter 38. The present
chapter does not claim the stronger form; it claims the epistemic form, and it notes that the
stronger form is established later.


18.4      The Proof
Proof of Theorem 18.1.       1. By (P1), every manifest identity appears in a receiving cognitive
      context.

   2. By (P2), the appearance of an identity in a receiving cognitive context is conveyed by
      epistemic light, which is the condition of possibility of legible relation.

   3. By (P3), epistemic light has a reflective direction: the structure-edge between two
      manifestations in the same receiving context is activated according to the rules of the
      context.

   4. From (1)–(3): the expression of a manifest identity is reflected; its manifestation, conveyed
      by epistemic light, activates a reflective edge in the receiving context.

   5. By the interpretive premise (Section 18.4.1): the rendering-legible of an expression in
      the reflection of another expression is what the chapter calls finding.

   6. Conclusion: every manifest identity stands in the structural relation of finding.


    Steps (1)–(4) are the logical part of the proof: they derive, from the three premises, the
conclusion that the expression of every manifest identity is reflected in the receiving context.
Step (5) is the interpretive part: it identifies the reflected expression with the relation of
finding. The two parts are distinguished so that the reader can see what is derived and what
is stipulated.
18.5. “Desire” Is Structural                                                                   265


18.4.1     The Interpretive Premise
Definition 18.1 (The Interpretive Premise of Finding). (A) Finding is the relation in which
an expression is rendered legible as the expression of its source, through the reflection of the
expression in another expression in the same receiving context. The definition is a stipulation
of the framework’s vocabulary; it identifies the relation derived in steps (1)–(4) with the name
“finding.”

    The definition is (A): it is stipulated. Its justification is that the relation derived in steps
(1)–(4) has the structure that the ordinary word “finding” names, and that the framework
needs a name for that structure. Its cost is that the ordinary word carries connotations that
the stipulation does not adopt; the framework states the cost in the section on the technical
definition of “desire” (Section 18.5.1), and it states what the alternative vocabulary would be.

Remark 18.9 (The Proof Does Not Assume the Conclusion). The proof does not assume
the conclusion. It assumes the three premises, and it derives, in steps (1)–(4), the conclusion
that the expression of every manifest identity is reflected. The derivation is not trivial—it
requires the identification of the reflection of an expression with the rendering-legible of
the expression—but it is not circular. The premises do not depend on the conclusion; the
conclusion depends on the premises and on the interpretive stipulation.

Remark 18.10 (The Proof Does Not Use the Principle of Expression). The proof does not use
the principle of expression. The principle is needed for the stronger form of the theorem, which
concerns every identity, manifest or not. The present chapter’s theorem concerns manifest
identities, and its proof uses only the definitions of Part III and the reflective character of
epistemic light.

Remark 18.11 (The Proof Is a Combination of Three Principles and an Interpretive Stipula-
tion). The proof is a combination of three principles and an interpretive stipulation, and the
combination is worth marking. The three principles (manifestation, epistemic light, reflective
character) are independently established; the interpretive stipulation is the chapter’s contribu-
tion. The proof shows that when the three principles and the stipulation are taken together,
the relation of finding follows. The combination is not a trivial consequence; it requires the
recognition that the reflection of an expression is the rendering-legible of the expression, and
that recognition is the chapter’s contribution.


18.5      “Desire” Is Structural
The theorem’s title uses the word “desire,” and the word must be fixed. In this book, “desire”
is a structural term. It names the direction of the relation by which an identity is rendered
legible in what reflects its expression. It is not a mental state, a conation, a want, or a value,
and the theorem does not move from the structure of identity to the psychology of a subject.
    The word “desire” is retained because the relation has the structure of a direction: the
identity is, as it were, oriented toward its own legibility in the reflection of another. The
orientation is structural, not psychological.

Remark 18.12 (The Term “Finding” Is Structural Too). The term “finding” is likewise
structural. It names the relation by which the reflection of an expression renders the expression
legible as the expression of its source. It is not a psychological event—not an act of discovery,
not a moment of recognition, not a feeling of having found. It is a structural relation: the
expression is rendered legible, in the reflection, as the expression of its source. Whether
anyone experiences the rendering is a separate question; the relation holds whether or not it is
experienced.
266                                                             Chapter 18. The Desire to Find


Remark 18.13 (The Two Terms Are Structural, Not Metaphorical). The two terms “desire”
and “finding” are structural, not metaphorical. The framework does not use them metaphor-
ically; it uses them to name structural relations, and it states the sense of each at its first
occurrence.

Remark 18.14 (No Psychological or Evaluative Claim). The chapter makes no psychological
or evaluative claim. It does not say that identities want to be found, or that finding is good,
or that the relation of finding is more important than other relations among identities. It
says that the relation of finding holds structurally, given the definitions of Part III and the
reflective character of epistemic light, and it leaves the psychological and evaluative questions
to other inquiries.

18.5.1      The Technical Definition of “Desire” and Its Criterion
The word “desire” is a technical term in this chapter, and the technical sense must be stated
once, at the strength of a definition, together with the criterion that distinguishes it from
psychological desire and behavioral motivation.

Definition 18.2 (Desire, Structural Sense). (A) In this book, desire is the structural orientation
of a manifest identity toward its own legibility in the reflection of its expression in another
identity’s expression. The orientation is structural, not psychological: it is a position in the
relation of finding, not a state of a subject.

      The definition has three components, and each is worth marking.

First component: the orientation is toward legibility. The orientation is not toward
being found by someone; it is toward being legible, which is the structural condition that
makes finding possible.

Second component: the orientation is in the reflection of the expression. The
orientation is not toward the source’s own expression; it is toward the reflection of that
expression in another expression.

Third component: the orientation is structural, not psychological. The orientation
is a position in the relation of finding, not a state of a subject. A subject may or may not
experience the orientation; the orientation holds whether or not it is experienced.

18.5.2      The Criterion of Distinction
The definition of “desire” is easily conflated with psychological desire and behavioral motivation.
The criterion that distinguishes them is stated here, so that the reader can identify, in a given
case, whether the structural sense applies.

Definition 18.3 (The Criterion of Structural Desire). (A) A relation is a case of structural
desire, rather than of psychological desire or behavioral motivation, when it satisfies all three
of the following conditions:

(D1) Independence of experience: the relation holds whether or not any subject experiences it.
     Psychological desire requires a subject who desires; structural desire does not.

(D2) Independence of motivation: the relation holds whether or not any subject is motivated
     by it. Behavioral motivation requires a subject who is moved to act; structural desire
     does not.
18.5. “Desire” Is Structural                                                                    267


(D3) Structural orientation: the relation is a position in the structure of expression and
     reflection—the orientation of a manifest identity toward its legibility in the reflection of
     another expression. Psychological desire is a state of a subject; behavioral motivation is
     a disposition to act; structural desire is neither.

The three conditions are (A): they are the framework’s stipulation of the criterion. A case
that satisfies all three is a case of structural desire; a case that fails any one is not (or is not
only) a case of structural desire.

    The criterion is (A): it is stipulated. Its justification is that it makes the structural sense
identifiable in cases; its cost is that some cases will satisfy the criterion and also satisfy the
conditions of psychological desire or behavioral motivation, and the framework does not claim
that the structural sense excludes the psychological or the behavioral. A case can be a case of
structural desire and also a case in which a subject desires; the framework’s claim is about the
structural sense, not about the exclusion of the others.

    The table states the criterion in a form that can be applied. A case that satisfies the
structural-desire column and not the other two is a case of structural desire alone; a case
that satisfies all three is a case in which the structural sense applies, and the psychological or
behavioral senses may also apply.

Remark 18.15 (What Is Lost by Using the Word “Desire”). The word “desire,” even as a
technical term, carries psychological connotations. What is lost by using the word is the ease
of reading that a more neutral term would provide. What is gained is the continuity with the
framework’s earlier and later uses, and the recognition that the structural orientation has the
form of a direction. The loss is real, and the framework states it.

Remark 18.16 (What Is Not Lost by Using the Word “Desire”). What is not lost is the
structural content. The definition states the three components of the structural orientation,
and the criterion distinguishes the structural sense from the psychological and the behavioral.
The psychological connotations of the word are not used in any premise of the theorem, and
no conclusion of the theorem depends on them.

Remark 18.17 (The Alternative Vocabulary). The framework considered a neutral alternative:
structural orientation toward legibility, or legibility-orientation for short. The alternative has
the advantage of being unambiguously structural; it has the disadvantage of being a coined
term, with no continuity in the framework’s vocabulary. The framework retains the word
“desire” for three reasons: (i) the structural orientation has the form of a direction, which the
word “desire” names; (ii) the word is used consistently in the framework’s later chapters; (iii)
the technical definition and the criterion are stated at the first occurrence, and the reader who
has followed them has the structural sense. The alternative is offered as a comparison, not as
a replacement.

18.6     The Dependence of the Theorem
The theorem depends on its premises, and the dependence has a consequence that must be
stated: the theorem cannot be used to support the premises.
    The theorem is a consequence of the definitions of Part III, the reflective character of
epistemic light, and the interpretive premise. To use the theorem to support the definitions,
the reflective character, or the interpretive premise would be to use a consequence to support
its own premise, and the framework does not do that.

Remark 18.18 (The Direction of Dependence). The dependence runs from the premises to
the theorem, not from the theorem to the premises. The reader who accepts the premises
should accept the theorem; the reader who does not accept the premises is not addressed by
the theorem.

Remark 18.19 (The Relation to Chapter 38). The stronger form of the theorem depends on
the principle of expression, which is argued in Chapter 38. The present chapter’s theorem does
not. The two forms of the theorem are related, but the relation is one-directional: the stronger
form entails the epistemic form, but the epistemic form does not entail the stronger form.


18.7     Manifestation as a Condition of Finding
The theorem has an implication: finding requires manifestation. If same-context identities
could find one another directly—without any expression—expression would not be needed for
finding. They find one another only through what each expresses.
    The implication is that manifestation is a condition of finding. An identity is found through
its manifestation; the manifestation is what is reflected, and the reflection is what renders
the identity legible. Without manifestation, there would be nothing to reflect, and without
reflection, nothing would be found.
    Two things must be separated, and the distinction is the section’s principal contribution.

First thing: finding through manifestation. An identity is rendered legible through its
manifestation. The manifestation is the expression; the reflection of the manifestation is what
renders the expression legible. The first is retained: it is what the theorem establishes.

Second thing: finding through a successive downward route. Finding might be
thought to require the identity to be manifested in every context between the source and the
finding. The theorem does not require this, and the framework does not hold it. The identity
may be manifested directly in the context in which the finding occurs, without passing through
every context between. This is the non-necessity of sequential passage (Chapter 9), applied to
the relation of finding.

18.7.1    A Step-by-Step Example of the Process of Finding
The distinction between the two things is abstract; the following example states the process of
finding step by step, so that the reader can see the distinction at work.

The case. A reader encounters an anonymous manuscript and wants to know who wrote it.
The manuscript is the manifestation; the author’s identity is the source.

Step 1: the manifestation is present. The reader has the manuscript. It is the expression
of the author’s identity, conveyed by epistemic light in the mode of the reader’s cognitive
context (a literary context, with its rules of reading).
18.8. The Two Directions of Finding                                                             269


Step 2: the reflection is activated. The reader’s cognitive context includes other expres-
sions: other manuscripts, letters, biographical documents. The reflective edge between the
manuscript and one of the other expressions is activated: the manuscript’s style resembles the
style of a known author’s letters.


Step 3: the expression is rendered legible. The activation of the reflective edge renders
the manuscript legible as the expression of that author’s identity. The reader sees, in the
manuscript, the features that the author’s other expressions display.


Step 4: the finding is achieved. The reader’s finding is the relation in which the manuscript
is rendered legible as the expression of the author’s identity, through the reflection of the
manuscript in the author’s other expressions. The finding is not the identity itself; it is the
identity as it appears in the reflection of its expression.


The distinction at work. The finding does not require the author’s identity to be manifested
in every context between the author and the reader. It requires only that the manuscript be
reflected in another expression in the reader’s context. The reflection is direct; the manifestation
is the manuscript; the finding is through manifestation, not through a successive downward
route. The example shows the distinction in a single case.

Remark 18.20 (The Example Shows the Process, Not a Sequence in Time). The four steps
are stated in order, but the order is analytical, not temporal. The manifestation, the reflection,
the rendering-legible, and the finding are four structural positions in one relation, not four
stages that unfold in time. The reader who reads the steps as a temporal sequence has misread
the example; the reader who reads them as a structural decomposition of the finding has read
it correctly.

Remark 18.21 (Why the Distinction Matters). The distinction matters for the parts of the
book that follow. When the book treats the epistemic economy of cognition (Part VI), it
will speak of finding through manifestation, not of finding through successive descent. The
distinction is what allows the framework to say that finding is structural, without committing
itself to a sequential metaphysic of descent.

Remark 18.22 (The Distinction Opens a Space). The distinction opens a space for what the
framework does not describe. If finding is through manifestation and not through successive
descent, then the relation of finding is compatible with a direct action that does not pass
through the intermediate contexts. The framework does not describe such a direct action, and
it does not deny it.


18.8     The Two Directions of Finding
The structural relation of finding has two directions, and the distinction is worth stating
because the two are easily confused.


First direction: the ascending direction. The structural direction of ascending epistemic
light, from a manifestation toward its source. When a listener hears a speaker’s words and
understands something about the speaker, the understanding is in the ascending direction:
from the expression back to the source.
270                                                              Chapter 18. The Desire to Find


Second direction: the reflective direction. The structural direction of reflective epistemic
light, from one manifestation to another in the same context. When a listener responds to
a speaker, and the speaker hears the response and comes to understand her own expression
better, the exchange is in the reflective direction.
    The ascending and the reflective directions are not two separate relations; they are two
directions of a single structural relation of finding.

Remark 18.23 (The Two Directions Are One Relation). The distinction between the two
directions is analytical, not substantial. The relation of finding is one relation, and the two
directions are two ways the relation can run. In any given encounter, the relation may run in
one direction, or in the other, or in both.

Remark 18.24 (No Claim About Emotion or Value). The description of the two directions
is structural. It says that the relation of finding can run in the ascending direction or in the
reflective direction, and it says what each direction relates. It does not say that one direction is
more valuable than the other, or that either direction is accompanied by emotion, motivation,
or any psychological state.


18.9     The Epistemic Conditions of Finding
The chapter’s positive contribution is the statement of the epistemic conditions under which
finding holds, stated within the chapter and without appeal to any external justification.

First condition: manifestation. Finding requires that the identity be manifested in some
receiving cognitive context. Without a manifestation, there is no expression to be reflected,
and no finding to be achieved. The condition is the condition of the theorem’s first premise
(P1).

Second condition: conveyance by epistemic light. Finding requires that the manifesta-
tion be conveyed by epistemic light, the condition of possibility of legible relation. Without
epistemic light, the manifestation is present but not legible, and the finding cannot be achieved.
The condition is the condition of the theorem’s second premise (P2).

Third condition: reflection in another expression. Finding requires that the manifes-
tation be reflected in another expression in the same receiving context. Without the reflection,
the manifestation is present and legible, but not rendered legible as the expression of its source.
The condition is the condition of the theorem’s third premise (P3) and of the interpretive
stipulation.

Fourth condition: the interpretive recognition. Finding requires that the reflection
be recognized as the rendering-legible of the expression. The recognition is the interpretive
stipulation of Section 18.4.1; without it, the relation derived from (P1)–(P3) is a relation of
reflection, but not yet the relation of finding. The condition is the condition of the chapter’s
interpretive contribution.
    The four conditions are the epistemic conditions of finding, stated within the chapter.
They are the conditions under which the theorem’s conclusion holds; they do not appeal to
any external justification, and they do not defer the conditions to another work. A reader who
satisfies the four conditions in a case has a case of finding; a reader who satisfies fewer has a
case in which some condition of finding is missing.

Remark 18.25 (The Four Conditions Are the Chapter’s Contribution). The four conditions
are the chapter’s positive contribution to the account of finding. They are not new premises of
18.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                    271


the theorem; they are the statement of what the theorem’s premises require, made explicit as
conditions. The first three are the conditions of the three premises; the fourth is the condition of
the interpretive stipulation. Together they state what finding is, in the framework’s vocabulary,
and what a case must satisfy for finding to hold.



Remark 18.26 (The Conditions Are Not Criteria of Psychological Experience). The four
conditions are epistemic conditions, not criteria of psychological experience. A subject may
satisfy the four conditions without experiencing the finding; a subject may experience something
like finding without satisfying the four conditions. The conditions are about the structure
of the relation, not about the psychology of the subject. The distinction is the distinction
between the epistemic conditions and the psychological experience; the framework keeps it
apart.




18.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the full account of what finding consists in, beyond the
four epistemic conditions stated in Section 18.9. The account of the content of finding, in any
particular case, is left to the parts of the book that treat the epistemic economy of cognition.
   Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether every identity is, in fact, found.
The theorem says that every manifest identity stands in the relation of finding; it does not say
that the relation is actualized for every manifest identity.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between finding and viability. The two
are related: viability is the structural character of the relation between an identity and its
manifestations (Chapter 36); finding is the structural relation by which an identity is rendered
legible in the reflection of its expression. Whether the two relations are the same, or whether
one is a condition of the other, is a question the chapter leaves open.
    Fourth, the chapter does not develop the connection between the theorem of the desire to
find and the theorem of unknownness (Chapter 19). The two theorems are related, but the
connection is stated in its own place, in Chapter 19.



Remark 18.27 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed seven things. It
has stated the theorem of the desire to find, in its epistemic form, with the three premises
made explicit and the scope of the conclusion stated. It has proved the theorem, distinguishing
the logical part of the proof from its interpretive part. It has distinguished the structural
sense of “desire” and “finding” from the psychological and the behavioral, with an explicit
criterion (D1)–(D3). It has defined “desire” as a technical term, and stated what is lost and
what is not lost by using the word. It has stated a step-by-step example of the process of
finding. It has stated the four epistemic conditions of finding, within the chapter and without
external justification. And it has stated the two directions of finding (ascending, reflective)
as directions of one relation. The chapter’s contribution is the theorem itself, the technical
definition and criterion of desire, the epistemic conditions of finding, and the distinctions that
the later parts of the book require.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you understood something about a person from what they said or
did. What was rendered legible in that moment? Was it the person’s identity, or the person’s
expression, or both? What does your answer tell you about the difference between finding and
18.11. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                              273


knowing?
     And consider the step-by-step example of Section 18.7.1: the reader, the anonymous
manuscript, and the author’s other expressions. Can you identify the four epistemic conditions
of finding in the example? Can you give a case in which one of the four conditions is missing,
and show what is lost when it is missing? What does your answer tell you about the difference
between finding and a mere correlation of expressions?
     Finally, consider the criterion of structural desire (Definition 18.3): can you give a case in
which the structural sense applies, and the psychological and behavioral senses do not? Can
you give a case in which all three senses apply? What does your answer tell you about the
difference between the structural sense and the ordinary sense, and about what is lost and
what is not lost by using the word “desire”? A reader who can answer all three questions has
understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before
them.

The next chapter states the theorem of the unknownness of same-category identities: the
structural condition under which reflection among identities in the same context is possible.
The present chapter has argued that every manifest identity stands in the relation of finding;
the next chapter argues that the relation requires the identities to be, in a certain structural
sense, unknown to one another.

Chapter 19

Unknownness of Same-Category
Identities

Scope
This chapter states a theorem about the structural condition under which reflection among
identities in the same cognitive context is possible, and it distinguishes two kinds of unknown-
ness. It separates three senses of impossibility (Section 19.6), so that the theorem’s claim is
stated at the precision the argument supports, and it distinguishes structural unknownness,
current non-recognition, and lack of information (Section 19.3), so that the theorem’s premise
is stated more narrowly. Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter is silent on questions
of emotion, love, or value, the silence is not a denial but a recognition that the epistemic
description is not the whole of what can be said. Where the chapter speaks of “finding,”
“direction,” “individuation,” “reflection,” or “unknownness,” these are structural terms; their
sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the previous chapters.


19.1     A Scene: The Two Mirrors
Consider two mirrors facing each other. Each reflects the other, and in the reflection each
shows what the other is. But notice what happens at the limit: if the two mirrors were
perfectly aligned, with nothing between them, and if each could see the other as clearly as it
sees itself, the reflection would collapse. The mirrors would cease to be two mirrors and would
become, in effect, one surface reflecting itself. The image of the other would be the image of
the self, and the image of the self would be the image of the other. There would be nothing
left to reflect, because there would be nothing between the two that could be reflected.
    The collapse does not happen with two ordinary mirrors, because the two mirrors are
separated: by distance, by angle, by the air between them, by the frame that holds them. The
separation is what makes the reflection possible. If the separation were removed—if the two
mirrors were fused into one—the reflection would cease. The two mirrors would be one mirror,
and one mirror cannot reflect itself.
    Now consider two identities in the same cognitive context. Each expresses itself; each
is rendered legible in the reflection of its expression in the other’s expression. This is the
relation of finding, stated in the previous chapter. But the relation of finding requires that the
two identities remain distinct. If the two were fused into one—if each had direct access to
the other, without the mediation of expression—there would be no reflection between them,
because reflection requires a relation between distinct terms. The two would be one, and one
cannot find itself in the reflection of another.
    The scene poses a question. What is the structural condition under which the relation of
finding is possible between two same-context identities? The framework’s answer is that the
276                                     Chapter 19. Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


condition is unknownness: each must be, in a certain structural sense, unknown to the other.
The unknownness is not a defect; it is the condition of possibility of the relation. The present
chapter states the theorem, distinguishes the three kinds of unknownness that the theorem
involves (Section 19.3), and draws its consequences.

Remark 19.1 (The Scene Shows That Separation Is the Condition of Reflection). The scene
shows a structural point that the theorem will apply to identities: reflection requires separation.
The two mirrors reflect each other because they are distinct and separated; if they were
fused, the reflection would collapse. The framework’s claim is that the same structural point
holds for identities: reflection requires distinctness, and distinctness is what the theorem calls
“unknownness.”

Remark 19.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the theorem; it makes the theorem intelligible
before it is stated. The proof is given in Section 19.5, and the scene carries no weight in it.


19.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated and proved the theorem of the desire to find: given the definitions
of Part III and the reflective character of epistemic light, every manifest identity stands in the
structural relation of finding, in which its expression is rendered legible in the reflection of
another’s expression. The theorem established that the relation of finding holds for manifest
identities; it did not yet ask what the relation requires of the identities it relates.
    The present chapter asks that question. What must be true of two identities, for the
relation of finding to hold between them? The framework’s answer is that they must be distinct,
and that their distinctness, in the structural sense the chapter will define, is unknownness.
    Two things must be distinguished at the outset, because the word “unknownness” is easily
misread.

First: unknownness is structural, not epistemic. It is not the state of a subject who
has not yet learned something. It is a structural feature of the relation between two distinct
identities: each is not directly accessible to the other, and the inaccessibility is what makes
expression necessary.

Second: unknownness is not a defect. It is not a lack that expression might eventually
fill. It is the condition of possibility of expression, and therefore of finding.
     The chapter treats the theorem in the next sections, distinguishes the senses of impossibility
in Section 19.6, distinguishes the three kinds of unknownness in Section 19.3, argues that
finding requires distinctness, and states the two structural directions of finding.

Remark 19.3 (The Question Is About the Condition of the Relation, Not Its Content).
The question the chapter asks is not about what the relation of finding amounts to in any
particular case; it is about the condition under which the relation is possible. The distinction
is the distinction between the condition of a relation and its content. The present chapter is
concerned with the first.


19.3     The Three Kinds of Unknownness
The word “unknownness” covers three different things, and the theorem uses it in only one of
the three senses. The three must be distinguished before the theorem can be stated precisely.
19.4. The Theorem                                                                                 277


Definition 19.1 (Structural Unknownness). Structural unknownness is the feature of the
relation between two distinct identities by which neither is directly accessible to the other:
each is available to the other only through its manifestation, and the manifestation is not the
identity. Structural unknownness is not a lack of information; it is the condition of possibility
of expression.

Definition 19.2 (Current Non-Recognition). Current non-recognition is the state of a subject
who does not, at a given time, recognize an identity that is in fact available through its
manifestation. Current non-recognition is a contingent fact about the subject’s present
condition; it can be removed by more manifestation or by a better grasp of the manifestation.

Definition 19.3 (Lack of Information). Lack of information is the state of a subject who has
not been presented with the manifestations that would be needed to identify an identity. Lack
of information is a contingent fact about the subject’s occasion; it can be removed by more
manifestation.

   The three definitions distinguish three things. Structural unknownness is the condition of
the relation; current non-recognition and lack of information are states of the subject, and
they are contingent. The theorem’s claim is about the first, not about the second or the third.

Remark 19.4 (The Three Kinds Are Not Three Degrees). The three kinds of unknownness
are not three degrees of one thing; they are three different things, with different criteria.
Structural unknownness has no degree: the relation between distinct identities either has it
or does not, and it has it whenever the identities are distinct. Current non-recognition and
lack of information have degrees: a subject can be more or less non-recognizing, more or less
lacking in information. The theorem’s claim is about the undegreed kind; the other two kinds
are the ones that progress can reduce.


19.4      The Theorem
Theorem 19.1 (Unknownness). (T) Given (P1) the Manifestation Premise (Chapter 13),
(P2) the Reflective Character of epistemic light (Chapter 16), and (P3) the Finding Premise
(Chapter 18, Theorem 18.1), the structural unknownness of same-context identities is the
structural condition of possibility of reflection, not a defect. If the other were directly accessible,
there would be no mirror; there would be no reflection. Structural unknownness is the structural
condition of individuation, and individuation is the structural condition of reflection among
distinct identities.

    The theorem has three premises and one conclusion. The premises are narrower than in
the earlier form of the theorem: the theorem no longer presupposes that “the other must be
unknown” in a general sense, but that the structural unknownness of same-context identities
is what makes reflection possible. The distinction between structural unknownness and the
other two kinds (Section 19.3) is what makes the premise precise.
    The theorem has two parts. The first part is negative: structural unknownness is not a
defect. The second part is positive: structural unknownness is the structural condition of
possibility of reflection. The two parts are not the same claim.
    The theorem is (T): it is argued from the three premises. The argument is given in the
next section.

Remark 19.5 (The Theorem Is About Same-Context Identities). The theorem concerns
identities in the same cognitive context. Its claim is not that identities in different contexts are
structurally unknown to one another, though they may be, but that the structural unknownness
of identities in the same context is what makes reflection possible among them.
278                                     Chapter 19. Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


Remark 19.6 (The Premises Are Narrower Than in the Earlier Form). The theorem’s premises
are narrower than in the earlier form. The earlier form used the premise that “the other
must be unknown,” which was ambiguous among the three kinds. The present form uses
(P1)–(P3), each of which is established in a specific chapter, and the conclusion is stated in
terms of structural unknownness, not in terms of unknownness in general. The narrowing is
the chapter’s contribution to the precision of the theorem.


19.5      The Proof
Proof of Theorem 19.1.     1. By (P1), every manifest identity is available to another only
      through its manifestation; the manifestation is not the identity.

   2. By (P2), epistemic light has a reflective direction: the structure-edge between two
      manifestations in the same context is activated, and the activation renders the expression
      legible.

   3. By (P3), every manifest identity stands in the relation of finding, in which its expression
      is rendered legible in the reflection of another’s expression.

   4. The reflection that (P3) establishes is a reflection between two distinct identities: if the
      two were not distinct, there would be no relation between them for the reflection to be
      of (the mirror case).

   5. The distinctness that the reflection requires is the structural unknownness of Defini-
      tion 19.1: each identity is available to the other only through its manifestation, and the
      manifestation is not the identity.

   6. Conclusion: structural unknownness is the structural condition of possibility of reflection,
      not a defect.


    The proof’s force is in step (4). The mirror case shows that reflection requires distinct
terms; if the two identities were not distinct, there would be nothing for the reflection to relate.
Step (5) identifies the distinctness with structural unknownness, in the sense of Definition 19.1.
The identification is not a new premise; it is the statement of what the distinctness consists in.
    The proof does not use current non-recognition or lack of information (Definitions 19.2
and 19.3). Those are states of the subject, and they are contingent; the theorem is about the
structure of the relation, not about the subject’s states. The three kinds of unknownness are
distinguished so that the proof uses only the first.

Remark 19.7 (The Proof Is Relative to the Three Premises). The proof depends on (P1)–(P3).
It cannot be used to support those premises. The dependence is one-directional: the theorem
of unknownness is a consequence of the three premises, not a premise of them.

Remark 19.8 (The Proof Does Not Use the Finitude of the Subject). The proof does not use
the finitude of the subject (Chapter 3). The structural unknownness is a feature of the relation
between distinct identities, not a limitation of a finite subject. A subject that is not finite
would still encounter the other through the other’s expression, because the other’s identity is
not directly accessible to any subject that is not the other.


19.6      The Vocabulary of Impossibility
The theorem’s conclusion is easily over-read. Three senses of impossibility must be distin-
guished.
19.7. The Table of Kinds of Unknownness                                                      279


Definition 19.4 (In Principle Impossible). A limit is in principle impossible when no possible
development of the subject’s capacities, tools, or context could remove it. The limit is entailed
by the structure of the subject’s relation to the object.


Definition 19.5 (Impossible with Current Tools). A limit is impossible with current tools
when the subject’s present capacities, tools, or context cannot remove it, but a possible
development could.


Definition 19.6 (Impossible for the Finite Subject). A limit is impossible for the finite subject
when the subject’s finitude—its occupation of finitely many contexts, its completion of finitely
many acts of reconstruction (Chapter 3)—entails that the limit cannot be removed.


    The three definitions distinguish three kinds of limit, and the theorem of unknownness
claims the first and the third, not the second.



The structural unknownness is in principle impossible to remove. The structural
unknownness of one identity to another is not a shortage of manifestation that more mani-
festation could fill. It is the structural fact that one identity is not another; no amount of
expression, however complete, can turn one identity into another.



The structural unknownness is also impossible for the finite subject. The finite
subject occupies finitely many contexts and completes finitely many acts of reconstruction.
Even if the structural unknownness were not in principle impossible, it would be impossible
for the finite subject to remove it, because the subject could not survey all the contexts in
which the other’s manifestations could be realized.



Current non-recognition and lack of information are impossible only with current
tools. Current non-recognition and lack of information are not structural; they are limits of
the subject’s present condition. A possible development could reduce them.


Remark 19.9 (The Vocabulary and the Theorem). The vocabulary of impossibility is the
chapter’s contribution to the precision of the theorem. The theorem claims that the structural
unknownness is (i) in principle impossible to remove, and (ii) impossible for the finite subject.
The theorem does not claim that current non-recognition or lack of information is impossible;
it claims that those can in principle be reduced.

19.8     Unknownness and Manifestational Partiality
The theorem states that structural unknownness is the condition of reflection. Two aspects of
the condition must be distinguished.

First aspect: structural unknownness. The other is unknown by the structure of
individuation itself. The unknownness cannot be removed by more manifestation, because it
is not a shortage of manifestation; it is the structural fact that one identity is not another.

Second aspect: manifestational partiality. The manifestation of an identity in a receiving
context is partial, because the receiving context’s capacity is finite (Chapter 13). The partiality
19.9. Finding Requires Distinctness                                                          281


is a feature of the manifestation, not of the identity; it is what the identity’s appearance in a
finite context can be.
    The two aspects are related. Structural unknownness is the condition under which
manifestation is necessary; manifestational partiality is the form that the manifestation takes
under that condition. The manifestation is necessary because the identity is structurally
unknown; the manifestation is partial because the receiving context is finite. The two together
are what the relation of finding works with.
Remark 19.12 (Partiality Is a Structural Feature, Not a Defect). That a manifestation gives
only a partial knowledge of its source does not make the manifestation a defective instance of
its kind. The partiality is structural: a manifestation is the appearance of an identity in a
receiving cognitive context, and the receiving context’s capacity determines how much of the
identity can appear (Chapter 13).
Remark 19.13 (Unknownness Is Not Ignorance). The word “unknownness” might suggest
ignorance—the state of a subject who does not know what could be known. The theorem’s
unknownness is not ignorance. Ignorance is the kind of unknownness that current non-
recognition and lack of information name; it can in principle be reduced. The theorem’s
unknownness is structural; it is not a state of the subject but a feature of the relation.


19.9     Finding Requires Distinctness
A structural implication of the theorem is stated in this section. It is stated as an independent
argument, so that the relation among distinctness, recognition, and the possibility of finding is
made explicit.
Principle 19.1 (Distinctness Is the Condition of Finding). (T) Finding, in the structural
sense of Chapter 18, requires the distinctness of the identities related. If the two identities
were fused, there would be no reflection between them, and therefore no finding.
Argument for the Principle.      1. Finding is the relation in which an expression is rendered
     legible as the expression of its source, through the reflection of the expression in another
     expression (Chapter 18, Definition 18.1).

   2. Reflection is a relation between two distinct expressions: the reflected and the reflecting
      (Chapter 16, the reflective direction).

   3. If the two identities were fused, there would be no two expressions: there would be one
      expression, and one expression cannot reflect itself (the mirror case).

   4. Therefore, finding requires the distinctness of the identities related.

   5. The distinctness is what the theorem calls structural unknownness (Definition 19.1).

   6. Therefore, structural unknownness is the condition of finding.


    The argument’s force is in step (3). The mirror case shows that reflection requires two
distinct surfaces; if the two are fused, there is no reflection. The argument applies the mirror
case to identities: if the two identities were fused, there would be no two expressions for the
reflection to relate.
Remark 19.14 (The Argument Is About Structure, Not About Value). The argument is about
the structure of the relation of finding, not about the value of distinctness. The framework
does not say that distinctness is a good, an end, or a value; it says that distinctness is the
structural condition under which the relation of finding is possible.
282                                    Chapter 19. Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


Remark 19.15 (Recognition Presupposes Distinctness). The argument also shows that
recognition presupposes distinctness. To recognize an expression as the expression of its source,
the recognizer must be distinct from the source; if the recognizer were the source, there would
be no recognition, because there would be nothing to recognize. The distinctness is what
makes recognition possible, and the recognition is what the finding consists in.

Remark 19.16 (What the Tradition Has Called “Love”). What the tradition has called “love”
is, in this framework, a particular form of the structural relation of finding under the condition
of distinctness. The framework states the structural condition of the relation, not its reality.
What love is, in the tradition’s sense, the framework does not describe; the distinction between
the structural condition and the reality of the relation is kept throughout the book. The
framework does not undertake the inquiry into love.


19.10      The Two Structural Directions of Finding
The structural relation of finding has two directions, and the distinction is worth stating
because the two are easily confused.

First direction: the ascending direction. The structural direction of ascending epistemic
light, from a manifestation toward its source. When a listener hears a speaker’s words and
understands something about the speaker, the understanding is in the ascending direction.

Second direction: the reflective direction. The structural direction of reflective epistemic
light, from one manifestation to another in the same context. When a listener responds to
a speaker, and the speaker hears the response and comes to understand her own expression
better, the exchange is in the reflective direction.
    The ascending and the reflective directions are not two separate relations; they are two
directions of a single structural relation of finding.

Remark 19.17 (The Two Directions Are One Relation). The distinction between the two
directions is analytical, not substantial. The relation of finding is one relation, and the two
directions are two ways the relation can run.

Remark 19.18 (No Claim About Emotion or Value). The description of the two directions is
structural. It does not say that one direction is more valuable than the other, or that either
direction is accompanied by emotion, motivation, or any psychological state.


19.11      The Epistemic Criterion of Structural Unknownness
The chapter’s positive contribution is the epistemic criterion by which structural unknownness
is diagnosed, stated within the chapter and without appeal to any external justification.

Definition 19.7 (The Epistemic Criterion of Structural Unknownness). (T) A case exhibits
structural unknownness when it satisfies all three of the following conditions:

(U1) Availability through manifestation only: the identity is available to any other identity
     only through its manifestation, and the manifestation is not the identity.

(U2) Non-removability by more manifestation: no increase in the quantity or adequacy of the
     manifestation would make the identity directly accessible to another identity.

(U3) Structural role in reflection: the condition is what makes the reflection between the two
     expressions possible; if it were removed, the reflection would cease (the mirror case).
19.12. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                   283


The three conditions are (T): they follow from (P1)–(P3) and from the mirror case. A case
that satisfies all three is a case of structural unknownness; a case that fails any one is not (or
is not only) a case of structural unknownness.
    The criterion is (T) relative to the three premises and to the mirror case. Its justification
is the argument of Section 19.5; its use is the diagnosis of a case.

Remark 19.19 (The Criterion Is Not a Psychological Criterion). The criterion is not a
psychological criterion. It does not say what a subject feels, believes, or desires. It says what
features a relation has. The three conditions are features of the relation, not states of the
subject.
Remark 19.20 (The Criterion Is the Chapter’s Positive Contribution). The criterion is the
chapter’s positive contribution to the account of structural unknownness. It is not a new
premise of the theorem; it is the statement of what the theorem’s premises require, made
explicit as a criterion. The criterion states what structural unknownness is, in the framework’s
vocabulary, and what a case must satisfy for structural unknownness to hold.


19.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the full account of what the relation of finding amounts
to, in the way of content, in any particular case. The theorem states the structural condition
under which the relation is possible; the development of the content is left to the parts of the
book that treat the epistemic economy of cognition.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether structural unknownness can
ever be removed. The theorem states that it cannot be removed by more manifestation, but it
does not rule out that some other structural change might remove it. Whether such a change
is possible is a question the framework leaves open.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between the two directions of finding
beyond the distinction stated above.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of structural unknownness.
It claims to have described the structure of structural unknownness and the epistemic criterion
by which it is diagnosed; what grounds the structure is not addressed in the present chapter.
Remark 19.21 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has stated and proved the theorem of structural unknownness, in its epistemic form, with the
three premises made explicit. It has distinguished three kinds of unknownness (structural,
current non-recognition, lack of information) and stated which kind the theorem claims. It
284                                     Chapter 19. Unknownness of Same-Category Identities


has distinguished three senses of impossibility and stated which senses the theorem claims. It
has stated a table of the kinds of unknownness with condition, diagnostic criterion, example,
and what progress can reduce. It has stated the principle that distinctness is the condition
of finding, with an independent argument. And it has stated the epistemic criterion of
structural unknownness, within the chapter. The chapter’s contribution is the theorem itself,
the vocabulary of impossibility, the three kinds of unknownness, the table, the distinctness
argument, and the epistemic criterion.
