while manifestational adequacy fails; each row is therefore a case in which manifestational
adequacy does work that the other criterion does not do. The independence is not an accident
of the list; it follows from the objects of the criteria: the other six are about the context or
the reconstruction, and manifestational adequacy is about the appearance.
 22.5. Acceptance and Rejection Conditions                                                      317


 22.5      Acceptance and Rejection Conditions
 The criterion is proposed. The framework states the conditions under which it would be
 accepted as a principle, and the conditions under which it would be rejected. The two sets of
 conditions are stated so that the criterion’s status is not left ambiguous: the framework states
 exactly what would settle it.

 22.5.1     The Acceptance Conditions
 The criterion would be accepted as a principle of the framework when three conditions are
 met.

 Definition 22.3 (Acceptance Conditions for Manifestational Adequacy). (A) The criterion is
 accepted as a principle when:

(AC1) The working definitions of capacity and aptitude (Definitions 22.1 and 22.2) are replaced
      by, or confirmed as, the independent account: an account that defines capacity and
      aptitude without circularity with the appearance whose fit is in question, and that is
      stated in the framework’s vocabulary.

(AC2) The criterion is shown to do work that the three criteria of Chapter 21 and the three
      criteria of Chapter 23 do not do: a case is exhibited in which all six other criteria are
      satisfied and the criterion fails, and the failure is recognized as an error of attribution by
      the framework’s own standards.

(AC3) The criterion’s work is shown to be consistent with the rest of the framework: no other
      principle of the framework is contradicted by the acceptance of the criterion, and the
      criterion’s conflicts with the other criteria are stated as structural differences, not as
      inconsistencies.

     The three conditions are (A): they are the framework’s stipulation of what would make
 the criterion a principle. The conditions are stated so that a reader who wishes to settle the
 criterion’s status knows what to supply; a reader who supplies all three has accepted the
 criterion; a reader who supplies fewer has not.

 22.5.2     The Rejection Conditions
 The criterion would be rejected as a principle of the framework when one of three conditions
 is met.

 Definition 22.4 (Rejection Conditions for Manifestational Adequacy). (A) The criterion is
 rejected as a principle when:

(RC1) It is shown to do no work: every case the criterion addresses is shown to be addressed
      by the three criteria of Chapter 21 or by the three criteria of Chapter 23.

(RC2) Its work is shown to be done by the criteria of Chapter 23: the criterion’s contribution
      is shown to be a consequence of the criteria of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity, not an
      independent condition.

(RC3) An independent account of capacity is supplied that does not support the criterion: the
      account defines capacity in a way that makes the criterion’s claim about fit false, or that
      makes the criterion’s claim follow from the definition alone (in which case the criterion
      is trivial).
318                                                     Chapter 22. Manifestational Adequacy


    The three conditions are (A): they are the framework’s stipulation of what would make
the criterion fail. The conditions are stated so that a critic who wishes to reject the criterion
knows what to supply; a critic who supplies one of the three has rejected the criterion.

Remark 22.10 (The Conditions Are Not a Decision Procedure). The conditions are not a
decision procedure. They state what would settle the criterion’s status; they do not state how
to determine, in advance, whether the conditions will be met. The framework’s claim is that
the criterion is a candidate whose status is to be settled by the conditions, and that the reader
is invited to supply what the conditions require.

Remark 22.11 (The Criterion Is Retained, Pending the Conditions). The criterion is retained
in the framework’s vocabulary, pending the conditions. The retention is not an adoption; it is
the recognition that the criterion states a real condition under which a context is usable for
the reconstruction of an identity, and that the condition is worth stating even before its full
justification is supplied. The reader who takes the retention as an adoption has read more
than the framework claims; the reader who takes it as a proposal pending the conditions has
read the framework’s claim.


22.6     What the Criterion Adds to the Three Criteria
The criterion adds to the three criteria in a specific way, and the specificity is worth stating.

The three criteria govern the use of contexts. Cross-checkability governs the identifi-
cation of elements; minimality governs the choice of frame; consistency governs the relation
between frames. All three are about the context, and about how the context is used.

The fourth criterion governs the attribution. The fourth criterion is about the appear-
ance that the context is used to study. It says that the appearance must be of a kind that the
context can bear and is suited to.

The three criteria would not catch the error the fourth addresses. A context could
be cross-checkable, minimal, and consistent, and yet be a context in which the appearance
attributed to it could not have been produced.

Remark 22.12 (A Second Illustration: The Physician and the Rash). Consider a physician
studying a patient’s rash. Her context is the dermatological one; the context is valid by the
three criteria of Chapter 21. Now suppose someone says: “The rash is a manifestation of the
patient’s moral character.” The attribution is an error—not because the patient has no moral
character, and not because the rash could not exist, but because the dermatological context
cannot bear the appearance of moral character. The three criteria would not catch the error;
the fourth criterion does.

Remark 22.13 (The Criterion Is Not a Restatement of the Three). The criterion is not a
restatement of the three criteria. The three are about the use of contexts; the fourth is about
the fit between the appearance and the context. The difference is structural.

Remark 22.14 (The Criterion and Principle 13.1). The criterion is related to the principle of
contextual manifestational capacity, stated as a proposal in Chapter 13 (Principle 13.1). The
principle is about the production of the manifestation; the criterion is about the attribution of
the manifestation. Both depend on the notion of capacity; both remain proposed; both wait
on the same independent account. The reader who has followed Chapter 13 will recognize the
same missing account in both.
22.7. The Relational Diagram                                                               319


22.7     The Relational Diagram
The criterion’s place among the other conditions is stated in a relational diagram. The diagram
shows how the context, the appearance, the receiving capacity, and the adequacy of the
reconstruction are related.


   The Context
   The question, the fixed elements, the rule, the standpoint (Chapter 10)
   ↓
   Context Validity (Chapter 21): cross-checkability, minimality, consistency
   ↓
   The Appearance
   The manifestation attributed to the context
   ↓
   Manifestational Adequacy (this chapter, proposed)
   Capacity: what the context can bear (Def. 22.1)
   Aptitude: what the context is suited to (Def. 22.2)
   ↓
   The Reconstruction
   The pseudo-identity formed from the appearance in the context
   ↓
   Pseudo-Identity Adequacy (Chapter 23): consistency, stability, fruitfulness


    The diagram is a summary, not a new argument. Its purpose is to show the layers of
conditions and the direction of their dependence: the context is the starting point; the
context validity criteria assess the context; the appearance is attributed to the context; the
criterion of manifestational adequacy assesses the attribution; the reconstruction is formed;
the pseudo-identity adequacy criteria assess the reconstruction.

What manifestational adequacy fills. It fills the gap between the validity of the context
and the adequacy of the reconstruction: a context can be valid, and a reconstruction can
be adequate, and yet the appearance attributed to the context can be of a kind the context
cannot bear. The criterion is what checks this case.

What manifestational adequacy does not duplicate. It does not duplicate the three
criteria of Chapter 21 (those are about the use of the context) and it does not duplicate the
criteria of Chapter 23 (those are about the reconstruction). The criterion is the intermediate
layer, and the gap it fills is between the two.

Can the criterion conflict with context validity? Yes, the criterion and the three
criteria of Chapter 21 can conflict. The contract example shows this. The criterion is an
independent condition, and its independence is what allows it to conflict with them. The
conflict is the framework’s way of stating that the validity of the context and the fit between
the appearance and the context are distinct conditions.

Can the criterion conflict with pseudo-identity adequacy? Yes, the criterion and
the three criteria of Chapter 23 can conflict. A reconstruction can be consistent, stable, and
fruitful (it passes the criteria of Chapter 23), and yet the appearances it is formed from can
be of a kind the context cannot bear (it fails the criterion). The two are distinct, and their
independence is what allows the conflict.
320                                                      Chapter 22. Manifestational Adequacy


Remark 22.15 (The Diagram Is a Map, Not a Hierarchy). The diagram is a map of the
layers, not a hierarchy of the criteria. The framework does not say that context validity is more
important than manifestational adequacy, or that manifestational adequacy is more important
than pseudo-identity adequacy. The layers are different conditions on different objects, and
each must be satisfied in its own place.
Remark 22.16 (The Diagram and the Fallacy of Super-Identity). The diagram is what makes
the fallacy of super-identity visible in its full structure. The record that the fallacy treats
as a reconstruction passes the three criteria of Chapter 21 (the contexts are valid) and the
three criteria of Chapter 23 (the record is consistent, stable, fruitful), and yet the record fails
the criterion of manifestational adequacy (the appearances it contains are of kinds that some
of the contexts cannot bear). The diagram is the framework’s statement of what the fallacy
leaves out.


22.8     The Criterion and the Criteria of Adequacy
The criterion is easily confused with the criteria of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity (Chap-
ter 23), and the distinction is worth marking.
    The criterion of manifestational adequacy is about the fit between the appearance and the
context in which it is attributed. The criteria of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity are about
the reconstruction formed from the manifestations available in a context.
    The two are different, and neither entails the other. A context can pass the criterion of
manifestational adequacy and still produce a reconstruction that fails the criteria of adequacy;
a reconstruction can pass the criteria of adequacy and still be formed from a context that fails
the criterion of manifestational adequacy.
Remark 22.17 (The Distinction Matters for the Fallacy of Super-Identity). The distinction
matters for the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28). The criterion of manifestational
adequacy is one of the checks: a manifestation attributed to a context that cannot bear it is a
manifestation that should not be aggregated with the others. The criteria of adequacy are
another check. The two checks are distinct, and the framework uses both.
Remark 22.18 (The Criterion Is Not a Criterion of Truth). The criterion is not a criterion
of truth. It says that attributing to a context an appearance of a kind that the context cannot
bear is an error of attribution; it does not say that the appearance is false.


22.9     What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not establish the criterion. The criterion is proposed, and the
acceptance and rejection conditions (Section 22.5) state exactly what would settle its status.
The chapter supplies working operational definitions of capacity and aptitude, but these are
marked as working, not as final.
    Second, the chapter does not supply the final independent definition of “capacity.” The
working definition (Definition 22.1) is the best the framework can supply at this stage; the
final definition is a condition of acceptance (AC1).
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the criterion is a criterion of
context validity. The framework’s claim is that it is, in the sense that it states a condition
under which a context is usable for the reconstruction of an identity; whether the criterion is a
criterion of context validity is a matter the acceptance conditions decide.
    Fourth, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the criterion, once the acceptance
conditions are met, would be adopted. The framework’s claim is that the criterion is a candidate;
whether the candidate is a principle is a question the framework leaves to the conditions.
22.10. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                             321

has stated the proposed fourth criterion of manifestational adequacy, with working operational

comparison matrix aligning the criterion with the three criteria of Chapter 21 and the three

A Question for Reflection
Consider a context you have used to study something, and an appearance you have attributed
to it. Apply the working definitions of capacity and aptitude (Definitions 22.1 and 22.2): does
the context have the capacity and the aptitude for the appearance? If it does, what makes it
so? If it does not, was the attribution an error, and what kind of error?
    And consider the contract—the scene that opened the chapter. The context of legal
obligation is valid by the three criteria, and yet the attribution of affection to the contract
is an error. Apply the comparison matrix (Section 22.4): which of the six other criteria are
satisfied, and which is not? What does your answer tell you about the difference between the
validity of a context and the fit between the appearance and the context?
    And consider the acceptance and rejection conditions (Section 22.5): can you supply what
AC1, AC2, or AC3 require for a case of your own? Can you supply what RC1, RC2, or RC3
would require, and show that the criterion fails for that case? What does your answer tell you
about the status of the criterion, and about what would settle it? A reader who can answer all
three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s
three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the criteria of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity: consistency, stability,
and fruitfulness. The present chapter has stated a proposed criterion of context validity; the
next chapter states the criteria by which the reconstruction formed from the context is assessed.
                                                                                                 323




Chapter 23

The Adequacy of a Pseudo-Identity

Scope
This chapter states the three criteria by which the adequacy of a pseudo-identity is assessed:
consistency, stability, and fruitfulness. It defines the three, states the assessment conditions of
each, gives a comparable example for each, explains the relation between the narrow definition
of fruitfulness and the use of predictive and practical success as diagnostic indicators, applies
the criteria to three rival reconstructions in a single worked example, and states the application
and the limits of the criteria. It distinguishes minimality from stability by a worked example
(Section 23.5.1). It does not yet state the three failures of reconstruction; that is the subject
of Chapter 24. Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “adequacy,” “consistency,”
“stability,” “fruitfulness,” “reconstruction,” “estimate,” or “indicator,” these are structural terms,
and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


23.1      A Scene: The Three Historians and the Treaty
Consider three historians, working independently on the same event: a treaty signed in the
winter of a particular year, by parties whose records have been partly lost. Each historian has
a different set of documents. The first has the diplomatic correspondence; the second has the
financial records; the third has the private letters of one of the signatories.
    Each historian reconstructs the event. The first reconstructs it as a settlement of a territorial
dispute, with the specific terms fixed by diplomatic bargaining. The second reconstructs it as
a settlement of a financial obligation, with the specific terms fixed by the parties’ debts. The
third reconstructs it as a settlement of a personal quarrel, with the specific terms fixed by the
signatory’s resentment.
    The three reconstructions differ. Each is partial; each is drawn from a different set of
documents; each makes visible something the others do not. The question is not which
reconstruction is “the” true one. The question is: what makes a reconstruction adequate, given
that every reconstruction is partial and every reconstruction is drawn from a different set of
documents?
    The scene poses a question that the previous chapters have prepared. The pseudo-identity,
defined in Chapter 12, is the observer’s approximation of an identity, constructed from the
available manifestations. It is an estimate of a signature, not a rival identity. The three
historians are each forming a pseudo-identity of the same identity. What distinguishes an
adequate pseudo-identity from an inadequate one?
    The present chapter’s answer is that an adequate pseudo-identity is one that satisfies three
criteria: it converges with other independent reconstructions (consistency); it is stable under
small perturbations of the observer’s context (stability); and it has the structural capacity to
produce further distinctions and to be continued (fruitfulness), with predictive and practical
324                                            Chapter 23. The Adequacy of a Pseudo-Identity


success functioning as its diagnostic indicators. The three criteria are the framework’s fallibilist
account of adequacy. The chapter applies them to three rival reconstructions in Section 23.7.

Remark 23.1 (The Scene Shows the Three Criteria at Work, Not Three Reconstructions).
The scene is easily read as an observation about three historians who happen to disagree. The
observation is not wrong, but it hides the structural point. The structural point is that the
three reconstructions, different as they are, can be assessed by the same three criteria: they
can be checked for convergence, for stability, and for fruitfulness. The three criteria are not
three alternative reconstructions; they are three ways of assessing one reconstruction.

Remark 23.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the criteria; it makes them intelligible before they
are stated.


23.2     The Question
The previous chapters of Part IV have stated the conditions of epistemic validity and adequacy.
Chapter 21 stated the three criteria of context validity: cross-checkability, minimality, and
consistency. Chapter 22 stated the proposed fourth criterion, manifestational adequacy. The
present chapter turns from the criteria of contexts to the criteria of the reconstruction formed
from the contexts.
    The question is: what makes a pseudo-identity adequate? The pseudo-identity is a working
model, the best the observer can achieve given the available manifestations and the costs
of reconstruction. The question is what distinguishes an adequate working model from an
inadequate one.
    The question is not about whether the pseudo-identity is the identity. No pseudo-identity is
the identity. The question is about whether the pseudo-identity is an adequate approximation
of the signature, given the available manifestations and the costs of reconstruction. The answer
is the three criteria of this chapter.

Remark 23.3 (The Question Is About Adequacy, Not About Truth). The question is about
adequacy, not about truth. A pseudo-identity is not true or false in the way a proposition is
true or false; it is adequate or inadequate in the way a model is adequate or inadequate. The
distinction is the distinction between the truth of a claim and the adequacy of a reconstruction.


23.3     The Three Criteria
Definition 23.1 (The Criteria of the Adequacy of a Pseudo-Identity). (A) A pseudo-identity
is adequate, to the extent that it satisfies the three criteria of consistency, stability, and
fruitfulness:

  (i) Consistency: observers working independently in different contexts arrive at the same
      pseudo-identity, up to isomorphism.

 (ii) Stability: the pseudo-identity is stable under small perturbations of the observer’s context
      or cognitive apparatus.

 (iii) Fruitfulness: the pseudo-identity has the structural capacity to produce further distinc-
       tions within the reconstruction and to be continued into further reconstructions of the
       same identity or of identities of the same kind. Predictive and practical success function
       as diagnostic indicators of fruitfulness, not as the criterion itself (Section 23.6.1).
23.3. The Three Criteria                                                                    325


   The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary. The three criteria are not the same claim: the first is about convergence of
independent reconstructions; the second is about stability of a single reconstruction under
perturbation; the third is about the structural capacity to distinguish and to continue, with
success as its indicator.




23.3.1    The Assessment Conditions of the Three Criteria

The definition states what the three criteria are; the assessment conditions state what must be
observed to apply them.




Assessment conditions for consistency. The reconstruction is assessed by comparing it
with the reconstructions of at least two observers working independently, in contexts that are
not shared. The assessment conditions are: (C1) the observers’ contexts are independently
constituted; (C2) the reconstructions are stated in a form that can be compared up to
isomorphism; (C3) the convergences and divergences are identified for each element of the
reconstruction.




Assessment conditions for stability. The reconstruction is assessed by perturbing the
observer’s context, means, or conceptual structure in small ways, and checking whether the
reconstruction remains the same up to isomorphism. The assessment conditions are: (S1)
the perturbations are small relative to the reconstruction’s object; (S2) the perturbations are
independent of one another; (S3) the changes in the reconstruction, if any, are recorded for
each perturbation.




Assessment conditions for fruitfulness. The reconstruction is assessed by checking
whether it can produce further distinctions within itself and whether it can be continued into
further reconstructions. The assessment conditions are: (F1) the reconstruction generates at
least one distinction that is not already stated in it; (F2) the reconstruction can be continued
into a further reconstruction of the same identity or of identities of the same kind; (F3) the
diagnostic indicators (predictive success, practical success) are recorded as evidence, not as
the criterion (Section 23.6.1).




23.3.2    Comparable Examples for the Three Criteria

The three criteria are stated abstractly; the comparable examples state what an instance of
each looks like.

Remark 23.4 (The Three Criteria Answer Three Different Questions). The three criteria
answer three different questions. Consistency: does the reconstruction converge with what
other observers, working independently, arrive at? Stability: does the reconstruction remain
the same when the observer’s context changes? Fruitfulness: does the reconstruction have the
structural capacity to distinguish and to continue? The three questions are distinct, and an
answer to one is not an answer to the others.
Remark 23.5 (The Criteria Are Fallibilist, Not Foundationalist). The three criteria are
fallibilist: they provide an account of adequacy of the same kind that scientific theories have,
not an account of certainty of the kind that foundationalist epistemologies have sought.
Remark 23.6 (The Criteria Are Not the Criteria of Context Validity). The three criteria of
this chapter are not the three criteria of context validity (Chapter 21). The criteria of context
validity are about the contexts; the criteria of adequacy are about the reconstruction formed
from the contexts. The word “consistency” appears in both sets, but it is used in different
senses.
Remark 23.7 (The Criteria Are Not the Criterion of Manifestational Adequacy). The three
criteria of this chapter are not the proposed criterion of manifestational adequacy (Chapter 22).
The proposed criterion is about the fit between the appearance and the context; the criteria of
adequacy are about the reconstruction formed from the appearances.


23.4        The First Criterion: Consistency
Consistency is convergence across independent observers. The criterion is stated at the level
of observers, not at the level of a single observer.
Remark 23.8 (What the Criterion Is Not). The criterion is not a demand for unanimity.
Observers may converge on the same pseudo-identity up to isomorphism, but not up to identity.
The criterion is also not a demand that every observer arrive at the pseudo-identity; it is a
demand that the observers who work independently in different contexts arrive at the same
pseudo-identity, and that this convergence is the evidence of the reconstruction’s adequacy.
Remark 23.9 (Why Convergence Is Evidence of Adequacy). Convergence is evidence of
adequacy because the observers do not share their contexts. If the reconstruction were a
projection of the observer’s context, the projections of different contexts would differ; they
would not converge on a single pseudo-identity unless the identity itself were the common
cause of the convergence. The claim is abductive, not deductive.
23.5. The Second Criterion: Stability                                                         327


Remark 23.10 (The Criterion Is Not a Proof of Adequacy). Convergence among independent
observers can be explained by shared convention, by shared training, or by shared error, and
not only by the identity’s being the common cause. The criterion is a reason for holding the
pseudo-identity adequate, not a guarantee that it is.


23.5     The Second Criterion: Stability
Stability is invariance across perturbations of one observer’s context. The criterion is stated at
the level of a single observer’s reconstruction, across perturbations.

Remark 23.11 (What Counts as a “Small Perturbation”). The word “small” is a structural
term, not a precise measure. A small perturbation is a change in the observer’s context,
means, or conceptual structure that is not large enough to make the reconstruction a different
reconstruction of a different identity. The criterion does not provide a threshold; it leaves the
identification of the threshold to the inquiry.

Remark 23.12 (Why Stability Is Evidence of Adequacy). Stability under small perturbations
is evidence of adequacy because a reconstruction that tracked only the perturbations would
change as the perturbations change. If the reconstruction remains the same across the
perturbations, the reconstruction is tracking something that is not the perturbations; it is
tracking the identity. The claim is abductive, not deductive.

Remark 23.13 (The Criterion Is Not a Proof of Adequacy). Stability under small perturbations
can be explained by the reconstruction’s insensitivity to the perturbations, not only by the
identity’s being the invariant that the reconstruction tracks. A reconstruction that is insensitive
to everything is stable under everything, and it is not an adequate reconstruction of anything.

Remark 23.14 (The Criterion Is Different from Consistency). Consistency is convergence
across observers; stability is invariance across perturbations of one observer’s context. A
reconstruction can be consistent and unstable; a reconstruction can be stable and inconsistent.

23.5.1    Minimality and Stability: A Worked Distinction
Minimality (Chapter 21) and stability are easily run together. Both concern a kind of economy:
minimality is the economy of the context, and stability is the economy of the reconstruction.

Remark 23.15 (The Two Criteria Concern Different Objects). Minimality is a condition
on the context (Chapter 21). It asks whether the context introduces elements or rules that
do no work in the explanation. Stability is a condition on the pseudo-identity formed from
the context. The distinction is the distinction between the economy of the context and the
economy of the reconstruction.

Case A: Minimal but not stable. Consider a reconstruction of a historical figure from
a single document, written by a single witness. The context is minimal: it uses only the
document, the witness, and the events the document records; it introduces no element or
rule that does no work. The context passes the minimality criterion of Chapter 21. But
the pseudo-identity formed from the document is not stable: a small change in the witness’s
testimony (a single word, a single date) would change the pseudo-identity significantly. The
reconstruction is minimal and not stable.

Case B: Stable but not minimal. Consider a reconstruction of a historical figure from
four documents, written by four witnesses, each of whom tells the same story with minor
variations, plus a fifth document that adds a detail no other document confirms. The fifth
328                                            Chapter 23. The Adequacy of a Pseudo-Identity


document’s detail is not needed; the context is not minimal. But the pseudo-identity formed
from the four witnesses is stable: a small change in any one witness’s testimony would not
change the pseudo-identity significantly. The reconstruction is stable and not minimal.

Remark 23.16 (The Two Criteria Are Independent). The two cases show that the two criteria
are independent. In Case A, minimality holds and stability fails. In Case B, stability holds
and minimality fails. The independence is not accidental; the two criteria concern different
objects.


23.6     The Third Criterion: Fruitfulness
Fruitfulness is the structural capacity of the pseudo-identity to produce further distinctions
within the reconstruction and to be continued into further reconstructions. The criterion is
stated at the level of the pseudo-identity, not at the level of the observer who formed it, and
not at the level of the practical success of a system that operates according to it.

23.6.1    The Narrow Definition and the Diagnostic Indicators
The apparent tension between the narrow definition of fruitfulness and the use of predictive or
practical success elsewhere in the framework is resolved by distinguishing the criterion from
its indicators. The narrow definition states the structural core of fruitfulness; the predictive
and practical success are the observable signs by which the structural core is detected, not the
criterion itself.

Definition 23.2 (Fruitfulness, Narrow Sense). (A) A pseudo-identity is fruitful in the narrow
sense when:

(F1) it can produce further distinctions within the reconstruction; and

(F2) it can be continued into further reconstructions of the same identity or of identities of
     the same kind.

The two conditions are the criterion. Predictive success and practical success are not conditions
of fruitfulness; they are its diagnostic indicators (Definition 23.3).

Definition 23.3 (The Diagnostic Indicators of Fruitfulness). (A) The diagnostic indicators
of fruitfulness are the observable signs by which the structural capacity of Definition 23.2 is
detected:

(I1) Predictive success: the reconstruction, when used to predict future manifestations of the
     identity, yields predictions that are confirmed by further manifestations.

(I2) Practical success: a system that operates according to the reconstruction succeeds in its
     environment.

The indicators are evidence of fruitfulness, not its criterion. A reconstruction can be fruitful
and fail an indicator; a reconstruction can pass an indicator and be unfruitful.

    The two definitions resolve the apparent tension. The narrow definition (Definition 23.2) is
the criterion: it states what fruitfulness consists in. The diagnostic indicators (Definition 23.3)
are the observable signs: they state how fruitfulness is detected. The framework uses the
indicators as evidence, and it does not substitute them for the criterion. The reader who
reads the framework’s use of prediction or practical success as a use of the criterion has read
the indicators for the criterion; the reader who distinguishes the two has read the framework
correctly.
23.6. The Third Criterion: Fruitfulness                                                         329


Remark 23.17 (Fruitfulness Is Not Practical Success). Practical success is the achievement of
a goal in the world. The framework’s fruitfulness is the structural capacity to distinguish and
to continue. A pseudo-identity that is fruitful in the framework’s sense may fail in practice; a
pseudo-identity that succeeds in practice may be unfruitful in the framework’s sense. The two
are distinct, and the framework keeps them apart.

Remark 23.18 (Fruitfulness Is Not Truth). Truth is the correspondence of a proposition to
what is. The framework’s fruitfulness is the structural capacity of the reconstruction to generate
further distinctions and to continue. A pseudo-identity that is fruitful in the framework’s sense
may be false; a pseudo-identity that is true may be unfruitful in the framework’s sense.

Pair 1: Fruitful but false. Consider a pseudo-identity of a historical figure that organizes
the available documents into a coherent narrative, distinguishes the figure’s motives from
the motives of the figure’s contemporaries, and can be continued into a reconstruction of the
figure’s later life. The pseudo-identity is fruitful in the narrow sense: it produces distinctions
and can be continued. It may also be false: the narrative may be internally coherent but
incompatible with facts that later documents reveal. The framework’s criterion calls the
pseudo-identity fruitful; it does not call it true.

Pair 2: True but unfruitful. Consider a pseudo-identity of the same historical figure that
consists in a list of verified facts, each of which is true, but with no organizing distinctions and
no capacity to be continued into a reconstruction of the figure’s later life. The pseudo-identity
is true, in the sense that each of its statements corresponds to a fact. It is not fruitful in the
narrow sense: it produces no distinctions and cannot be continued.

Pair 3: Fruitful with failing indicator. Consider a reconstruction of a period that
produces new distinctions and can be continued, but whose predictions about the period’s
economic trends fail when tested. The reconstruction is fruitful in the narrow sense; its
predictive indicator (I1) fails. The framework’s criterion calls the reconstruction fruitful; the
indicator is evidence that the reconstruction’s fruitfulness may be limited in a particular
respect.

Pair 4: Unfruitful with passing indicator. Consider a reconstruction of a period that is
a list of verified facts and produces no distinctions and no continuation, but whose practical
predictions about the period’s weather turn out to be correct. The reconstruction is unfruitful
in the narrow sense; its practical indicator (I2) passes. The framework’s criterion calls the
reconstruction unfruitful; the indicator is evidence that may be coincidental, and the criterion
is not overridden by it.

Remark 23.19 (The Indicators Are Evidence, Not the Criterion). The four pairs of cases
show that the indicators are evidence, not the criterion. Pair 3 shows a fruitful reconstruction
with a failing indicator; Pair 4 shows an unfruitful reconstruction with a passing indicator. In
both cases, the criterion (fruitfulness in the narrow sense) and the indicator diverge, and the
framework’s claim is that the criterion, not the indicator, is decisive. The indicators are the
observable signs by which the criterion is detected; the criterion is the structural capacity the
signs point to.

Remark 23.20 (Fruitfulness Is a Condition on the Reconstruction, Not on the Facts).
Fruitfulness is a condition on the reconstruction; it is not a condition on the facts. A
reconstruction can be fruitful even when the facts it contains are false; a reconstruction can be
unfruitful even when the facts it contains are true.
330                                           Chapter 23. The Adequacy of a Pseudo-Identity


23.7     The Worked Example: Assessing Three Rival Reconstruc-
         tions
The three criteria are abstract; the worked example applies them to the three historians’
reconstructions of the treaty, and selects the more adequate one. The example is the chapter’s
principal contribution to the application of the criteria.

The three reconstructions. Let R1 be the reconstruction from the diplomatic correspon-
dence (the treaty as a settlement of a territorial dispute, fixed by diplomatic bargaining). Let
R2 be the reconstruction from the financial records (the treaty as a settlement of a financial
obligation, fixed by the parties’ debts). Let R3 be the reconstruction from the private letters
of one signatory (the treaty as a settlement of a personal quarrel, fixed by the signatory’s
resentment).

Step 1: assess consistency. Each reconstruction is compared with a fourth independent
reconstruction, carried out by a fourth historian who has not seen the three. The fourth
historian’s reconstruction agrees, up to isomorphism, with R1 ’s description of the treaty’s terms
and with R2 ’s description of the parties’ obligations; it does not agree with R3 ’s description
of the signatory’s motive. The assessment: R1 and R2 pass consistency for the terms and
obligations; R3 fails consistency for the motive.

Step 2: assess stability. Each reconstruction is perturbed by correcting one date in one
document. R1 ’s description of the territorial terms is unchanged; R2 ’s description of the
financial obligations is unchanged; R3 ’s description of the signatory’s resentment changes
significantly (the correction of the date makes the resentment’s timing incompatible with the
treaty’s signing). The assessment: R1 and R2 pass stability; R3 fails stability.

Step 3: assess fruitfulness. Each reconstruction is tested for whether it can produce
further distinctions and be continued. R1 generates a distinction between the territorial terms
that were negotiated and those that were imposed, and can be continued into a reconstruction
of the treaty’s implementation; it passes. R2 generates a distinction between the obligations
that were recognized and those that were deferred, and can be continued into a reconstruction
of the parties’ subsequent financial relations; it passes. R3 generates a distinction between
the signatory’s private resentment and his public conduct, and can be continued into a
reconstruction of his later correspondence; it passes.

Step 4: assess the diagnostic indicators. R1 ’s predictions about the treaty’s territorial
implementation are confirmed by later documents (I1 passes); R2 ’s predictions about the
parties’ financial relations are confirmed (I1 passes); R3 ’s predictions about the signatory’s
later conduct are partly confirmed, partly not (I1 mixed). R1 ’s and R2 ’s practical use by later
historians is documented (I2 passes); R3 ’s practical use is limited (I2 weak).

The verdict. R1 and R2 pass all three criteria and their indicators; R3 passes fruitfulness
but fails consistency and stability. The framework’s verdict is: R1 and R2 are adequate
reconstructions; R3 is fruitful but not adequate. Between R1 and R2 , the criteria do not
decide; the choice between them is a matter for the inquiry, and it depends on the question
the inquiry is asking (the territorial question for R1 , the financial question for R2 ).

Remark 23.21 (The Worked Example Shows the Criteria at Work, Not a Decision Procedure).
The worked example shows the criteria at work on three rival reconstructions. It is not a
decision procedure that can be applied mechanically to any case; it is a display of the criteria’s
23.8. Application and Limits of the Three Criteria                                             331


application, and it depends on the judgments made at each step (the identification of the
elements, the perturbations, the distinctions, the indicators). The framework’s claim is that
the criteria discipline the judgment, not that they eliminate it.
Remark 23.22 (The Verdict Is Not a Proof). The verdict of the worked example is not a
proof that R1 and R2 are adequate. The verdict is the result of the assessment by the three
criteria; it is a reason for holding the reconstructions adequate, not a guarantee. The fallibility
of the assessment is the price of finite inquiry, and the worked example exhibits it.
Remark 23.23 (The Choice Between R1 and R2 Is Not Settled by the Criteria). The choice
between R1 and R2 is not settled by the criteria; both pass all three. The criteria answer
whether a reconstruction is adequate; they do not answer which of two adequate reconstructions
is the better. The choice depends on the question the inquiry is asking, and the framework
leaves the choice to the inquiry.


23.8     Application and Limits of the Three Criteria
The criteria are used to assess a reconstruction; the present section states how they are applied
and where their application stops.

First step of application: identify the reconstruction’s object. The criteria are
applied to a pseudo-identity of a specific identity, formed from a specific set of manifestations,
in a specific context. The first step is to state the object, the manifestations, and the context
in a form that can be examined.

Second step: apply consistency. Compare the reconstruction with the reconstructions of
at least two independent observers, and identify the convergences and divergences for each
element.

Third step: apply stability. Perturb the observer’s context, means, or conceptual structure
in small ways, and identify the changes in the reconstruction for each perturbation.

Fourth step: apply fruitfulness. Check whether the reconstruction produces further
distinctions and can be continued; record the diagnostic indicators (predictive and practical
success) as evidence.

Fifth step: assess. The reconstruction is adequate to the extent that it satisfies the three
criteria; the assessment is the assessment of the three together, not of each alone.
Remark 23.24 (The Limits of Application: No Absolute Proof). The application of the
criteria does not yield an absolute proof of adequacy. The criteria are fallibilist; the assessment
is a reason for holding the reconstruction adequate, not a guarantee. The application is fallible
like every identification in the framework.
Remark 23.25 (The Limits of Application: No Elimination of Partiality). The application
of the criteria does not eliminate the partiality of the reconstruction. The pseudo-identity is
partial, because it is drawn from the available manifestations, and the available manifestations
are finite. The criteria assess the adequacy of the partial reconstruction; they do not make it
complete.
Remark 23.26 (The Limits of Application: No Choice Among Adequate Reconstructions).
The application of the criteria does not choose among adequate reconstructions. If two
reconstructions both satisfy the three criteria, the criteria do not say which is the better. The
choice is a matter for the inquiry, and it depends on the purposes the inquiry serves.
332                                            Chapter 23. The Adequacy of a Pseudo-Identity


Remark 23.27 (The Limits of Application: No Substitution for the Context Criteria or the
Manifestational Adequacy Criterion). The application of the criteria does not replace the
criteria of context validity (Chapter 21) or the proposed criterion of manifestational adequacy
(Chapter 22). The three criteria are about the reconstruction; the other criteria are about the
contexts and the appearances. The framework uses all of them, and each has its own place.

Remark 23.28 (The Criteria Are the Best the Finite Subject Can Supply). The criteria are
the best the finite subject can supply. The framework does not claim that they are the best
possible criteria; it claims that they are the best available to a finite subject.


23.9     The Criteria and the Context
The criteria are used within a context, and the relation between the criteria and the context is
worth marking.
    A pseudo-identity is formed from the manifestations available in a context. The context
is assessed by the criteria of context validity (Chapter 21); the reconstruction is assessed by
the criteria of adequacy (the present chapter). The two assessments are distinct, and the
framework uses both.

Remark 23.29 (The Two Assessments Are Compatible). The two assessments are compatible
because they concern different things: the context is assessed by the criteria of context validity,
and the reconstruction is assessed by the criteria of adequacy. The two are not rivals; they are
two assessments of the same inquiry, at two different levels.

Remark 23.30 (The Criteria and the Fallacy of Super-Identity). The criteria of adequacy
are used against the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28). The fallacy is the error of treating
a record formed by aggregating manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the
identity. The criteria of adequacy are one of the checks: a reconstruction that fails them is not
a candidate for the reconstruction of the identity.


23.10      The Criteria and the Three Failures of Reconstruction
The criteria are stated here, and their relation to the three failures of reconstruction is stated
in the next chapter. The distinction is worth marking briefly.
    The three failures of reconstruction (Chapter 24) are three structurally different ways in
which a reconstruction can go wrong. The criteria of adequacy are the criteria by which a
reconstruction that has not failed is assessed as adequate. The two are distinct: the failures
are the ways a reconstruction can go wrong; the criteria are the conditions a reconstruction
must satisfy if it is not to go wrong in those ways.

Remark 23.31 (The Criteria and the Failures Are Not the Same). The criteria are conditions;
the failures are the ways in which the conditions can be missed. The first states what adequacy
is; the second states the ways in which a reconstruction can fall short of it.


23.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not state the three failures of reconstruction. The three failures are
stated in Chapter 24.
    Second, the chapter does not compare the criteria with the criteria of other epistemologies.
The criteria are the framework’s own criteria; the comparison with other frameworks belongs
to a different inquiry.
23.11. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                  333


    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of how the three criteria are to be weighted
relative to one another. The framework’s claim is that the three are distinct, and that the
assessment is the assessment of the three together; whether one criterion is more important
than another is a question the chapter leaves open.




   Fourth, the chapter does not claim that the criteria can be applied in every case without
judgment. The application of the criteria to a particular case is a matter for the inquiry.




Remark 23.32 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed eight things.
It has stated the three criteria of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity: consistency, stability,
fruitfulness. It has stated the assessment conditions of each criterion and given a comparable
example for each. It has resolved the apparent tension between the narrow definition of
fruitfulness and the use of predictive and practical success elsewhere, by distinguishing the
criterion from its diagnostic indicators, and has given four pairs of cases (fruitful but false,
true but unfruitful, fruitful with failing indicator, unfruitful with passing indicator). It has
distinguished minimality from stability by a worked example. It has stated the fallibilist
character of the assessment. It has applied the three criteria to three rival reconstructions in
a full worked example, and selected the more adequate ones. It has stated the application
and the limits of the criteria. And it has distinguished the criteria from the criteria of context
validity (Chapter 21) and the proposed criterion of manifestational adequacy (Chapter 22).
The chapter’s contribution is the framework’s account of the adequacy of a reconstruction,
stated at the strength its arguments support, the assessment conditions, the worked example,
and the clarification of fruitfulness that the later parts of the book require.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a reconstruction you have formed of something you know only partly. Apply
the assessment conditions of Section 23.3.1: is your reconstruction consistent with other
independent reconstructions? Is it stable under new evidence? Does it have the structural
capacity to distinguish and to continue? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between the adequacy of a reconstruction and the partiality of the evidence?
    And consider the worked example of Section 23.7: can you apply the same four steps to
three rival reconstructions of your own? Can you show, for each step, which reconstruction
passes and which fails? Can you state the verdict, and can you explain why the choice between
the two adequate reconstructions is not settled by the criteria?
    Finally, consider the distinction between the narrow definition of fruitfulness and its
23.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                            335


diagnostic indicators (Section 23.6.1): can you give a case in which a reconstruction is fruitful
but its predictive indicator fails, and a case in which a reconstruction is unfruitful but its
practical indicator passes? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the
criterion and its indicators, and about the framework’s claim that the criterion, not the
indicator, is decisive? A reader who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter;
a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the three failures of reconstruction: the failure from a shortage of
manifestations, the failure from incompatibility of manifestations, and the failure from the
false assumption that an aggregate can replace the source. The present chapter has stated the
criteria of adequacy; the next chapter states the ways in which a reconstruction can fall short
of them.

Chapter 24

The Three Failures of Reconstruction

Scope
This chapter states the three structurally different ways in which an attempt to reconstruct
an identity from its manifestations can fail. It states the three failures, gives for each a
diagnostic sign, an assessment question, its consequence, and its remedy, states the logical
relations among the three with a diagram (Section 24.7.1), examines the claim that the third
is the most fundamental with an independent argument and two counterexamples, and adds a
diagnostic table for identifying the failure in a real reconstruction (Section 24.10). Its claims
are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “failure,” “shortage,” “incompatibility,” “aggregate,”
“misattribution,” or “confounded record,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by
the definitions in this chapter.


24.1      A Scene: Three Attempts to Reconstruct a Song
Consider three attempts to reconstruct the same thing: a song that has been transmitted
orally for several generations, and whose original performances are lost.
    The first attempt is made by a scholar who has collected three recordings. The three
recordings are of the same song, but each is short, and each was recorded in a different village.
The scholar tries to reconstruct the song from the three recordings. The reconstruction is
incomplete: too few manifestations are available, and the invariant cannot be isolated from
the small sample. This is the first failure: the failure from a shortage of manifestations.
    The second attempt is made by a scholar who has collected three hundred recordings, from
many villages and many generations. The recordings conflict: some have the same melody but
different words; some have the same words but a different melody; some seem to be a different
song entirely, misattributed to the original. The scholar tries to reconstruct the song from the
three hundred recordings. The reconstruction is confounded: the manifestations conflict, and
the invariant cannot be isolated from the conflict. This is the second failure: the failure from
incompatibility of manifestations.
    The third attempt is made by a scholar who has collected three hundred recordings, and
who has sorted them, separated the conflicting ones, and verified that the rest are recordings
of the same song. The recordings are rich and compatible. The scholar builds a complete
record of every feature that appears in any recording, and calls the record “the song.” But the
record is not the song. The song is the identity that the recordings manifest; the record is a
collection of manifestations, sorted and verified, but still a collection. This is the third failure:
the failure from the false assumption that an aggregate can replace the source.
    The three attempts fail in different ways. The first fails because there are too few
manifestations; the second fails because the manifestations conflict; the third fails because
338                                          Chapter 24. The Three Failures of Reconstruction


even a rich and compatible aggregate is not the identity. The present chapter gives, for each
failure, its diagnostic sign, its assessment question, its consequence, and its remedy.

Remark 24.1 (The Scene Shows Three Trajectories, Not Three Scholars). The scene is
easily read as an observation about three scholars who happen to fail in different ways. The
observation is not wrong, but it hides the structural point. The structural point is that the
three failures are three trajectories of the same inquiry. The three scholars are not three
different people; they are three possible outcomes of the same project.

Remark 24.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the three
failures at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the distinction between them; it makes
the distinction intelligible before it is stated.


24.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated the three criteria of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity (Chapter 23).
The criteria state what an adequate reconstruction is; they do not yet state the ways in which
a reconstruction can fall short of them.
    The present chapter asks: what are the structurally different ways in which a reconstruction
can go wrong? The question is not idle. A reconstruction can fail in more than one way, and
the ways are not the same. If the ways are distinguished, the failure can be diagnosed, and
the appropriate remedy can be sought. If the ways are run together, every failure looks like
every other failure, and no remedy is available.
    The chapter’s answer has three parts. A reconstruction can fail from a shortage of
manifestations; it can fail from incompatibility of manifestations; and it can fail from the false
assumption that an aggregate can replace the source. The three failures are distinct, and
they have different remedies. The chapter also states the logical relations among the three
(Section 24.7), examines the claim that the third is the most fundamental (Section 24.8), and
adds a diagnostic table (Section 24.10).

Remark 24.3 (The Three Failures Are Not Degrees of the Same Failure). The three failures
are not three degrees of the same failure. They are three structurally different ways in which a
reconstruction can go wrong, and each has its own diagnosis and its own remedy.

Remark 24.4 (The Three Failures Can Occur Together). The three failures are distinct,
but they are not mutually exclusive. A reconstruction can suffer from a shortage and from
incompatibility at the same time; a reconstruction can suffer from incompatibility and from
the aggregate-replacing-source at the same time. The framework distinguishes the three so
that each can be diagnosed, not because they cannot occur together.


24.3     The First Failure: Shortage of Manifestations
Definition 24.1 (The First Failure: Shortage of Manifestations). (A) A reconstruction suffers
from the first failure when the manifestations gathered are too few, or too uniform, for the
invariant to be isolated. The failure is quantitative: the reconstruction has not gathered
enough evidence.

Diagnostic sign. The reconstruction’s description varies widely under small additions of
new manifestations; the reconstruction does not converge on a single pseudo-identity; the
criteria of consistency, stability, and fruitfulness are not satisfied, and the failure is traced to
the sample size.
24.4. The Second Failure: Incompatibility of Manifestations                                     339


Assessment question. Is the sample of manifestations large enough, and varied enough,
for the invariant to be isolated from it?

Consequence. The reconstruction is incomplete: it is an inadequate reconstruction of the
identity, because the invariant cannot be isolated from the small sample.

Remedy. More manifestations, gathered under varied contexts. The remedy is the ordinary
remedy of empirical inquiry.

Remark 24.5 (The Failure Is Real). The first failure is a real failure. The reconstruction
that suffers from it is not an adequate reconstruction of the identity; it is an inadequate
reconstruction.

Remark 24.6 (The Failure Is Remediable in Principle). The first failure is remediable in
principle. With enough manifestations, under sufficiently varied contexts, the invariant can be
isolated.

Remark 24.7 (The Failure and the Finitude of the Subject). The first failure is compounded
by the finitude of the subject (Chapter 3). The finite subject cannot complete the survey of
manifestations (Chapter 27); every reconstruction is formed from a finite sample. The first
failure is therefore not only a failure of a particular reconstruction; it is a structural condition
of finite inquiry. The failure is a failure of completeness, not a failure of the reconstruction’s
adequacy.

Remark 24.8 (The Failure Is a Limit of Evidence). The first failure is a limit of evidence. A
limit of evidence is a limit that more evidence, in principle, could overcome. The distinction
between a limit of evidence and a limit of conception is what the chapter will use to distinguish
the first and second failures from the third.


24.4     The Second Failure: Incompatibility of Manifestations
Definition 24.2 (The Second Failure: Incompatibility of Manifestations). (A) A reconstruction
suffers from the second failure when the manifestations conflict, because some of them are
not manifestations of the identity (misattribution), or are taken from contexts not mutually
translatable (the precondition of the fallacy of super-identity). The failure is structural: the
reconstruction has gathered manifestations, and the manifestations conflict.

Diagnostic sign. The reconstruction’s description is internally inconsistent; the manifes-
tations cannot be brought under a single invariant without excluding some of them; the
reconstruction oscillates between incompatible descriptions, and the oscillation is traced to the
conflict among the manifestations.

Assessment question. Are the manifestations attributed to the identity all manifestations
of the identity, and are the contexts from which they are drawn mutually translatable?

Consequence. The reconstruction is confounded: the invariant cannot be isolated from the
conflict, because the conflict is in the evidence.

Remedy. Better sorting: remove the manifestations that are not manifestations of the
identity, and handle the contexts that cannot be translated into one another with the care
that the criteria of context validity (Chapter 21) require.
340                                          Chapter 24. The Three Failures of Reconstruction


Remark 24.9 (The Failure Is Real). The second failure is a real failure. The reconstruction
that suffers from it is not an adequate reconstruction of the identity; it is a confounded
reconstruction.

Remark 24.10 (The Failure Is Remediable in Principle). The second failure is remediable in
principle. With the right sorting and the right handling of the contexts, the manifestations
that are not manifestations of the identity are removed, and the manifestations that are from
mutually translatable contexts are kept.

Remark 24.11 (The Failure and the Fallacy of Super-Identity). The second failure is not the
fallacy of super-identity. The fallacy (Chapter 28) is the error of treating a record formed by
aggregating manifestations across contexts whose elements are not mutually translatable as a
reconstruction of the identity. The second failure is the more general failure of incompatibility,
of which the fallacy is a particular case.

Remark 24.12 (The Failure Is a Limit of Use, Not a Limit of Amount). The first failure
is a limit of the amount of evidence. The second failure is a limit of the use of evidence:
the manifestations are enough, but they are not sorted. The remedy for the first failure is
more evidence; the remedy for the second failure is better use of the evidence that is already
available.


24.5     The Third Failure: Aggregate Replacing the Source
Definition 24.3 (The Third Failure: Aggregate Replacing the Source). (A) A reconstruction
suffers from the third failure when it treats the aggregate of manifestations, however rich and
compatible, as if it were the identity. The aggregate is not the identity: the identity is the
invariant that the manifestations manifest; the aggregate is a collection of manifestations,
sorted and verified, but still a collection. The failure is conceptual: the reconstruction fails in
its understanding of what it is doing.

Diagnostic sign. The reconstruction states the aggregate of manifestations as if it were the
identity; it presents the collection as the source; it does not distinguish the pseudo-identity
it has formed from the identity it was meant to approximate. The failure is traced to the
conception, not to the evidence or the sorting.

Assessment question. Does the reconstruction present the aggregate of manifestations as
the identity, or does it present it as a pseudo-identity, an estimate of a signature, that is not
the identity?

Consequence. The reconstruction is a spurious composite: it is a record without a corre-
sponding invariant, and it is not an adequate reconstruction of the identity. The failure is not
a shortage of evidence, and it is not a conflict in the evidence; it is a failure of the conception
of what the reconstruction is.

Remedy. A correction of the conception: the reconstruction must recognize that it has
produced a pseudo-identity, an estimate of a signature, and not the identity itself (Chapter 12).
The remedy is not more evidence, and it is not better sorting; it is the recognition of what
kind of object a reconstruction is.

Remark 24.13 (The Failure Is Real). The third failure is a real failure. The reconstruction
that suffers from it is not an adequate reconstruction of the identity; it is a record without a
corresponding invariant, a spurious composite.
24.6. The Three Failures Compared                                                               341


Remark 24.14 (The Failure Is Not Remediable by More Evidence). The third failure is not
remediable by more evidence. More evidence makes the aggregate larger, not more adequate
as a reconstruction of the identity.

Remark 24.15 (The Failure Is Not Remediable by Better Sorting). The third failure is
not remediable by better sorting. The manifestations may be perfectly sorted and perfectly
compatible; the aggregate is still not the identity.

Remark 24.16 (The Failure Is a Limit of Conception). The first failure is a limit of evidence;
the second is a limit of use; the third is a limit of conception. The limit of conception is
the deepest, because it is not a limit of the inquiry’s resources; it is a limit of the inquiry’s
understanding of what it is doing.

24.7      The Logical Relations Among the Three Failures
The three failures are distinct, and the present section states their logical relations. The
relations are three: (i) the three are not mutually exclusive; (ii) the three are not jointly
exhaustive; (iii) the three can overlap, and the overlap has a pattern.
342                                          Chapter 24. The Three Failures of Reconstruction


Principle 24.1 (The Logical Relations Among the Three Failures). (A) The three failures
are not mutually exclusive, and they are not jointly exhaustive. A reconstruction can suffer
from more than one of the three at the same time, and a reconstruction can fail in a way that
is none of the three. The three are the kinds of failure the framework has identified, not the
complete partition of the space of failures.


24.7.1    The Diagram of the Relations
The relations among the three failures can be displayed in a diagram. The diagram has three
regions, one for each failure, and the regions overlap.


  Region F1                       Region F2                     Region F3
  Shortage of manifestations      Incompatibility of manifesta- Aggregate replacing          the
                                  tions                         source
  Overlaps:
  F1 ∩ F2: small sample                                            F2 ∩ F3: sorted aggregate
  with misattributed manifes-                                      mistaken for identity
  tations
  The pattern of overlap: F3 often follows F2 (sorting leads to treating the sorted aggre-
  gate as the identity). F1 can lead to F2 (a small sample may contain misattributions).
  The three regions do not exhaust the space: the absence of manifestations is a failure
  none of the three names.


    The diagram is a summary, not a proof. Its purpose is to show that the three failures
are distinct regions that can overlap, and that the overlap has a characteristic pattern. The
framework’s claim is that the three are the kinds it has identified, not the complete partition
of the space; a fourth kind (the absence of manifestations) is named in the diagram as outside
the three regions.


Not mutually exclusive: an overlapping example. A reconstruction of a historical
figure from three letters written by the figure’s contemporaries, each of which reports a different
version of the same event. The reconstruction suffers from shortage and from incompatibility
at once.


Not jointly exhaustive: an independent example. A reconstruction of an identity that
has no manifestations at all in the reconstruction’s context. The reconstruction fails in a way
the three failures do not name: the failure from the absence of manifestations.


Overlap with a pattern: the third failure follows the second. When a reconstruction
suffers from incompatibility, the remedy is to sort the manifestations. If the sorted aggregate
is then treated as if it were the identity, the reconstruction passes from the second failure to
the third.

Remark 24.18 (The Three Failures and the Criteria of Exhaustiveness). The principle states
that the three failures are not jointly exhaustive. The claim is not that a fourth failure is
likely, or that the three are a poor classification; the claim is that the three are the kinds the
framework has identified, and that the framework does not claim to have partitioned the space
of failures.
24.8. Why the Third Failure Is the Most Fundamental                                              343


Remark 24.19 (The Three Failures and the Criteria of Exclusiveness). The principle states
that the three failures are not mutually exclusive. The claim is not that the three are the
same; the claim is that a reconstruction can suffer from more than one at the same time. The
distinction is the distinction between the distinctness of the kinds and the exclusiveness of the
instances.


24.8      Why the Third Failure Is the Most Fundamental
The third failure is the most fundamental of the three, and the claim is stated with an
independent argument and examined with two counterexamples.

24.8.1     The Independent Argument
Principle 24.2 (The Third Failure Is the Most Fundamental). (T) The third failure is more
fundamental than the first and the second, in the sense that a reconstruction that suffers
from the third failure cannot be made adequate by any improvement of its evidence or its
sorting, while a reconstruction that suffers from the first or the second can be made adequate
in principle by such improvements.

Argument for the Principle.   1. A reconstruction that suffers from the first failure can, in
     principle, be made adequate by more evidence (the remedy of Section 24.3).

   2. A reconstruction that suffers from the second failure can, in principle, be made adequate
      by better sorting (the remedy of Section 24.4).

   3. A reconstruction that suffers from the third failure cannot be made adequate by more
      evidence or by better sorting: the aggregate, however large and however well sorted,
      remains an aggregate, not the identity (Section 24.5).

   4. Therefore the third failure is more fundamental: it is a limit that the remedies of the
      first two cannot remove.


    The principle’s force is in step (3). The first two failures are limits of the inquiry’s resources
(the amount of evidence, the use of evidence); the third failure is a limit of the inquiry’s
conception of what it is doing. The remedies of the first two are remedies within the conception;
the remedy of the third is a correction of the conception. The distinction is the distinction
between a limit within the inquiry and a limit of the inquiry.

24.8.2     Counterexample 1: A Reconstruction Where the First Failure Is
           More Fundamental
A critic might object that the first failure can be more fundamental than the third. Consider a
reconstruction of an identity whose manifestations are so few, and so uniform, that the recon-
struction cannot even form an aggregate to be mistaken for the identity. The reconstruction
suffers from the first failure; it does not yet reach the third. The first failure, in this case, is
the limit that prevents the inquiry from proceeding at all; the third failure is not even on the
horizon.
    The framework’s response is that the first failure, in this case, is more fundamental in the
order of inquiry (it comes first, and it blocks the inquiry), but not in the order of conception
(it does not change what the inquiry is doing). The third failure, once it occurs, cannot be
removed by more evidence; the first failure, once the evidence is supplied, can be removed.
The distinction is the distinction between the order of inquiry and the order of conception; the
344                                          Chapter 24. The Three Failures of Reconstruction


framework’s claim that the third is more fundamental is a claim about the order of conception,
not about the order of inquiry.


24.8.3    Counterexample 2: A Reconstruction Where the Second Failure Is
          More Fundamental
A critic might object that the second failure can be more fundamental than the third. Consider
a reconstruction whose manifestations are irreducibly in conflict, so that no sorting can remove
the conflict. The reconstruction suffers from the second failure; the conflict is structural to the
evidence, and no amount of sorting can remove it. The second failure, in this case, is the limit
that prevents the reconstruction from being adequate; the third failure is a consequence of the
second, and the second is more fundamental.
    The framework’s response is that the second failure, in this case, is more fundamental in
the order of evidence (it is the limit of what the evidence can be), but not in the order of
conception (it does not change what the inquiry is doing). The third failure, when it follows
the second, is not removed by resolving the second; the third requires a correction of the
conception, and the correction is not supplied by the resolution of the second. The distinction
is the same as in the first counterexample: the order of inquiry and the order of evidence are
distinguished from the order of conception.

Remark 24.20 (The Two Counterexamples Are Answered, Not Dismissed). The two coun-
terexamples are answered, not dismissed. Each shows a case in which one of the first two
failures is more fundamental in one order (the order of inquiry, the order of evidence), and the
framework acknowledges the cases. The framework’s claim is that the third failure is more
fundamental in the order of conception; the counterexamples do not touch that claim, because
they concern other orders. The distinction among the orders is what the counterexamples
reveal, and the framework states it.

Remark 24.21 (The Third Failure Is Not a Failure of the Identity). The third failure is not
a failure of the identity. The identity is what it is; the reconstruction’s treating the aggregate
as if it were the identity does not make the identity an aggregate. The failure is a failure of
the reconstruction, not a failure of the identity.



24.9     The Three Failures and the Criteria of Adequacy
The criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23) state what an adequate reconstruction is. The three
failures state the ways in which a reconstruction can fall short of the criteria.
    The first failure is a failure of consistency, stability, and fruitfulness, all at once: a
reconstruction from too few manifestations is unlikely to converge, to be stable, or to be
fruitful. The remedy is more evidence.
    The second failure is a failure of consistency in particular: a reconstruction from conflicting
manifestations is unlikely to converge, because the conflict is in the evidence. The remedy is
better sorting.
    The third failure is a failure of the conception of what the reconstruction is. The remedy
is a correction of the conception, not a change in the criteria.

Remark 24.22 (The Criteria and the Failures Are Complementary). The criteria and the
failures are complementary. The criteria state what adequacy is; the failures state the ways in
which a reconstruction can fall short of it.
24.10. The Diagnostic Table for a Real Reconstruction                                        345

which failure a given reconstruction suffers from. The table is applied to a real reconstruction,
so that the reader can see the instrument at work.
