Chapter 27

The Impossibility of Super-Identity

Scope
This chapter opens Part V by stating the theorem of the impossibility of super-identity: no
finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity in all cognitive contexts. It gives two
independent arguments for the theorem—the reductio from the four premises (Section 27.5),
and the diagonal construction (Section 27.6)—states the diagonal construction in a coherent
formalization that defines the symbols and states each inference step (Section 27.7), states
the configuration-dependence strengthening (Section 27.8), and draws the three consequences:
the limit of reconstruction, the plurality of perspectives, and the fallacy of super-identity
(which is stated in full in Chapter 28). It closes with the falsification conditions of the
principle (Section 27.10) and with the epistemic result of the principle as a guide to the
limits of reconstruction and to the claim of completeness (Section 27.11). Its claims are
epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “super-identity,” “survey,” “context,” “configuration,” or
“completeness,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this
chapter.


27.1     A Scene: The Catalog of the Library
Consider a catalog that attempts to list every book in a library. The catalog is itself a book in
the library. If it is complete, it must list itself. But when it lists itself, the listing is a new
entry, and the catalog is no longer the catalog it was: it is a catalog that lists itself, which is
different from the catalog before it listed itself. To be complete, the new catalog must list the
new entry, which is a new listing, and so on without end.
    The catalog cannot be complete—not because the librarian is lazy, but because the task is
self-undermining. Every attempt to complete the catalog generates a new item outside the
attempt. The incompleteness is not a shortage of effort; it is a structural feature of the task
itself.
    The scene poses a question. What is the structure of this regress? Is it a peculiarity of
catalogs, or is it a general feature of any attempt to complete a survey? The present chapter’s
answer is that it is general: it is the structure of any attempt at super-identity.

Remark 27.1 (The Scene Shows Self-Undermining Structure). The scene is easily read as a
puzzle about catalogs. The puzzle is real, but it hides the structural point. The structural
point is that the catalog is a case of a self-undermining task: a task whose completion generates
a new item outside the completion.

Remark 27.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the structure
of the impossibility in a familiar case. It does not prove the theorem; it makes the theorem
intelligible before it is stated.
378                                            Chapter 27. The Impossibility of Super-Identity


27.2     The Question
The previous parts of the book have developed the structure of epistemic relations and the
conditions of epistemic validity and adequacy. The present part turns from the conditions of
validity to the limits of cognition. The first limit, and the one from which the others follow, is
the impossibility of super-identity.
    The question is: what is a super-identity claim, and why can no finite subject make one?

Remark 27.3 (The Impossibility Is on the Side of the Subject). The impossibility established
here is an impossibility for the finite subject. The framework does not claim that no subject
whatsoever can know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts; it claims that no finite
subject can.

Remark 27.4 (The Question Comes at the Start of Part V). The question comes at the start
of Part V because the limits are not a failure of the conditions of validity, but a condition of
the subject. A cognition which satisfies all the conditions of Part IV is still subject to the
limits that the present part states.


27.3     The Principle Restated
Definition 27.1 (Super-Identity). A super-identity claim is a subject’s claim to have known,
or to be able to know, all manifestations of an identity in all contexts, so that nothing about
the identity’s expression remains outside its knowledge.

Principle 27.1 (Impossibility of Super-Identity). (T) No finite subject can know all manifes-
tations of an identity in all contexts. The super-identity claim is therefore self-undermining.
Moreover, the impossibility is not a matter of degree of effort: any attempt to complete the
survey generates new contexts that lie outside it.

    The principle has two claims. The first is the impossibility itself; the second is the character
of the impossibility (structural, not contingent). The first is established by the reductio and
the diagonal construction; the second by the configuration-dependence strengthening.

Remark 27.5 (The Two Claims Are Not Independent). The first claim (no finite subject
can know all manifestations in all contexts) is what the second claim (the impossibility is
structural, not contingent) makes precise: without the second claim, the first would be a
contingent fact that a more powerful subject might overcome.


27.4     The Scope of the Sets and the Finitude Premise
Before the arguments are stated, the sets and the finitude premise must be defined precisely,
so that the arguments are assessable.

Definition 27.2 (The Set of Contexts). (A) Let C be the set of cognitive contexts in which
an identity I can be manifested. The set is defined by the condition: C ∈ C if and only if C is
a cognitive context (Chapter 10), and I has a manifestation in C (Chapter 13).

Definition 27.3 (The Subject’s Standing). (A) Let CS ⊆ C be the set of contexts in which
the finite subject S has standing: the contexts the subject occupies at some time, in the sense
of the finitude axiom (Chapter 3). The set is finite by the finitude axiom.

Definition 27.4 (The Finitude Premise). (A) For every finite subject S, CS is finite. The
premise is the finitude axiom of Chapter 3, stated in the vocabulary of the present chapter.
27.5. The First Argument: The Reductio                                                      379


Remark 27.6 (The Scope of the Set of Contexts). The set C is defined by the condition of
the definition; the framework does not require that C be given in extension. The set is what
the arguments quantify over; the arguments use the openness of relations to show that C is
not exhausted by any finite subset.

Remark 27.7 (The Finitude Premise Is Not a Contingent Fact). The finitude premise is not
a contingent fact about the subject’s present resources; it is the finitude axiom of Chapter 3.
The subject that the framework’s arguments are about is the finite subject; the infinite subject
is not the subject the arguments address.


27.5     The First Argument: The Reductio
The first argument is a reductio from four premises.

First Argument: The Reductio. The premises are:

(P1) Finitude of the subject (Definition 27.4): for every finite subject S, CS is finite.

(P2) Infinity of contexts (Chapter 11): C is not finite.

(P3) Manifestation is a product (Chapter 13): the manifestation of I in C, f (C), is determined
     jointly by I and by C, not by I alone.

(P4) Knowing is situated (Chapters 10 and 14): to know f (C) is a cognition, and every
     cognition occurs in a context; the subject must have standing in C for f (C) to be known.

   The reductio proceeds:

  1. Suppose a finite subject S knows all manifestations of I in all contexts: for every C ∈ C,
     S knows f (C).

  2. By (P4), for every C ∈ C, S has standing in C; hence C ⊆ CS .

  3. By (P1), CS is finite; hence C is finite.

  4. This contradicts (P2). Hence the supposition is false: no finite subject knows all
     manifestations of I in all contexts.



    The weight of the proof falls on (P4). The other three premises are the framework’s finitude
axiom, its infinity principle, and its account of manifestation; (P4) is the substantive premise
that links the subject’s knowledge to the contexts the subject occupies.

Remark 27.8 (The Generative-Rule Objection). It may be objected that a subject could
know the invariant structure itself, and from it generate every manifestation by a rule,
without entering each context. The framework’s reply is (P4) together with (P3): because
manifestations are products of identity and receiving context, no rule stated in terms of the
identity alone yields them. A generative rule would need the receiving contexts as inputs,
and having the inputs is having standing in the contexts. Whoever exhibits a rule that
generates every manifestation from the identity alone, without the receiving contexts, refutes
the principle.

Remark 27.9 (The Four Premises Are Not Equally Weighty). (P1) and (P2) are the frame-
work’s own axioms; (P3) and (P4) are the framework’s account of manifestation and cognition.
The reductio is only as strong as its weakest premise; the second argument below is designed
to reach the same conclusion without (P3).
380                                              Chapter 27. The Impossibility of Super-Identity


27.6      The Second Argument: The Diagonal Construction

The second argument is independent of (P3). It uses only the openness of relations and the
situatedness of knowing.


Second Argument: The Diagonal Construction.             1. Suppose a finite subject S has surveyed
     a collection of contexts L = {C1 , . . . , Cn } ⊆ CS and claims that these are all the contexts
     in which I is manifested: C ⊆ L.

   2. The survey is itself a cognition, carried out in some context CS (the fourth column;
      Chapter 7).

   3. By the openness of relations (Chapter 11), the pair (L, f (L)), where f (L) = {f (C1 ), . . . , f (Cn )},
      is a fixed element in some context C ∗ ∈ C that is not among C1 , . . . , Cn . The context
      C ∗ contains the survey as an element, but the survey does not contain C ∗ .

   4. The manifestation f (C ∗ ) is defined, but f (C ∗ ) ∈
                                                          / f (L).

                                            / f (L), but the survey claimed f (L) is the whole of
   5. So the survey is incomplete: f (C ∗ ) ∈
      the manifestations.

   6. Hence the claim to have surveyed all the contexts is false.




   The argument is diagonal in the strict sense: whatever list of contexts is offered, a context
outside the list can be constructed from the list itself.

Remark 27.10 (The Argument Is Diagonal in the Strict Sense). The construction works by
taking the list and its content together and producing a new item that is not among the items
the list contains. The form is the same as Cantor’s diagonal argument, applied to contexts
rather than to real numbers.

Remark 27.11 (The Argument Is Not a Proof That Every Survey Fails). The argument
shows that any claim to have surveyed all contexts is false. It does not show that no survey is
useful, or that no partial survey can be adequate for its purposes.

Remark 27.12 (The Argument Depends on the Openness of Relations). The argument uses
the openness of relations (Chapter 11); it does not invoke the motion of fluid elements. The
distinction is the distinction between knowing a rule and completing a survey; the framework’s
claim is about the second, not the first.



27.7      The Coherent Formalization

The diagonal argument is stated in prose in the previous section. The present section states it
in a coherent formalization, with symbols defined and each inference step stated.
27.7. The Coherent Formalization                                                                381


27.7.1      The Symbols

Symbol              Meaning
S                   A finite subject
I                   An identity
C                   The set of cognitive contexts in which I can be manifested (Defini-
                    tion 27.2)
CS                  The set of contexts in which S has standing (Definition 27.3), finite by
                    the finitude axiom
M                   The collection of manifestations of I in the contexts of C
f                   The representation function f : C → M; f (C) is the manifestation of I
                    in C
L                   A finite list of contexts, L = {C1 , . . . , Cn } ⊆ CS
f (L)               The collection {f (C1 ), . . . , f (Cn )} of manifestations in L

27.7.2      The Formalization, Step by Step
The formalization has the following form.

     1. The finitude of the subject. CS is finite (Definition 27.3).

     2. The representation function is defined on C. f : C → M is a function; for every
        C ∈ C, f (C) is a determinate manifestation. (This is the formal counterpart of the
        definition of manifestation, Chapter 13.)

     3. The subject’s access is restricted to CS . S has access to f (C) only for C ∈ CS .
        (This is the formal counterpart of the situatedness of knowing, (P4).)

     4. The openness of relations. For every finite list L ⊆ CS and its manifestation set f (L),
                                                                        / L. (This is the formal
        the pair (L, f (L)) is a fixed element in some C ∗ ∈ C with C ∗ ∈
        counterpart of the openness of relations, Chapter 11.)

     5. The diagonal stage. Given L, construct C ∗ as in step 4. Then f (C ∗ ) is defined by
                             / f (L) by the construction in step 4 (since C ∗ ∈
        step 2, and f (C ∗ ) ∈                                                / L).

     6. The conclusion. Any finite list L ⊆ CS omits the manifestation f (C ∗ ), where C ∗ is
        constructed from L. Hence no finite list is complete.

     7. The epistemic conclusion. Since S’s access is restricted to CS (step 3), and since CS
        is finite (step 1), no finite subject can survey all contexts. Hence no finite subject knows
        all manifestations of I in all contexts.

    The formalization makes explicit what the prose argument leaves implicit: the symbols, the
function f , the finitude of CS , the access restriction, the openness premise, and the diagonal
stage. Each step is a stated premise or a stated inference; the reader who accepts the premises
accepts the conclusion.
382                                           Chapter 27. The Impossibility of Super-Identity


Remark 27.13 (The Formalization Does Not Require the Infinity of Contexts). The formal-
ization does not require that C be infinite. It requires only that CS be finite and that openness
of relations holds: for any finite list L, there is C ∗ ∈ C outside L. If C were finite but larger
than CS , the conclusion would still hold: any survey of CS omits contexts in C that are not in
CS . The infinity of contexts makes the impossibility more dramatic, but it is not required for
it.

Remark 27.14 (The Formalization and the Prose Argument). The formalization and the
prose argument are the same argument, stated at two levels of detail. The prose argument
states the structure; the formalization states the structure in symbols. The reader who has
followed the prose argument will recognize the formalization; the reader who has followed the
formalization will recognize the prose argument.

Remark 27.15 (The Conclusion Is Epistemic, Not Metaphysical). The conclusion of the
formalization is epistemic: it is a claim about the finite subject’s access, not a claim about the
identity’s nature. The framework’s claim is that the finite subject cannot survey all contexts,
not that there are no more contexts, and not that the identity is in itself unknowable.


27.8     The Strengthening: Configuration-Dependence
The configuration-dependence strengthening is stated here in summary form; its full develop-
ment is the work of Chapter 29.

Definition 27.5 (Configuration-Dependence (summary)). (A) The manifestation of I in C
depends on what passes through the epistemic light of C, and this in turn depends on the
whole configuration of C: on what other fixed elements are present, and in what state.

The Strengthened Argument.      1. By the conveyor principle (Chapter 8), every manifestation
     of I in C is conveyed by epistemic light of C.

  2. By configuration-dependence, what the epistemic light conveys depends on the configu-
     ration of C.

  3. The configuration of C changes with time and with the other identities in it.

  4. So the set of manifestations of I in a single context C is not fixed once and for all, and
     cannot be exhaustively listed at any one time.

  5. Hence super-identity is impossible not only because contexts are non-finitely many, but
     also because even a single context yields manifestations that vary with its configuration.


Remark 27.16 (The Strengthening Is the Strongest of the Three Arguments). The two
arguments (reductio, diagonal) show that the impossibility holds for any finite subject. The
strengthening shows that the impossibility holds even if the number of contexts were finite,
because a single context’s configuration changes. The strengthening is the strongest because it
survives the denial of the infinity of contexts.

Remark 27.17 (The Strengthening Is Developed in Chapter 29). The configuration-dependence
strengthening is stated here in summary form because it belongs to the argument for the impos-
sibility. Its full development—the definition, the argument, the scope, and the vulnerability—is
the work of Chapter 29.
27.9. The Three Consequences                                                                   383


27.9      The Three Consequences
First consequence: the limit of reconstruction. No subject can occupy a view that
captures an identity as it is in itself, independent of any context. What a finite subject can
achieve is a pseudo-identity of increasing adequacy, not an exhaustive acquaintance with the
source. ((T))

Second consequence: the plurality of perspectives. The plurality of perspectives is a
structural consequence of the relation between a finite subject and an identity, not a defect.
Different perspectives are partial, but not arbitrary: each is answerable to the criteria of
adequacy and of context validity stated in Part IV. ((T))

Third consequence: the fallacy of super-identity. Any attempt to aggregate manifes-
tations across contexts into a single flat record is not a reconstruction of identity. The fallacy
is stated and argued in Chapter 28. ((T))
Remark 27.18 (The Three Consequences Are One Structure). The three consequences are
aspects of one structural fact: the relation between a finite subject and an identity is a relation
of partial access, not of exhaustive comprehension. The first names the limit of the access; the
second names the form the access takes; the third names the error that the limit invites.
Remark 27.19 (The Consequences Are Structural, Not Evaluative). The framework does
not claim that the limit of reconstruction is a deficiency to be lamented, or that the plurality
of perspectives is a good to be celebrated. It claims that the three are structural features of
the relation between finite subjects and identities.
Remark 27.20 (The First Consequence Is Not Skepticism). A skeptic claims that knowledge
is impossible; the framework claims that knowledge is partial. The first is a denial of knowledge;
the second is a description of its condition.
Remark 27.21 (The Second Consequence Is Not Relativism). Relativism is the thesis that
every perspective is as good as every other. The framework’s claim is that every perspective is
partial, not that every perspective is equally adequate.


27.10      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in the preceding sections. The falsification
conditions are stated here with real examples and possible counter-models.

27.10.1     The Falsification Conditions of the Reductio
The reductio would be refuted by a case in which a finite subject knows all manifestations of
an identity in all contexts. Four real examples are the possible counter-models:

Counter-model 1: a finite subject with infinite standing. A finite subject that
occupies infinitely many contexts at once. If such a subject could be exhibited, (P1) would fail,
and the reductio would not go through. The framework does not claim that such a subject is
impossible; it claims that no such subject is known, and that the framework’s arguments are
about finite subjects.

Counter-model 2: a finite number of contexts. An identity whose contexts are finitely
many. If such an identity could be exhibited, (P2) would fail, and the reductio would not go
through. The framework claims that the contexts are not finite (Chapter 11); the reader who
exhibits a finite set of contexts for an identity refutes the infinity principle.
384                                            Chapter 27. The Impossibility of Super-Identity


Counter-model 3: a manifestation not a product of context. An identity whose
manifestations are fixed by the identity alone, not by the receiving context. If such an identity
could be exhibited, (P3) would fail, and the reductio would not go through. The framework’s
account of manifestation (Chapter 13) denies this; the reader who exhibits a manifestation
fixed by the identity alone refutes (P3).


Counter-model 4: a cognition without a context. A cognition that does not occur in a
context. If such a cognition could be exhibited, (P4) would fail, and the reductio would not go
through. The framework’s account of cognition (Chapters 7 and 10) denies this.


27.10.2     The Falsification Conditions of the Diagonal Construction
The diagonal construction would be refuted by a case in which a finite subject’s survey of CS
is complete. Three possible counter-models:


Counter-model 5: no context outside the list. A case in which the openness of relations
fails, so that the pair (L, f (L)) is not a fixed element in any context outside L. If such a case
could be exhibited, step 4 of the diagonal construction would fail.


Counter-model 6: the representation function is undefined outside CS . A case in
which f is not defined on C \ CS . If such a case could be exhibited, step 5 of the diagonal
construction would fail.


Counter-model 7: the subject’s access is not restricted to CS . A case in which the
                                  / CS . If such a case could be exhibited, step 3 of the diagonal
subject has access to f (C) for C ∈
construction would fail.


27.10.3     The Falsification Conditions of the Strengthening
The strengthening would be refuted by a case in which the configuration of a context does not
affect the manifestations produced in it:


Counter-model 8: configuration-independent manifestation. A manifestation of I in
C that is the same regardless of what other fixed elements are present in C, and in what state.
If such a case could be exhibited, the configuration-dependence premise would fail, and the
strengthening would not go through.

Remark 27.22 (The Falsification Conditions Are Concrete). The eight counter-models are
concrete: each is a specific claim that would, if true, refute one of the premises of the argument.
The reader who wishes to challenge the principle knows where to press: on one of the eight
premises. The framework does not claim that no such counter-model can be constructed;
it claims that no such counter-model has been constructed that survives the framework’s
arguments, and it states the premises so that the reader can assess them.

Remark 27.23 (The Two Arguments Are Independent). The two arguments for the impossi-
bility are independent, and each can be assessed separately. A reader who rejects the first,
because of a disagreement about (P4), can still accept the second. A reader who rejects the
second, because of a disagreement about openness, can still accept the first.
27.11. The Epistemic Result of the Principle                                                   385


27.11      The Epistemic Result of the Principle
The chapter’s positive contribution is the epistemic result of the principle: a guide to the
limits of reconstruction and to the claim of completeness. The present section states the result,
so that the reader knows what the principle gives, not only what it excludes.


27.11.1     The Guide to the Limits of Reconstruction
The principle gives a guide to the limits of reconstruction. For any attempt to reconstruct an
identity, the guide states:


First rule: state the contexts of the reconstruction. A reconstruction is always
a reconstruction in some contexts. The first rule is to state the contexts in which the
reconstruction is carried out, so that the reader knows what the reconstruction covers.


Second rule: state the aspects of the identity that the contexts make available.
The contexts make available some aspects of the identity and not others. The second rule
is to state which aspects the contexts make available, so that the reader knows what the
reconstruction can and cannot capture.


Third rule: do not claim completeness. No reconstruction in finitely many contexts is
complete. The third rule is to state the reconstruction’s claim at the strength its contexts
support: the reconstruction is adequate to the extent the criteria of Chapter 23 support, and
it is not a super-identity claim.


Fourth rule: distinguish adequacy from completeness. A reconstruction can be
adequate for its purposes without being complete. The fourth rule is to distinguish the
question of the reconstruction’s adequacy (assessed by the criteria of Chapter 23) from the
question of its completeness (which the present chapter establishes is impossible for the finite
subject).


27.11.2     The Guide to the Claim of Completeness
The principle gives a guide to the claim of completeness. For any attempt to claim completeness,
the guide states:


First rule: identify the claim. A claim of completeness is a claim that the reconstruction
covers all manifestations in all contexts. The first rule is to identify whether the claim is a
claim of completeness or a claim of adequacy.


Second rule: test the claim against the principle. If the claim is a claim of completeness,
the principle states that the claim is false for any finite subject. The second rule is to test the
claim against the principle, and to recognize that the claim cannot be sustained.


Third rule: reformulate the claim. The claim of completeness can be reformulated as
a claim of adequacy: the reconstruction is adequate to the extent the criteria of Chapter 23
support, and it does not claim to be complete. The third rule is to reformulate the claim, so
that the reconstruction is stated at the strength its contexts support.
386                                            Chapter 27. The Impossibility of Super-Identity


Fourth rule: state what the reconstruction leaves out. A reconstruction that recognizes
its own limits can state what it leaves out: the contexts it does not survey, the aspects it
does not capture, the manifestations it does not know. The fourth rule is to state what the
reconstruction leaves out, so that the reader knows what the reconstruction is not.



Remark 27.24 (The Two Guides Are One Result). The guide to the limits of reconstruction
and the guide to the claim of completeness are aspects of one result: the principle’s contribution
to the practice of reconstruction. The first guide states what the reconstruction must do; the
second guide states what the reconstruction must not claim.



Remark 27.25 (The Result Is Epistemic, Not Evaluative). The result is epistemic, not
evaluative. The principle does not say that the reconstruction is a poor thing, or that the
reconstruction is a good thing; it says that the reconstruction is limited, and that its limits
are structural. The reader who takes the result as an evaluation has misread it; the reader
who takes it as an epistemic guide has read it correctly.




27.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
   First, the chapter does not develop the fallacy of super-identity in full. That is the work of
Chapter 28.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the configuration-dependence strengthening in full.
That is the work of Chapter 29.
    Third, the chapter does not state the other limits of finite cognition. Those are stated in
their own places in Part V (Chapters 30–33).
    Fourth, the chapter does not develop the connection between the impossibility of super-
identity and the framework’s account of viability and the cost of cognition. That is developed
in Part VI.



Remark 27.26 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed seven things. It
has defined super-identity and stated the principle of its impossibility, with the two claims
the principle makes. It has stated the scope of the sets and the finitude premise. It has given
two independent arguments for the principle: the reductio from the four premises, and the
diagonal construction. It has given a coherent formalization of the diagonal construction, with
the symbols defined and each inference step stated. It has stated the configuration-dependence
strengthening and marked it as the strongest of the three arguments. It has stated the
falsification conditions of the principle, with eight concrete counter-models. And it has stated
the epistemic result of the principle as a guide to the limits of reconstruction and to the claim
of completeness.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a subject you know well—a discipline, a tradition, a person’s life. What would it
mean to know all of it? What would the attempt to know all of it generate that would be
outside the attempt?
    And consider the catalog—the scene that opened the chapter. The catalog cannot be
complete because the act of listing itself generates a new entry. Is super-identity a task of the
same kind?
    And consider the two guides of Section 27.11: can you apply the four rules of the guide to
the limits of reconstruction to a reconstruction of your own? Can you apply the four rules of
the guide to the claim of completeness to a claim of your own? What does your answer tell
you about the difference between an adequate reconstruction and a complete one? A reader
who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none
has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the fallacy of super-identity: the error of treating a record formed by
aggregating manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the identity. The present
chapter established that the reconstruction cannot be completed; the next chapter states the
error of treating the completed record as if it were the identity.
                                                                                               389




Chapter 28

The Fallacy of Super-Identity

Scope
This chapter states and proves the fallacy of super-identity: the error of treating a record formed
by aggregating manifestations across contexts whose elements are not mutually translatable
as a reconstruction of the identity. It distinguishes aggregation, compatibility, and numerical
unity with independent examples; it states the principle of the non-reduction of identity to
its manifestations; it states the logical relation between the impossibility of Chapter 27 and
the fallacy with a table of premises and conclusions; it states the Golden Record Illusion
with a non-library example; and it states the conditions for correct aggregation, so that the
fallacy can be avoided by a stated method. Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks
of “aggregation,” “compatibility,” “numerical unity,” “context-confounded record,” “spurious
composite,” or “Golden Record,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter.


28.1     A Scene: The Library and the Complete Record
Consider a library that decides to compile a single record of everything it knows about a single
book. The record is to contain every fact that any catalog, any reader, any review, and any
bibliography has recorded about the book: its publication data, its contents, its reception, its
translations, its misreadings, its influence, its presence in courses and in libraries, and every
annotation that any reader has ever written in any copy.
    The record is compiled. It is enormous, and it is consistent: no fact in the record contradicts
any other. Every entry in the record is accurate. The record is complete, in the sense that
nothing any catalog or reader or review has said about the book is missing from it.
    Now suppose the librarian says: “We now have the book. Not a copy, not a catalog
entry—the book itself. The record is the book.”
    The librarian has made an error. The record is not the book. The record is a collection of
facts about the book, drawn from many contexts, sorted and made consistent. The book is
the identity that the facts are about.
    The scene poses a question. What exactly is the librarian’s error? It is not an error of
accuracy, consistency, or completeness. The error is of a different kind: it is the error of
treating an aggregate of facts drawn from different contexts as if it were the identity that the
facts are about. The present chapter names this error, states it as a principle, and proves it.

Remark 28.1 (The Scene Shows the Difference Between the Source and the Aggregate). The
scene is easily read as an observation about a librarian who happens to confuse a record with
the thing recorded. The structural point is that the record is an aggregate and the book is a
source. The fallacy is the error of treating the aggregate as the source.
390                                                 Chapter 28. The Fallacy of Super-Identity


Remark 28.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the fallacy
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the principle; it makes the principle intelligible
before it is stated.


28.2     The Question
The previous chapter established the impossibility of super-identity: no finite subject can
know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27). The impossibility is a limit
on what the finite subject can do; it is not yet an account of the error that a finite subject can
make when it tries to do what cannot be done.
     The present chapter states the error. The question is: what is the error of treating an
aggregate of manifestations, drawn from different contexts, as a reconstruction of the identity?
     The distinction between the impossibility and the fallacy is worth marking. The impossi-
bility is a fact about what the finite subject cannot do. The fallacy is an error that the finite
subject can commit, and can commit with a small amount of data as easily as with a large
amount.

Remark 28.3 (The Fallacy Is Not the Impossibility). The fallacy is not the impossibility.
The impossibility is a limit on what the finite subject can know; the fallacy is an error of
method. The two are related, but they are not the same.

Remark 28.4 (The Fallacy Is a Failure of Method, Not a Failure of Belief). The fallacy is a
failure of method, not a failure of belief. A subject can commit the fallacy while believing
that its record is merely a record; the fallacy is in the method the subject uses to form the
record, not in the subject’s belief about what the record is.


28.3     The Principle of the Fallacy
Principle 28.1 (Fallacy of Super-Identity). (T) A record formed by aggregating manifestations
drawn from contexts whose elements are not mutually translatable is not a reconstruction of
the identity. It is a context-confounded record: an object that corresponds to no identity at
all.

    The principle is (T): it is argued from the definition of reconstruction, from the definition
of manifestation as a product, and from the criteria of context validity.

Remark 28.5 (The Principle Is About Method, Not About Knowledge). The principle
says that a particular method of forming a record —aggregation across contexts without
translation—does not yield a reconstruction of the identity. It does not say that the subject
who uses the method lacks knowledge.

Remark 28.6 (The Principle Is a Particular Case of the Non-Reduction Principle). The
fallacy principle is the non-reduction principle (stated below as Principle 28.2) applied to the
specific case of a record formed across contexts.


28.4     The Proof
Proof of the Fallacy of Super-Identity.    1. To reconstruct an identity is to find what remains
      invariant across its manifestations (Chapter 12).

   2. Each manifestation is the product of the identity and the context in which it appears
      (Chapter 13). It therefore contains two components, contributed by the identity and by
      the context, and these are not separated in the manifestation as given.
28.5. The Logical Relation Between the Impossibility and the Fallacy                           391


  3. Invariants are isolated by comparing manifestations while the context varies and the
     identity is held constant (Chapter 12).
  4. Mere concatenation does not compare; it only collects. A record that concatenates
     manifestations from different contexts does not vary the context while holding the
     identity constant.
  5. A concatenated record therefore mixes the identity’s contribution with the contributions
     of every context it has absorbed, and gives no way of telling which is which.
  6. Hence concatenation does not reconstruct the identity. A record that treats the mixture
     as an identity has no corresponding identity; call it a spurious composite.


    The proof’s force is in step (4). If concatenation compared the manifestations while varying
the context, it would isolate the invariant. But concatenation does not compare; it collects.
Remark 28.7 (The Proof Is a Diagnosis of a Method). The proof is a diagnosis of a method,
not a condemnation of a subject. The proof shows that the method of concatenation does not
yield a reconstruction; it does not show that the subject who uses the method is irrational.

Remark 28.8 (The Two Claims Are Independent in Their Premises). The two claims are

the finite subject cannot survey all manifestations; it does not establish that the identity has
no complete manifestation. The fallacy establishes that the aggregate is not a reconstruction;
it does not establish that the aggregate is unreal. The framework’s claim is that the two are
epistemic, and that their being epistemic is what makes them assessable.


28.6     Aggregation, Compatibility, and Numerical Unity
The fallacy is not only a fault of gathering conflicting information. Three things are separate,
and the distinction is developed here with independent examples.

Aggregation. Collecting manifestations.

Compatibility. The absence of conflict among them.

Numerical unity. The oneness of the source identity.

28.6.1    Independent Examples for the Three Concepts
Example of aggregation. A historian collects all the surviving letters of a person, all the
references to the person in other people’s letters, and all the official documents that mention
the person. The collection is an aggregation: many manifestations, gathered together. Nothing
yet has been done to distinguish what is contributed by the person from what is contributed
by the contexts.

Example of compatibility. The historian compares the letters and finds that no letter
contradicts any other: the person’s stated beliefs, the person’s reported actions, and the
person’s reported relations are all consistent. The absence of conflict is compatibility. Nothing
yet has been done to isolate the person’s invariant; the compatibility is a relation among the
manifestations.

Example of numerical unity. The historian forms a reconstruction of the person: the
person’s identity, as it appears across the manifestations. The reconstruction is a pseudo-
identity (Chapter 12), and it approximates the numerical unity of the source. The numerical
unity is not achieved by the aggregation or by the compatibility; it is the oneness of the source,
which the reconstruction approximates but does not reach.

Principle 28.2 (Non-Reduction of Identity to Manifestations). (T) An identity is not identical
with the aggregate of its manifestations, nor with their compatible aggregate.

Proof of the Non-Reduction Principle.      1. A manifestation is the product of the identity
      and a receiving context, and is not the identity (Chapter 13).
28.7. The Golden Record Illusion                                                                393


   2. An aggregate of products is a plurality of products. A plurality of things is not, as such,
      a single thing of another kind.

   3. Compatibility among the products is a relation among them and does not bring in the
      thing that they are products of.

   4. Hence the identity is not the aggregate, nor the compatible aggregate.


Remark 28.10 (The Three Are Not the Same). The three—aggregation, compatibility, and
numerical unity—are not the same, and the fallacy is the confusion of the first two with the
third. The examples above show that each can be present without the others: aggregation
without compatibility (conflicting letters), compatibility without numerical unity (the letters
are consistent but the person is not reconstructed), numerical unity without aggregation (the
reconstruction is formed from a small sample, not from an aggregate).

Remark 28.11 (The Three Are Not the Three Failures of Reconstruction). The three—
aggregation, compatibility, and numerical unity—are not the three failures of reconstruction
(Chapter 24). The three failures are the ways a reconstruction can go wrong; the three of the
present section are the elements of the relation between a record and the source.


28.7      The Golden Record Illusion
The fallacy is closely related to what we may call the Golden Record Illusion: the belief that
there is, or could be, a single record that contains all attributes of an entity across all contexts.
    The framework treats this ideal as ill-posed. There is no Golden Record, not because
we lack the resources to construct it, but because collecting attributes does not isolate an
invariant, and an invariant is what an identity is.

28.7.1     A Non-Library Example: The Patient’s Medical Record
Consider a patient’s medical record. The record contains every test result, every physician’s
note, every imaging scan, every prescription, and every nurse’s observation. The record is
enormous, and it is consistent: no entry contradicts any other. Every entry is accurate.
    Now suppose a physician says: “We now have the patient. Not a summary, not a diagnosis—
the patient herself. The record is the patient.”
    The physician has made the same error as the librarian. The record is an aggregate of facts
about the patient, drawn from many contexts (laboratory, clinic, imaging center, pharmacy,
bedside), and the patient is the identity that the facts are about. The record is not the patient,
however complete and consistent it is.
    The medical example shows the fallacy at work in a domain where the aggregation is
most advanced and the temptation is most acute: the more data we collect, the more we are
tempted to think the data is the thing. The fallacy is not the belief that the data is useful; it
is the belief that the data is the thing.

Remark 28.12 (The Golden Record Is Not a Limit of Technology). The Golden Record is
not a limit of technology. The framework does not say that a sufficiently powerful computer
could construct the record; it says that the record is not the kind of object a reconstruction of
an identity can be.

Remark 28.13 (The Golden Record Is Not a Limit of Effort). The Golden Record is not a limit
of effort. The framework does not say that a sufficiently diligent subject could construct the
record; it says that the record, however diligently constructed, would not be a reconstruction
of the identity.
394                                                 Chapter 28. The Fallacy of Super-Identity


Remark 28.14 (The Illusion Is a Temptation, Not a Theory). The illusion is a temptation,
not a theory. A subject who commits the fallacy need not hold the Golden Record Illusion as
an explicit theory; the subject need only treat the record it has as if it were the identity.


28.8     The Fallacy and the Criteria of Context Validity
The fallacy is what the criteria of context validity (Chapter 21) are designed to prevent. The
connection is worth stating.
    The criteria of context validity—cross-checkability, minimality, and consistency—discipline
the use of cognitive contexts. A record formed from contexts that fail the criteria is a record
formed from contexts that are not candidates for the reconstruction of an identity.
Remark 28.15 (The Criteria Are Necessary, Not Sufficient). The criteria of context validity
are necessary, not sufficient, for avoiding the fallacy. A record formed from contexts that pass
the criteria can still be a spurious composite, if the record is a mere concatenation of the
manifestations without the comparison that isolates the invariant.
Remark 28.16 (The Fallacy and the Three Failures of Reconstruction). The fallacy is a
particular case of the second failure of reconstruction (incompatibility of manifestations;
Chapter 24), and it leads to the third (aggregate replacing the source; Chapter 24).


28.9     Conditions for Correct Aggregation
The fallacy is the error of aggregating across non-translatable contexts. The present section
states the conditions under which aggregation is correct, so that the fallacy can be avoided by
a stated method.
Definition 28.1 (Conditions for Correct Aggregation). (A) An aggregation of manifestations
drawn from contexts C1 , . . . , Cn is correct when:
(A1) Translatability: the contexts are mutually translatable, in the sense that their elements
     can be identified as the same elements across them (Chapter 21, criterion of cross-
     checkability).
(A2) Comparison: the aggregation is accompanied by a comparison that varies the context
     while holding the identity constant, so that the invariant can be isolated.
(A3) Separation of contributions: the contributions of the identity and the contributions of
     the contexts are distinguished, and the reconstruction is stated in terms of the former.
(A4) Non-claim of completeness: the aggregation does not claim to be complete; it claims to
     be adequate to the extent the criteria of Chapter 23 support.
   The four conditions are (A): they are the framework’s stipulation of the correct aggregation.
An aggregation that satisfies all four is a correct aggregation; an aggregation that fails any
one is an aggregation that risks the fallacy.

28.9.1    What Each Condition Excludes
A1 excludes aggregation across non-translatable contexts. The first condition excludes
the fallacy’s central case: a record formed by aggregating manifestations from contexts whose
elements cannot be identified as the same elements across them.

A2 excludes mere concatenation. The second condition excludes the method of pure
collection, without the comparison that isolates the invariant.
28.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                  395


A3 excludes the spurious composite. The third condition excludes the record that mixes
the identity’s contribution with the contexts’ contributions, without distinguishing them.

A4 excludes the super-identity claim. The fourth condition excludes the claim that the
aggregation is complete; it states that the aggregation is adequate, not that it is complete.

28.9.2    What Correct Aggregation Is Not
The conditions state what correct aggregation is; the present subsection states what it is not,
so that the conditions are not misread.

Correct aggregation is not a denial that records are useful. A record of manifestations
can be useful for many purposes; the conditions state what the record must satisfy to be a
candidate for the reconstruction of the identity, not whether the record is useful.

Correct aggregation is not a demand for unanimity. The contexts may disagree; the
conditions require that the disagreements be translatable, not that they be absent.

Correct aggregation is not a demand for completeness. The conditions require that
the aggregation not claim completeness, not that the aggregation be complete.

Correct aggregation is not a denial of the fallacy’s possibility. The conditions state
what correct aggregation is; they do not guarantee that every aggregation that satisfies them
is adequate. The adequacy of the reconstruction is a separate question, assessed by the criteria
of Chapter 23.

Remark 28.17 (The Conditions Are a Method, Not a Guarantee). The conditions are a
method for avoiding the fallacy, not a guarantee that the fallacy is avoided. An aggregation
that satisfies the four conditions is a candidate for the reconstruction of the identity; the
adequacy of the reconstruction is a separate question. The distinction is the distinction
between the method and the outcome; the framework keeps it apart.


28.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not establish the impossibility of super-identity. That is the subject
of Chapter 27. The present chapter states the fallacy that the impossibility makes intelligible.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the criteria of context validity.
That is the subject of Chapter 21.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the full account of the three failures of reconstruction.
That is the subject of Chapter 24.
    Fourth, the chapter does not develop the relation between the fallacy and the framework’s
account of viability (Chapter 36).

Remark 28.18 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed seven things. It
has stated and proved the fallacy of super-identity. It has stated the logical relation between
the impossibility and the fallacy, with a table of premises and conclusions. It has distinguished
aggregation, compatibility, and numerical unity with independent examples, and stated the
non-reduction principle. It has stated the Golden Record Illusion, with a non-library example
(the patient’s medical record). And it has stated the conditions for correct aggregation, with
the exclusion of each condition.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a record you have formed of something you know only through records—a person
from their letters, a period from its documents, a practice from its manuals. Does the record
satisfy the four conditions of Definition 28.1? If it does, the record is a candidate for the
reconstruction. If it does not, which condition does it fail?
    And consider the librarian and the physician—the two scenes of the chapter. The librarian
confuses the record of the book with the book; the physician confuses the medical record with
the patient. Are the two errors the same? If they are, what does that tell you about the
generality of the Golden Record Illusion? If they are different, what does that tell you about
the domains in which the fallacy is most tempting?
    And consider the table of Section 28.5: can you apply the table to a case of your own, and
show what the impossibility establishes and what the fallacy establishes? Can you show a case
in which the impossibility applies but the fallacy does not, and a case in which the fallacy
applies but the impossibility does not? What does your answer tell you about the difference
between the limits of the finite subject and the errors of the method it uses? A reader who
can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has
the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter develops the configuration-dependence strengthening that Chapter 27 stated in
summary form. It argues that super-identity is impossible even within a single context, because
a context’s configuration changes with time and with the other identities in it.

Chapter 29

Configuration-Dependence

Scope

This chapter develops the configuration-dependence strengthening that Chapter 27 stated in
summary form. It defines configuration-dependence, distinguishes three kinds of dependence
on configuration and states their epistemic standing (Section 29.4), argues that configuration-
dependence is a consequence of the conveyor principle, states the strengthened argument for
the impossibility of super-identity with a diagram of the dependence of the appearance on
the configuration (Section 29.5), and states the conditions of application and the limits of the
inference (Section 29.6). Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “configuration,”
“context,” “conveyance,” “manifestation,” or “exhaustive listing,” these are structural terms,
and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.



29.1     A Scene: The Crowd and the Two Photographs

Consider a photograph of a crowd. The photograph is taken at a moment; it records what is
in the frame at that moment. Now consider a second photograph of the same crowd, taken
a moment later. The two photographs are of the same crowd, but they are not the same
photograph. The crowd has changed: someone has moved, someone has arrived, someone has
left.
     Now ask: what is the crowd? Not the sum of the photographs; the photographs are records
of the crowd at particular moments. The crowd is what the photographs record, and the crowd
changes from moment to moment. What the photographs record changes with the crowd.
     The scene poses a question. If the configuration of a context changes, can a finite subject
exhaustively list the manifestations of an identity in that context, even in a single context?
The present chapter’s answer is that it cannot. The impossibility of super-identity is not a
consequence of the number of contexts; it is a consequence of the nature of manifestation.

Remark 29.1 (The Scene Shows Configuration, Not Mere Succession). The scene is easily
read as an observation about two photographs that happen to be taken at different moments.
The structural point is that the difference between the two photographs is not merely a
difference of time; it is a difference of configuration.

Remark 29.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the structure
of the claim in a familiar case. It does not prove the argument; it makes the argument intelligible
before it is stated.
398                                                    Chapter 29. Configuration-Dependence


29.2       The Question
The previous chapter stated the fallacy of super-identity: the error of treating a record formed
by aggregating manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the identity (Chapter 28).
    The impossibility, as stated in Chapter 27, was supported by two arguments: the reductio
from the four premises, and the diagonal construction. Both arguments turn on the non-
finiteness of the number of contexts. If the number of contexts were finite, the first argument
would fail; if the openness of relations failed, the second would fail.
    The present chapter asks: is the impossibility deeper than the number of contexts? The
answer is yes. Even if the number of contexts were finite—even if there were only one context—
the impossibility would survive, because the configuration of the context changes, and the
manifestations vary with it.

Remark 29.3 (The Strengthening Does Not Replace the Previous Arguments). The strengthen-
ing is an additional argument, which shows that the impossibility holds even under assumptions
that would make the previous arguments fail.

Remark 29.4 (The Question Is Not About the Number of Contexts). The question is whether
the impossibility survives even if the number of contexts were finite. The distinction is the
distinction between the number of contexts and the nature of manifestation.


29.3       The Definition of Configuration-Dependence
Definition 29.1 (Configuration-Dependence). (A) The manifestation of an identity I in a
cognitive context C depends on what passes through the epistemic light of C, and this in turn
depends on the whole configuration of C: on what other fixed elements are present, and in
what state.

      The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.

The first part: the manifestation of I in C. The manifestation is the contextually
realized appearance of an identity in a receiving cognitive context (Chapter 13).

The second part: what passes through the epistemic light of C. The epistemic light
is the medium of legible relation (Chapter 15), sharpened into an active structure of legibility
(Chapter 16).

The third part: the whole configuration of C. The configuration of a context is the set
of fixed elements present in it, together with their states and their relations.

Remark 29.5 (The Definition Is About Dependence, Not About Determination). The
definition is about dependence, not about determination. The manifestation depends on the
configuration; it does not say that the configuration alone determines the manifestation.

Remark 29.6 (The Definition Is a Consequence of the Conveyor Principle). The definition is a
consequence of the conveyor principle (Chapter 8), applied to the specific case of manifestations
in a context.

Remark 29.7 (Configuration-Dependence Is Not Context-Dependence). Configuration-dependence
is not the context-dependence principle of Chapter 10. Context-dependence is about the roles
elements play in an explanation; configuration-dependence is about what the manifestation
depends on.
29.4. Three Kinds of Dependence and Their Epistemic Standing                                   399


29.4     Three Kinds of Dependence and Their Epistemic Standing
The claim that manifestation depends on configuration can be true in three ways. The three
are distinguished by their epistemic standing: what kind of claim each is, and what role each
can play in the epistemic argument. Only the second and third kinds are retained in the main
argument of the chapter; the first is marked as outside the epistemic argument.


29.4.1    Causal Dependence: Outside the Epistemic Argument
Definition 29.2 (Causal Dependence on Configuration). (A) A manifestation causally depends
on configuration when the presence, state, or relations of the other elements in the context are
among the causes of the manifestation’s occurring as it does.


Epistemic standing. The causal claim is a claim about the causal order; it is not a claim
about the epistemic order. The framework’s argument is epistemic, and it does not use the
causal claim.


Why it is not used. The causal claim, if true, would not establish the impossibility. A
subject who knew the causal laws governing the appearance could, in principle, compute
the manifestation from the laws and the configuration. The impossibility would then be a
consequence of the subject’s ignorance of the configuration, not of the nature of manifestation.
The causal dependence is therefore marked as outside the epistemic argument; it is a claim
the framework does not need and does not use.


Status. The causal claim is not asserted by the framework; the definition is stated so that
the kind can be distinguished, not so that it can be adopted.


29.4.2    Epistemic Dependence: The Kind the Diagonal Argument Uses
Definition 29.3 (Epistemic Dependence on Configuration). (A) A manifestation epistemically
depends on configuration when what the manifestation is legible as—what it can be recognized
as—depends on the configuration’s capacity and aptitude to render it legible.


Epistemic standing. The epistemic claim is a claim about what the manifestation is legible
as; it is a claim about the structure of legibility, not about the causal order. It is the kind of
claim the framework’s argument requires.


Example. A face appears friendly in a familiar setting and menacing in an unfamiliar one;
the same configuration of facial features is legible as different things in different configurations
of the surrounding context. The epistemic dependence is not a change in the face, but a change
in what the face can be recognized as.


Why the diagonal argument uses it. The diagonal argument of Chapter 27 constructs a
context outside any given list, using the list’s content as a legible element of the new context.
The construction requires that the list’s content be legible as an element of the new context;
this is epistemic dependence. The argument does not require that the manifestation in the
new context be causally determined by the list.
400                                                     Chapter 29. Configuration-Dependence


29.4.3      Structural Dependence: The Kind the Strengthened Argument Uses
Definition 29.4 (Structural Dependence on Configuration). (A) A manifestation structurally
depends on configuration when the manifestation is what it is only as a position in the
configuration; the configuration is not an external condition on the manifestation but part of
what the manifestation is.

Epistemic standing. The structural claim is a claim about the constitution of the mani-
festation; it is a claim about what the manifestation is, not about its causes and not about
what it is legible as. It is the strongest of the three claims, and it is the one the strengthened
argument requires.

Example. A word in a sentence means what it means partly because of its position in the
sentence; the same word in a different sentence has a different meaning, not because the word
has changed, but because its position in the configuration of the sentence is part of its meaning.

Why the strengthened argument uses it. The strengthened argument’s conclusion is
that the set of manifestations is not fixed even in a single context. The conclusion requires
that the manifestations be what they are only as positions in the configuration, and that the
configuration not be fixed. A reader who accepted only causal dependence would find the
strengthened argument unable to reach its conclusion.

    The table states the epistemic standing of the three kinds and the role each plays in the
epistemic argument. The main argument of the chapter uses only the epistemic and structural
kinds; the causal kind is marked as outside the epistemic argument.

Remark 29.8 (Why Only Two Kinds Are Retained). Only two of the three kinds are retained
in the main argument, because the causal kind does not establish the impossibility. The
impossibility is an epistemic claim; it requires an epistemic dependence. The causal claim, if
true, would leave open the possibility that the impossibility could be overcome by knowing
the causal laws. The epistemic and structural kinds do not leave that possibility open, and
they are the kinds the argument uses.

Remark 29.9 (The Three Kinds Are Not Alternatives). The three kinds are not alternatives;
they are three ways the claim of configuration-dependence can be true. The framework asserts
the epistemic and structural kinds; it marks the causal kind as outside the epistemic argument.
29.5. The Strengthened Argument                                                            401


Remark 29.10 (The Distinction Is Structural, Not Verbal). The three kinds are distinguished
by what they claim, not by the words used to state them.


29.5     The Strengthened Argument
The strengthened argument uses configuration-dependence to show that super-identity is
impossible even within a single context.

29.5.1    The Diagram of the Dependence
The dependence of the appearance on the configuration of the context can be displayed as a
diagram.

   The Configuration of the Context C
   The fixed elements present, their states, and their relations
   ↓
   What passes through the epistemic light of C
   The active structure of legibility, shaped by the configuration
   ↓
   The Manifestation of I in C
   The appearance, as a position in the configuration
   ↓
   The Set of Manifestations of I in C
   Not fixed once and for all, because the configuration changes

    The diagram is a summary, not a new argument. Its purpose is to show the direction of
the dependence: the configuration shapes what passes through the epistemic light, and what
passes through the epistemic light shapes the manifestation; the set of manifestations is not
fixed because the configuration changes.

29.5.2    The Argument
The Strengthened Argument.      1. By the conveyor principle, every manifestation of I in C
     is conveyed by epistemic light of C.

  2. By configuration-dependence (in its structural form, Definition 29.4), what the epistemic
     light conveys depends on the configuration of C, and the manifestation is what it is only
     as a position in the configuration.

  3. The configuration of C changes with time and with the other identities in it.

  4. So the set of manifestations of I in a single context C is not fixed once and for all, and
     cannot be exhaustively listed at any one time.

  5. Hence super-identity is impossible not only because contexts are non-finitely many, but
     also because even a single context yields manifestations that vary with its configuration.


    The argument’s force is in step (3). If the configuration of a context did not change, the
set of manifestations in the context would be fixed, and the subject could in principle list
them exhaustively at one time.
Remark 29.11 (The Argument Does Not Use the Finitude of the Subject). The argument’s
conclusion is about the set of manifestations, not about the subject who surveys them.
 402                                                   Chapter 29. Configuration-Dependence


 Remark 29.12 (The Strengthened Argument Is the Strongest of the Three). The strengthened
 argument survives the denial of both the infinity of contexts and the openness of relations. A
 reader who rejects both can still accept the strengthened argument.


 29.6      The Conditions of Application and the Limits of the Infer-
           ence
 The claim is stated at the strength its argument supports. The present section states the
 conditions under which the claim applies, and the limits of the inference that the argument
 supports.

 29.6.1    The Conditions of Application
 The claim applies when three conditions are met, and the conditions are worth stating.

 Definition 29.5 (Conditions of Application of Configuration-Dependence). (A) The claim of
 configuration-dependence applies to a context C when:

(CA1) The conveyor principle holds: the manifestations of I in C are conveyed by the epistemic
      light of C (Chapter 8).

(CA2) The configuration changes: the fixed elements present in C, their states, and their
      relations are not fixed for all time.

(CA3) The structural dependence holds: the manifestation of I in C is what it is only as a
      position in the configuration (Definition 29.4).

    The three conditions are the framework’s statement of the conditions under which the claim
 applies. The claim does not apply when any one of the three conditions fails; the framework
 does not pretend otherwise.

 29.6.2    The Limits of the Inference
 The inference from configuration-dependence to the impossibility of super-identity has limits,
 and the limits are worth stating.

 Definition 29.6 (Limits of the Inference). (A) The inference from configuration-dependence
 to the impossibility of super-identity is limited in three ways:

 (LI1) Scope limit: the inference applies to contexts that satisfy the conditions of application
       (Definition 29.5); it does not apply to contexts that do not.

 (LI2) Premise limit: the inference depends on the conveyor principle and on the structural
       form of configuration-dependence; a reader who rejects either premise has a reason to
       reject the inference.

 (LI3) Conclusion limit: the inference concludes that the set of manifestations is not fixed;
       it does not conclude that the identity has no fixed structure, or that the identity is
       unknowable in itself. The conclusion is epistemic, not metaphysical.

    The three limits are the framework’s statement of the limits of the inference. A reader who
 applies the inference beyond the limits has applied it beyond what the argument supports; a
 reader who applies it within the limits has applied it correctly.
29.7. The Claim and the Limits of Part V                                                     403


29.6.3    What the Limits Exclude
LI1 excludes application to non-applicable contexts. The inference does not apply to
contexts that fail the conditions of application; the framework does not claim that it does.

LI2 excludes the inference’s independence from its premises. The inference is as
strong as its premises; the framework states the premises so that the reader can assess the
inference.

LI3 excludes the metaphysical over-reading of the conclusion. The conclusion is
about the set of manifestations, not about the identity’s nature.

29.6.4    What the Conditions of Application and the Limits Are Not
The conditions of application and the limits of the inference are not:

Not a denial that configuration-dependence holds. The conditions state when the
claim applies; they do not deny that the claim holds in the cases in which it applies.

Not a demand that the configuration be known. The conditions state when the claim
applies; they do not require that the configuration be known to the subject.

Not a guarantee that the inference is valid in every case. The limits state the scope
of the inference; they do not guarantee that the inference is valid in every case within the
scope.

Remark 29.13 (The Conditions and the Limits Are the Framework’s Statement of the Claim’s
Scope). The conditions of application and the limits of the inference are the framework’s
statement of the claim’s scope. The framework does not claim that the claim applies everywhere;
it claims that the claim applies where the conditions are met, and that the inference is valid
where the limits permit.


29.7     The Claim and the Limits of Part V
The configuration-dependence claim is one of the limits of Part V, and its relation to the other
limits is worth marking.
    The impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27) is the first and most fundamental limit.
The configuration-dependence strengthening (the present chapter) deepens the impossibility.
The fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28) is the error that the impossibility makes intelligible.

Remark 29.14 (The Claim and the Other Limits). The claim is one of the limits, and it does
not replace the others. The limits of self-knowledge, the impossibility of complete knowledge of
epistemic light, and the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness are distinct
limits, with their own arguments and their own scope.


29.8     What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
   First, the chapter does not develop the other limits of Part V. Those are stated in
Chapters 30–33.
   Second, the chapter does not develop the connection between configuration-dependence
and the epistemic economy of cognition. That is developed in Part VI.
404                                                    Chapter 29. Configuration-Dependence


    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the configuration of a context
can, in some special case, be fixed. The conditions of application (Definition 29.5) state that
the configuration changes; a critic who proposes a case in which it does not is invited to do so.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim that the strengthened argument is the only argument
for the impossibility. It is one of three.

Remark 29.15 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has defined configuration-dependence, and argued that it is a consequence of the conveyor
principle. It has distinguished three kinds of dependence on configuration—causal, epistemic,
and structural—and stated their epistemic standing, marking the causal kind as outside the
epistemic argument and retaining the epistemic and structural kinds in the main argument. It
has stated the strengthened argument for the impossibility of super-identity, with a diagram
of the dependence of the appearance on the configuration. It has stated the conditions of
application and the limits of the inference. And it has marked the strengthening as the
strongest of the three arguments. The chapter’s contribution is the framework’s account of
the deepest form of the impossibility of super-identity, the distinction among the three kinds
of dependence, and the conditions and limits that the later parts of the book require.
