A Question for Reflection
Consider a context you know well—a conversation, a classroom, a practice—and a manifestation
of an identity in that context. Does the manifestation depend on what else is present in
the context, and in what state? If the configuration of the context changed, would the
manifestation change?
    And consider the crowd—the scene that opened the chapter. The two photographs are of
the same crowd, and they are not the same photograph, because the crowd’s configuration has
changed. Is the difference between the photographs a difference in the crowd, or a difference
in the configuration?
    And consider the three kinds of dependence (Section 29.4): can you give a case in which
the dependence is only causal, a case in which it is epistemic, and a case in which it is
structural? Apply the conditions of application (Definition 29.5) and the limits of the inference
(Definition 29.6) to your cases: which cases satisfy the conditions, and which cases fall within
the limits? What does your answer tell you about the difference between the dependence that
the diagonal argument requires and the dependence that the strengthened argument requires?
A reader who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can
answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the limits of self-knowledge: the application of the impossibility of
super-identity to the subject’s own identity. The present chapter has shown that the impossibility
survives even a single context; the next chapter shows that it applies even to the subject’s
knowledge of itself.
                                                                                              407




Chapter 30

The Limits of Self-Knowledge

Scope
This chapter defines the structural limits of self-knowledge: the limits that follow, for any
finite subject, from the impossibility of super-identity, when that impossibility is applied to
the subject’s own identity. It distinguishes the kinds of self-knowledge data (Section 30.3),
argues that the limits follow from the impossibility, states three consequences, distinguishes
four kinds of first-person access with a table of what each supplies and what it cannot establish
(Section 30.9), states a self-knowledge audit protocol (Section ??), and states the epistemic
result of the chapter as a method of controlling self-knowledge claims (Section 30.12). It does
not address psychological and normative questions. Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter
speaks of “self-knowledge,” “self-model,” “reconstruction,” “introspection,” or “privilege,” these
are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


30.1     A Scene: The Autobiography and the Reviewer
Consider a person writing an autobiography. She has three kinds of source for the book: her
own memories of the events; her journals, kept across several decades; and what others have
said about her—letters, testimony, the recollections of friends and rivals.
    She works through the sources. Her memories are vivid for some periods and blank for
others; her journals record what she thought worth writing at the time; what others say is
sometimes recognizable and sometimes strange. Each source gives her something the others
do not, and none gives her the whole.
    She writes the book. The book is a reconstruction of her life from the manifestations
available to her. It is her own reconstruction—she is the one who has gathered the sources
and made the selection—but it is still a reconstruction, drawn from manifestations, and it is
not the same thing as the life it describes.
    Now suppose a reviewer says: “This is not a biography. It is the person, written down. She
has captured herself completely.”
    The reviewer has said something that sounds like praise, and is in fact a claim the framework
cannot accept. The book is not the person. The book is a reconstruction of the person from
the manifestations available to her, sorted and selected, but still a reconstruction.
    The scene poses a question. What is the structure of the subject’s knowledge of its own
identity? Is it different in kind from the subject’s knowledge of other identities—privileged,
direct, exhaustive—or is it subject to the same structural constraints? The present chapter’s
answer is that it is subject to the same constraints.

Remark 30.1 (The Scene Shows the Structure of Self-Knowledge). The scene is easily read
as an observation about a person writing an autobiography. The structural point is that the
408                                                  Chapter 30. The Limits of Self-Knowledge


autobiography is a reconstruction—a pseudo-identity formed from the manifestations available
to the author—and not the identity it describes.
Remark 30.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the claim; it makes the claim intelligible before it
is stated.


30.2       The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have stated the limits of finite cognition. Chapter 27 stated
the impossibility of super-identity: no finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity
in all contexts. Chapter 28 stated the fallacy of super-identity. Chapter 29 stated the
configuration-dependence strengthening.
    The present chapter asks a different kind of question. The impossibility of Chapter 27
was stated for any identity and any finite subject. The present chapter asks: what follows
when the identity is the subject’s own? Is the subject’s knowledge of itself subject to the
impossibility, or is it privileged?
    The framework does not accept the exception. The chapter’s answer is that the subject’s
knowledge of its own identity is subject to the same structural constraints as its knowledge of
any other identity.
Remark 30.3 (The Question Is About Identity, Not About Mental States). The question is
about the subject’s knowledge of its own identity, not about its knowledge of its own mental
states. A subject may have privileged access to some of its mental states and still be subject
to the structural limits of self-knowledge.
Remark 30.4 (The Question Is About Privilege, Not About Existence). The question the
chapter asks is not whether self-knowledge exists; the framework grants that it does, and that
it can be adequate. The question is whether self-knowledge is privileged, in the sense of being
direct, exhaustive, or exempt from the structural constraints.


30.3       The Kinds of Self-Knowledge Data
Before the definition is stated, the kinds of self-knowledge data must be distinguished, so that
the definition is not read as a claim about all of them.
Definition 30.1 (The Kinds of Self-Knowledge Data). (A) Four kinds of self-knowledge data
are distinguishable:
(S1) Introspection: the subject’s direct observation of its own mental states. Introspection
     supplies the subject with the content of its states (what it feels, thinks, desires) in a way
     that is not inferred from other evidence.

(S2) Self-report: the subject’s statements about its own states, dispositions, and history.
     Self-report is a linguistic act, and it is subject to the norms of reporting (sincerity,
     accuracy, completeness).

(S3) Reconstruction from behavior : the subject’s inference from its own behavior, its own
     history, and the testimony of others to a model of its own traits, patterns, and dispositions.

(S4) Reconstruction from identity-manifestations: the subject’s inference from the mani-
     festations of its own identity to a pseudo-identity of that identity. It is the kind of
     self-knowledge the chapter’s limits concern.
      The four kinds are not the same, and the chapter’s claims must be distinguished for each.
30.4. The Definition of the Structural Limits of Self-Knowledge                              409


(S1) Introspection. Introspection is a source of knowledge of mental states. It is not, by
itself, a source of knowledge of the subject’s identity. The subject can introspect a feeling
without introspecting the identity that the feeling manifests.

(S2) Self-report. Self-report is a linguistic act that draws on introspection, memory, and
the subject’s model of itself. It is not a direct access to the identity; it is a statement about
manifestations.

(S3) Reconstruction from behavior. The subject’s inference from its own behavior is
a reconstruction. It is subject to the same constraints as any reconstruction: it is partial,
fallible, and indexed to the contexts in which the behavior is observed.

(S4) Reconstruction from identity-manifestations. The subject’s reconstruction of its
own identity is the kind the chapter’s limits concern. It is a pseudo-identity, formed from the
manifestations available to the subject, and it is subject to the impossibility of super-identity.

Remark 30.5 (The Four Kinds Are Not Independent). The four kinds are not independent.
Self-report draws on introspection and on the subject’s model of itself; the model of itself
draws on the reconstruction from behavior; the reconstruction from identity-manifestations
draws on all of the other three. The framework distinguishes them so that the chapter’s claims
can be stated for the kind to which they apply, not because they are separate sources.

Remark 30.6 (The Chapter’s Claims Apply to (S4), Not to (S1)–(S3) as Such). The chapter’s
claims apply to (S4), the reconstruction of the subject’s own identity. They do not, as such,
apply to (S1), (S2), or (S3). The limits of introspection, self-report, and reconstruction from
behavior are real limits, but they are different limits, and the present chapter does not address
them. The four kinds of first-person access (Section 30.9) are the chapter’s statement of what
the claims cover and what they do not.


30.4     The Definition of the Structural Limits of Self-Knowledge
Definition 30.2 (The Structural Limits of Self-Knowledge). The structural limits of self-
knowledge are the limits that follow, for any finite subject, from the impossibility of super-
identity, when that impossibility is applied to the subject’s own identity: a subject can form
only pseudo-identities of its own identity, never the identity as such.

   The definition has two parts, and both are worth marking.

The first part: the limits follow from the impossibility of super-identity. The limits
are the impossibility itself, applied to the specific case of the subject’s own identity.

The second part: the subject can form only pseudo-identities of its own identity.
The self-model the subject forms of itself is a pseudo-identity, not the identity.

Remark 30.7 (The Definition Is About Identity, Not About Mental States). The definition is
about the subject’s knowledge of its own identity, not about its knowledge of its own mental
states.

Remark 30.8 (The Definition Is About the Finite Subject). The definition is about the finite
subject. It does not claim that no subject whatsoever can know its own identity exhaustively;
it claims that no finite subject can.
410                                                  Chapter 30. The Limits of Self-Knowledge


Remark 30.9 (The Definition Is a Particular Case of the Impossibility). The definition is
a particular case of the impossibility of super-identity, not a new principle. The framework
states the definition separately because the application to the subject’s own identity is not
trivial—it overturns a long tradition—and because the application has consequences of its
own.


30.5     The Argument
Argument for the Structural Limits of Self-Knowledge. 1. By the impossibility of super-
     identity (Chapter 27), no finite subject can know all manifestations of an identity
     in all contexts.
   2. The subject’s own identity is an identity among others. Nothing in the framework’s
      account of identity (Chapter 12) exempts it from the impossibility, and nothing in the
      framework’s account of the subject (Chapter 20) exempts it either.
   3. Therefore no finite subject can know all manifestations of its own identity in all contexts.
   4. The subject’s knowledge of its own identity is, by (S4) of Definition 30.1, a reconstruction
      from manifestations; it is a pseudo-identity, not the identity.
   5. Therefore the subject’s self-knowledge is subject to the structural limits of self-knowledge,
      in the sense of Definition 30.2.


    The argument’s force is in step (2). If the subject’s own identity were exempt from the
impossibility, the argument would fail, and self-knowledge would be privileged. But nothing in
the framework exempts it.
Remark 30.10 (The Argument Does Not Deny That Self-Knowledge Exists). The argument
does not deny that self-knowledge exists. It denies that self-knowledge is exhaustive or
privileged.
Remark 30.11 (The Argument Is Relative to the Impossibility). The argument is (T) relative
to the impossibility of Chapter 27.
Remark 30.12 (The Argument’s Structure Is the Same as Chapter 29’s). Chapter 29 argued
that the impossibility holds even within a single context, because the configuration of the
context changes. The present chapter argues that the impossibility holds even for the subject’s
own identity, because the subject’s own identity is manifested in the same way as any other
identity.


30.6     Self-Knowledge Is Not Privileged
The first consequence is that self-knowledge is not privileged. The subject has access to its
own manifestations, as it has access to the manifestations of other identities; it does not have
direct access to its own identity.
Remark 30.13 (The Privilege of Mental States Is Not the Privilege of Identity). A subject
can know its own mental states more directly than it knows the mental states of others. What
the framework denies is that the same privilege applies to the subject’s knowledge of its own
identity.
Remark 30.14 (The Privilege Is Not a Denial of Self-Knowledge). The denial of privilege is
not a denial of self-knowledge. The subject can know a great deal about itself; its self-knowledge
can be more adequate than its knowledge of many other identities.
30.7. Self-Knowledge Is a Reconstruction from Manifestations                                   411


30.7     Self-Knowledge Is a Reconstruction from Manifestations
The second consequence is that self-knowledge is a reconstruction from manifestations. The
subject forms its pseudo-identity of itself from the manifestations available to it.
    The subject is one of its own manifestations. Its self-knowledge is therefore a reconstruction
from at least one manifestation—itself—and from whatever other manifestations of its identity
it can gather.
    The reconstruction is subject to the three criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23): consistency,
stability, and fruitfulness.

Remark 30.15 (The Self-Model Is a Pseudo-Identity, Not a Manifestation). The self-model
the subject forms of itself is a pseudo-identity, not a manifestation.

Remark 30.16 (The Reconstruction Is Subject to Configuration-Dependence). The recon-
struction is subject to configuration-dependence (Chapter 29).

Remark 30.17 (The Reconstruction Is Subject to the Fallacy of Super-Identity). The
reconstruction is subject to the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28).


30.8     Self-Knowledge Is Subject to the Same Structural Con-
         straints
The third consequence is that self-knowledge is subject to the same structural constraints as
knowledge in general.

Remark 30.18 (The Continuity Is Not a Denial of Difference). The subject has more
manifestations of itself available to it than it has of any other identity, and its access to those
manifestations is more direct. The difference is real.

Remark 30.19 (The Continuity Is Not a Denial of Self-Understanding). The subject can
understand itself, in the sense of forming an adequate pseudo-identity of its own identity.

Remark 30.20 (The Three Consequences Are One Structure). The three consequences are
aspects of one structural fact: the subject’s knowledge of its own identity is a relation between
a manifestation and its source, and the relation has the character that every such relation has.


30.9     The Strongest First-Person Objection
The strongest objection to the present chapter is that the chapter’s claim is too broad: that it
treats all first-person access as if it were a reconstruction from manifestations. The objection
is stated in its strongest form, and the chapter’s answer is stated with equal care.


30.9.1    The Objection Stated
The objection. “A subject is not only a manifestation of its own identity; the subject is its
own identity, in the sense that the subject’s first-person access to itself is not mediated by
manifestations. When I feel a pain, I do not reconstruct the pain from manifestations; I have
the pain. The chapter’s claim that self-knowledge is a reconstruction from manifestations is
therefore false for at least some kinds of first-person access.”
412                                                 Chapter 30. The Limits of Self-Knowledge


30.9.2    Four Kinds of First-Person Access
Definition 30.3 (Four Kinds of First-Person Access). (A) Four kinds of first-person access
are distinguishable:

(A1) First-person access to a mental state. The subject has a sensation, thought, emotion, or
     desire, and is aware of having it. The awareness is direct.

(A2) First-person access to the subject’s own awareness. The subject is aware that it is aware;
     it has a second-order awareness of a first-order awareness.

(A3) First-person access to the subject’s own character. The subject forms a model of its
     own traits, patterns, and dispositions. The access is not direct; the subject must gather
     evidence.

(A4) First-person access to the subject’s own identity. The subject forms a pseudo-identity
     of the identity that its manifestations manifest. The access is a reconstruction from
     the manifestations, and it is subject to the same structural constraints as any other
     reconstruction of an identity.

   The table states what each kind of first-person access supplies and what it cannot establish.
The first three kinds supply direct access to manifestations; the fourth kind is a reconstruction,
and its access to the identity is indirect.

Remark 30.21 (The Chapter Limits (A4), Not (A1), (A2), or (A3)). The chapter’s argument
is about (A4). It does not deny (A1), (A2), or (A3); it does not claim that the subject’s access
to its own mental states is mediated.

Remark 30.22 (The Objection Is Right About (A1), (A2), and (A3), and Not About (A4)).
The objection is right about (A1), (A2), and (A3). The objection is not right about (A4).
The subject’s access to its own identity is a reconstruction from manifestations, and the
impossibility of super-identity applies to it.
 30.10. The Structural Limits and Introspection                                                413


 30.9.4    The Chapter’s Claim Restated
 The chapter’s claim, restated in the light of the distinction, is: the subject’s access to its own
 identity (A4) is a reconstruction from manifestations, and it is subject to the impossibility of
 super-identity; the subject’s access to its own mental states (A1), to its own awareness (A2),
 and to its own character (A3) is not, as such, a reconstruction from manifestations, and the
 chapter does not deny its directness.

 Remark 30.23 (The Restatement Does Not Weaken the Argument). The restatement clarifies
 the argument’s scope; it does not reduce its force.


 30.10      The Structural Limits and Introspection
 The structural limits of self-knowledge are easily confused with the limits of introspection, and
 the distinction is worth marking.
     Introspection is the subject’s observation of its own mental states. The framework does
 not deny that introspection occurs, or that it can yield knowledge of mental states.
     The structural limits of self-knowledge are different. They are about the subject’s knowledge
 of its own identity, not about its knowledge of its mental states.

 Remark 30.24 (The Two Are Related but Distinct). Introspection is one of the sources from
 which the subject forms its self-model; the structural limits of self-knowledge are the limits on
 what the self-model can be.

 30.10.1     A Self-Knowledge Audit Protocol
 The distinction between introspection and the structural limits of self-knowledge suggests a
 protocol by which a subject can audit its own self-knowledge claims. The protocol has four
 steps.

 Definition 30.4 (The Self-Knowledge Audit Protocol). (A) A subject audits its self-knowledge
 claims by four steps:

(SK1) Identify the claim. State the claim the subject is making about itself. Is it a claim about
      a mental state (A1), a claim about its own awareness (A2), a claim about its character
      (A3), or a claim about its identity (A4)?

(SK2) Identify the kind of access. State the kind of access the claim is based on (introspection,
      self-report, reconstruction from behavior, reconstruction from identity-manifestations).
      The kind of access determines what the claim can and cannot establish (Section 30.9.3).

(SK3) State the limits of the kind. For the kind identified in (SK2), state what the kind can
      establish and what it cannot. A claim of kind (A4) cannot be established by any kind of
      access, because (A4) is a reconstruction and is subject to the structural limits.

(SK4) Reformulate the claim at its proper strength. If the claim is a claim of kind (A4) and is
      stated as an exhaustive or privileged claim, reformulate it as a claim of adequacy: the
      self-model is adequate to the extent the criteria of Chapter 23 support, and it is not a
      claim to completeness.

     The protocol is (A): it is the framework’s stipulation of the audit. Its justification is its
 use in controlling self-knowledge claims; its cost is that the identification of the kind in (SK1)
 and (SK2) is fallible.
414                                                Chapter 30. The Limits of Self-Knowledge


Remark 30.25 (The Protocol and the Chapter’s Claims). The protocol is the chapter’s
positive contribution to the practice of self-knowledge. The chapter’s argument states the
limits; the protocol states the method by which a subject can apply the limits to its own
claims.

Remark 30.26 (The Protocol Is Not a Psychological Procedure). The protocol is not a
psychological procedure. It is an epistemic procedure: it asks the subject to identify the kind
of claim and the kind of access, and to state what the kind can and cannot establish. The
protocol does not require the subject to feel anything, or to introspect anything; it requires
the subject to state the claim at its proper strength.


30.11      The Structural Limits and the Unknownness of Chapter
           19
The structural limits of self-knowledge are related to the unknownness of same-category
identities (Chapter 19).
    Chapter 19 stated the theorem of unknownness: the unknownness of same-context identities
is the structural condition of possibility of reflection, not a defect. The unknownness there
was the unknownness between two distinct identities.
    The present chapter’s limits concern a different unknownness: the unknownness between a
subject and its own identity.

Remark 30.27 (The Two Unknownnesses Are Different). Chapter 19’s unknownness is
between two distinct identities; the present chapter’s unknownness is between a manifestation
and its own source. Both are intrinsic; both are structural; but they are not the same.

Remark 30.28 (The Two Unknownnesses Are One Structure). The structure is the structure
of the relation between an identity and its manifestations. The framework states the two
cases separately because the cases are different and the consequences of each are different; the
underlying structure is one.


30.12      The Epistemic Result: A Method of Controlling Self-
           Knowledge Claims
The chapter’s positive contribution is the epistemic result: a method of controlling self-
knowledge claims. The present section states the result, so that the reader knows what the
chapter gives, not only what it excludes.

30.12.1    The Method
The method has four rules, each of which states a condition on a self-knowledge claim.

First rule: identify the kind of claim. Before a self-knowledge claim is asserted, the
subject identifies whether the claim is about a mental state (A1), about its own awareness
(A2), about its character (A3), or about its identity (A4). The kind determines what the claim
can and cannot establish.

Second rule: state the kind of access. For the claim identified, the subject states the
kind of access the claim rests on (introspection, self-report, reconstruction from behavior, or
reconstruction from identity-manifestations). The kind of access determines what the claim
can and cannot establish.
30.13. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                 415


Third rule: state the limits. The subject states the limits of the kind of access: what
the kind can establish and what it cannot. A claim of kind (A4) cannot be established as
exhaustive or privileged, because the kind is a reconstruction and is subject to the structural
limits.

Fourth rule: reformulate at the proper strength. If the claim is a claim of kind (A4)
and is stated as exhaustive or privileged, the subject reformulates it as a claim of adequacy:
the self-model is adequate to the extent the criteria of Chapter 23 support, and it is not a
claim to completeness.

30.12.2     The Result Stated
The method’s result is the framework’s statement of how self-knowledge claims are to be
controlled. The result has three parts.

First part: the four kinds of self-knowledge are distinct. Mental states, awareness,
character, and identity are four kinds of self-knowledge, and the chapter’s claims apply to the
fourth, not to the first three.

Second part: the claim about identity is a reconstruction. The subject’s access to
its own identity is a reconstruction from manifestations, and it is subject to the impossibility
of super-identity.

Third part: the claim about identity is controlled by the method. The method of
the four rules is the framework’s statement of how a self-knowledge claim is to be stated at its
proper strength. A claim that satisfies the four rules is a controlled claim; a claim that fails
any one is an uncontrolled claim.

Remark 30.29 (The Result Is a Method, Not a Doctrine). The result is a method, not a
doctrine. The framework does not say what the subject’s self-knowledge should be; it says how
a claim about self-knowledge is to be stated at its proper strength. The reader who takes the
result as a doctrine has misread it; the reader who takes it as a method has read it correctly.

Remark 30.30 (The Method Is the Chapter’s Positive Contribution). The method is the
chapter’s positive contribution to the practice of self-knowledge. The chapter’s argument
states the limits; the method states how a subject can apply the limits to its own claims.


30.13      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the subject’s own identity is, in
some special case, exempt from the impossibility. The framework’s claim is that nothing in
the framework exempts it.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the self-model. The self-model is
stated here as a pseudo-identity, in the sense of Chapter 12; its development is the work of the
chapters on the criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23) and on the three failures of reconstruction
(Chapter 24).
    Third, the chapter does not claim that the structural limits of self-knowledge are the only
limits on the subject’s knowledge of itself. The limits of introspective access, of memory, and
of the coherence of the self-model are limits in the ordinary sense, and the framework does not
deny them.
416                                                  Chapter 30. The Limits of Self-Knowledge


   Fourth, the chapter does not develop the relation between the structural limits of self-
knowledge and the epistemic economy of cognition (Part VI).


Remark 30.31 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It has
defined the structural limits of self-knowledge, and it has marked the definition as a particular
case of the impossibility of super-identity. It has distinguished the kinds of self-knowledge
data (introspection, self-report, reconstruction from behavior, reconstruction from identity-
manifestations), and it has stated which kind the chapter’s claims apply to. It has argued that
the limits follow from the impossibility. It has stated the four kinds of first-person access, with
a table of what each supplies and what it cannot establish. It has stated the self-knowledge
audit protocol. And it has stated the epistemic result of the chapter as a method of controlling
self-knowledge claims. The chapter’s contribution is the framework’s account of the limits that
the impossibility of super-identity imposes on the subject’s knowledge of itself, the distinction
among the four kinds of first-person access, the self-knowledge audit protocol, and the method
of controlling self-knowledge claims.

Chapter 31

The Impossibility of Complete
Knowledge of Epistemic Light

Scope
This chapter states the impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light. It draws the first
epistemological consequence of the encompassment principle stated in Chapter 17: because we
are encompassed in epistemic light, and complete knowledge would require standing outside
its object, no finite subject can know epistemic light completely. The chapter argues the
standpoint premise independently (Section 31.3), examines the objection from reflective or
internal knowledge (Section 31.4), states the principle, proves it, distinguishes three senses
of “complete knowledge” of epistemic light with separate criteria (Section 31.7), distinguishes
the impossibility from skepticism and from the impossibility of super-identity, and states a
method of partial knowledge of epistemic light and its indicators of assessment (Section 31.10).
Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “complete knowledge,” “encompassment,”
“standpoint,” “partial knowledge,” or “mode,” these are structural terms, and their sense is
fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


31.1     A Scene: The Fish and the Water
Consider a fish in a tank, trying to describe the water. The fish can describe the water in
many ways: the temperature, the salinity, the currents, the pressure. It can describe what
the water does to its gills, what it does to its motion, what it does to the light that passes
through it. The fish can give a very detailed description.
    But the fish cannot describe the water as a whole, from outside the water. To describe the
water as a whole, the fish would have to stand outside the water, and the fish cannot stand
outside the water. Every description the fish gives is a description from within the water.
    Now consider us, in relation to epistemic light. We are encompassed in epistemic light
(Chapter 17). We can know epistemic light in its modes; we cannot know epistemic light as a
whole, because to know it as a whole we would have to stand outside it, and standing outside
epistemic light would be standing outside the condition of our own cognition.
    The scene poses a question. What is the structure of our relation to epistemic light,
such that complete knowledge of it is impossible? Is the impossibility a limit of our present
resources, or is it a structural feature of the relation between a finite subject and the medium
of its cognition?

Remark 31.1 (The Scene Shows the Difference Between Modes and the Whole). The scene is
easily read as an observation about a fish that happens to be unable to leave the water. The
420                Chapter 31. The Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light


structural point is that the fish’s description is a description of the water in its modes, and
not a description of the water as a whole.

Remark 31.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the
impossibility at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the principle; it makes the
principle intelligible before it is stated.


31.2     The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have stated the limits of finite cognition. The present chapter
turns to a different limit: not the finite subject’s access to an identity, but its access to the
medium by which any identity is known: epistemic light.
     The question is: can the finite subject know epistemic light completely?
     The framework’s answer is that it cannot. The answer is the principle of this chapter, and
it is proved from the encompassment principle of Chapter 17. The chapter also argues the
standpoint premise independently, and it examines the objection from reflective knowledge.

Remark 31.3 (The Question Is About the Medium, Not the Object). The question is about
the medium, not about the object. The previous limits of Part V concern the finite subject’s
knowledge of an identity; the present limit concerns its knowledge of the medium of all
knowledge.


31.3     The Standpoint Premise Argued Independently
The proof of the impossibility depends on a premise: complete knowledge requires an external
standpoint. The premise is easily assumed, and the present section argues it independently, so
that the argument does not rest on an unexamined assumption.

Definition 31.1 (The Standpoint Premise). (A) The standpoint premise: complete knowledge
of a medium requires a standpoint that is not itself within the medium—a standpoint from
which the medium can be surveyed as a whole.

   The premise is (A): it is stipulated as part of what “complete knowledge” means in the
framework. The present section argues for it, so that the stipulation is not arbitrary.

First argument: the model of complete knowledge. The standard epistemological
model of complete knowledge is the model of a survey: the knower surveys the object from
a standpoint, and the survey is complete when no part of the object is left out. The model
requires a standpoint, and the standpoint must be distinct from the object; if the standpoint
were within the object, the survey would be a part of what is surveyed, and it would not be
a survey of the whole. The model is the model of complete knowledge that the framework
uses; a reader who uses a different model has a different notion of complete knowledge, and
the framework’s argument is not addressed to that notion.

Second argument: the regress. Suppose that a subject could know a medium completely
from within the medium. Then the knowledge would itself be a part of the medium, and the
medium would include the knowledge of itself. If the knowledge is complete, it must include
the knowledge of the knowledge, and so on. The regress is the same as the regress of the
catalog (Chapter 27): any complete account of a medium from within the medium generates
a new item outside the account. To stop the regress, the account must be from outside the
medium; that is, it must have an external standpoint.
31.4. The Objection from Reflective Knowledge                                                421


Third argument: the distinction between the mode and the whole. A mode of a
medium is an appearance of the medium in a context. A complete knowledge of a medium
would be a knowledge of the medium as it is in itself, not merely in some mode. The distinction
between the mode and the whole is the distinction between what appears in a context and
what the medium is independent of any context. The knowledge of the whole would require
a standpoint that is not itself a context of the medium’s appearance; that is, an external
standpoint.
    The three arguments support the standpoint premise at the strength of a stipulation: they
show that the premise is the natural reading of what “complete knowledge” means, and that
the alternatives face either a regress or a confusion of mode and whole.

Remark 31.4 (The Premise Is Not a Dogma). The premise is not a dogma. It is argued
from the model of complete knowledge, from the regress of a complete account from within a
medium, and from the distinction between the mode and the whole. A reader who proposes a
different model of complete knowledge has proposed a different notion, and the framework’s
argument is offered at the strength of its own notion. The distinction is the distinction between
the framework’s notion and a rival notion; the framework states its own, and invites the reader
to assess the argument in the notion it states.


31.4     The Objection from Reflective Knowledge
The most serious objection to the standpoint premise is that a subject might know a medium
completely through reflective knowledge: knowledge that the medium has of itself, from within,
by its own structure. The objection is worth stating in its strongest form, and the framework’s
answer is worth stating with equal care.

31.4.1    The Objection Stated
The objection. “A medium can know itself from within, by a reflective structure. A mind
knows its own states by introspection; a language can describe itself in its own vocabulary; a
formal system can prove theorems about itself. The knowledge is internal, but it is knowledge
of the medium, and it can be complete. The standpoint premise is therefore false: complete
knowledge does not require an external standpoint; it can be achieved from within, by
reflection.”

31.4.2    The Framework’s Answer
The framework’s answer has two parts.

First part: reflective knowledge is knowledge of a mode. Reflective knowledge is a
knowledge that the medium has of itself from within. The knowledge is real, and the framework
does not deny it. But the knowledge is knowledge of the medium as it appears in the reflective
context, not of the medium as a whole. A mind that introspects its own states knows the states
as they appear in the introspective context; the knowledge is a mode of the medium, not the
medium as a whole. A language that describes itself describes itself in its own vocabulary, and
the description is a mode of the language, not the language as a whole.

Second part: reflective knowledge is subject to the regress. Reflective knowledge, if
it claims to be complete, is subject to the regress of Section 31.3. If the reflective knowledge
is complete, it must include the knowledge of the knowledge, and so on. The regress is not
stopped by reflection; it is stopped by the external standpoint, which is what the standpoint
premise requires.
422                 Chapter 31. The Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light


    The framework’s answer is not a denial that reflective knowledge exists. It is a denial that
reflective knowledge can be complete. The distinction is the distinction between the knowledge
of a mode and the knowledge of the whole; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 31.5 (The Answer Is Not a Denial of Reflection). The answer is not a denial of
reflection. Reflective knowledge is real, and the framework uses it throughout (Chapters 12,
13, 20). The answer is a denial that reflection can be complete, and the denial is based on the
distinction between the mode and the whole.
Remark 31.6 (The Objection Is the Strongest Form of the Challenge). The objection is the
strongest form of the challenge to the standpoint premise. It grants that the medium can know
itself; it denies that the knowledge must be from an external standpoint. The framework’s
answer is that the knowledge is a knowledge of a mode, not of the whole; the distinction
between the mode and the whole is what the answer turns on.
Remark 31.7 (The Objection Points Beyond Itself). The objection points beyond itself. The
reflective knowledge that the objection describes is a real knowledge, and it is knowledge of a
mode of the medium. The distinction between the mode and the whole points beyond itself to
what the medium is in itself, and to what the medium is independent of any reflective context.
The framework’s claim is that the distinction is real, and that the medium in itself is not
described by any reflection. The distinction is the distinction between the reflective knowledge
and the ground of the medium; it is kept throughout the book.


31.5       The Principle
Principle 31.1 (Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light). (T) No finite
subject can know epistemic light completely, because the finite subject is encompassed in
epistemic light, and complete knowledge requires standing outside the object of knowledge—and
no finite subject can stand outside epistemic light.
      The principle has two parts, and both are worth marking.

The first part: the impossibility itself. No finite subject can know epistemic light
completely.

The second part: the reason for the impossibility. The impossibility follows from the
encompassment principle (Chapter 17) and from the standpoint premise (Section 31.3).
Remark 31.8 (The Principle Is About the Finite Subject). The principle is about the finite
subject. It does not claim that no subject whatsoever can know epistemic light completely.
Remark 31.9 (The Principle Is Not About What Epistemic Light Is in Itself). The principle
says that complete knowledge of epistemic light is impossible for the finite subject; it does not
say what epistemic light is.
Remark 31.10 (The Principle Is a Particular Case of the Encompassment Principle). The
principle is a particular case of the encompassment principle, applied to the specific question
of the subject’s knowledge of epistemic light.


31.6       The Proof
Proof of the Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light.       1. By the standpoint
      premise (Definition 31.1, argued in Section 31.3), complete knowledge requires an external
      standpoint.
31.7. Three Senses of Complete Knowledge, with Criteria                                      423


  2. By the encompassment principle (Chapter 17), the finite subject is encompassed in
     epistemic light; it has no standpoint outside epistemic light.
  3. By the answer to the reflective objection (Section 31.4), reflective knowledge from within
     the medium is knowledge of a mode, not of the whole, and it is subject to the regress if
     it claims completeness.
  4. Therefore the finite subject cannot know epistemic light completely.


   The argument’s force is in the combination of steps (1), (2), and (3). Step (1) states
what complete knowledge requires; step (2) states that the finite subject does not satisfy the
requirement; step (3) states that the only apparent alternative—reflective knowledge—does
not satisfy it either. The combination yields the conclusion.
Remark 31.11 (The Proof Depends on the Two Principles and the Objection’s Answer).
The proof depends on the standpoint premise, on the encompassment principle, and on the
answer to the reflective objection. A reader who accepts the three has a reason to accept the
conclusion; a reader who rejects one has a reason to reject the conclusion.
Remark 31.12 (The Proof Is Not a Denial of Knowledge of Epistemic Light). The proof
does not deny that the finite subject can know anything about epistemic light. It denies that
the finite subject can know epistemic light completely.
Remark 31.13 (The Proof Is Not a Denial of Physics). The proof does not deny that physics
studies light, or that the physical description of light is a real description at its own level.


31.7     Three Senses of Complete Knowledge, with Criteria
The claim that complete knowledge of epistemic light is impossible is ambiguous, and the
ambiguity must be resolved. Three senses of “complete knowledge” must be distinguished,
each with its own criterion, and the chapter states which sense the impossibility claim covers.

31.7.1    Complete Knowledge of the Structure
Definition 31.2 (Complete Knowledge of Structure). Complete knowledge of the structure of
epistemic light is knowledge of the full structural description of epistemic light: its place in
the framework’s architecture, its character as the medium of legibility, its relation to the four
columns, its appearance in the modes of the apparatuses.

Criterion. The criterion of completeness at this level is the framework’s own completeness:
the structural description is complete when it states all the roles and relations the framework’s
architecture assigns to epistemic light. The criterion is internal to the framework; the
framework’s chapters 15–17 are the statement of the structural description, and they are the
standard by which the description is assessed.

Possible for the finite subject? Yes. The structural description is within the reach of the
finite subject; it is what the framework’s chapters on epistemic light provide.

31.7.2    Complete Knowledge of the Instances
Definition 31.3 (Complete Knowledge of Instances). Complete knowledge of the instances
of epistemic light is knowledge of all the actual and possible activations of epistemic light in
all contexts: every edge that has been or could be activated, in every apparatus, under every
condition.
424                Chapter 31. The Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light


Criterion. The criterion of completeness at this level is the exhaustive survey: the knowledge
is complete when no activation of epistemic light is left out. The criterion is external to any
particular context; it requires a survey of all contexts.

Possible for the finite subject? No. The finite subject occupies finitely many contexts
(Chapter 3), and the activations of epistemic light are not finite (Chapter 11 and Chapter 29).

31.7.3      Final Encompassment
Definition 31.4 (Final Encompassment). Final encompassment of epistemic light is the
standpoint from which epistemic light could be surveyed as a whole—the standpoint of a
subject not encompassed in epistemic light.

Criterion. The criterion of final encompassment is the external standpoint: the standpoint
is available when the subject is not itself within the medium it surveys. The criterion is
structural; it is the criterion the standpoint premise (Section 31.3) states.

Possible for the finite subject? No. The finite subject is encompassed in epistemic light
in every act of cognition (Chapter 17); it has no external standpoint.

31.7.4      The Three Senses Compared

Sense              Criterion                       Possible for the fi- What the im-
                                                   nite subject?        possibility claim
                                                                        covers

   The table states the three senses, their criteria, and what the impossibility claim covers.
The claim covers the second and third senses; it does not cover the first.
Remark 31.14 (The Three Senses and the Impossibility Claim). The distinction among the
three senses is what makes the impossibility claim precise. The claim is not that the finite
subject cannot know anything about epistemic light; it is that the finite subject cannot know
all instances of epistemic light, and cannot occupy the standpoint of final encompassment. The
first sense (complete knowledge of structure) is possible, and Chapters 15–17 are a contribution
to it.
Remark 31.15 (The Three Senses Are Not a Hierarchy of Value). The three senses are not
a hierarchy of value. The framework does not claim that complete knowledge of structure
is more valuable than complete knowledge of instances, or that final encompassment is the
highest good.


31.8        The Impossibility Is Not Skepticism
Skepticism is the thesis that knowledge is impossible. The principle of this chapter is not
skepticism. It claims that a particular kind of knowledge—complete knowledge of epistemic
light—is impossible for the finite subject, not that knowledge in general is impossible.
 31.9. The Impossibility Is Not the Impossibility of Super-Identity                             425


 Remark 31.16 (The Impossibility Is Not a Defect of the Subject). The impossibility is a
 structural feature of the relation between the finite subject and the medium of its cognition.
 Remark 31.17 (The Impossibility Is Not a Denial of Progress). The finite subject can refine
 its knowledge of epistemic light; it can develop better descriptions of the modes. What it
 cannot do is reach a complete knowledge of epistemic light.


 31.9      The Impossibility Is Not the Impossibility of Super-Identity
 The impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light is related to the impossibility of
 super-identity (Chapter 27), but the two are distinct.
 Remark 31.18 (The Two Impossibilities Are Different in Object). The first is about an
 identity; the second is about the medium.
 Remark 31.19 (The Two Impossibilities Are Related in Structure). Both are impossibilities
 for the finite subject, and both are consequences of structural features of the subject’s condition.
 Remark 31.20 (The Two Impossibilities Together). The two impossibilities together yield a
 stronger conclusion: not only can the finite subject not know all manifestations of an identity,
 but it also cannot know the medium by which the manifestations are known.


 31.10      The Method of Partial Knowledge and Its Indicators
 The principle denies complete knowledge, not all knowledge. The present section states the
 method of partial knowledge of epistemic light and the indicators of its assessment.

 31.10.1     The Method
 Definition 31.5 (The Method of Partial Knowledge of Epistemic Light). (A) The method of
 partial knowledge of epistemic light has four steps:
(PK1) Identify the mode. State the context in which epistemic light is being studied, and the
      mode in which it appears in that context (perceptual, formal, practical, or another
      mode).

(PK2) State the conditions. State the conditions under which the mode appears: the configura-
      tion of the context, the cognitive apparatus of the subject, and the question the inquiry
      is asking.

(PK3) Describe the effects. Describe the effects of epistemic light in the mode: what it renders
      legible, what it fails to render legible, and what its structural features are.

(PK4) Assess by the indicators. Assess the description by the indicators of Section 31.10.2.
     The method is (A): it is the framework’s stipulation of the method of partial knowledge.
 Its justification is its use in the assessment of descriptions of epistemic light; its cost is that
 the identification of the mode in (PK1) is fallible.

 31.10.2     The Indicators of Assessment
 Definition 31.6 (The Indicators of Partial Knowledge). (A) A description of a mode of
 epistemic light is assessed by three indicators:
  (I1) Consistency with other descriptions: the description converges with the descriptions of
       other inquirers who have studied the same mode (Chapter 23, consistency).
426                Chapter 31. The Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light


 (I2) Stability under perturbation: the description remains the same under small perturbations
      of the context, the apparatus, or the question (Chapter 23, stability).

 (I3) Fruitfulness: the description generates further distinctions within the mode, and can be
      continued into further descriptions of the same mode or of related modes (Chapter 23,
      fruitfulness).

The three indicators are the framework’s statement of what it is for a description of a mode of
epistemic light to be adequate. They are the same indicators as the criteria of Chapter 23,
applied to the specific case of epistemic light.

31.10.3     What the Method and the Indicators Establish
The method and the indicators establish that partial knowledge of epistemic light is real
knowledge, and that its adequacy is assessable by the same criteria as any other reconstruction.
They do not establish complete knowledge; the impossibility of complete knowledge is what
the principle of this chapter establishes.

Remark 31.21 (The Modes Are Not the Whole). The modes are the appearances of epistemic
light in the contexts in which the finite subject cognizes; the whole would be epistemic light
as it is in itself. The distinction is the distinction between the appearance and the medium.

Remark 31.22 (The Knowledge of the Modes Is Subject to the Limits of Part V). The
knowledge of the modes is subject to the other limits of Part V: the impossibility of super-
identity (Chapter 27), the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28), configuration-dependence
(Chapter 29), and the limits of self-knowledge (Chapter 30).

Remark 31.23 (The Partial Knowledge Is Not a Substitute for Complete Knowledge). The
partial knowledge is real, and it is the form of knowledge available to the finite subject. It is
not a substitute for complete knowledge; it is the knowledge the finite subject can have.


31.11      The Impossibility Is Not the Fallacy of Super-Identity
The fallacy of super-identity is an error of method; the impossibility of complete knowledge of
epistemic light is a structural limit.

Remark 31.24 (The Two Are Not the Same). The impossibility is a fact about what the
finite subject cannot know; the fallacy is an error the finite subject can commit.

Remark 31.25 (The Fallacy Is Not a Denial of the Impossibility). A subject that commits
the fallacy does not deny the impossibility; it ignores the impossibility.


31.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
     First, the chapter does not settle what epistemic light is in itself. The principle is about
the limits of the finite subject’s knowledge of epistemic light, not about the nature of epistemic
light.
     Second, the chapter does not develop the distinction between intrinsic and temporary
unknownness. That distinction is the subject of Chapter 32.
     Third, the chapter does not develop the plurality of perspectives. That is the subject of
Chapter 33.
     Fourth, the chapter does not deny that physics studies light, or that the physical description
of light is a real description at its own level.
31.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                            427


Remark 31.26 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed seven things.
It has argued the standpoint premise independently, and it has examined the objection from
reflective knowledge. It has stated the principle of the impossibility of complete knowledge of
epistemic light, and proved it. It has distinguished three senses of “complete knowledge” of
epistemic light, each with its own criterion, and stated which senses the impossibility claim
covers. It has distinguished the impossibility from skepticism and from the impossibility of
super-identity. It has stated a method of partial knowledge of epistemic light, with four steps,
and the three indicators of its assessment. And it has distinguished the impossibility from the
fallacy of super-identity, and stated its relation to the other limits of Part V.

A Question for Reflection
Consider something you have studied for a long time. Can you name what you know about
it, and what you know you cannot know about it? Is what you cannot know a limit of your
resources, or a limit of the kind of thing you are trying to know?
     And consider the fish—the scene that opened the chapter. The fish can describe the water
in its modes, but cannot describe the water as a whole. Are we in the same position with
respect to epistemic light?
     And consider the reflective objection (Section 31.4): can you state the objection in your
own words, and the framework’s answer? Can you give a case in which reflective knowledge
is possible, and show why the framework says that the reflective knowledge is a knowledge
of a mode, not of the whole? What does your answer tell you about the difference between
reflection and final encompassment?
     Finally, consider the method of partial knowledge (Definition 31.5): can you apply its
four steps to a mode of epistemic light, and assess your description by the three indicators?
What does your answer tell you about the difference between partial and complete knowledge?
A reader who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can
answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness: the two
kinds of unknownness that the impossibility of super-identity and the impossibility of complete
knowledge of epistemic light make intelligible.
                                                                                               429




Chapter 32

Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness

Scope
This chapter develops the distinction between two kinds of unknownness: intrinsic unknownness,
which cannot be removed by more manifestation, because it is a structural feature of the
relation between distinct identities; and temporary unknownness, which can in principle be
reduced, because it is a contingent feature of the present state of a relation. The chapter
defines the two kinds and states an independent criterion for distinguishing them (Section 32.3),
states the principle of their distinction, argues that only the intrinsic kind is structural, states
the independent criterion with a decision tree and the evidence that refutes the attribution
(Section 32.6), states the structural features of each kind with the epistemic response and the
appropriate action for each (Section 32.7), and states the practical result of the distinction for
the management of evidence and reconstruction (Section 32.8). Its claims are epistemic; where
the chapter speaks of “intrinsic,” “temporary,” “unknownness,” “manifestation,” “capacity,”
“occasion,” “response,” or “recognition,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by
the definitions in this chapter.


32.1      A Scene: The Translator
Consider a translator working on a poem in a language she has studied for twenty years. She
has three kinds of difficulty with the poem.
    The first difficulty is a matter of vocabulary. Some words in the poem are archaic, and
their meanings are uncertain. With more context—more documents, more parallel usages,
more scholarship—the difficulty could in principle be resolved. The unknownness of the words
is temporary: it can be reduced by more evidence.
    The second difficulty is a matter of grammar. Some constructions in the poem are
ambiguous, and the translator cannot tell which of two grammatical analyses is correct. With
more linguistic analysis, the difficulty could in principle be resolved. The unknownness of the
grammar is also temporary.
    The third difficulty is a matter of what the poem means as a whole. The translator can
render each word, each line, each image; she can produce a translation that is accurate word
by word and line by line. But she cannot say what the poem means in a way that exhausts it.
The poem means more than any translation can capture; the meaning is not a collection of
word-meanings or line-meanings, but the unity that the words and lines express. No amount
of translation will exhaust it, because the exhaustion would require a translation that is the
poem, and a translation that is the poem is not a translation.
    The three difficulties are not the same. The first two are difficulties of evidence or of
analysis; they could in principle be resolved by more work. The third is a difficulty of a
430                                       Chapter 32. Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness


different kind; it could not be resolved by more work, because it is not a shortage of evidence
or of analysis.

Remark 32.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the two
kinds of unknownness at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the distinction; it makes
the distinction intelligible before it is stated.


32.2       The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have stated the limits of finite cognition. The present chapter
turns to a distinction that the previous chapters have used but not developed: the distinction
between two kinds of unknownness.
   The question is: what distinguishes the unknownness that can be reduced by more
manifestation from the unknownness that cannot? The framework’s answer is the distinction
between temporary and intrinsic unknownness. The distinction matters because it determines
what response the finite subject should make to its unknownness.

Remark 32.2 (The Chapter Develops Chapter 19). The chapter develops the distinction
that Chapter 19 named, in the theorem of unknownness (Theorem 19.1). In Chapter 19, the
distinction was stated so that the theorem of unknownness could be stated precisely. The
present chapter develops the distinction, so that the reader can see what each kind is, what
each kind is a feature of, and what response each kind invites.


32.3       The Two Kinds of Unknownness and the Criterion of Dis-
           tinction
Definition 32.1 (Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness). (A) Intrinsic unknownness: the
other is unknown by the structure of individuation itself. The unknownness cannot be removed
by more manifestation, because it is not a shortage of manifestation; it is the structural fact
that one identity is not another.
   Temporary unknownness: the other is unknown for now, because of limited capacity, limited
manifestation, or limited occasion. The unknownness can in principle be reduced: with more
manifestation, more capacity, or more occasion, the other can become more fully known.

      The definition has two parts, and both are worth marking.

The first part: intrinsic unknownness. The unknownness is intrinsic when it is a feature
of the relation between distinct identities. No amount of manifestation can turn one identity
into another, and no amount of reflection can render one identity directly present to another.

The second part: temporary unknownness. The unknownness is temporary when it is
a feature of the present state of a relation. With more manifestation, more capacity, or more
occasion, the unknownness can be reduced.

32.3.1      The Independent Criterion of Distinction
The definition states what the two kinds are; the criterion states how they are distinguished in
a particular case, independently of the subject’s failure or success.

Definition 32.2 (The Criterion of Distinction). (A) A case of unknownness is intrinsic when
it satisfies all three conditions:
32.4. The Principle of the Distinction                                                         431


(C1) Structural source: the unknownness is a feature of the relation between distinct identities,
     not of the present state of the relation.
(C2) Non-removability by manifestation: no amount of manifestation, capacity, or occasion
     could remove the unknownness, because the unknownness is entailed by the distinctness
     of the identities.
(C3) Independence from inquiry: the attribution of the unknownness does not depend on the
     failure of any inquiry; the unknownness would be present even if no inquiry had been
     undertaken.
A case that fails any one of the three is a case of temporary unknownness, or a case in which
the kind has not been determined.
    The criterion is (A): it is the framework’s stipulation of the distinction. Its justification is
that it makes the distinction applicable without depending on the subject’s success or failure;
its cost is that the identification of (C1) and (C2) is fallible.
Remark 32.3 (The Criterion Is Independent of the Failure). The criterion is independent
of the failure. A subject that has failed to solve an unknownness may be facing an intrinsic
unknownness or a temporary one; the failure alone does not determine which. The criterion
requires the structural source and the non-removability, not the failure.
Remark 32.4 (The Criterion Is Not a Decision Procedure). The criterion is not a decision
procedure. It states the conditions under which a case is intrinsic; it does not tell the subject
how to determine, in a given case, whether the conditions are met. The decision tree of
Section 32.6.1 states the steps by which the criterion is applied.


32.4     The Principle of the Distinction
Principle 32.1 (The Distinction of Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness). (T) Intrinsic
unknownness and temporary unknownness are structurally distinct: the first is a feature of
the relation between distinct identities, and the second is a feature of the present state of a
relation. Neither entails the other, and each can be present without the other.
    The principle is (T): it is argued from the definitions and from the criterion of distinction.
Its force is the force of the distinction.

Argument for Principle 32.1.       1. Intrinsic unknownness is a feature of the relation between
     distinct identities; it follows from the structural fact that one identity is not another.
   2. Temporary unknownness is a feature of the present state of a relation; it follows from
      the limited capacity, limited manifestation, or limited occasion of the present state.
   3. The first kind is structural; the second is contingent.
   4. The two kinds are distinct, and each can be present without the other.



32.5     Only the Intrinsic Kind Is Structural
Principle 32.2 (Only the Intrinsic Kind Is Structural). (T) Only intrinsic unknownness is
structural in the sense the impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27) requires. Temporary
unknownness is contingent on the present state of a relation, and the impossibility of super-
identity does not claim that temporary unknownness cannot be reduced; it claims that intrinsic
unknownness cannot be removed.
 432                                        Chapter 32. Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness


     The principle is (T): it is argued from the definition of the two kinds and from the statement
 of the impossibility of super-identity.


 Argument for Principle 32.2.    1. The impossibility of super-identity is a structural feature
      of the relation between the finite subject and the identity (Chapter 27).

    2. Intrinsic unknownness is a feature of the relation between distinct identities; it is not a
       shortage of manifestation.

    3. Temporary unknownness is a feature of the present state of the relation; it can be reduced
       by more manifestation.

    4. The impossibility of super-identity does not claim that temporary unknownness cannot
       be reduced; it claims that intrinsic unknownness cannot be removed.

    5. Hence only the intrinsic kind is structural in the sense the impossibility requires.




 32.6      The Independent Criterion and the Decision Tree
 The distinction is easily misused. A subject that has failed to solve an unknownness may be
 tempted to call it intrinsic, on the ground that the failure has not been overcome. The present
 section states the independent criterion with a decision tree, and the evidence that would
 refute the attribution.


 32.6.1     The Decision Tree
 Definition 32.3 (The Decision Tree for Attributing Unknownness). (A) The kind of an
 unknownness is determined by the following steps:

(DT1) Is the unknownness a feature of the relation between distinct identities, or of the present
      state of the relation? If it is a feature of the present state, the unknownness is temporary;
      proceed to (DT2) to confirm. If it is a feature of the relation between distinct identities,
      proceed to (DT3).

(DT2) Can more manifestation, more capacity, or more occasion reduce the unknownness? If
      yes, the unknownness is temporary; if no, the case is undetermined and requires further
      inquiry.

(DT3) Would any amount of manifestation, capacity, or occasion remove the unknownness? If
      no, the unknownness is intrinsic; if yes, the case is undetermined and the subject has
      not yet identified the structural feature.

(DT4) Is the attribution independent of the failure of any inquiry? If yes, the attribution of
      intrinsic is warranted; if no, the attribution is not warranted.

     The decision tree is (A): it is the framework’s stipulation of the steps by which the criterion
 is applied. Its justification is its use in the assessment of cases; its cost is that the steps
 (DT1)–(DT4) are fallible and may require iteration.
32.7. The Structural Features and the Response of Each Kind                                  433
