32.6.2    The Evidence That Would Refute the Attribution
The attribution of intrinsic unknownness is a structural claim, and it is refutable. Three kinds
of evidence would refute it.

Definition 32.4 (The Evidence That Refutes the Attribution). (A) The attribution of intrinsic
unknownness to a case is refuted by any one of the following:

(R1) A manifestation that removes the unknownness: a manifestation is produced that removes
     the unknownness; the unknownness was temporary, not intrinsic.

(R2) A generative rule that yields the manifestation from the identity alone: a generative rule
     is exhibited that yields the manifestation from the identity alone, without the receiving
     contexts; the unknownness was not a structural feature of the relation between distinct
     identities.

(R3) A demonstration that the unknownness is a feature of the present state: the unknownness
     is shown to be a feature of the present capacity, the present manifestation, or the present
     occasion, rather than a feature of the relation itself.

Remark 32.5 (The Criterion Protects Against the Misuse). The criterion and the decision
tree protect against the misuse of the distinction. Without them, a subject could call any
unsolved unknownness intrinsic. With them, the subject must identify the structural feature
and must state what would refute the attribution.


32.7     The Structural Features and the Response of Each Kind
The two kinds of unknownness have different structural features, and each kind invites a
different epistemic response and a different appropriate action. The present section states the
features, the response, and the action for each kind.

32.7.1    Intrinsic Unknownness
First feature: not a defect. Intrinsic unknownness is not a lack that expression might
eventually fill. It is the condition of possibility of expression, and therefore of finding (Chap-
ter 18).

Second feature: not ignorance. Ignorance is the temporary state; the intrinsic unknown-
ness is not a state of the subject but a feature of the relation.
434                                       Chapter 32. Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness


Third feature: what the finding requires. The finding (Chapter 18) requires the
distinctness of the two identities, and the distinctness is what the intrinsic unknownness
names.

The epistemic response. The appropriate response to intrinsic unknownness is recognition:
the subject recognizes that the unknownness is structural, that its knowledge is partial by
condition, and that the recognition is the condition of the finding. The recognition is not a
resignation; it is the recognition of the condition under which the finding is possible.

The appropriate action. The appropriate action is to hold the claim at the strength the
arguments support, and to state what the reconstruction leaves out. The subject does not
pursue what cannot be removed; it states the reconstruction at the adequacy the criteria of
Chapter 23 support, and it states the unknownness that the reconstruction does not remove.

32.7.2    Temporary Unknownness
First feature: a feature of the present state. Temporary unknownness is a feature of
the present state of the relation, not of the relation itself.

Second feature: reducible. Temporary unknownness can be reduced by more manifestation,
more capacity, or more occasion.

Third feature: not the unknownness the impossibility concerns. The impossibility
of super-identity concerns the intrinsic kind, not the temporary kind.

The epistemic response. The appropriate response to temporary unknownness is inquiry:
the subject gathers more manifestation, develops better models, and refines the criteria of
adequacy. The response is fallible; it may turn out that the unknownness is intrinsic in some
respects, and the subject should be prepared to revise the attribution.

The appropriate action. The appropriate action is to pursue the reduction, and to record
what the reduction leaves unreduced. The subject does not give up on what can be reduced; it
pursues the reduction, and it records the intrinsic unknownness that the reduction does not
remove.

Remark 32.6 (The Two Responses Are Not Rivals). The two responses are not rivals. The
ordinary case is the case in which both kinds of unknownness are present at once; the subject
should respond to the temporary unknownness by inquiry, and to the intrinsic unknownness
by recognition. The two responses are complementary, not exclusive.

Remark 32.7 (The Response Is Not a Rule). The response is not a rule. The framework
does not say that the subject must respond in a particular way in a particular case; it says
that the two kinds of unknownness invite different responses, and that the distinction is what
makes the difference visible.


32.8     The Practical Result: Managing Evidence and Reconstruc-
         tion
The chapter’s positive contribution is the practical result of the distinction for the management
of evidence and reconstruction. The present section states the result, so that the reader knows
what the chapter gives, not only what it excludes.
32.9. What the Distinction Does Not Establish                                              435


32.8.1    The Result for the Management of Evidence
The distinction gives three rules for the management of evidence.

First rule: distinguish the kind before gathering. Before gathering more evidence,
the subject determines, by the decision tree (Definition 32.3), whether the unknownness is
intrinsic or temporary. If the unknownness is intrinsic, more evidence will not remove it, and
the subject should not spend its finite resources on a pursuit that cannot succeed. If the
unknownness is temporary, more evidence can reduce it, and the subject should gather the
evidence.

Second rule: record what the evidence does not remove. The evidence that the
subject gathers may reduce the temporary unknownness without removing the intrinsic
unknownness. The subject records the intrinsic unknownness that the evidence leaves, so that
the reconstruction is stated at the strength the evidence supports.

Third rule: revise the attribution when the evidence refutes it. If the evidence
refutes the attribution (Definition 32.4), the subject revises the attribution. The revision is
the ordinary progress of inquiry; it is what the criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23) measure.

32.8.2    The Result for Reconstruction
The distinction gives three rules for reconstruction.

First rule: state the reconstruction at its proper strength. The reconstruction is
stated at the strength the criteria of Chapter 23 support, with the intrinsic unknownness
acknowledged. The reconstruction does not claim completeness; it claims adequacy.

Second rule: distinguish what the reconstruction reduces from what it does not.
The reconstruction reduces the temporary unknownness (by more manifestation and better
model) and does not remove the intrinsic unknownness. The subject states both, so that the
reader knows what the reconstruction achieves and what it does not.

Third rule: record the open questions. The intrinsic unknownness that the reconstruc-
tion does not remove is recorded as an open question, in the sense of Chapter 34. The record is
the reconstruction’s statement of what it leaves open, and it is what makes the reconstruction
assessable.

Remark 32.8 (The Result Is a Method, Not a Doctrine). The result is a method, not a
doctrine. The framework does not say what the subject’s reconstruction should be; it says
how the reconstruction is to be stated at its proper strength. The reader who takes the result
as a doctrine has misread it; the reader who takes it as a method has read it correctly.

Remark 32.9 (The Result and the Epistemic Economy of Cognition). The result is the
condition of the epistemic economy of cognition. The finite subject’s inquiry is subject to
a cost; the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness is what prevents the
subject from spending its finite capacity on a pursuit that cannot succeed. The distinction is
therefore not only a limit on knowledge; it is a condition of the economy of inquiry.


32.9     What the Distinction Does Not Establish
The distinction is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
436                                        Chapter 32. Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness


The distinction does not deny that temporary unknownness is real. The temporary
kind is real unknownness; it is what the finite subject’s inquiry aims at reducing.



The distinction does not deny that intrinsic unknownness is real. The intrinsic kind
is real unknownness; it is what the finite subject’s inquiry cannot remove.



The distinction does not say that every case is clearly one kind or the other. The
ordinary case is mixed; the distinction is a distinction of kinds, not of cases.



The distinction does not say that intrinsic unknownness cannot be experienced as
a loss. The framework makes no evaluative claim about intrinsic unknownness.



The distinction is not a definition of knowledge. The distinction is a distinction
between two kinds of unknownness; it does not define what knowledge is.


Remark 32.10 (The Distinction Is a Diagnosis, Not a Condemnation). The distinction is a
diagnosis, not a condemnation. The framework does not say that intrinsic unknownness is
bad, or that temporary unknownness is good. It says that the two are structurally different,
and that the difference matters for what the finite subject can hope to achieve.



32.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not settle the question of whether every case of unknownness falls
clearly into one of the two kinds. The decision tree and the criterion state the conditions; the
application to a particular case is the work of the inquiry.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of what the intrinsic unknownness is
a feature of. The intrinsic unknownness is a feature of the relation between distinct identities
(Chapter 19); its full development is the work of Chapter 19.
    Third, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of unknownness. It claims
to have described the structure of unknownness, and the structure is what the chapter’s claims
concern.
    Fourth, the chapter does not develop the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33) that the
distinction makes intelligible. The plurality is the positive form that the limits take; it is the
subject of the next chapter.


Remark 32.11 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has defined the two kinds of unknownness, with an independent criterion of distinction. It has
stated and argued the principle of their distinction, and the principle that only the intrinsic
kind is structural. It has stated the independent criterion with a decision tree, and the evidence
that would refute the attribution. It has stated the structural features of each kind, with the
epistemic response and the appropriate action for each. And it has stated the practical result
of the distinction for the management of evidence and reconstruction.

A Question for Reflection
Consider something you have tried to understand and have not understood. Apply the decision
tree of Definition 32.3: is the unknownness a feature of the relation between distinct identities,
or of the present state of the relation? Can more manifestation reduce it, or would no amount
of manifestation remove it? What does your answer tell you about the kind of unknownness
you face?
     And consider the translator—the scene that opened the chapter. The third difficulty—the
meaning of the poem as a whole—is the kind of unknownness that no amount of translation
can remove. Apply the criterion of Definition 32.2: does the case satisfy (C1), (C2), and (C3)?
If it does, the attribution of intrinsic unknownness is warranted; if it does not, the case is one
of temporary unknownness, or the kind has not been determined.
     Finally, consider the practical result of Section 32.8: can you apply the three rules for the
management of evidence and the three rules for reconstruction to a case of your own? Can
you show, for each rule, what the rule requires and why? What does your answer tell you
about the difference between a controlled inquiry and an uncontrolled one? A reader who can
answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the
438                                        Chapter 32. Intrinsic and Temporary Unknownness


chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter states the plurality of perspectives: the structural consequence of the relation
between a finite subject and an identity. The present chapter has distinguished the two kinds of
unknownness; the next chapter states what the plurality of perspectives is, and why it is not a
defect of cognition but a condition of it.

Chapter 33

The Plurality of Perspectives

Scope
This chapter states the plurality of perspectives as a structural consequence of the relation
between a finite subject and an identity. It defines the plurality (Definition 33.1), gives the
criteria for identifying independent and overlapping perspectives (Section 33.3.1), argues that
the plurality is structural (Principle 33.1), states the assessment of perspectives (Principle 33.2),
states the comparison matrix and the adjudication criteria with a worked real conflict (Sec-
tion 33.6), and states the conditions for comparing and adjudicating perspectives (Section 33.7).
Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “perspective,” “plurality,” “assessment,”
“adjudication,” “viewpoint,” or “position,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed
by the definitions in this chapter and by the definition of perspective in Chapter 14.

Remark 33.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part V). The chapter is the eighth of the nine
chapters of Part V. The previous chapters stated the limits of finite cognition: the impossibility
of super-identity (Chapter 27), the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28), configuration-
dependence (Chapter 29), the limits of self-knowledge (Chapter 30), the impossibility of
complete knowledge of epistemic light (Chapter 31), and the distinction between intrinsic and
temporary unknownness (Chapter 32). The present chapter states the positive form that those
limits take: the plurality of perspectives.


33.1      A Scene: The Mountain from Three Valleys
Consider a mountain, seen from three valleys. From the northern valley, the mountain has a
steep face of grey rock and a single peak. From the southern valley, it has a rounded summit
and a forested slope. From the eastern valley, it has two peaks and a saddle between them.
The three views are of the same mountain, and none of them is the mountain.
     A traveler who has seen the mountain from one valley knows something about the mountain,
and does not know everything. A traveler who has seen it from three valleys knows more, and
still does not know everything. No number of valley-views is the mountain.

Remark 33.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the plurality
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the claim; it makes the claim intelligible before it
is stated.


33.2      The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have stated the limits of finite cognition. The present chapter
states a further consequence: the plurality of perspectives.
440                                                   Chapter 33. The Plurality of Perspectives


   The question is: what is the plurality of perspectives, why is it structural, how is it assessed,
and how are the perspectives related to one another?

Remark 33.3 (The Chapter States What the Previous Chapters Implied). The impossibility
of super-identity, the fallacy of super-identity, the configuration-dependence, the limits of
self-knowledge, the impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light, and the distinction
between intrinsic and temporary unknownness all imply that cognition is from a perspective.
The present chapter makes the implication explicit.


33.3     The Plurality Defined
Definition 33.1 (The Plurality of Perspectives). (A) The plurality of perspectives is the
structural fact that an identity can be cognized from more than one perspective, and that the
perspectives are not all the same.

33.3.1     The Criteria for Identifying Independent and Overlapping Perspec-
           tives
The plurality is a plurality of perspectives that are related in various ways. Before the relations
can be assessed, the perspectives must be identified, and the identification requires criteria
that distinguish independent perspectives (perspectives that differ in their point, means, or
conceptual structure) from overlapping perspectives (perspectives that share some of the same
structural features).

Definition 33.2 (Independent and Overlapping Perspectives). (A) Two perspectives P1 and
P2 on an identity I are:

(I1) Independent when they differ in at least one of the three structural parts of perspective
     (the point, the means, the conceptual structure), and neither can be derived from the
     other without loss of the difference.

(I2) Overlapping when they share at least one of the three structural parts, and the shared
     part is the same in both; the overlap can be partial (sharing the point but not the means)
     or total (sharing all three).

Remark 33.4 (Independence and Overlap Are Criteria, Not Values). The criteria are descrip-
tive: they state what it is for perspectives to be independent or overlapping. They do not say
that independent perspectives are better than overlapping ones, or vice versa. A subject may
find overlapping perspectives more useful for a given purpose, and independent perspectives
more useful for another.
33.4. The Plurality Is Structural                                                              441


Remark 33.5 (Overlap Is Not Identity). Overlap is not identity. Two perspectives that share
all three structural parts are not two perspectives; they are the same perspective viewed twice.
The plurality of perspectives is a plurality of distinct perspectives; an overlap of all three parts
collapses the plurality into one.


33.4      The Plurality Is Structural
Principle 33.1 (The Structural Character of the Plurality). (T) The plurality of perspectives
is a structural condition of finite cognition, not a defect. It is the condition under which a
finite subject cognizes an identity, and it cannot be removed by a better perspective, because
no finite subject can occupy every position.
Argument for Principle 33.1.   1. A perspective is the structural position of an observer
    within a cognitive context (Chapter 14).
   2. A perspective is partial because it is located.
   3. An identity can be cognized from more than one position; the positions differ, the
      perspectives differ, and each makes visible aspects the others do not.
   4. If the plurality were a defect, it would be removable by a better perspective. But no
      finite subject can occupy every position.
   5. Therefore the plurality is the structural condition under which a finite subject cognizes
      an identity.


Remark 33.6 (The Plurality Is Not a Limit of Resources). A subject with more resources
would occupy more positions, but it would still occupy perspectives, and the plurality would
still be the condition of its cognition.
Remark 33.7 (The Plurality and the Impossibility of Super-Identity). The impossibility says
that no finite subject can know all manifestations in all contexts; the plurality says that, given
the impossibility, every cognition of an identity is from a perspective, and the perspectives are
many.


33.5      The Assessment of Perspectives
Principle 33.2 (The Assessment of Perspectives). (T) Perspectives are assessed indirectly,
through two things: the context in which the perspective is located, assessed by the criteria
of context validity (Chapter 21); and the reconstruction that the perspective makes possible,
assessed by the criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23). The assessment is not a ranking of
perspectives; it is the discipline by which the plurality is made usable for the reconstruction of
the identity.
Argument for Principle 33.2.    1. A perspective is not a claim; it is a position. What is
     assessed is the context in which the perspective is located and the reconstruction the
     perspective makes possible.
   2. The context is assessed by the criteria of context validity.
   3. The reconstruction is assessed by the criteria of adequacy.
   4. Hence the assessment of a perspective is the assessment of the two things it makes
      possible.
442                                                   Chapter 33. The Plurality of Perspectives


Remark 33.8 (The Assessment Is Not a Ranking). The assessment says which perspectives
are candidates and which reconstructions are adequate; it does not say which perspective is
the best. The choice among adequate perspectives is a matter for the inquiry.


33.6     The Comparison Matrix of Perspectives
The plurality is a plurality of perspectives related in various ways. The present section states
the fourfold matrix of perspective relations, the criteria of adjudication for each, and a worked
real conflict.

33.6.1     The Four Relations and the Adjudication Criteria
Definition 33.3 (The Four Relations of Perspective). (A) Two perspectives P1 and P2 on
the same identity are related in one of four ways:
(R1) Complementary: each makes visible aspects of the identity that the other does not, and
     the aspects can be combined into a single reconstruction without loss.
(R2) Conflicting: each makes a claim about the same aspect of the identity, and the claims
     cannot both be true in the same respect.
(R3) Asymmetric: one perspective can be reconstructed from the other, but not the reverse.
(R4) Incomparable: the two perspectives cannot be brought under a common respect, and
     neither can be reconstructed from the other.

33.6.3    A Worked Real Conflict
Consider two historians, H1 and H2 , studying a treaty signed in a particular year. H1 claims
the treaty was signed in January; H2 claims March. Both cite documents.

Step 1: identify the perspectives. H1 ’s perspective is the diplomatic context (the
negotiation records); H2 ’s perspective is the legal context (the registry of ratifications). The
two perspectives are independent in their point (the negotiation room vs. the registry office)
and in their means (diplomatic correspondence vs. legal records), but they overlap in their
conceptual structure (both are documentary inquiries).

Step 2: identify the relation. The two perspectives make claims about the same aspect
of the identity (the date of the signing) and cannot both be true in the same respect. The
relation is conflicting (R2).

Step 3: identify the respect. The conflict is within the same respect (the date of the
signing), not across different respects. The adjudication criterion (R2) applies: at most one of
the two claims is adequate in the respect.

Step 4: translate or decide. If the two dates refer to different events (signing vs. rat-
ification), the conflict is apparent and the translation resolves it. If the two dates refer to
the same event, the conflict is real, and the adjudication requires deciding between the two
claims. The criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23) assess which reconstruction is more adequate:
consistency with other documents, stability under correction of single documents, fruitfulness
in explaining the subsequent events.

The verdict. If the ratification date is March and the signing date is January, the two claims
are compatible and the perspectives are complementary after translation. If both documents
refer to the same event, the conflict is real, and the more adequate reconstruction is chosen by
the criteria of adequacy.

Remark 33.9 (The Worked Conflict Shows the Adjudication at Work). The worked conflict
shows the four steps of adjudication: identify the perspectives, identify the relation, identify
the respect, and translate or decide. The four steps are the framework’s application of the
matrix and of the criteria to a real case.

Remark 33.10 (The Matrix and the Fallacy of Super-Identity). The matrix makes the fallacy
visible in the case of the plurality. The fallacy is the error of treating two perspectives as if
they were complementary when they are conflicting, or as if they were comparable when they
are incomparable. The matrix and the criteria state the relations and the adjudication that
avoid the fallacy.


33.7     Conditions for Comparing and Adjudicating Perspectives
The present section states the conditions under which perspectives can be compared and
adjudicated, and what distinguishes comparison and adjudication from mere plurality, mere
relativism, or mere skepticism.

33.7.1    The Conditions for Comparison
Definition 33.4 (The Conditions for Comparing Perspectives). (A) Two perspectives P1 and
P2 on an identity can be compared when:
444                                                   Chapter 33. The Plurality of Perspectives


(C1) Common identity: they are perspectives on the same identity.

(C2) Identifiable relation: the relation between them (complementary, conflicting, asymmetric,
     incomparable) can be identified by the criteria of the matrix.

(C3) Common respect or translatable respects: the respects in which they are said can be
     identified as the same, or as two respects that can be related by a stated translation.

(C4) Assessable reconstruction: the reconstruction each makes possible can be assessed by the
     criteria of adequacy.

33.7.2    The Conditions for Adjudication
Definition 33.5 (The Conditions for Adjudicating Perspectives). (A) Two perspectives P1
and P2 can be adjudicated when:

(A1) The comparison conditions are met (Definition 33.4).

(A2) The relation is identified : the relation is complementary, conflicting, asymmetric, or
     incomparable (Definition 33.3).

(A3) The adjudication criteria are applied : the criteria of context validity (Chapter 21) and of
     adequacy (Chapter 23) are applied to the reconstructions.

(A4) The result is stated at its proper strength: the adjudication yields a combination (com-
     plementary), a decision (conflicting), a direction (asymmetric), or a recognition of
     incomparability (incomparable).

33.7.3    What the Conditions Distinguish
The conditions distinguish comparison and adjudication from three positions that the plurality
is easily confused with.

From mere plurality. Mere plurality is the fact that perspectives are many, without any
discipline. The conditions add the discipline: they require the identity, the relation, the respect,
and the assessment. Mere plurality is a fact; the conditions are the discipline that makes the
fact usable.

From relativism. Relativism is the thesis that every perspective is as good as every other,
or that there is no fact of the matter. The conditions deny relativism: they require that the
perspectives be assessed by the criteria of context validity and of adequacy, and that the
assessment yield a result at its proper strength. The conditions do not say that every perspective
is equally valid; they say which perspectives are candidates and which reconstructions are
adequate.

From skepticism. Skepticism is the thesis that knowledge is impossible. The conditions
deny skepticism: they require that the perspectives be assessed, and they state the conditions
under which the assessment yields knowledge. The conditions do not say that every assessment
is certain; they say which assessments are adequate.

Remark 33.11 (The Conditions Are the Framework’s Discipline on the Plurality). The
conditions are the framework’s discipline on the plurality. They do not deny the plurality;
they make it usable. They do not claim that the assessment is certain; they claim that the
assessment is adequate to the extent the criteria support.
33.8. The Plurality and the Other Limits of Part V                                             445


Remark 33.12 (The Conditions and the Criteria of the Framework). The conditions are
stated in terms of the framework’s criteria: the criteria of context validity (Chapter 21), the
criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23), and the matrix of perspective relations (Definition 33.3).
The conditions are not a new set of criteria; they are the framework’s statement of how the
existing criteria are applied to the plurality.



33.8      The Plurality and the Other Limits of Part V

The plurality is one of the limits of Part V, and its relation to the other limits is worth marking.

Remark 33.13 (The Plurality Is the Positive Side of the Limits). The limits say what the
finite subject cannot do; the plurality says what the finite subject does do, given the limits.
The finite subject cognizes from a perspective, and the perspectives are many.

Remark 33.14 (The Plurality and the Epistemic Humility of Chapter 35). The humility is
the recognition of the limits; the plurality is the form that inquiry takes under the limits. The
two are related as the disposition and the form that the disposition takes in inquiry.

Remark 33.15 (The Plurality and the Epistemic Economy of Part VI). The plurality is
relevant to the epistemic economy of Part VI: a subject that recognizes the plurality can
distribute its finite capacity across the perspectives that are most adequate for its purposes,
instead of pursuing a single exhaustive perspective that is not available to it.



33.9      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
     First, the chapter does not develop the criteria of context validity and of adequacy in
full. Those criteria are stated in Chapters 21 and 23; the present chapter states how they are
applied to the perspectives.
     Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the plurality of perspectives is
a plurality of partial perspectives or a plurality of equally valid perspectives. The framework
holds the first; the conditions (Definition 33.4) state the discipline by which the partial
perspectives are assessed.
     Third, the chapter does not develop the connection between the plurality and the epistemic
humility of Chapter 35 beyond the remark of the previous section.
     Fourth, the chapter does not develop the boundaries of epistemology (Chapter 34) that
the plurality implies. The boundaries state what the framework can and cannot establish, and
the open questions that it leaves.

Remark 33.16 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has defined the plurality of perspectives. It has stated the criteria for identifying independent
and overlapping perspectives. It has argued that the plurality is structural, not a defect. It
has stated the assessment of perspectives. It has stated the comparison matrix of perspectives
with the adjudication criteria, and a worked real conflict. And it has stated the conditions for
comparing and adjudicating perspectives, which distinguish comparison from mere plurality,
relativism, and skepticism.

A Question for Reflection
Consider an identity you have come to know from more than one perspective. Are the
perspectives independent or overlapping, by the criteria of Definition 33.2? Which of the four
relations (complementary, conflicting, asymmetric, incomparable) holds between them? Apply
the adjudication criteria: what would the assessment yield, and at what strength?
    And consider the worked real conflict (Section 33.6.3): can you apply the four steps to
a conflict of your own? Can you identify the perspectives, the relation, the respect, and the
adjudication? What does your answer tell you about the difference between the plurality of
perspectives and the chaos of perspectives that the conditions are meant to prevent?
    Finally, consider the conditions of Section 33.7: can you apply the conditions for comparison
and adjudication to a pair of perspectives of your own? Can you show, for each condition, what
the condition requires and why? What does your answer tell you about the difference between
a pluralistic inquiry and a relativistic one? A reader who can answer all three questions has
understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before
them.

The next chapter states the boundaries of epistemology: what epistemic inquiry can and cannot
do, what it can and cannot establish, and what questions it leaves to other inquiries.

Chapter 34

The Boundaries of Epistemology

Scope
This chapter states the boundaries of the epistemic framework developed in this volume. It
says what the framework can and cannot establish, what questions it leaves open, and what
conditions govern its further internal development. It states the coherence of the framework,
the framework’s role as a conceptual foundation, the three principles of the boundary, the
internal domain and competence of epistemic analysis (Section 34.6), the open questions with
their place, reason, consequence, and method (Sections 34.7 through 34.9), the classification
of the fourteen questions by their relation to the core (Section 34.10), the open problems in
epistemic reconstruction (Section 34.11), and the conditions for further internal development
(Section 34.12). It closes Part V.
    Its claims are epistemic and meta-epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “boundary,”
“coherence,” “foundation,” “competence,” “open question,” or “development,” these are structural
terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.

Remark 34.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part V). The chapter is the eighth of the nine chapters
of Part V. The previous chapters stated the limits of finite cognition: the impossibility of super-
identity (Chapter 27), the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28), configuration-dependence
(Chapter 29), the limits of self-knowledge (Chapter 30), the impossibility of complete knowledge
of epistemic light (Chapter 31), the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness
(Chapter 32), and the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33). The present chapter turns from
the limits of the finite subject to the limits of the framework’s account of the finite subject.
The next chapter (Chapter 35) states epistemic humility, the disposition that the limits and
the open questions require, and it closes Part V.


34.1      A Scene: The Map
Consider a map. A map is not the territory it represents; it is a representation of the territory,
drawn for a purpose, at a scale, with a selection of what to include and what to leave out. A
topographic map shows elevation but not population; a political map shows borders but not
climate; a road map shows routes but not soil. Each map is accurate in its own terms, and
none is the territory. The map has a boundary—the edge of the sheet, the region it covers,
the features it represents—and the boundary is not a defect. It is what makes the map useful.
    The scene poses a question. What are the boundaries of the framework? Where does its
description stop being useful, and where does it begin to be misleading? And what are the
questions it leaves open?

Remark 34.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the answer; it makes the answer intelligible
448                                                Chapter 34. The Boundaries of Epistemology


before it is stated.


34.2      The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have stated the limits of finite cognition. The present chapter
asks: what are the limits on what the framework itself can establish?
    The question is not idle. A framework that did not know its boundaries would claim more
than it can support. The framework’s honesty about its limits is part of what the framework
is. The present chapter states the boundaries, and it states them as an axiom so that the
reader knows, from the outset, what the framework claims and what it does not.


34.3      The Coherence of the Framework
Over thirty-three chapters, the book has built an epistemic framework. What can be said of
it is that it is coherent: its definitions are fixed, its arguments state their premises, and its
statuses are declared.
Remark 34.3 (Coherence Is Not Completeness). Coherence is not completeness. The
framework is coherent in the sense that its principles are mutually consistent and its arguments
are stated; it is not complete in the sense that every question it raises is answered.
Remark 34.4 (Coherence Is Not Finality). Coherence is not finality. A coherent framework
can be revised; a framework that is not coherent cannot be revised, because there is no single
structure to revise.
Remark 34.5 (Coherence Is Relative to the Framework’s Scope). Coherence is relative to
the framework’s scope. The framework is coherent as an epistemic framework, for the scope it
declares. It does not claim coherence with the whole of what is.


34.4      The Framework as a Conceptual Foundation
The framework supplies primitives, abstractions, and invariants for the structural description
of explanatory cognition.

Primitives. The framework’s primitives are identity, manifestation, epistemic light, context,
expression, and cost.

Abstractions. The framework’s abstractions are the pseudo-identity, signature, intra-
category epistemic light, cognitive sediment, returning light, category-relative predication,
reflection, the action chain, the crystallization of effect, and the structural duality of expression.

Invariants. The framework’s invariants are identity rigidity and conservation, non-duplicability,
non-reduction of identity to manifestations, essential homogeneity of manifestation, non-
sequential connectivity, expression as structural necessity, and the limits of the finite observer.
Remark 34.6 (The Framework’s Role Is Foundational, Not Directive). The framework
describes the structure of explanatory cognition; the empirical inquiries answer their specific
questions by their own methods. The framework states the conditions under which the inquiries
can develop; the authority of those inquiries comes from their own methods.
Remark 34.7 (Description and Prescription). The framework describes structure; it does
not prescribe conduct. A structural description is not a normative prescription, but neither
is it irrelevant to one. The description provides an epistemic basis on which a normative
prescription may be built; it does not itself supply that prescription.
34.5. The Three Principles of the Boundary                                                    449


34.5     The Three Principles of the Boundary
Three principles fix the boundary of the framework.
Principle 34.1 (Autonomy of Epistemic Justification). (A) The validity of an epistemic
principle, within the domain of epistemology, does not depend on confirmation from outside
epistemology.
    The principle separates autonomy from exclusivity. Autonomy says that epistemology’s
justification is internal to epistemology; exclusivity would say that epistemology is the only
domain of valid discourse. The framework holds the first and denies the second.
Principle 34.2 (Internal Definition). (T) The concepts of the framework are defined and
justified within its own system, from its premises.
Principle 34.3 (Meaning Is Not Exported). (T) The use of a word or concept in another
domain does not determine its epistemic sense here.
Remark 34.8 (Where a Conflict Is Felt). If someone judges that an epistemic principle here is
mistaken, the ground for revising it is an epistemic one: incoherence with other commitments,
a better rival commitment, or the showing that the principle does no work.


34.6     Internal Domain and Competence of Epistemic Analysis
The framework’s boundary is not a fence against other domains; it is a statement of what the
framework’s analysis can do, and under what conditions it can be applied. The present section
states the internal domain and the competence of the epistemic analysis, so that the reader
knows what the framework is for.

34.6.1    The Internal Domain
The internal domain of the framework is the structure of explanatory cognition: the roles an
explanation assigns, the relations among the roles, the conditions of validity and adequacy,
the limits of finite cognition, and the epistemic economy of cognition. The framework’s claims
are within this domain; its arguments are assessed by the standards of this domain.

34.6.2    The Competence of the Analysis
The epistemic analysis has four competences, and each is worth stating.

First competence: structural description. The framework can describe the structure of
any explanatory cognition in the four columns, in the categories of identity and manifestation,
and in the terms of the criteria of validity and adequacy. The competence is the framework’s
primary contribution; it is what the analysis is for.

Second competence: assessment of reconstructions. The framework can assess a
reconstruction of an identity by the criteria of adequacy (consistency, stability, fruitfulness)
and by the criteria of context validity (cross-checkability, minimality, consistency). The
assessment is fallible, and it is the best the finite subject can supply.

Third competence: identification of limits. The framework can identify the limits of
finite cognition—the impossibility of super-identity, the fallacy of super-identity, configuration-
dependence, the limits of self-knowledge, the impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic
light, the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness, and the plurality of
perspectives. The identification is structural; it does not require empirical confirmation.
450                                               Chapter 34. The Boundaries of Epistemology


Fourth competence: preparation of further analysis. The framework can prepare the
further analysis of the epistemic economy of cognition, the cost of cognition, the cognitive
sediment and its integration, the balance criterion, and the concept of viability. The preparation
is the framework’s contribution to the parts of the book that follow; it is the internal domain’s
extension into the economy of cognition.

34.6.3    The Conditions of Application
The four competences are exercised under three conditions, and the conditions are worth
stating.

First condition: the question is about explanatory cognition. The framework’s
competences apply to questions about the structure of explanatory cognition. A question
about what is, independent of any cognition, is outside the framework’s competence; the
framework can describe the structure of the cognition that asks the question, but it cannot
answer the question itself.

Second condition: the question is asked at the strength the framework’s arguments
support. The framework’s competences are exercised at the strength of its arguments. A
question that presupposes a stronger claim than the framework establishes is outside the
framework’s competence; the framework can state what it does establish, and it can mark the
presupposition as outside its scope.

Third condition: the question is assessed by the framework’s standards. The
framework’s competences are exercised in the framework’s standards of assessment: coherence,
explanatory power, fruitfulness, and the criteria of validity and adequacy. A question that is
asked by another domain’s standards is outside the framework’s competence; the framework
can describe the structure of the question, and it can mark the standards as another domain’s.

Remark 34.9 (The Three Conditions Are the Framework’s Competence). The three conditions
are the framework’s competence. The framework does not claim that every question can
be answered within its domain; it claims that the questions it can answer are those that
satisfy the three conditions, and that the questions it cannot answer are marked as outside its
competence.

Remark 34.10 (The Framework Does Not Deny Other Inquiries). The framework does not
deny that other inquiries ask questions outside its competence. It says that its competence is
the structure of explanatory cognition, and that the questions outside that structure belong to
other inquiries. The framework’s silence on those questions is not a denial of their reality; it is
the recognition that the framework’s analysis is not the whole of what can be said.


34.7     The Open Questions: Conceptual
The framework’s principles make visible a set of questions that the framework does not settle.
Each question is stated with its place of arising, the reason it remains open, its consequence
for the framework, and the method of its further investigation.

First question: the structural conditions of joint realizability of viabilities. Place
of arising. Chapter 36 (viability) and Chapter 37 (the three components).
    Reason it remains open. The framework states the structural conditions of joint realizability,
but the account of the joint realizability of two viabilities in one context is not developed.
34.8. The Open Questions: Argumentative                                                      451


    Consequence for the framework. The question does not threaten the framework’s core; it is
an extension of the framework’s account of viability.
    Method of investigation. A structural analysis of the joint realizability of two viabilities,
stated at the strength the framework’s account of viability supports.

Second question: the structural boundary between the reduction of viability and
the singularity. Place of arising. Chapter 37, Section 37.7 (Definition 37.2: the threshold
at which the cost of restoring a manifestation exceeds the cost of producing a new one).
    Reason it remains open. The singularity is defined; the exact function that maps a degree
of reduction of viability onto a position relative to the threshold is not.
    Consequence for the framework. The question limits the framework’s application to the
gradient of viability; it does not threaten the framework’s core.
    Method of investigation. A formalization of the boundary, or a demonstration that the
boundary is not definable within the framework’s resources.

Third question: the conceptual relation of epistemic light and expression. Place
of arising. Chapter 15 (epistemic light) and Chapter 38 (expression).
    Reason it remains open. The framework states that epistemic light is the medium of legible
relation and that expression is the enactment of the identity; the exact conceptual relation
between the two is not developed.
    Consequence for the framework. The question is an extension; it does not threaten the
framework’s core.
    Method of investigation. A conceptual analysis of the relation, stated at the strength the
framework’s arguments support.

Fourth question: the mode of the relation between the structural epistemic light
and its ground. Place of arising. Chapter 15 and Chapter 31.
    Reason it remains open. The framework states the relation of condition to ground; the
finer account of how the structural epistemic light is given by its ground is not developed.
    Consequence for the framework. The question is an extension; it does not threaten the
framework’s core.
    Method of investigation. A structural analysis of the mode, or a demonstration that the
mode is not describable within the framework’s resources.

Remark 34.11 (The Fourteen Questions Are Recorded, Not Deferred). The fourteen questions

what would settle it.


34.10      The Classification of the Open Questions
The fourteen open questions are classified into three groups by their relation to the core.
Definition 34.1 (The Three Groups of Open Questions). (A) The fourteen open questions
are classified into three groups:
(G1) Threatening-validity questions: questions whose settlement or non-settlement bears on
     the framework’s core commitments.

(G2) Operationalization questions: questions whose settlement is needed for the framework’s
     application in a given domain, without threatening the framework’s core.
454                                               Chapter 34. The Boundaries of Epistemology


(G3) Developmental questions: questions that the framework invites as extensions, without
     requiring them for its validity or its operation.

34.11       Open Problems in Epistemic Reconstruction
The chapter’s positive contribution to the reader’s navigation of the framework’s open problems
is the statement of the problems that the framework’s reconstruction of explanatory cognition
leaves open. The present section states these problems, so that the reader knows where the
framework’s work is not finished.

First problem: the exact measurement of the two measures. Chapter 26 stated the
scales of intensity and breadth as ordinal-structural, with the comparison criteria and the
34.12. Conditions for Further Internal Development                                              455


normalization; the exact measurement of the two measures in a given case is left open. The
framework states the scale and the conditions; the measurement procedure is a matter for the
applications of the framework.

Second problem: the exact form of the joint realizability of viabilities. Chapter 36
states the structural character of viability; the joint realizability of two viabilities in a single
context is an extension that the framework invites (Q1).

Third problem: the exact boundary between the gradient of viability and the
singularity. Chapter 37 defines the singularity; the function that maps a degree of reduction
onto a position relative to the threshold is left open (Q2).

Fourth problem: the exact conceptual relation between epistemic light and ex-
pression. Chapters 15 and 38 state the two concepts; the exact relation between them is
left open (Q3).

Fifth problem: the exact form of the bridge between description and prescription.
Chapter 4 states that description grounds prescription without replacing it; the exact form of
the bridge is left open (Q9).

Sixth problem: the temporal structure of self-awareness. Chapter 20 distinguishes
phenomenal time and structural time; the development of either kind is left open (Q14).

Remark 34.13 (The Six Problems Are the Framework’s Own Statement). The six problems
are the framework’s own statement of where its reconstruction is not finished. They are
not a denial of the framework’s achievements; they are the recognition that the framework’s
achievements are partial, and that the further work is internal to the framework’s own
standards.


34.12      Conditions for Further Internal Development
The framework’s further development is internal to the framework’s own standards, and the
present section states the conditions under which the development can proceed.

First condition: the development is by the framework’s standards. A further
development of the framework is assessed by the framework’s own standards: coherence,
explanatory power, fruitfulness, and the criteria of validity and adequacy. A development
that is assessed by another domain’s standards is not a development of the framework; it is a
development of the other domain.

Second condition: the development is within the framework’s competence. A
further development of the framework is within the framework’s competence (Section 34.6). A
development that asks a question outside the framework’s competence is not a development of
the framework; it is a development of another inquiry.

Third condition: the development is stated at the strength the framework’s
arguments support. A further development of the framework is stated at the strength of
the framework’s arguments. A development that claims more than the arguments support is
not a development of the framework; it is a claim the framework does not support.
456                                              Chapter 34. The Boundaries of Epistemology


Fourth condition: the development is recorded as an extension of the framework.
A further development of the framework is recorded as an extension of the framework, so
that the reader knows what the framework claims and what the development adds. The
record is the framework’s statement of its own development; it is what makes the development
assessable.

Remark 34.14 (The Four Conditions Are the Framework’s Discipline on Its Own Develop-
ment). The four conditions are the framework’s discipline on its own development. They do
not deny that other inquiries can develop; they say that the framework’s own development is
by its own standards, within its own competence, at the strength of its own arguments, and
recorded as an extension of itself.

Remark 34.15 (The Living Framework). The framework is not a static hierarchy. When a
conceptual difficulty appears at one level, it can lead to refinement of a principle at another,
and the refined principle in turn changes what can be said below. This is what keeps the
system revisable. The framework is a living framework, not a finished monument.


34.13      Closing Part V
Part V has stated the limits, errors, and unknownness that any finite cognition must acknowl-
edge. The summary is worth giving, because Part VI builds on it.

  1. The impossibility of super-identity. No finite subject can know all manifestations of
     an identity in all contexts; the impossibility is structural, not contingent on the subject’s
     resources (Chapter 27).

  2. The fallacy of super-identity. A record formed by aggregating manifestations across
     contexts whose elements are not mutually translatable is not a reconstruction of the
     identity (Chapter 28).

  3. Configuration-dependence. The manifestation of an identity in a context depends
     on the configuration of the context, and the configuration changes; super-identity is
     impossible even within a single context (Chapter 29).

  4. The limits of self-knowledge. The subject’s knowledge of its own identity is subject
     to the impossibility of super-identity; it is not privileged (Chapter 30).

  5. The impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light. Because we are
     encompassed in epistemic light, complete knowledge of it is impossible for the finite
     subject (Chapter 31).

  6. Intrinsic and temporary unknownness. Only the intrinsic kind is structural in the
     sense of the impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 32).

  7. The plurality of perspectives. The plurality is a structural consequence of the
     relation between a finite subject and an identity (Chapter 33).

  8. The boundaries of epistemology. The framework is coherent, foundational, and
     autonomous; it has an internal domain and four competences; it leaves open fourteen
     questions, classified by their relation to the core (G1, G2, G3); and its further development
     is governed by four conditions (the present chapter).

    Part VI turns from the limits of cognition to the epistemic economy of cognition and to
the concept of viability.

A Question for Reflection
Consider one of the fourteen open questions. What is its place of arising, its reason for
remaining open, its consequence for the framework, and the method of its further investigation?
What does your answer tell you about the difference between the questions the framework
raises and the questions it settles?
    And consider the four competences (Section 34.6.2): can you apply each of the four to a
case of your own? Can you show, for each, what the framework can do and what the framework
cannot? What does your answer tell you about the difference between the framework’s
competence and the framework’s silence?
    And consider the six open problems in epistemic reconstruction (Section 34.11): can you
state, for each problem, what the framework has established and what remains open? What
does your answer tell you about the difference between the framework’s achievements and its
458                                               Chapter 34. The Boundaries of Epistemology


unfinished work? A reader who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a
reader who can answer none has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter states epistemic humility, the disposition that the limits and the open questions
require, and it closes Part V. Part VI develops the epistemic economy of cognition and the
concept of viability.

Chapter 35

Open Questions and Epistemic
Humility

Scope
This chapter states epistemic humility as the structural disposition that follows from the
limits of Part V and from the open questions identified in Chapter 34. It defines humility
as a practical rule for calibrating confidence and revising claims (Definition 35.1), states the
principle of its structural character (Principle 35.1), distinguishes three modes of epistemic
miscalibration (Section 35.5), connects humility to the method of Chapter 2, to the boundaries
of Chapter 34, and to the distinctions of Chapters 32 and 33, calibrates it for the three groups
of open questions with a confidence-level table (Section 35.8), states a practical checklist
for applying humility in reconstruction (Section 35.9), and closes Part V. It does not repeat
the open questions; they are stated in Chapter 34 (fourteen questions in three groups: four
conceptual, five argumentative, five epistemic), and the present chapter refers to them.
    Its claims are epistemic and meta-epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “humility,”
“calibration,” “confidence,” “miscalibration,” “open question,” “practice,” or “recognition,” these
are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.

Remark 35.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part V). The chapter is the ninth and last chapter
of Part V. The previous chapters have stated the limits of finite cognition (Chapters 27–33)
and the boundaries of the framework with its fourteen open questions (Chapter 34). The
present chapter states the disposition that those limits and those questions require, and it
closes Part V. The next chapter (Chapter 36) opens Part VI.


35.1     A Scene: The Scholar at the End of a Career
Consider a scholar at the end of a long career. She is asked what she has learned. She does
not say: “I have learned the truth about my subject.” She does not say: “I have learned that
nothing can be known.” She says: “I have learned which questions are the real ones, and I
have learned that I will not answer all of them. I have learned which answers are adequate,
and I have learned that adequacy is not the same as completeness. I have learned to hold
my conclusions at the strength my arguments support, and to let the questions I have not
answered remain open, without either giving up on them or pretending to have settled them.”
    The scholar’s answer is one instance of a structural disposition. The disposition is not the
disposition of the scholar who claims to have settled everything, and it is not the disposition
of the scholar who claims that nothing can be settled. It is the disposition of the scholar who
knows what the limits of inquiry are, and who holds her conclusions at the strength the limits
permit.
460                                        Chapter 35. Open Questions and Epistemic Humility


Remark 35.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the
disposition at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the claim; it makes the claim
intelligible before it is stated.


35.2      The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have stated the limits of finite cognition. Chapter 34 stated
the boundaries of the framework and identified fourteen open questions in three groups. The
present chapter asks: what disposition does the framework’s account of the limits, together
with its identification and classification of the open questions, require of the finite subject?
The framework’s answer is epistemic humility.
Remark 35.3 (The Chapter Does Not Repeat the Open Questions). The chapter does not
repeat the open questions of Chapter 34. The questions are stated there; the present chapter
states the disposition that the questions, together with the limits, require.


35.3      The Definition of Epistemic Humility as a Practical Rule
Definition 35.1 (Epistemic Humility as a Practical Rule). (A) Epistemic humility is the
practical rule by which a subject:
(H1) States each claim at the epistemic status its arguments support (A, T, E, Q, S, or
     Proposed), and does not state it above or below that status.
(H2) Calibrates confidence to the status: full confidence for (A) and (T) claims whose arguments
     have been given; limited confidence for (E) claims; no closure for (Q) and (S) claims;
     and provisional confidence for Proposed claims.
(H3) Leaves open the questions the arguments do not settle, and states them at the status (Q)
     or (S) they are given in Chapter 34, not as settled claims.
(H4) Revises the claim when the arguments change, and states the revision at the status the
     new arguments support.
    The definition is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary about what humility
requires. Its justification is that it converts the disposition into a rule that can be applied; its
cost is that the identification of the status of a claim is fallible, like every identification in the
framework.
    The rule has four parts, and each is worth marking.

Part H1: stating each claim at its status. The subject does not state a (T) claim as if
it were (A) (which would overstate the claim) and does not state an (A) claim as if it were (T)
(which would understate the claim). The status is the claim’s proper strength, and the rule
requires that the claim be stated at that strength.

Part H2: calibrating confidence to the status. The subject’s confidence is not a separate
matter from the claim’s status; it is the subjective counterpart of the status. The rule requires
that the confidence be calibrated to the status, so that the subject’s belief and the claim’s
support are aligned.

Part H3: leaving the open questions open. The subject does not treat a (Q) or (S)
question as a settled claim, and does not treat it as a claim that cannot be settled. The open
question is held at the status it is given, and the subject continues the inquiry that might
settle it.
35.4. The Principle of Epistemic Humility                                                     461


Part H4: revising the claim when the arguments change. The subject does not hold
the claim fixed when the arguments change. The rule requires that the claim be revised at the
status the new arguments support, so that the claim’s strength tracks the arguments’ strength.

Remark 35.4 (The Rule Is Not a Psychological Procedure). The rule is not a psychological
procedure. It does not require that the subject feel a certain way, or that the subject introspect
a certain state. It requires that the subject state the claim at the status its arguments support,
calibrate its confidence to the status, hold the open questions as open, and revise the claim
when the arguments change. These are actions, not feelings; the rule is a practical rule, not a
psychological one.


35.4     The Principle of Epistemic Humility
Principle 35.1 (Epistemic Humility as Structural Disposition). (T) Epistemic humility is
the structural disposition that follows, for a finite subject, from the limits of finite cognition
(Part V) and from the open questions that the framework’s principles make visible (Chapter 34).
It is not an optional virtue added to the framework’s epistemic claims; it is what the claims
require, if the subject takes them seriously.

    The principle is (T): it is argued, and the argument is given below.

Argument for Principle 35.1.     1. By the limits of Part V, no finite subject can know all
     manifestations of an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), cannot complete its knowledge
     of epistemic light (Chapter 31), and is subject to the other limits stated in Part V.

   2. By the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28), a subject that treats an aggregate of
      manifestations across contexts as a reconstruction of the identity has committed an error,
      not achieved a completeness.

   3. By the boundaries of the framework (Chapter 34), there are questions the framework
      itself leaves open—fourteen of them, in three groups—and the framework’s principles
      make those questions visible without settling them.

   4. A subject that accepts the limits and the open questions, and that claims to have settled
      what cannot be settled, has committed the error of false certainty (M1).

   5. A subject that accepts the limits and the open questions, and that refuses to settle what
      the arguments do settle, has committed the error of excessive suspension (M2).

   6. Therefore the disposition that avoids both errors is epistemic humility, in the sense of
      Definition 35.1.


Remark 35.5 (The Argument Is Relative to the Limits and the Open Questions). The
argument is (T) relative to the limits of Part V and the open questions of Chapter 34. A
reader who rejects the limits has a reason to reject the argument; a reader who accepts the
limits has a reason to accept the argument.


35.5     Three Modes of Epistemic Miscalibration
The rule of humility (Definition 35.1) is defined against three modes of epistemic miscalibration.
The present section states the three modes, so that the rule is not read as a vague disposition
but as a rule that can be applied against specific failures.
462                                      Chapter 35. Open Questions and Epistemic Humility


Definition 35.2 (The Three Modes of Epistemic Miscalibration). (A) A subject’s epistemic
stance is miscalibrated when it exhibits one of three modes:
(M1) False certainty: the subject states a claim at a status stronger than its arguments support.
     The subject treats a (T) claim as (A), an (E) claim as (T), a (Q) question as settled,
     or a Proposed claim as established. The error is the error of claiming more than the
     arguments deliver.
(M2) Excessive suspension: the subject states a claim at a status weaker than its arguments
     support. The subject treats an (A) or (T) claim as (E) or (Q), or holds a question as
     unanswerable when the arguments settle it. The error is the error of claiming less than
     the arguments deliver.
(M3) Unjustified under-estimation: the subject states a claim at a status weaker than its
     arguments support, not because the arguments are weak, but because the subject
     distrusts its own arguments without reason. The error is a form of (M2), distinguished
     by its motive: the subject under-estimates not because the arguments are insufficient,
     but because the subject does not trust its own capacity to assess them.
    The three modes are (A): they are the framework’s stipulation of what miscalibration is.
The three modes are the failures that the rule of humility is designed to avoid; the rule is the
discipline that prevents them.

Mode              What it is                          What the rule requires

Remark 35.6 (The Three Modes Are Not Three Degrees). The three modes are not three
degrees of one miscalibration. They are three structurally different failures: M1 is overstatement,
M2 is understatement, and M3 is a specific form of understatement distinguished by its motive.
The rule of humility addresses all three, and the framework’s status labels (Chapter 2) are the
instrument by which the rule is applied.
Remark 35.7 (The Three Modes and the Open Questions). The three modes are especially
visible in the treatment of the open questions. M1 treats a (Q) question as settled; M2
treats a (Q) question as unanswerable; M3 treats a (Q) question as unanswerable because the
subject does not trust its own capacity to investigate it. The humble subject holds the (Q)
question at (Q), continues the inquiry, and does not confuse the question’s openness with its
unanswerability.
Remark 35.8 (The Three Modes and the Fourteenth Question). The fourteenth question
(Question 14, the temporal structure of self-awareness) is a special case. Chapter 20 flags it as
a gap that Book I does not fill; the humble subject holds it as a gap, not as a question the
framework has settled (M1) and not as a question that cannot be settled (M2 or M3). The
distinction between a gap and a question is the distinction between a limit the framework
has reached and a question the framework has raised; the humble subject holds both at their
stated strength.
35.6. Humility and the Method                                                                463


35.6     Humility and the Method
Humility is related to the method of Chapter 2, and the relation is worth stating.
    The method of Chapter 2 has three parts: the removal test for necessity, the reducibility
test for sufficiency, and the test of fruitfulness. Each part yields a conclusion at a declared
strength. The method is the instrument by which the claims’ statuses are assigned; humility
is the disposition that holds the claims at the assigned statuses.

Remark 35.9 (The Method Is Humility’s Instrument). The method is humility’s instrument.
The removal test, the reducibility test, and the test of fruitfulness are the disciplines by which
the subject holds its claims at the strength the arguments support. The epistemic status labels
are the method’s vocabulary; humility is the method’s disposition.


35.7     Humility and the Open Questions
Humility is the disposition that the open questions of Chapter 34 require, and the relation is
worth stating.
    The open questions are the questions the framework raises but does not settle. They
are stated in three groups: conceptual (Questions 1–4), argumentative (Questions 5–9), and
epistemic (Questions 10–14), including the fourteenth question (Question 14), the temporal
structure of self-awareness, which Chapter 20 flagged as a gap. The questions are marked (Q);
they are not unanswered because the framework has not tried, but because the framework’s
arguments do not settle them.
    The humble subject holds the open questions as open. It does not treat them as settled
(M1); it does not treat them as unanswerable (M2 or M3); it continues the inquiry that might
settle them, and it leaves them open until the inquiry does.

Remark 35.10 (The Open Questions Are Invitations). The open questions are invitations,
not defeats. They are the framework’s statement of where the inquiry continues; they are
what a reader who wishes to extend the framework is invited to address.


35.8     The Calibration of Humility for the Three Groups
Chapter 34 classified the fourteen open questions into three groups by their relation to the
core: threatening-validity (G1), operationalization (G2), and developmental (G3). The present
section states how humility is calibrated differently for each group, and it gives a table of the
confidence level and the epistemic response appropriate to each group.

35.8.1    The Three Calibrations
Humility toward G1 questions. The G1 questions are the questions whose settlement
or non-settlement bears on the framework’s core commitments. The G1 questions are Q7,
Q9, Q12, and Q14. Humility toward a G1 question is the disposition to hold the framework’s
claims that depend on the question at their stated strength, and to acknowledge that, if the
question cannot be settled, the claims that depend on it are conditional on the core.

Humility toward G2 questions. The G2 questions are the questions whose settlement is
needed for the framework’s application. The G2 questions are Q2, Q5, Q6, and Q8. Humility
toward a G2 question is the disposition to recognize that the framework’s application in a
given domain is limited by the question, and to leave the question open without claiming that
the framework’s application is complete.
 464                                      Chapter 35. Open Questions and Epistemic Humility


 Humility toward G3 questions. The G3 questions are the questions the framework invites
 as extensions. The G3 questions are Q1, Q3, Q4, Q10, Q11, and Q13. Humility toward a G3
 question is the disposition to recognize the question as an extension the framework invites,
 and to hold it open without treating it as a threat to the framework’s core.

 35.9     A Practical Checklist for Applying Humility
 The rule of humility (Definition 35.1) is stated in four parts; the present section states a
 practical checklist by which the rule is applied in the process of reconstruction. The checklist
 has five steps, and each step corresponds to a part of the rule.

 Definition 35.3 (The Practical Checklist for Applying Humility). (A) A subject applies
 humility in reconstruction by five steps:

(CL1) Identify the claim. State the claim in one sentence. Identify what the claim asserts and
      what it does not.

(CL2) Identify the status. State the epistemic status of the claim (A, T, E, Q, S, or Proposed),
      and the arguments that support the status. If the status is not clear, the claim is not
      yet ready to be asserted.

(CL3) Check for miscalibration. Compare the claim’s status with the subject’s actual confidence:
      is the confidence stronger than the status (M1), weaker (M2), or weaker for the wrong
      reason (M3)?

(CL4) State the claim at its status. Reformulate the claim so that it is stated at the status
      identified in (CL2), with the confidence calibrated in (CL3).
 35.10. Humility and the Unknownness of Chapter 32                                             465


(CL5) Record what the claim leaves open. State the open questions the claim leaves open, in
      the sense of Chapter 34 (with their group, G1, G2, or G3), and state what would settle
      them.

     The checklist is (A): it is the framework’s stipulation of the procedure. Its justification is
 that it makes the rule of humility applicable in the process of reconstruction; its cost is that
 the identification of the status in (CL2) is fallible.
