 Remark 35.12 (The Checklist Is Not a Guarantee). The checklist is not a guarantee. A
 subject can follow the five steps and still misidentify the status of a claim, or still misjudge
 the arguments. The checklist is the discipline by which the rule is applied; it does not replace
 the arguments, and it does not make the arguments infallible.

 Remark 35.13 (The Checklist Is the Practice of Humility). The checklist is the practice
 of humility. The rule (Definition 35.1) states what humility is; the checklist states how it
 is applied. The two are the same disposition, stated at two levels of detail: the rule is the
 substance, and the checklist is the procedure.

 Remark 35.14 (The Checklist and the Open Questions of Chapter 34). The checklist’s
 fifth step records the open questions. The recording is the practice of humility’s third part
 (H3): the subject does not treat the open questions as settled, and it does not treat them as
 unanswerable. It records them at their stated status (Q or S), together with their group (G1,
 G2, or G3) and what would settle them. The record is the subject’s statement of what its
 claim leaves open; it is what makes the claim assessable.


 35.10      Humility and the Unknownness of Chapter 32
 Humility is related to the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness (Chap-
 ter 32), and the relation is worth marking.
     The distinction between the two kinds of unknownness is what makes humility precise.
 The temporary unknownness is what the inquiry can reduce; the humility that responds to it
 is the humility of the inquirer who continues to gather evidence and to refine the criteria. The
 intrinsic unknownness is what the inquiry cannot reduce; the humility that responds to it is
466                                     Chapter 35. Open Questions and Epistemic Humility


the humility of the inquirer who recognizes that the finite subject’s knowledge is partial by
condition, not by failure.
Remark 35.15 (The Two Responses and the Three Modes). The two responses are what
avoid the three modes. False certainty (M1) treats the intrinsic unknownness as if it were tem-
porary; excessive suspension (M2) and unjustified under-estimation (M3) treat the temporary
unknownness as if it were intrinsic. Humility holds the two kinds of unknownness apart, and
responds to each with the response it invites.


35.11      Humility and the Plurality of Chapter 33
Humility is related to the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33), and the relation is worth
marking.
   The plurality is the form that the limits take: the finite subject cognizes an identity from
a perspective, and the perspectives are many, assessed by criteria, and none is exhaustive.
Humility is the disposition that makes the plurality bearable: the recognition that the subject’s
perspective is one among many, that it is assessed by criteria, and that it is not exhaustive.
Remark 35.16 (The Humility and the Assessment of Perspectives). Humility is what makes
the assessment of perspectives possible. The assessment (Chapter 33) is the discipline on the
plurality; humility is the disposition that accepts the discipline, and that does not claim for
its own perspective a status that the discipline does not give it.


35.12      Closing Part V
Part V has stated the limits, errors, and unknownness that any finite cognition must acknowl-
edge, and it has stated the disposition that the limits and the open questions require.

  1. The limits. The impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27), the fallacy of super-
     identity (Chapter 28), configuration-dependence (Chapter 29), the limits of self-knowledge
     (Chapter 30), the impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic light (Chapter 31),
     the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness (Chapter 32), and the
     plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33).

  2. The boundaries. The framework is coherent, foundational, and autonomous; it leaves
     open fourteen questions in three groups, classified into G1, G2, and G3 (Chapter 34).

  3. The disposition. Epistemic humility is the practical rule for calibrating confidence
     and revising claims (the present chapter). The rule has four parts (H1–H4); it is defined
     against three modes of miscalibration (M1–M3); it is calibrated for the three groups of
     open questions; and it is applied by a five-step checklist (CL1–CL5).

    Part VI turns from the limits of cognition to the epistemic economy of cognition and to
the concept of viability.


35.13      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not settle the open questions of Chapter 34. The questions are
stated there; the present chapter states the disposition that the questions require, not the
answers to the questions.
    Second, the chapter does not claim that humility is the only epistemically appropriate
disposition. It claims that humility is the disposition that the limits and the open questions
35.14. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                              467


require; whether other dispositions are also appropriate, in other respects, is a question the
chapter leaves open.
    Third, the chapter does not claim that humility is a virtue in any evaluative sense. The
chapter’s claim is epistemic: humility is the practical rule that the limits and the open questions
require. Whether humility is a virtue, and what kind of virtue it is, is a question that belongs
to other inquiries.
    Fourth, the chapter does not develop the full connection between humility and the epistemic
economy of Part VI. The full connection is the work of Part VI.

Remark 35.17 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has defined epistemic humility as a practical rule for calibrating confidence and revising
claims (Definition 35.1). It has stated and argued the principle of its structural character
(Principle 35.1). It has distinguished three modes of epistemic miscalibration (false certainty,
excessive suspension, unjustified under-estimation) and stated the rule’s response to each. It has
calibrated humility for the three groups of open questions (G1, G2, G3) with a confidence-level
table. And it has stated a five-step practical checklist for applying humility in reconstruction.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a claim you hold with confidence. Apply the checklist of Definition 35.3: what is the
claim, what is its status, is your confidence calibrated to the status, and what does the claim
leave open? If the checklist reveals a miscalibration, which of the three modes (M1, M2, M3)
is it?
     And consider the calibration of humility for the three groups of open questions (Section 35.8):
can you identify, among the fourteen questions, a G1 question that, if unanswerable, would
leave the framework’s claims conditional on the core; a G2 question whose settlement is
needed for the framework’s application in a domain you care about; and a G3 question whose
settlement would be an extension of the framework rather than a threat to it? For each, apply
the checklist: what confidence level does the group require, and what epistemic response?
What does your answer tell you about the difference between humility toward the framework’s
defender and humility toward the framework’s extender? A reader who can answer both
questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer neither has the chapter’s two
tasks before them.

Part V is complete. Part VI develops the epistemic economy of cognition and the concept of
viability: the three components of viability, the cost of cognition, the cognitive sediment and its
integration, and the balance criterion. The humility stated here is the disposition that Part VI’s
economy of cognition requires; the reader who has followed the argument to this point has the
framework, and Part VI is the framework’s final development.

            Part VI

Epistemic Economy and Viability

Chapter 36

Viability as Epistemic Structural
Character

Scope
This chapter opens Part VI by stating the framework’s central concept: viability. It defines
viability as the structural character of an epistemic reconstruction of an identity from its
manifestations in a cognitive context (Definition 36.1); it states the principle of the structural
character and its compatibility with the limits of Part V (Principle 36.1); it shows which problem
each limit of Part V creates for the assessment of viability and which component responds; it
states the structural relations of viability to adequacy, identity, intensity, and breadth in one
positive section (Section 36.5); it names the three components—fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability—with a diagnostic question, required data, assessment output, and failure mode
for each (Section 36.6); it gives a conceptual model of the relation between viability and the
cost of cognition (Section 36.7); and it states the conditions of validity of the definition and
the criteria of its revision (Section 36.8).
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “viability,” “fidelity,” “sustainability,”
“recoverability,” “structural character,” “reconstruction,” or “relation,” these are structural
terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.
Remark 36.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI). The chapter is the first of the eight chapters
of Part VI. Part V closed with epistemic humility (Chapter 35). The present chapter opens
the part that the disposition makes possible: the epistemic economy of cognition, and the
concept that names the framework’s central contribution.


36.1      A Scene: Three Translations of the Same Poem
Consider two translators of the same poem, working fifty years apart. The first produces
the best translation of her time; the second works later, corrects some errors, preserves some
achievements, and produces the best translation of her time. Now consider a third translator,
working at the same time as the first, who produces a translation that is accurate and readable
but imposes her own theory of poetry on the poem. Her version cannot be corrected, extended,
or recovered, because its errors are not distinguishable from its theory.
    The three translations are all epistemic reconstructions of the same poem, and each
is partial. But the first and the second are viable reconstructions, and the third is not.
The difference is not in the amount of knowledge; it is in the structural character of the
reconstruction.
Remark 36.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the concept
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the definition; it makes the definition intelligible
472                                  Chapter 36. Viability as Epistemic Structural Character


before it is stated.


36.2      The Question
The previous parts of the book have developed the framework’s epistemic structure. The
present part turns to the epistemic economy of cognition, and the concept that names the
framework’s central contribution: viability.
    The question is: given the limits and the criteria, what is the structural character of an
epistemic reconstruction of an identity from its manifestations, such that the reconstruction
can be sustained, corrected, extended, and recovered?


36.3      The Definition of Viability
Definition 36.1 (Viability). (A) The viability of an epistemic reconstruction of an identity in
a cognitive context is the structural character of the reconstruction in three respects:
  (i) fidelity: the reconstruction preserves the essential determination of the identity, so that
      the reconstruction records an appearance of that identity and not of another. Fidelity
      has the role of the source-relation of the reconstruction (Chapter 13, Principle 13.2;
      developed in Chapters 37 and 38).

 (ii) sustainability: the cost of producing and maintaining the reconstruction does not exceed
      what the receiving cognitive context can bear. Sustainability has the role of the cost-
      relation of the reconstruction (Chapter 39).

 (iii) recoverability: the identity retains its structural capacity to manifest in the context;
       the singularity at which restoring a manifestation would cost more than producing a
       new one has not been crossed. Recoverability has the role of the future-relation of the
       reconstruction (Chapter 37, Section 37.7).
    The definition has three components, and each has a distinct role in the structure of
the reconstruction: the source-relation (fidelity), the cost-relation (sustainability), and the
future-relation (recoverability). The three roles are not interchangeable; each answers a
different question about the reconstruction, and the three together state the character of the
reconstruction.
Remark 36.3 (Viability Admits of Degrees). Viability admits of degrees: the reconstruction
can satisfy the three components more or less completely.
Remark 36.4 (Viability Is Not a Value). Viability is a structural character of the reconstruc-
tion; it states a condition on the reconstruction, and it attaches no value, end, or good to the
condition.


36.4      Viability and the Limits of Part V
The limits of Part V create problems for the assessment of viability, and the three components
are the framework’s response to those problems. The present section states, for each limit, the
problem it creates and the component that responds.
Principle 36.1 (Viability as Structural Character Compatible with the Limits). (T) Viability
is a structural character of an epistemic reconstruction, compatible with the limits of Part V.
It does not claim completeness of knowledge; it claims that the reconstruction can satisfy the
three components more or less completely, within the limits that the finite subject’s condition
imposes.

Remark 36.5 (The Components Are the Framework’s Response to the Limits). The com-
ponents are the framework’s response to the limits. The limits say what the finite subject
cannot do; the components say what the finite subject can assess in the reconstruction, given
the limits.

Remark 36.6 (Viability and the Humility of Chapter 35). The humble subject is the subject
474                                   Chapter 36. Viability as Epistemic Structural Character


that can form a viable reconstruction: it holds the claims at the strength the arguments
support (fidelity), it does not demand more of the context’s capacity than the context can bear
(sustainability), and it leaves the inquiry open to correction and continuation (recoverability).


36.5      The Structural Relations of Viability to Adequacy, Identity,
          Intensity, and Breadth
The present section states, in one positive statement, the structural relations between viability
and the concepts it is easily confused with. The relations are not negations; they are the
framework’s account of how the concepts are related.

The relation to identity. Identity is the invariant an explanatory cognition holds fixed
across a class of allowable transformations of its manifestations (Chapter 12); it admits of
no degrees. Viability is the structural character of the reconstruction of the identity, and it
admits of degrees. The relation is the relation between the invariant and the character of its
reconstruction: identity is what is reconstructed; viability is the character of the reconstruction.
The two are related as the source to the character of its reconstruction, not as two properties
of the same subject.

The relation to the criteria of adequacy. The criteria of adequacy (consistency, stability,
fruitfulness; Chapter 23) are the criteria by which the reconstruction is assessed. Viability
is the structural character of the reconstruction that the criteria assess. The relation is the
relation between the assessment and the character assessed: the criteria yield a verdict on the
reconstruction’s adequacy; viability is the character that the verdict concerns. The two are
related, but neither entails the other: a reconstruction can satisfy the criteria and be less than
fully viable; a reconstruction can be viable and fail the criteria in some respect.

The relation to intensity and breadth. Intensity and breadth (Chapter 26) are the
two measures of the epistemic relation between a manifestation and its source. Viability is
the three-component character of the reconstruction. The relation is the relation between
the manifestation’s measures and the reconstruction’s character: the two measures assess the
manifestation; viability assesses the reconstruction that the manifestation makes possible.
The three components of viability are not the two measures taken together: fidelity is the
source-relation, sustainability is the cost-relation, and recoverability is the future-relation;
intensity and breadth are the measure of confirmation and articulation of the manifestation.

The relation to value. Viability is a structural character, not a value. The relation between
viability and value is the relation between a structural description and an evaluative claim:
the framework’s description of viability provides an epistemic basis on which an inquiry into
value may be built; the framework does not itself supply the evaluative claim, and it does not
replace it.

Remark 36.7 (The Relations Are Structural, Not Negations). The relations are structural,
not negations. Each states how the two concepts are related in the framework’s architecture,
not merely that they are different. The reader who has followed the argument to this point
has the vocabulary to state each relation; the reader who has not is directed to the chapters
that define the concepts.

Remark 36.8 (The Distinctions Are the Concept’s Precision). The distinctions are the
concept’s precision. A concept that were identical with identity, or with the criteria, or with
the two measures, or with a value, would not be the framework’s concept.
 36.6. The Three Components Named, with Diagnostic Instruments                             475


 36.6      The Three Components Named, with Diagnostic Instru-
           ments
 The definition names the three components; the present section states, for each component,
 its diagnostic question, the data required for the assessment, the assessment output, and the
 failure mode.

 36.6.1    Fidelity
 Definition 36.2 (Fidelity: Diagnostic Instruments). (A) The component of fidelity is assessed
 by four instruments:

(DF1) Diagnostic question: does the reconstruction preserve the essential determination of the
      identity, so that it records an appearance of that identity and not of another?

(DF2) Required data: the reconstruction, the essential features of the identity (as identified
      by the reconstruction’s identification of the defining invariants, Chapter 12), and the
      comparison with at least one other reconstruction of the same identity.

(DF3) Assessment output: the verdict that the reconstruction preserves, partially preserves, or
      fails to preserve the essential determination of the identity.

(DF4) Failure mode: distortion (the reconstruction carries features that conflict with the
      essential determination of the identity) or misattribution (the reconstruction records an
      appearance of a different identity).

 36.6.2    Sustainability
 Definition 36.3 (Sustainability: Diagnostic Instruments). (A) The component of sustainability
 is assessed by four instruments:

(DS1) Diagnostic question: does the cost of producing and maintaining the reconstruction
      exceed what the receiving cognitive context can bear?

(DS2) Required data: the reconstruction, the account of the cost of cognition (Chapter 39), and
      the assessment of the context’s capacity.

(DS3) Assessment output: the verdict that the reconstruction is sustainable, partially sustain-
      able, or unsustainable in the context.

(DS4) Failure mode: exhaustion (the cost exceeds the context’s capacity) or fragility (the cost
      is within the capacity, but small perturbations of the context would push it beyond).

 36.6.3    Recoverability
 Definition 36.4 (Recoverability: Diagnostic Instruments). (A) The component of recover-
 ability is assessed by four instruments:

(DR1) Diagnostic question: does the identity retain its structural capacity to manifest in the
      context, or has the singularity been crossed?

(DR2) Required data: the reconstruction, the account of the singularity (Chapter 37, Sec-
      tion 37.7), and the assessment of the identity’s capacity for further manifestation.

(DR3) Assessment output: the verdict that the reconstruction is recoverable, partially recover-
      able, or unrecoverable.
 476                                     Chapter 36. Viability as Epistemic Structural Character


(DR4) Failure mode: crossing the singularity (the cost of restoring the manifestation exceeds
      the cost of producing a new one) or loss of capacity (the identity no longer has the
      structural capacity to manifest in the context).

 Remark 36.9 (The Three Components Are Not Independent). The three components are
 aspects of one structural character: the character of the reconstruction. A reconstruction can
 satisfy two of the three and fail the third; the framework’s claim is that the three are aspects
 of one character, not three separate conditions.

 Remark 36.10 (The Three Components Point Beyond Themselves). The three components
 state the structural character of the reconstruction; they do not state the ground of the
 reconstruction, or the value of the reconstruction, or the telos for which the reconstruction
 exists.


 36.7       Viability and the Epistemic Economy of Part VI
 Viability is the central concept of the epistemic economy that Part VI develops. The present
 section states the relation between viability and the cost of cognition as a conceptual model,
 with a diagram.

 Definition 36.5 (The Conceptual Model of Viability and Cost). (A) The relation between
 viability and the cost of cognition is a three-place relation:

 (M1) The reconstruction: what the subject forms from the manifestations.

 (M2) The cost: what the reconstruction demands of the context’s capacity (Chapter 39).

 (M3) The viability: the character of the reconstruction, assessed by the three components, of
      which sustainability is the cost-relation.

 The cost is the demand; the sustainability is the condition on the demand; the viability is the
 character of the reconstruction under the three relations (source, cost, future).

 Remark 36.11 (The Diagram Shows the Direction of the Relation). The diagram shows the
 direction of the relation: the reconstruction demands a cost, the sustainability is the condition
 on the cost, and the viability is the character of the reconstruction under the three relations.
 The direction is from the reconstruction to the cost to the sustainability to the viability; the
 reverse direction is not the framework’s claim.

 Remark 36.12 (Viability and the Sediment of Chapter 40). The sediment is what the
 reconstruction leaves behind after the demand has been met (Chapter 40); it is not a fourth
 component of viability, but it is one of the conditions that can bring the singularity about,
 and it is one of the terms of the balance (Chapter 42).

 Remark 36.13 (Viability and the Balance of Chapter 42). The balance is the framework’s
 measure of the relation between the identity and the epistemic light it receives (Chapter 42);
 it is a measure of the flow, not the character of the reconstruction. Viability is the character;
 the balance is the measure.


 36.8      The Conditions of Validity and the Criteria of Revision
 The definition is stated at the strength its argument supports. The present section states the
 conditions under which the definition is valid, and the criteria by which it would be revised.


 36.8.1     The Conditions of Validity
 Definition 36.6 (The Conditions of Validity of the Definition of Viability). (A) The definition
 of viability is valid when three conditions are met:

(CV1) The definition is stated for an epistemic reconstruction: the subject of the definition is
      the reconstruction of an identity from its manifestations, not the identity in itself and
      not the manifestation alone.

(CV2) The three components have distinct roles: fidelity is the source-relation, sustainability is
      the cost-relation, and recoverability is the future-relation, and the three roles are not
      interchangeable.

(CV3) The definition is compatible with the limits of Part V : the definition does not claim
      completeness of knowledge, and it does not require a standpoint the finite subject cannot
      occupy.
 478                                   Chapter 36. Viability as Epistemic Structural Character


 36.8.2     The Criteria of Revision

 Definition 36.7 (The Criteria of Revision of the Definition of Viability). (A) The definition
 is revised when one of three cases is exhibited:

(CR1) A case that satisfies the three components but is not a viable reconstruction: the definition
      is incomplete, and a fourth component must be added or the three revised.

(CR2) A case that lacks one of the three components but is a viable reconstruction: the definition
      is too strong, and the component must be removed or weakened.

(CR3) A case in which the role of one component overlaps with the role of another : the definition
      is not precise, and the roles must be redefined.

 Remark 36.14 (The Definition Is Fallible). The definition is fallible, like every identification
 in the framework. The conditions of validity and the criteria of revision state what would
 confirm or revise it; they do not claim that the definition is beyond revision.

 Remark 36.15 (The Definition Is the Framework’s Central Concept). The definition is the
 framework’s central concept, and its precision is the framework’s contribution. The reader who
 has followed the argument to this point has the vocabulary to state the concept; the present
 chapter states it, and the chapters that follow develop it in each of its three components.



 36.9      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
 Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
     First, the chapter does not develop the three components. The three components are
 named here with their diagnostic instruments, and they are defined in Chapter 37. The
 present chapter states the definition and the conditions of its validity; the development of the
 components is the work of the chapters that follow.
     Second, the chapter does not develop the framework’s account of the cost of cognition.
 The cost is named here, in the second component; its development is the work of Chapter 39.
     Third, the chapter does not develop the framework’s account of the singularity. The
 singularity is named here, in the third component; it is defined in Chapter 37, Section 37.7,
 and the present chapter refers to it.
     Fourth, the chapter does not settle the first open question of Chapter 34 (Question 1): the
 joint realizability of two viabilities in one context. The present chapter states the concept
 of a single reconstruction’s viability; the joint realizability is left open, and it is one of the
 framework’s invitations to an extension.

 Remark 36.16 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
 has defined viability as the structural character of an epistemic reconstruction, with the three
 components distinguished by role. It has shown which problem each limit of Part V creates
 for the assessment of viability and which component responds. It has stated the structural
 relations of viability to adequacy, identity, intensity, and breadth in one positive section. It
 has given a diagnostic question, required data, assessment output, and failure mode for each
 component. It has given a conceptual model and a diagram of the relation between viability
 and the cost of cognition. And it has stated the conditions of validity of the definition and the
 criteria of its revision.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a reconstruction you have formed of something you know only partly. Apply
the diagnostic instruments of Section 36.6: what is the diagnostic question for fidelity, for
sustainability, and for recoverability? What data would you need to assess each, and what
would the assessment output be? If any component fails, which failure mode is it?
    And consider the limits of Part V: which limit creates the most serious problem for your
assessment of the reconstruction’s fidelity, and which component responds to it? What does
your answer tell you about the relation between the limits and the components?
    Finally, consider the conditions of validity and the criteria of revision (Section 36.8): can
you apply the three conditions and the three criteria to the definition of viability in a case
of your own? Can you exhibit a case that would satisfy the conditions or trigger a revision?
What does your answer tell you about the definition’s precision and its fallibility? A reader
who can answer all three questions has understood the chapter; a reader who can answer none
has the chapter’s three tasks before them.

The next chapter (Chapter 37) states the three components of viability in their own place:
fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. The present chapter has defined viability and stated
the diagnostic instruments; the next chapter defines each component, argues for the minimality
of the three, and develops the third (recoverability) through the account of the singularity.

Chapter 37

Fidelity, Sustainability, Recoverability

Scope
This chapter states the three components of viability in their own place. The previous
chapter defined viability as the epistemic structural character of an epistemic reconstruction
(Chapter 36, Definition 36.1), and named the three components: fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability. The present chapter gives each component an operational definition and an
assessment scale (Definition 37.1), defines the fidelity matrix (Section 37.3), distinguishes the
four kinds of cost (Section 37.4), distinguishes the objects of recoverability (Section 37.5),
develops the singularity as a precise threshold with comparability conditions and context-
dependence (Section 37.6), argues for the minimality of the three components with elimination
examples and counter-examples (Section 37.7), states the trade-off matrix (Section 37.8), and
states the conditions of application of the model (Section 37.9).
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “fidelity,” “sustainability,” “recover-
ability,” “cost,” “capacity,” “singularity,” or “threshold,” these are structural terms, and their
sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.

Remark 37.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI). The chapter is the second of the eight
chapters of Part VI. It defines the three components, develops recoverability through the
singularity, and prepares the ground for Chapters 38 (fidelity) and 39 (sustainability).


37.1     A Scene: Three Gardens
Consider three attempts to keep a garden alive in a dry climate. The first gardener plants
the right plants for the climate and maintains them within her means; the garden is faithful,
sustainable, and recoverable. The second plants more beautiful plants that cost more than
she can afford; the garden is faithful but unsustainable. The third plants the same as the
second in a drier time; the garden is faithful and (for a season) sustainable, but unrecoverable,
because the climate can no longer restore it.

Remark 37.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the three
components at work. It does not prove the three-fold structure; it makes the structure
intelligible.


37.2     The Three Components Defined, with Operational Scales
Definition 37.1 (The Three Components of Viability, with Operational Scales). (A) The
viability of an epistemic reconstruction R of an identity I in a cognitive context C has three
components, each with an operational definition and an assessment scale:
 482                                           Chapter 37. Fidelity, Sustainability, Recoverability


    (i) Fidelity: the reconstruction preserves the essential determination of I, so that the
        reconstruction records an appearance of I and not of another. The operational definition
        is the fidelity matrix (Section 37.3). The assessment scale is ordinal: F3 (full preservation),
        F2 (substantial preservation with identified omissions), F1 (partial preservation with
        identified distortions), F0 (failure of preservation).

   (ii) Sustainability: the cost of the reconstruction does not exceed what C can bear. The
        operational definition is the fourfold cost account (Section 37.4). The assessment scale is
        ordinal: S3 (cost well within capacity), S2 (cost within capacity with margin), S1 (cost
        at the margin of capacity), S0 (cost exceeds capacity).

  (iii) Recoverability: the identity retains its structural capacity to manifest in C; the singularity
        at which restoring the reconstruction would cost more than producing a new one has not
        been crossed. The operational definition is the fourfold object account (Section 37.5).
        The assessment scale is ordinal: R3 (all four objects recoverable), R2 (three of the
        four recoverable), R1 (one or two recoverable), R0 (none recoverable, or the singularity
        crossed).

     The definition is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary. Its justification is
 that it makes the three components applicable; its cost is that the identification of the scale
 level in a given case is fallible.



 37.3      Fidelity and the Fidelity Matrix
 Fidelity is the first component. Its operational definition is a matrix that classifies the essential
 features of the identity by their fate in the reconstruction.

 Definition 37.2 (The Fidelity Matrix). (A) For each essential feature e of the identity I (as
 identified by the reconstruction’s identification of the defining invariants, Chapter 12), the
 reconstruction assigns e to one of five cells:

(FM1) Reference: e is present in the reconstruction and is the same feature as in the identity;
      the reconstruction’s description of e matches the identity’s essential determination of e.

(FM2) Preserved : e is present in the reconstruction and is compatible with the identity’s
      essential determination, though its description is partial.

(FM3) Omitted : e is not present in the reconstruction, and the omission is identified.

(FM4) Distorted : e is present in the reconstruction, but the reconstruction’s description of e
      conflicts with the identity’s essential determination of e.

(FM5) Unknown: the reconstruction does not determine whether e is preserved, omitted, or
      distorted.

 The matrix is the operational definition of fidelity. A reconstruction that has no feature in
 (FM4) has not distorted the identity; a reconstruction that has no feature in (FM3) and no
 feature in (FM5) has preserved the identity fully; a reconstruction that has features in (FM4)
 has distorted the identity, at the features in question.
37.4. Sustainability and the Four Kinds of Cost                                               483

Remark 37.3 (The Matrix Is the Operational Definition of Fidelity). The matrix is the
operational definition: it states, for each essential feature, what the reconstruction does with
it. The fidelity of the reconstruction, as a whole, is the pattern of cells across the essential
features; the ordinal scale of Definition 37.1 (F3 , F2 , F1 , F0 ) is the summary of the pattern.

Remark 37.4 (The Matrix Requires the Essential Features to Be Identified). The matrix
requires that the essential features of the identity be identified (Chapter 12, Definition 12.1
and the identification of the defining invariants). The identification is the work of the inquiry,
and it is fallible; the matrix is only as good as the identification. A reader who finds the
identification inadequate has found a limit of the fidelity assessment, not a defect of the matrix.

Remark 37.5 (Fidelity Is Not Intensity, Not Breadth, Not a Degree of Identity). Fidelity
is not intensity (Chapter 26), not breadth (Chapter 26), and not a degree of the identity
(Chapter 12). It is the preservation of the essential determination, as recorded by the matrix;
the other concepts are about the manifestation’s confirmation, articulation, or invariance, and
the framework keeps them apart.


37.4       Sustainability and the Four Kinds of Cost
Sustainability is the second component. Its operational definition distinguishes four kinds of
cost, each of which can be assessed separately.

Definition 37.3 (The Four Kinds of Cost). (A) The cost of a reconstruction R in a context
C has four kinds:

(C1) Collection cost: the cost of gathering the manifestations from which R is formed. The
     assessment method is the measure of the time, resources, and access required to gather
     the manifestations.

(C2) Processing cost: the cost of forming R from the manifestations (the comparison, the
     isolation of the invariants, the formation of the reconstruction). The assessment method
     is the measure of the cognitive effort, the time, and the resources required for the
     comparison and the formation.

(C3) Maintenance cost: the cost of keeping R adequate as the manifestations and the context
     change. The assessment method is the measure of the effort required to keep the
     reconstruction adequate over the period in which it is used.
484                                         Chapter 37. Fidelity, Sustainability, Recoverability


(C4) Revision cost: the cost of revising R when the manifestations or the context change in a
     way that requires the reconstruction’s revision. The assessment method is the measure
     of the effort required to revise the reconstruction, as a function of the kind of change.


The total cost of R in C is the sum (or the weighted sum) of the four kinds. The reconstruction
is sustainable in C when the total cost does not exceed what C can bear.


Remark 37.6 (The Four Kinds Are Distinct). The four kinds of cost are distinct. A
reconstruction can have low collection cost and high processing cost (the manifestations are
easy to gather but hard to compare); low processing cost and high maintenance cost (the
reconstruction is easy to form but hard to keep adequate); low maintenance cost and high
revision cost (the reconstruction is stable but hard to revise). The framework distinguishes
them so that the assessment of sustainability can locate the cost that exceeds the capacity.


Remark 37.7 (The Cost Is Context-Relative). The cost is context-relative: what is cheap in
one context may be expensive in another. The sustainability of a reconstruction is therefore
indexed to the context in which it is assessed; a reconstruction that is sustainable in one
context may be unsustainable in another.



37.5     Recoverability and the Four Objects of Recovery

Recoverability is the third component. Its operational definition distinguishes four objects
that can be recovered, each of which can be assessed separately.


Definition 37.4 (The Four Objects of Recoverability). (A) The recoverability of a reconstruc-
tion R of an identity I in a context C has four objects:


(O1) The evidence: the manifestations from which R was formed are still available, or can be
     re-gathered at a cost lower than the cost of producing a new reconstruction.


(O2) The reconstruction structure: the structure of R (the four columns, the relations among
     them, the identification of the defining invariants) is still available, or can be re-formed
     at a cost lower than the cost of producing a new structure.


(O3) The argumentative links: the arguments by which the elements of R are connected
     are still available, or can be re-formed at a cost lower than the cost of producing new
     arguments.


(O4) The capacity to continue: the identity retains its structural capacity to manifest in C,
     so that the reconstruction can be continued into further reconstructions of the same
     identity or of identities of the same kind.


The reconstruction is recoverable when all four objects are recoverable; the singularity is
crossed when at least one of the four objects is not recoverable (the cost of restoring it exceeds
the cost of producing a new one).

Remark 37.8 (The Four Objects Are Distinct). The four objects are distinct. A reconstruction
can be recoverable at the level of the evidence (the manifestations are still available) and not
at the level of the capacity (the identity has lost its capacity to manifest in the context). The
framework distinguishes them so that the assessment of recoverability can locate the object
that is not recoverable.
Remark 37.9 (Recoverability Is Not Sustainability). Recoverability is not sustainability. A
reconstruction can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the context’s capacity
has been exhausted; if the cost of restoring it exceeds the cost of producing a new one, the
reconstruction is not recoverable, even though it was sustainable.


37.6     The Singularity: A Precise Threshold
The singularity is the threshold at which the cost of restoring an existing reconstruction in a
context exceeds the cost of producing a new one there. The present section states the threshold
precisely, the conditions under which the two costs are comparable, and the context-dependence
of the threshold.
Definition 37.5 (The Singularity). (A) The singularity of a reconstruction R of an identity
I in a context C is the threshold at which

                                     κr (R, C) > κn (I, C),

where κr (R, C) is the cost of restoring R in C, and κn (I, C) is the cost of producing a new
reconstruction of I in C. The singularity is crossed when the inequality holds; it is not crossed
when
                                     κr (R, C) ≤ κn (I, C).

37.6.1    The Conditions of Comparability
The singularity is defined by a comparison of two costs, and the comparison is meaningful
only when the two costs are comparable.
Definition 37.6 (The Conditions of Comparability of the Two Costs). (A) The two costs
κr (R, C) and κn (I, C) are comparable when:
 486                                        Chapter 37. Fidelity, Sustainability, Recoverability


(CC1) Same context: both costs are assessed in the same context C, with the same capacity
      and constraints.

(CC2) Same object: both costs are for the same identity I, not for different identities or for
      different aspects of the same identity.

(CC3) Same kind of cost: both costs are computed with the same four kinds of cost (Defini-
      tion 37.3), so that the comparison is not between a collection cost and a revision cost, or
      between a processing cost and a maintenance cost.

(CC4) Same time horizon: both costs are computed over the same period, so that the comparison
      is not between a cost computed over a short period and a cost computed over a long
      period.
 When the four conditions are met, the comparison is meaningful; when they are not, the
 singularity is not yet defined for the case, and the comparison must be preceded by the
 normalization of the two costs.

 37.6.2    The Context-Dependence of the Threshold
 The singularity is context-dependent. The threshold is not a fixed point in the abstract; it
 depends on the context’s capacity, the identity’s essential determination, and the four kinds of
 cost in that context.
 Remark 37.10 (The Threshold Is Indexed to the Context). The threshold is indexed to the
 context: κr (R, C) and κn (I, C) are both computed in C, and the threshold is the point at
 which the inequality holds in C. A threshold in one context is not a threshold in another; the
 two are different points, and the assessment of recoverability is the assessment of the threshold
 in the context in which the reconstruction is used.
 Remark 37.11 (The Threshold Is an Estimate, Not a Precise Measurement). The threshold
 is an estimate, not a precise measurement. The two costs are assessed by the four kinds of cost
 (Definition 37.3), and the assessment is fallible. The threshold is a structural point, and its
 location in a given case is the work of the inquiry; the framework does not offer an algorithm
 for computing it.

 37.6.3    The Monotonicity and Threshold Conditions
 The singularity argument depends on two independent premises, and they are stated here as
 the framework’s proposals for the behavior of the cost functions.
 Remark 37.12 (The Monotonicity and Threshold Conditions). The monotonicity condition.
 For a fixed C and I, as the context’s capacity for I’s manifestation is exhausted, the ratio
 κr /κn is non-decreasing.
     The threshold condition. The ratio κr /κn is bounded below by a value less than 1 in
 states of ample capacity, and unbounded above as the context’s capacity for I’s manifestation
 approaches zero.
     The two conditions are stated as independent premises. They are not derived from the
 framework’s other principles; they are the framework’s proposal for the behavior of the cost
 functions, and they are stated at exactly that strength. The singularity argument is therefore
 (E) conditional on the two conditions.
 The Argument for the Singularity.   1. The four kinds of cost (Definition 37.3) are finite
      demands on the context’s capacity.

    2. The context’s capacity is finite (Chapter 39).
37.7. The Minimality of the Three Components                                                  487


   3. By the monotonicity and threshold conditions (Remark 37.12), the ratio κr /κn is non-
      decreasing and unbounded above as the capacity is exhausted.

   4. Hence there is a threshold at which the ratio crosses 1; that threshold is the singularity.

   5. Therefore the singularity is the threshold of recoverability, and recoverability is the
      condition under which the threshold has not been crossed.


Remark 37.13 (The Argument Is Conditional on the Two Conditions). The argument is
(E) conditional on the monotonicity and threshold conditions. The framework does not claim
that the conditions hold for every cognitive context; it claims that they hold for the class of
contexts the framework treats, and it invites the reader to assess them.


37.7     The Minimality of the Three Components
The three components are minimal: each is needed, and no fourth is required. The argument
is strengthened here with elimination examples and counter-examples for each component.


37.7.1    The Elimination Examples
For each component, an elimination example shows what is lost when the component is
removed.

Elimination of fidelity. Without fidelity, the reconstruction would not distinguish a
manifestation of the identity from a manifestation of another. The relation between the
identity and its manifestations could not be assessed as a relation of the identity; it would
be a relation of some identity or other. The elimination example is a reconstruction that is
sustainable and recoverable but records the appearance of a different identity; the reconstruction
has no claim to be a reconstruction of the intended identity.

Elimination of sustainability. Without sustainability, the reconstruction could be fidelious
and recoverable, but its cost would exceed the context’s capacity. The relation between the
identity and its manifestations could not be maintained; it would be a relation that the context
cannot bear. The elimination example is a reconstruction that preserves the identity’s essential
determination and can be restored after a lapse, but whose cost of production exceeds the
context’s capacity; the reconstruction is not viable in that context.

Elimination of recoverability. Without recoverability, the reconstruction could be fidelious
and sustainable, but the identity would have no structural capacity to manifest in the context
after the reconstruction has been used. The relation between the identity and its manifestations
would be a relation that cannot continue. The elimination example is a reconstruction that
preserves the identity’s essential determination and whose current cost is within the context’s
capacity, but whose cost of restoration after a lapse exceeds the cost of producing a new
reconstruction; the reconstruction is not viable beyond its present use.


37.7.2    The Counter-Examples
For each component, a counter-example shows what happens when the component is required
but cannot be assessed.
488                                          Chapter 37. Fidelity, Sustainability, Recoverability


Counter-example to the necessity of fidelity. A critic might propose a reconstruction
that is sustainable and recoverable, but that does not preserve the identity’s essential deter-
mination, and yet is viable. The framework’s response is that such a reconstruction is not a
reconstruction of the identity; it is a reconstruction of another identity, or of no identity at all.
The critic’s proposal does not refute the necessity of fidelity; it shows that the reconstruction
the critic describes is not the reconstruction the framework is about.

Counter-example to the necessity of sustainability. A critic might propose a recon-
struction that is fidelious and recoverable, but whose cost exceeds the context’s capacity, and
yet is viable. The framework’s response is that such a reconstruction is not viable in the
context; it is viable in a context with greater capacity, but not in the context in which its cost
exceeds the capacity. The critic’s proposal does not refute the necessity of sustainability; it
shows that the context in which the reconstruction is viable is a different context.

Counter-example to the necessity of recoverability. A critic might propose a recon-
struction that is fidelious and sustainable, but whose restoration after a lapse would cost
more than a new reconstruction, and yet is viable. The framework’s response is that such
a reconstruction is not viable beyond its present use; it is a reconstruction whose viability
is limited to its present use, and the framework’s claim is that the reconstruction is not
recoverable in the sense the framework requires.

Remark 37.14 (The Counter-Examples Are Answered, Not Dismissed). The counter-examples
are answered, not dismissed. Each shows a case in which the component’s removal seems
possible; the framework’s answer locates the case in the framework’s vocabulary, and shows
that the component’s role is not refuted by the case. The minimality argument is therefore
(E): it is an estimate, supported by the elimination examples and the counter-examples, and
subject to revision if a further counter-example is found.


37.8      The Trade-Off Matrix
The three components are not independent; they trade off against one another. The present
section states the trade-off matrix.

Definition 37.7 (The Trade-Off Matrix of the Three Components). (A) For each pair of
components, the trade-off matrix states the direction of the trade-off and the kind of conflict
or reinforcement:

(T1) Fidelity vs. sustainability: a more fidelious reconstruction may cost more than a less
     fidelious one; the trade-off is a conflict when the fidelity requires a cost that exceeds
     the context’s capacity, and a reinforcement when the fidelity can be achieved within the
     capacity.

(T2) Fidelity vs. recoverability: a more fidelious reconstruction may be less recoverable if its
     essential determination is harder to restore than a less fidelious one; the trade-off is a
     conflict when the cost of restoring the fidelity exceeds the cost of a new reconstruction,
     and a reinforcement when the fidelity is restorable within the capacity.

(T3) Sustainability vs. recoverability: a more sustainable reconstruction may be less recoverable
     if the sustainability is achieved by a structure that is hard to restore; the trade-off is a
     conflict when the sustainable structure is not recoverable, and a reinforcement when the
     sustainable structure is also restorable.

 Remark 37.15 (The Trade-Offs Are Structural, Not a Defect). The trade-offs are structural:
 they are what the three-fold structure implies. The framework does not claim that the
 trade-offs can be eliminated; it claims that the assessment of viability is the assessment of the
 trade-offs in a given case, and that the assessment is the work of the inquiry.

 Remark 37.16 (The Trade-Offs Are Not a Ranking). The trade-offs are not a ranking of
 the three components. The framework does not say that fidelity is more important than
 sustainability, or that sustainability is more important than recoverability. The ranking, if
 there is one, belongs to the inquiry, not to the framework.


 37.9      The Conditions of Application of the Model
 The three-fold structure is a model of the relation between an identity and its reconstruction.
 The model applies under conditions, and the conditions are worth stating.

 37.9.1     The Conditions of Application
 Definition 37.8 (The Conditions of Application of the Three-Fold Model). (A) The three-fold
 model applies to a reconstruction R of an identity I in a context C when:

(CA1) The reconstruction is an epistemic reconstruction: R is the reconstruction of I from its
      manifestations (Chapter 36, Definition 36.1).

(CA2) The identity’s essential features are identified : the essential features of I are identified
      by the inquiry (Chapter 12, Definition 12.1).

(CA3) The four kinds of cost are comparable: the costs κr (R, C) and κn (I, C) satisfy the
      comparability conditions (Definition 37.6).

(CA4) The four objects of recovery are assessable: each of the four objects (evidence, structure,
      links, capacity) can be assessed by the framework’s definitions (Definition 37.4).

 When the four conditions are met, the model applies; when they are not, the model’s application
 is limited, and the limitation is stated as a limit of the model.

 37.9.2     The Limits of the Model
 The model has limits, and the limits are stated as the conditions under which the model’s
 application is qualified.
490                                         Chapter 37. Fidelity, Sustainability, Recoverability


First limit: the identification of essential features. The fidelity matrix requires the
essential features to be identified; the identification is fallible, and the matrix is only as good
as the identification. The limit is the limit of the identification, not of the matrix.


Second limit: the comparability of the costs. The singularity requires the two costs
to be comparable; when they are not comparable, the singularity is not defined, and the
recoverability assessment is limited to the objects that can be assessed independently of the
singularity.


Third limit: the context-dependence of the threshold. The threshold is indexed to
the context; a threshold in one context is not a threshold in another. The limit is the limit of
the context-relative assessment, not of the model.


Fourth limit: the monotonicity and threshold conditions. The singularity argument
depends on the two conditions (Remark 37.12); when they are not met, the singularity argument
is not available, and the recoverability assessment is limited to the object-level assessment.


Fifth limit: the open question of the gradient. The exact boundary between the
gradient of viability and the threshold of the singularity (Question 2 of Chapter 34) is left
open; the model states the threshold, and it leaves the gradient’s exact function to the inquiry.

Remark 37.17 (The Limits Are the Model’s Conditions of Application). The limits are the
model’s conditions of application. They state when the model applies and when it does not;
they do not deny the model’s validity within the conditions. A reader who finds a case outside
the conditions has found a limit of the model, not a defect of the model.


37.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop fidelity and sustainability in their own right. Fidelity
is developed in Chapter 38, and sustainability in Chapter 39. The present chapter states the
operational definitions, and it develops recoverability through the singularity.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the trade-offs among the three components in a given
case. The trade-offs are structural, and their resolution is the work of the inquiry.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the exact boundary between the gradient of viability
and the threshold of the singularity (Question 2 of Chapter 34).
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim that the three-fold structure is the only structure that
could describe the relation. The framework’s claim is that it is the one the framework uses,
and that it is minimal for the framework’s purposes.

Remark 37.18 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed eight things. It
has given each component an operational definition and an assessment scale. It has defined the
fidelity matrix. It has distinguished the four kinds of cost. It has distinguished the four objects
of recoverability. It has stated the singularity as a precise threshold, with the comparability
conditions and the context-dependence. It has strengthened the minimality argument with
elimination examples and counter-examples. It has stated the trade-off matrix. And it has
stated the conditions of application of the model.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a reconstruction you have formed of something you know only partly. Apply the
fidelity matrix: for each essential feature, is it in FM1, FM2, FM3, FM4, or FM5? What is
the fidelity level (F3 , F2 , F1 , F0 )? Apply the four kinds of cost: what is the collection cost,
the processing cost, the maintenance cost, and the revision cost? What is the sustainability
level (S3 , S2 , S1 , S0 )? Apply the four objects of recoverability: are the evidence, the struc-
ture, the links, and the capacity to continue recoverable? What is the recoverability level
(R3 , R2 , R1 , R0 )?
    And consider the trade-offs: does your reconstruction trade fidelity for sustainability, or
sustainability for recoverability? Which of the three pairs is the most significant in your case?
What does your answer tell you about the relation between your reconstruction and the source,
and about the three-fold structure as the model of the relation?

The next chapter (Chapter 38) develops the first component in its own place: fidelity. The
chapter after that (Chapter 39) develops the second component, in the account of the cost of
cognition.

Chapter 38

Fidelity and the Conditions of
Epistemic Reconstruction

Scope
This chapter develops the first component of viability—fidelity— as the preservation of the
determining structure of an identity in an epistemic reconstruction. It defines fidelity (Def-
inition 38.2), states the conditions of epistemic reconstruction (Section 38.3), distinguishes
preservation from non-realization (Section 38.5), distinguishes identity rigidity from recon-
struction gradation (Section 38.6), distinguishes loss, distortion, and omission (Section 38.7),
states the place of fidelity among the three components of viability with executable criteria
(Section 38.8), states a measurement method (Section 38.9), and applies the method to a
complete example (Section 38.10).
    The chapter makes no appeal to any intrinsic tendency of identity to express itself, and it
defers no part of the concept to another work. Fidelity is defined entirely within this volume,
on the basis of the framework’s account of identity (Chapter 12), of manifestation (Chapter 13),
and of reconstruction (Chapter 36).
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “fidelity,” “preservation,” “determining
structure,” “loss,” “distortion,” “omission,” or “reconstruction,” these are structural terms, and
their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.

Remark 38.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI). The chapter is the third of the eight chapters
of Part VI. Chapter 36 defined viability and named its three components; Chapter 37 defined
the three components and developed recoverability through the singularity. The present chapter
develops the first component (fidelity) by the preservation of the determining structure of the
source in the reconstruction. The next chapter (Chapter 39) develops the second component
(sustainability) through the account of the cost of cognition.


38.1      A Scene: Two Reconstructions of a Poem
Consider two reconstructions of a poem whose original is lost. The first reconstruction preserves
the poem’s meter, its imagery, and the relation between its stanzas; the second preserves
the meter and the imagery but replaces the poem’s central image with one the reconstructor
prefers. The two reconstructions are both epistemic reconstructions of the same poem, and
both are partial. But the first preserves the determining structure of the poem, and the second
distorts it.
    The difference between the two reconstructions is a difference in fidelity. The first is faithful
to the poem; the second is not. The question the scene poses is: what is the determining
 494                       Chapter 38. Fidelity and the Conditions of Epistemic Reconstruction


 structure that the first reconstruction preserves and the second does not, and how is the
 preservation of that structure assessed?
 Remark 38.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the concept
 at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the definition; it makes the definition intelligible.


 38.2      The Question
 Chapter 37 stated fidelity as the first component of viability, argued from the principle of
 essential homogeneity (Chapter 13, Principle 13.2), and noted that fidelity would be developed
 in its own place. The present chapter is that place.
     The question is: what is fidelity, exactly, and by what conditions is it assessed in an
 epistemic reconstruction? The framework’s answer is that fidelity is the preservation of the
 determining structure of the source in the reconstruction, and that it is assessed by the
 conditions of epistemic reconstruction stated in the next section.


 38.3      The Conditions of Epistemic Reconstruction
 The assessment of fidelity presupposes that the reconstruction is an epistemic reconstruction
 in the framework’s sense. The conditions under which a reconstruction is an epistemic
 reconstruction are stated here.
 Definition 38.1 (The Conditions of Epistemic Reconstruction). (A) A reconstruction R of
 an identity I in a cognitive context C is an epistemic reconstruction when it satisfies four
 conditions:
(EC1) Identifying the source: R identifies I as the identity it reconstructs, and does not
      substitute another identity for I.
(EC2) Identifying the essential features: R identifies the essential features of I (Chapter 12,
      Definition 12.1), so that the fidelity of R can be assessed feature by feature.
(EC3) Bearing a relation to the source’s manifestations: R is formed from the manifestations
      of I in C (Chapter 13), and its relation to the source is stated explicitly.
(EC4) Being assessable by the criteria of adequacy: R can be assessed by the criteria of adequacy
      of Chapter 23 (consistency, stability, fruitfulness), so that its fidelity is assessable alongside
      its adequacy.
     The four conditions are (A): they are the framework’s stipulation of what it is for a
 reconstruction to be an epistemic reconstruction. Their justification is that they make the
 fidelity assessment applicable; their cost is that the identification of the essential features in
 (EC2) is fallible.


 38.4      Fidelity Defined
 Definition 38.2 (Fidelity). (A) The fidelity of an epistemic reconstruction R of an identity I
 is the extent to which R preserves the determining structure of I. The determining structure
 is the totality of I’s essential features (Chapter 12, Definition 12.1), together with the relations
 among them that the identification of the essential features fixes. The preservation is assessed
 feature by feature, and the fidelity of R as a whole is the pattern of the feature-level assessments.
     The definition is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary. Its justification is
 that it makes fidelity assessable without appeal to any intrinsic tendency of identity; its cost
 is that the identification of the determining structure is fallible.
38.5. Preservation and Non-Realization                                                         495


Remark 38.3 (Fidelity Is Graded). Fidelity admits of degrees: R can preserve the determining
structure of I more or less completely. The degrees are the degrees of the preservation, not of
the identity (Chapter 12, Principle 12.1).

Remark 38.4 (Fidelity Is Not a Value). Fidelity is a structural character of the reconstruction;
it states a condition on the reconstruction, and it attaches no value, end, or good to the
condition.


38.5      Preservation and Non-Realization
The first thing to be distinguished is preservation from non-realization. A reconstruction can
preserve the determining structure of the source without realizing every manifestation that the
source could have in every context; and a reconstruction can fail to preserve the determining
structure even when it realizes many manifestations of the source.

Principle 38.1 (Preservation Is Not Universal Realization). (T) The preservation of the
determining structure of an identity in a reconstruction does not require the realization of every
manifestation of the identity in every context. Preservation is a property of the reconstruction’s
relation to the determining structure; realization is a property of the manifestations in their
contexts.

Proof of Principle 38.1.     1. The determining structure of I is the totality of its essential
      features and their relations (Definition 38.2).

   2. The manifestations of I in various contexts are many, and the reconstruction R is formed
      from the manifestations available in a particular context (Definition 38.1, EC3).

   3. R can preserve the determining structure of I while being formed from a finite subset of
      the manifestations, because the determining structure is what the manifestations express,
      not the sum of the manifestations.

   4. Therefore preservation does not require universal realization.


Remark 38.5 (Preservation Is Feature-Relative). Preservation is assessed feature by feature:
for each essential feature of I, R either preserves it, omits it, or distorts it (Section 38.7).
The preservation of the determining structure as a whole is the pattern of the feature-level
assessments, not a single verdict.


38.6      Identity Rigidity and Reconstruction Gradation
The second thing to be distinguished is the rigidity of identity from the gradation of the
reconstruction.

Principle 38.2 (Identity Rigidity and Reconstruction Gradation). (T) The rigidity of identity
(Chapter 12, Principle 12.1) does not entail the rigidity of its reconstructions, and the gradation
of its reconstructions does not entail the gradation of the identity.

Proof of Principle 38.2.    1. Identity is rigid: it admits no degrees (Chapter 12, Principle
     12.1). The rigidity is a feature of the identity.

   2. The fidelity of a reconstruction admits of degrees (Definition 38.2). The gradation is a
      feature of the reconstruction, in its relation to the determining structure.
496                     Chapter 38. Fidelity and the Conditions of Epistemic Reconstruction


   3. The two features are features of different things: the rigidity of the identity; the gradation
      of the reconstruction. The compatibility is the compatibility of two features of different
      things.

   4. Therefore the rigidity of identity and the gradation of the reconstruction are compatible,
      and neither entails the other.


Remark 38.6 (The Distinction Is an Application of Category-Relative Predication). The
distinction is an application of the principle of category-relative predication (Chapter 25):
“rigid” is said of the identity in one respect; “graded” is said of the reconstruction in another
respect. The distinction of respects removes the apparent conflict.


38.7     Loss, Distortion, and Omission
The third thing to be distinguished is the three ways in which a reconstruction can fail to
preserve the determining structure of its source.
Definition 38.3 (Loss, Distortion, and Omission). (A) For each essential feature e of the
identity I, the reconstruction R is in one of three failure states:
(F1) Loss: e is not present in R, and its absence is not marked as an omission; the reconstruc-
     tion presents itself as complete with respect to e.

(F2) Distortion: e is present in R, but R’s description of e conflicts with the identity’s
     determining structure of e (Chapter 13, Principle 13.2).

(F3) Omission: e is not present in R, and its absence is marked as an omission; the recon-
     struction states that e is not determined by the available manifestations, or is left open
     for further reconstruction.
The three states are distinct: loss presents absence as completeness; distortion presents a
conflict as a preservation; omission presents absence as absence.
Remark 38.7 (Omission Is Not Loss). Omission is not loss. Omission is a failure of preservation
that is marked as a failure; loss is a failure of preservation that is not marked. A reconstruction
that omits e and marks the omission is faithful to the determining structure in the sense that
it does not present itself as preserving e; a reconstruction that loses e and does not mark the
loss presents itself as preserving e when it does not, and is therefore not faithful.
Remark 38.8 (Omission Is Not Distortion). Omission is not distortion. Omission leaves e
out; distortion puts a conflicting e in. The two are different failures, and the framework keeps
them apart.
Remark 38.9 (The Three States and the Fidelity Matrix). The three states correspond to
the fidelity matrix of Chapter 37 (Definition 37.2): FM1 and FM2 are the preservation states;
FM3 is the omission state; FM4 is the distortion state; FM5 is the unknown state, which is
not a failure state but a state of indeterminacy.


38.8     Fidelity as the First Component of Viability
Fidelity is the first component of viability (Chapter 37, Definition 37.1), and its place among
the three components is stated here with executable criteria.
Definition 38.4 (The Executable Criteria for the Fidelity Component). (A) The fidelity of a
reconstruction R is assessed by four executable criteria, aligned with the criteria of Chapter 23:
  38.9. A Measurement Method for Fidelity                                                            497


(Fid1) Identification completeness (aligned with consistency, Chapter 23): the essential features
       of the identity are identified, and the identification is consistent with the identification
       of the defining invariants (Chapter 12, Definition 12.1).

(Fid2) Preservation consistency (aligned with consistency, Chapter 23): the reconstruction’s
       description of each identified essential feature is consistent with the identity’s determining
       structure of the feature.

(Fid3) Stability of preservation (aligned with stability, Chapter 23): the reconstruction’s preser-
       vation of the essential features is stable under small perturbations of the reconstruction’s
       context or of the available manifestations.

(Fid4) Fruitfulness of preservation (aligned with fruitfulness, Chapter 23): the reconstruction’s
       preservation of the essential features supports further reconstruction of the identity (in
       further contexts, or in further manifestations).

  Remark 38.10 (The Executable Criteria and the Fidelity Matrix). The four executable
  criteria operationalize the fidelity matrix of Chapter 37 (Definition 37.2): Fid1 and Fid2 assess
  the pattern of the matrix across the essential features; Fid3 and Fid4 assess the matrix’s
  behavior under perturbation and its fruitfulness. The matrix and the criteria are the same
  assessment, stated at two levels of detail.
 Remark 38.11 (Fidelity and the Other Components). The executable criteria for fidelity are
 complemented by the executable criteria for sustainability (Chapter 39) and for recoverability
 (Chapter 37, Section 37.6). The three sets of criteria are the framework’s account of the three
 components of viability, and the assessment of viability is the assessment of the three sets
 together.


  38.9      A Measurement Method for Fidelity
  The executable criteria are stated; the present section states a measurement method that
  applies them to a case.
  Definition 38.5 (The Fidelity Measurement Method). (A) The fidelity of a reconstruction R
  of an identity I is measured by five steps:
(FM1) List the essential features. List the essential features e1 , . . . , en of I, as identified by the
      identification of the defining invariants (Chapter 12).
 498                       Chapter 38. Fidelity and the Conditions of Epistemic Reconstruction


(FM2) Locate each feature in the fidelity matrix. For each ei , determine whether R is in FM1
      (reference), FM2 (preserved), FM3 (omitted), FM4 (distorted), or FM5 (unknown).

(FM3) Compute the preservation pattern. Record the count of features in each cell, and the
      pattern of the matrix.

(FM4) Apply the executable criteria. Assess the pattern by Fid1–Fid4 (Definition 38.4).

(FM5) Assign the fidelity level. Assign the ordinal level F3 , F2 , F1 , F0 of Chapter 37 (Definition
      37.1), together with the matrix pattern and the executable criteria that support the
      level.
 Remark 38.12 (The Method Is Fallible). The method is fallible: the identification of the
 essential features (FM1) is the work of the inquiry, and the location of each feature in the
 matrix (FM2) is fallible. The method is the framework’s instrument, not a guarantee of the
 verdict.


  38.10       A Complete Example
 The measurement method is applied to a complete example, so that the reader can see the
 method at work.

  The case. A reconstruction R of a historical figure I from three sources: a collection of
  letters, a diary, and the testimony of a contemporary. The essential features of I, as identified
  by the inquiry, are: e1 (the figure’s stated beliefs), e2 (the figure’s patterns of action), e3 (the
  figure’s relations to contemporaries), and e4 (the figure’s self-presentation).

  Step FM1: list the essential features. The list is e1 , e2 , e3 , e4 .

  Step FM2: locate each feature in the matrix.
       • e1 : R describes the figure’s stated beliefs, and the description matches the letters; FM1
         (reference).

       • e2 : R describes the figure’s patterns of action, and the description is compatible with
         the diary, though partial; FM2 (preserved).

       • e3 : R does not describe the figure’s relations to contemporaries, and the absence is
         marked as an omission; FM3 (omitted).

       • e4 : R describes the figure’s self-presentation, but the description conflicts with the
         contemporary’s testimony; FM4 (distorted).

  Step FM3: compute the pattern. The pattern is: one FM1, one FM2, one FM3, one
  FM4, zero FM5.

  Step FM4: apply the executable criteria.
       • Fid1: identification completeness — the four essential features are identified; pass.

       • Fid2: preservation consistency — three of the four features are consistent; the fourth
         (e4 ) is distorted; partial pass.

       • Fid3: stability of preservation — the preservation of e1 and e2 is stable under small
         perturbations of the sources; the preservation of e4 is not; partial pass.
38.11. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                    499


   • Fid4: fruitfulness of preservation — the preservation of e1 and e2 supports further
     reconstruction of the figure’s later life; the distortion of e4 does not; partial pass.




Step FM5: assign the fidelity level. The pattern is one FM1, one FM2, one FM3, one
FM4. The level is F2 (substantial preservation with identified omissions), with the note that
e4 is distorted, which prevents full preservation.




The verdict. R is fidelious at the substantial level, with identified omissions and one
identified distortion. The distortion of e4 is the most serious failure; the omission of e3 is
recorded as an omission and does not present itself as preservation. The reconstruction is a
candidate for further revision, with the distortion of e4 as the target.



Remark 38.13 (The Example Shows the Method at Work). The example shows the five-step
method at work on a complete case. It is not a proof of the method; it is a display of its
application.




38.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish

Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not settle the question of what degree of fidelity a given reconstruc-
tion realizes. The method is stated, and the application to a given case is the work of the
inquiry.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the essential features of any
identity. The essential features are identified by the inquiry (Chapter 12, Definition 12.1), and
the identification is the work of the inquiry, not of the chapter.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between fidelity and the other components
of viability beyond the executable criteria stated in Section 38.8. The trade-offs among the
three components are structural, and their resolution is the work of the inquiry.
    Fourth, the chapter does not settle the open questions of Chapter 34 that the fidelity
assessment raises (Questions 1 and 2).



Remark 38.14 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed seven things. It
has defined fidelity as the preservation of the determining structure of the source in the epistemic
reconstruction (Definition 38.2). It has stated the conditions of epistemic reconstruction
(Definition 38.1). It has distinguished preservation from non-realization (Principle 38.1),
identity rigidity from reconstruction gradation (Principle 38.2), and loss from distortion
and from omission (Definition 38.3). It has stated the executable criteria for the fidelity
component, aligned with Chapter 23 (Definition 38.4). It has stated a measurement method
(Definition 38.5). And it has applied the method to a complete example (Section 38.10).
