A Question for Reflection
Consider a reconstruction you have formed of something you know only partly. Apply the
five-step measurement method of Definition 38.5: what are the essential features, where does
each fall in the fidelity matrix, what is the pattern, what does each executable criterion yield,
and what is the fidelity level? Can you distinguish, in your case, the loss, the distortion, and
the omission? What does your answer tell you about the relation between your reconstruction
and its source?
    And consider the example of Section 38.10: the reconstruction was at level F2 , with one
distortion and one omission. If you were to revise it, which failure would you target first, and
why? What does your answer tell you about the relation between fidelity and the criteria of
adequacy of Chapter 23? A reader who can answer both questions has understood the chapter;
a reader who can answer neither has the chapter’s two tasks before them.

The next chapter (Chapter 39) develops the second component of viability in its own place:
sustainability, through the account of the cost of cognition. The present chapter has developed
the first component, fidelity, as the preservation of the determining structure in the epistemic
reconstruction.

Chapter 39

The Cost of Cognition

Scope
This chapter develops the second component of viability—sustainability—through the frame-
work’s account of the cost of cognition. It defines the cost of cognition (Definition 39.1),
distinguishes three kinds of cost (realization, reconstruction, and maintenance-and-recovery)
(Definition 39.2), distinguishes three aspects of cost (extent, reach, and duration) (Defini-
tion 39.3), states the principle of epistemic economy (Principle 39.1), states the variational
principle of sustainability (Principle 39.2), and connects sustainability to the cost (Princi-
ple 39.3).
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “cost,” “economy,” “sustainability,”
“optimum,” “extent,” “reach,” or “duration,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed
by the definitions in this chapter. The chapter’s silence on questions of value is not a denial
but a recognition that the epistemic description is not the whole of what can be said.
Remark 39.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI). The chapter is the fourth of the eight chapters
of Part VI. The previous chapters defined viability and its three components (Chapters 36
and 37), and developed the first component (fidelity) through the distinction between the
tendency to express and the degree of structural fidelity (Chapter 38). The present chapter
develops the second component (sustainability), through the account of the cost of cognition.
The third component (recoverability) was developed in Chapter 37, through the singularity. The
chapters that follow state the cognitive sediment (Chapter 40), its integration (Chapter 41), the
balance criterion (Chapter 42), and the core commitments and dependency map (Chapter 43).
The present chapter’s role is to state the cost at the strength its argument supports, and to
prepare the ground for the chapter that states what the cost leaves behind (the sediment).


39.1     A Scene
Consider a scholar with a finite working life. She has three projects she wants to complete: a
large reference work on a body of texts, a series of close readings of individual passages, and a
study of the transmission of the texts across centuries. She has, let us suppose, ten years of
full-time work, and she has no way to extend the time.
    The reference work demands the most extensive labor: she must read every text, catalogue
every variant, compile every index. The close readings demand less extensive labor but
more intensive concentration: she must live with each passage for weeks, work through every
ambiguity, trace every allusion. The study of transmission demands labor that is ongoing: she
must gather documents as they become available, maintain her archive, and revise her account
as the archive grows.
    Suppose the scholar attempts all three projects at once, with equal attention, and without
distinguishing the cost of each. She will complete none of them well. The reference work will
502                                                          Chapter 39. The Cost of Cognition


be incomplete; the close readings will be rushed; the study of transmission will be abandoned
midway. The cost of each project, in the time and attention available, has exceeded what she
can bear.
    Suppose, instead, that she considers the cost of each project, and chooses among them
according to what her capacity permits. She might complete the close readings, because they
are within her capacity, and defer the reference work to a later generation. Or she might
complete the study of transmission, because the documents are available now and may not be
available later, and defer the close readings. The choice is hers; the framework does not make
it for her. But the choice is informed by the cost of each project, and by what her capacity
permits.
    The scene poses a question. What is the cost of cognition, and how does it bear on what
the finite subject can sustain? The present chapter’s answer is that the cost of cognition has
three kinds and three aspects, and that sustainability is the condition under which the cost
does not exceed the context’s capacity. The chapter states the cost, the kinds, the aspects,
and the condition.

Remark 39.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the cost at
work in a familiar case. It does not prove the definitions that follow; it makes them intelligible
before they are stated. The definitions and the principles are stated in the sections that follow,
and the scene carries no weight in them.

Remark 39.3 (The Scene Shows the Three Kinds and Three Aspects at Work). The scene is
easily read as an observation about a scholar. The observation is not wrong, but it hides the
structural point. The structural point is that the three projects differ in the three kinds of cost
(the reference work is high in the cost of realization and reconstruction; the close readings are
high in the cost of reconstruction; the study of transmission is high in the cost of maintenance
and recovery) and in the three aspects (the reference work is high in extent; the close readings
are high in reach; the study of transmission is high in duration). The scene is the framework’s
way of showing that the three kinds and the three aspects are not three separate properties
of a project; they are three dimensions in which the demand of the project on the scholar’s
capacity can be assessed. A reader who takes the scene as a display of three projects has read
the scene; a reader who takes it as a display of the three kinds and the three aspects has read
the structural point.


39.2      The Question
The previous chapters of Part VI have developed the concept of viability and its first component.
Chapter 36 defined viability as the epistemic structural character of the relation between
an identity and its manifestations, and named the three components: fidelity, sustainability,
and recoverability. Chapter 37 defined the three components and argued for their minimality.
Chapter 38 developed the first component (fidelity) by distinguishing the tendency to express
from the degree of structural fidelity.
    The present chapter develops the second component: sustainability. The question is not
what fidelity is; Chapter 38 has said that. The question is what sustainability is, and what it
depends on. The framework’s answer is that sustainability depends on the cost of cognition:
the cost of producing and maintaining a manifestation, and the relation of that cost to the
receiving cognitive context’s capacity. Sustainability is the condition under which the cost
does not exceed the capacity.
    The question is not idle. Sustainability is a component of viability, and the concept of
viability is the framework’s central contribution. If sustainability is not understood, the concept
of viability is not understood; and if the cost of cognition is not understood, sustainability
39.3. The Definition of the Cost of Cognition                                                 503


is not understood. The present chapter states the cost, so that sustainability can be stated
precisely.
    The chapter’s method is fivefold. It defines the cost of cognition (39.1). It distinguishes
three kinds of cost (39.2) and three aspects of cost (39.3). It states the principle of epistemic
economy (39.1) and the variational principle of sustainability (39.2). It connects sustainability
to the cost (39.3), and states the trade-offs between sustainability and the other two components
of viability. And it connects the cost to the limits of Part V, to the humility of Chapter 35,
and to the chapters that follow.
Remark 39.4 (The Question and the Limits of Part V). The question is related to the limits
of Part V, and the relation is worth marking. The limits say what the finite subject cannot do:
it cannot know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it cannot complete
its knowledge of epistemic light (Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic unknownness of
the other (Chapter 32), and it cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33). The cost of
cognition is what the finite subject must bear, given the limits: the cognition of an identity
demands capacity of the context, and the demand cannot be eliminated. The distinction is the
distinction between the limits and the cost that the limits impose; the framework holds both.


39.3     The Definition of the Cost of Cognition
Definition 39.1 (Cost of Cognition). (A) The cost of cognition is what the cognition of an
identity demands of the receiving cognitive context’s capacity. It is not a single quantity; it is
a family of demands, distinguished by what is demanded and by the aspect under which the
demand is made.
    The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary: it says what the cost is. The definition is not derived from the framework’s other
principles; it is the framework’s proposal for what the cost is, and it is stated at exactly that
strength. It rests on the framework’s account of capacity (Chapter 13), and it is one of the
primitives of the framework (Chapter 34, the list of primitives).
    The definition has two parts, and both are worth marking.

The first part: the cost is a demand on capacity. The cost is what the cognition of an
identity demands of the context’s capacity. The context has a capacity—what it can bear,
and what it is suited to (Chapter 13)—and the cognition of an identity makes a demand on
that capacity. The demand is not a defect of the cognition; it is a structural feature of the
relation between the cognition and its context.

The second part: the cost is a family of demands. The cost is not a single quantity; it
is a family of demands, distinguished by what is demanded and by the aspect under which the
demand is made. The next two sections state the two distinctions: three kinds of cost, and
three aspects of cost.
Remark 39.5 (The Cost Is Structural, Not Evaluative). The cost is structural, not evaluative.
It is what the cognition of an identity demands of the context’s capacity; it is not a value, a
good, or an end. The framework does not say that lower cost is better or that higher cost
is worse; it says what the cost is, and it leaves the evaluation to other inquiries. The reader
who imports an evaluative sense into the cost has misread it; the reader who reads it as a
structural demand has read it correctly.
Remark 39.6 (The Cost Is Not a Defect of the Cognition). The cost is not a defect of the
cognition. It is a structural feature of the relation between the cognition and its context.
A cognition that demands more of the context is not thereby a defective cognition; it is a
504                                                         Chapter 39. The Cost of Cognition


cognition whose relation to the context is at a particular cost. The framework’s claim is that
the cost is real, not that it is a defect.


39.4     The Three Kinds of Cost
The cost has three kinds, and the three are distinguished by what the cognition demands.
Definition 39.2 (Three Kinds of Cost). (A) The cost of cognition has three kinds:
  (i) the cost of realization: what it takes for the cognition to come to be—the conditions that
      the context must supply for the cognition to be realized;

 (ii) the cost of reconstruction: what it takes to form a pseudo-identity of the identity—the
      observation, the comparison, the inference that the reconstruction requires;

 (iii) the cost of maintenance and recovery: what it takes to keep, or to regain, the cognition—
       the conditions that the context must sustain for the cognition to continue, and the
       conditions that must be restored if the cognition is to be recovered after a lapse.
    The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary: it says what the three kinds of cost are. The definition is not derived from the
framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the three kinds, and it is stated
at exactly that strength.
    The three kinds are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.

The cost of realization. What it takes for the cognition to come to be. The conditions
that the context must supply for the cognition to be realized: the material, the relations, the
structural possibilities that the cognition’s realization requires. The cost is the demand that
the realization makes on the context’s capacity.

The cost of reconstruction. What it takes to form a pseudo-identity of the identity
(Chapter 12). The conditions that the subject must satisfy in order to reconstruct the identity
from its manifestations: the observation, the comparison, the inference that the reconstruction
requires. The cost is the demand that the reconstruction makes on the context’s capacity.

The cost of maintenance and recovery. What it takes to keep, or to regain, the cognition.
The conditions that the context must sustain for the cognition to continue, and the conditions
that must be restored if the cognition is to be recovered after a lapse. The cost is the demand
that the continuation or restoration makes on the context’s capacity.
Remark 39.7 (The Three Kinds Are Not Three Components of One Quantity). The three
kinds are not three components of one quantity that could be added up. They are three kinds
of demand on the context’s capacity, and their relation is not simply additive. How they stand
to one another in a given case is a conceptual question the framework leaves open, and it is
one of the fourteen open questions of Chapter 34 (Question 8). The framework’s claim is that
the three are distinct; their sum is not the total cost.
Remark 39.8 (The Three Kinds Are Related). The three kinds are related. The cost of
realization is what the cognition demands in order to be; the cost of reconstruction is what its
reconstruction demands in order to be known; the cost of maintenance and recovery is what
its continuation or restoration demands in order to persist. The three are distinct, but they
are not unrelated; a cognition that is expensive to realize may be inexpensive to reconstruct,
and a cognition that is inexpensive to realize may be expensive to maintain. The relation is
structural, not contingent, and the framework keeps the three kinds apart.
39.5. The Three Aspects of Cost                                                             505


Remark 39.9 (The Three Kinds Are Not a Ranking). The three kinds are not a ranking of
importance. The framework does not say that the cost of realization is more important than
the cost of reconstruction, or that the cost of reconstruction is more important than the cost
of maintenance and recovery. It says that the three are distinct kinds of demand, and that the
assessment of the cost is the assessment of the three kinds in a given case. The ranking, if
there is one, belongs to the inquiry, not to the framework.


39.5     The Three Aspects of Cost
The cost has three aspects, and the three are distinguished by the aspect under which the
demand is made.

Definition 39.3 (Three Aspects of Cost). (A) The cost of cognition has three aspects:

  (i) extent: how much of the context’s capacity is taken —the quantity of capacity that the
      cognition demands;

 (ii) reach: how much cognition and attention it takes to hold it—the quantity of reconstruction
      that the cognition demands;

(iii) duration: how long it must be kept up—the quantity of time that the cognition demands.

    The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary: it says what the three aspects of cost are. The definition is not derived from the
framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the three aspects, and it is
stated at exactly that strength.
    The three aspects are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.

The aspect of extent. How much of the context’s capacity is taken. The extent is the
quantity of capacity that the cognition demands: how much material, how many relations,
how many structural possibilities. The cognition that is high in extent demands much of the
context’s capacity; the cognition that is low in extent demands little.

The aspect of reach. How much reconstruction it takes to hold the cognition. The reach
is the quantity of reconstruction that the cognition demands: how much observation, how
much comparison, how much inference is required to form a pseudo-identity of the identity.
The cognition that is high in reach demands much of the subject’s reconstructive effort; the
cognition that is low in reach demands little.

The aspect of duration. How long the cognition must be kept up. The duration is the
quantity of time that the cognition demands: how long the capacity must be sustained for the
cognition to continue. The cognition that is high in duration demands much of the context’s
capacity over time; the cognition that is low in duration demands little.

Remark 39.10 (The Three Aspects Are Not Three Quantities). The three aspects are not
three quantities that could be added up. They are three dimensions of one demand on capacity,
and their relation is not simply additive. How they stand to one another in a given case is a
conceptual question the framework leaves open, and it is one of the fourteen open questions
of Chapter 34 (Question 8). The framework’s claim is that the three are distinct; their
combination is not the total cost.

Remark 39.11 (The Three Aspects Are Not Independent). The three aspects are not
independent. A cognition can be high in extent and low in reach and short in duration (a
506                                                        Chapter 39. The Cost of Cognition


large material object that is easily recognized and soon gone); or high in reach and low in
extent and long in duration (a subtle relation that demands much reconstruction, occupies
little capacity, and persists). The three aspects answer different questions, and an answer to
one does not answer the others. The combinations are structural, not contingent, and the
framework keeps the three aspects apart.

Remark 39.12 (The Three Aspects Are Not a Ranking). The three aspects are not a ranking
of importance. The framework does not say that extent is more important than reach, or that
reach is more important than duration. It says that the three are distinct dimensions of the
demand, and that the assessment of the cost is the assessment of the three aspects in a given
case. The ranking, if there is one, belongs to the inquiry, not to the framework.


39.6     The Principle of Epistemic Economy
The distinction among the kinds and aspects of cost leads to a principle about the cost as
such.

Principle 39.1 (Epistemic Economy). (E) Every realization of a cognition, every reconstruc-
tion of an identity, and every maintenance of a cognition bears a cost that cannot be wholly
removed. Cost is a structural feature of the relation between the cognition and its context; it
is not a value, a burden to be minimized as an end, or a good.

    The principle is (E): it is an estimate, not a primitive commitment and not a proved
conclusion. Its support is the structure of the relation between the cognition and its context:
the context has finite capacity, and no cognition is free of what it asks of that capacity. The
principle would be refuted by a case in which a cognition demands nothing of the context’s
capacity; the framework argues that none can be coherently described, given the finite capacity
of every context. The estimate is offered at that strength, and the reader who wishes to
challenge it knows where to press.
    The principle has three components, and each is worth marking.

The first component: cost is irreducible. Cost belongs to the relation between the
cognition and its context. A context has finite capacity, and no cognition is free of what it
asks of that capacity. The cost cannot be eliminated; it can only be distributed, deferred, or
transformed.

The second component: cost is a family of demands. Cost is not a single quantity.
The three kinds and the three aspects distinguished above are ways in which cognition asks
something of capacity. Their relation is not simply additive; how they stand to one another in
a given case is not fixed in advance.

The third component: complete reconstruction is structurally unavailable. Com-
plete reconstruction is impossible (the impossibility of super-identity, Chapter 27), and it
would demand unbounded cost. The framework states this as a structural limit, not as a
deficiency to be overcome.

Remark 39.13 (The Economy Is Structural, Not Economic). The economy at issue is
structural: it names what cognition demands of a finite capacity, not a system of exchange or
a market. The framework uses the word because the structural feature is analogous to what
economy studies; it imports no assumption of economic theory. The structural economy is a
statement about the relation between cognition and finite capacity, and it is to be read at that
level.
39.7. The Variational Principle of Sustainability                                               507


Remark 39.14 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Thrift). The principle is not a denial of
thrift. A subject that economizes on the cost of cognition is a subject that tries to satisfy
the demands with the least cost; the framework does not deny that this is possible, or that it
is sometimes desirable. What the framework denies is that the cost can be eliminated. The
subject can reduce the cost, distribute it, or transform it; the subject cannot make it vanish.
The distinction is the distinction between the reduction of cost and the elimination of cost;
the framework affirms the first and denies the second.
Remark 39.15 (The Principle Is About the Relation, Not About the Subject). The principle
is about the relation between the cognition and its context, not about the subject who bears
the cost. The cost is what the cognition demands of the context; the subject may bear the
cost, or may distribute it, or may defer it, but the cost is a feature of the relation, not of the
subject. The distinction is the distinction between the structural feature and the subject’s
experience of it; the framework keeps it apart.


39.7      The Variational Principle of Sustainability
The principle of epistemic economy raises a further question. Given that cost is irreducible,
what is the structural optimum of cognition? The framework states the optimum in a principle.
Principle 39.2 (Variational Principle of Sustainability). (E) For any identity and any receiving
context, the structural optimum of cognition is the point at which cost is minimized subject
to the constraints of fidelity and recoverability. There is no single structural optimum across
contexts; each is indexed to the context and to the identity.
    The principle is (E): it is an estimate, not a primitive commitment and not a proved
conclusion. Its support is the structure of the relation between cost, fidelity, and recoverability:
the three are the components of viability (Chapter 37), and the structural optimum is the
point at which the cost is as low as it can be while fidelity and recoverability are still satisfied.
The estimate is offered at that strength.
    The principle’s claim is precise. Cost alone is not the criterion of sustainability. Cost can
be lowered by lowering fidelity: a thinner cognition is cheaper and is a less complete reflection
of the source. Sustainability is the three-fold structural relation of fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability. Cost and fidelity are therefore taken together: the structural optimum is the
least cost consistent with fidelity.
Remark 39.16 (Cost Alone Is Not Sustainability). The criterion is fidelity-constrained cost,
not cost alone. Viability has three components—fidelity, sustainability, recoverability—and the
structural optimum is the point at which cost is as low as it can be while these are satisfied. A
cheap cognition with low fidelity is not at the optimum; it is simply cheap. The framework’s
claim is structural: the optimum is indexed to the relation among the three components, not
to cost taken in isolation.
Remark 39.17 (No Single Structural Optimum). The structural optimum depends on the
receiving context, its capacity, and the identity. The principle states a family of structural
optima, each indexed to a context. There is no single structural optimum across contexts,
because the contexts differ in capacity, and the identities differ in their essential determination.
The framework’s claim is structural: for any given identity and context, there is a structural
optimum; across identities and contexts, there is no single optimum.
Remark 39.18 (The Variational Principle Is Not a Formula). The variational principle is not
a formula. It states the structural optimum, but it does not offer an algorithm for computing
it. The identification of the optimum in a given case is the work of the inquiry, not of the
principle. The principle’s role is to state the condition the inquiry aims at, not to substitute
for the inquiry.
508                                                          Chapter 39. The Cost of Cognition


39.8     Sustainability as the Second Component
Given the cost and the variational principle, sustainability (the second component of viability)
can be stated precisely.

Principle 39.3 (Sustainability). (T) A relation between an identity and its manifestations in
a cognitive context is sustainable when the cost of the cognition—in its three kinds and three
aspects—does not exceed what the context’s capacity can bear, at the level of fidelity and
recoverability that the identity’s nature permits.

   The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of cost and from the variational principle.
The argument is the definition’s application to the relation between the cognition and the
context, and the variational principle’s condition on the optimum.
   The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.

The first part: the cost in its three kinds and three aspects. The cost is the whole
family of demands: the three kinds (realization, reconstruction, maintenance and recovery)
and the three aspects (extent, reach, duration). Sustainability is the condition under which
the whole family does not exceed the context’s capacity; it is not the condition under which
one kind or one aspect does not exceed the capacity, while the others do.

The second part: the context’s capacity. The context has a capacity (Chapter 13):
what it can bear, and what it is suited to. The capacity is not a quantity of the same kind
as the cost; it is the structural feature that the cost demands. The cost is measured in the
demands it makes; the capacity is measured in what it can bear.

The third part: fidelity and recoverability as constraints. The sustainability is not
the condition under which the cost is lowest, period. It is the condition under which the cost
does not exceed the capacity, at the level of fidelity and recoverability that the identity’s
nature permits. A cognition that is cheap because it distorts the source is not sustainable in
the framework’s sense; it is cheap, but it fails the fidelity condition.

Remark 39.19 (Sustainability Is Not the Absence of Cost). Sustainability is not the absence
of cost. The cost is irreducible (Principle 39.1); every cognition has a cost. Sustainability
is the condition under which the cost does not exceed the capacity, not the condition under
which there is no cost. The reader who reads sustainability as the absence of cost has misread
it; the reader who reads it as the condition of cost relative to capacity has read it correctly.

Remark 39.20 (Sustainability Is Not Cheapness). Sustainability is not cheapness. A cognition
can be cheap and unsustainable (if the context’s capacity is very small, or if the cognition’s
fidelity is low); a cognition can be expensive and sustainable (if the context’s capacity is very
large, or if the cognition’s fidelity is high and the cost is within the capacity). The two are
related, but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.

Remark 39.21 (Sustainability Is Not Fidelity). Sustainability is not fidelity. A cognition can
be high in fidelity and unsustainable (if the cost of the fidelity exceeds the context’s capacity);
a cognition can be sustainable and low in fidelity (if the cognition is cheap but distorts the
source). The two are different components of viability, and the framework keeps them apart.

Remark 39.22 (Sustainability Is Not Recoverability). Sustainability is not recoverability. A
cognition can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the context’s capacity has
been exhausted; the cognition is not recoverable if the cost of restoring it would exceed the
cost of producing a new one (Chapter 37, Section 37.7). The two are different components of
viability, and the framework keeps them apart.
39.9. The Trade-Offs with the Other Components                                                  509


39.9      The Trade-Offs with the Other Components
Sustainability is related to the other two components of viability, and the trade-offs are worth
stating.

Sustainability and fidelity. A cognition that is high in fidelity is often high in cost (a more
complete preservation of the source’s essential determination may require more of the context’s
capacity); a cognition that is low in fidelity is often low in cost (a less complete preservation
may require less of the context’s capacity). The trade-off is structural, not contingent; the
assessment of viability is the assessment of the trade-off in a given case.

Sustainability and recoverability. A cognition that is sustainable for a long duration often
exhausts the context’s capacity for restoration, and is therefore less recoverable; a cognition
that is sustainable for a short duration often leaves the capacity for restoration, and is therefore
more recoverable. The trade-off is structural, and the assessment of viability is the assessment
of the trade-off.

The three components together. The three components are conditions on the relation
between the identity and its manifestations, and the conditions can be satisfied at different
degrees. The trade-offs are the framework’s account of what the assessment of viability is;
they are not a defect of the three-fold structure.

Remark 39.23 (The Trade-Offs Are Not a Ranking). The trade-offs are not a ranking of the
components. The framework does not say that sustainability is more important than fidelity,
or that fidelity is more important than recoverability. It says that the three are conditions on
the relation, and that the assessment of viability is the assessment of the trade-offs in a given
case. The ranking, if there is one, belongs to the inquiry, not to the framework.

Remark 39.24 (The Trade-Offs Are Not a Promise of Compensation). The trade-offs are
not a promise of compensation. A cognition that is cheap in sustainability is not thereby
compensated for its low sustainability by high fidelity; it is simply a cognition that realizes
the three components at different degrees. The reader who reads the trade-offs as a promise
of compensation has misread them; the reader who reads them as a distinction of the three
components has read them correctly.


39.10      The Cost and the Limits of Part V
The cost of cognition is related to the limits of Part V, and the relation is worth marking.
    The limits say what the finite subject cannot do: it cannot know all manifestations of
an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it cannot complete its knowledge of epistemic light
(Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic unknownness of the other (Chapter 32), and it
cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33). The cost of cognition is what the finite subject
must bear, given the limits: the cognition of an identity demands capacity of the context, and
the demand cannot be eliminated. The distinction is the distinction between the limits and
the cost that the limits impose; the framework holds both.
    The cost is also related to the disposition of Chapter 35. The humble subject is the subject
that can assess the cost of its cognition: it recognizes that the cognition of an identity demands
capacity, that the demand cannot be eliminated, and that the assessment of the cost is the
work of the inquiry. The humility is the disposition that accepts the cost; the cost is what
the disposition recognizes. The distinction is the distinction between the disposition and the
structural feature that the disposition recognizes; the framework keeps it apart.
510                                                       Chapter 39. The Cost of Cognition


Remark 39.25 (The Cost and the Intrinsic Unknownness). The cost is related to the
distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness (Chapter 32), and the relation is
worth marking. The temporary unknownness is what the assessment of the cost can reduce:
more manifestation, more analysis, and more comparison can make the assessment of the cost
more precise. The intrinsic unknownness is what the assessment cannot remove: the finite
subject cannot exhaust the relation, and the cost is always assessed within the partiality that
the intrinsic unknownness imposes. The distinction is the distinction between the assessment
and the completeness of the assessment; the framework keeps it apart.


39.11      The Cost and the Open Questions of Chapter 34
The cost is related to four of the fourteen open questions of Chapter 34, and the relation is
worth marking.
    The first is the question of the exact boundary between the reduction of viability and the
singularity (Question 2). The present chapter states the cost of restoration as a kind of cost
(the cost of maintenance and recovery); the relation between that cost and the singularity is
left open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations to an extension.
    The second is the question of the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of the
balance criterion (Question 6). The present chapter states the cost; the balance criterion
(Chapter 42) uses the cost as one of its terms, but the exact relation between the cost and the
balance is left open.
    The third is the question of whether the proposed criterion of manifestational adequacy
and the principle of contextual manifestational capacity can be given independent definition
and support (Question 7). The present chapter develops the notion of what a context can
bear (the capacity), and the development is genuine, but it does not supply the independent
account of capacity that the proposed criterion and the principle need. The settlement of the
question is left open.
    The fourth is the question of the relation among the aspects of cost (Question 8). The
present chapter distinguishes the three aspects (extent, reach, duration), but their exact
relation is left open.

Remark 39.26 (The Open Questions Are Invitations, Not Defeats). The four open questions
are invitations to an extension of the framework, not defeats of it. The framework states the
cost and its kinds and aspects at the strength its arguments support; the questions that the
cost raises but does not settle are the framework’s statement of where the inquiry continues.
A reader who settles one of the questions has extended the framework; a reader who shows
that the question is not real has shown a limit of the framework’s formulation.


39.12      The Cost and the Sediment of Chapter 40
The cost of cognition is related to the cognitive sediment, and the relation is worth marking,
because the two are distinguished by the distinction between the demand and the residue.
    The cost is what the cognition demands of the context’s capacity; the sediment (Chapter 40)
is what the cognition leaves behind after the demand has been met. The two are related: a
cognition that is high in cost may leave more sediment than a cognition that is low in cost.
But the two are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart. The cost is the demand;
the sediment is the residue. The distinction is structural, not verbal.

Remark 39.27 (The Sediment Is Not a Kind of Cost). The sediment is not a kind of cost. The
three kinds of cost (realization, reconstruction, maintenance and recovery) are the demands
that the cognition makes on the context’s capacity; the sediment is what the cognition leaves
39.13. The Cost and the Balance of Chapter 42                                                    511


in the context after the demand has been discharged. The framework states the cost here, and
the sediment in Chapter 40; the two are distinct, and neither is reducible to the other.


39.13       The Cost and the Balance of Chapter 42
The cost of cognition is related to the balance criterion, and the relation is worth marking.
    The cost is what the cognition demands of the context’s capacity; the balance criterion
(Chapter 42) is the framework’s measure of the relation between an identity and the epistemic
light it receives. The balance uses the sediment as its negative term; the sediment is the residue
of the cost. The cost is the demand; the balance is the measure of the flow that the demand
produces. The two are related as the demand and the measure of the flow; the framework
keeps them apart.
Remark 39.28 (The Cost Is Not the Balance). The cost is not the balance. The cost is what
the cognition demands; the balance is the measure of the relation between the identity and
the epistemic light it receives. A cognition can be high in cost and the relation between the
identity and its manifestations can still be at a high balance; a cognition can be low in cost
and the relation can still be at a low balance. The two are different, and the framework keeps
them apart.


39.14       The Cost and the Core Commitments of Chapter 43
The cost of cognition is related to the core commitments of the framework, and the relation is
worth marking.
    The cost is one of the framework’s primitives (Chapter 34, the list of primitives); the
account of the cost in the present chapter is one of the chapters that the core commitments
of Chapter 43 make possible. The three components of viability (fidelity, sustainability,
recoverability) are the framework’s central character; the cost is one of the structural features
of the relation that the character describes. The cost is not one of the ten core commitments,
but it is one of the structural features that the core commitments make intelligible.
Remark 39.29 (The Cost and the Core Commitments). The cost is not one of the ten core
commitments (Chapter 43), but it is a structural feature that the core commitments make
intelligible. The commitment to the finitude of the epistemic subject (C1) is what makes the
cost irreducible; the commitment to the autonomy of epistemic justification (C3) is what makes
the assessment of the cost internal to epistemology; the commitment to the identity of the
framework (C4, C10) is what makes the relation between the identity and its manifestations
the subject of the cost. The cost is not a core commitment, but it is a structural feature of
the relation that the core commitments describe.


39.15       Scope and Vulnerability
The account is stated at the strength its argument supports, and its scope and vulnerability
are worth stating.
    The account is valid for the class of relations the framework treats: the relations between
identities and their manifestations in cognitive contexts, under the conditions the framework’s
definitions specify. It says that the cost has three kinds and three aspects, and that sustainability
is the condition under which the cost does not exceed the context’s capacity. It does not say
that the cost can be measured with a common unit, or that the optimum can be computed by
a formula.
    The account rests on the framework’s account of identity (Chapter 12), of manifestation
(Chapter 13), and of the three components of viability (Chapter 37). The account’s force is no
512                                                        Chapter 39. The Cost of Cognition


greater than the force of these commitments; a reader who rejects one of them has a reason to
reject the corresponding part of the account, and the framework does not pretend otherwise.
    The account would be put in question by two things.

First challenge. A case in which the cost of a cognition demands nothing of the context’s
capacity. If such a case could be given, the principle of epistemic economy would be refuted,
and the account would need to be revised. The framework does not claim that no such case can
be described; it claims that none has been described that survives the framework’s definitions,
and it argues that none can be.

Second challenge. A case in which the cost of a cognition exceeds the context’s capacity,
and yet the cognition is sustainable in the framework’s sense. If such a case could be given,
the definition of sustainability would be too strong, and the framework would need to revise it.
The framework holds that sustainability is the condition under which the cost does not exceed
the capacity, and it states the account at exactly the strength its arguments support.

Remark 39.30 (The Account Is Not a Formula). The account is not a formula. It states the
cost, its kinds and aspects, and the condition of sustainability; it does not offer an algorithm
for computing the cost or the optimum in a given case. The identification of the cost in a
particular case is the work of the inquiry, not of the account. The account’s role is to state
the conditions the inquiry aims at, not to substitute for the inquiry.

Remark 39.31 (The Account Points Beyond Itself). The account points beyond itself. The
cost and the condition of sustainability are real structural features of the relation between an
identity and its manifestations; the features are describable, and the description is what the
framework offers. But the features are not the whole of what the relation is; the relation is
between an identity and its manifestations, and the identity and the manifestations are what
they are. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of the relation and what lies
beyond it; the framework keeps it throughout.


39.16      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Five things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the cognitive sediment. The sediment is treated
in Chapter 40; the present chapter states the cost, not what the cost leaves behind. The
distinction is the distinction between the demand and the residue; the framework keeps it
apart.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the balance criterion. The balance criterion is stated
in Chapter 42; the present chapter states the cost, not the measure of the relation between
the identity and the epistemic light it receives. The distinction is the distinction between the
demand and the measure; the framework keeps it apart.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of how the cost is to be measured in a
particular case. The cost’s kinds and aspects are stated; their measurement is a matter for the
inquiry, not for the chapter.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim that the cost can be reduced to a single quantity. The
cost is a family of demands, and the framework does not offer a common unit. A reader who
expects a single quantity is invited to propose one; the framework’s account is offered at the
strength of a family of demands.
    Fifth, the chapter does not settle the four open questions of Chapter 34 that the cost raises
(Questions 2, 6, 7, and 8). The present chapter states the cost; the questions that the cost
raises but does not settle are the framework’s invitations to an extension.
39.17. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                              513


Remark 39.32 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has defined the cost of cognition (Definition 39.1). It has distinguished three kinds of cost
(realization, reconstruction, maintenance and recovery) (Definition 39.2) and three aspects
(extent, reach, duration) (Definition 39.3). It has stated the principle of epistemic economy
(Principle 39.1) and the variational principle of sustainability (Principle 39.2). It has connected
sustainability (the second component of viability) to the cost (Principle 39.3), and stated the
trade-offs with the other two components. It has connected the cost to the limits of Part V,
to the humility of Chapter 35, to the open questions of Chapter 34, and to the sediment of
Chapter 40, the balance of Chapter 42, and the core commitments of Chapter 43. And it has
stated the scope and vulnerability of the account.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a cognition you have maintained for a long time—a relationship, a practice, a
research project. Which kind of cost was most demanding—the cost of realization, the cost of
reconstruction, or the cost of maintenance and recovery? Which aspect was most demanding—
the extent, the reach, or the duration? And consider the scholar of the scene: which of the three
projects demanded the most of the three kinds, and which of the three aspects? What does
your answer tell you about the relation between the cost of cognition and the sustainability of
the relation?

The next chapter (Chapter 40) states what the cognition leaves behind after the demand has
been met: the cognitive sediment. The present chapter has developed the second component
of viability, sustainability, through the account of the cost of cognition. The chapter after
that (Chapter 41) states the integration of the sediment; the chapter after that (Chapter 42)
states the balance criterion. The third component of viability, recoverability, was developed in
Chapter 37 through the singularity.
