Chapter 40

Cognitive Sediment

Scope
This chapter defines the cognitive sediment: the epistemic counterpart, at the level of the
relation between an identity and its manifestations, of what the previous chapter called the cost
of cognition. The cost of cognition is what the cognition demands of the receiving context’s
capacity (Chapter 39); the sediment is what the cognition leaves behind in the context after
the demand has been met.
    The chapter states the distinction between hard and soft manifestation (Section 40.3,
Definitions 40.1 and 40.2), the action chain by which an effect is produced and received
(Section 40.4, Definition 40.3), the crystallization of effect (Section 40.5, Definition 40.4),
the definition of sediment (Section 40.6, Definition 40.5), the definition of returning light
as the complement of sediment (Section 40.7, Definition 40.6), the three layers of sediment
(Section 40.8, Definition 40.7), the three forms of integration (Section 40.9, Definition 40.8),
and the distinction of sediment from transformation and from loss of identity (Section 40.11).
It connects the sediment to the three components of viability (Section 40.10).
    The singularity and recoverability, which the first edition of Book I referenced to Chapter 41,
are now developed in Chapter 37, Section 37.7 and Section 37.6, because Book I has no
separate singularity chapter: Chapter 41 is the integration of cognitive sediment, and the
singularity belongs in the chapter that states the third component of viability. The present
chapter therefore develops the sediment’s full structural context—hard/soft, action chain,
crystallization, returning light—and it prepares Chapter 41 (the integration of sediment) and
Chapter 42 (the balance criterion).
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “sediment,” “lodging,” “integration,”
“crystallization,” “returning light,” “transformation,” “loss,” or “layer,” these are structural
terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter. The chapter’s silence on
questions of value is not a denial but a recognition that the epistemic description is not the
whole of what can be said.

Remark 40.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI). The chapter is the fifth of the eight chapters
of Part VI. The previous chapters defined viability and its three components (Chapters 36
and 37), developed the first component (fidelity) through the distinction between the tendency
to express and the degree of structural fidelity (Chapter 38), and developed the second
component (sustainability) through the account of the cost of cognition (Chapter 39). The
third component (recoverability) was developed in Chapter 37, through the singularity. The
present chapter states what the cognition leaves behind after the demand has been met:
the cognitive sediment. The chapters that follow state the integration of the sediment
(Chapter 41), the balance criterion (Chapter 42), and the core commitments and dependency
map (Chapter 43). The present chapter’s role is to state the sediment at the strength its
argument supports, and to prepare the ground for the chapter that states its integration.
516                                                            Chapter 40. Cognitive Sediment


40.1     A Scene
Consider a house that has been lived in for a hundred years. Every generation that lived in it
left something behind. In the attic, there are boxes of letters that no one has opened in decades.
In the basement, there are tools from a trade that no one in the family practices anymore. In
the walls, there are pipes that were installed, replaced, and abandoned; the abandoned ones
are still there, rusting, no longer connected to anything. The house has absorbed the lives
that were lived in it, and what it has absorbed has not all been processed.
     Some of what the house absorbed is active. The letters, when they are read, still speak;
the tools, when they are understood, still tell of the trade; the pipes, when they are inspected,
still show the shape of the plumbing that was. What has been absorbed can be integrated: it
can be brought into the network of relations that the house holds, and it can become part of
what the house is. Some of what the house absorbed is not active. The rust in the abandoned
pipes does not speak; the dust in the unopened boxes does not tell; the mold in the walls
does not show the shape of anything. What has been absorbed can also not be integrated: it
persists, it is not connected to anything, and it lays a claim on the house’s capacity that the
house cannot discharge.
     The scene is one instance of a structural relation. Whenever a cognition leaves something
behind in its context, what is left behind is either integrated into the context’s relations or
lodged in it. The framework names the lodged residue, and the process of integration, and the
cost that the whole relation bears.
     The scene poses a question. What is it for a cognition to leave something behind? What
is it for the residue to be lodged, or integrated? And what does the relation between the
cognition and its residue have to do with the three components of viability? The present
chapter answers these questions. Its principal contributions are the definition of the cognitive
sediment, the statement of the action chain and the crystallization of effect, the definition of
returning light, the distinction among the three layers of sediment, the statement of the three
forms of integration, and the distinction of the sediment from transformation and from loss of
identity.

Remark 40.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the sediment
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the definitions that follow; it makes them
intelligible before they are stated. The definitions are stated in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them.

Remark 40.3 (The Scene Shows the Distinction Between Lodged and Integrated). The scene
is easily read as an observation about a house. The observation is not wrong, but it hides the
structural point. The structural point is that what the house has absorbed is of two kinds:
what is integrated into the network of the house’s relations (the letters, when read; the tools,
when understood; the pipes, when inspected) and what is lodged in it (the rust, the dust, the
mold). The two are not the same, and the difference is the framework’s distinction between the
integrated light and the lodged sediment. A reader who takes the scene as a display of a house
has read the scene; a reader who takes it as a display of the distinction between integration
and lodging has read the structural point.


40.2     The Question
The previous chapters of Part VI have developed the concept of viability and its components.
Chapter 36 defined viability as the epistemic structural character of the relation between
an identity and its manifestations, and named the three components: fidelity, sustainability,
and recoverability. Chapter 37 defined the three components, argued for their minimality,
and developed recoverability through the account of the singularity; it stated fidelity as the
40.3. Hard and Soft Manifestations                                                           517


first component (developed in Chapter 38) and sustainability as the second (developed in
Chapter 39). Chapter 38 developed fidelity by distinguishing the tendency to express from the
degree of structural fidelity. Chapter 39 developed sustainability through the account of the
cost of cognition.
    The present chapter turns to a different question. The previous chapters have stated what
the cognition demands of the context’s capacity (the cost) and what the cognition preserves
of the source (fidelity). The present chapter asks: what does the cognition leave behind in
the context, after the demand has been met and the preservation has been achieved? The
framework’s answer is the cognitive sediment.
    The question is not idle. The sediment is not the same as the cost, and not the same as the
manifestation. The cost is the demand the cognition makes; the sediment is what the cognition
leaves behind after the demand has been discharged. The manifestation is the appearance of
the identity in the context; the sediment is what the appearance leaves in the context after the
appearance has been cognized. The three are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
    The chapter’s method is fivefold. It states the hard/soft distinction that the sediment
presupposes. It states the action chain by which an effect is produced and received, and the
crystallization of effect by which the residue becomes a hard manifestation. It defines the
sediment and the returning light that is its complement. It distinguishes the three layers
of sediment, and the three forms of integration. And it connects the sediment to the three
components of viability, to the limits of Part V, to the open questions of Chapter 34, and to
the core commitments of Chapter 43.

Remark 40.4 (The Sediment Is Not the Cost). The sediment is not the cost. The cost is
what the cognition demands of the context’s capacity (Chapter 39); the sediment is what the
cognition leaves behind after the demand has been met. The two are related: a cognition that
is high in cost may leave more sediment than a cognition that is low in cost. But the two are
not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.

Remark 40.5 (The Sediment Is Not the Manifestation). The sediment is not the manifestation.
The manifestation is the contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving context
(Chapter 13); the sediment is what the appearance leaves in the context after the appearance
has been cognized. The two are related: the manifestation is the appearance; the sediment is
the residue of the appearance. But the two are not the same, and the framework keeps them
apart.


40.3     Hard and Soft Manifestations
Before the sediment can be defined, a distinction must be stated between two kinds of
manifestation—the hard and the soft—because the sediment is defined in terms of it. The
distinction was flagged in Chapter 13 (the manifestational effect, which Chapter 13 forwards
here), and it is stated here in its own place.
    The distinction is structural, not psychological. It does not name two kinds of experience,
or two degrees of vividness, or two intensities of attention. It names two ways in which an
appearance can stand to the context in which it appears: one that persists and resists change,
and one that exists only as the act by which the first is activated.

Definition 40.1 (Hard Manifestation). (A) A hard manifestation of an identity in a context
is a manifestation with structural inertia: it resists change, and its persistence is a condition
of the unity of the manifestation. The material forms of an identity, the relations it sustains,
and the meanings it carries are hard manifestations in the appropriate context.

Definition 40.2 (Soft Manifestation). (A) A soft manifestation of an identity in a context
is a manifestation without structural inertia: it exists only as the act by which a subject’s
518                                                            Chapter 40. Cognitive Sediment


self-awareness activates a hard manifestation. The soft manifestation is the product of a hard
manifestation and the self-awareness of the identity.

    The distinction is worth stating because the sediment is what the hard manifestation leaves
in the context after the activation has ceased. The soft manifestation is the act; the hard
manifestation is what the act activates; the sediment is what the hard manifestation leaves
behind when the act is over.

Remark 40.6 (The Soft Manifestation Is the Product of the Pair). The soft manifestation
is the product of the pair (hard manifestation, self-awareness): it is the act by which the
hard manifestation is activated. Without the hard manifestation, there is nothing to activate;
without the self-awareness, there is no activation. The soft manifestation is therefore not a
third thing alongside the hard manifestation and the self-awareness; it is the act of the pair.

Remark 40.7 (The Distinction and the Limits of Part V). The distinction is related to the
limits of Part V, and the relation is worth marking. The hard manifestation is what the finite
subject can cognize; the soft manifestation is the act by which it is cognized. The limits
say that the finite subject cannot know all manifestations in all contexts (Chapter 27); the
distinction is the framework’s way of stating what the subject can and cannot cognize: it can
cognize the hard manifestation (the appearance), and it cannot cognize the identity itself (the
source that the hard manifestation manifests).


40.4     The Action Chain
The distinction between hard and soft manifestation raises a further question: by what chain
does an effect pass from the soft manifestation to a receiving hard manifestation? The
framework distinguishes four stages, and the distinction is worth stating because the sediment
is what the fourth stage leaves behind.

Definition 40.3 (Action Chain). (A) An action chain is a sequence of four stages:

  (i) Emission: the self-awareness of an identity activates a hard manifestation to emit a
      signal into the receiving context;

 (ii) Transmission: the signal travels through the context via epistemic light (the fluid
      element);

 (iii) Reception: the signal meets a receiving hard manifestation in the context;

 (iv) Effect: the receiving hard manifestation is modified by the signal.

   The action is actual only when all four stages occur. Before the fourth stage, the action is
potential: an emitted signal that has not yet landed.

Example 40.1 (The Radio Station). A radio employee, out of mischief, announces that
extraterrestrials are attacking. The announcement is an emission (stage i): the employee’s
voice, a hard manifestation, is activated by her self-awareness. The radio waves travel through
the air (stage ii): the transmission. As long as the waves are in the air and have not been
received, the action is potential, not actual. When a listener hears the announcement and
panics, the action becomes actual (stages iii–iv): the listener’s body and psychology, hard
manifestations, are modified by the signal. The panic, the rumor, and the social disruption
are the effects of the action.

Remark 40.8 (The Radio Metaphor Is Structural). The radio metaphor is not decorative. It
makes visible the structure of the action chain: the action is not complete until the signal lands
40.5. The Crystallization of Effect                                                             519


on a hard manifestation. The metaphor distinguishes three things that are easily run together:
the emission (the signal), the transmission (the medium), and the effect (the modification of
the receiver). The emission is the soft manifestation; the transmission is the fluid element
(epistemic light); the effect is the modification of the receiving hard manifestation.
Remark 40.9 (The Action Chain and the Locus of Evaluation). The action chain locates the
effect at stage (iv): an action is actual only when a receiving hard manifestation is modified.
Before stage (iv), the action is potential, and the framework does not treat a potential action as
an actual one. This is a structural claim about the action chain, not a normative claim about
when an action is subject to evaluation; the normative question belongs to the metaethical
volume, where the expansion criterion and the threefold ethical taxonomy are stated. Book I
states the action chain as a structural feature of the relation between manifestation and effect;
the ethical consequence is flagged in the later volume.


40.5      The Crystallization of Effect
The action chain states how an effect is received. The present section states what happens to the
effect after it has been received: it tends to crystallize—to become itself a hard manifestation.
Definition 40.4 (Crystallization). (A) The crystallization of an action is the process by which
the effect of the action, initially a modification of a receiving hard manifestation, becomes
itself a hard manifestation in the context: a sediment, a habit, a structure, an institution.
Example 40.2 (The Panic as Sediment). The panic that follows the radio announcement is
initially a soft effect (a modification of the listeners’ bodies and psychologies). Over time, it
crystallizes: it becomes a habit of fear (a hard manifestation in the listeners), a rumor (a hard
manifestation in the relational context), and a social disruption (a hard manifestation in the
material context). The action has become sediment.
Principle 40.1 (The Crystallization Principle). (T) Every actual action tends toward crystal-
lization: its effect, once received, becomes a hard manifestation in the context, and the hard
manifestation becomes the condition of further soft manifestations.
Proof of Principle 40.1.       1. By Definition 40.3, an actual action modifies a receiving hard
      manifestation.
   2. By Definition 40.1, a hard manifestation exhibits structural inertia: it resists change,
      and its persistence is a condition of unity.
   3. Hence the modification, once received, tends to persist and to become itself a hard
      manifestation.
   4. The principle follows.


    The principle is (T): it follows from the definitions of the action chain and of the hard
manifestation. The argument’s force is in step (2): if the hard manifestation did not exhibit
structural inertia, the modification would not tend to persist, and crystallization would not
occur.
Remark 40.10 (Crystallization and Sediment). Crystallization is the process by which the
effect of an action becomes a hard manifestation. The sediment (Section 40.6) is a species of
hard manifestation: the hard manifestation that is lodged—that persists, is not integrated
into the network of relations, and lays a lasting claim on the context’s capacity. Not every
crystallized effect is sediment; only the crystallized effect that is not integrated is sediment. The
distinction is the distinction between the process (crystallization) and the species (sediment);
the framework keeps it throughout.
520                                                            Chapter 40. Cognitive Sediment


40.6     The Definition of Sediment
The sediment is a species of intra-category epistemic light, and the definition states what the
species is.

Definition 40.5 (Cognitive Sediment). (A) Cognitive sediment is intra-category epistemic
light that has become lodged: light that has descended and not ascended, persists beyond the
activity that carried it, is not integrated into the relations of its context, and lays a lasting
claim on that context’s capacity.

   The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary: it says what the sediment is. The definition is not derived from the framework’s
other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for what the sediment is, and it is stated at
exactly that strength.
   The definition has three marks, and each is worth marking.


The first mark: persistence. The sediment persists beyond the activity that carried
it. The activity is the cognition that produced the manifestation; the persistence is the
continuation of the manifestation after the activity has ceased. The persistence is what makes
the sediment a residue, not a momentary product.


The second mark: non-integration. The sediment is not integrated into the relations of
its context. The relations of the context are the network of cognitions that hold the context
together; the non-integration is the sediment’s exclusion from that network. The sediment
is not connected to the relations that would make it active; it is a deposit, not a part of the
network.


The third mark: a lasting claim on capacity. The sediment lays a lasting claim on the
context’s capacity. The capacity is what the context can bear (Chapter 13); the claim is the
demand the sediment makes on the capacity without discharging it. The sediment occupies
the capacity without contributing to the network; it is a burden, not a part.

Remark 40.11 (The Three Marks Are Not Independent). The three marks are not independent.
They are three aspects of one structure—lodging—and hold or fail together. A sediment that
persisted but was integrated would not be sediment; a sediment that was not integrated but
did not persist would not be sediment; a sediment that persisted and was not integrated but
made no claim on capacity would not be sediment. The three marks are the three conditions
of lodging, and the framework keeps them together.

Remark 40.12 (The Sediment Is Not Every Unreturned Light). The sediment is not every
unreturned epistemic light. Intra-category epistemic light is light that has descended and not
ascended; it is the wider class within which the sediment is a species. Light that is still in
the course of its return, or that has been integrated, is intra-category epistemic light but not
sediment. The three marks of lodging separate the sediment from the wider class. The light
that is in the course of its return is what the next section calls returning light.

Remark 40.13 (The Sediment Is Not a Defect of the Cognition). The sediment is not a
defect of the cognition. It is a structural feature of the relation between the cognition and
its context: the cognition leaves something behind, and what it leaves is either integrated or
lodged. The framework’s claim is that the sediment is real, not that the cognition that leaves
it is defective.
40.7. Returning Light                                                                          521


40.7      Returning Light
The sediment is the light that has lodged. The complement of the sediment is the light that
returns: the returning light. The framework defines it here, because the definition of the
sediment is incomplete without the definition of its complement, and because the balance
criterion (Chapter 42) uses both.

Definition 40.6 (Returning Light). (A) Returning light is the epistemic light that continues
after the pause of an expression, and refers back to its source through what the identity left in
other manifestations.

    The definition states a structure, not a process. The structure is that of a light that
continues after the manifestation has ceased, and that refers back to the source through the
traces the source left in other manifestations. The traces are not the source; they are what the
source left behind. The returning light is the light that carries the effect of the traces back to
the source, without the source being manifested in the context of the traces.

Remark 40.14 (A Sketch of the Mechanism). An identity’s expression leaves traces in other
manifestations (effects, records, relations). When other identities take up these traces, reflective
epistemic light is generated; when they are affected, it may become ascending epistemic light,
which refers to the source. It is a return through other manifestations and not a direct return.
The sketch is offered as an estimate ((E)); its details are left for the chapters that treat the
specific contexts and their rules.

Remark 40.15 (Returning Light Is Not the Sediment). Returning light is not the sediment.
The sediment is the light that has lodged: it persists, is not integrated, and lays a lasting
claim on capacity. Returning light is the light that is in the course of its return: it has not
lodged, and its claim on capacity is being discharged through the network. The two are the
complements of the same structural relation: the sediment is the light that does not return,
and the returning light is the light that does.

Remark 40.16 (Returning Light and the Balance Criterion). The balance criterion (Chap-
ter 42) uses returning light as one of its positive terms and the sediment as its negative term.
The balance of an identity in a context is the received light preserved plus the ascending light
given, minus the received light become sediment; the returning light is the mechanism by
which the ascending light is given. The connection is stated here so that the reader knows
where the criterion’s terms come from; the criterion itself is the subject of Chapter 42.

Remark 40.17 (Returning Light and the Limits of Part V). The returning light is related
to the limits of Part V, and the relation is worth marking. The intrinsic unknownness
(Chapter 32) is what the returning light cannot remove: the light can return through the
traces, and the unknownness that the identity is not the subject remains. The returning
light is the framework’s account of how the light can return, within the partiality that the
intrinsic unknownness imposes. The distinction is the distinction between the return and the
completeness of the return; the framework keeps it apart.


40.8      The Three Layers of Sediment
The definition of sediment applies across the contexts of cognition. The framework distinguishes
three layers of sediment, according to the context in which the lodging occurs and the kind of
relations in which the lodging is embedded.

Definition 40.7 (Three Layers of Sediment). (A) Cognitive sediment has three layers:
522                                                             Chapter 40. Cognitive Sediment


  (i) cognitive sediment: the lodging is in the cognitive context, in the network of meanings
      that the identity’s expressions have produced;

 (ii) affective sediment: the lodging is in the cognitive context, in the experiences of feeling
      that the identity’s expressions have produced;

 (iii) ontological sediment: the lodging is in the material context, in the material forms that
       the identity’s expressions have produced.

    The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary:
it says what the three layers are. The definition is not derived from the framework’s other
principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the three layers, and it is stated at exactly that
strength.
    The three layers are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.

The first layer: cognitive sediment. The lodging is in the cognitive context. The
lodged epistemic light is meanings that have not been integrated into the network of relations.
The meanings persist, but they are not connected to the meanings that the identity’s other
expressions have produced; they lay a claim on the identity’s capacity for meaning that the
identity’s relations do not discharge.

The second layer: affective sediment. The lodging is in the cognitive context, but in
the register of feeling. The lodged epistemic light is experiences of feeling that have not been
worked through. The feelings persist, but they are not integrated into the relations that the
identity’s other expressions have produced; they lay a claim on the identity’s capacity for
feeling that the identity’s relations do not discharge.

The third layer: ontological sediment. The lodging is in the material context. The
lodged epistemic light is material forms that conflict with the structure of the identity. The
forms persist, but they are not integrated into the material relations that the identity’s
other expressions have produced; they lay a claim on the identity’s capacity for material
manifestation that the identity’s relations do not discharge.

Remark 40.18 (The Three Layers Are Distinguished Structurally). The three layers are
distinguished structurally, not evaluatively: by the context in which the lodging occurs and
by the kind of relation in which the lodging is embedded. The cognitive sediment is in
the cognitive context; the ontological sediment is in the material context. The framework’s
distinction between cognitive and material contexts is what the three layers follow from.

Remark 40.19 (The Order of the Layers Is an Estimate). A common pattern is that cognitive
sediment gives rise to affective, and affective to ontological, and that deeper layers are harder
to process. This is a possible pattern (E), not a necessity of logic: the framework does not
show that the layers must arise in that order, or that every case follows it. The pattern is
stated as an estimate, not as a universal.

Remark 40.20 (The Three Layers Are Not a Ranking). The three layers are not a ranking
of severity or of importance. The framework does not say that ontological sediment is worse
than cognitive sediment, or that cognitive sediment is more important than affective sediment.
It says that the three are distinguished by the context in which the lodging occurs and by the
kind of relation in which the lodging is embedded. The difference is structural, not evaluative.

Remark 40.21 (The Three Layers Point Beyond Themselves). The three layers are real
structural features of the relation between a cognition and its context; the features are
describable, and the description is what the framework offers. But the features are not the
40.9. The Integration of Sediment                                                               523


whole of what the relation is; the relation is between an identity and its manifestations, and the
identity and the manifestations are what they are. The distinction is the distinction between
the structure of the relation and what lies beyond it; the framework keeps it throughout.


40.9     The Integration of Sediment
The definition of sediment raises a further question. Can sediment be integrated? The
framework’s answer is that it can, and the answer is stated in a structural account of the forms
of integration. The full development of the integration is the work of Chapter 41; the present
section states the three forms in summary, so that the reader knows what integration is before
Chapter 41 develops it.
    Sediment can be integrated into the relations of its context. Integration is the process
by which lodged epistemic light is returned to the network of relations from which it was
separated. Three structural forms of integration are distinguished.
Definition 40.8 (Three Forms of Integration). (A) Sediment can be integrated in three
structural forms:
  (i) identification: the recognition of the lodged epistemic light as lodged—the discernment
      of sediment by its three marks;
 (ii) structural recognition: the recognition that lodging is a structural condition of the relation
      between a cognition and its context, not a deviation from a norm;
 (iii) return: the re-entry of the lodged epistemic light into the network of relations of its
       context, through expression in some form.
    The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary:
it says what the three forms are. The definition is not derived from the framework’s other
principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the three forms, and it is stated at exactly that
strength.
    The three forms are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart. The first form is
the recognition that the epistemic light is not on its way back, and that it is claiming capacity
that the context cannot discharge. The second form is the recognition that the lodging is not
a failure of the identity or of the context, but a structural feature of the relation between
them. The third form is the re-entry of the epistemic light into the network from which it was
separated; the epistemic light becomes active again, and its claim on capacity is discharged.
Remark 40.22 (The Three Forms Are Not a Sequence). The three forms are not a temporal
sequence that every integration must traverse. They are three structural forms of integration,
and a given case of integration may involve one, two, or all three. The first form is the
recognition; the second is the structural understanding; the third is the return. The three are
related, but they are not a sequence. The conditions under which integration is possible, and
the limits of integration, are the subject of Chapter 41.
Remark 40.23 (Integration Is Structural Transformation). Integration is structural trans-
formation, not elimination. The lodged epistemic light is returned to the relations of its
context; the epistemic light becomes active, and its claim on capacity is discharged. What
integration produces is the transformation of sediment into returning light; the sediment is
not removed but integrated. The framework’s claim is structural: integration is the return of
lodged epistemic light to the relations of its context.
Remark 40.24 (No Terminal State). Sediment accumulates; there is no final state in which it
is absent. This is a structural feature of the relation between a cognition and its context, not a
task to be completed. The framework claims the possibility of integration, within a structure
in which sediment continues to arise.
524                                                             Chapter 40. Cognitive Sediment


40.10      The Sediment and the Three Components of Viability
The sediment is related to the three components of viability (Chapter 37), and the relation is
worth stating.

The sediment and fidelity. The sediment is not a failure of fidelity; it is what the cognition
leaves behind after the manifestation has been cognized. A cognition can be high in fidelity
(the manifestation preserves the essential determination of the source) and still leave sediment
(the manifestation’s residue is not integrated into the context’s relations). The two are different,
and the framework keeps them apart.

The sediment and sustainability. The sediment is a claim on the context’s capacity
(Chapter 39). It is what makes the sustainability of the relation more demanding: the sediment
occupies the capacity without discharging it, and the cognition must bear the cost of the
sediment in addition to the cost of the manifestation. The sediment is not the cost, but it
adds to the cost, and the framework keeps the two related but distinct.

The sediment and recoverability. The sediment is one of the conditions that can cross
the singularity (Chapter 37, Section 37.7). The singularity is the threshold at which the cost of
restoring a manifestation exceeds the cost of producing a new one; the sediment, by occupying
the capacity without discharging it, can raise the cost of restoration to the point where the
singularity is crossed. The sediment is not the singularity, but it is one of the conditions that
bring it about, and the framework keeps the two related but distinct.
Remark 40.25 (The Sediment Is Not a Component of Viability). The sediment is not a
fourth component of viability. Viability has three components: fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability (Chapter 37). The sediment is what the cognition leaves behind in the context,
and it is related to the three components (it is not a failure of fidelity, it adds to the cost, and
it can cross the singularity). But it is not a fourth component; it is the residue of the relation,
not the character of the relation.
Remark 40.26 (The Sediment Points Beyond Itself). The sediment is a real structural
feature of the relation between a cognition and its context; the feature is describable, and
the description is what the framework offers. But the feature is not the whole of what the
relation is; the relation is between an identity and its manifestations, and the identity and the
manifestations are what they are. The distinction is the distinction between the structure of
the relation and what lies beyond it; the framework keeps it throughout.


40.11      Sediment, Transformation, and Loss of Identity
The concept of sediment is related to two other concepts that are easily confused with it:
transformation and loss of identity. The chapter states the distinctions.

First concept: sediment. Lodged epistemic light in a context, with the three marks of
lodging (persistence, non-integration, and a lasting claim on capacity). The sediment is a
feature of the relation between an identity and its context; it is not a feature of the identity.

Second concept: transformation. A change of manifestation or structure that the
identity’s allowable class permits, with no loss of identity. The transformation is a change
in the manifestations; it is not a change in the identity. The identity is conserved across
the transformation, as the framework’s account of conservation established (Chapter 12,
Section 12.7).
40.12. The Sediment and the Limits of Part V                                                  525


Third concept: loss of identity. A change in which the identity ceases to be the identity it
was. The loss of identity is not a matter of degree; the principle of identity rigidity established
that identity admits no degrees (Chapter 12, Principle 12.1). Sediment and transformation
can alter the structural viability of manifestations; neither is, by itself, a loss of identity.
    The three concepts are distinct, and the distinctions are structural. Sediment is a feature
of the relation between identity and manifestation; transformation is a change in the manifes-
tations; loss of identity is a change in the identity. The three answer different questions, and
an answer to one does not answer the others.

Remark 40.27 (Sediment Threatens Viability, Not Identity). The accumulation of sediment
does not entail loss of identity. An identity can be surrounded by sediment, can be hindered
by sediment, can have its capacity for manifestation reduced by sediment, and still be the
identity it was; the conservation of identity (Chapter 12, Section 12.7) is what makes this
possible. Sediment threatens the viability of the relation; the identity itself is conserved.

Remark 40.28 (Transformation Is Not Loss). A transformation of manifestations is not a loss
of identity. The manifestations may change in structure, in context, in mode; the identity is
conserved. The distinction was drawn in Chapter 25, in the resolution of the tension between
rigidity and dynamism; the present section applies it to the specific case of sediment and
transformation. Transformation is a change in the manifestations with the identity conserved.

Remark 40.29 (Loss of Identity Is Not a Matter of Degree). The loss of identity is not a
matter of degree. Identity admits no degrees (Chapter 12, Principle 12.1); a change either is a
change within the identity’s allowable class, or it is not. Sediment and transformation can be
more or less; loss of identity cannot. The framework’s claim is that the three concepts are
distinct, and that the distinctions are structural, not evaluative.

Remark 40.30 (The Three Concepts Are Not a Ranking). The three concepts are not a ranking
of severity. The framework does not say that loss of identity is worse than transformation, or
that transformation is worse than sediment. It says that the three are distinct, and that each
names a different kind of change or residue. The difference is structural, not evaluative.


40.12      The Sediment and the Limits of Part V
The sediment is related to the limits of Part V, and the relation is worth marking, because the
relation is what makes the concept of sediment precise.
    The limits say what the finite subject cannot do: it cannot know all manifestations of
an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it cannot complete its knowledge of epistemic light
(Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic unknownness of the other (Chapter 32), and it
cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33). The sediment is what the cognition leaves
behind, given the limits: the sediment is a residue of the cognition, and the residue is subject
to the same partiality that the limits impose. The distinction is the distinction between the
limits and the residue that the limits impose; the framework holds both.
    The sediment is also related to the disposition of Chapter 35. The humble subject is the
subject that can recognize the sediment: it recognizes that the cognition leaves something
behind, that the residue is either integrated or lodged, and that the integration is the work of
the inquiry. The humility is the disposition that accepts the sediment; the sediment is what
the disposition recognizes. The distinction is the distinction between the disposition and the
structural feature that the disposition recognizes; the framework keeps it apart.

Remark 40.31 (The Sediment and the Intrinsic Unknownness). The sediment is related to
the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness (Chapter 32), and the relation
is worth marking. The temporary unknownness is what the assessment of the sediment can
526                                                            Chapter 40. Cognitive Sediment


reduce: more manifestation, more analysis, and more comparison can make the recognition of
the sediment more precise. The intrinsic unknownness is what the assessment cannot remove:
the finite subject cannot exhaust the relation, and the sediment is always recognized within the
partiality that the intrinsic unknownness imposes. The distinction is the distinction between
the recognition and the completeness of the recognition; the framework keeps it apart.

Remark 40.32 (The Sediment and the Plurality of Perspectives). The sediment is related to
the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33), and the relation is worth marking. The sediment is
what the cognition leaves behind in one context; the plurality of perspectives is the fact that
the identity can be cognized from more than one perspective. The sediment of one context is
not the sediment of another; the recognition of the sediment is perspective-bound, and the
plurality of perspectives is the condition under which the sediment can be recognized from
more than one angle. The distinction is the distinction between the sediment and the plurality
of perspectives; the framework keeps it apart.


40.13      The Sediment and the Open Questions of Chapter 34
The sediment is related to three of the fourteen open questions of Chapter 34, and the relation
is worth marking.
    The first is the question of the exact boundary between the reduction of viability and the
singularity (Question 2). The present chapter states the sediment as one of the conditions that
can bring the singularity about; the exact relation between the sediment and the singularity is
left open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations to an extension.
    The second is the question of the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of the
balance criterion (Question 6). The present chapter states the sediment and the returning
light, which are the two terms of the balance criterion; the exact relation between the sediment
and the balance is left open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations to an extension.
    The third is the question of the relation among the aspects of cost (Question 8). The
present chapter states the sediment as the residue of the cost; the exact relation between the
sediment and the three aspects of cost is left open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations
to an extension.

Remark 40.33 (The Open Questions Are Invitations, Not Defeats). The three open questions
are invitations to an extension of the framework, not defeats of it. The framework states the
sediment at the strength its arguments support; the questions that the sediment raises but
does not settle are the framework’s statement of where the inquiry continues. A reader who
settles one of the questions has extended the framework; a reader who shows that the question
is not real has shown a limit of the framework’s formulation.


40.14      The Sediment and the Core Commitments of Chapter 43
The sediment is related to the core commitments of the framework, and the relation is worth
marking.
    The sediment is not one of the ten core commitments (Chapter 43), but it is a structural
feature that the core commitments make intelligible. The commitment to the finitude of the
epistemic subject (C1) is what makes the sediment unavoidable: the finite subject cannot
process all the light it receives, and the unprocessed light becomes sediment. The commitment
to identity conservation (C4) is what makes the sediment not a loss of identity: the identity is
conserved across the sediment, and the sediment is a feature of the relation between the identity
and its manifestations, not of the identity itself. The commitment to the non-duplicability of
identity (C10) is what makes the sediment specific to a context: the sediment of one context
40.15. Scope and Vulnerability                                                                527


is not the sediment of another, and the identity that the sediment is the residue of is not
duplicated in the sediment.

Remark 40.34 (The Sediment and the Core Commitments). The sediment is not one of the
ten core commitments (Chapter 43), but it is a structural feature that the core commitments
make intelligible. The commitment to the finitude of the epistemic subject (C1) is what makes
the sediment unavoidable; the commitment to identity conservation (C4) is what makes the
sediment not a loss of identity; the commitment to the non-duplicability of identity (C10) is
what makes the sediment specific to a context. The sediment is not a core commitment, but it
is a structural feature of the relation that the core commitments describe.


40.15      Scope and Vulnerability
The account is stated at the strength its argument supports, and its scope and vulnerability
are worth stating.
    The account is valid for the class of relations the framework treats: the relations between
identities and their manifestations in cognitive contexts, under the conditions the framework’s
definitions specify. It says that the sediment has three layers and three forms of integration; it
does not say that the sediment can be measured in a common unit, or that the integration
can always be achieved.
    The account rests on the framework’s account of identity (Chapter 12), of manifestation
(Chapter 13), of the three components of viability (Chapter 37), and of the cost of cognition
(Chapter 39). The account’s force is no greater than the force of these commitments; a reader
who rejects one of them has a reason to reject the corresponding part of the account, and the
framework does not pretend otherwise.
    The account would be put in question by two things.

First challenge. A case in which a cognition leaves nothing behind in its context. If such a
case could be given, the definition of sediment would be empty for that case, and the account
would need to be revised. The framework does not claim that no such case can be described;
it claims that none has been described that survives the framework’s definitions, and it argues
that none can be.

Second challenge. A case in which what is left behind is integrated in a way that the three
forms do not cover. If such a case could be given, the account of the three forms would be
incomplete, and the framework would need to add a fourth form. The framework holds that
the three forms are the ones the framework has identified, and it states the account at exactly
the strength its arguments support.

Remark 40.35 (The Account Is Not a Formula). The account is not a formula. It states the
sediment, its three layers, and the three forms of integration; it does not offer an algorithm for
measuring the sediment or for achieving the integration in a given case. The identification of
the sediment in a particular case is the work of the inquiry, not of the account. The account’s
role is to state the conditions the inquiry aims at, not to substitute for the inquiry.

Remark 40.36 (The Account Points Beyond Itself). The account points beyond itself. The
sediment and the integration are real structural features of the relation between a cognition and
its context; the features are describable, and the description is what the framework offers. But
the features are not the whole of what the relation is; the relation is between an identity and
its manifestations, and the identity and the manifestations are what they are. The distinction
is the distinction between the structure of the relation and what lies beyond it; the framework
keeps it throughout.

40.16      What This Chapter Does Not Establish


Six things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.

    First, the chapter does not develop the singularity. The singularity is the threshold at
which the cost of restoring a manifestation exceeds the cost of producing a new one; it is
developed in Chapter 37, Section 37.7, in the chapter that states the third component of
viability. The present chapter states the sediment, which is one of the conditions that can
bring the singularity about, but it does not develop the singularity itself.

    Second, the chapter does not develop the balance criterion. The balance criterion is the
framework’s measure of the relation between an identity and the epistemic light it receives; it
is the subject of Chapter 42. The present chapter states the sediment and the returning light,
which are the two terms of the balance criterion, but it does not develop the criterion itself.

    Third, the chapter does not develop the integration of sediment beyond the statement
of the three forms. The full account of the integration—the conditions under which it is
possible, the limits of integration, the relation between integration and self-awareness, and the
relation between integration and the singularity—is the subject of Chapter 41. The present
chapter states the three forms in summary, so that the reader knows what integration is before
Chapter 41 develops it.

   Fourth, the chapter does not settle the question of how the sediment is to be measured in
a particular case. The three layers are distinguished; their measurement is a matter for the
inquiry, not for the chapter.

    Fifth, the chapter does not develop the ethical consequence of the action chain. The action
chain locates the effect at stage (iv); the ethical consequence—whether a potential action is
subject to ethical evaluation—is a question for the metaethical volume, where the expansion
criterion and the threefold ethical taxonomy are stated. Book I states the action chain as a
structural feature of the relation between manifestation and effect; the ethical consequence is
flagged in the later volume.

    Sixth, the chapter does not settle the three open questions of Chapter 34 that the sediment
raises (Questions 2, 6, and 8). The present chapter states the sediment; the questions that the
sediment raises but does not settle are the framework’s invitations to an extension.




Remark 40.37 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It has
stated the hard/soft distinction (Definitions 40.1 and 40.2), the action chain (Definition 40.3),
and the crystallization of effect (Definition 40.4). It has defined the cognitive sediment
(Definition 40.5) and the returning light (Definition 40.6). It has distinguished the three
layers of sediment (cognitive, affective, ontological) (Definition 40.7). It has stated the three
forms of integration (identification, structural recognition, return) (Definition 40.8). It has
distinguished sediment from transformation and from loss of identity (Section 40.11), and
connected the sediment to the three components of viability (Section 40.10). And it has
connected the sediment to the limits of Part V (Section 40.12), to the open questions of
Chapter 34 (Section 40.13), and to the core commitments of Chapter 43 (Section 40.14).

A Question for Reflection
Consider something you have carried with you for a long time—a habit, a memory, a com-
mitment, a grief. Is it integrated into the rest of your life, or has it become lodged? If it has
lodged, is it cognitive, affective, or ontological sediment? What would it take for it to be
integrated? And consider the light that returns: is there something in your life that refers back
to its source through what you have left in other manifestations—a trace that still speaks, a
meaning that still carries? And consider the house of the scene: which of the three layers is
most visible in the letters, the tools, the pipes, the rust, the dust, the mold? What does your
answer tell you about the relation between what cognition leaves behind, the returning light,
and the viability of the relation between you and the source?

Chapter 41

The Integration of Cognitive Sediment

Scope
This chapter develops the integration of cognitive sediment. The previous chapter (Chapter 40)
defined the sediment, stated the hard/soft distinction, the action chain, the crystallization of
effect, and the returning light, and named the three forms of integration in summary; the present
chapter states what integration is (Definition 41.1), states the three forms in their own place
(Definition 41.2), states the four conditions under which integration is possible (Section 41.5),
connects integration to self-awareness (Chapter 20), to returning light (Chapter 40), and to the
three components of viability (Chapter 37), and states the limits of integration (Section 41.12).
    The chapter is written after the rewrites of Chapters 20 and 40, and it is consistent with
them. The relation to self-awareness uses the wide/reflexive distinction, and the unconscious as
weak self-awareness, that Chapter 20 states; the fourth condition of integration (Section 41.5)
is stated in terms of that distinction, and the unconscious is stated as one of the conditions
that can block integration. The relation to returning light uses the definition that Chapter 40
gives; the integration of sediment is what produces returning light, and the balance criterion
of Chapter 42 uses the two as its positive and negative terms.
    The singularity and recoverability, which the first edition of Book I referenced to Chapter 42,
are now developed in Chapter 37 (Section 37.7 and Section 37.6), the chapter that states the
third component of viability. Chapter 42 is the balance criterion, not the singularity; the
chapter’s references to the singularity point to Chapter 37, and its references to the balance
criterion point to Chapter 42.
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “integration,” “identification,” “struc-
tural recognition,” “return,” “condition,” or “returning light,” these are structural terms, and
their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in Chapter 40. The chapter’s silence
on questions of value is not a denial but a recognition that the epistemic description is not the
whole of what can be said.

Remark 41.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI). The chapter is the sixth of the eight chapters of
Part VI. The previous chapters defined viability and its three components (Chapters 36 and 37),
developed the first component (fidelity) through the distinction between the tendency to express
and the degree of structural fidelity (Chapter 38), the second component (sustainability)
through the account of the cost of cognition (Chapter 39), and the sediment (the residue of the
cost) in its own place (Chapter 40). The present chapter states the integration of the sediment:
what it is, in what forms it is achieved, under what conditions it is possible, and what its limits
are. The next chapter (Chapter 42) states the balance criterion; the last chapter of Part VI
(Chapter 43) states the core commitments and the dependency map. The chapter’s role is to
state the integration at the strength its argument supports, and to prepare the ground for the
chapter that states the balance criterion.
