41.1     A Scene
Consider a person who has spent twenty years in a profession, and who has recently come to
see that the profession was not for her. She has left it, but she has not left it behind. The
habits of the profession are still with her: the way she reads a document, the way she sizes up
a room, the way she answers a question. Some of these habits she values; some she resents;
some she does not notice. The profession is gone, but what it taught her is still lodged in her.
     She has three options, and each is a different way of dealing with what is lodged.
     The first option is to ignore it. She can act as if the profession never existed, and let the
habits persist unexamined. This is what the framework would call the persistence of sediment
without integration: the lodged epistemic light persists, is not connected to the rest of her life,
and continues to lay a claim on her capacity.
     The second option is to fight it. She can try to eliminate the habits, to unlearn what the
profession taught, to become someone who never had them. This is what the framework would
call the attempt to remove the sediment by rejection: the lodged epistemic light is resisted,
but resisting it does not integrate it; it only adds another layer of lodging on top of the first.
     The third option is to integrate it. She can come to understand the habits, to see what
they were for, to decide which are still useful and which are not, and to make the ones that
are useful part of her present life. This is what the framework would call integration: the
lodged epistemic light is returned to the network of her present relations, and its claim on her
capacity is discharged.
     The three options are not the same. Ignoring the sediment leaves it lodged. Fighting it adds
to it. Integrating it transforms it. The transformation is not the elimination of the sediment;
it is the return of the sediment to the network of relations from which it was separated.
     The scene poses a question. What is integration, exactly, and how is it possible? The
present chapter’s answer is that integration is the return of lodged epistemic light to the
network of relations of its context, and that it is possible under four conditions, in three forms,
and with limits that the framework states.

Remark 41.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows integration
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the definitions that follow; it makes them
intelligible before they are stated. The definitions and the argument are given in the sections
that follow, and the scene carries no weight in them.

Remark 41.3 (The Scene Shows Three Responses, Not Three People). The scene is easily
read as an observation about a person’s choices. The observation is not wrong, but it hides the
structural point. The structural point is that the three options (ignoring, fighting, integrating)
are three structural responses to the lodged sediment, and the three are distinguished by what
they do to the lodging. Ignoring leaves the lodging unchanged; fighting adds a new layer of
lodging; integrating transforms the lodging into returning light. The scene is the framework’s
way of showing that the integration is not one option among others; it is the response that
transforms the sediment, and the other two responses are failures to make the transformation.
A reader who takes the scene as a display of a person’s choices has read the scene; a reader
who takes it as a display of the three structural responses has read the structural point.


41.2     The Question
The previous chapters of Part VI have developed the concept of viability and its relation
to the cost of cognition and to the sediment. Chapter 36 defined viability and named its
three components. Chapter 37 defined the three components, argued for their minimality,
and developed recoverability through the account of the singularity. Chapter 38 developed
fidelity. Chapter 39 developed sustainability through the account of the cost of cognition.
41.3. The Definition of Integration                                                           533


Chapter 40 defined the cognitive sediment, stated the hard/soft distinction, the action chain,
the crystallization of effect, and the returning light, distinguished its three layers, and named
the three forms of integration in summary.
    The present chapter asks: what is the integration of cognitive sediment, and how is it
possible? The question is not what the sediment is; Chapter 40 has said that. The question is
what it is to integrate the sediment, what conditions make integration possible, and what the
integration can and cannot achieve.
    The question is not idle. The sediment is one of the conditions that can cross the singularity
(Chapter 37, Section 37.7); if integration were impossible, the sediment would accumulate
without remedy, and the relation between an identity and its manifestations would become
unsustainable. If integration were easy, the sediment would not be a structural problem. The
framework’s claim is that integration is possible, but not easy, and not always achievable; and
that the conditions, forms, and limits of integration are what the present chapter states.
    The chapter’s method is fivefold. It defines integration (41.1), and distinguishes integration
from mere removal. It states the three forms of integration in their own place (41.2). It
states the four conditions under which integration is possible (41.5), and connects them to
self-awareness (Chapter 20) and to the unconscious as weak self-awareness. It states the
relation between integration and returning light (Chapter 40). And it states the limits of
integration (41.12), and the relation between integration and the three components of viability
(Chapter 37).

Remark 41.4 (The Question and the Limits of Part V). The question is related to the
limits of Part V, and the relation is worth marking. The limits say what the finite subject
cannot do: it cannot know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it
cannot complete its knowledge of epistemic light (Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic
unknownness of the other (Chapter 32), and it cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33).
The integration is what the finite subject can do, given the limits: it can return the lodged
light to the network of relations, and it can transform the sediment into returning light, within
the partiality that the limits impose. The distinction is the distinction between the limits and
the activity that the limits permit; the framework holds both.


41.3     The Definition of Integration
Definition 41.1 (Integration of Cognitive Sediment). (A) The integration of cognitive sediment
is the return of lodged epistemic light to the network of relations of its context. It is the
transformation of sediment into returning light; it is not the elimination of the sediment, and
it is not the removal of the lodged light from the context.

   The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary: it says what integration is. The definition is not derived from the framework’s
other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for what integration is, and it is stated at
exactly that strength.
   The definition has two parts, and both are worth marking.

The first part: return to the network. Integration is the return of the lodged epistemic
light to the network of relations of its context. The lodged light is not removed from the
context; it is returned to the network. The return makes the light active again; its claim on
capacity is discharged, not by removing it, but by integrating it.

The second part: transformation into returning light. Integration is the transformation
of sediment into returning light (Chapter 40, Definition 40.6). The sediment is not removed; it
is transformed. The returning light is the light that continues after the pause of the expression,
534                                         Chapter 41. The Integration of Cognitive Sediment


and refers back to its source through what the identity left in other manifestations; the
integration is the activity by which the lodged light becomes returning light. The distinction
is the distinction between transformation and elimination; the framework keeps it throughout.
A reader who reads integration as the removal of the sediment has misread it; a reader who
reads it as the transformation of the sediment into returning light has read it correctly.

Remark 41.5 (Integration Is Not Removal). Integration is not removal. The lodged epistemic
light is not removed from the context; it is returned to the network. Removal would leave the
capacity of the context intact, but it would not transform the sediment; it would only move it.
Integration transforms the sediment, by making it active in the network from which it was
separated.

Remark 41.6 (Integration Is Not Rejection). Integration is not rejection. The lodged
epistemic light is not resisted; it is recognized, understood, and returned. Rejection would add
a new layer of lodging on top of the existing one, because the effort to resist the sediment is
itself a form of lodged light. Integration does not resist the sediment; it transforms it.

Remark 41.7 (Integration Is Not Ignorance). Integration is not ignorance. The lodged
epistemic light is not ignored; it is recognized. Ignoring the sediment leaves it lodged;
integration returns it to the network. The distinction is the distinction between not noticing
and noticing; the framework keeps it throughout.

Remark 41.8 (The Definition and the Limits of Part V). The definition is related to the limits
of Part V, and the relation is worth marking. The integration does not claim completeness:
the finite subject cannot integrate all the sediment it produces, and the integration is always
partial, within the intrinsic unknownness that the limits impose (Chapter 32). The definition
is the framework’s statement of what the integration is, within the partiality that the limits
permit; it does not claim that the integration is exhaustive.


41.4     The Three Forms of Integration
The definition of integration raises a question: what are the forms in which integration is
achieved? The framework distinguishes three, which were named in summary in Chapter 40
and are stated here in their own place.

Definition 41.2 (Three Forms of Integration). (A) Integration of cognitive sediment takes
three forms:

  (i) identification: the recognition of the lodged epistemic light as lodged—the discernment
      of the sediment by its three marks;

 (ii) structural recognition: the recognition that the lodging is a structural condition of the
      relation between a cognition and its context, not a deviation from a norm;

 (iii) return: the re-entry of the lodged epistemic light into the network of relations of its
       context, through expression in some form.

    The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary:
it says what the three forms are. The definition is not derived from the framework’s other
principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the three forms, and it is stated at exactly that
strength.
    The three forms are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
41.5. The Conditions of Integration                                                          535


The first form: identification. The recognition of the lodged epistemic light as lodged.
The discernment of the sediment by its three marks (persistence, non-integration, and a lasting
claim on capacity). The identification is the first step: the subject must recognize that there
is a sediment, and recognize it for what it is. Without the identification, the other forms are
not possible; the subject does not know what it is trying to integrate.


The second form: structural recognition. The recognition that the lodging is a structural
condition of the relation between a cognition and its context, not a deviation from a norm.
The structural recognition is the second step: the subject must understand that the sediment is
not a failure of the identity or of the context, but a structural feature of the relation. Without
the structural recognition, the subject may misinterpret the sediment as a defect, and the
attempt to integrate may become an attempt to eliminate.


The third form: return. The re-entry of the lodged epistemic light into the network of
relations of its context, through expression in some form. The return is the third step: the
subject must return the lodged light to the network, by expressing it in a way that makes
it active again. Without the return, the identification and the structural recognition remain
theoretical; the sediment is still lodged. The return is what produces the returning light of
Chapter 40.

Remark 41.9 (The Three Forms Are Not a Sequence). The three forms are not a temporal
sequence that every integration must traverse. They are three structural forms of integration,
and a given case may involve one, two, or all three. The first form is the recognition; the
second is the structural understanding; the third is the return. The three are related, but they
are not a sequence.

Remark 41.10 (The Three Forms Are Not Independent). The three forms are not independent.
Identification without structural recognition may lead to a rejection of the sediment, not to its
integration. Structural recognition without return may lead to a theoretical understanding
that does not change the relation. Identification without return, or structural recognition
without return, does not integrate the sediment; it only prepares for the integration.

Remark 41.11 (The Three Forms Are Not a Formula). The three forms are not a formula.
The framework states the three forms, but it does not offer an algorithm for achieving them in
a given case. The identification of the sediment in a particular case is the work of the inquiry,
not of the framework. The three forms are the conditions the inquiry aims at, not a procedure
that guarantees the outcome.


41.5     The Conditions of Integration
The definition and the three forms raise a further question: under what conditions is integration
possible? The framework states four conditions. The fourth is stated in terms of the distinction
between wide and reflexive self-awareness, and between full and weak self-awareness, that
Chapter 20 draws.


The first condition: the sediment must be recognizable. The lodged epistemic light
must be recognizable by the three marks of lodging. If the sediment cannot be recognized—if
the lodged light is indistinguishable from the integrated light—the subject cannot begin the
integration. The recognizability is the first condition.
536                                         Chapter 41. The Integration of Cognitive Sediment


The second condition: the context must have capacity for the return. The context
must have the capacity to receive the returned light. If the context’s capacity is exhausted—if
the sediment has occupied all the capacity that the return would require—the return is not
possible. The capacity for the return is the second condition.

The third condition: the subject must have the reflexive self-awareness to recognize
the sediment and its structure. The subject must be able to recognize the lodged light
(identification) and to understand its structural character (structural recognition). The reflexive
self-awareness (Chapter 20, Remark 20.11) is the third condition: it is the special case of
self-awareness in which a subject regulates its relation to its own self-model, and it is the case
that the first two forms of integration require.

The fourth condition: the subject’s self-awareness must not be weak in the relevant
respect. The return (the third form of integration) requires the full exercise of the mechanism
of regulation, not the weak self-awareness that Chapter 20 calls the unconscious (Chapter 20,
Definition 20.4). A subject whose self-awareness is weak—whose regulation of its relation
to its source is incomplete— cannot make the return, because the return is the activity by
which the lodged light is returned to the network, and the return requires the mechanism to
be operative. The fourth condition is the condition that the unconscious can block integration:
not because the unconscious is a separate mechanism, but because the weak self-awareness
that the unconscious names is the mode of the mechanism in which the return is not fully
made.
    The four conditions are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart. The first is
a condition on the sediment; the second is a condition on the context; the third and fourth
are conditions on the subject—the third on the subject’s reflexive self-awareness, the fourth
on the subject’s full self-awareness. The four together are the framework’s account of what
integration requires.
Remark 41.12 (The Conditions Are Not Sufficient). The conditions are not sufficient. A
case can satisfy all four conditions and still not achieve integration, because the integration
depends on factors the conditions do not control: the exercise of the subject’s self-awareness
in the return, the context’s conditions, the identity’s capacity for further manifestation. The
conditions are necessary, not sufficient; the framework does not claim that they guarantee the
outcome. The exercise of self-awareness is not a volitional posit added to the framework; it is
the activity that Chapter 20’s mechanism of regulation names, and the framework states it as
a structural activity, not as a free choice.
Remark 41.13 (The Conditions Are Not a Formula). The conditions are not a formula.
They state what integration requires, but they do not offer an algorithm for achieving it. The
application of the conditions to a given case is the work of the inquiry, not of the framework.
Remark 41.14 (The Conditions and Self-Awareness). The third and fourth conditions connect
integration to self-awareness (Chapter 20). Self-awareness is the mechanism of regulation by
which the manifestation adjusts its relation to its source; integration is one of the forms that
the regulation takes. The subject that integrates the sediment is a subject that exercises its
self-awareness in the reflexive mode (for identification and structural recognition) and in the
full mode (for the return). The unconscious—weak self-awareness—is the mode in which the
return is blocked.


41.6      Integration and Self-Awareness
The connection between integration and self-awareness is worth stating in its own place, and
it is stated in terms of the distinction that Chapter 20 draws.
41.7. Integration and Returning Light                                                         537


    Self-awareness, as defined in Chapter 20, is the mechanism of regulation by which a
manifestation adjusts its relation to its source. It has three channels: the descending channel
(reception), the reflective channel (emission), and the ascending channel (return). Integration
is the activity of the third channel: the return of the lodged epistemic light to the network of
relations of its context.
    The integration is not a separate mechanism, added to self-awareness. It is one of the
activities of self-awareness, in its ascending channel. The subject that integrates the sediment
is a subject that exercises its self-awareness in the ascending direction, returning the lodged
light to its source.
Remark 41.15 (Integration Requires Reflexive and Full Self-Awareness). Integration requires
both the reflexive mode and the full mode of self-awareness (Chapter 20, Remark 20.11). The
reflexive mode is required for the identification and the structural recognition: the subject
must be able to cognize its own sediment, and this is a reflexive act of self-awareness. The
full mode is required for the return: the subject must be able to return the lodged light to
the network, and this requires the mechanism of regulation to be operative, not weak. The
distinction between the two modes is the distinction between cognizing the sediment and
returning it; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 41.16 (Integration Is Not Reflexive Consciousness). Integration is not reflexive
consciousness (Chapter 20). Reflexive consciousness is the subject’s consciousness of its own
consciousness; it is a specific act of consciousness in the relational context. Integration is
the return of the lodged light to the network; it is an activity of the ascending channel of
self-awareness, not the subject’s consciousness of itself. The two are related (the subject that
integrates the sediment must be conscious of what it is integrating, which is the reflexive
mode), but they are not the same.
Remark 41.17 (Integration Is the Ascending Channel). Integration is the ascending channel
of self-awareness. The descending channel is the reception of the light; the reflective channel is
the emission of the light; the ascending channel is the return of the light. Integration is the
return. The distinction is structural, not metaphorical; the framework uses the language of
the channels to state the structural relations among the three activities of self-awareness.
Remark 41.18 (The Unconscious Can Block Integration). The unconscious—weak self-
awareness (Chapter 20, Definition 20.4)—can block integration. It does not block it by being
a separate mechanism; it blocks it by being the mode of the mechanism in which the return is
not fully made. A subject whose self-awareness is weak in the relevant respect cannot complete
the third form of integration (the return), and the sediment remains lodged. The framework’s
claim is that the unconscious is one of the conditions that can block integration; the condition
is stated in Section 41.5, and the present remark connects it to the account of the unconscious
in Chapter 20.
Remark 41.19 (Integration Points Beyond Itself). The integration points beyond itself. The
integration is the activity of self-awareness; it is not the ground of the self. The integration
points beyond itself to what makes the self-awareness possible, and to what makes the
integration possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is
pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the
integration and the ground of the self; it is kept throughout the book.


41.7     Integration and Returning Light
Integration is related to returning light, and the relation is worth stating in its own place,
because Chapter 40 defined returning light as the complement of the sediment, and the
integration is what produces it.
538                                         Chapter 41. The Integration of Cognitive Sediment


Remark 41.20 (Integration Produces Returning Light). Integration is the transformation of
sediment into returning light (Definition 41.1; Chapter 40, Definition 40.6). The sediment is
the light that has lodged: it persists, is not integrated, and lays a lasting claim on capacity.
The returning light is the light that continues after the pause of the expression, and refers
back to its source through what the identity left in other manifestations. The integration is
the activity by which the lodged light becomes returning light; without the integration, the
light remains lodged, and no returning light is produced. The two are the complements of the
same structural relation: the sediment is the light that does not return, and the returning
light is the light that does; the integration is the activity that moves the one to the other.

Remark 41.21 (Returning Light and the Balance Criterion). The balance criterion (Chap-
ter 42) uses returning light as one of its positive terms and the sediment as its negative
term. The integration is the activity that increases the positive term (the returning light) and
decreases the negative term (the sediment); the balance criterion is the measure of the result.
The relation is stated here so that the reader knows where the criterion’s terms come from,
and what activity moves them; the criterion itself is the subject of Chapter 42.


41.8     Integration and the Three Components of Viability
Integration is related to the three components of viability (Chapter 37), and the relation is
worth stating.

Integration and fidelity. Integration does not change the fidelity of the manifestation; the
manifestation’s relation to its source is what it is. What integration changes is the relation
between the lodged light and the network; it returns the lodged light to the network, so that its
claim on the subject’s capacity is discharged. The fidelity of the manifestation is not affected
by the integration; the integration is about the sediment, not about the manifestation.

Integration and sustainability. Integration improves the sustainability of the relation
between an identity and its manifestations. The sediment is a claim on capacity that the
context cannot discharge (Chapter 40); integration discharges the claim by returning the
lodged light to the network. The sustainability is improved, because the capacity that the
sediment occupied is released for the relation. The integration is one of the activities by which
the relation is made more sustainable.

Integration and recoverability. Integration can prevent the crossing of the singularity
(Chapter 37, Section 37.7). The singularity is the threshold at which the cost of restoring a
manifestation exceeds the cost of producing a new one; the sediment, by occupying the capacity
without discharging it, can raise the cost of restoration to the point where the singularity
is crossed. Integration reduces the cost of restoration, by returning the lodged light to the
network; it can prevent the crossing of the singularity, and preserve the recoverability of the
relation.

Remark 41.22 (Integration Is Not the Restoration of Identity). Integration is not the restora-
tion of identity. The identity is conserved across the integration (Chapter 12, Section 12.7);
the integration is about the sediment, not about the identity. A relation that has lost its
recoverability may still be integrated; the integration does not restore the recoverability that
has been lost. The two are related, but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them
apart.

Remark 41.23 (Integration Is Not a Guarantee of Viability). Integration is not a guarantee of
viability. A relation can be integrated and still fail one of the three components; the integration
41.9. Integration and the Limits of Part V                                                    539


improves the sustainability, but it does not guarantee the fidelity or the recoverability. The
integration is one of the activities that the subject can perform; it is not the whole of the
viability of the relation.
Remark 41.24 (Integration Points Beyond Itself). The integration points beyond itself. The
integration is the activity of returning the lodged light to the network; it is not the ground of
the viability of the relation. The integration points beyond itself to what makes the relation
possible, and to what makes the viability possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing
is real, and that what is pointed to is not described by the framework. The distinction is the
distinction between the integration and the ground of the relation; it is kept throughout the
book.


41.9      Integration and the Limits of Part V
The integration is related to the limits of Part V, and the relation is worth marking, because
the relation is what makes the concept of integration precise.
    The limits say what the finite subject cannot do: it cannot know all manifestations of
an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it cannot complete its knowledge of epistemic light
(Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic unknownness of the other (Chapter 32), and it
cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33). The integration is what the finite subject can
do, given the limits: it can return the lodged light to the network of relations, and it can
transform the sediment into returning light, within the partiality that the limits impose. The
distinction is the distinction between the limits and the activity that the limits permit; the
framework holds both.
    The integration is also related to the disposition of Chapter 35. The humble subject is the
subject that can recognize the integration: it recognizes that the integration is possible, that
the integration is not guaranteed, and that the integration is the work of the inquiry. The
humility is the disposition that accepts the integration; the integration is what the disposition
recognizes. The distinction is the distinction between the disposition and the structural activity
that the disposition recognizes; the framework keeps it apart.
Remark 41.25 (The Integration and the Intrinsic Unknownness). The integration is related
to the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness (Chapter 32), and the relation
is worth marking. The temporary unknownness is what the integration can reduce: more
manifestation, more analysis, and more comparison can make the integration more complete.
The intrinsic unknownness is what the integration cannot remove: the finite subject cannot
exhaust the relation, and the integration is always partial, within the partiality that the
intrinsic unknownness imposes. The distinction is the distinction between the integration and
the completeness of the integration; the framework keeps it apart.
Remark 41.26 (The Integration and the Plurality of Perspectives). The integration is related
to the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33), and the relation is worth marking. The integration
is what the subject can do from one perspective; the plurality of perspectives is the fact that
the identity can be cognized from more than one perspective. The integration from one
perspective is not the integration from another; the integration is perspective-bound, and the
plurality of perspectives is the condition under which the integration can be made from more
than one angle. The distinction is the distinction between the integration and the plurality of
perspectives; the framework keeps it apart.


41.10      Integration and the Open Questions of Chapter 34
The integration is related to three of the fourteen open questions of Chapter 34, and the
relation is worth marking.
540                                         Chapter 41. The Integration of Cognitive Sediment


    The first is the question of the exact boundary between the reduction of viability and the
singularity (Question 2). The present chapter states the integration as one of the activities
that can prevent the crossing of the singularity; the exact relation between the integration and
the singularity is left open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations to an extension.
    The second is the question of the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of the
balance criterion (Question 6). The present chapter states the integration, which produces the
returning light that the balance criterion uses as its positive term; the exact relation between
the integration and the balance is left open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations to an
extension.
    The third is the question of whether the proposed criterion of manifestational adequacy
and the principle of contextual manifestational capacity can be given independent definition
and support (Question 7). The present chapter states the integration as the return of the
lodged light to the network; the exact relation between the integration and the capacity is left
open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations to an extension.
Remark 41.27 (The Open Questions Are Invitations, Not Defeats). The three open questions
are invitations to an extension of the framework, not defeats of it. The framework states the
integration at the strength its arguments support; the questions that the integration raises
but does not settle are the framework’s statement of where the inquiry continues. A reader
who settles one of the questions has extended the framework; a reader who shows that the
question is not real has shown a limit of the framework’s formulation.


41.11      Integration and the Core Commitments of Chapter 43
The integration is related to the core commitments of the framework, and the relation is worth
marking.
    The integration is not one of the ten core commitments (Chapter 43), but it is a structural
activity that the core commitments make intelligible. The commitment to the finitude of
the epistemic subject (C1) is what makes the integration necessary: the finite subject cannot
process all the light it receives, and the unprocessed light becomes sediment that must be
integrated. The commitment to identity conservation (C4) is what makes the integration not
a restoration of identity: the identity is conserved across the integration, and the integration is
an activity of the relation between the identity and its manifestations, not of the identity itself.
The commitment to the non-duplicability of identity (C10) is what makes the integration
specific to a context: the integration of one context is not the integration of another, and the
identity that the integration is the activity of is not duplicated in the integration.
Remark 41.28 (The Integration and the Core Commitments). The integration is not one
of the ten core commitments (Chapter 43), but it is a structural activity that the core
commitments make intelligible. The commitment to the finitude of the epistemic subject (C1)
is what makes the integration necessary; the commitment to identity conservation (C4) is what
makes the integration not a restoration of identity; the commitment to the non-duplicability
of identity (C10) is what makes the integration specific to a context. The integration is not a
core commitment, but it is a structural activity of the relation that the core commitments
describe.


41.12      The Limits of Integration
Integration is possible, but it is not unlimited, and the limits are worth stating.

The first limit: not every sediment is integrable. Some sediment is not integrable.
The lodged epistemic light may be so thoroughly separated from the network that the return is
41.13. Integration and the Singularity                                                        541


not possible; or the context’s capacity may be so exhausted that the return cannot be made; or
the subject’s self-awareness may be so weak in the relevant respect that the return is blocked
(Section 41.6, Remark on the unconscious). The framework does not claim that every sediment
can be integrated; it claims that some can, and that the conditions of integration state when
it can.

The second limit: integration has no terminal state. The sediment accumulates, and
the integration is an ongoing activity, not a terminal state. This is a structural feature of the
relation between a cognition and its context, not a task to be completed (Chapter 40). The
subject that integrates the sediment will find, in time, that new sediment has accumulated,
and will need to integrate again. The integration is the form that the relation takes, not the
state that the relation reaches.

The third limit: integration is not a substitute for sustainability. Integration
improves sustainability, but it is not a substitute for it. A relation that is unsustainable
because the cost of the manifestation exceeds the context’s capacity cannot be made sustainable
by integrating the sediment; the sustainability is a condition on the cost, not on the sediment.
The integration is one of the activities that the subject can perform; it is not a substitute for
the reduction of the cost.

The fourth limit: integration is not a substitute for recoverability. Integration can
prevent the crossing of the singularity, but it is not a substitute for recoverability. A relation
whose recoverability has been lost cannot be made recoverable by integrating the sediment;
the recoverability is a condition on the identity’s capacity to manifest, not on the sediment.
The integration is one of the activities that the subject can perform; it is not a substitute for
the preservation of the recoverability.
Remark 41.29 (The Limits Are Not Deficiencies). The limits are not deficiencies of the
integration. They are the conditions under which integration is possible, and they are stated
so that the reader knows what integration can and cannot achieve. A reader who accepts
the limits may still accept integration; a reader who rejects the limits is invited to show that
integration can achieve what the limits exclude.
Remark 41.30 (The Limits Point Beyond Themselves). The limits point beyond themselves.
The limits are the limits of the integration, not the limits of what is. The integration is the
activity of the finite subject; the limits are the limits of the finite subject’s activity. The
distinction is the distinction between the limits of integration and the limits of what is; the
framework keeps it throughout.


41.13      Integration and the Singularity
Integration is related to the singularity (Chapter 37, Section 37.7), and the relation is worth
marking.
    The singularity is the threshold at which the cost of restoring a manifestation exceeds
the cost of producing a new one (Chapter 37, Definition 37.2). The sediment is one of the
conditions that can cross the singularity; the integration is one of the activities that can
prevent the crossing.
    The relation between integration and the singularity is the relation between prevention
and the threshold. Integration prevents the crossing of the singularity, by returning the lodged
light to the network; without the integration, the sediment accumulates, the cost of restoration
rises, and the singularity may be crossed. The integration is the activity; the singularity is the
threshold that the activity prevents.
542                                        Chapter 41. The Integration of Cognitive Sediment


Remark 41.31 (Integration Is Not the Only Prevention). Integration is not the only prevention.
The singularity can be prevented by other activities: by the reduction of the cost of the
manifestation, by the preservation of the identity’s capacity for further manifestation, by the
maintenance of the context’s capacity. The integration is one of the activities; it is not the
only one. The framework’s claim is that the integration is one of the activities, and that its
relation to the singularity is as prevention to threshold.

Remark 41.32 (The Ethical Consequence of the Action Chain Is Not Developed Here).
Chapter 40 stated the action chain, and flagged that the ethical consequence of the action
chain—whether a potential action is subject to ethical evaluation—is a question for the
metaethical volume. The present chapter does not develop that consequence either. The
integration is the activity by which the sediment is returned to the network; the ethical
evaluation of the integration, and of the action chain that produced the sediment, belongs to
the metaethical volume, where the expansion criterion and the threefold ethical taxonomy are
stated. Book I states the integration as a structural feature of the relation between a cognition
and its context; the ethical consequence is flagged in the later volume.


41.14      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Six things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the singularity. The singularity is the threshold at
which the cost of restoring a manifestation exceeds the cost of producing a new one; it is
developed in Chapter 37 (Section 37.7), in the chapter that states the third component of
viability. The present chapter states the integration, and its relation to the singularity, but it
does not develop the singularity itself.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the balance criterion. The balance criterion is the
framework’s measure of the relation between an identity and the epistemic light it receives; it
is the subject of Chapter 42. The present chapter states the integration, and its relation to
the balance criterion, but it does not develop the criterion itself.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of how the integration is to be measured
in a particular case. The three forms are stated, and the four conditions are stated; their
measurement is a matter for the inquiry, not for the chapter.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim that the integration can always be achieved. The three
forms and the four conditions are necessary, not sufficient; the integration depends on factors
the conditions do not control. The framework holds that integration is possible, not that it is
guaranteed.
    Fifth, the chapter does not develop the ethical consequence of the action chain or of the
integration. The action chain was stated in Chapter 40, and the ethical consequence was
flagged there as a question for the metaethical volume; the integration’s ethical evaluation,
and the action chain’s, belong to the same volume. The present chapter states the integration
as a structural activity; the ethical consequence is flagged in the later volume.
    Sixth, the chapter does not settle the three open questions of Chapter 34 that the integration
raises (Questions 2, 6, and 7). The present chapter states the integration; the questions that
the integration raises but does not settle are the framework’s invitations to an extension.

Remark 41.33 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It has
defined the integration of cognitive sediment (Definition 41.1), and distinguished integration
from mere removal, from rejection, and from ignorance. It has stated the three forms of
integration in their own place (Definition 41.2). It has stated the four conditions of integration
(Section 41.5), and connected them to self-awareness (Chapter 20), to the unconscious as weak
self-awareness, and to returning light (Chapter 40). It has stated the limits of integration
(Section 41.12), and its relation to the three components of viability (Chapter 37) and to
41.15. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                           543


the singularity (Chapter 37). And it has connected the integration to the limits of Part V
(Section 41.9), to the open questions of Chapter 34 (Section 41.10), and to the core commitments
of Chapter 43 (Section 41.11).

A Question for Reflection
Consider something you have carried with you for a long time that has not been integrated
into your life—a memory, a habit, a resentment, a loyalty. What would it take for it to be
integrated? Would you need to recognize it as lodged (identification), to understand it as a
structural condition (structural recognition), to return it to your life in some form (return)?
544                                        Chapter 41. The Integration of Cognitive Sediment


Would your self-awareness need to be reflexive (to cognize the sediment) and full (to return
it, not weak)? And consider the person of the scene: which of the three options (ignoring,
fighting, integrating) is the one that transforms the sediment, and which are the ones that
leave it lodged or add to it? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the
integration of sediment, the returning light, and the viability of the relation between you and
the source?

The next chapter (Chapter 42) states the balance criterion: the framework’s measure of the
relation between an identity and the epistemic light it receives. The present chapter has stated
the integration, and its relation to the singularity (Chapter 37) and to the three components of
viability (Chapter 37); the next chapter states the criterion by which the flow of epistemic light
is measured, using returning light as its positive term and sediment as its negative term. The
last chapter of Part VI (Chapter 43) states the core commitments and the dependency map.
