Chapter 42

The Balance Criterion

Scope

This chapter states the framework’s measure of the relation between an identity and the
epistemic light it receives: the balance criterion. The criterion measures the extent to which
the received epistemic light is preserved or returned, less the extent to which it has become
cognitive sediment (Chapter 40). It is distinguished from viability (Chapter 36) and from
the three components of viability (Chapter 37); it is connected to the sediment (Chapter 40),
to the returning light (Chapter 40), and to the integration of sediment (Chapter 41); and
it is stated at the strength of an axiom (Definition 42.1), with the open question of how its
quantities are to be compared in a given case marked accordingly (Section 42.5).
    The chapter is written after the rewrites of Chapters 37, 40, and 41, and it is consistent
with them. The singularity, which the first edition of Book I referred to as a development of
the later volume, is now developed in Chapter 37 (Section 37.7, Definition 37.2); the present
chapter’s references to the singularity point there. The returning light, which the first edition
of Book I did not define, is now defined in Chapter 40 (Definition 40.6); the present chapter
states how the second term of the balance (the ascending light given) is produced by the
integration (Chapter 41) through the returning light, and the definition is the one Chapter 40
gives.
    Its claims are epistemic; where the chapter speaks of “balance,” “preserved,” “returned,”
“sediment,” “returning light,” “threshold,” or “measure,” these are structural terms, and their
sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in Chapters 40 and 41. The chapter’s
silence on questions of value is not a denial but a recognition that the epistemic description is
not the whole of what can be said.


Remark 42.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI). The chapter is the seventh of the eight
chapters of Part VI. The previous chapters defined viability and its three components (Chap-
ters 36 and 37), developed the first component (fidelity) through the distinction between the
tendency to express and the degree of structural fidelity (Chapter 38), the second component
(sustainability) through the account of the cost of cognition (Chapter 39), the sediment in
its own place (Chapter 40), and the integration of the sediment (Chapter 41). The present
chapter states the balance criterion: the framework’s measure of the relation between an
identity and the epistemic light it receives. The last chapter of Part VI (Chapter 43) states
the core commitments and the dependency map. The chapter’s role is to state the criterion at
the strength its argument supports, and to prepare the ground for the chapter that states the
commitments on which the criterion, and the whole framework, rest.
546                                                         Chapter 42. The Balance Criterion


42.1     A Scene
Consider a scholar who has spent her working life in a field, and who has just retired. Her
career can be described in three ways, and each is a different balance.
    The first way. She has read the field’s literature, mastered its methods, written its history.
She has taken what the field gave her—its texts, its problems, its standards—and she has
preserved it: she has carried it forward in her teaching, her scholarship, and her memory.
Little of it has been lost, and little of it has been left unprocessed. The balance is high: the
received light has been preserved, and little has become sediment.
    The second way. She has read the literature and mastered the methods, but she has not
been able to integrate what she has learned into a coherent account. Her notes are extensive,
her reading is broad, but her writing is thin. The received light has neither been preserved in
a form she can use nor returned to the field in a form others can use; it has lodged in her,
unprocessed. The balance is low: the received light has become sediment, and little has been
returned.
    The third way. She has read the literature and mastered the methods, and she has
integrated what she has learned into a coherent account. She has written the field’s history,
taught its methods, and trained its next generation. The received light has been preserved
and returned; little of it has lodged. The balance is high, and it is high in the second sense:
not only preserved, but returned.
    The three ways are not the same. The first is preservation without return; the second is
lodging without preservation; the third is preservation and return. The framework’s balance
criterion measures the difference: it measures the extent to which the received light has been
preserved or returned, less the extent to which it has lodged.
    The scene poses a question. What is the balance criterion, exactly, and how does it relate
to the three components of viability? The present chapter’s answer is that the balance criterion
is a measure of the relation between an identity and the epistemic light it receives, and that it
is distinct from viability and from the three components, though related to them. The chapter
states the criterion, the thresholds, and the relation.

Remark 42.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the balance
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the criterion; it makes the criterion intelligible
before it is stated. The criterion is stated in the sections that follow, and the scene carries no
weight in them.

Remark 42.3 (The Scene Shows the Two Positive Terms and the Negative Term). The scene
is easily read as an observation about a scholar. The observation is not wrong, but it hides
the structural point. The structural point is that the three careers differ in the three terms of
the balance. The first career is high in the first positive term (the received light preserved),
and low in the negative term (the sediment); the second career is low in the first positive term,
low in the second (the ascending light given), and high in the negative term (the sediment);
the third career is high in both positive terms and low in the negative term. The scene is the
framework’s way of showing that the balance is not a single quantity but a measure of three
terms, and that the three terms can be realized at different degrees. A reader who takes the
scene as a display of three careers has read the scene; a reader who takes it as a display of the
three terms of the balance has read the structural point.


42.2     The Question
The previous chapters of Part VI have developed the concept of viability and its components.
Chapter 36 defined viability as the epistemic structural character of the relation between an
identity and its manifestations, and named the three components: fidelity, sustainability, and
42.3. The Definition of the Balance Criterion                                                547


recoverability. Chapter 37 defined the three components, argued for their minimality, and
developed recoverability through the account of the singularity. Chapter 38 developed fidelity.
Chapter 39 developed sustainability through the account of the cost of cognition. Chapter 40
defined the cognitive sediment, the hard/soft distinction, the action chain, the crystallization
of effect, and the returning light. Chapter 41 developed the integration of cognitive sediment.
    The present chapter asks: is there a measure of the relation between an identity and
the epistemic light it receives, and if so, what is it? The framework’s answer is the balance
criterion. The criterion is not the same as viability, and not the same as any of the three
components; it is a measure that the framework uses to assess the relation under a particular
aspect, the aspect of the flow of epistemic light.
    The question is not idle. Viability is a structural character; the three components are
conditions on the relation. Neither is a measure. The balance criterion is the framework’s
measure of the flow of epistemic light, and it is what the framework uses to assess the relation
under the aspect of the flow. Without the criterion, the framework would have a structural
character and a set of conditions, but no measure; with the criterion, the framework has a way
of assessing the relation in a given case.
    The chapter’s method is fivefold. It defines the balance criterion (42.1). It distinguishes
the criterion from viability and from the three components. It states the three thresholds
(42.2), and the status of the criterion (42.5). It states the relation between the balance and
the returning light (Chapter 40) and the integration (Chapter 41). And it states the scope
and vulnerability of the criterion (42.11), and connects it to the limits of Part V, to the open
questions of Chapter 34, and to the core commitments of Chapter 43.

Remark 42.4 (The Question and the Limits of Part V). The question is related to the limits
of Part V, and the relation is worth marking. The limits say what the finite subject cannot do:
it cannot know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it cannot complete
its knowledge of epistemic light (Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic unknownness of
the other (Chapter 32), and it cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33). The balance
criterion is the measure that the finite subject can apply, given the limits: it measures the
extent to which the received light has been preserved or returned, less the extent to which
it has become sediment, within the partiality that the limits impose. The distinction is the
distinction between the limits and the measure that the limits permit; the framework holds
both.


42.3     The Definition of the Balance Criterion
Definition 42.1 (The Balance Criterion). (A) The balance of an identity in a cognitive
context is the extent to which the descending epistemic light it has received is preserved or
returned, less the extent to which it has become cognitive sediment:

Balance = (received light preserved)+(ascending light given)−(received light become sediment).

   The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary: it says what the balance is. The definition is not derived from the framework’s
other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the measure, and it is stated at exactly
that strength.
   The definition has three terms, and each is worth marking.

The first term: the received light preserved. The epistemic light that the identity has
received, and that it has preserved in its manifestations. The preservation is the retention of
the light in a form that the identity can use; it is the first positive term in the balance. The
preservation is what fidelity (Chapter 38) measures, at the level of the single manifestation;
548                                                         Chapter 42. The Balance Criterion


the balance’s first term is the aggregate of the preserved light across the manifestations of the
identity.

The second term: the ascending light given. The epistemic light that the identity has
returned to its source, or to other identities, in the form of ascending or reflective epistemic
light. The return is the light that goes back; it is the second positive term in the balance.
The ascending light given is what the returning light (Chapter 40, Definition 40.6) carries,
and what the integration (Chapter 41) produces: the integration is the activity by which the
lodged light is returned to the network, and the returning light is the light that the integration
returns. The second term of the balance is therefore the measure of what the integration has
achieved.

The third term: the received light become sediment. The epistemic light that the
identity has received, and that has become cognitive sediment (Chapter 40). The sediment is
the light that has not been preserved and has not been returned; it is the negative term in the
balance.
    The balance is the sum of the two positive terms minus the negative term. A high balance
is a relation in which the received light has been preserved or returned, and little has become
sediment. A low balance is a relation in which more has become sediment than has been
preserved or returned.
Remark 42.5 (The Three Terms Are Not the Same Kind of Quantity). The three terms are
not the same kind of quantity. The received light preserved and the ascending light given are
positive terms; the received light become sediment is a negative term. The framework’s claim
is that the balance is the sum of the two positive terms minus the negative term; it does not
claim that the three terms can be measured in a common unit, and it leaves the question of
how they are to be compared to the inquiry (see Section 42.5).
Remark 42.6 (The Balance Is a Measure, Not a Character). The balance is a measure, not a
character. Viability (Chapter 36) is a structural character of the relation; the balance is a
measure of the relation under the aspect of the flow of epistemic light. The two are different,
and the framework keeps them apart. A relation can be highly viable and have a moderate
balance, or have a high balance and be less than fully viable; the two are different assessments,
and neither entails the other.
Remark 42.7 (The Balance Is Not a Value). The balance is not a value. It is a measure of
the relation between an identity and the epistemic light it receives; it states a condition on
the relation, and it attaches no value, end, or good to the condition. A relation with a high
balance is not thereby more valuable than a relation with a low balance; the framework makes
no evaluative claim. The reader who imports an evaluative sense into the balance has misread
it; the reader who reads it as a structural measure has read it correctly.


42.4     The Three Thresholds
The definition raises a question: what are the states of the balance, and how are they
distinguished? The framework distinguishes three thresholds.
Definition 42.2 (Three Thresholds of the Balance). (A) The balance can be distinguished
into three thresholds:
  (i) high balance: the received light has been preserved or returned; little sediment;

 (ii) balance near zero: neither returned nor lodged; the structural possibility of return
      remains;
42.5. The Status of the Criterion                                                            549


 (iii) low balance: more has been lodged than returned.
    The definition is stated as an axiom, because it is a stipulation of the framework’s
vocabulary: it says what the three thresholds are. The definition is not derived from the
framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the thresholds, and it is stated
at exactly that strength.
    The three thresholds are worth marking.

The first threshold: high balance. The received light has been preserved or returned;
little has become sediment. The relation is one in which the identity has taken what it has
received and made it active; the light has been preserved in the identity’s manifestations, and
has been returned to the source or to other identities.

The second threshold: balance near zero. The received light has neither been returned
nor lodged; the structural possibility of return remains. The relation is one in which the light
is still in the course of its return; it has not yet been preserved or returned, and it has not
yet become sediment. The balance is near zero because the positive and negative terms are
approximately equal.

The third threshold: low balance. The received light has become lodged; more has
become sediment than has been returned. The relation is one in which the identity has not
been able to integrate what it has received; the light has lodged in the identity’s sediment,
and the claim on the identity’s capacity has not been discharged.
Remark 42.8 (The Thresholds Are Not Places). The thresholds are not places. They are
states of the balance, and the framework states them to make the balance criterion usable.
The framework does not claim that the thresholds are precise, or that every case falls clearly
into one of the three; the thresholds are the framework’s distinctions, and the application of
the distinctions to a given case is the work of the inquiry.
Remark 42.9 (The Thresholds Are Not a Ranking). The thresholds are not a ranking of
the relation. The framework does not say that a relation with a high balance is better than
a relation with a low balance. It says that the three thresholds are states of the balance,
and that the assessment of the relation is the assessment of the state in a given case. The
evaluation, if there is one, belongs to the inquiry, not to the framework.
Remark 42.10 (The Thresholds Are Not the Three Components). The thresholds are not the
three components of viability (Chapter 37). The components are conditions on the relation;
the thresholds are states of the balance. A relation can be at the second threshold (balance
near zero) and still satisfy the three components (the manifestation is fidelious, the cost is
sustainable, the identity retains its capacity to manifest). The two are different, and the
framework keeps them apart.


42.5     The Status of the Criterion
The criterion is stated as an axiom, and its status is worth marking.
    The criterion is (A): it is a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary. It says what the
balance is, and it leaves the operational question—how the three terms are to be measured,
and how they are to be compared in a given case—to the inquiry. The framework’s claim is
that the criterion is the measure the framework uses, and that the measure is structural, not
evaluative.
    The operational question is marked as an open philosophical question ((Q)). The framework
does not claim that the balance can be measured in every case; it claims that the balance
550                                                         Chapter 42. The Balance Criterion


is the measure the framework uses, and that the measure is the one the framework can
supply, given the framework’s account of the cost of cognition (Chapter 39), of the sediment
(Chapter 40), of the returning light (Chapter 40), and of the integration (Chapter 41). The
operational question is the same question that the boundaries of epistemology list among the
open questions (Chapter 34, Question 6 on the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and
of the balance criterion); the present chapter states the criterion and marks the question as
open, and it does not settle the question that Chapter 34 has already marked as open.
Remark 42.11 (The Operational Question Is Open). The operational question is open. How
the three terms are to be measured, and how they are to be compared in a given case, is
a question the framework leaves open. A reader who settles the question has extended the
framework; a reader who shows that the question cannot be settled has shown a limit of
the framework’s formulation. The question is the one listed in Chapter 34 (Question 6); the
present chapter does not repeat the whole of the question, and it states the criterion at the
strength that question permits.
Remark 42.12 (The Status Is Not a Claim of Precision). The status is not a claim of precision.
The framework does not claim that the balance is a precise measure, or that it is the only
measure. It claims that the balance is a measure, and that the measure is structural. A reader
who seeks a precise measure will not find one in the framework; a reader who seeks a structural
measure will find one.
Remark 42.13 (The Status Is Not a Claim of Uniqueness). The status is not a claim of
uniqueness. The framework’s claim is that the balance is the measure the framework uses, not
that it is the only measure. A reader who proposes a different measure is invited to do so; the
framework does not claim that its own measure is the only one.


42.6     The Balance and the Three Components
The balance is related to the three components of viability (Chapter 37), and the relation is
worth stating.

The balance and fidelity. The first term of the balance—the received light preserved—is
related to fidelity. A manifestation that is high in fidelity is a manifestation that preserves
the source’s essential determination (Chapter 38); the received light that is preserved in the
manifestation is the light that the manifestation carries, in a form that preserves the source’s
determination. The two are related, but they are not the same: fidelity is a condition on the
manifestation; the balance is a measure of the relation.

The balance and sustainability. The second term of the balance—the ascending light
given—is related to sustainability. A relation that is sustainable is a relation in which the cost
of the manifestation does not exceed the context’s capacity (Chapter 39); the ascending light
that is given is the light that the relation returns, in a form that the context can bear. The
two are related, but they are not the same: sustainability is a condition on the relation; the
balance is a measure of the relation.

The balance and recoverability. The third term of the balance—the received light become
sediment—is related to recoverability. The sediment is what the relation leaves behind when
the light has not been preserved and has not been returned (Chapter 40); the sediment’s claim
on the context’s capacity is what can cross the singularity (Chapter 37, Section 37.7), and
what can make the relation less recoverable. The two are related, but they are not the same:
recoverability is a condition on the identity’s capacity to manifest; the balance is a measure of
the flow of light.
42.7. The Balance, the Sediment, and the Integration                                          551


Remark 42.14 (The Balance Is Not a Substitute for the Components). The balance is not a
substitute for the components. The components are conditions on the relation; the balance is
a measure of the flow. A relation can satisfy the components and have a balance that is less
than high (if the relation is near the second threshold, with the light still in the course of its
return). The two assessments are different, and the framework keeps them apart.

Remark 42.15 (The Balance Is Not Derived from the Components). The balance is not
derived from the components. The three components are the structural character of the
relation; the balance is a measure of the flow. The two are related, but the balance is not a
consequence of the components; it is a distinct measure that the framework uses to assess the
relation under the aspect of the flow.

Remark 42.16 (The Balance Points Beyond Itself). The balance points beyond itself. The
balance is the measure of the flow of epistemic light; it is not the ground of the flow. The
balance points beyond itself to what makes the flow possible, and to what makes the relation
possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not
described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the balance and the
ground of the flow; it is kept throughout the book.


42.7     The Balance, the Sediment, and the Integration
The balance is related to the cognitive sediment (Chapter 40), to the returning light (Chap-
ter 40), and to the integration of sediment (Chapter 41), and the relation is worth stating.
    The sediment is the third term of the balance: the received light that has become cognitive
sediment. The balance criterion measures the extent to which the received light has become
sediment, less the extent to which it has been preserved or returned; the sediment is the
negative term in the balance.
    The returning light (Chapter 40, Definition 40.6) is the light that continues after the
pause of the expression, and refers back to its source through what the identity left in other
manifestations. The returning light is what the second term of the balance measures: the
ascending light that is given is the returning light that the identity returns to its source or to
other identities. The distinction between the sediment and the returning light is the distinction
between the light that has lodged (the negative term) and the light that has returned (the
positive term); the balance criterion measures the difference.
    The integration of sediment (Chapter 41) is the activity by which the lodged light is
returned to the network of relations. Integration transforms sediment into returning light
(Chapter 41, Definition 41.1; Chapter 40, Definition 40.6); it increases the second term of the
balance (the ascending light given) and decreases the third term (the received light become
sediment); it improves the balance. The two are related: the integration is the activity; the
balance is the measure of the result.

Remark 42.17 (The Balance Is Not the Same as the Integration). The balance is not the
same as the integration. The integration is the activity; the balance is the measure of the
result. A relation can be integrated and still have a moderate balance (if the integration has
returned the light, but not all of it); a relation can have a high balance and not be integrated
(if the received light has been preserved without being returned). The two are related, but
they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.

Remark 42.18 (The Balance and the Integration Are Complementary). The balance and the
integration are complementary. The integration is the activity that improves the balance; the
balance is the measure that assesses the result of the integration. The two are different, and
the framework uses both. A subject that integrates the sediment is a subject that improves
the balance; a subject that measures the balance is a subject that assesses the integration.
552                                                        Chapter 42. The Balance Criterion


Remark 42.19 (The Balance Points Beyond Itself). The balance points beyond itself. The
balance is the measure of the flow of epistemic light; it is not the ground of the flow. The
balance points beyond itself to what makes the flow possible, and to what makes the relation
possible. The framework’s claim is that the pointing is real, and that what is pointed to is not
described by the framework. The distinction is the distinction between the balance and the
ground of the flow; it is kept throughout the book.


42.8     The Balance and the Limits of Part V
The balance is related to the limits of Part V, and the relation is worth marking, because the
relation is what makes the balance criterion precise.
    The limits say what the finite subject cannot do: it cannot know all manifestations of
an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it cannot complete its knowledge of epistemic light
(Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic unknownness of the other (Chapter 32), and it
cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33). The balance criterion is the measure that the
finite subject can apply, given the limits: it measures the extent to which the received light
has been preserved or returned, less the extent to which it has become sediment, within the
partiality that the limits impose. The distinction is the distinction between the limits and the
measure that the limits permit; the framework holds both.
    The balance is also related to the disposition of Chapter 35. The humble subject is the
subject that can assess the balance: it recognizes that the balance is a measure, not a value;
that the balance is not a precise measure; and that the assessment of the balance is the work
of the inquiry. The humility is the disposition that accepts the measure; the balance is what
the disposition assesses. The distinction is the distinction between the disposition and the
structural measure that the disposition assesses; the framework keeps it apart.
Remark 42.20 (The Balance and the Intrinsic Unknownness). The balance is related to
the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness (Chapter 32), and the relation
is worth marking. The temporary unknownness is what the assessment of the balance can
reduce: more manifestation, more analysis, and more comparison can make the balance more
precise. The intrinsic unknownness is what the assessment cannot remove: the finite subject
cannot exhaust the relation, and the balance is always assessed within the partiality that the
intrinsic unknownness imposes. The distinction is the distinction between the assessment and
the completeness of the assessment; the framework keeps it apart.
Remark 42.21 (The Balance and the Plurality of Perspectives). The balance is related to
the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33), and the relation is worth marking. The balance
of one perspective is not the balance of another; the balance is perspective-bound, and the
plurality of perspectives is the condition under which the balance can be assessed from more
than one angle. The distinction is the distinction between the balance and the plurality of
perspectives; the framework keeps it apart.


42.9     The Balance and the Open Questions of Chapter 34
The balance is related to three of the fourteen open questions of Chapter 34, and the relation
is worth marking.
    The first is the question of the exact boundary between the reduction of viability and the
singularity (Question 2). The present chapter states the sediment as the negative term of the
balance and its relation to the singularity; the exact relation between the balance and the
singularity is left open, and it is one of the framework’s invitations to an extension.
    The second is the question of the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of the
balance criterion (Question 6). The present chapter defines the criterion and the thresholds;
42.10. The Balance and the Core Commitments of Chapter 43                                    553


the conceptual foundations are left open, and the present chapter marks the operational
question of measurement as open.
    The third is the question of the relation among the aspects of cost (Question 8). The
present chapter uses the cost as one of the terms of the balance (the sediment is the residue of
the cost); the exact relation between the aspects of cost and the balance is left open, and it is
one of the framework’s invitations to an extension.
Remark 42.22 (The Open Questions Are Invitations, Not Defeats). The three open questions
are invitations to an extension of the framework, not defeats of it. The framework states the
balance criterion at the strength its arguments support; the questions that the criterion raises
but does not settle are the framework’s statement of where the inquiry continues. A reader
who settles one of the questions has extended the framework; a reader who shows that the
question is not real has shown a limit of the framework’s formulation.


42.10      The Balance and the Core Commitments of Chapter 43
The balance criterion is related to the core commitments of the framework, and the relation is
worth marking.
    The balance is not one of the ten core commitments (Chapter 43), but it is a structural
measure that the core commitments make intelligible. The commitment to the finitude of the
epistemic subject (C1) is what makes the balance necessary: the finite subject cannot preserve
or return all the light it receives, and the unprocessed light becomes sediment that the balance
measures. The commitment to identity conservation (C4) is what makes the balance not a
measure of the identity: the identity is conserved across the balance, and the balance is a
measure of the relation between the identity and its manifestations, not of the identity itself.
The commitment to the non-duplicability of identity (C10) is what makes the balance specific
to a context: the balance of one context is not the balance of another, and the identity that
the balance is the measure of the relation to is not duplicated in the balance.
Remark 42.23 (The Balance and the Core Commitments). The balance is not one of the ten
core commitments (Chapter 43), but it is a structural measure that the core commitments
make intelligible. The commitment to the finitude of the epistemic subject (C1) is what
makes the balance necessary; the commitment to identity conservation (C4) is what makes the
balance not a measure of the identity; the commitment to the non-duplicability of identity
(C10) is what makes the balance specific to a context. The balance is not a core commitment,
but it is a structural measure of the relation that the core commitments describe.


42.11      Scope and Vulnerability
The criterion is stated at the strength its argument supports, and its scope and vulnerability
are worth stating.
    The criterion is valid for the class of relations the framework treats: the relations between
identities and their manifestations in cognitive contexts, under the conditions the framework’s
definitions specify. It says that the balance is the sum of the two positive terms minus the
negative term; it does not say that the balance can be measured with a common unit, or that
the thresholds are precise.
    The criterion rests on the framework’s account of the cost of cognition (Chapter 39), of the
sediment (Chapter 40), of the returning light (Chapter 40), and of the integration (Chapter 41).
The criterion’s force is no greater than the force of these commitments; a reader who rejects
one of them has a reason to reject the corresponding term of the criterion, and the framework
does not pretend otherwise.
    The criterion would be put in question by two things.
554                                                           Chapter 42. The Balance Criterion


First challenge. A case in which the balance is high, and yet the relation between the
identity and its manifestations is not what the framework would count as viable. If such a
case could be given, the criterion would be shown to be misleading, and the framework would
need to revise it. The framework does not claim that no such case can be described; it claims
that none has been described that survives the framework’s definitions, and it argues that
none can be.

Second challenge. A case in which the balance is low, and yet the relation is what the
framework would count as viable. If such a case could be given, the criterion would be shown
to be too strong, and the framework would need to revise it. The framework holds that the
balance is a measure, not the character; a low balance is compatible with viability, and a high
balance is compatible with a lack of viability, because the two assessments are different. The
challenge would be effective only if it showed that the balance is not a measure at all.

Remark 42.24 (The Criterion Is Not a Formula). The criterion is not a formula. It states the
balance, but it does not offer an algorithm for measuring it in a given case. The identification
of the balance in a particular case is the work of the inquiry, not of the criterion. The criterion’s
role is to state the measure the inquiry aims at, not to substitute for the inquiry.

Remark 42.25 (The Criterion Points Beyond Itself). The criterion points beyond itself.
The balance is a real measure of the relation between an identity and the epistemic light it
receives; the measure is describable, and the description is what the framework offers. But the
measure is not the whole of what the relation is; the relation is between an identity and its
manifestations, and the identity and the manifestations are what they are. The distinction is
the distinction between the measure of the relation and what lies beyond it; the framework
keeps it throughout.


42.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Six things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not settle the operational question of how the three terms of the
balance are to be measured. The criterion is stated; the measurement is marked as an open
question ((Q)), and the framework leaves it to the inquiry. The question is the one listed in
Chapter 34 (Question 6); the present chapter states the criterion at the strength that question
permits, and it does not repeat the whole of the question.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the singularity. The singularity is the threshold at
which the cost of restoring a manifestation exceeds the cost of producing a new one; it is
developed in Chapter 37 (Section 37.7, Definition 37.2), in the chapter that states the third
component of viability. The present chapter uses the singularity in its account of the third
term of the balance (the received light become sediment) and of its relation to recoverability;
it does not re-derive the singularity, and it does not defer it to the later volume. The first
edition of Book I deferred the singularity to the later volume; the present edition develops it
in Chapter 37, and the present chapter’s reference to it points there.
    Third, the chapter does not compare the balance criterion with other measures of the
relation between an identity and its manifestations. The criterion is the framework’s measure;
the comparison with other measures belongs to a different inquiry, and the chapter does not
undertake it.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim that the balance is the only measure the framework
uses. The framework’s claim is that the balance is one measure, and that the measure is
structural; a reader who proposes a different measure is invited to do so, and the framework
does not claim that its own measure is the only one.
42.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                               555


    Fifth, the chapter does not develop the balance criterion in the specific contexts in which
the framework’s applications are worked out. The criterion is stated at the strength the
framework can support; the application to specific cases is the work of the inquiry, not of the
chapter.
    Sixth, the chapter does not settle the three open questions of Chapter 34 that the balance
criterion raises (Questions 2, 6, and 8). The present chapter states the criterion; the questions
that the criterion raises but does not settle are the framework’s invitations to an extension.

Remark 42.26 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed six things. It
has defined the balance criterion (Definition 42.1), with the three terms (the received light
preserved, the ascending light given, the received light become sediment). It has distinguished
the criterion from viability and from the three components of viability. It has stated the
three thresholds (Definition 42.2), and the status of the criterion (Section 42.5). It has stated
the relation between the balance and the returning light (Chapter 40) and the integration
(Chapter 41), so that the second and third terms of the balance are anchored in the chapters
that define them. It has connected the balance to the limits of Part V (Section 42.8), to the
open questions of Chapter 34 (Section 42.9), and to the core commitments of Chapter 43
(Section 42.10). And it has stated the scope and vulnerability of the criterion.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a relation you have had with something you have received—a tradition, a teacher,
a field of study. Is the relation at the first threshold (high balance), the second (balance
near zero), or the third (low balance)? What has been preserved, what has been returned,
and what has lodged? Consider also the returning light: is there a light that continues after
the pause of the relation, and refers back to its source through what you have left in other
manifestations—a trace that still speaks, a meaning that still carries? And consider the three
careers of the scene: which of the three terms of the balance is most visible in the first career,
and which in the second? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the
balance of the relation and the viability of the relation?

The next chapter (Chapter 43) is the final chapter of Part VI. It gathers the framework’s core
epistemic commitments and states the dependency map of the whole. The present chapter has
stated the balance criterion, the framework’s measure of the relation between an identity and
the epistemic light it receives; the next chapter states the commitments on which the measure,
the criterion, and the whole framework rest.

Chapter 43

Core Epistemic Commitments and the
Dependency Map

Scope
This chapter closes Part VI and the book. It states the audit of the framework’s commitments:
it gathers the framework’s core epistemic commitments (C1–C10), distinguishes them from
definitions, consequences, estimates, proposals, open questions, and speculation, states the
dependency map of the whole (Section 43.7), states the dependencies of the four formal
theorems on the core (Section 43.8), and closes with the framework’s self-description as a
conditional architecture on a core (Principle 43.1). Its claims are meta-epistemic; where the
chapter speaks of “core,” “definition,” “consequence,” “estimate,” “proposal,” “dependency,” or
“architecture,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this
chapter. The chapter’s silence on questions of value is not a denial but a recognition that the
meta-epistemic description is not the whole of what can be said.

Remark 43.1 (The Chapter’s Place in Part VI and in the Book). The chapter is the eighth
and last chapter of Part VI, and the forty-third and last chapter of the book’s body. The
previous chapters developed the framework’s central concept (viability, Chapter 36), its three
components (Chapter 37), the fidelity component (Chapter 38), the sustainability component
(Chapter 39), the sediment (Chapter 40), the integration of the sediment (Chapter 41), and
the balance criterion (Chapter 42). The present chapter does not develop a new concept; it
states the audit of the whole. It closes Part VI, and it closes the book. The chapter after it
does not exist; the book’s body ends here. The back matter (Bibliography, Glossary, Index of
Arguments, Index of Epistemic Principles, Index of Formalizations) follows, and the reader
who wishes to locate a specific claim is directed to the indexes.


43.1     A Scene
Consider a surveyor at the end of a survey. She has walked the whole territory; she has marked
every boundary, every elevation, every landmark; she has drawn the map. Now she sits at
the table, at the end of the work, and does what a surveyor does at the end of the work: she
checks the map against the territory.
    She does not check every detail again. She checks the landmarks—the points on which the
whole map depends. If a landmark is misplaced, the map is wrong in a way that the correction
of no other point can fix. If a landmark is correctly placed, the map’s other points can be
corrected one by one, without the whole map collapsing.
    She asks three questions of each landmark. First: is it a landmark, or is it a derived point
that could be computed from other landmarks? Second: on what other landmarks does its
558                     Chapter 43. Core Epistemic Commitments and the Dependency Map


placement depend? Third: what would be lost if it were moved?
    The surveyor’s questions are the questions of the audit. The present chapter is that
audit, applied to the framework developed in the preceding chapters. The landmarks are the
framework’s core epistemic commitments. The derived points are the definitions, consequences,
estimates, and proposals. The dependencies are stated in the dependency map, and the cost
of moving a landmark is stated with it.
    The scene poses a question. What are the framework’s landmarks, and what depends on
them? The present chapter’s answer is the audit. Its principal contribution is the dependency
map, and its closing claim is that the framework is a conditional architecture on a core.

Remark 43.2 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the audit at
work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the audit’s results; it makes the results intelligible
before they are stated. The audit is stated in the sections that follow, and the scene carries no
weight in them.

Remark 43.3 (The Scene Shows the Difference Between Landmarks and Derived Points).
The scene is easily read as an observation about a surveyor. The observation is not wrong, but
it hides the structural point. The structural point is that the surveyor does not check every
point; she checks the landmarks, because the landmarks are what the other points depend on.
The distinction is the distinction between the core (the landmarks) and the derived points
(the definitions, consequences, estimates, and proposals). The audit is the framework’s way
of making the distinction visible, so that the reader knows which claims are the landmarks
and which are the derived points. A reader who takes the scene as a display of a surveyor has
read the scene; a reader who takes it as a display of the distinction between the core and the
derived points has read the structural point.


43.2      The Question
The previous chapters of Part VI have developed the framework’s central concept and its
components. Chapter 36 defined viability. Chapter 37 defined the three components and devel-
oped the third (recoverability) through the account of the singularity. Chapter 38 developed
fidelity. Chapter 39 developed sustainability through the cost of cognition. Chapter 40 defined
the cognitive sediment. Chapter 41 developed the integration of sediment. Chapter 42 stated
the balance criterion.
    The present chapter asks the audit’s questions. What are the framework’s core commitments—
the landmarks on which the whole depends? What kind of commitment is each of the frame-
work’s other claims—a definition, a consequence, an estimate, a proposal, an open question,
or a speculation? And what is lost, for the framework, if a given commitment is rejected?
    The questions are not idle. A framework that does not distinguish its landmarks from its
derived points is a framework that cannot be assessed. A reader who rejects a derived point
has a reason to reject only that point; a reader who rejects a landmark has a reason to reject
the whole structure that depends on it. The framework’s honesty about which is which is
part of what the framework is. The present chapter states the audit, so that the reader knows
which is which.

Remark 43.4 (The Audit Is Not a Demand for Certainty). The audit is not a demand for
certainty. It does not claim that the core commitments are certain; it claims that they are
the commitments on which the framework’s other claims depend. The core commitments are
(A): they are adopted, not proved; their justification is coherence, explanatory power, and
fruitfulness (Chapter 2), not certainty. The audit’s function is to make the core visible, so that
the reader can see what the framework is committed to, and what is lost if a commitment is
rejected.
43.3. The Audit and Its Criteria                                                             559


Remark 43.5 (The Audit and the Limits of Part V). The audit is related to the limits of
Part V, and the relation is worth marking. The limits say what the finite subject cannot do: it
cannot know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts (Chapter 27), it cannot complete
its knowledge of epistemic light (Chapter 31), it cannot remove the intrinsic unknownness of
the other (Chapter 32), and it cannot occupy every perspective (Chapter 33). The audit is the
framework’s statement of what it is committed to, given the limits: the ten core commitments
are (A), and their justification is coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness, not certainty.
The distinction is the distinction between the limits and the commitments that the limits
permit; the framework holds both.


43.3     The Audit and Its Criteria
The audit distinguishes six classes of claim: core commitments, definitions, consequences,
estimates, proposals, and open questions or speculations. The last class contains two different
statuses: (Q) for an unsettled question and (S) for a speculative extension.

Definition 43.1 (The Classes of the Audit). (i) Core: a primitive commitment that is not
     derived from the other entries and on which conclusions in at least two parts of the
     book depend. Rejecting a core commitment withdraws the support it gives to those
     conclusions; it does not leave the dependent structure unchanged.

 (ii) Definition: a stipulation of the sense of a term or of the criteria for its application.
      Rejecting a definition changes the framework’s vocabulary and requires the claims using
      that term to be restated; it does not, by itself, establish a contrary fact.

 (iii) Consequence: a claim that follows, by the argument given in the chapter that states
       it, from other commitments and definitions. A consequence is (T); rejecting it requires
       identifying which premise or inferential step is not accepted.

 (iv) Estimate: a substantive assessment offered at a stated strength, rather than presented
      as a necessary consequence. Estimates include judgments about sufficiency, minimality,
      order, and explanatory adequacy. In the book’s status notation, an estimate is (E).

 (v) Proposal : a claim or formulation put forward for consideration but not presented as
     established. A proposal remains open to assessment and is not counted as a settled
     result.

 (vi) Open question or speculation: an issue the framework explicitly leaves unsettled (Q), or
      a possible extension presented tentatively and with caution (S). An open question and
      a speculation are not interchangeable: the former identifies a gap to be addressed; the
      latter marks a conjectural possibility.

    The definition is a stipulation of the audit’s vocabulary, and it is stated at that strength.
Its purpose is to make the framework’s commitments visible, not to prove them.

Remark 43.6 (Why the Audit Separates the Classes). The audit separates the classes because
the first edition’s labels were too coarse. In the earlier classification, the label (A) covered
several different kinds of claim: a primitive commitment, a stipulated definition, a derivable
consequence, and a provisional assessment or modelling assumption. The audit separates them.
A reader who rejects a primitive commitment has a reason to reject the conclusions that depend
on it; a reader who rejects a stipulated definition has proposed another vocabulary; a reader
who rejects a consequence has denied one of its premises; a reader who rejects an estimate has
rejected that assessment and the claims that specifically rely on it. The distinctions make the
framework assessable.
560                     Chapter 43. Core Epistemic Commitments and the Dependency Map


Remark 43.7 (The Audit and the Open Questions of Chapter 34). The audit is related to
the open questions of Chapter 34, and the relation is worth marking. The open questions are
fourteen, in three groups: four conceptual (Questions 1–4), five argumentative (Questions 5–9),
and five epistemic (Questions 10–14), including the fourteenth question (Question 14), the
temporal structure of self-awareness, which Chapter 20 flagged as a gap. The audit’s sixth
class marks the open questions as (Q), and the same class marks the one speculation (the
countability of the infinity of contexts, Chapter 11) as (S). The audit is the framework’s way of
stating what is foundational (the core), stipulated (the definitions), argued (the consequences),
provisionally assessed (the estimates), proposed (the proposals), and left open or conjectural
(the questions and speculation). A reader who wishes to see the questions is directed to
Chapter 34; a reader who wishes to see the audit’s classification of them is directed to the
present chapter.


43.4     The Core Epistemic Commitments
The framework’s core has ten epistemic commitments. Each is stated with its basis, and each
is marked with the part or parts of the book in which it does load-bearing work.

C1. Finitude of the Epistemic Subject (Chapter 3). Every cognizing subject occupies,
    at any time, finitely many cognitive contexts, and completes, in any finite span, only
    finitely many acts of reconstruction. Load-bearing in: Part V (the impossibility of
    super-identity, Chapter 27; the limits of self-knowledge, Chapter 30; the impossibility of
    complete knowledge of epistemic light, Chapter 31; intrinsic unknownness, Chapter 32;
    the plurality of perspectives, Chapter 33).

C2. Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos (Chapter 4). Epistemology, as prac-
    ticed in this book, describes the structure of explanatory cognition; it does not establish
    the telos of cognition. Load-bearing in: Part I (the method), Part V (the boundaries),
    Part VI (the scope of viability).

C3. Autonomy of Epistemic Justification (Chapter 4). No epistemic principle in this
    book takes confirmation from a non-epistemic domain as its ground. The fact that C5 is
    defended in a later volume is an inter-volume placement of its philosophical argument,
    not an appeal to non-epistemic evidence. Load-bearing in: Part I (the method), Part V
    (the boundaries), Part VI (the status of the coherence tests).

C4. Identity Rigidity and Conservation (Chapter 12, Sections 12.6–12.7). Identity
     is rigid—it admits of no degrees (Principle 12.1)—and identity is conserved—it is invariant
     under all temporal transformations of its manifestations (Principle 12.2). Load-bearing
     in: Part III (the distinction between identity and signature, Section 12.4; the argument
     from the logic of identity for rigidity, Section 12.6; the transcendental and abductive
     arguments for conservation, Section 12.7; the thread-and-beads model, Section 12.9),
     Part VI (the distinction between viability and identity, Chapter 36; the distinction
     between sediment and loss of identity, Chapter 40).

C5. Expression as Structural Tendency (Chapter 38). Every identity tends toward
    expression; the tendency cannot be structurally unrealized, only structurally hindered.
    Load-bearing in: Part VI (fidelity, Chapter 38; the three components, Chapter 37). The
    tendency itself is defined in Chapter 38; the principle of expression, of which the tendency
    is the core, is argued in the later volume. The present volume borrows the commitment
    from the later volume, and states it here as a core commitment of the present volume’s
    account of fidelity; the full defense of the principle of expression belongs to the later
    volume (see Remark 43.11, below).
43.4. The Core Epistemic Commitments                                                          561


C6. Openness of Relations (Chapter 11). For every cognitive context C and every man-
    ifestation m that an identity has in C, there is a cognitive context C ′ in which m is itself
    a fixed element, related by epistemic light and dynamics not available in C. Load-bearing
    in: Part II (the infinity of contexts), Part V (the diagonal argument for the impossibility
    of super-identity).

C7. Trans-Categorical Character of Epistemic Light (Chapter 15). Epistemic light
    is the medium of legible relation: the condition of possibility of a relation’s being legible
    as a relation between these terms. It is not a term in the relation, and it is not a relation
    among relations. Load-bearing in: Part III (the medium of relation, the desire to find,
    the unknownness of same-category identities), Part V (the impossibility of complete
    knowledge of epistemic light).

C8. Category-Relative Predication (Chapter 25). Epistemic predicates are not abso-
    lute; they are defined relative to a cognitive context and to a respect. Load-bearing in:
    Part IV (the resolution of the tensions between intensity and breadth), Part VI (the
    resolution of the tension between rigidity and grading, Chapter 38).

C9. Configuration-Dependence (Chapter 29). The manifestation of an identity in a
    context depends on what passes through the epistemic light of the context, and this
    in turn depends on the whole configuration of the context. Load-bearing in: Part V
    (the strengthening of the impossibility of super-identity), Part VI (the cost of cognition,
    Chapter 39).

C10. Non-Duplicability of Identity (Chapter 12, Section 12.8). Identity cannot be
    copied; signatures, pseudo-identities, and information can be duplicated, but identity
    cannot. A copy of a system reproduces its signature; if the copy expresses at all, it
    expresses an identity of its own. Load-bearing in: Part III (the distinction between
    identity and signature, Section 12.4; the argument for non-duplicability, Section 12.8;
    primitive thisness, Section 12.8), Part VI (the distinction between the identity that is
    expressed and the reconstruction that approximates it, on which the whole account of
    viability depends, Chapters 36–42).

Remark 43.8 (The Core Is Small). The core is small—ten commitments—and its smallness is
the point. A framework whose core is small is a framework whose foundations can be examined;
a framework whose core is large is a framework whose foundations are hidden among its claims.
The framework’s claim is that the ten commitments are the framework’s landmarks. Other
claims are defined in relation to the core, derived from it, assessed at a stated strength, or left
open to revision.
Remark 43.9 (The Core Is Not a Claim of Certainty). The core is not a claim of certainty.
The ten commitments are (A): they are adopted, not proved. Their justification is coherence,
explanatory power, and fruitfulness (Chapter 2); the framework’s honest position is that these
are the criteria by which the core is to be tested. A reader who rejects a core commitment
has a reason to reject the conclusions that depend on it; a reader who accepts the core has a
reason to accept the framework at the strength its arguments support.
Remark 43.10 (The Core Is Not the Only Possible Starting Point). The core is not the only
possible starting point. It is the set of commitments that the argument of the book cannot do
without; a different framework might start from a different core, and the comparison of the
two frameworks would be a different inquiry. The framework’s claim is that its own core is
coherent, explanatory, and fruitful, not that no other core could be.
Remark 43.11 (C5 Is Borrowed From the Later Volume). C5 states a commitment that
is argued, not in the present volume, but in the later volume. The tendency to express is
562                     Chapter 43. Core Epistemic Commitments and the Dependency Map


defined in Chapter 38; the principle of expression, of which the tendency is the core, is argued
in the later volume. The present volume borrows the commitment because its account of
fidelity (Chapter 38) and of the three components (Chapter 37) depends on it. The cost of the
borrowing is that a reader who rejects the principle of expression, as it is argued in the later
volume, has a reason to reject C5 and the conclusions that depend on it; the present volume
does not undertake to defend the principle, and it states the borrowing openly. The borrowing
is not a weakness of the present volume’s audit; it is the recognition that the present volume is
one volume of a series, and that its core includes a commitment whose full argument is given
elsewhere in the series.


43.5     The Definitions That Do Load-Bearing Work
Most of the framework’s definitions are stipulations of vocabulary, and rejecting one of them
changes the vocabulary, not any fact. A few do load-bearing work, and they are worth marking
because their role in the framework is more than vocabulary.
Definition of identity (Chapter 12). The invariant that an explanatory cognition holds
     fixed across a class of allowable transformations of its manifestations. Role: it fixes the
     sense of “identity” for the whole framework; rejecting it changes the vocabulary, and
     the framework’s claims about identity, signature, and pseudo-identity would need to be
     restated.
Definition of signature (Chapter 12). The structural description of the invariance of an
     identity. Role: it fixes the distinction between the identity and what reconstruction
     recovers; the distinction between identity and pseudo-identity depends on it.
Definition of pseudo-identity (Chapter 12). The observer’s approximation of an identity,
     constructed from the available manifestations. Role: it fixes the epistemic status of what
     the observer actually has; the criteria of adequacy (Chapter 23) are its criteria.
Definition of thread (Chapter 12). An identity as a structural invariant that holds a
     sequence of manifestations together. Role: it gives a precise form to the invariance
     of identity and to the conservation of identity under the loss of lower manifestations
     (Theorem 12.1).
Definition of recursive manifestation (Chapter 12). The structure by which a mani-
     festation realized in one context can itself be the occasion for further manifestations
     of the same identity. Role: it makes precise the distinction between the plurality of
     manifestations and the plurality of identities; the unity of the source is not the unity of
     an aggregate.
Definition of manifestation (Chapter 13). The contextually realized appearance of an
     identity in a receiving cognitive context, according to the context’s capacity, aptitude,
     and constraints. Role: it fixes the sense of “manifestation” for the whole framework;
     its product-character is a commitment, and rejecting it would change the framework’s
     account of reconstruction.
Definition of epistemic light (Chapter 15). The medium of legible relation. Role: it
     fixes the sense of “epistemic light” for the whole framework; the trans-categorical character
     of light (C7) depends on it.
Definition of viability (Chapter 36). The epistemic structural character of the relation
     between an identity and its manifestations in a cognitive context, in the three respects of
     fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. Role: it fixes the framework’s central concept;
     the three components (Chapter 37) are the specifications of the definition.
43.6. The Consequences, Estimates, Proposals, and Open Questions                                563


Definition of the three components (Chapter 37). Fidelity, sustainability, and recover-
     ability. Role: the three components are the substance of viability; Chapter 38 develops
     fidelity, Chapter 39 develops sustainability, and Chapter 37 develops recoverability.

Definition of the singularity (Chapter 37). The threshold at which the cost of restoring
     an existing manifestation in a context exceeds the cost of bringing about a new one there.
     Role: it fixes the sense of “recoverability”; without it, the third component of viability
     would be undefined.

Definition of the balance criterion (Chapter 42). The balance of an identity in a con-
     text as the received light preserved plus the ascending light given, minus the received
     light become sediment. Role: it fixes the framework’s measure of the relation; the audit
     does not count it as a core commitment, because the framework can be stated without
     the measure (the measure is a diagnostic, not a foundation).

Remark 43.12 (The Definitions Are Not the Core). The definitions are not the core. The core
is the set of primitive commitments on which the framework’s claims depend; the definitions
are the vocabulary in which the claims are stated. The two are different classes in the audit,
and the framework keeps them apart. A reader who rejects a definition has proposed another
vocabulary; a reader who rejects a core commitment has denied one of the framework’s
premises.

Speculation (S). The speculative extensions. The framework’s one (S) claim is the question
whether the infinity of contexts is countable or uncountable (Chapter 11).

    The map is a summary, not a new argument. Its purpose is to make the framework’s
structure visible: which commitments are foundational, which conclusions depend on which,
and what is lost if any commitment is rejected. A reader who rejects one of the entries knows
exactly which conclusions are no longer supported.



Remark 43.13 (The Map Is Not the Framework). The map is not the framework. The
map states the dependencies among the framework’s commitments; it does not restate the
arguments for them. A reader who wishes to assess a conclusion is directed to the chapter that
states it and to the arguments that support it. The map’s role is to locate the conclusions in
the structure, not to substitute for them.



Remark 43.14 (The Map Is Not a Proof of the Core). The map is not a proof of the core.
The core’s ten commitments are (A): they are adopted, not proved. The map states what
depends on them; it does not justify them. The justification of each is its coherence, its
explanatory power, and its fruitfulness (Chapter 2), and the framework’s honest position is
that these are the criteria by which the core is to be tested.



Remark 43.15 (The Map Is Not Exhaustive). The map is not exhaustive. It lists the
conclusions that depend on each core commitment; it does not list every claim in the book. A
reader who wishes to see the full set of claims is directed to the Index of Epistemic Principles
and to the Index of Arguments; the map states the dependencies among the core and the most
important conclusions, and it leaves the rest to the indexes. The dependencies of the four
formal theorems are stated in Section 43.8, and the full formal system is stated in Appendix .15.



Remark 43.16 (The Map and the Open Questions of Chapter 34). The map is related to
the open questions of Chapter 34, and the relation is worth marking. The map states the
dependencies among the core commitments and the conclusions; the open questions state
what the framework does not settle. The two are complementary: the map states what the
framework is committed to, and the open questions state what the framework leaves open.
The fourteen open questions are stated in Chapter 34; the map states the dependencies among
the core commitments and the conclusions, and it does not restate the questions. A reader
who wishes to see the questions is directed to Chapter 34; a reader who wishes to see the
dependencies is directed to the map.

but also which formal theorems depend on which core commitments.

and the prose arguments are not rivals. The prose arguments are the substance, and the
formal theorems are their precise form. The reader who is content with the prose arguments
of Chapters 6 and 7 has the principle, the arguments, and the limits; the reader who wishes to
see the principle in a precise form has the formal theorems. The two are the same arguments,
stated at two levels of detail; the formal theorems do not replace the prose arguments, and the
prose arguments do not make the formal theorems unnecessary.

Remark 43.19 (The Formal Theorems and the Reader). The formal theorems are offered for

who wishes to assess the framework at the level of its formal structure. They are not offered as
a requirement: the philosophical reader who is content with the prose of Chapters 6 and 7 has
the principle and the arguments, and does not need the formal theorems. The formal theorems
are a supplement, not a substitute; they are the framework’s way of being assessable at the
level of its formal structure, and they are offered at the strength that a supplement can have.


43.9     The Book as a Conditional Architecture on a Core
The audit’s result is the framework’s self-description: the book is a conditional architecture on
a core.

Principle 43.1 (The Book Is a Conditional Architecture on a Core). (A) The book is a
conditional architecture on a core of ten epistemic commitments. Every other claim of the
book is a definition that fixes vocabulary, a consequence that follows from the core and the
definitions, an estimate that is offered at a stated strength, a proposal that is stated but not
established, an open question that is stated but not settled, or a speculation that is flagged for
caution. The book is not a closed system: it does not claim that its conclusions are necessary,
nor that its list of commitments is complete, nor that its estimates are final.

    The principle is (A): it is adopted as the book’s self-description. It classifies the status of
the book’s claims; it does not independently prove the commitments it records.
    The principle has four consequences (the fourth is new, and it records the formal theorems).

First consequence: conditionality is stated, not hidden. The dependency of each
conclusion on the core is stated in the map of the previous section. A conclusion of the book
is asserted given the core commitments on which it depends, not unconditionally. Where the
dependency is a single core commitment, the reader can see that it is; where a conclusion has
several dependencies, the reader can see which.

Second consequence: rejecting a commitment has a known cost. A reader who
rejects a core commitment has a map of what is affected: the conclusions that depend on
the commitment are placed in question, and the other conclusions remain. A reader who
rejects a definition has proposed another vocabulary. A reader who rejects an estimate or a
proposal loses only the estimate or the proposal. The cost of each rejection is stated with the
commitment that is rejected.

Third consequence: revision is expected. The book’s self-description as a conditional
architecture is a statement that the book is open to revision. The framework’s living character
(Chapter 34) is what makes revision possible; the framework’s core is what makes the revision
checkable. A reader who finds a claim unconvincing has located a place where the framework
can be revised, and the map of the previous section states what the revision would affect.

Fourth consequence: the formal theorems are part of the architecture. The four
formal theorems of Appendix .15 are the formal counterparts of the arguments of Chapters 6
and 7; they depend on the core commitments stated in Section 43.8. The formal theorems
are not an addition to the architecture; they are the architecture stated in a precise form. A
reader who accepts the core commitments and the formal system of Appendix .15 has the
570                     Chapter 43. Core Epistemic Commitments and the Dependency Map


formal counterparts of the framework’s arguments; a reader who rejects a core commitment
knows which formal theorems are affected.
Remark 43.20 (The Conditional Architecture Is Not a Weakness). The conditional architec-
ture is not a weakness. It is what the framework is: a structure whose foundations are visible,
and whose claims can be assessed at the strength the foundations support. A framework that
presented itself as unconditional would claim more than its arguments support; a framework
that presented itself as conditional is honest about what it is, and is assessable at the strength
its arguments support.
Remark 43.21 (The Conditional Architecture Is Not Relativism). The conditional architecture
is not relativism. It does not say that every framework is as good as every other; it says that
the framework’s claims are conditional on the framework’s core, and that the core is assessed
by the framework’s own criteria (coherence, explanatory power, fruitfulness). A different
framework with a different core would be assessed by its own criteria, and the comparison of the
two frameworks would be a different inquiry. The conditional architecture is the framework’s
statement of its own conditionality, not a denial of the possibility of assessment.
Remark 43.22 (The Conditional Architecture and the Central Concept). The conditional
architecture is related to the framework’s central concept, viability (Chapter 36), and the
relation is worth marking. Viability is the epistemic structural character of the relation
between an identity and its manifestations, in the three respects of fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability. The conditional architecture is the framework’s statement of what the concept
of viability depends on: the ten core commitments, the definitions, and the consequences that
the chapters of Parts I–VI develop. The two are related as the concept and the audit of its
foundations; the framework states both, and the reader who has followed the argument to this
point has the vocabulary to state them.


43.10      What the Audit Does Not Do
The audit is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.

The audit does not prove the core. The ten commitments are (A): they are adopted, not
proved. The audit states what depends on them; it does not justify them. The justification of
each is its coherence, its explanatory power, and its fruitfulness; the audit’s role is to make
the core visible, not to establish it.

The audit does not claim that the core is complete. The ten commitments are the
ones the framework uses; the framework does not claim that no further commitment is needed.
A reader who finds a commitment that the framework uses but has not listed has found an
omission in the audit, and the audit can be revised to include it.

The audit does not claim that the core is minimal. The ten commitments are the ones
the framework cannot do without; the framework does not claim that a smaller core would
not do. A reader who shows that two of the ten are the same, or that one is derivable from
the others, has shown that the core can be reduced, and the audit can be revised accordingly.

The audit does not substitute for the arguments. The map states the dependencies
among the framework’s commitments; it does not restate the arguments for them. A reader
who wishes to assess a conclusion is directed to the chapter that states it; the map’s role
is to locate the conclusion in the structure. The formal theorems of Section 43.8 are the
formal counterparts of the arguments of Chapters 6 and 7; they do not substitute for the prose
arguments, and the prose arguments do not make the formal theorems unnecessary.
43.11. Closing the Book                                                                           571


The audit does not close the book. The audit is the book’s statement of its own structure;
it is not the book’s conclusion. The book’s conclusion is stated in the closing note of the
chapter, and the book’s open questions are stated in Chapter 34. The audit is the framework’s
self-description, and the self-description is part of what the framework is.

Remark 43.23 (The Audit Is a Discipline, Not a Verdict). The audit is a discipline on the
book’s claims, not a verdict on them. It makes the core visible, states what depends on what,
and states the cost of each rejection. It does not decide which commitments are true; it states
what the framework is committed to, so that the reader can decide whether to accept the
framework on its own terms.

Remark 43.24 (The Audit and the Framework’s Limits). The audit is related to the
framework’s limits, and the relation is worth marking. The framework’s limits are stated
in Part V: the impossibility of super-identity, the fallacy of super-identity, configuration-
dependence, the limits of self-knowledge, the impossibility of complete knowledge of epistemic
light, the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness, the plurality of perspectives.
The audit does not claim to overcome the limits; it states the framework’s commitments within
them. The distinction is the distinction between the limits and the commitments that the
limits permit; the framework holds both.


43.11       Closing the Book
The book ends here. Its closing claims are three, and they are stated at the strength the
book’s arguments support.

First: the framework is a conditional architecture on a core. The framework’s
ten epistemic commitments are its landmarks; the framework’s other claims are definitions,
consequences, estimates, proposals, open questions, and speculation. The framework’s claim
is that the architecture is coherent, foundational, and autonomous; the framework does not
claim that the architecture is certain, complete, or final.

Second: the framework’s central character is viability. The viability of an identity in
a cognitive context is the epistemic structural character of the relation between the identity
and its manifestations, in the three respects of fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. The
concept is descriptive, not evaluative; it states a condition on the relation, and it attaches
no value, end, or good to the condition. The framework’s claim is that the concept is real,
invariant, and describable; the framework does not claim that the concept is the whole of what
the relation is.

Third: the framework’s honesty about its limits is part of what it is. The frame-
work’s limits are stated in Part V: the impossibility of super-identity, the fallacy of super-identity,
configuration-dependence, the limits of self-knowledge, the impossibility of complete knowledge
of epistemic light, the distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness, the plurality
of perspectives. The framework’s open questions are stated in Chapter 34. The framework’s
humility is stated in Chapter 35. The framework’s claim is that its honesty about its limits is
not a weakness but a condition of its precision; the framework does not claim that the limits
are the limits of what is, and it does not claim that nothing lies beyond them.

The framework is offered as a philosophical proposal, not as a closed system. Its worth is to
be assessed by its coherence, by the distinctions it makes possible, and by the strength of
its arguments. The reader who has followed the argument from beginning to end has seen
the architecture built, part by part, each part presupposing only what has come before. The
572                     Chapter 43. Core Epistemic Commitments and the Dependency Map


reader who has entered in the middle has seen one part in its context. Both readers have
seen the same architecture, and both are invited to continue the inquiry that the architecture
makes possible.

The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.
