.10      Comparative Profiles: Convergences and Decisive Differ-
         ences
The matrix identifies points of proximity, but a matrix necessarily compresses arguments.
This section expands selected comparisons where the danger of false equivalence is greatest.
The aim is not to provide a complete history of each tradition; it is to identify what must be
compared if the relation is to be philosophically exact.


.10.1      Aristotle: Explanation, Causes, and the Organization of Inquiry
Aristotle is a primary comparison for the framework’s architecture of explanation, but the
relation must be stated carefully. The four causes (material, formal, efficient, and final) classify
explanatory factors in accounts of natural and substantial things. The framework’s four
.10. Comparative Profiles: Convergences and Decisive Differences                             607


columns classify analytical roles within explanatory cognition. The first is a causal-explanatory
taxonomy; the second is an epistemic architecture. Their number does not establish identity
of structure.
    The more productive comparison concerns the relation between explanatory completeness
and the plurality of explanatory questions. Aristotle’s account of knowing through causes offers
a historical precedent for refusing explanations that leave the relevant “because” unanswered.
The framework’s four questions—what, how, on what basis, and where—are broader in function:
they distinguish the object or content to be explained, its mode or process, its grounding, and
the context in which the explanation is intelligible. Whether these four roles are necessary and
jointly sufficient is a question for the framework’s own argument, not something established
by Aristotle’s four causes.
    The comparison with Aristotle’s potentiality and actuality is similarly limited. It can
illuminate the difference between a capacity and its realization, but the framework’s tendency
to manifest is explicitly treated in this volume as an epistemic-structural notion whose full
grounding is deferred. It should not be identified with Aristotelian dynamis without an
argument showing that the two concepts share their grounds and inferential consequences.

.10.2    Hume and Locke: Experience, Representation, and the Limits of
         Inference
Locke and Hume are important because they make the origin, content, and limits of human
knowledge central questions. Locke’s distinction between sensation and reflection provides
a comparison for the framework’s concern with reception and cognitive access. Yet Locke’s
account is principally concerned with the origin of ideas and the operations of the understanding;
the framework asks how an identity is epistemically reconstructed through manifestations in
contexts. The objects of analysis overlap, but the explanatory tasks differ.
    Hume’s analysis of impressions, ideas, association, causation, and induction is a close
point of contact for the limits of justification. The framework’s account of unknownness
and finite reconstruction, however, is not simply Humean skepticism. Hume’s problem of
induction concerns the rational warrant for projecting regularities beyond observed cases. The
framework’s distinction between intrinsic and temporary unknownness concerns whether a
limitation belongs to the structure of access or can be reduced through further reconstruction.
These questions can intersect, but neither entails the other.
    The comparison also clarifies that the framework’s viability is not a measure of the
probability or evidential strength of a belief in the Humean sense. Fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability concern the structural relation between identity and manifestation. A belief may
be well supported yet costly to maintain; it may be sustainable yet misrepresent its object.
The three components therefore should not be collapsed into a single measure of confidence or
confirmation.

.10.3    Kant: Conditions, Limits, and the Two Orders
Kant is one of the closest comparisons for the framework’s concern with conditions and limits,
but the objects of the two inquiries differ. Kant investigates the a priori conditions under which
objects can be experienced and known by finite human cognition. The framework investigates
the analytical roles and relations through which an explanation is constituted and assessed.
The former is transcendental in the specifically Kantian sense; the latter should not be called
transcendental merely because it asks about conditions.
    The comparison is strongest in three areas: the finitude of cognition; the distinction
between what appears and what cannot be known as an object of possible experience; and
the need to distinguish the conditions of cognition from claims about things as they are
independently of those conditions. It is weaker where the framework’s identity/manifestation
608                         Appendix . A Comparative Study of the Philosophy of Viability


distinction is treated as if it were equivalent to Kant’s phenomenon/noumenon distinction.
In the framework, identity is not simply a noumenal object and manifestation is not simply
a phenomenon. The distinction is introduced to explain the relation between an invariant
identity and its context-conditioned epistemic appearances, not to reproduce Kant’s two-aspect
or two-world interpretations.
    The distinction between the order of cognition and the order of grounding must also remain
separate from Kant’s distinction between epistemic conditions and things in themselves. It is
a distinction between two explanatory orders in the book’s own architecture. A comparison
may show a family resemblance, but not identity of doctrine.

.10.4    Hegel: Mediation, Development, and the Question of Totality
Hegel offers a strong comparison for mediation, relational determination, and the integration
of apparently separate moments. This is relevant to the framework’s governing dynamics,
non-sequential connectivity, and integration of cognitive sediment. Nevertheless, Hegelian
mediation belongs to a systematic dialectical account in which determinations are intelligible
through their relations and development. The framework’s connectivity is an account of
relations among analytical roles in explanatory cognition; it does not, by itself, commit the
framework to dialectical logic or to the Hegelian account of the development of Spirit.
    The contrast is particularly important concerning totality. The framework’s account of
the impossibility of super-identity and the limits of complete reconstruction should not be
presented as a simple rejection of Hegel. Hegel’s notion of the true as the whole is embedded
in a distinctive account of mediation and conceptual development. To establish a direct
disagreement, one would need to compare the framework’s precise definition of complete
reconstruction with Hegel’s account of the whole, rather than treating “totality” as a single
univocal concept.

.10.5    Husserl and Heidegger: Givenness, Horizon, and Situated Under-
         standing
Husserl is a particularly important interlocutor for manifestation, intentionality, horizon, and
the unity of an object across changing modes of givenness. The framework’s distinction
between identity and manifestation can be compared with the distinction between an object
and its profiles or modes of appearance. The comparison is structural: Husserl’s analyses
concern intentional constitution and the structures of appearing, whereas the framework
uses manifestation within an account of explanatory reconstruction. It would therefore be
inaccurate to say that the framework merely renames phenomenological givenness.
    Heidegger’s analysis of being-in-the-world and the fore-structure of understanding is relevant
to context-dependence. Understanding is not an isolated operation performed by a context-free
subject; it is situated within practical and interpretive involvement. The framework also denies
context-free explanatory cognition, but it gives context a specified role in the architecture of
explanation. Heidegger’s existential analytic and the framework’s epistemic context should
not be treated as interchangeable.
    Merleau-Ponty’s account of embodied and perspectival perception adds a further compar-
ison: the object is disclosed through situated perspectives rather than from an impossible
view from nowhere. The framework’s plurality of perspectives is comparable at this point,
although its account should be assessed on its own terms and not reduced to embodiment or
phenomenological perspectivism.

.10.6    Peirce and Dewey: Inquiry, Correction, and Practical Consequences
Peirce and Dewey are important for the dynamics of inquiry and the correction of cognition.
Peirce’s fallibilism and account of inquiry provide a comparison for the framework’s reconstruc-
.10. Comparative Profiles: Convergences and Decisive Differences                             609


tion, adequacy, and epistemic humility. Dewey’s account of inquiry as a transformation of an
indeterminate situation is relevant to the framework’s attention to context and cognitive cost.
    The difference concerns the criterion of success. Pragmatist accounts often connect meaning,
warranted assertion, or inquiry to practical consequences and the resolution of problematic
situations. The framework explicitly treats viability as descriptive rather than normative. It
therefore cannot equate viability with usefulness, successful coping, or practical satisfaction.
A reconstruction may function effectively in a situation and still fail fidelity to the identity;
conversely, a faithful reconstruction may be costly or difficult to sustain. The comparative task
is to explain how the framework relates these dimensions without reducing one to another.

.10.7    Avicenna: Perception, Intellect, and Self-Knowledge
Avicenna provides a major comparison for the gradation of cognitive faculties, the relation
between sensation, imagination, estimation, and intellect, and the analysis of self-awareness.
The famous “flying man” thought experiment is relevant to the question of self-awareness without
ordinary sensory awareness. It is not, however, equivalent to the framework’s distinctions
among self-regulation, self-awareness, consciousness, and awareness. The thought experiment
establishes a particular point about the soul’s awareness of itself; the framework classifies
epistemic functions and their relations.
    The comparison with knowledge by presence (al-`ilm al-h.ud.ūrı̄) requires similar care.
Avicenna’s account of self-knowledge and later Islamic elaborations of knowledge by presence
cannot be compressed into one doctrine. The framework’s identity/manifestation relation is not
automatically a form of knowledge by presence. A substantive comparison must ask whether
the identity is directly present to cognition, whether it is inferred through manifestations, and
what role representation plays in each account.

.10.8    Suhrawardi and Ibn `Arabı̄: Light and Manifestation
Suhrawardi is a central comparison for the language of light and illumination. In illuminationist
philosophy, light is not merely a metaphor for clarity; it is bound to a metaphysical account
of reality and knowledge. The framework’s epistemic light, by contrast, is introduced as a
condition and active structure of epistemic legibility. The resemblance is significant at the
level of function and vocabulary, but the difference in grounding is decisive. The framework’s
use of “light” must not be read as silently importing Suhrawardi’s ontology.
    Ibn `Arabı̄ is relevant to the multiplicity of manifestations and the relation between the
Real and loci of manifestation. Yet his doctrine of manifestation belongs to a metaphysical
and theological vision. The framework’s manifestation is an epistemic appearance within a
receiving context. The comparison can illuminate the question of how one referent may be
disclosed in multiple modes, but it cannot identify epistemic manifestation with ontological
tajallı̄.

.10.9    Mulla Sadra: Gradation, Change, and the Identity of the Subject
Mulla Sadra’s account of substantial motion, gradation of existence, and the relation between
soul and perception is a valuable comparison for continuity through change and the development
of cognitive capacities. The framework’s account of identity across manifestations may appear
close to the Sadrian concern with persistence and transformation. The difference is that Mulla
Sadra’s account is ultimately grounded in ontology, while the present volume restricts itself to
the epistemic conditions under which identity is reconstructed.
    This distinction is not a claim that the two systems are incompatible. It means that an
epistemological homology does not establish agreement about the nature of existence, the soul,
or substantial motion. Those questions belong to a different level of comparison and, within
the book’s own project, to a different volume.
610                         Appendix . A Comparative Study of the Philosophy of Viability


.10.10    Nāgārjuna, Yogācāra, and Nyāya: Three Distinct Eastern Compar-
          isons
These schools should not be grouped under a single “Eastern” epistemology. Their points of
contact with the framework are distinct.
    Madhyamaka, especially Nāgārjuna’s critique of svabhāva, provides a comparison for the
critique of reified identity and for the limits of conceptual determination. But the framework’s
claim that an identity cannot be exhaustively reconstructed from its manifestations does
not entail the Madhyamaka thesis that phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. One is an
epistemic limitation; the other is part of a philosophical critique of intrinsic existence and
dependent arising.
    Yogācāra offers comparisons concerning the structure of cognition, representation, and the
conditioning of experience. Its theories, however, vary across texts and interpreters; it should
not be reduced to the slogan that “everything is consciousness”. The framework’s epistemic
light and manifestation should be compared with specific Yogācāra accounts of cognition and
appearance, not with a simplified school label.
    Nyāya is especially relevant to Part IV because it develops detailed accounts of valid
cognition (pramān.a), error, and the sources of knowledge. This is a closer comparison
for epistemic validity than Madhyamaka or Daoism. Yet Nyāya’s realism and its theories
of knowledge-source reliability differ from the framework’s analysis of context validity and
reconstruction adequacy. A precise comparison must map each criterion to the Nyāya account
of perception, inference, comparison, and testimony rather than treating all criteria of validity
as equivalent.


.10.11    Interim Comparative Result
The profiles suggest that no single predecessor supplies the whole architecture. Different
traditions are close to different components: Aristotle to explanatory organization; Kant to
conditions and limits; Husserl to manifestation and horizon; Heidegger to situated understand-
ing; Peirce and Dewey to inquiry and correction; Avicenna to perception and self-awareness;
Suhrawardi to light; Ibn `Arabı̄ to manifestation; Mulla Sadra to continuity through change;
and the Buddhist and Nyāya traditions to distinct questions about identity, cognition, and
validity.
    This distribution supports a limited conclusion: the framework is synthetic in the sense
that it addresses a range of problems that have been treated in different traditions. It does not
yet establish historical independence, originality in the strong sense, or superiority over those
traditions. Those conclusions require textual, historical, and argumentative tests beyond the
identification of points of proximity.


.11      The Independence of the Framework
This section is separated from the historical comparison because the question “to which
philosopher is the book closest?” is not the same as the question “does the book have an
independent apparatus?” On the basis of the structure of the book, six distinct axes can be
identified.

   1. The four-column architecture of explanation. Four analytical roles—fixed, fluid,
      dynamics, context—with principles of necessity (removal test), sufficiency (reducibility
      test), and distinctness (Chapters 6–7), and with the conveyor principle (Chapter 8),
      non-sequential connectivity (Chapter 9), context-dependence (Chapter 10), and the
      infinity of contexts (Chapter 11).
.12. The Most Important Distinctions of the Framework                                       611


  2. The theory of epistemic relation. The distinction among identity, signature, pseudo-
     identity, manifestation, context, and perspective (Chapters 12–14); the sharpened account
     of epistemic light as an active structure of legibility (Chapters 15–16); the encompassment
     in epistemic light (Chapter 17); the desire to find (Chapter 18); the unknownness of same-
     category identities (Chapter 19); the distinction among self-awareness, consciousness,
     and awareness (Chapter 20).

  3. Epistemic light. The formulation of the condition of the possibility of legibility of
     relation as an active structure (Chapters 15–17), with the three directions (descending,
     ascending, reflective) and the non-travel of the light (Chapter 16).

  4. The theory of the limits of reconstruction. The impossibility of super-identity
     (Chapter 27), the fallacy of super-identity (Chapter 28), configuration-dependence
     (Chapter 29), the limits of self-knowledge (Chapter 30), the impossibility of complete
     knowledge of epistemic light (Chapter 31), the distinction between intrinsic and temporary
     unknownness (Chapter 32), the plurality of perspectives (Chapter 33).

  5. The criteria of validity and adequacy. The three criteria of context validity
     (Chapter 21), the proposed criterion of manifestational adequacy (Chapter 22), the
     three criteria of the adequacy of a pseudo-identity (Chapter 23), the three failures of
     reconstruction (Chapter 24), the principle of category-relative predication (Chapter 25),
     and the two measures of intensity and breadth (Chapter 26).

  6. The epistemic economy and viability. Fidelity, sustainability, recoverability (Chap-
     ter 37), the tendency to express and the degree of structural fidelity (Chapter 38), the
     cost of cognition (Chapter 39), the cognitive sediment (Chapter 40), the integration of
     sediment (Chapter 41), the balance criterion (Chapter 42), and the audit of the core
     commitments (Chapter 43).

    These six axes, taken together, present the book’s proposed architecture of explanatory
cognition. Their completeness is a structural claim to be assessed by the dependency map
and by the arguments for the individual commitments; the comparative survey alone does not
prove that no further axis is required. The important point is that the six axes depend on one
another. For example, without the theory of manifestation, the concept of pseudo-identity
cannot be understood; without the concept of pseudo-identity, the criteria of the adequacy
of reconstruction lose their subject matter; and without the cognitive limits, the concept of
viability cannot be formulated correctly. This interconnection is one of the important features
of the book’s structure.

.13    Limits of the Comparative Study and Outstanding Tests

merely by showing that its concepts have analogues in earlier traditions. It can, however,
identify the exact burden of proof. The following limitations are therefore part of the result,
not qualifications to be hidden.

     to others. The entries on Kant, Husserl, Avicenna, and the major Islamic illuminationist

.13. Limits of the Comparative Study and Outstanding Tests                                  613


     and philosophical traditions identify substantial points of contact; several other entries
     remain orientation-level comparisons. They should not be cited as if they were exhaustive
     interpretations of those thinkers.

  2. Primary-source verification. A number of comparisons are stated at the level of
     widely recognized positions. A full scholarly edition should attach precise primary-
     text references and, where relevant, distinguish the philosopher’s own text from later
     commentary and school interpretation.

  3. Translation risk. Terms such as identity, manifestation, light, context, consciousness,
     and viability do not have stable one-to-one equivalents across Greek, Arabic, Sanskrit,
     German, and English. Lexical resemblance is therefore insufficient; the comparison must
     be functional and inferential.

  4. Internal diversity. “Western”, “Islamic”, and “Eastern” are convenient organizing
     headings, not unified theoretical positions. The comparison must preserve disagreements
     within each tradition and avoid attributing one doctrine to an entire civilization or
     school.

  5. Asymmetry of scope. The present volume is epistemological, whereas several inter-
     locutors develop integrated metaphysical, theological, ethical, or soteriological systems.
     A comparison limited to epistemology can identify differences of grounding but cannot
     adjudicate the full systems.

  6. Originality is not established by difference alone. A framework may use a different
     vocabulary while reproducing an earlier structure; conversely, it may share a structure
     while making a genuinely new inferential move. Originality must be tested at the level
     of definitions, dependencies, arguments, and consequences.

   The most important outstanding comparative tests are these:

Four-column necessity. Does the removal of each column produce a determinate explanatory
     failure, and can that failure be shown without presupposing the four-column model?

Four-column sufficiency. Can every relevant explanatory function be assigned to one or
     more of the four columns without adding a fifth primitive role or forcing unlike functions
     together?

Identity and manifestation. Does the distinction resolve specific identity problems, or
     does it relocate them into the definition of identity? The answer requires case-by-
     case comparison with theories of persistence, individuation, intentional object, and
     appearance.

Epistemic light. Is epistemic light indispensable to the intelligibility of the relation, or can
     its explanatory work be reconstructed from other concepts already in the framework?

Viability. Are fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability jointly necessary and sufficient for
    the descriptive notion of viability? Are they independent, or can one be reduced to
    another?

Non-normativity. Can viability remain descriptive in every application, especially where
    sustainability and balance might be mistaken for practical success, value, or optimality?

   These tests connect the comparative appendix to the book’s own methodological standards.
They do not decide the outcome in advance. They specify what a successful defense of the
framework must establish.

.14     Conclusion of the Appendix
Three main results follow from the comparative study of the book’s six parts.

First result. The book is within the problem-tradition of epistemology, but its central
problem differs from that of many classical apparatuses. Many philosophical systems focus on
one of the following: the foundation of knowledge; the sources of knowledge; the possibility
of knowledge; the conditions of cognition; the relation of subject and object; the validity of
belief; or the limits of reason. The book attempts to organize these problems within a single
architecture of explanatory cognition. This is a claim about the organization of the present
volume, not a claim that the framework has already solved every problem that it brings into
relation.

Second result. The closest families for deep comparison are Western phenomenology, Islamic
epistemology, and pragmatism. Each at a particular level: Husserl, Heidegger, and Merleau-
Ponty for appearance, perspective, and context; Avicenna, Suhrawardi, Ibn `Arabı̄, and Mulla
Sadra for perception, light, manifestation, and identity; Peirce, Dewey, and Popper for validity,
reconstruction, and the correction of knowledge; Kant and Hume for the limits of cognition
and the finitude of the subject; Nāgārjuna and Yogācāra for the comparison with unknownness
and the structure of consciousness; Lakatos for the audit of Chapter 43.

Third result. The concept of viability in Part VI should be placed at the center of the
comparative assessment of the whole book, because it joins the architecture of cognition to the
economy of cognition, and brings together three problems in one framework: the preservation
of the fidelity of reconstruction to the structure of identity; the possibility of the continuation of
cognition with a bearable cost; and the possibility of recovering the capacity for manifestation
and reconstruction. This combination is the most important locus for the examination of the
conceptual independence of the framework.


.15     A Methodological Note on the Result of This Study
In this comparison, three kinds of claim are not to be confused with one another.

   1. Historical precedent. A problem was stated earlier in the work of a philosopher.

   2. Structural homology. Two frameworks organize a problem with analogous structures.

   3. Theoretical independence. A framework organizes a problem with its own definitions,
      principles, and inferential relations.

    For example, the presence of the concept of light in Suhrawardi and of epistemic light in
the book creates a historical precedent and a comparable structural homology; but to establish
or deny theoretical independence, one must examine the definition of light, its place in the
apparatus, its inferential function, and its results in both systems separately.
    This study is a philosophical and conceptual comparison, not a historical proof of the book’s
independence from all earlier traditions. Such a proof would require a historical examination
of the sources and the formation of the work.

The final result. The Philosophy of Viability, in this volume, is an epistemological project
centered on the architecture of explanatory cognition, the structure of manifestation and the
reconstruction of identity, the limits of cognition, and the epistemic economy of viability. Its
comparison with Kant, Husserl, Heidegger, Avicenna, Suhrawardi, Ibn `Arabı̄, Mulla Sadra,
.15. A Methodological Note on the Result of This Study                                    615


Peirce, and Nāgārjuna has the greatest philosophical capacity; but none of them is, alone,
representative of the whole framework.
    To reach a comparison at the level of academic research, the study should be supplemented
by a source-based dossier for each major comparison: primary-text passages, reliable transla-
tions, the precise claim being compared, the inferential role of that claim, and the strongest
objection to the proposed homology. Chapter-by-chapter extension can then proceed where
the comparison is substantive, rather than forcing every chapter into a parallel with every
tradition.

Formal Reconstruction of the
Four-Column Architecture

Scope
This appendix gives a formal reconstruction of the four-column architecture developed in
Chapters 6–10. It also makes explicit the methodological qualifications stated in Chapter 2
and the conditional status of the framework stated in Chapter 43. The reconstruction specifies
a formal language, a set of structural axioms, definitions, formal counterparts of the removal
and reducibility tests, a consistency model, and the limits of the formal treatment.
    The formalization is a supplement to the philosophical arguments. It does not replace the
prose, and it does not claim that the four columns are four ontological kinds of entity. They
are analytical roles within explanatory cognition: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing
dynamics, and context.
    The strength of the claims is deliberately differentiated. The removal test supports
a conditional necessity conclusion, given the commitment that explanatory failure can be
recognized. The reducibility test supports an estimate of sufficiency concerning the standard
candidates examined in the book. It does not prove that no future candidate could resist
reduction. The consistency result establishes only that the explicitly stated formal system
has a model. None of these results, by itself, establishes the metaphysical nature of what is
explained or the telos of cognition.


.16    Purpose and Methodological Status
The formal reconstruction serves three purposes. First, it separates primitive commitments
from definitions and makes the inferential structure inspectable. Second, it clarifies which
claims follow from the formal stipulations and which depend on substantive interpretations.
Third, it makes the limits of the formal claims visible.
    The three tests in Chapter 2 answer different questions. The removal test asks whether
a proposed column can be dropped while a complete explanation remains. The reducibility
test asks whether a proposed additional column can be reassigned to the existing columns
without loss. The test of fruitfulness asks whether the framework supports the arguments and
distinctions developed in the book. The present appendix formalizes aspects of the first two
tests; it does not formalize fruitfulness as a theorem.

Remark .25 (Necessity is conditional). The necessity result is conditional on the removal-test
commitment: when removal leaves a recognizable explanatory failure, the removed column is
necessary for the explanation under examination. The formal system can state the structure of
this inference, but it does not independently prove the epistemic commitment that recognizable
failure can be identified.

Remark .26 (Sufficiency is an estimate). The book does not claim to prove that no fifth
column could ever be found. Its sufficiency claim is an estimate supported by examining
618                        Appendix . Formal Reconstruction of the Four-Column Architecture


standard candidates. A candidate that resists reduction would count against that estimate.
The formal reconstruction preserves this open-ended status and does not convert the estimate
into an unrestricted theorem.

Remark .27 (Analytical, not metaphysical, reduction). To reassign the explanatory role
of purpose or normativity to the governing-dynamics column is not to claim that purposes
or norms are unreal, nor that their content is exhausted by the formal analysis. The claim
concerns the form of an explanation, not the whole reality or content to which the explanation
refers.


.17       The Formal Language
The language is a many-sorted first-order language. Variables range only over the sorts specified
below. The sorts classify entities appearing in explanatory relations; they are not the four
columns.

.17.1      Sorts
The language has four principal sorts, corresponding to the four categories of the material in
which the four analytical roles are assigned (Chapter 6, Section 6.9):

      • E: elements;

      • R: rules;

      • C: contexts;

      • X: explanations.

    It also has four auxiliary sorts, which are used in the finitude axioms (Group F) and in
the application predicate:

      • S: states;

      • P: subjects or cognizers;

      • A: acts or reconstructions;

      • T: times.

    The four principal sorts are those introduced in Chapter 6 (Section 6.9); the four auxiliary
sorts are added here because the finitude claims concern subjects, acts, states, and temporal
intervals, and because the application predicate Apply takes a state as its last argument. The
distinction between principal and auxiliary sorts is stated so that the reader who has followed
Chapter 6 meets the same four principal sorts here, and so that the addition of the auxiliary
sorts is visible as an addition, not as a silent change of the language.
    The additional sorts P, A, and T are typed so that the finitude claims can be stated without
untyped variables; the additional sort S is typed so that the application predicate can take a
state as its last argument.

.17.2      Predicates
The four role predicates are:

      • InF (e, x): e occupies the fixed-element role in x;

      • InΦ (e, x): e occupies the fluid-element role in x;
.18. Axioms                                                                                         619


   • Dyn(x, r): r is a governing rule of x;

   • Ctx(x, c): c is a context of x.

   The remaining predicates are:

   • Carries(eϕ , e1 , e2 ): the fluid element eϕ conveys an effect from e1 to e2 ;

   • Apply(r, e1 , e2 , eϕ , s): applying rule r to the ordered relation involving e1 , e2 , eϕ yields s;

   • Complete(x): x is complete in the primitive sense;

   • WF(x): x is well-formed;

   • ValidConveyance(x): x has valid conveyance;

   • DynCoherent(x): x is dynamically coherent;

   • StructuralComplete(x): x is structurally complete;

   • DeterminedBy(e, c): the role of e is determined relative to context c;

   • Occupies(p, c, t): subject p occupies context c at time t;

   • Completes(p, a, t): subject p completes act a at time t.

    The language also contains a removal operation x \ κ, where κ ranges over the four role
symbols F, Φ, D, K. This operation is stipulated at the formal level; its relevant properties
are stated in Group S below. Role-set comparisons used in the reducibility and distinctness
discussions are meta-theoretical set comparisons, not first-order predicates in the sorted
language.


.17.3   Abbreviations
For readability, the following abbreviations will be used:

                                    Has(x, F ) :≡ ∃e InF (e, x),
                                    Has(x, Φ) :≡ ∃e InΦ (e, x),
                                    Has(x, D) :≡ ∃r Dyn(x, r),
                                    Has(x, K) :≡ ∃c Ctx(x, c).

   We also write Four(x) for the conjunction

                         Has(x, F ) ∧ Has(x, Φ) ∧ Has(x, D) ∧ Has(x, K).

The axioms are grouped by their role in the reconstruction. Their status is not uniform:
some articulate the proposed structure, some state the formal test conditions, and some are
substantive commitments of the reconstruction. The grouping is organizational and does not
imply that every axiom is derivable from the others.

.18.5   Group E: Completeness Axioms
The primitive predicate Complete is not defined to mean structural completeness. The following
axioms state the relation adopted in this reconstruction.

E1 (Structural completeness implies primitive completeness).

                              ∀x(StructuralComplete(x) → Complete(x)).

E2 (Well-formed structural failure).

                     ∀x((WF(x) ∧ ¬StructuralComplete(x)) → ¬Complete(x)).

E3 (Failure of well-formedness).

                                      ∀x(¬WF(x) → ¬Complete(x)).

    E1 has only the direction displayed. It does not assert that primitive completeness implies
structural completeness by itself. E2 applies to well-formed but structurally incomplete
explanations; E3 applies to explanations that are not well-formed. Together, E1, E2, and E3
yield the equivalence
                            Complete(x) ↔ StructuralComplete(x),
provided the cases WF(x) and ¬WF(x) are exhaustive, as they are in classical first-order logic.

.18.6   Group F: Finitude Axioms
The finitude claims are stated using the appropriate sorts. Their set-cardinality notation is a
metatheoretical abbreviation.

F1 (Finitude of occupied contexts). For every subject and time, the set of contexts oc-
     cupied by that subject at that time is finite:

                         ∀p ∈ P, t ∈ T     {c ∈ C : Occupies(p, c, t)} < ∞.

F2 (Finitude of completed acts over a finite interval). For every subject and every
     bounded interval of time, the set of acts completed within that interval is finite:

            ∀p ∈ P, t1 , t2 ∈ T, t1 ≤ t2   {a ∈ A : ∃t ∈ [t1 , t2 ] Completes(p, a, t)} < ∞.

    These axioms formalize finitude claims relevant to the framework; they do not assert that
the total number of possible contexts, acts, or times in the universe is finite.

.18.7   Group S: Removal Axioms
For each structurally complete explanation, removal deletes the relevant constituent. The
stated retention conditions apply only where explicitly listed. Restricting these axioms to
structurally complete inputs makes their scope match the removal test; no assumption is made
about repeated removal from an already damaged explanation.

S1 (Removal of fixed elements).
                                                                        
                          ∀x, e StructuralComplete(x) → ¬InF (e, x \ F ) .

S2 (Fluid elements retained under fixed-role removal).

                    ∀x, e(StructuralComplete(x) → (InΦ (e, x) ↔ InΦ (e, x \ F ))).

S3 (Dynamics retained under fixed-role removal).

                   ∀x, r(StructuralComplete(x) → (Dyn(x, r) ↔ Dyn(x \ F, r))).

S4 (Context retained under fixed-role removal).

                    ∀x, c(StructuralComplete(x) → (Ctx(x, c) ↔ Ctx(x \ F, c))).

S5 (Removal of fluid elements).
                                                                       
                          ∀x, e StructuralComplete(x) → ¬InΦ (e, x \ Φ) .

S6 (Removal of governing dynamics).
                                                                      
                          ∀x, r StructuralComplete(x) → ¬Dyn(x \ D, r) .

S7 (Removal of context).
                                                                      
                          ∀x, c StructuralComplete(x) → ¬Ctx(x \ K, c) .

    The removal operation is required to produce an explanation in the sort X. S1, S5, S6, and
S7 guarantee that the corresponding removed explanation lacks one of the four constituents
required by well-formedness. No claim is made here that removal preserves every other feature
of the original explanation; only the stated retention conditions are assumed.

.19     Definitions
Definition .2 (Well-formedness). An explanation is well-formed exactly when it contains at
least one fixed element, at least one fluid element, a governing rule, and a context:
                        WF(x) :≡ ∃e1 , e2 , r, c InF (e1 , x) ∧ InΦ (e2 , x)
                                                                          
                                                   ∧ Dyn(x, r) ∧ Ctx(x, c) .
Definition .3 (Valid conveyance). An explanation has valid conveyance when every ordered
pair of distinct fixed elements in it is connected by at least one fluid carrier:
           ValidConveyance(x) :≡ ∀e1 , e2 InF (e1 , x) ∧ InF (e2 , x) ∧ e1 ̸= e2
                                                                                            
                                               → ∃eϕ (InΦ (eϕ , x) ∧ Carries(eϕ , e1 , e2 )) .
Definition .4 (Dynamical coherence). An explanation is dynamically coherent when every
carrying relation has a governing rule and a resulting state:
         DynCoherent(x) :≡ ∀e1 , e2 , eϕ Carries(eϕ , e1 , e2 )
                                                                                            
                                             → ∃r, s(Dyn(x, r) ∧ Apply(r, e1 , e2 , eϕ , s)) .
Definition .5 (Structural completeness).
         StructuralComplete(x) :≡ WF(x) ∧ ValidConveyance(x) ∧ DynCoherent(x).
Definition .6 (The four analytical roles). The predicates InF , InΦ , Dyn, and Ctx express,
respectively, the roles of fixed element, fluid element, governing dynamics, and context. The
predicates classify explanatory functions in a context; they do not classify four ontological
kinds of entity.
Definition .7 (Necessity under the removal test). A role κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K} is necessary for a
structurally complete explanation when removing that role yields an explanation that is not
primitively complete:
                   Necessary(κ) :≡ ∀x (StructuralComplete(x) ∧ Has(x, κ))
                                                          
                                       → ¬Complete(x \ κ) .
Definition .8 (Explanatory role sets). For each analytical role κ, let R(κ) be the set of
explanatory functions assigned to that role in the analysis under consideration. For a candidate
q, let R(q) be the set of explanatory functions performed by that candidate. These are sets in
the metatheory. Their membership and inclusion require substantive interpretation; they are
not consequences of the many-sorted syntax alone.
Definition .9 (Pointwise reducibility of a candidate). A candidate q is reducible to the four
columns when each explanatory function performed by q can be reassigned, without loss, to at
least one of the four existing columns:
                             R(q) ⊆ R(F ) ∪ R(Φ) ∪ R(D) ∪ R(K).
The inclusion is pointwise: each function is assigned to an existing column. It does not create
a fifth column, and it does not require all functions of a candidate to be assigned to one and
the same column. Where a candidate’s functions divide between columns, the analysis must
state that division explicitly.
624                     Appendix . Formal Reconstruction of the Four-Column Architecture


Definition .10 (The formal counterparts of the two tests). The removal test is represented
by Definition .7 and Theorem .1. The reducibility test is represented by Definition .9 and the
candidate-by-candidate assessment in Section .21.2. The tests answer different questions and
neither substitutes for the other.

Definition .11 (Finitude principle). The formal counterpart of the finitude principle is given
by F1 and F2: F1 concerns the finite set of contexts occupied by a subject at a given time; F2
concerns the finite set of acts completed by a subject over a bounded interval.


.20     Formal Results
Theorem .1 (Formal necessity). For each κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K}, Necessary(κ).

Theorem .2 (Reduction of the examined candidates). On the candidate-role analyses stated
in Section .21.2, each of the four standard candidates—purpose, time, observer, and the
normative dimension—is reducible to the four columns in the sense of Definition .9. The
theorem is conditional on the examined candidates: it does not quantify over every possible
future candidate, and it does not establish that no irreducible fifth column can be found.
Its proper epistemic status is an estimate concerning the standard candidates examined, in
keeping with Chapter 2.

Theorem .3 (Distinctness of the analytical roles). If the role-specificity condition stated in
Section .21.3 is accepted, then no one of the four role-sets is included in another. This is a
conditional result about analytical functions, not a claim that the four columns are four kinds
of entity.

Theorem .4 (Consistency). The axioms and definitions stated in this appendix have a model.

Remark .28 (Why the four results are stated as theorems). The four results are stated as
theorems, not as propositions, because they are the formal counterparts of the framework’s
central claims: the necessity of the four columns (Chapter 7), the sufficiency estimate for
the standard candidates (Chapter 7), the distinctness of the four roles (Chapter 7), and
the consistency of the formal system. Chapters 6, 7, and 43 refer to them as theorems,
and the Index of Formalizations records them as theorems. The word “theorem” does not
overstate their status: each theorem states its conditionality in its own statement (necessity
is conditional on the removal-test commitment; sufficiency is conditional on the examined
candidates; distinctness is conditional on the role-specificity premise). The theorem’s status is
the status of a formal result at a stated strength, not the status of an unconditional truth.


.21     Proofs and Candidate Assessments
.21.1    Proof of Necessity
Proof of Theorem .1. Let x be structurally complete, and let κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K} be a role that
x has. We show that ¬Complete(x \ κ).
    Case κ = F . By S1, the removed explanation x \ F has no fixed element. It therefore fails
the first existential condition in Definition .2, so ¬WF(x \ F ). By E3, ¬Complete(x \ F ).
    Case κ = Φ. By S5, x \ Φ has no fluid element. Hence ¬WF(x \ Φ), and E3 gives
¬Complete(x \ Φ).
    Case κ = D. By S6, x \ D has no governing rule. Hence ¬WF(x \ D), and E3 gives
¬Complete(x \ D).
    Case κ = K. By S7, x \ K has no context. Hence ¬WF(x \ K), and E3 gives ¬Complete(x \
K).
.21. Proofs and Candidate Assessments                                                         625


    In every case, removal defeats well-formedness and therefore defeats primitive completeness
by E3. E2 is not used in these four cases, because its antecedent requires the removed
explanation to remain well-formed. E1 concerns the original structurally complete explanation;
it does not establish the failure of its removal. Since x and κ were arbitrary, the definition of
necessity is satisfied.

Remark .29 (What the proof establishes). The proof establishes necessity relative to the
stipulated well-formedness conditions, removal operation, and completeness axioms. It does not
independently prove that these stipulations are the only possible account of explanation. The
philosophical force of the removal test remains conditional on the methodological commitment
that the resulting failure is recognizable as explanatory failure.


.21.2    Assessment of the Standard Candidates
The following candidate assessments are the formal counterparts of the examples examined in
Chapters 2 and 7. They are not deductions from the first-order axioms. Each is an explicit
interpretation of the candidate’s explanatory function, and each remains open to challenge by
a counterexample. The four candidates are the same four that Chapter 2 (Section 2.4.2) and
Chapter 7 (Section 7.4) examine: purpose, time, observer, and the normative dimension.


Candidate 1: Purpose or goal. A teleological explanation states a target or direction
toward which a system tends. In the explanatory form under examination, that function
is performed by a governing rule. Thus the relevant candidate functions are reassigned to
dynamics:
                                  R(purpose) ⊆ R(D).

This is an analytical reduction of the role of purpose in an explanation. It is not a metaphysical
denial of purposes or goals.


Candidate 2: Time. Temporal order may enter an explanation as a feature of succession and
change, in which case it is represented under governing dynamics; or it may enter as part of the
frame or scale at which elements are individuated, in which case it is represented under context.
Accordingly, the candidate’s explanatory functions are partitioned into temporal-dynamical
and temporal-contextual functions:

                              RD (time) ⊆ R(D),
                              RK (time) ⊆ R(K),
                               R(time) = RD (time) ∪ RK (time).

This does not posit a fifth temporal column. It states that the functions attributed to time in
the examined explanations are assigned to the dynamics or context column according to their
explanatory use.


Candidate 3: The observer. The standpoint of the cognizer is represented through the
context: the question asked, the means used, and the scale adopted. Thus

                                     R(observer) ⊆ R(K).

The claim is that the observer’s explanatory role is made explicit by context, not that the
observer is unreal or unimportant.
626                       Appendix . Formal Reconstruction of the Four-Column Architecture


Candidate 4: The normative dimension. A normative explanation may be represented,
at the level of its explanatory form, as invoking a rule concerning what ought to be done
or what state ought to be approached. In that form, its explanatory function is assigned to
governing dynamics:
                                   R(normative) ⊆ R(D).
This does not claim that the content of a norm is exhausted by the formal role of a governing
rule. It claims only that the form of the normative explanation can be analyzed through the
four columns. The normative candidate remains the most serious challenge to the sufficiency
estimate: a reader who shows that its explanatory form cannot be analyzed through the four
columns has supplied a counterexample to the estimate.

Remark .30 (Status of the sufficiency theorem). Theorem .2 is supported by the four candidate
analyses just stated. It does not quantify over every possible future candidate, and it does
not establish that no irreducible fifth column can be found. Its proper epistemic status is
an estimate concerning the standard candidates examined, in keeping with Chapter 2. The
theorem’s title (“Reduction of the examined candidates”) records this scope, and the theorem’s
statement states it explicitly.

.21.3    Proof of Distinctness
The first-order axioms establish some structural distinctions. For example, A4 excludes
simultaneous fixed/fluid membership of one element in one explanation, while the sorts
distinguish elements, rules, contexts, and explanations. Those facts alone do not prove that
all four meta-theoretical role-sets are pairwise incomparable.
     For the conditional distinctness result, the following role-specificity condition is required:

                           ∀κi ̸= κj ∈ {F, Φ, D, K},         R(κi ) ⊈ R(κj ).                  (RS)

Condition (RS) says that each analytical role contains at least one explanatory function not
performed by any one of the other roles. It is an interpretive premise about the role-sets, not
a theorem obtained from A1–A4.

Proof of Theorem .3. Assume (RS). Let κi and κj be distinct columns. By (RS), there is at
least one explanatory function in R(κi ) that is not in R(κj ). Therefore R(κi ) ⊈ R(κj ). Since
the ordered pair was arbitrary, no role-set is included in another. The conclusion is conditional
on (RS), as stated.

Remark .31 (Why typed sorts are not enough). The fact that elements, rules, and contexts
occupy different formal sorts does not by itself establish the non-inclusion of all role-sets.
The fixed and fluid columns are both roles played by elements, and role-set inclusion is a
comparison of explanatory functions rather than of the underlying sorts. The role-specificity
premise must therefore be stated rather than inferred from typing alone.

.21.4    Proof of Consistency
Proof of Theorem .4. We give a finite model. Let the domains be

non-well-formed explanation in the model is not complete. E1 holds because each structurally

relation has no intermediate two-edge factorization. C1 holds because each application input
has only one output state. C2 holds by the displayed application tuples. D1 and D2 hold
by the interpretation of DeterminedBy and the role predicates. F1 and F2 hold because the
occupancy and completion relations are empty. Ex holds because x1 and x2 are complete.
    Thus every axiom has been satisfied in the same structure M. The formal system therefore
has a model and is consistent.


Remark .32 (Scope of the consistency model). The model is a consistency witness, not a
complete representation of the philosophical framework. It shows that the displayed axioms
can be jointly satisfied. It does not prove that the axioms are true of every explanatory
practice, nor does it settle the philosophical interpretation of the role predicates.

.23     Limits of the Formalization
First limit: supplement, not substitute. The formal reconstruction supplements the
prose arguments. It does not replace their philosophical content or the interpretive work
performed by the chapters.

Second limit: one possible formalization. The language and axioms constitute one
possible formal rendering. Other formal languages may capture the same analytical distinctions
with different primitives or definitions.

Third limit: structure, not telos. The formal system concerns the structure of explanatory
cognition. It does not establish the purpose or telos of cognition.

Fourth limit: necessity depends on a methodological commitment. The necessity
proof is valid relative to the stipulated removal operation, well-formedness condition, and
completeness axioms. The philosophical force of the removal test depends on the declared
commitment that explanatory failure can be recognized.

Fifth limit: sufficiency remains revisable. The candidate assessment concerns purpose,
time, observer, and the normative dimension. It does not rule out every possible future
candidate. An irreducible candidate would count against the sufficiency estimate.

Sixth limit: role-set assumptions are interpretive. The reducibility assessment and
distinctness result depend on interpretations of explanatory functions. In particular, the
role-specificity condition (RS) is an explicit premise for incomparability; it is not derived from
the mere fact that the language has different sorts.
630                      Appendix . Formal Reconstruction of the Four-Column Architecture


Seventh limit: analytical roles are context-sensitive. The columns classify roles within
explanatory cognition. The same entity may occupy different roles in different explanatory
contexts, provided the formal representation does not assign it both fixed and fluid roles within
the same explanation. This is the distinction captured by A4 and D2.

Remark .34 (The reader’s point of assessment). A reader may accept the formal derivations
while questioning a substantive premise, such as the criterion of well-formedness, the removal
operation, or a candidate-role analysis. Such a challenge is not hidden by the formal notation;
it identifies precisely where the philosophical argument must be assessed.

Remark .35 (Closing note). The formal reconstruction makes a specified part of the four-
column principle inspectable. Its value lies in clarifying assumptions, inferential steps, and
limitations. The prose remains the philosophical substance; the formalization is a disciplined
supplement.


A Note on the Formal Reconstruction and the Indexes
The formal reconstruction is recorded in the Index of Formalizations and in the Index of
Epistemic Principles. The present appendix is the source for those entries.


A Note on the Status of the Formal Reconstruction
The vocabulary and axioms of this appendix are stipulated for the purpose of formal recon-
struction. The necessity result is conditional on the removal-test commitments. The sufficiency
result is an estimate concerning the standard candidates examined, and is stated as Theorem .2
with the scope of its estimate made explicit. The distinctness result is conditional on the
role-specificity premise (RS), and is stated as Theorem .3 with that conditionality made
explicit. The consistency result is supported by the finite model constructed above.

The formal reconstruction is offered as a supplement, not as a substitute. The prose is the
substance; the formalization makes a specified part of that substance assessable in a precise
form.
