An Independent Comparative Stress
Test against Six Major Epistemological
Traditions

Scope
This appendix is a supplementary study of the theoretical independence of the epistemology
developed in Book I, Epistemology of Viability. It has seven parts. The first part states
the question, the scope, and the method of the comparison. The second part compares the
framework with Kant. The third part compares it with Husserl. The fourth part compares it
with Peirce. The fifth part compares it with Suhrawardi. The sixth part compares it with
Mulla Sadra. The seventh part compares it with Dharmakirti. The appendix then states the
cross-comparative assessment, the internal stress tests, and the final assessment.
    The study is designed as a supplementary appendix to Book I. It does not replace the book’s
existing comparative study, whose scope is broader. The present inquiry isolates six demanding
interlocutors and asks whether the architecture developed in Book I can withstand comparison
with them. The terminology and distinctions used here follow Book I. In particular, this study
preserves the distinction between cognitive and ontological architecture, treats viability as a
descriptive epistemic concept, and does not import the metaphysical commitments of Book II
into the epistemological argument.
    The study distinguishes four claims that are often conflated: historical priority, conceptual
resemblance, functional equivalence, and theoretical independence. A concept may have
precedents without being reducible to them; two theories may resemble one another without
performing the same explanatory work; and functional equivalence does not by itself establish
identity of foundations. Conversely, different terminology is not evidence of originality. The
relevant question is whether the definitions, principles, and inferential dependencies of Book I
can be reconstructed from a rival framework without adding commitments that the rival does
not contain.
    The central claim of Book I is that explanatory cognition has a four-column analytical
architecture: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context. Its account of
epistemic relations distinguishes identity, signature, pseudo-identity, manifestation, perspective,
and epistemic light. It further examines context-validity, manifestational adequacy, limits and
forms of unknownness, epistemic economy, and viability. Viability is the structural character
of the relation between an identity and its manifestations in a cognitive context, considered
through fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.
    The comparative result is deliberately qualified. No one of the six traditions, taken by
itself, reproduces the whole architecture of Book I. Yet this absence does not prove originality,
historical independence, or superiority. The strongest case for distinctiveness lies in the
integration of the four analytical roles with the account of epistemic relations, limits, and
epistemic economy, together with the specific derivation of viability. That case remains
answerable to objections concerning redundancy, circularity, scope, and the status of its
632                                     Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


foundational commitments.
    The study’s claims are comparative; where the appendix speaks of “precedent,” “resem-
blance,” “equivalence,” “reconstructibility,” or “independence,” these are technical terms of
the comparative method, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in Section .24.4. The
appendix’s silence on questions of value is not a denial but a recognition that the comparative
assessment is not the whole of what can be said.


.24     Question, Scope, and Method
.24.1    What Is Being Tested
The object of comparison is the epistemology of Book I, not the entire eighteen-volume
series and not the metaphysics developed in Book II. Book I explicitly distinguishes cognitive
architecture from ontological architecture. Its four columns are introduced as analytical roles
in explanatory cognition; they are not initially offered as an ontology or as a doctrine of what
exists. Any comparison that silently turns the epistemological framework into a metaphysical
system misstates the target.
    The relevant question is therefore not whether Kant, Husserl, Peirce, Suhrawardi, Mulla
Sadra, or Dharmakirti anticipated the entire Philosophy of Viability. It is whether their
accounts contain resources that can reproduce the explanatory work assigned in Book I to its
four columns, epistemic relations, validity conditions, limits, and viability.

.24.2    The Book’s Own Architecture
Book I begins with explanatory cognition and four questions: What? How? On what basis?
Where? These are not four material causes. They are four analytical questions that an
adequate explanatory cognition must address. They are articulated as four distinct roles:

   1. Fixed elements: what the explanation holds fixed, including the relevant identities
      and determinations.

   2. Fluid elements: what makes relations among the fixed elements possible and intelligible.

   3. Governing dynamics: the rules, constraints, and modal structures that govern what
      can occur or be asserted.

   4. Context: the cognitive setting in which the other roles are assigned, interpreted, and
      related.

The Four-Column Principle argues for the necessity of the four roles by a removal test and
supports their joint sufficiency by a reducibility test. The book is careful about the different
strengths of these results: necessity is argued; sufficiency is supported as an estimate rather
than presented as an unrestricted theorem about every possible form of cognition. The
distinctness of the roles matters as much as their joint presence.
    The book’s account of epistemic relations includes identity, signature, and pseudo-identity;
manifestation as epistemic appearance; context and perspective; and epistemic light as the
medium or condition of relation. Epistemic light is not a physical ray, a metaphysical substance,
or an unargued identification with Suhrawardian Light. It names a trans-categorical condition
under which relations become legible in cognition. The account also examines the desire to find,
unknownness among same-category identities, self-regulation, self-awareness, consciousness,
and awareness.
    The later parts of Book I address context validity, manifestational adequacy, pseudo-
identity, failures of reconstruction, category-relative predication, intensity and breadth, the
impossibility and fallacy of super-identity, configuration-dependence, limits of self-knowledge,
.24. Question, Scope, and Method                                                              633


unknownness, plurality of perspectives, epistemic humility, cognitive cost, cognitive sediment,
and the balance criterion.


.24.3    Viability: The Book’s Specific Concept
Book I defines viability as the structural character of the relation between an identity and its
manifestations in a cognitive context. The identity itself does not admit of degrees: something
is or is not that identity. Viability admits of degrees because it characterizes the relation
through which an identity is cognitively manifested.

   1. Fidelity: the manifestation preserves the essential determination of the identity, so that
      what cognition records is recognizable as an appearance of that identity rather than
      another.

   2. Sustainability: the cost of producing and maintaining the manifestation does not
      exceed what the receiving cognitive context can bear.

   3. Recoverability: the identity retains the structural capacity to manifest in that context;
      the threshold at which restoring a manifestation would cost more than producing a new
      one has not been crossed.

These are structural and descriptive conditions. Sustainability is not mere temporal endurance
or practical success. Recoverability is not simply memory or psychological recollection. Viability
does not, by definition, mean that a belief is good, morally desirable, useful, or true. Its
epistemological role must be assessed within the book’s account of validity and adequacy; it
must not be converted into a substitute definition of truth.


.24.4    Method of Comparison
Each interlocutor is examined under six headings: (i) the problem addressed and the achieve-
ment; (ii) the commitments and questions left open; (iii) the point of convergence with Book I;
(iv) the decisive difference; (v) the strongest objection that the rival perspective can raise; and
(vi) the extent to which Book I’s answer can be reconstructed from the rival’s own resources.
    The comparison uses four levels:

Historical precedent
     A problem or concept has appeared earlier in a tradition.

Structural resemblance
     Two theories arrange concepts or relations in a similar pattern.

Functional equivalence
    Two concepts perform substantially the same explanatory task.

Inferential reconstructibility
     The claims of one framework can be derived from the principles of another without
     importing additional premises.

Only the last level directly bears on the strongest form of theoretical independence. Even then,
independence is a matter of degree and scope, not a binary verdict established by terminology.
634                                     Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


.25     Kant: Conditions and Limits of Cognition
.25.1    Problem and Achievement
Kant’s critical philosophy asks how synthetic a priori cognition is possible and what makes
objective experience possible. In the Critique of Pure Reason, sensibility gives intuitions and
understanding thinks them through concepts. The categories are conditions under which
the manifold of intuition can be unified as experience. Their legitimate theoretical use is
restricted to objects of possible experience. Kant’s achievement is therefore double: he explains
conditions of objective experience and, by the same move, establishes limits on speculative
cognition.
    The proximity to Book I is substantial at the level of the question. Both approaches ask
after conditions that make cognition possible and both refuse to treat the knowing subject as
an unlimited spectator. Both also distinguish the conditions of cognition from claims that
exceed those conditions.

.25.2    Open Questions and Differences
The interpretation of the phenomenon/noumenon distinction remains contested: it may be
read as a distinction between two standpoints or as involving a stronger distinction between
domains. The relation between the affection of sensibility and the unknowability of things
in themselves is also difficult. These are not simple defects; they are enduring interpretive
problems within Kant scholarship.
     Book I, however, is not primarily a transcendental deduction of the categories. It asks
for the analytical roles required by explanatory cognition and tests them by removal and
reducibility. Kant’s categories are not equivalent to the four columns. The fixed elements,
fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context are roles in an explanatory architecture, not
a list of pure concepts of the understanding. Nor does Kant develop an account corresponding
in detail to cognitive cost, cognitive sediment, recoverability, and the balance criterion.

.25.3    The Viability Framework’s Distinct Response
Book I offers a more differentiated map of explanatory cognition. Instead of treating the
conditions of experience as a single transcendental problem, it separates what is held fixed,
what mediates relation, what governs possibility, and the context in which cognition operates.
It then asks how identity is manifested, how a manifestation can be adequate, and what limits
arise from the finitude of the epistemic subject and the plurality of contexts.
    The relation to Kant is therefore one of shared critical ambition but different architecture.
Kant can illuminate the need to distinguish conditions and limits; he does not, without further
argument, yield the four-column framework or the three components of viability.

.25.4    Strongest Kantian Objection
A Kantian may object that Book I treats its four roles as if they were discovered through
analysis, while the very possibility of identifying and distinguishing those roles may depend on
conditions of synthesis that the book has not independently justified. The removal test may
show that a role is needed within the chosen practice of explanation, not that it is a necessary
condition of cognition as such. The Kantian will ask whether the framework has established
its transcendental scope or merely described a familiar class of explanatory activity.
    The proper reply is not to claim that Book I has refuted Kant. It must clarify its scope:
explanatory cognition is the target, and the Four-Column Principle is to be assessed at the
strength and domain stated in the book. If the claim is generalized to all cognition, a stronger
argument is required.
.26. Husserl: Givenness, Horizon, and Constitution                                                635


.25.5    Reconstructibility and Verdict
Kant can reconstruct the general idea that cognition has enabling conditions and limits. He
cannot straightforwardly reconstruct the specific four-role architecture, the distinction between
identity, signature, and pseudo-identity, or viability as fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.
The overlap is strong concerning conditions and limits, but limited concerning the book’s
detailed architecture and epistemic economy. The Kantian comparison is a serious test of
scope, not a demonstration that Book I is reducible to transcendental idealism.


.26     Husserl: Givenness, Horizon, and Constitution
.26.1    Problem and Achievement
Husserl’s phenomenology investigates how objects are given in experience and how their
identity is intended across changing profiles. An object is not ordinarily given all at once in a
single exhaustive presentation. It appears through adumbrations, within horizons of possible
further experience. Intentionality, fulfilment, evidence, and the structures of temporal and
horizonal consciousness provide tools for describing how something is meant and recognized as
the same through varying appearances.
    This is a close point of contact with Book I’s distinction between identity and manifestation.
Both approaches resist identifying an object with one isolated appearance. Both treat the
context or horizon of appearance as relevant to what can be given and how it can be understood.

.26.2    Open Questions and Differences
Phenomenology contains multiple methodological and transcendental developments, and the
relation between descriptive phenomenology and transcendental constitution is not reducible
to one formula. Husserl’s analyses also do not present the same four analytical roles as Book I.
A horizon is not simply the book’s context column; intentionality is not identical to the fluid
element; and no direct equivalence should be asserted between phenomenological fulfilment
and viability.
    Book I’s concern with cognitive cost, the structural threshold of recoverability, and the
integration of the three viability conditions is not a central Husserlian project. Phenomenology
may describe horizons and modes of givenness in great detail without thereby deriving a
general account of the sustainability of manifestation within a finite cognitive context.

.26.3    The Viability Framework’s Distinct Response
Book I distinguishes identity, its signature, pseudo-identity, and manifestation. This allows it to
ask not only how an object is given through profiles, but also how a cognitive reconstruction can
preserve or distort the identity it purports to present. It adds a systematic account of context
validity and manifestational adequacy, then considers the costs and limits of maintaining a
manifestation in a cognitive context.
    The book’s epistemic light should not be equated with phenomenological givenness. It is
introduced as a condition of legibility of relation, not as a synonym for the appearing of an
object. A phenomenological reconstruction may illuminate aspects of the relation, but the
equivalence requires argument.

.26.4    Strongest Husserlian Objection
A Husserlian may argue that Book I’s talk of identity and manifestation presupposes an
account of intentionality and evidence that it has not fully supplied. What warrants the
claim that a manifestation preserves an identity rather than merely fitting a prior conceptual
636                                      Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


scheme? If fidelity is assessed by the same cognitive context that constructs the manifestation,
the criterion may be circular. Phenomenology will demand an account of fulfilment, evidence,
and the modes in which the object itself can correct an anticipation.
    This objection presses Book I to show how fidelity is assessed without reducing it to
coherence with the subject’s expectations. The answer must be found in the book’s own
account of identity, signature, pseudo-identity, reconstruction, and context validity; it cannot
be supplied merely by renaming phenomenological evidence.

.26.5    Reconstructibility and Verdict
Husserl offers strong resources for understanding appearance, horizon, and the identity of
an object across profiles. He does not by himself supply Book I’s four-column architecture
or its integrated account of cognitive economy and recoverability. The overlap is strong
concerning manifestation and context, moderate concerning identity, and limited concerning
the three viability conditions. Husserl is among the closest interlocutors, but not a complete
reconstruction of Book I.


.27     Peirce: Inquiry, Fallibilism, and Correction
.27.1    Problem and Achievement
Peirce’s epistemology is inseparable from signs, inference, and inquiry. His account of abduction,
deduction, and induction explains how hypotheses are proposed, consequences derived, and
claims tested. Fallibilism rejects the idea that any finite belief is immune to correction. Inquiry
is a communal and potentially self-correcting process oriented toward the stabilization of belief
under continued investigation. Peirce’s pragmatic maxim clarifies the meaning of concepts
through their conceivable practical bearings.
    Peirce is especially relevant to Book I’s concern with reconstruction, error, the finitude
of the epistemic subject, and the correction of cognitive claims. His work also provides a
strong challenge to any framework that might appear to make the individual subject the final
measure of validity.

.27.2    Open Questions and Differences
Peirce’s semiotic and pragmatic framework is not a four-column analysis of explanatory
cognition. The triadic structure of sign, object, and interpretant cannot simply be mapped
onto fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context. The categories of
Firstness, Secondness, and Thirdness likewise perform a different systematic role.
    Peirce’s communal and long-run account of inquiry also differs from Book I’s analysis of
a finite subject operating across cognitive contexts. The latter does not reduce validity to
eventual communal convergence. Nor is viability equivalent to pragmatic success: Book I
explicitly treats viability as descriptive structural character, not as a value or telos.

.27.3    The Viability Framework’s Distinct Response
Book I’s account of cognitive cost, cognitive sediment, integration, and balance asks how a
finite cognitive context can maintain and revise manifestations without exceeding its capacities.
Recoverability adds a structural question: whether the identity retains the capacity to manifest
again in that context, and whether restoration remains viable relative to the cost of producing
a new manifestation. This is not identical to Peircean correction, though both address the
temporality and revisability of cognition.
     The book’s epistemic status labels—axiom or foundational commitment (A), argued (T),
estimate (E), open epistemic question (Q), speculation (S), and proposed—also make explicit
.28. Suhrawardi: Illumination and Knowledge by Presence                                         637


differences in argumentative strength. This is compatible with fallibilist discipline, but it is
not simply derived from Peirce.

.27.4    Strongest Peircean Objection
A Peircean may object that the framework’s account of context and viability risks becoming
too subject-relative unless it explains how cognitive contexts are corrected through public
signs, communal testing, and resistance from the object. A criterion of sustainability might
reward a cheap and stable but false representation. Recoverability might preserve a distorted
construction rather than facilitate correction. The Peircean question is: what secures the
difference between an enduring cognitive habit and a belief that survives because it has escaped
adequate testing?
    Book I must answer by keeping viability distinct from truth and by showing how its
conditions operate alongside, rather than in place of, its account of epistemic validity and
adequacy. It must also explain how a manifestation can fail fidelity even when it is cognitively
inexpensive or easy to recover.

.27.5    Reconstructibility and Verdict
Peirce can reconstruct fallibilism, inquiry, correction, and the importance of inferential practice.
He cannot straightforwardly reconstruct the four columns or the specific triad of fidelity,
sustainability, and recoverability. The overlap is strong concerning correction and epistemic
discipline, moderate concerning the limits of finite inquiry, and limited concerning the archi-
tecture as a whole. Peirce is a major methodological interlocutor and a source of stringent
objections, not a sufficient substitute for Book I.


.28     Suhrawardi: Illumination and Knowledge by Presence
.28.1    Problem and Achievement
Suhrawardi’s Illuminationist philosophy gives light a central metaphysical and epistemological
role. Light is not merely a metaphor for clarity; it belongs to an ordered account of reality
and manifestation. His account of knowledge by presence is particularly important: some
forms of knowing are not primarily representational descriptions of an object but involve the
presence of the known to the knower. This challenges theories that reduce all knowledge to
the acquisition of concepts or representations.
    The point of contact with Book I is obvious but must be handled carefully. Both frameworks
use the language of light and both are concerned with the conditions under which something
becomes manifest or intelligible. Both also raise questions about forms of knowing that cannot
be reduced to ordinary representation.

.28.2    Open Questions and Differences
The similarity of the word “light” does not establish identity of concept. In Suhrawardi, Light
is embedded in an ontological hierarchy and has a metaphysical status. Book I’s epistemic
light is defined within an epistemological architecture as a condition of the legibility of relation.
It is not identified with the Light of Lights, a physical entity, or a metaphysical substance. To
import Suhrawardi’s ontology into Book I would violate the distinction between cognitive and
ontological architecture that Book I insists upon.
     Knowledge by presence also differs from Book I’s general account of explanatory cognition.
The latter addresses the architecture of explanatory understanding, including contexts, relations,
reconstruction, and epistemic economy. It does not claim that all knowing is reducible to
explanatory cognition, nor that presence and manifestation are interchangeable.
638                                       Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


.28.3    The Viability Framework’s Distinct Response
Book I treats epistemic light as the medium or condition through which relations become
legible. Its account is deliberately trans-categorical: light is not one more fixed element or
governing rule. The book further considers light as active structure and the limits of complete
knowledge of epistemic light. This is a distinctive epistemological treatment, but its novelty
cannot be established by contrasting terminology alone.
    The crucial question is whether the explanatory work assigned to epistemic light can
be performed by Suhrawardi’s account of illumination without importing its metaphysical
hierarchy. If it can, the difference may be largely one of scope and formulation. If it cannot,
the divergence is more substantial.

.28.4    Strongest Illuminationist Objection
A Suhrawardian may argue that Book I has abstracted light from the ontological reality that
makes illumination intelligible. If light is only a condition of legibility, what explains its
efficacy? Is it a formal relation, a condition of cognition, or a name for the fact that relations
are understood? Without a more precise account, epistemic light may risk being explanatorily
idle or circular: relations are legible because of light, and light is identified because relations
are legible.
     This is among the most important tests of Book I. It must show that epistemic light
contributes explanatory work not already performed by context, fixed elements, or governing
dynamics. Its trans-categorical status must be argued, not protected from criticism by
definition.

.28.5    Reconstructibility and Verdict
Suhrawardi offers a close historical and conceptual interlocutor for light, manifestation, and
presence. But his metaphysical Light cannot simply be identified with Book I’s epistemic
light. The overlap is strong at the level of illumination and intelligibility, but the difference in
theoretical status is decisive. The independence claim is plausible only if Book I can demonstrate
the non-redundant explanatory role of epistemic light without relying on Suhrawardi’s ontology.


.29     Mulla Sadra: Existence, Intellect, and Presence
.29.1    Problem and Achievement
Mulla Sadra’s philosophy integrates several strands of Islamic philosophy and develops a
distinctive account of existence, substantial motion, and the relation between being and
knowledge. His epistemology cannot be separated from his metaphysics: knowledge, intellect,
and the knower-known relation are situated within a broader account of existence and its
degrees. His treatment of knowledge by presence and the transformation of the knower is
particularly relevant to questions about identity, change, and cognition.
    The proximity to Book I lies in the attention to identity through change, the relation
between what is known and how it is known, and the limits of a purely static account of
cognition. Sadra’s philosophy is a serious interlocutor for any framework that distinguishes
invariant identity from changing manifestations.

.29.2    Open Questions and Differences
The decisive difference is methodological and architectural. Mulla Sadra’s account of knowledge
is embedded in an ontology of existence and its gradations. Book I, by contrast, initially
presents its four columns as an analytical architecture of explanatory cognition and explicitly
.30. Dharmakirti: Perception, Inference, and Epistemic Validity                              639


distinguishes that architecture from an ontological structure. Book II later develops metaphys-
ical claims conditionally in relation to Book I; those claims must not be retroactively treated
as premises of Book I.
    Nor should Sadra’s substantial motion be equated with Book I’s distinction between identity
and manifestation. The terms may approach related problems while performing different roles.
A full comparison must distinguish the metaphysical transformation of the existent from the
epistemic reconstruction of an identity across manifestations.


.29.3    The Viability Framework’s Distinct Response
Book I’s account of identity, signature, pseudo-identity, and manifestation is designed to
explain how cognition tracks an identity without confusing it with any one appearance or with
an inadequate reconstruction. Its account of finitude and unknownness then explains why no
finite subject can possess every manifestation across every context. Viability characterizes the
relation between identity and manifestations through fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.
     This account can be compared with Sadra’s treatment of knowledge by presence and the
transformation of the knower, but it does not derive its epistemological architecture from
Sadra’s metaphysics. The distinction is essential if the claim of epistemological autonomy is to
remain coherent.


.29.4    Strongest Sadrian Objection
A Sadrian may argue that Book I’s separation of cognitive architecture from ontology is
unstable. If identity and manifestation are intelligible only through some account of being, how
can an epistemology claim autonomy from metaphysical commitments? Further, if knowledge
is itself a mode or degree of existence, a merely analytical account may omit the ontological
reality of knowing. The Sadrian may also question whether identity can be treated as an
invariant without explaining the metaphysical ground of its persistence.
     The appropriate response is to distinguish methodological autonomy from the claim that
cognition has no ontological conditions. Book I’s claim is that its epistemic principles are
not justified by importing a particular metaphysics. It does not follow that cognition exists
independently of being. Whether this distinction is sufficient is a substantive point for debate.


.29.5    Reconstructibility and Verdict
Mulla Sadra offers strong resources for the relation between knowledge, existence, change,
and presence. He does not by himself reconstruct Book I’s four-column architecture or its
account of epistemic economy. The overlap is substantial around identity and change, but the
frameworks differ in their order of explanation. Sadra is a crucial test of the boundary between
epistemology and metaphysics, not evidence that Book I is a derivative version of his system.


.30     Dharmakirti: Perception, Inference, and Epistemic Validity
.30.1    Problem and Achievement
Dharmakirti’s epistemology examines the sources and validity of cognition, especially perception
and inference. His work develops rigorous accounts of non-conceptual perception, conceptual
construction, inference, and the relation between cognition and its objects. The distinction
between perception and inference, together with the analysis of reliable cognition, makes his
work a demanding interlocutor for any theory that proposes criteria of epistemic validity and
reconstruction.
640                                      Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


   The point of contact with Book I is the insistence that cognition must be assessed rather
than merely described. Both approaches distinguish modes of cognition and ask under what
conditions a cognitive act can count as successful or valid.


.30.2    Open Questions and Differences
Dharmakirti’s epistemology is developed within Buddhist philosophical debates about mo-
mentariness, causal efficacy, exclusion, and the status of conceptual construction. These
commitments differ from Book I’s account of identity and manifestation. In particular, the
book’s treatment of identity as invariant under a class of allowable transformations should not
be assimilated to a Buddhist account of momentary particulars or apoha without a detailed
argument.
    The two systems also organize their questions differently. Dharmakirti’s distinction
between perception and inference does not map directly onto the four columns. Nor does his
account of reliable cognition automatically yield the book’s triad of fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability.


.30.3    The Viability Framework’s Distinct Response
Book I asks how an identity is manifested in a cognitive context, how a manifestation is recon-
structed, and how the reconstruction may fail. It examines context validity, manifestational
adequacy, pseudo-identity, and failures of reconstruction. The account of intensity and breadth
further differentiates epistemic measures. These distinctions are not identical to the Buddhist
distinction between perception and inference, though they can be compared at the level of
epistemic assessment.
    The three components of viability add an account of the cognitive economy of manifestation.
A cognition may be accurate in one respect yet too costly to maintain in a given context; a
manifestation may be recoverable or may cross a threshold at which restoration is no longer
structurally available. Such questions do not replace truth or reliable cognition; they concern
the structure of the relation between identity and manifestation.


.30.4    Strongest Dharmakirti Objection
A Dharmakirti-inspired objection would ask whether Book I’s identity and manifestation
are sufficiently connected to causal efficacy and non-deceptive cognition. If a manifestation
preserves an identity only according to a conceptual signature, how does the framework
distinguish a genuine manifestation from a coherent but misleading construction? A further
objection is that sustainability and recoverability may be epistemically irrelevant to truth: a
false belief can be cheap, stable, and easy to restore.
    Book I must accept the force of the second objection insofar as viability is descriptive and
not a truth criterion. Its answer must show how viability complements, rather than displaces,
validity and adequacy. The first objection requires a clear account of how identity, signature,
pseudo-identity, and reconstruction constrain one another.


.30.5    Reconstructibility and Verdict
Dharmakirti provides a powerful account of perception, inference, and epistemic reliability. He
does not straightforwardly reconstruct the four-column architecture or the book’s account of
cognitive economy. The overlap is strong concerning epistemic assessment, moderate concerning
reconstruction and error, and limited concerning viability. Dharmakirti is a demanding test of
the distinction between viability and truth, and of the account of pseudo-identity.

.31.2    What the Comparison Establishes
The comparison establishes a distribution of proximity, not a single nearest predecessor. Kant
is closest on conditions and limits; Husserl on appearance and horizon; Peirce on fallibilism
and correction; Suhrawardi on light and manifestation; Mulla Sadra on knowledge, identity,
and change; Dharmakirti on perception, inference, and epistemic validity. Each tradition
illuminates a different region of Book I.
    This distribution matters. If one tradition reproduced the whole framework, the indepen-
dence claim would be substantially weakened. Since the relevant resources are distributed
across different systems, the possibility remains that Book I offers a distinctive integration.
But integration itself must be shown to be explanatory rather than merely encyclopedic. A
framework does not become original simply by placing familiar concepts next to one another.

.31.3    The Strongest General Objections
Four objections cut across the six comparisons.

  1. Redundancy: the four columns may redescribe familiar distinctions without adding
642                                      Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


      explanatory power. The book must show what is lost when any column is removed and
      why the roles cannot be reduced to one another.

   2. Circularity: fidelity and epistemic light may be assessed by the same context whose
      adequacy they are supposed to explain. The book must identify independent constraints
      on the assessment of manifestations.

   3. Subject-relativity: if context contributes to manifestation, the framework must explain
      how it distinguishes context-sensitive appearance from arbitrary construction.

   4. Category error: viability may be mistaken for truth, value, usefulness, or survival.
      Book I must maintain the distinctions it explicitly draws and show how viability relates
      to validity without replacing it.


.32     Internal Stress Tests
.32.1    Are the Four Columns Necessary?
The book’s removal test is the right starting point: remove one analytical role and ask whether
the explanatory task can still be performed without silently reintroducing that role under
another name. The test is persuasive only if the examples are not selected to guarantee the
result. It should be applied to heterogeneous cases, including scientific, historical, practical,
and interpretive explanations, and should make explicit what counts as a successful explanation
in each case.
    The central vulnerability is role overlap. A critic may argue that context is part of governing
dynamics, or that fluid elements are reducible to relations among fixed elements. Book I’s
answer must show that these roles answer different questions and that any apparent reduction
either changes the meaning of a role or leaves an explanatory question unanswered.

.32.2    Are the Four Columns Jointly Sufficient?
The reducibility test supports an estimate of joint sufficiency. It should not be overstated as
a proof that no other analytical role could ever be required. A strong test would examine
candidate additions—purpose, norm, evidence, agency, temporal scale, or standpoint—and
determine whether each is a genuinely independent role or can be assigned to one of the four
columns without loss. The book’s own distinction between structure and telos is especially
relevant: purpose should not be inserted as a universal fifth column merely because some
explanations concern purposes.

.32.3    Are the Three Components of Viability Independent?
The three components must each do distinct work. Fidelity concerns preservation of identity;
sustainability concerns the cost borne by the receiving cognitive context; recoverability concerns
the retained structural capacity for renewed manifestation. The independence test asks whether
a case can satisfy two while failing the third.
    The claim of independence is ambiguous, and the ambiguity must be resolved before the
test can be applied. Three senses are distinguishable.

Logical independence
     None of the three components is derivable from the other two by the framework’s
     principles alone. This sense is not claimed by Book I. In some cases, the failure of
     one component may entail the failure of another: a manifestation that fails fidelity
    (it is a distortion, not a manifestation of the identity) may make the question of its
.32. Internal Stress Tests                                                                   643


      sustainability or recoverability moot. Logical independence is therefore not asserted, and
      the framework does not need it.
Conceptual independence
    Each of the three components states a distinct structural condition on the relation, not
    a re-description of one of the other two. This sense is claimed.
Non-equivalence
    No two of the three components are equivalent (neither entails the other in both
    directions). This sense is claimed.

    The independence test must therefore be understood as a test of conceptual independence
and non-equivalence, not of logical independence. The test asks whether a case can be described
in which two components are satisfied and the third fails. Three conceptual test patterns are
stated below; they are not empirical proofs, and they are offered at the strength of a conceptual
distinctness argument.

Test 1: Fidelity fails, sustainability and recoverability hold
     A manifestation distorts the identity it purports to manifest (it introduces a feature
     incompatible with the identity’s essential determination), but the distortion is cheap to
     produce and maintain (sustainability holds) and can be restored after a lapse at a cost
     lower than producing a new manifestation (recoverability holds). The pattern shows
     that fidelity is not entailed by sustainability and recoverability.
Test 2: Sustainability fails, fidelity and recoverability hold
     A manifestation preserves the identity’s essential determination (fidelity holds) and can be
     restored after a lapse at a cost lower than producing a new manifestation (recoverability
     holds), but its cost of production and maintenance exceeds what the receiving context
     can bear (sustainability fails). The pattern shows that sustainability is not entailed by
     fidelity and recoverability.
Test 3: Recoverability fails, fidelity and sustainability hold
     A manifestation preserves the identity’s essential determination (fidelity holds) and its
     current cost of production and maintenance is within the context’s capacity (sustainability
     holds), but the context’s capacity for restoring the manifestation after a lapse has been
     exhausted, so that the cost of restoration would exceed the cost of producing a new
     manifestation (recoverability fails). The pattern shows that recoverability is not entailed
     by fidelity and sustainability.

    The three patterns are the conceptual test patterns of the independence claim. They show
that the three components are conceptually independent and non-equivalent in the senses
stated above. They do not show that the three components are logically independent, and the
framework does not claim that they are. The patterns are stated at exactly that strength; a
reader who shows that one of the patterns is not internally consistent with the framework’s
definitions has refuted the corresponding distinctness claim, and the framework can be revised
accordingly.
Remark .36 (The Independence Claim and the Distinctness Tests). The independence claim
of Book I is the claim of conceptual independence and non-equivalence, and it is supported by
the three distinctness tests stated above. It is not the claim of logical independence, which
the framework does not assert and does not need. The distinction matters, because a reader
who expects logical independence will find the claim overstated; a reader who understands the
claim as conceptual independence and non-equivalence will find it supported by the tests. The
same distinction is stated in Chapter 37 (Section 37.8, Remarks 37.8a and 37.8b), and the two
statements are the same statement.
644                                      Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


Remark .37 (The Sufficiency Claim and the Minimality Argument). The claim that the
three components are sufficient (no fourth is required) is an estimate (E) supported by the
minimality argument of Chapter 37 (Section 37.8). It is not a theorem, and it is not established
by the three distinctness tests above. The distinctness tests establish conceptual independence
and non-equivalence; the sufficiency claim is established by the separate argument that the
three relations the character must describe (source, context, future capacity) are exhaustive.
The two claims are distinct, and the framework keeps them apart. A reader who accepts the
distinctness tests has a reason to accept the independence claim; a reader who accepts the
minimality argument has a reason to accept the sufficiency claim. The two acceptances are
not the same acceptance, and the framework does not collapse one into the other.

.32.4    Is Epistemic Light Non-Circular?
The most delicate question is whether epistemic light explains the legibility of relations or
merely renames it. The framework needs to identify what follows from the presence or absence
of epistemic light that does not already follow from context, fixed elements, or governing
dynamics. It must also clarify why light is trans-categorical rather than an additional element
within one of the columns.
    The Suhrawardian comparison intensifies this demand. Book I is right to distinguish its
epistemic concept from metaphysical Light; but a difference in ontological status does not
by itself establish explanatory independence. A successful account must state the specific
inferential work performed by epistemic light and specify what would count against the account.

.32.5    Does Viability Collapse into Truth or Value?
Book I defines viability descriptively. It follows that a viable manifestation need not thereby
be true, morally good, or practically desirable. A false representation can be inexpensive and
stable; a true but complex account can be costly to maintain. Fidelity is the component most
directly connected to preservation of identity, but even fidelity must be assessed through the
book’s account of identity and manifestation rather than treated as an unexplained synonym
for truth.
    The distinction between description and prescription must also be preserved. The fact
that a cognitive structure is sustainable does not imply that it ought to be sustained. Nor
does recoverability establish that an identity is valuable. Any normative conclusion requires
additional premises and belongs to a different inquiry.

.32.6    Can the Framework Correct Itself ?
Book I’s epistemic status labels are an important safeguard. Foundational commitments,
argued claims, estimates, open questions, speculations, and proposals are not interchangeable.
The dependency map and the audit of core epistemic commitments make it possible to ask
which conclusions depend on which premises. This is a strength only if the labels are applied
consistently and if claims can be revised when their dependencies fail.
    A framework that calls itself fallible but protects its central principles from counterexample
would fail its own methodological standard. The strongest independence claim must therefore
remain open to revision. The book should identify not only what would support the four-column
principle, but also what would falsify or materially weaken it.


.33     Final Assessment
.33.1    What Can Be Claimed
The comparison supports the following limited conclusions.
.33. Final Assessment                                                                          645


   1. None of the six interlocutors, considered alone, reproduces the complete architecture of
      Book I.

   2. Each tradition offers resources that illuminate a significant part of the project, and each
      supplies objections that Book I must answer.

   3. The strongest candidate for distinctiveness is not any isolated term—especially not the
      word “viability” or “light”—but the proposed integration of the four analytical roles,
      the account of epistemic relations, the analysis of limits and reconstruction, and the
      three-part account of viability.

   4. The independence of that integration is plausible but not established merely by the
      comparative survey. It depends on the success of the internal tests concerning necessity,
      sufficiency, conceptual independence and non-equivalence of the three components of
      viability, non-redundancy of epistemic light, non-circularity of fidelity, and revisability.
      The internal test of the three components (Section .32.3) states the sense in which
      independence is claimed (conceptual independence and non-equivalence, not logical
      independence) and gives the three distinctness tests that support the claim at that
      strength.

.33.2    What Cannot Yet Be Claimed
This study does not establish that Book I is historically unprecedented, that no earlier
philosopher anticipated any of its components, that it is superior to the six traditions, or
that its principles are immune to reconstruction. Nor does it show that the four columns
are necessary for every possible form of cognition. Its claims are restricted to the scope and
argumentative status stated in Book I.
    The study also does not settle the full relation between epistemic light and metaphysical
light, the ultimate ground of identity, or the metaphysical status of cognition. Those questions
require arguments beyond the present comparative test and, where appropriate, belong to the
separate work of Book II and later volumes.

.33.3    Calibrated Verdict
The most defensible verdict is that Epistemology of Viability presents a distinctive and
potentially independent analytical architecture of explanatory cognition. Its strongest claim
to originality lies in the systematic integration of its components and in the specific role
assigned to viability as a descriptive structural character of the relation between identity
and manifestation. The comparison with Kant, Husserl, Peirce, Suhrawardi, Mulla Sadra,
and Dharmakirti does not disclose a single system from which the whole framework can be
straightforwardly derived.
    That is a meaningful result, but it is not a final proof of independence. The framework’s
independence remains a reasoned hypothesis supported by comparative differentiation and
subject to further internal testing. The decisive work is not to insist that the framework is
unlike its predecessors, but to demonstrate that its distinctions are necessary, non-redundant,
explanatorily productive, and open to correction. The internal test of the three components of
viability (Section .32.3) is a step in this direction: it states the sense in which independence is
claimed (conceptual independence and non-equivalence, not logical independence), and it gives
the three distinctness tests that support the claim at that strength. The sufficiency claim is
stated as an estimate (E) supported by the minimality argument of Chapter 37 (Section 37.8),
not as a theorem; the framework does not claim more than its arguments support.

Remark .38 (The Comparative Study and the Prose). The comparative study and the prose
of Book I are not rivals. The prose is the substance, and the comparative study is its assessment
646                                      Appendix . An Independent Comparative Stress Test


at the level of its relation to the tradition. The reader who is content with the prose has the
framework and the arguments; the reader who wishes to see the framework in the context
of the tradition has the comparative study. The two are complementary, and the framework
invites both.


A Note on the Status of the Comparative Study
The comparative study is (C): it is a comparative assessment, offered at the strength of a
comparative assessment, and it is marked (C) where the comparison is a judgment. Its verdicts
are not (A) or (T); they are the strength that the comparative method supports. The study’s
internal cross-references (to the sections of this appendix) are stated in the header; its external
cross-references (to Chapters of Book I and to the book’s existing comparative appendix) are
hard-coded to their correct numbers.
    The reader who wishes to see the statuses of the comparative study in the context of the
book’s other statuses is directed to the Index of Epistemic Principles (Part VII). The reader
who wishes to see the comparative study alongside the book’s existing comparative study is
directed to the appendix A Comparative Study of the Philosophy of Viability.


A Note on Terminological Consistency
Throughout this appendix, the following English expressions are retained in the sense estab-
lished by Book I: explanatory cognition; fixed elements; fluid elements; governing dynamics;
context; identity; signature; pseudo-identity; manifestation; epistemic light; context validity;
manifestational adequacy; cognitive cost; cognitive sediment; fidelity; sustainability; and recov-
erability. These terms should not be replaced with near-synonyms merely for stylistic variation
where the distinction is philosophically significant.

The comparative study is offered as a supplement, not as a substitute. The prose is the substance;
the comparison is the abbreviation. The framework’s claim is that the comparison is assessable
at the strength its method supports; the reader’s task is to assess it at that strength, and to
decide what to make of it.

A Note on the Bibliography and the Audit
The bibliography is not part of the framework’s core commitments; it is not one of the ten
commitments of the audit (Chapter 43). It records the works that the body of the book cites,
and it does not add any claim to the framework. The audit of Chapter 43 states, in its class
(v), that the works cited are not premises of the framework’s arguments: the framework’s
principles are established by the philosophical arguments of the chapters, and the works cited
are used to make or assess claims within those arguments, not to ground the framework from
outside.
    The bibliography is consistent with two of the framework’s core commitments, and the
consistency is worth marking. The first is C3, the autonomy of epistemic justification (Chap-
ter 4): the framework’s principles do not depend on confirmation from outside epistemology,
and the works cited in the bibliography are not a ground of justification for the framework.
The second is C2, that philosophy describes structure, not telos (Chapter 4): the works cited
are used to describe the structure of explanatory cognition, and the bibliography does not,
and cannot, establish the telos for which cognition exists.
Remark .39 (The Bibliography and the Separate Treatise). The bibliography is the bibliogra-
phy of the present volume. The comparative treatment of the philosophical traditions is given
in the separate treatise, Dialogues with the Philosophical Traditions, and that treatise has its
own bibliography. The two bibliographies are distinct, and the present volume’s arguments
do not depend on the separate treatise. The distinction is stated in the Preface, and it is
observed here: the present bibliography records the works cited in this volume, and it does
not anticipate the works that the separate treatise will cite.
Remark .40 (The Bibliography and the Coherence Tests). The scientific works cited in the
bibliography (Einstein, Maxwell, Weinberg, and Maupertuis) appear only in the coherence
tests of the framework (Chapter 4 and the coherence tests of Chapters 16 and 17). The
coherence tests show that the framework’s claims are not at odds with the way the established
inquiries describe their own structure; they do not confirm the framework, and they are not
a ground of justification. The works are cited because they are the sources of the inquiries
that the coherence tests engage, not because the framework’s principles depend on them. The
distinction is the distinction between the coherence test and the justification; the framework
keeps it throughout (Chapter 4).
Remark .41 (The Bibliography and the Reader). The bibliography is a service to the reader.
It records the works that the body of the book cites, so that the reader who wishes to assess a
claim is directed to its sources. It does not claim to be complete, and it does not claim that
the works cited are the only works that bear on the framework’s claims. A reader who finds a
work that the framework should have cited has found an omission in the bibliography, and the
bibliography can be revised to include it.


A Note on the Separate Treatise
The comparative treatment of the philosophical traditions is given in a separate treatise, Dia-
logues with the Philosophical Traditions, to be published independently. The separate treatise
has its own bibliography, covering the primary and secondary sources for the comparative
treatment.
    The two bibliographies are distinct. The present bibliography records the works cited in
this volume; the separate treatise’s bibliography records the works cited in the comparative
treatment. The reason for the separation is stated in the Preface: a comparison of structures
is a different genre from a systematic reconstruction, and keeping them in one volume would
encourage a misreading of the framework’s authority. The present volume’s arguments do not
Bibliography                                                                           653


depend on the separate treatise, and the separate treatise presupposes the present volume’s
framework.
