Glossary of Epistemic Terms

A Note on the Glossary
This glossary collects the technical terms of the framework, with the definition or principle
that fixes each term’s sense, and a cross-reference to the place in the book where the term is
defined. The cross-references use the numbers of the definitions and principles stated in the
chapters; the reader who wishes to see a definition in its context is directed to the chapter and
section where it appears.
    The terms are listed alphabetically. A term that has more than one definition, or that is
defined in more than one place, is listed with each definition, distinguished by the place of
definition.
    Every term in this glossary is a structural term. No term carries normative, ethical, or
evaluative weight in this book. Where a term used here has a normative use elsewhere, the
entry states that its sense in this book is fixed entirely by the book’s own structural definitions.
    The glossary also contains a separate section at the end, Formal Terms of the Reconstruction,
which collects the terms of the formal system of Appendix .15. The section is separate because
the formal terms are not part of the body of the book’s vocabulary; they are the vocabulary
of the formal system, and the reader who wishes to see them in context is directed to the
appendix.


A
Action Chain. A sequence of four stages by which an effect is produced and received:
     emission, transmission, reception, effect. (Definition 40.3; Chapter 40.)

Active Structure of Legibility. A structure that always is, is a structure of connection,
     has edges that are activated or deactivated according to rules, and itself does not move.
     Epistemic light is an active structure of legibility. (Definition 16.1; Chapter 16.)

Adequacy (of a Pseudo-Identity). The extent to which a pseudo-identity satisfies the
    three criteria of consistency, stability, and fruitfulness (Definition 23.1; Chapter 23).

Aggregation. Collecting manifestations. One of three things that the fallacy of super-identity
    confuses with the other two—compatibility and numerical unity (Chapter 28).

Awareness. The regulation of a manifestation for the reception of reflective epistemic light and
    intra-category epistemic light. A species of self-awareness. (Definition 20.3; Chapter 20).


B
Balance Criterion. The balance of an identity in a cognitive context is the extent to which
    the descending epistemic light it has received is preserved or returned, less the extent to
    which it has become cognitive sediment. (Definition 42.1; Chapter 42.)
656                                                              Glossary of Epistemic Terms


Barzakhic Realm. Not used in this volume. The barzakhic realms belong to the ontological
    architecture of the later volumes; the present volume mentions them only to mark them
    off (Chapter 5).


C
Capacity (of a Cognitive Context). What a context’s mode of cognition permits to appear
    in it and what it constrains. (Chapter 13; developed in Chapter 39.)

Category-Relative Predication. The principle that epistemic predicates are not absolute,
    but are defined relative to a cognitive context and to a respect. (Principle 25.1; Chap-
    ter 25.)

Cognitive Context. The frame in which something is cognized: the question asked, the
    elements held fixed, the rule applied, and the standpoint from which the partition into
    fixed and fluid is made. A cognitive context is fixed by the question, and there are
    indefinitely many of them. (Definition 10.1; Chapter 10; restated Definition 14.1 in
    Chapter 14.)

Cognitive Sediment. Intra-category epistemic light that has become lodged: light that has
    descended and not ascended, persists beyond the activity that carried it, is not integrated
    into the relations of its context, and lays a lasting claim on that context’s capacity.
    (Definition 40.5; Chapter 40.)

Compatibility. The absence of conflict among manifestations. One of three things that the
   fallacy of super-identity confuses with the other two—aggregation and numerical unity
   (Chapter 28).

Conditional Architecture on a Core. The book’s self-description: the book is a condi-
    tional architecture on a core of ten epistemic commitments (C1–C10), and every other
    claim of the book is a definition, a consequence, an estimate, a proposal, an open question,
    or a speculation. (Principle 43.1; Chapter 43.)

Configuration-Dependence. The manifestation of an identity in a cognitive context depends
    on what passes through the epistemic light of the context, and this in turn depends on
    the whole configuration of the context. (Definition 29.1; Chapter 29.)

Consciousness. The intensity of the connection between a manifestation and its source.
    (Definition 20.2; Chapter 20.)

Consistency (as Criterion of Adequacy). Observers working independently in different
    contexts arrive at the same pseudo-identity, up to isomorphism. (Chapter 23.)

Consistency (as Criterion of Context Validity). A valid context is consistent in all its
    overlaps with other valid contexts. (Principle 21.3; Chapter 21.)

Context. The background in which cognition occurs; determines what counts as a fixed
    element, what counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics governs. (Definition 6.4;
    Chapter 6.) The framework distinguishes two kinds of context; see Cognitive Context
    and Existential Context.

Context-Dependence. The fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive
    context, not on the element’s essence. (Principle 10.1; Chapter 10.)
Glossary of Epistemic Terms                                                                 657


Conveyor Principle. No explanation of how one fixed element bears on another is complete
    unless it invokes a fluid element: a carrier, medium, signal, or process by which the effect
    passes. (Principle 8.1; Chapter 8.)

Core Epistemic Commitments (C1–C10). The ten primitive commitments of the frame-
    work, on which the framework’s other claims depend. They are stated in Chapter 43
    (§43.4), and each is marked with the part or parts of the book in which it does load-bearing
    work.

Cost of Cognition. What the cognition of an identity demands of the receiving cognitive
     context’s capacity. Not a single quantity; a family of demands, distinguished by kind
    (realization, reconstruction, maintenance and recovery; Definition 39.2) and by aspect
    (extent, reach, duration; Definition 39.3). (Definition 39.1; Chapter 39.)

Cross-Checkability. A valid context is one whose fixed and fluid elements can be identified
    and distinguished from at least one other valid context. (Principle 21.1; Chapter 21.)

Crystallization. The process by which the effect of an action, initially a modification of
    a receiving hard manifestation, becomes itself a hard manifestation in the context: a
    sediment, a habit, a structure, an institution. (Definition 40.4; Chapter 40.)

Crystallization Principle. Every actual action tends toward crystallization: its effect, once
    received, becomes a hard manifestation in the context, and the hard manifestation
    becomes the condition of further soft manifestations. (Principle 40.1; Chapter 40.)


D
Death. Not developed in this volume. The framework’s account of death belongs to the later
    volumes; the present volume does not state it.

Defining Invariants. The features that constitute an identity’s determination: those that
     distinguish it from its alternatives and are fixed by what it is. Taken as primitive in the
     framework. (Definition 12.2; Chapter 12.)

Degree of Structural Fidelity. The extent to which a manifestation preserves the essential
    determination of its source. Not necessary; an identity can be realized at varying degrees
    of structural fidelity. (Definition 38.2; Chapter 38.)

Descent (Epistemic). The appearance of epistemic light in the mode of a receiving cognitive
    context, without epistemic light going from one context to another. Not to be confused
    with travel. (Principle 16.4; Chapter 16.)

Desire to Find. The structural relation by which an identity is rendered legible in the reflec-
     tion of its expression in another identity’s expression. Not a mental state. (Theorem 18.1;
     Chapter 18.)

Diagonal Argument. The second, independent argument for the impossibility of super-
    identity (Chapter 27). It proceeds by constructing, from any finite list of contexts
    surveyed by a subject, a context outside the list.


E
Energy. Not developed in this volume. The framework’s account of energy belongs to the
    later volumes; the present volume names energy only to mark it off (Chapter 17).
658                                                                Glossary of Epistemic Terms


Epistemic Economy. Every realization of a cognition, every reconstruction of an identity,
     and every maintenance of a cognition bears a cost that cannot be wholly removed. Cost
     is a structural feature of the relation between the cognition and its context; it is not a
     value, a burden to be minimized as an end, or a good. (Principle 39.1; Chapter 39.)

Epistemic Humility. The disposition to hold one’s epistemic claims at the strength the
     arguments support, and to leave the questions one has not settled open, without either
     claiming to have settled them or claiming that they cannot be settled. (Definition 35.1;
     Chapter 35.)

Epistemic Humility as Structural Disposition. Epistemic humility is the structural dis-
     position that follows, for a finite subject, from the limits of finite cognition and from the
     open questions that the framework’s principles make visible. It is not an optional virtue
     added to the framework’s epistemic claims; it is what the claims require, if the subject
     takes them seriously. (Principle 35.1; Chapter 35.)

Epistemic Light. The medium of legible relation: the condition of possibility of a relation’s
     being legible as a relation between these terms. Not a term in the relation, and not a
     relation among relations. (Definition 15.1; Chapter 15.)

Essential Feature. A feature of an identity that belongs to its defining invariants. A non-
     essential feature is one that may vary among the manifestations of the identity without
     altering its essential determination. (Definition 13.2; Chapter 13.)

Essential Homogeneity (of Manifestation). A manifestation is essentially homogeneous
    with its source insofar as it preserves the source’s essential determination. Structural
    variation among manifestations of one identity is permissible where it does not introduce
     a feature incompatible with that determination. (Principle 13.2; Chapter 13.)

Existential Context. The setting in which a manifestation is realized, with the capacity and
     the constraints of that setting. Named in this volume to mark it off from the cognitive
     context; the existential context is not developed as an ontology here. (Definition 10.2;
     Chapter 10; restated Definition 14.2 in Chapter 14.)

Explanatory Cognition. Cognition whose aim is to understand how some things stand to
    one another. (Definition 1.1; Chapter 1.)

Expression (as Structural Tendency). Every identity tends toward expression; the ten-
    dency cannot be structurally unrealized, only structurally hindered. The tendency is a
    structural direction of what an identity is, not a choice and not a mechanism. (Defini-
    tion 38.1; Chapter 38. The principle of expression, of which the tendency is the core, is
    argued in the later volume.)


F
Fallacy of Super-Identity. A record formed by aggregating manifestations drawn from
     contexts whose elements are not mutually translatable is not a reconstruction of the
     identity. It is a context-confounded record: an object that corresponds to no identity at
     all. (Principle 28.1; Chapter 28.)

Fidelious / Infidelious. A manifestation is fidelious when it preserves the essential deter-
     mination of its source, so that the cognition records an appearance of that identity and
     not of another; a manifestation is infidelious when it does not. The pair is the adjectival
     form of fidelity and its privative. The terms are technical terms of the framework; they
Glossary of Epistemic Terms                                                                    659


      are not synonyms for “faithful” and “unfaithful” in the ordinary sense. (Principle 13.2;
      Chapter 13; Principle 37.1; Chapter 37; developed in Chapter 38.)

Fidelity. The first component of viability: the manifestation preserves the essential determi-
     nation of the identity, so that the cognition records an appearance of that identity and
     not of another. (Principle 37.1; Chapter 37; developed in Chapter 38.)

Finitude of the Epistemic Subject. Every cognizing subject is finite: at any time it oc-
     cupies finitely many cognitive contexts, and in any finite span of inquiry it completes
     only finitely many acts of reconstruction. (Principle 3.1; Chapter 3.)

Fixed Element. An entity selected as an invariant term within a given explanatory cognition.
     Its fixedness is methodological: it is held stable for the purpose of explaining its relations.
    (Definition 6.1; Chapter 6.)

Fluid Element. An entity that conveys effect. A fluid element is an edge in the network of
     cognition, connecting fixed elements to one another. (Definition 6.2; Chapter 6.)

Formal Counterpart. The expression in the formal language of Appendix .15 of a prose
    principle, definition, or argument. The formal counterpart of a prose principle is not a
    substitute for the prose; it is the same principle, stated at a higher level of precision.
    (Appendix F; see also the entries under Formal Terms of the Reconstruction.)

Four-Column Principle. Every explanatory cognition requires the simultaneous presence
     of four columns: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context. If any
     one of the four is absent, the cognition is incomplete as an explanation. (Principle 7.1;
     Chapter 7.) The necessity half is (T); the sufficiency half is (E).

Fruitfulness (as Criterion of Adequacy). A system that operates according to the pseudo-
     identity is able to operate within its environment, predict future manifestations, and
     preserve the structural viability of its expressions. (Chapter 23.)


G
Golden Record Illusion. The belief that there is, or could be, a single record that contains
    all attributes of an entity across all contexts. The framework treats this ideal as ill-posed.
    (Chapter 28.)

Governing Dynamics. A rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements. Dy-
    namics determines the behavioral pattern of the network of cognition. (Definition 6.3;
    Chapter 6.)


H
Hard Manifestation. A manifestation with structural inertia: it resists change, and its
    persistence is a condition of the unity of the manifestation. (Definition 40.1; Chapter 40.)

Hindrance. The structural condition in which the tendency to express is not realized at the
    degree the identity’s nature would permit, because the receiving context’s capacity or
    the configuration of the context does not permit the realization. Hindrance is not failure.
    (Principle 38.3; Chapter 38.)
660                                                               Glossary of Epistemic Terms


I
Identity. The invariant that an explanatory cognition holds fixed across a specified class of
     allowable transformations of its manifestations. (Definition 12.1; Chapter 12.)

Identity Conservation. Identity is invariant under all temporal transformations of its man-
     ifestations. (Principle 12.2; Chapter 12; the conservation principle is C4 of the audit,
     Chapter 43.)

Identity Rigidity. Identity does not admit of degrees. A structure either is invariant under
     the specified transformations, or it is not. (Principle 12.1; Chapter 12.)

Identity-Preserving Transformation. A transformation whose resulting state remains
     within the range of structural possibilities compatible with the identity’s defining invari-
     ants. (Definition 12.3; Chapter 12.)

Impossibility of Complete Knowledge of Epistemic Light. No finite subject can know
    epistemic light completely, because the finite subject is encompassed in epistemic light,
    and complete knowledge would require standing outside the object of knowledge—and
    no finite subject can stand outside epistemic light. (Principle 31.1; Chapter 31.)

Impossibility of Super-Identity. No finite subject can know all manifestations of an iden-
    tity in all contexts. (Principle 27.1; Chapter 27.) Supported by the reductio from the four
    premises and by the diagonal construction; strengthened by configuration-dependence
    (Chapter 29).

Intensity. The degree to which a manifestation confirms the source as a whole, in its unity
     (the completeness of reflection). (Definition 26.1; Chapter 26.)

Intrinsic Unknownness. The other is unknown by the structure of individuation itself. The
     unknownness cannot be removed by more manifestation, because it is not a shortage of
     manifestation; it is the structural fact that one identity is not another. (Definition 32.1;
     Chapter 32.)

Intra-Category Epistemic Light. Epistemic light that has descended into a cognitive
     context and has not ascended. The wider class within which cognitive sediment is a
     species (Chapter 40).


L
Legibility. The recognizability of a relation as a relation between these terms. Epistemic
     light is what makes a relation legible; epistemic light itself is not legible in the same
     sense (Chapter 15).


M
Manifestation. The contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving cognitive
    context, according to the context’s capacity, aptitude, and constraints. (Definition 13.1;
    Chapter 13.)

Manifestational Adequacy (Proposed). The cognitive context in which a manifestation is
    attributed must have the capacity and the aptitude for the kind of appearance attributed
    to it. (Principle 22.1; Chapter 22.) Proposed, not yet assigned a status.
Glossary of Epistemic Terms                                                                   661


Manifestational Capacity (Contextual). The form that a manifestation takes in a receiv-
    ing cognitive context is fixed jointly by the source identity and by the capacity of the
    context, and contexts differ in capacity. (Principle 13.1; Chapter 13.) Proposed; not yet
    assigned (A) or (T).

Minimality. A valid context is the smallest context that can still explain the phenomenon.
    (Principle 21.2; Chapter 21.)

Mixed Nature. Not used in this volume. The mixed nature of a barzakhic realm belongs to
    the ontological architecture of the later volumes.


N
Non-Duplicability of Identity. Identity cannot be copied. Signatures, pseudo-identities,
    and information can be duplicated; identity cannot. A copy of a system reproduces its
    signature; if the copy expresses at all, it expresses an identity of its own. (Principle 12.3;
    Chapter 12; C10 of the audit, Chapter 43.)

Non-Reduction of Identity to Manifestations. An identity is not identical with the ag-
    gregate of its manifestations, nor with their compatible aggregate. (Principle 28.2;
    Chapter 28.)

Non-Sequential Connectivity. The conveyor principle does not require that the connection
    between two fixed elements pass through all intermediate fixed elements. A fluid element
    may connect two fixed elements directly. (Principle 9.1; Chapter 9.)

Non-Travel of Epistemic Light. Epistemic light does not travel. (Principle 16.2; Chap-
    ter 16.)

Numerical Unity. The oneness of the source identity. One of three things that the fallacy of
   super-identity confuses with the other two—aggregation and compatibility (Chapter 28).


O
Only the Intrinsic Kind Is Structural. Only intrinsic unknownness is structural in the
    sense the impossibility of super-identity requires. Temporary unknownness is contingent
    on the present state of a relation, and the impossibility of super-identity does not claim
    that temporary unknownness cannot be reduced; it claims that intrinsic unknownness
    cannot be removed. (Principle 32.2; Chapter 32.)

Openness of Relations. For every cognitive context C and every manifestation m that an
    identity has in C, there is a cognitive context C ′ in which m is itself a fixed element,
    related by epistemic light and dynamics not available in C. (Definition 11.1; Chapter 11.)


P
Perspective. The structural position of an observer within a cognitive context: the point from
    which, the means by which, and the conceptual structure through which a manifestation
    is apprehended. A perspective is located, partial, and revisable. (Definition 14.3;
    Chapter 14.)

Plurality Is Structural. The plurality of perspectives is a structural condition of finite
     cognition, not a defect. It is the condition under which a finite subject cognizes an
662                                                              Glossary of Epistemic Terms


      identity, and it cannot be removed by a better perspective, because no finite subject can
      occupy every position. (Principle 33.1; Chapter 33.)

Plurality of Perspectives. The structural fact that an identity can be cognized from more
     than one perspective, and that the perspectives are not all the same. (Definition 33.1;
     Chapter 33.)

Primary Cognitive Apparatus. A cognitive apparatus whose fixed elements are general
    and whose fluid element is foundational. (Definition 17.1; Chapter 17.)

Principle of the Distinction (Intrinsic and Temporary). Intrinsic unknownness and tem-
     porary unknownness are structurally distinct: the first is a feature of the relation between
     distinct identities, and the second is a feature of the present state of a relation. Neither
     entails the other, and each can be present without the other. (Principle 32.1; Chapter 32.)

Pseudo-Identity. The observer’s approximation of an identity, constructed from the available
    manifestations. It is an estimate of a signature, not a rival identity. (Definition 12.8;
    Chapter 12.)


R
Recoverability. The third component of viability: the identity retains its structural capacity
    to manifest in the context; the singularity at which restoring a manifestation would cost
    more than producing a new one has not been crossed. (Principle 37.3; Chapter 37.)

Recursive Manifestation. The structure by which a manifestation that is realized in one
    context can itself be the occasion for further manifestations of the same identity, in
    the same context or another, without the identity being multiplied. (Definition 12.7;
    Chapter 12.)

Reducibility. A candidate fifth column is reducible when its role in explanation can be
    reassigned to one of the four columns without loss. (Definition 2.2; Chapter 7.)

Relational Manifestation. Not developed in this volume. The relational manifestation
     belongs to the ontological architecture of the later volumes.

Removal Test. A proposed column of explanatory cognition is necessary if the removal
   of that column from an otherwise complete explanation leaves an account that is a
   recognizable explanatory failure. (Definition 2.1; Chapter 2.)

Returning Light. The epistemic light that continues after the pause of an expression, and
    refers back to its source through what the identity left in other manifestations. (Defini-
    tion 40.6; Chapter 40.)


S
Secondary Cognitive Apparatus. A cognitive apparatus whose fixed elements are specific
    and whose fluid element is derived. (Definition 17.2; Chapter 17.)

Self-Awareness. The mechanism of regulating the connection between a manifestation and
     its source: the activity by which a manifestation adjusts how much descending epistemic
     light it receives, how much reflective epistemic light it emits, and how much ascending
     epistemic light it returns. (Definition 20.1; Chapter 20.)
Glossary of Epistemic Terms                                                                  663


Signature. The structural description of an identity’s invariance: what can be read off,
     compared, recorded, and reproduced about the pattern. (Definition 12.4; Chapter 12.)
Singularity (The). The threshold at which the cost of restoring an existing manifestation in
     a context exceeds the cost of bringing about a new one there. Cost, in the framework’s
     sense, is the demand that a manifestation makes on the capacity of a context; the
     singularity is the point at which the demand for restoration exceeds the demand for a
     new manifestation of the same identity in the same context. (Definition 37.2; Chapter 37.)
Soft Manifestation. A manifestation without structural inertia: it exists only as the act
     by which a subject’s self-awareness activates a hard manifestation. (Definition 40.2;
     Chapter 40.)
Stability (as Criterion of Adequacy). The pseudo-identity is stable under small pertur-
     bations of the observer’s context or cognitive apparatus. (Chapter 23.)
Structural Duality of Expression. Intensity and breadth are two measures of one expres-
     sion, not two quantities on one scale. They are structurally distinct: each can vary
     independently of the other. (Principle 26.1; Chapter 26.)
Structural Fluidity. “Fluid element” is an analytical role, not an ontological essence. Epis-
     temic light plays the role of conveyor, so it is the fluid element; the role is independent
     of whether epistemic light moves or not. (Principle 16.3; Chapter 16.)
Super-Identity. A subject’s claim to have known, or to be able to know, all manifestations
    of an identity in all contexts. (Definition 27.1; Chapter 27.)
Sustainability. The second component of viability: the cost of producing and maintain-
     ing the manifestation does not exceed what the receiving cognitive context can bear.
    (Principle 37.2; Chapter 37; developed in Chapter 39.)


T
Tendency to Express. The structural direction of an identity toward its own manifestation.
    It is what the identity is, not a choice the identity makes, and not a mechanism imposed
    from without. The tendency cannot be structurally unrealized; it can only be structurally
    hindered. (Definition 38.1; Chapter 38.)
Temporary Unknownness. The other is unknown for now, because of limited capacity,
   limited manifestation, or limited occasion. The unknownness can in principle be reduced.
   (Definition 32.1; Chapter 32.)
The Assessment of Perspectives. Perspectives are assessed indirectly, through two things:
    the context in which the perspective is located, assessed by the criteria of context validity
    (cross-checkability, minimality, consistency); and the reconstruction that the perspective
    makes possible, assessed by the criteria of adequacy (consistency, stability, fruitfulness).
    The assessment is not a ranking of perspectives; it is the discipline by which the plurality
    is made usable for the reconstruction of the identity. (Principle 33.2; Chapter 33.)
Theorem of Unknownness. The unknownness of same-context identities is the structural
    condition of possibility of reflection, not a defect. If the other were directly known, there
    would be no mirror; there would be no reflection. (Theorem 19.1; Chapter 19.)
Three Aspects of Cost. The cost of cognition has three aspects: extent (how much of the
    context’s capacity is taken), reach (how much cognition and attention it takes to hold
    it), and duration (how long it must be kept up). (Definition 39.3; Chapter 39.)
664                                                               Glossary of Epistemic Terms


Three Components of Viability. Fidelity, sustainability, recoverability. (Definition 37.1;
    Chapter 37.)

Three Kinds of Cost. The cost of cognition has three kinds: the cost of realization (what
    it takes for the cognition to come to be), the cost of reconstruction (what it takes to
    form a pseudo-identity of the identity), and the cost of maintenance and recovery (what
    it takes to keep, or to regain, the cognition). (Definition 39.2; Chapter 39.)

Three Thresholds of the Balance. High balance; balance near zero; low balance. (Defini-
    tion 42.2; Chapter 42.)

Trans-Categorical Character of Epistemic Light. Epistemic light is the medium of leg-
    ible relation: it is not a term in the relation, and it is not a relation among relations.
    (Principle 15.2; Chapter 15.)


U
Unknownness. See Theorem of Unknownness under T.


V
Variational Principle of Sustainability. For any identity and any receiving cognitive con-
     text, the structural optimum of cognition is the point at which cost is minimized subject
     to the constraints of fidelity and recoverability. (Principle 39.2; Chapter 39.)

Viability. The epistemic structural character of the relation between an identity and its
    manifestations in a cognitive context, in the three respects of fidelity, sustainability, and
    recoverability. A descriptive concept; not a value, an end, or a good. (Definition 36.1;
    Chapter 36.)

Viability as Structural Character Compatible with Limits. Viability is a structural
    character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations, compatible with
    the limits of Part V. It does not claim completeness of knowledge; it claims that the
    relation can satisfy the three components more or less completely, within the limits that
    the finite subject’s condition imposes. (Principle 36.1; Chapter 36.)

Viability Is Not Identity. Identity does not admit of degrees; viability admits of degrees.
    The two statements do not conflict, because viability is a property of the relation between
    an identity and its manifestations in a context, not of the identity itself. (Principle 36.2;
    Chapter 36.)

Viability Is Not the Criteria of Adequacy. Viability is the structural character of the
    relation between an identity and its manifestations in a context. The criteria of adequacy
    are the criteria by which a reconstruction (a pseudo-identity) is assessed. The two are
    different, and neither entails the other. (Principle 36.3; Chapter 36.)

Viability Is Not the Two Measures. Viability is a three-component character of the rela-
    tion between an identity and its manifestations. Intensity and breadth are two measures of
    the epistemic relation between a manifestation and its source. The two are different, and
    the three-component character is not the two measures taken together. (Principle 36.4;
    Chapter 36.)
Glossary of Epistemic Terms                                                                  665


Terms Used Without a Formal Definition
The following terms appear in the body of the book and are used in senses that the surrounding
prose fixes. They are collected here for the reader’s convenience.

Capacity (of a Cognitive Context). See the entry under C. The full account is given in
    Chapter 39, where capacity is the structural feature that the cost of cognition demands.
Channel (of Self-Awareness). The descending, reflective, and ascending channels of self-
    awareness are the three directions in which the mechanism of regulation operates.
    (Chapter 20; the three directions of epistemic light are stated in Chapter 16.)
Coherence Test. A test that shows an inquiry in another domain can develop itself within the
    framework without contradiction. Marked “not evidence, not justification” (Chapters 4,
    16, and 17).
Conditionality (of the Book). The book’s self-description as a conditional architecture on
    a core of ten epistemic commitments. (Chapter 43.)
Configuration (of a Context). The set of fixed elements present in a context, together
    with their states and their relations. (Chapter 29.)
Conservation (of Identity). See the entry under I.
Dependency Map. The table that states, for each core commitment, which conclusions
    depend on it, and what is lost if it is rejected. (Chapter 43.)
Formal System. The system of sorts, predicates, axioms, definitions, and theorems that is
    stated in full in Appendix .15. The formal system is the formal counterpart of the prose
    arguments of Chapters 2, 3, 6, and 7. (Appendix F; see also the entries under Formal
    Terms of the Reconstruction.)
Four Columns. The four analytical roles of explanatory cognition: fixed elements, fluid
     elements, governing dynamics, and context. (Chapters 6 and 7.)
Humility. See the entry under E for Epistemic Humility.
Integration (of Cognitive Sediment). The return of lodged epistemic light to the network
     of relations of its context. Transformation, not elimination. (Definition 41.1; Chapter 41.)
Living Character (of the Framework). The framework’s capacity to be refined and re-
     vised by its own inquiries. (Chapter 34.)
Order of Cognition. The order in which a finite subject comes to understand the structure
    of explanatory cognition. The order of the body of the book. (Chapter 5.)
Order of Grounding. The order in which what is depends on what. Marked in this volume;
    not developed here. (Chapter 5.)
Perspective (as Distinct from Context). See the entry under P; the distinction between
    context and perspective is stated in Chapter 14.
Pseudo-Identity (as Approximation). See the entry under P.
Two Measures. Intensity and breadth. (Chapter 26.)
Three Forms of Integration. Identification, structural recognition, return. (Definition 41.2;
    Chapter 41.)
Three Layers of Sediment. Cognitive, affective, ontological. (Definition 40.7; Chapter 40.)

Formal Terms of the Reconstruction
The following terms are the terms of the formal system of Appendix .15. They are collected
in a separate section because they are not part of the body of the book’s vocabulary; they
are the vocabulary of the formal system, and the reader who wishes to see them in context is
directed to the appendix.

Sort. One of the five categories of the formal system: elements (E), rules (R), contexts (C),
     explanations (X), and states (S). The sorts are stated in Appendix .15.

Role Predicate. One of the four predicates that assign a role to an element in an explanation:
     InF (e, x) for the fixed elements, InΦ (e, x) for the fluid elements, Dyn(x, r) for the governing
     dynamics, and Ctx(x, c) for the context. The role predicates are the formal counterparts
     of the four columns; they are stated in Chapter 6, Section 6.10, and in Appendix .15.

Completeness Predicate. The primitive predicate Complete(x) that states that an explana-
   tion is complete. It is the formal counterpart of the methodological commitment, stated
   in Chapter 2, that we can recognize an explanatory failure when we see one; it is stated
   in Chapter 6, Section 6.10, and in Appendix .15.

Structural Completeness. The condition, defined in the formal system, that all four roles
     are assigned and the roles are coherent with one another. It is defined in Definition .5 of
     Appendix .15.

Necessity (Formal). The property of a role κ, defined in the formal system, that the
    removal of κ from a structurally complete explanation yields an explanation that is not
    complete. It is defined in Definition .7 of Appendix .15, and it is the formal counterpart
    of Definition 2.1 (the removal test).

Reducibility (Formal). The property of a candidate role κ5 , defined in the formal system,
    that the role of κ5 is a subset of the role of one of the four columns. It is defined in
    Definition .9 of Appendix .15, and it is the formal counterpart of Definition 2.2 (the
    reducibility test).

Finitude (Formal). The formal statement, in the formal system, of the finitude of the
     epistemic subject: the set of contexts occupied at a time is finite, and the set of acts
     completed in a finite span is finite. It is stated in Definitions ?? and ?? of Appendix .15,
     and it is the formal counterpart of Principle 3.1.

Formal Theorem of Necessity. The theorem, proved in the formal system, that the four
    columns are necessary. It is Theorem .1 of Appendix .15, and it is the formal counterpart
    of the necessity half of Principle 7.1.

Formal Theorem of Sufficiency. The theorem, proved in the formal system, that the four
    columns are sufficient for the standard candidates. It is Theorem .2 of Appendix .15,
    and it is the formal counterpart of the sufficiency half of Principle 7.1.

Formal Theorem of Distinctness. The theorem, proved in the formal system, that the
    four roles are distinct. It is Theorem .3 of Appendix .15, and it is the formal counterpart
    of Principle 7.2.

Formal Theorem of Consistency. The theorem, proved in the formal system, that the
    formal system has a model, and therefore is consistent. It is Theorem .4 of Appendix .15,
    and it is the formal counterpart of the framework’s claim to coherence (Chapter 34).
Glossary of Epistemic Terms                                                                   667


A Note on the Comparative Glossary
The original edition of this work contained a comparative glossary, relating the framework’s
terms to the vocabularies of the Islamic tradition. The comparative glossary is not included
in the present volume, because the volume’s scope is the epistemology of viability and not
the comparative treatment of the traditions. The comparison is part of the separate treatise
Dialogues with the Philosophical Traditions, and the reader who comes to the framework from
a tradition is directed there.
    The framework’s terms stand on their own. They are defined within the book, and no
argument of the book depends on the reader’s acquaintance with any tradition. The separate
treatise’s comparison is offered as an aid to dialogue, not as a means of proof; the framework’s
principles are justified by their own arguments, and the tradition’s claims are justified by their
own sources.

Index of Arguments

A Note on the Index
This index lists the arguments of the framework, organized by part and chapter. Each entry
gives the name of the argument, its epistemic status, and a cross-reference to the chapter and
section in which it is stated.
     An argument is listed as a proof where a complete argument is given from stated premises.
It is listed as an argument where the argument is given at a lower degree of completeness, or
where the argument is relative to named commitments. The status labels are those introduced
in the front matter: (T) (argued), (E) (estimate), (T) relative to (an argument that depends
on a named commitment), and conditional (an argument that establishes a conditional but
not its antecedent).
     The entries are listed in the order in which they appear in the book, not alphabetically, so
that the reader can follow the development of the framework’s case from its foundation to its
close. A reader who wishes to locate an argument by name is directed to the glossary and to
the general index.
     The index covers the epistemic body of the book only. The later volumes’ arguments (the
ontological, the modal, the theological) are not part of this volume, and are not indexed here.
The appendices of the original edition are not part of the present volume, and are not indexed
here.

is stated in Chapter 27 and restated in the summary of Chapter 29; the argument for the fallacy

restatement is counted separately, because each has its own argumentative role. The count is
offered as a summary of the index’s structure, not as a judgment about the framework’s case.

32–43): the principles of Chapters 32, 33, 35, 36, 38, 40, 42, and 43 have been included.


A Note on the Arguments and the Dependency Map
The index lists the arguments; the dependency map at the end of Chapter 43 states what
depends on what. The two are complementary: the index locates each argument; the map
states its dependencies. A reader who wishes to assess an argument is directed to the chapter
that states it; a reader who wishes to see the structure of the whole is directed to the map.
     The index also distinguishes the arguments that are complete proofs from those that are
relative to named commitments. The distinction is structural, not evaluative: a (T) argument
is not more important than a (T) relative to argument; it is a different kind of argument, and
it invites a different kind of criticism. The framework’s honesty about which is which is part
of what the framework is.
Remark .42 (The Index and the Audit). The index and the audit of Chapter 43 are related
but distinct. The audit states the framework’s core commitments and their dependencies; the
676                                                                        Index of Arguments


index states the framework’s arguments and their statuses. The audit is about the framework’s
foundations; the index is about the framework’s case. The two together make the framework
assessable: the reader can see what the framework is committed to, and what arguments the
framework gives for its claims.

Remark .43 (The Index and the Glossary). The index and the glossary are complementary.
The glossary is alphabetical; the index is in the order of the book. The glossary fixes the sense
of each term; the index locates each argument in its chapter. A reader who wishes to see a
term’s definition is directed to the glossary; a reader who wishes to see an argument’s place in
the book is directed to the index.

Index of Epistemic Principles



A Note on the Index




This index lists the principles, definitions, theorems, and proposed principles of the framework,
organized by part and chapter. Each entry gives the name of the entry, its epistemic status,
and a cross-reference to the chapter and section in which it is stated.




    The status labels are those introduced in the front matter: (A) (axiom or foundational
commitment), (T) (argued), (E) (estimate), (Q) (open epistemic question), (S) (speculation),
and proposed (not yet assigned a status). The labels are used in the chapters themselves;
the index records them.




    The entries are listed in the order in which they appear in the book, not alphabetically,
so that the reader can follow the development of the framework from its foundation to its
close. A reader who wishes to locate a principle by name is directed to the glossary, which is
alphabetical.




    An entry marked “restated” is a statement of a principle that was already stated earlier
in the book; the restatement is counted separately, because each restatement has its own
argumentative role. The dependency map at the end of Chapter 43 states which conclusions
depend on which core commitments. The formal reconstruction of the four columns is stated
in Appendix .15, and its entries are listed in Part VII of this index.

Remark .44 (The Counts Are Not a Ranking). The counts are not a ranking of the statuses.
A (T) claim is not more important than an (A) claim; it is a different kind of claim, and
it invites a different kind of criticism. The counts are offered as a summary of the index’s
structure, not as a judgment about the framework’s claims.

map at the end of Chapter 43 states what depends on what. The two are complementary: the
Index of Epistemic Principles                                                               687


index locates each entry; the map states its dependencies. A reader who wishes to assess a
claim is directed to the chapter that states it; a reader who wishes to see the structure of the
whole is directed to the map. The dependencies of the four formal theorems are stated in
Chapter 43, Section 43.8, and the formal system itself is stated in Appendix .15.

Remark .46 (The Index and the Glossary). The index and the glossary are complementary.
The glossary is alphabetical; the index is in the order of the book. The glossary fixes the sense
of each term; the index locates each principle in its chapter. A reader who wishes to see a
term’s definition is directed to the glossary; a reader who wishes to see a principle’s place in
the book is directed to the index.

Remark .47 (The Index and the Formal Reconstruction). The index lists the formal entries
of Appendix F in Part VII. The formal reconstruction is the formal counterpart of the prose
arguments of Chapters 2, 3, 6, and 7; it is offered as a supplement, not as a substitute for the
prose. A reader who wishes to see the formal system in full is directed to Appendix .15; a
reader who wishes to see the formal entries in the context of the index is directed to Part VII
of this index.

Index of Formalizations

A Note on the Index

This index lists the formalizations of the framework: the symbolic notation, the formal
expressions, and the formal structures (reductio, dilemma, transcendental argument, diagonal
construction) that appear in the book. Its purpose is to make the framework’s formal apparatus
visible in one place.
    The framework uses formalization sparingly in the body of the book (Preface; Chapter 2).
Every principle appears first in full philosophical prose, and only then in symbolic form. The
symbols abbreviate the prose, and the prose carries the principle; the entries of the index are
few, and each is cross-referenced to the prose that it abbreviates. The formal reconstruction of
the four columns (Appendix .15) is the exception: it states the formal system in full, with its
sorts, predicates, axioms, definitions, and theorems, and it is the formal counterpart of the
prose arguments of Chapters 2, 3, 6, and 7.
    The index covers the epistemic body of the book only. The formal apparatus of the later
volumes—the modal space Ω, the actualization chain X, the structural order R, the tower of
refinement, the categorical model of the hubs, the trans-categorical triad—is not part of this
volume, and is not indexed here. The appendices of the original edition are not part of the
present volume, and are not indexed here. A reader who wishes to see those formalisms is
directed to the later volumes and to the separate treatise on the dialogues.
     The index has five parts. The first part, Symbolic Notation, lists the symbols used in
the book, with their meaning and the chapters in which they appear. The second part,
Formalizations by Chapter, lists the formal expressions, organized by the chapter in which
they appear. The third part, Formal Structures, lists the four formal structures and the
places where each is used. The fourth part, The Formal Reconstruction of the Four Columns,
lists the formal system of Appendix .15 and its four theorems. The fifth part, The Status of
Formalization, states what the framework’s formal apparatus is.

Remark .48 (On the Use of the Quantifiers). The universal and existential quantifiers are
used in the book in their standard senses: ∀x means “for all x,” and ∃x means “there exists an
x.” The negation ¬ is used in its standard sense. The conditional → and the biconditional ↔
are used in their standard senses. The book uses only the standard logical symbols, and the
formal expressions are transparent to a reader who knows them.

Remark .49 (On the Use of the Tuple Notation). The tuple notation ⟨F, S, R⟩ is used in
Chapters 36 and 37 to abbreviate the three components of viability. The notation is purely
abbreviatory; it does not introduce a formal object, and it does not claim that viability
is a mathematical tuple. The prose that surrounds the notation states what the notation
abbreviates.

Remark .50 (On the Absence of the Later Volumes’ Symbols). The later volumes of the
series use symbols that are not used in this volume: Ω (the modal space), X (the actualization
chain), R (the structural order), the tower’s projection maps πi , and the categorical notation
of the hubs. Those symbols are not part of the present volume’s formal apparatus, and they
are not listed here. A reader who has met them elsewhere is directed to the later volumes for
their introduction and their use.


Part II: Formalizations by Chapter
The following subsections list the formal expressions and formal structures of the book,
organized by the chapter in which they appear. Each entry gives the formal expression, its
prose counterpart, and the definition or principle it abbreviates. The formal reconstruction of
the four columns (Appendix .15) is listed in Part IV of this index.

Chapter 1: Explanatory Cognition and the Four Questions
The definition of explanatory cognition.

          EC (x) ↔ x aims to understand how some things stand to one another.

The expression abbreviates Definition 1.1. It is not a premise of any argument; it fixes the
scope of the book.

The four questions.

             Q1 = what?,     Q2 = how?,    Q3 = on what basis?,     Q4 = where?

The expression abbreviates the four questions of Chapter 1. It is a summary, not a formal
system; the four questions are stated in prose, and the symbols abbreviate the prose.

The expression abbreviates Definition 2.1 (the removal test) in the formal language of Ap-
pendix .15 (Definition ??). The prose version states the test in terms of “a recognizable
explanatory failure”; the formal version states the test in terms of the primitive completeness
predicate.

               Reducible(κ5 ) :≡ ∃κ ∈ {F, Φ, D, K} : RoleSet(κ5 ) ⊆ RoleSet(κ).

The expression abbreviates Definition 2.2 (the reducibility test) in the formal language of

Chapter 3: Finitude of the Epistemic Subject
The formal counterpart of the first half of the principle.

The expression abbreviates the first half of Principle 3.1 (the finitude of the subject) in the
formal language of Appendix .15 (Definition ??). It states that, for every subject s and every
time t, the set of contexts occupied by s at t is finite.

The formal counterpart of the second half of the principle.

                 ∀s, t1 , t2 : |{a : Completes(s, a, t) for some t ∈ [t1 , t2 ]}| < ∞.

The expression abbreviates the second half of Principle 3.1 (the finitude of the subject) in the
formal language of Appendix .15 (Definition ??). It states that, for every subject s and every
finite interval of time [t1 , t2 ], the set of acts completed by s in the interval is finite.

Part III: Formal Structures
The framework uses four formal structures, each of which appears in more than one chapter.
The structures are stated here in their general form, with cross-references to the chapters in
which they are used.

The Reductio
The reductio is the framework’s most common formal structure. It proceeds by supposing the
negation of what is to be proved, deriving a contradiction, and concluding that the supposition
is false. The framework uses the reductio in the following places.

The Dilemma
The dilemma is used in one place: the argument for non-duplicability from the identity of
indiscernibles (Chapter 12). The argument has two horns—the identity of indiscernibles holds,
or it does not—and in both horns, the conclusion follows. The dilemma’s force is that it
removes the dependence of the principle on the identity of indiscernibles, without settling the
dispute over the principle itself.

The Transcendental Argument
The transcendental argument is used in two places in this volume: the argument for the
necessity of expression (Chapter 38, in outline), and the argument for the conservation of
identity (Chapter 12, developed further in the audit of Chapter 43). Both arguments proceed
from the possibility of experience to its condition. The first proceeds from the experience
of manifestation to the condition of expression; the second proceeds from the experience of
temporal continuity to the presumption of sameness.

The Diagonal Construction
The diagonal construction is used in one place in this volume: the second argument for the
impossibility of super-identity (Chapter 27). The argument proceeds by constructing, from
any finite list of contexts surveyed by a subject, a context outside the list. The construction
uses the list’s own content (the manifestations it surveys) as a fixed element of a new context,
and the new context is outside the list.

Remark .51 (The Counting Argument Is Not Used in This Volume). The counting argument—
used in the original edition for the minimality of the three hubs—is not part of the present
volume. The three components of viability (Chapter 37) are argued for minimality by the
distinctness of the three relations they describe, not by a count. The reader who has met the
counting argument elsewhere is directed to the later volumes.


Part IV: The Formal Reconstruction of the Four Columns
The formal reconstruction of the four columns is stated in full in Appendix .15. The present
part of the index lists the formal system’s sorts, predicates, axioms, definitions, and theorems,
with a cross-reference to the appendix.

The Sorts of the Formal System
The formal system has five sorts: E (elements), R (rules), C (contexts), X (explanations), and
S (states). The sorts are stated in Appendix .15.

The Predicates of the Formal System
The formal system has the following predicates:

   • InF (e, x), InΦ (e, x) — the role predicates for the fixed and the fluid elements;

   • Dyn(x, r) — the role predicate for the governing dynamics;

   • Ctx(x, c) — the role predicate for the context;

   • Apply(r, e1 , e2 , e3 , s) — the application predicate;

   • Complete(x) — the primitive completeness predicate;
702                                                                        Index of Formalizations


      • Carries(eϕ , e1 , e2 ) — the conveyance predicate;
      • DeterminedBy(e, c) — the context-determination predicate;
      • Occupies(s, c, t), Completes(s, a, t) — the predicates of the finitude principle;
      • WF(x), ValidConveyance(x), DynCoherent(x), StructuralComplete(x) — the structural
        predicates;
      • Necessary(κ), Reducible(κ5 ), RoleSet(κ), x \ κ, Has(x, κ) — the predicates and operations
        of the two tests.
The predicates are stated in Appendix .15.

The Axioms of the Formal System
The formal system has the following groups of axioms:
      • Structural axioms (A1–A4): the existence of distinct elements; the uniqueness of
        the dynamics and of the context; the absence of overlap between the fixed and the fluid
        elements.
      • Conveyance axioms (B1, B1′ , B2): the existence of a carrier for each pair of fixed
        elements; the distinctness of the carrier; the non-necessity of sequential passage.
      • Dynamical axioms (C1–C2): the determinacy of the state; the existence of a state
        for each valid conveyance.
      • Context axioms (D1–D2): the determination of roles by the context; the variety of
        roles across contexts.
      • Completeness axioms (E1–E2): the relation between the structural completeness
        and the primitive completeness; the failure of the structural completeness implies the
        failure of the primitive completeness.
      • Finitude axioms (F1–F2): the formal counterparts of the two halves of the finitude
        principle.
      • Syntactic axioms (S1–S7): the behavior of the removal operation x \ κ.
      • Existence axiom (Ex): there exists at least one complete explanation.
The axioms are stated in Appendix .15.

The Definitions of the Formal System
The formal system has the following definitions:
      • WF(x) — well-formedness;
      • ValidConveyance(x) — valid conveyance;
      • DynCoherent(x) — dynamical coherence;
      • StructuralComplete(x) — structural completeness;
      • Necessary(κ) — necessity;
      • Reducible(κ5 ) — reducibility;
      • Has(x, κ) — having a role.
The definitions are stated in Appendix .15.
Index of Formalizations                                                                     703


The Theorems of the Formal System
The formal system has four theorems:
   • Theorem .1 (Necessity): the four columns are necessary.
   • Theorem .2 (Sufficiency): the four columns are sufficient for the standard candidates.
   • Theorem .3 (Distinctness): the four roles are distinct.
   • Theorem .4 (Consistency): the formal system is consistent.
The theorems are stated and proved in Appendix .15, and their dependencies on the ten core
commitments are stated in Chapter 43, Section 43.8.
Remark .52 (The Formal Reconstruction and the Prose). The formal reconstruction is the
formal counterpart of the prose arguments of Chapters 2, 3, 6, and 7. It is not a substitute for
the prose; it is the same arguments, stated at a higher level of precision. The reader who is
content with the prose has the arguments; the reader who wishes to assess the framework at
the level of its formal structure has the formal reconstruction.


Part V: The Status of Formalization
The framework uses formalization at a specific strength, and the strength is stated here.
Formalization here means brief notation, explicit formulation of principles, dependency tables,
and epistemic labels. It also includes the formal reconstruction of Appendix .15, which states
the formal system in full; but the formal reconstruction is offered as a supplement, not as a
substitute for the prose.
   Three consequences follow, and they are stated here as a closing note on the index.

First consequence: the prose is primary. Every principle appears first in full philo-
sophical prose, and only then in symbolic form. The prose carries the principle; the symbol
abbreviates it. The symbols can be set aside without loss of the principle; the prose cannot be
set aside without loss. The index is a guide to the symbols; the prose is the substance. The
formal reconstruction is the exception that confirms the rule: it is offered as a supplement,
and it does not replace the prose.

Second consequence: the symbols are few. The body of the book uses a small number
of symbols, each of which is introduced with its meaning. The formal reconstruction uses a
larger number of symbols, but each is introduced in the appendix, and the appendix states
the formal system in full. The reader who follows the formal reconstruction has the appendix
as a guide; the reader who follows the prose has the prose as a guide.

Third consequence: formalization summarizes, and the argument justifies. The
formal expressions summarize the principles they abbreviate, and they are offered at the
strength the principles’ arguments support. The argument for a principle is the place where
the principle is assessed; the symbolic form presents the principle in abbreviated form. A
principle is justified by its argument, and the symbolic form is a way of seeing the principle.
Remark .53 (The Index and the Framework’s Formal Apparatus). The index makes the
framework’s formal apparatus visible in one place, so that the reader can see at a glance
what the framework formalizes and what it leaves in prose. The formalization is present in
the framework at the places the index records, and the index notes its presence. The formal
reconstruction of the four columns (Appendix .15) is the most extensive part of the framework’s
formal apparatus, and it is recorded in Part IV of this index.
704                                                                     Index of Formalizations


Remark .54 (The Formalization Is Sparse). The formalization of the body of the book
is sparse because the framework’s subject—the structure of explanatory cognition—is not
naturally formal. The subject is structural, but not mathematical; the framework’s precision
is philosophical, not computational. The formalization serves the precision where it can, and
the prose carries the rest. The formal reconstruction of the four columns is the exception: it is
the one part of the framework where the formalization is extensive, and it is offered because
the four-column principle invites a precise formulation.




Remark .55 (The Index and the Rewritten Chapters). The index has been revised to be
consistent with the rewritten chapters (Chapters 1–43). The chapter references are hard-coded
to their correct numbers, and the labels match the labels of the chapters. The formalization of
the singularity (Definition 37.2) has been added; the count of Chapter 37 has been corrected
from one to two; the formal reconstruction of the four columns (Appendix .15) has been added,
with its own symbols, definitions, and theorems; and the summary table has been updated
accordingly. A reader who finds a formal expression in the rewritten chapters that the index
does not list has found an omission in the index, and the index can be revised to include it.

The count is small in the body of the book, and the smallness is the point. The framework
uses formalization where it aids precision, and it withholds formalization where formalization
would substitute for understanding. The formal reconstruction of the four columns is the
exception: it is the one part of the framework where the formalization is extensive, and it is
706                                                                  Index of Formalizations


offered because the four-column principle invites a precise formulation. The index is a guide
to what is formalized. The prose is the substance; the formalization is the abbreviation.

Remark .56 (The Counts Are Approximate). The counts are approximate in the following
sense. Some formal expressions are schemas rather than formulas; some are stated in prose and
not in symbols; some are restatements of expressions stated earlier. The count is offered as a
summary of the index’s structure, not as a judgment about the framework’s formal precision.

Remark .57 (The Index and the Prose). The index is a guide to the symbols; the prose
is the substance. A reader who has followed the prose has the principles; a reader who has
followed the index has the symbols that abbreviate them. The framework’s claim is that the
prose is assessable on its own, and that the symbols are a help, not a substitute. The formal
reconstruction of the four columns is the exception: it is offered as a supplement, and it is
assessable at the strength its proofs support.
